Here, Mahānāma, a noble disciple, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome qualities, enters and abides in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. With the stilling of thought and examination, he enters and abides in the second jhāna… With the fading away of rapture… he enters and abides in the third jhāna… With the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and sorrow… he enters and abides in the fourth jhāna. In this way, Mahānāma, a noble disciple is an obtainer at will, without difficulty, and without trouble of the four jhānas, which pertain to the higher mind and are pleasant abidings in this very life.

27. “Yato kho, mahānāma, ariyasāvako evaṃ sīlasampanno hoti, evaṃ indriyesu guttadvāro hoti, evaṃ bhojane mattaññū hoti, evaṃ jāgariyaṃ anuyutto hoti, evaṃ sattahi saddhammehi samannāgato [P 1.0357] hoti, evaṃ catunnaṃ jhānānaṃ ābhicetasikānaṃ diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārānaṃ nikāmalābhī hoti akicchalābhī akasiralābhī, ayaṃ vuccati, mahānāma, ariyasāvako sekho pāṭipado apuccaṇḍatāya [M 2.0020] samāpanno, bhabbo abhinibbhidāya, bhabbo sambodhāya, bhabbo anuttarassa yogakkhemassa adhigamāya. Seyyathāpi, mahānāma, kukkuṭiyā aṇḍāni aṭṭha vā dasa vā dvādasa vā tānāssu kukkuṭiyā sammā adhisayitāni sammā pariseditāni sammā paribhāvitāni, kiñcāpi tassā kukkuṭiyā na [T 2.0030] evaṃ icchā uppajjeyya – ‘aho vatime kukkuṭapotakā pādanakhasikhāya vā mukhatuṇḍakena vā aṇḍakosaṃ padāletvā sotthinā abhinibbhijjeyyu’nti, atha kho bhabbāva te kukkuṭapotakā pādanakhasikhāya vā mukhatuṇḍakena vā aṇḍakosaṃ padāletvā sotthinā abhinibbhijjituṃ. Evameva kho, mahānāma, yato ariyasāvako evaṃ sīlasampanno hoti, evaṃ indriyesu guttadvāro hoti, evaṃ bhojane mattaññū hoti, evaṃ jāgariyaṃ anuyutto hoti, evaṃ sattahi saddhammehi samannāgato hoti, evaṃ catunnaṃ jhānānaṃ ābhicetasikānaṃ diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārānaṃ nikāmalābhī hoti akicchalābhī akasiralābhī, ayaṃ vuccati, mahānāma, ariyasāvako sekho pāṭipado apuccaṇḍatāya samāpanno[V 2.0022], bhabbo abhinibbhidāya, bhabbo sambodhāya, bhabbo anuttarassa yogakkhemassa adhigamāya.

27. Mahānāma, when a noble disciple is thus endowed with virtue, thus has guarded doors in the sense faculties, thus knows moderation in eating, thus is devoted to wakefulness, thus is possessed of the seven qualities of a good person, and thus is an obtainer at will, without difficulty, without trouble, of the four jhānas that are of the higher mind and are pleasant dwellings in this very life, this noble disciple, Mahānāma, is called a trainee on the path, endowed with the state of unspoilability, capable of breaking through, capable of enlightenment, capable of attaining the unsurpassed security from the yokes. Just as, Mahānāma, a hen might have eight, ten, or twelve eggs, and those eggs are properly sat upon, properly warmed, and properly brooded over by the hen. Even if the wish should not arise in that hen, ‘Oh, may these chicks of mine, having pierced the eggshell with the tips of their claws or with their beaks, break out safely!’, still, those chicks are capable of piercing the eggshell with the tips of their claws or with their beaks and breaking out safely. In the same way, Mahānāma, when a noble disciple is thus endowed with virtue, thus has guarded doors in the sense faculties, thus knows moderation in eating, thus is devoted to wakefulness, thus is possessed of the seven qualities of a good person, and thus is an obtainer at will, without difficulty, without trouble, of the four jhānas that are of the higher mind and are pleasant dwellings in this very life, this noble disciple, Mahānāma, is called a trainee on the path, endowed with the state of unspoilability, capable of breaking through, capable of enlightenment, capable of attaining the unsurpassed security from the yokes.

28. “Sa kho so, mahānāma, ariyasāvako imaṃyeva anuttaraṃ upekkhāsatipārisuddhiṃ āgamma anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati, seyyathidaṃ – ekampi jātiṃ dvepi jātiyo…pe… iti sākāraṃ sauddesaṃ anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati, ayamassa paṭhamābhinibbhidā hoti kukkuṭacchāpakasseva aṇḍakosamhā.

28. Mahānāma, that noble disciple, relying on this very unsurpassed purity of mindfulness through equanimity, recollects his manifold past abodes, that is: one birth, two births... and so on... thus he recollects his manifold past abodes with their aspects and details. This is his first breaking through, like that of a chick from the eggshell.

“Sa kho so, mahānāma, ariyasāvako imaṃye anuttaraṃ upekkhāsatipārisuddhiṃ āgamma dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena satte passati cavamāne upapajjamāne hīne paṇīte suvaṇṇe dubbaṇṇe sugate duggate…pe… yathākammūpage satte pajānāti, ayamassa dutiyābhinibbhidā hoti kukkuṭacchāpakasseva aṇḍakosamhā.

Mahānāma, that noble disciple, relying on this very unsurpassed purity of mindfulness through equanimity, with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, sees beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, of good appearance and bad appearance, in good destinations and bad destinations... and so on... he knows beings in detail as they fare according to their kamma. This is his second breaking through, like that of a chick from the eggshell.

“Sa kho so, mahānāma, ariyasāvako imaṃyeva anuttaraṃ upekkhāsatipārisuddhiṃ āgamma āsavānaṃ khayā anāsavaṃ cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ [T 2.0031] diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja [P 1.0358] viharati, ayamassa tatiyābhinibbhidā hoti kukkuṭacchāpakasseva aṇḍakosamhā.

Mahānāma, that noble disciple, relying on this very unsurpassed purity of mindfulness through equanimity, through the destruction of the taints, having realized for himself with higher knowledge in this very life, attains and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom. This is his third breaking through, like that of a chick from the eggshell.

29. “Yampi [M 2.0021] yampi kho (ka.), mahānāma, ariyasāvako sīlasampanno hoti, idampissa hoti caraṇasmiṃ; yampi, mahānāma, ariyasāvako indriyesu guttadvāro hoti, idampissa hoti caraṇasmiṃ; yampi, mahānāma, ariyasāvako bhojane mattaññū hoti, idampissa hoti caraṇasmiṃ; yampi, mahānāma, ariyasāvako jāgariyaṃ anuyutto hoti, idampissa hoti caraṇasmiṃ; yampi, mahānāma, ariyasāvako sattahi saddhammehi samannāgato hoti, idampissa hoti caraṇasmiṃ; yampi, mahānāma, ariyasāvako catunnaṃ jhānānaṃ ābhicetasikānaṃ diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārānaṃ nikāmalābhī hoti akicchalābhī akasiralābhī, idampissa hoti caraṇasmiṃ.

29. Mahānāma, that the noble disciple is endowed with virtue—this, for him, is 'conduct'. That the noble disciple has guarded doors in the sense faculties—this, for him, is 'conduct'. That the noble disciple knows moderation in eating—this, for him, is 'conduct'. That the noble disciple is devoted to wakefulness—this, for him, is 'conduct'. That the noble disciple is possessed of the seven qualities of a good person—this, for him, is 'conduct'. That the noble disciple is an obtainer at will, without difficulty, without trouble, of the four jhānas that are of the higher mind and are pleasant dwellings in this very life—this, for him, is 'conduct'.

“Yañca kho, mahānāma, ariyasāvako anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati, seyyathidaṃ [V 2.0023] – ekampi jātiṃ dvepi jātiyo…pe… iti sākāraṃ sauddesaṃ anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati, idampissa hoti vijjāya; yampi, mahānāma, ariyasāvako dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena satte passati cavamāne upapajjamāne hīne paṇīte suvaṇṇe dubbaṇṇe sugate duggate…pe… yathākammūpage satte pajānāti, idampissa hoti vijjāya. Yampi, mahānāma, ariyasāvako āsavānaṃ khayā anāsavaṃ cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharati, idampissa hoti vijjāya.

Mahānāma, that the noble disciple recollects his manifold past abodes, that is: one birth, two births... and so on... thus he recollects his manifold past abodes with their aspects and details—this, for him, is 'knowledge'. Mahānāma, that the noble disciple, with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, sees beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, of good appearance and bad appearance, in good destinations and bad destinations... and so on... he knows beings in detail as they fare according to their kamma—this, for him, is 'knowledge'. Mahānāma, that the noble disciple, through the destruction of the taints, having realized for himself with higher knowledge in this very life, attains and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom—this, for him, is 'knowledge'.

“Ayaṃ [T 2.0032] vuccati, mahānāma, ariyasāvako vijjāsampanno itipi caraṇasampanno itipi vijjācaraṇasampanno itipi.

This noble disciple, Mahānāma, is called 'one endowed with knowledge', also 'one endowed with conduct', and also 'one endowed with knowledge and conduct'.

30. “Brahmunāpesā, mahānāma, sanaṅkumārena gāthā bhāsitā –

30. Moreover, Mahānāma, this verse was spoken by the Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra:

‘Khattiyo seṭṭho janetasmiṃ, ye gottapaṭisārino;

Vijjācaraṇasampanno, so seṭṭho devamānuse’ti.

‘The Khattiya is best among the populace who rely on lineage; but one endowed with knowledge and conduct is best among devas and humans.’

“Sā kho panesā, mahānāma, brahmunā sanaṅkumārena gāthā sugītā no duggītā, subhāsitā no dubbhāsitā, atthasaṃhitā no anatthasaṃhitā, anumatā bhagavatā”ti.

Now, Mahānāma, that verse by the Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra was well-sung, not ill-sung; well-spoken, not ill-spoken; connected with benefit, not unconnected with benefit; and it was approved by the Blessed One.

Atha [M 2.0022] kho bhagavā uṭṭhahitvā āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ āmantesi – “sādhu sādhu, ānanda, sādhu kho tvaṃ, ānanda, kāpilavatthavānaṃ sakyānaṃ sekhaṃ pāṭipadaṃ abhāsī”ti.

Then the Blessed One rose from his seat and addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “Good, good, Ānanda! It is good, Ānanda, that you have spoken on the trainee's path for the Sakyans of Kapilavatthu.”

Idamavocāyasmā [P 1.0359] ānando. Samanuñño satthā ahosi. Attamanā kāpilavatthavā sakyā āyasmato ānandassa bhāsitaṃ abhinandunti.

The Venerable Ānanda said this. The Teacher approved. The Sakyans of Kapilavatthu, delighted, greatly rejoiced in what was spoken by the Venerable Ānanda.

Sekhasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ tatiyaṃ.

The Sekha Sutta, the third, is concluded.

4. Potaliyasuttaṃ

4. The Potaliya Sutta

31. Evaṃ [T 2.0033][V 2.0024] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā aṅguttarāpesu viharati āpaṇaṃ nāma aṅguttarāpānaṃ nigamo. Atha kho bhagavā pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya āpaṇaṃ piṇḍāya pāvisi. Āpaṇe piṇḍāya caritvā pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto yenaññataro vanasaṇḍo tenupasaṅkami divāvihārāya. Taṃ vanasaṇḍaṃ ajjhogāhetvā ajjhogahetvā (sī. syā. kaṃ.), ajjhogāhitvā (pī. ka.) aññatarasmiṃ rukkhamūle divāvihāraṃ nisīdi. Potaliyopi kho gahapati sampannanivāsanapāvuraṇo pāpuraṇo (sī. syā. kaṃ.) chattupāhanāhi chattupāhano (ka.) jaṅghāvihāraṃ anucaṅkamamāno anuvicaramāno yena so vanasaṇḍo tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā taṃ vanasaṇḍaṃ ajjhogāhetvā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavatā saddhiṃ sammodi. Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Ekamantaṃ ṭhitaṃ kho potaliyaṃ gahapatiṃ bhagavā etadavoca – “saṃvijjanti kho, gahapati, āsanāni; sace ākaṅkhasi nisīdā”ti. Evaṃ vutte, potaliyo gahapati “gahapativādena maṃ samaṇo gotamo samudācaratī”ti kupito anattamano tuṇhī ahosi. Dutiyampi kho bhagavā…pe… [T 2.0034] tatiyampi kho bhagavā potaliyaṃ gahapatiṃ etadavoca – “saṃvijjanti kho, gahapati, āsanāni; sace ākaṅkhasi nisīdā”ti. “Evaṃ vutte, potaliyo gahapati gahapativādena maṃ samaṇo gotamo samudācaratī”ti kupito anattamano bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “tayidaṃ, bho [P 1.0360] gotama, nacchannaṃ, tayidaṃ nappatirūpaṃ, yaṃ maṃ tvaṃ gahapativādena samudācarasī”ti. “Te hi te, gahapati, ākārā, te liṅgā[M 2.0023], te nimittā yathā taṃ gahapatissā”ti. “Tathā hi pana me, bho gotama, sabbe kammantā paṭikkhittā, sabbe vohārā samucchinnā”ti. “Yathā kathaṃ pana te, gahapati, sabbe kammantā paṭikkhittā, sabbe vohārā samucchinnā”ti? “Idha me, bho gotama, yaṃ ahosi dhanaṃ vā dhaññaṃ vā rajataṃ vā jātarūpaṃ vā sabbaṃ taṃ puttānaṃ dāyajjaṃ niyyātaṃ, tatthāhaṃ anovādī anupavādī ghāsacchādanaparamo viharāmi. Evaṃ kho me evañca me (syā.), evaṃ me (ka.), bho gotama, sabbe kammantā paṭikkhittā, sabbe vohārā samucchinnā”ti. “Aññathā kho tvaṃ, gahapati, vohārasamucchedaṃ vadasi, aññathā ca pana ariyassa vinaye vohārasamucchedo hotī”ti. “Yathā kathaṃ pana, bhante, ariyassa vinaye vohārasamucchedo hoti? Sādhu me, bhante[V 2.0025], bhagavā tathā dhammaṃ desetu yathā ariyassa vinaye vohārasamucchedo [T 2.0035] hotī”ti. “Tena hi, gahapati, suṇāhi, sādhukaṃ manasi karohi, bhāsissāmī”ti. “Evaṃ, bhante”ti kho potaliyo gahapati bhagavato paccassosi.

31. Thus have I heard: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Aṅguttarāpas, in their market town named Āpaṇa. Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning, took his bowl and outer robe and entered Āpaṇa for alms. Having walked for alms in Āpaṇa, after the meal, on returning from the alms round, he approached a certain grove for the day's abiding. Having entered that grove, he sat down at the foot of a certain tree for the day's abiding. Potaliya the householder, fully clad in lower and upper garments, with umbrella and sandals, was walking for exercise when he approached that grove. Having approached and entered the grove, he went to where the Blessed One was. Having approached, he exchanged courteous greetings and amiable talk with the Blessed One, and then stood to one side. To Potaliya the householder standing to one side, the Blessed One said this: “There are seats, householder; if you wish, sit down.” When this was said, Potaliya the householder, thinking, “The ascetic Gotama addresses me with the term ‘householder,’” became angry and displeased, and remained silent. A second time... and a third time the Blessed One said to Potaliya the householder: “There are seats, householder; if you wish, sit down.” When this was said, Potaliya the householder, angry and displeased that the ascetic Gotama was addressing him with the term ‘householder,’ said to the Blessed One: “It is not proper, Master Gotama, it is not suitable, that you address me with the term ‘householder.’” “But, householder, you have the characteristics, the signs, and the marks of a householder.” “But, Master Gotama, all my worldly activities have been rejected, all my dealings have been cut off.” “In what way, householder, have all your worldly activities been rejected and all your dealings cut off?” “Here, Master Gotama, whatever wealth, grain, silver, or gold I had, all that I have handed over to my sons as their inheritance. In that matter, I am not one who advises or reproaches; I live concerned only with my food and clothing. That is how, Master Gotama, all my worldly activities have been rejected and all my dealings have been cut off.” “Householder, you speak of the cutting off of dealings in one way, but in the Noble One's Discipline, the cutting off of dealings is otherwise.” “In what way, venerable sir, is there the cutting off of dealings in the Noble One's Discipline? It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in such a way that there is the cutting off of dealings in the Noble One's Discipline.” “Then, householder, listen and attend carefully; I will speak.” “Yes, venerable sir,” Potaliya the householder replied to the Blessed One.

32. Bhagavā etadavoca – “aṭṭha kho ime, gahapati, dhammā ariyassa vinaye vohārasamucchedāya saṃvattanti. Katame aṭṭha? Apāṇātipātaṃ nissāya pāṇātipāto pahātabbo; dinnādānaṃ nissāya adinnādānaṃ pahātabbaṃ; saccavācaṃ saccaṃ vācaṃ (syā.) nissāya musāvādo pahātabbo; apisuṇaṃ vācaṃ nissāya pisuṇā vācā pahātabbā; agiddhilobhaṃ nissāya giddhilobho pahātabbo; anindārosaṃ nissāya nindāroso pahātabbo; akkodhūpāyāsaṃ nissāya kodhūpāyāso pahātabbo; anatimānaṃ nissāya atimāno pahātabbo. Ime kho, gahapati, aṭṭha dhammā saṃkhittena vuttā, vitthārena avibhattā, ariyassa vinaye vohārasamucchedāya saṃvattantī”ti. “Ye me ye me pana (syā. ka.), bhante, bhagavatā aṭṭha dhammā saṃkhittena vuttā, vitthārena avibhattā, ariyassa vinaye vohārasamucchedāya saṃvattanti, sādhu me, bhante, bhagavā ime aṭṭha dhamme vitthārena vitthāretvā (ka.) vibhajatu anukampaṃ upādāyā”ti. “Tena hi, gahapati, suṇāhi, sādhukaṃ manasi karohi, bhāsissāmī”ti. “Evaṃ, bhante”ti kho potaliyo gahapati bhagavato paccassosi. Bhagavā etadavoca –

32. The Blessed One said this: “Householder, these eight principles in the Noble One's Discipline lead to the cutting off of dealings. What are the eight? Relying on not taking life, the taking of life is to be abandoned; relying on taking what is given, taking what is not given is to be abandoned; relying on true speech, false speech is to be abandoned; relying on non-divisive speech, divisive speech is to be abandoned; relying on non-covetousness, covetousness is to be abandoned; relying on non-censure and non-malice, censure and malice are to be abandoned; relying on non-anger and non-vexation, anger and vexation are to be abandoned; relying on non-arrogance, arrogance is to be abandoned. These, householder, are the eight principles, stated in brief but not analyzed in detail, that in the Noble One's Discipline lead to the cutting off of dealings.” “Venerable sir, these eight principles that the Blessed One has stated in brief but not analyzed in detail, which in the Noble One's Discipline lead to the cutting off of dealings—it would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One, out of compassion, would analyze these eight principles for me in detail.” “Then, householder, listen and attend carefully; I will speak.” “Yes, venerable sir,” Potaliya the householder replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:

33. “‘Apāṇātipātaṃ [M 2.0024][P 1.0361] nissāya pāṇātipāto pahātabbo’ti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ kiñcetaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ[T 2.0036]? Idha, gahapati, ariyasāvako iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘yesaṃ kho ahaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ hetu pāṇātipātī assaṃ, tesāhaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ pahānāya samucchedāya paṭipanno. Ahañceva ahañce (?) kho pana pāṇātipātī assaṃ, attāpi maṃ upavadeyya pāṇātipātapaccayā, anuviccāpi maṃ viññū anuvicca viññū (sī. syā. pī.) garaheyyuṃ pāṇātipātapaccayā, kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā duggati pāṭikaṅkhā pāṇātipātapaccayā. Etadeva kho pana saṃyojanaṃ etaṃ nīvaraṇaṃ yadidaṃ pāṇātipāto. Ye ca pāṇātipātapaccayā uppajjeyyuṃ āsavā vighātapariḷāhā, pāṇātipātā paṭiviratassa evaṃsa te āsavā vighātapariḷāhā na honti’. ‘Apāṇātipātaṃ nissāya pāṇātipāto pahātabbo’ti – iti yantaṃ vuttaṃ idametaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ.

33. “‘By relying on non-killing, killing is to be abandoned’—this was said. With reference to what was this said? Here, householder, a noble disciple reflects thus: ‘On account of which fetters would I kill living beings? I am practicing for the abandoning and utter destruction of those fetters. If I were to kill living beings, I myself would reproach myself on account of killing living beings; and the wise, having investigated, would censure me on account of killing living beings; and with the breaking up of the body, after death, a woeful destination would be expected on account of killing living beings. This killing of living beings is itself a fetter, this is a hindrance. And the taints, distresses, and fevers that would arise on account of killing living beings do not exist for one who abstains from killing living beings.’ ‘By relying on non-killing, killing is to be abandoned’—that was said with reference to this.”

34. “‘Dinnādānaṃ [V 2.0026] nissāya adinnādānaṃ pahātabba’nti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ, kiñcetaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ? Idha, gahapati, ariyasāvako iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘yesaṃ kho ahaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ hetu adinnādāyī assaṃ, tesāhaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ pahānāya samucchedāya paṭipanno. Ahañceva kho pana adinnādāyī assaṃ, attāpi maṃ upavadeyya adinnādānapaccayā, anuviccāpi maṃ viññū garaheyyuṃ adinnādānapaccayā, kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā duggati pāṭikaṅkhā adinnādānapaccayā. Etadeva kho pana saṃyojanaṃ etaṃ nīvaraṇaṃ yadidaṃ adinnādānaṃ. Ye ca adinnādānapaccayā uppajjeyyuṃ āsavā vighātapariḷāhā adinnādānā [T 2.0037] paṭiviratassa evaṃsa te āsavā vighātapariḷāhā na honti’. ‘Dinnādānaṃ nissāya adinnādānaṃ pahātabba’nti – iti yantaṃ vuttaṃ idametaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ.

34. “‘By relying on taking what is given, taking what is not given is to be abandoned’—this was said. With reference to what was this said? Here, householder, a noble disciple reflects thus: ‘On account of which fetters would I take what is not given? I am practicing for the abandoning and utter destruction of those fetters. If I were to take what is not given, I myself would reproach myself on account of taking what is not given; and the wise, having investigated, would censure me on account of taking what is not given; and with the breaking up of the body, after death, a woeful destination would be expected on account of taking what is not given. This taking what is not given is itself a fetter, this is a hindrance. And the taints, distresses, and fevers that would arise on account of taking what is not given do not exist for one who abstains from taking what is not given.’ ‘By relying on taking what is given, taking what is not given is to be abandoned’—that was said with reference to this.”

35. “‘Saccavācaṃ nissāya musāvādo pahātabbo’ti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ kiñcetaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ? Idha, gahapati, ariyasāvako iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘yesaṃ kho ahaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ hetu musāvādī assaṃ, tesāhaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ pahānāya samucchedāya paṭipanno. Ahañceva kho pana musāvādī assaṃ, attāpi maṃ upavadeyya musāvādapaccayā, anuviccāpi maṃ viññū garaheyyuṃ musāvādapaccayā, kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā duggati pāṭikaṅkhā musāvādapaccayā. Etadeva kho pana saṃyojanaṃ etaṃ nīvaraṇaṃ yadidaṃ [M 2.0025] musāvādo[P 1.0362]. Ye ca musāvādapaccayā uppajjeyyuṃ āsavā vighātapariḷāhā, musāvādā paṭiviratassa evaṃsa te āsavā vighātapariḷāhā na honti’. ‘Saccavācaṃ nissāya musāvādo pahātabbo’ti – iti yantaṃ vuttaṃ idametaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ.

35. “‘By relying on truthful speech, false speech is to be abandoned’—this was said. With reference to what was this said? Here, householder, a noble disciple reflects thus: ‘On account of which fetters would I speak falsely? I am practicing for the abandoning and utter destruction of those fetters. If I were to speak falsely, I myself would reproach myself on account of speaking falsely; and the wise, having investigated, would censure me on account of speaking falsely; and with the breaking up of the body, after death, a woeful destination would be expected on account of speaking falsely. This false speech is itself a fetter, this is a hindrance. And the taints, distresses, and fevers that would arise on account of false speech do not exist for one who abstains from false speech.’ ‘By relying on truthful speech, false speech is to be abandoned’—that was said with reference to this.”

36. “‘Apisuṇaṃ vācaṃ nissāya pisuṇā vācā pahātabbā’ti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ kiñcetaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ? Idha, gahapati, ariyasāvako iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘yesaṃ kho ahaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ hetu pisuṇavāco assaṃ, tesāhaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ pahānāya samucchedāya paṭipanno. Ahañceva kho pana pisuṇavāco assaṃ, attāpi maṃ upavadeyya pisuṇavācāpaccayā[T 2.0038], anuviccāpi maṃ viññū garaheyyuṃ pisuṇavācāpaccayā, kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā duggati pāṭikaṅkhā pisuṇavācāpaccayā. Etadeva kho pana saṃyojanaṃ etaṃ nīvaraṇaṃ yadidaṃ pisuṇā vācā. Ye ca pisuṇavācāpaccayā uppajjeyyuṃ āsavā vighātapariḷāhā, pisuṇāya [V 2.0027] vācāya paṭiviratassa evaṃsa te āsavā vighātapariḷāhā na honti’. ‘Apisuṇaṃ vācaṃ nissāya pisuṇā vācā pahātabbā’ti – iti yantaṃ vuttaṃ idametaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ.

36. “‘By relying on non-divisive speech, divisive speech is to be abandoned’—this was said. With reference to what was this said? Here, householder, a noble disciple reflects thus: ‘On account of which fetters would I speak divisively? I am practicing for the abandoning and utter destruction of those fetters. If I were to speak divisively, I myself would reproach myself on account of divisive speech; and the wise, having investigated, would censure me on account of divisive speech; and with the breaking up of the body, after death, a woeful destination would be expected on account of divisive speech. This divisive speech is itself a fetter, this is a hindrance. And the taints, distresses, and fevers that would arise on account of divisive speech do not exist for one who abstains from divisive speech.’ ‘By relying on non-divisive speech, divisive speech is to be abandoned’—that was said with reference to this.”

37. “‘Agiddhilobhaṃ nissāya giddhilobho pahātabbo’ti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ, kiñcetaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ? Idha, gahapati, ariyasāvako iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘yesaṃ kho ahaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ hetu giddhilobhī assaṃ, tesāhaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ pahānāya samucchedāya paṭipanno. Ahañceva kho pana giddhilobhī assaṃ, attāpi maṃ upavadeyya giddhilobhapaccayā, anuviccāpi maṃ viññū garaheyyuṃ giddhilobhapaccayā, kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā duggati pāṭikaṅkhā giddhilobhapaccayā. Etadeva kho pana saṃyojanaṃ etaṃ nīvaraṇaṃ yadidaṃ giddhilobho. Ye ca giddhilobhapaccayā uppajjeyyuṃ āsavā vighātapariḷāhā, giddhilobhā paṭiviratassa evaṃsa te āsavā vighātapariḷāhā na honti’. ‘Agiddhilobhaṃ nissāya giddhilobho pahātabbo’ti – iti yantaṃ vuttaṃ idametaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ.

37. “‘By relying on non-covetousness, covetousness is to be abandoned’—this was said. With reference to what was this said? Here, householder, a noble disciple reflects thus: ‘On account of which fetters would I be covetous? I am practicing for the abandoning and utter destruction of those fetters. If I were to be covetous, I myself would reproach myself on account of covetousness; and the wise, having investigated, would censure me on account of covetousness; and with the breaking up of the body, after death, a woeful destination would be expected on account of covetousness. This covetousness is itself a fetter, this is a hindrance. And the taints, distresses, and fevers that would arise on account of covetousness do not exist for one who abstains from covetousness.’ ‘By relying on non-covetousness, covetousness is to be abandoned’—that was said with reference to this.”

38. “‘Anindārosaṃ nissāya nindāroso pahātabbo’ti iti kho [T 2.0039] panetaṃ vuttaṃ, kiñcetaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ? Idha, gahapati, ariyasāvako iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘yesaṃ kho ahaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ hetu nindārosī assaṃ, tesāhaṃ [M 2.0026] saṃyojanānaṃ pahānāya [P 1.0363] samucchedāya paṭipanno. Ahañceva kho pana nindārosī assaṃ, attāpi maṃ upavadeyya nindārosapaccayā, anuviccāpi maṃ viññū garaheyyuṃ nindārosapaccayā, kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā duggati pāṭikaṅkhā nindārosapaccayā. Etadeva kho pana saṃyojanaṃ etaṃ nīvaraṇaṃ yadidaṃ nindāroso. Ye ca nindārosapaccayā uppajjeyyuṃ āsavā vighātapariḷāhā, anindārosissa evaṃsa te āsavā vighātapariḷāhā na honti’. ‘Anindārosaṃ nissāya nindāroso pahātabbo’ti – iti yantaṃ vuttaṃ idametaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ.

38. “‘By relying on non-censure and non-domineering, censure and domineering are to be abandoned’—this was said. With reference to what was this said? Here, householder, a noble disciple reflects thus: ‘On account of which fetters I might be given to censure and domineering, I am practicing for the abandoning and utter destruction of those fetters. If I were to be given to censure and domineering, I myself would reproach myself on account of censure and domineering; and the wise, having investigated, would censure me on account of censure and domineering; and with the breakup of the body, after death, an unfortunate destination is to be expected on account of censure and domineering. Indeed, this very censure and domineering is a fetter, this is a hindrance. And whatever taints, vexations, and fevers would arise on account of censure and domineering, for one who is without censure and domineering, those taints, vexations, and fevers do not exist.’ ‘By relying on non-censure and non-domineering, censure and domineering are to be abandoned’—that which was said, was said with reference to this.”

39. “‘Akkodhūpāyāsaṃ nissāya kodhūpāyāso pahātabbo’ti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ, kiñcetaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ? Idha, gahapati, ariyasāvako iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘yesaṃ kho ahaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ hetu kodhūpāyāsī assaṃ, tesāhaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ pahānāya samucchedāya paṭipanno. Ahañceva kho pana kodhūpāyāsī assaṃ, attāpi maṃ upavadeyya kodhūpāyāsapaccayā[V 2.0028], anuviccāpi maṃ viññū garaheyyuṃ kodhūpāyāsapaccayā, kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā duggati pāṭikaṅkhā kodhūpāyāsapaccayā. Etadeva kho pana saṃyojanaṃ etaṃ nīvaraṇaṃ yadidaṃ kodhūpāyāso. Ye ca kodhūpāyāsapaccayā uppajjeyyuṃ āsavā vighātapariḷāhā, akkodhūpāyāsissa [T 2.0040] evaṃsa te āsavā vighātapariḷāhā na honti’. ‘Akkodhūpāyāsaṃ nissāya kodhūpāyāso pahātabbo’ti – iti yantaṃ vuttaṃ idametaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ.

39. “‘By relying on non-anger and non-animosity, anger and animosity are to be abandoned’—this was said. With reference to what was this said? Here, householder, a noble disciple reflects thus: ‘On account of which fetters I might be angry and bear animosity, I am practicing for the abandoning and utter destruction of those fetters. If I were to be angry and bear animosity, I myself would reproach myself on account of anger and animosity; and the wise, having investigated, would censure me on account of anger and animosity; and with the breakup of the body, after death, an unfortunate destination is to be expected on account of anger and animosity. Indeed, this very anger and animosity is a fetter, this is a hindrance. And whatever taints, vexations, and fevers would arise on account of anger and animosity, for one who is without anger and animosity, those taints, vexations, and fevers do not exist.’ ‘By relying on non-anger and non-animosity, anger and animosity are to be abandoned’—that which was said, was said with reference to this.”

40. “‘Anatimānaṃ nissāya atimāno pahātabbo’ti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ, kiñcetaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ? Idha, gahapati, ariyasāvako iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘yesaṃ kho ahaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ hetu atimānī assaṃ, tesāhaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ pahānāya samucchedāya paṭipanno. Ahañceva kho pana atimānī assaṃ, attāpi maṃ upavadeyya atimānapaccayā, anuviccāpi maṃ viññū garaheyyuṃ atimānapaccayā, kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā duggati pāṭikaṅkhā atimānapaccayā. Etadeva kho pana saṃyojanaṃ etaṃ nīvaraṇaṃ yadidaṃ atimāno. Ye ca atimānapaccayā uppajjeyyuṃ āsavā vighātapariḷāhā, anatimānissa evaṃsa te āsavā vighātapariḷāhā na honti’. ‘Anatimānaṃ nissāya atimāno pahātabbo’ti – iti yantaṃ vuttaṃ idametaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ.

40. “‘By relying on non-arrogance, arrogance is to be abandoned’—this was said. With reference to what was this said? Here, householder, a noble disciple reflects thus: ‘On account of which fetters I might be arrogant, I am practicing for the abandoning and utter destruction of those fetters. If I were to be arrogant, I myself would reproach myself on account of arrogance; and the wise, having investigated, would censure me on account of arrogance; and with the breakup of the body, after death, an unfortunate destination is to be expected on account of arrogance. Indeed, this very arrogance is a fetter, this is a hindrance. And whatever taints, vexations, and fevers would arise on account of arrogance, for one who is not arrogant, those taints, vexations, and fevers do not exist.’ ‘By relying on non-arrogance, arrogance is to be abandoned’—that which was said, was said with reference to this.”

41. “Ime [M 2.0027][P 1.0364] kho, gahapati, aṭṭha dhammā saṃkhittena vuttā, vitthārena vibhattā avibhattā (syā. ka.), ye ariyassa vinaye vohārasamucchedāya saṃvattanti; na tveva tāva ariyassa vinaye sabbena sabbaṃ sabbathā sabbaṃ vohārasamucchedo hotī”ti.

41. “These, householder, are the eight qualities stated in brief and analyzed in detail, which conduce to the utter cutting off of conventions in the Noble One’s Discipline. Yet, in the Noble One’s Discipline, the cutting off of all conventions, completely and in every way, has not yet come to be.”

“Yathā kathaṃ pana, bhante, ariyassa vinaye sabbena sabbaṃ sabbathā sabbaṃ vohārasamucchedo hoti? Sādhu me, bhante, bhagavā tathā dhammaṃ desetu yathā ariyassa [T 2.0041] vinaye sabbena sabbaṃ sabbathā sabbaṃ vohārasamucchedo hotī”ti. “Tena hi, gahapati, suṇāhi, sādhukaṃ manasi karohi, bhāsissāmī”ti. “Evaṃ, bhante”ti kho potaliyo gahapati bhagavato paccassosi. Bhagavā etadavoca –

“But how, venerable sir, in the Noble One’s Discipline, does the utter cutting off of all conventions, completely and in every way, come to be? It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in such a way that in the Noble One’s Discipline the utter cutting off of all conventions, completely and in every way, comes to be.” “In that case, householder, listen and apply your mind well; I will speak.” “Yes, venerable sir,” the householder Potaliya replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:

Kāmādīnavakathā

Discourse on the Dangers of Sensual Pleasures

42. “Seyyathāpi[V 2.0029], gahapati, kukkuro jighacchādubbalyapareto goghātakasūnaṃ paccupaṭṭhito assa. Tamenaṃ dakkho goghātako vā goghātakantevāsī vā aṭṭhikaṅkalaṃ sunikkantaṃ nikkantaṃ nimmaṃsaṃ lohitamakkhitaṃ upasumbheyya upacchubheyya (sī. pī.), upacchūbheyya (syā. kaṃ.), upaccumbheyya (ka.). Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, gahapati, api nu kho so kukkuro amuṃ aṭṭhikaṅkalaṃ sunikkantaṃ nikkantaṃ nimmaṃsaṃ lohitamakkhitaṃ palehanto jighacchādubbalyaṃ paṭivineyyā”ti?

42. “Suppose, householder, a dog overcome by hunger and debility were to approach a slaughterhouse. Then a skilled butcher or a butcher's apprentice were to toss to it a skeleton-bone scraped clean, fleshless, and smeared with blood. What do you think, householder? Would that dog, by licking that skeleton-bone scraped clean, fleshless, and smeared with blood, allay its hunger and debility?”

“No hetaṃ, bhante”.

“No, venerable sir.”

“Taṃ kissa hetu”?

“For what reason?”

“Aduñhi, bhante, aṭṭhikaṅkalaṃ sunikkantaṃ nikkantaṃ nimmaṃsaṃ lohitamakkhitaṃ. Yāvadeva pana so kukkuro kilamathassa vighātassa bhāgī assāti. Evameva kho, gahapati, ariyasāvako iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘aṭṭhikaṅkalūpamā kāmā vuttā bhagavatā bahudukkhā bahupāyāsā bahūpāyāsā (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.), ādīnavo ettha bhiyyo’ti. Evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya disvā yāyaṃ upekkhā nānattā nānattasitā taṃ abhinivajjetvā, yāyaṃ upekkhā ekattā ekattasitā yattha sabbaso lokāmisūpādānā aparisesā nirujjhanti tamevūpekkhaṃ bhāveti.

“Because, venerable sir, that skeleton-bone is scraped clean, fleshless, and smeared with blood. That dog will only get weariness and vexation from it.” “Even so, householder, a noble disciple reflects thus: ‘Sensual pleasures have been compared by the Blessed One to a skeleton-bone—of much suffering, of much tribulation, and there is greater danger in them.’ Seeing this as it truly is with right wisdom, he avoids that equanimity which is diverse and based on diversity, and develops that very equanimity which is unified and based on unity, where all grasping for the baits of the world ceases without remainder.

43. “Seyyathāpi, gahapati, gijjho vā kaṅko vā kulalo vā maṃsapesiṃ [T 2.0042] ādāya uḍḍīyeyya uḍḍayeyya (syā. pī.). Tamenaṃ gijjhāpi kaṅkāpi kulalāpi anupatitvā [M 2.0028] anupatitvā vitaccheyyuṃ vissajjeyyuṃ virājeyyuṃ (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.). Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, gahapati, sace so gijjho vā kaṅko vā kulalo vā taṃ maṃsapesiṃ na khippameva paṭinissajjeyya, so tatonidānaṃ maraṇaṃ vā nigaccheyya maraṇamattaṃ vā dukkha”nti?

43. “Suppose, householder, a vulture, a heron, or a hawk were to carry off a piece of meat and fly away. Then other vultures, herons, and hawks would follow it, pursuing, tearing at it and trying to make it let go. What do you think, householder? If that vulture, heron, or hawk does not quickly relinquish that piece of meat, would it not, on account of that, meet with death or suffering like unto death?”

“Evaṃ, bhante”.

“So it is, venerable sir.”

“Evameva [V 2.0030] kho, gahapati, ariyasāvako iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘maṃsapesūpamā kāmā vuttā bhagavatā bahudukkhā bahupāyāsā, ādīnavo ettha bhiyyo’ti. Evametaṃ [P 1.0365] yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya disvā yāyaṃ upekkhā nānattā nānattasitā taṃ abhinivajjetvā yāyaṃ upekkhā ekattā ekattasitā yattha sabbaso lokāmisūpādānā aparisesā nirujjhanti tamevūpekkhaṃ bhāveti.

“Even so, householder, a noble disciple reflects thus: ‘Sensual pleasures have been compared by the Blessed One to a piece of meat—of much suffering, of much tribulation, and there is greater danger in them.’ Seeing this as it truly is with right wisdom, he avoids that equanimity which is diverse and based on diversity, and develops that equanimity which is unified and based on unity, where all grasping for the baits of the world ceases without remainder.

44. “Seyyathāpi, gahapati, puriso ādittaṃ tiṇukkaṃ ādāya paṭivātaṃ gaccheyya. Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, gahapati, sace so puriso taṃ ādittaṃ tiṇukkaṃ na khippameva paṭinissajjeyya tassa sā ādittā tiṇukkā hatthaṃ vā daheyya bāhuṃ vā daheyya aññataraṃ vā aññataraṃ vā aṅgapaccaṅgaṃ daheyya. aññataraṃ vā aṅgapaccaṅga (sī. pī.) daheyya, so tatonidānaṃ maraṇaṃ vā nigaccheyya maraṇamattaṃ vā dukkha”nti?

44. “Suppose, householder, a man were to take a blazing grass-torch and go against the wind. What do you think, householder? If that man does not quickly relinquish that blazing grass-torch, would that blazing grass-torch not burn his hand or his arm or some other of his major or minor limbs? And would he not, on account of that, meet with death or suffering like unto death?”

“Evaṃ, bhante”.

“So it is, venerable sir.”

“Evameva kho, gahapati, ariyasāvako iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘tiṇukkūpamā kāmā vuttā bhagavatā bahudukkhā bahupāyāsā, ādīnavo ettha bhiyyo’ti. Evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya disvā…pe… tamevūpekkhaṃ bhāveti.

“Even so, householder, a noble disciple reflects thus: ‘Sensual pleasures have been compared by the Blessed One to a grass-torch—of much suffering, of much tribulation, and there is greater danger in them.’ Seeing this as it truly is with right wisdom… he develops that very equanimity.

45. “Seyyathāpi[T 2.0043], gahapati, aṅgārakāsu sādhikaporisā, pūrā aṅgārānaṃ vītaccikānaṃ vītadhūmānaṃ. Atha puriso āgaccheyya jīvitukāmo amaritukāmo sukhakāmo dukkhappaṭikkūlo. Tamenaṃ dve balavanto purisā nānābāhāsu gahetvā aṅgārakāsuṃ upakaḍḍheyyuṃ. Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, gahapati, api nu so puriso iticiticeva kāyaṃ sannāmeyyā”ti?

45. “Suppose, householder, there were a pit of coals, deeper than a man’s height, full of embers, flameless and smokeless. Then a man would come along—desiring to live, not desiring to die, desiring happiness, and averse to suffering. Then two strong men, seizing him by his arms, would drag him toward the pit of coals. What do you think, householder? Would that man not struggle with his body this way and that?”

“Evaṃ, bhante”.

“So it is, venerable sir.”

“Taṃ kissa hetu”?

“For what reason?”

“Viditañhi[V 2.0031], bhante, tassa purisassa imañcāhaṃ aṅgārakāsuṃ papatissāmi, tatonidānaṃ maraṇaṃ vā nigacchissāmi maraṇamattaṃ vā dukkha”nti. “Evameva kho, gahapati, ariyasāvako iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘aṅgārakāsūpamā kāmā vuttā bhagavatā bahudukkhā bahupāyāsā, ādīnavo ettha bhiyyo’ti. Evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya disvā…pe… tamevūpekkhaṃ bhāveti.

“Because, venerable sir, that man knows: ‘I will fall into this pit of coals, and on account of that, I will meet with death or suffering like unto death.’” “Even so, householder, a noble disciple reflects thus: ‘Sensual pleasures have been compared by the Blessed One to a pit of coals—of much suffering, of much tribulation, and there is greater danger in them.’ Seeing this as it truly is with right wisdom… he develops that very equanimity.

46. “Seyyathāpi[M 2.0029], gahapati, puriso supinakaṃ passeyya ārāmarāmaṇeyyakaṃ vanarāmaṇeyyakaṃ bhūmirāmaṇeyyakaṃ pokkharaṇirāmaṇeyyakaṃ. So paṭibuddho na kiñci paṭipasseyya passeyya (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.). Evameva kho, gahapati, ariyasāvako iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘supinakūpamā kāmā vuttā bhagavatā bahudukkhā bahupāyāsā, ādīnavo ettha bhiyyo’ti…pe… tamevūpekkhaṃ bhāveti.

46. “Suppose, householder, a man were to see in a dream a delightful park, a delightful forest, a delightful land, and a delightful pond. When he awoke, he would see nothing of it. Even so, householder, a noble disciple reflects thus: ‘Sensual pleasures have been compared by the Blessed One to a dream—of much suffering, of much tribulation, and there is greater danger in them.’… he develops that very equanimity.

47. “Seyyathāpi, gahapati, puriso yācitakaṃ bhogaṃ yācitvā yānaṃ [P 1.0366] vā yānaṃ (syā. kaṃ. pī.) poriseyyaṃ poroseyyaṃ (sī. pī. ka.), oropeyya (syā. kaṃ.) pavaramaṇikuṇḍalaṃ. So tehi yācitakehi bhogehi purakkhato parivuto [T 2.0044] antarāpaṇaṃ paṭipajjeyya. Tamenaṃ jano disvā evaṃ vadeyya – ‘bhogī vata, bho, puriso, evaṃ kira bhogino bhogāni bhuñjantī’ti. Tamenaṃ sāmikā yattha yattheva passeyyuṃ tattha tattheva sāni hareyyuṃ. Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, gahapati, alaṃ nu kho tassa purisassa aññathattāyā”ti?

47. “Suppose, householder, a man, having borrowed possessions—a fine carriage and excellent jeweled earrings—were to go into the marketplace, preceded and surrounded by those borrowed possessions. People seeing him would say: ‘Sirs, this man is truly wealthy! This is how the wealthy enjoy their wealth.’ But the owners, wherever they might see him, would take back their property. What do you think, householder? Is that not enough to cause a change in that man’s state?”

“Evaṃ, bhante”.

“So it is, venerable sir.”

“Taṃ kissa hetu”?

“For what reason?”

“Sāmino hi, bhante, sāni harantī”ti. “Evameva kho, gahapati, ariyasāvako iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘yācitakūpamā kāmā vuttā bhagavatā bahudukkhā bahupāyāsā, ādīnavo ettha bhiyyo’ti…pe… [V 2.0032] tamevūpekkhaṃ bhāveti.

“Because, venerable sir, the owners are taking back their property.” “Even so, householder, a noble disciple reflects thus: ‘Sensual pleasures have been compared by the Blessed One to borrowed goods—of much suffering, of much tribulation, and there is greater danger in them.’… he develops that very equanimity.

48. “Seyyathāpi, gahapati, gāmassa vā nigamassa vā avidūre tibbo vanasaṇḍo. Tatrassa rukkho sampannaphalo ca upapannaphalo uppannaphalo (syā.) ca, na cassu kānici phalāni bhūmiyaṃ patitāni. Atha puriso āgaccheyya phalatthiko phalagavesī phalapariyesanaṃ caramāno. So taṃ vanasaṇḍaṃ ajjhogāhetvā taṃ rukkhaṃ passeyya sampannaphalañca upapannaphalañca. Tassa evamassa – ‘ayaṃ kho rukkho sampannaphalo ca upapannaphalo ca, natthi ca kānici phalāni bhūmiyaṃ patitāni. Jānāmi kho panāhaṃ rukkhaṃ ārohituṃ āruhituṃ (sī.). Yaṃnūnāhaṃ imaṃ rukkhaṃ ārohitvā yāvadatthañca khādeyyaṃ ucchaṅgañca pūreyya’nti. So taṃ rukkhaṃ ārohitvā yāvadatthañca khādeyya ucchaṅgañca pūreyya. Atha [T 2.0045] dutiyo puriso āgaccheyya phalatthiko phalagavesī phalapariyesanaṃ caramāno tiṇhaṃ kuṭhāriṃ kudhāriṃ (syā. kaṃ. ka.) ādāya. So taṃ vanasaṇḍaṃ ajjhogāhetvā [M 2.0030] taṃ rukkhaṃ passeyya sampannaphalañca upapannaphalañca. Tassa evamassa – ‘ayaṃ kho rukkho sampannaphalo ca upapannaphalo ca, natthi ca kānici phalāni bhūmiyaṃ patitāni. Na kho panāhaṃ jānāmi rukkhaṃ ārohituṃ. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ imaṃ rukkhaṃ mūlato chetvā yāvadatthañca khādeyyaṃ ucchaṅgañca pūreyya’nti. So taṃ rukkhaṃ mūlatova chindeyya. Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, gahapati, amuko asu (sī. pī.) yo so puriso paṭhamaṃ rukkhaṃ ārūḷho sace so na khippameva oroheyya tassa so rukkho papatanto hatthaṃ vā bhañjeyya pādaṃ vā bhañjeyya aññataraṃ vā aññataraṃ vā aṅgapaccaṅgaṃ bhañjeyya, so tatonidānaṃ [P 1.0367] maraṇaṃ vā nigaccheyya maraṇamattaṃ vā dukkha”nti?

48. “Suppose, householder, not far from a village or a town there was a dense thicket. In it there might be a tree with sweet and abundant fruit, and no fruits whatsoever might have fallen to the ground. Then a man might come along, wanting fruit, seeking fruit, wandering in search of fruit. Having entered that thicket, he might see that tree with sweet and abundant fruit. It might occur to him thus: ‘Indeed, this tree has sweet and abundant fruit, and no fruits whatsoever have fallen to the ground. Indeed, I know how to climb a tree. What if I were to climb this tree, eat as much as I wish, and fill my lap?’ He, having climbed that tree, might eat as much as he wishes and fill his lap. Then a second man might come along, wanting fruit, seeking fruit, wandering in search of fruit, taking a sharp axe. Having entered that thicket, he might see that tree with sweet and abundant fruit. It might occur to him thus: ‘Indeed, this tree has sweet and abundant fruit, and no fruits whatsoever have fallen to the ground. Indeed, I do not know how to climb a tree. What if I were to cut this tree at the root, eat as much as I wish, and fill my lap?’ He might cut that tree right at the root. What do you think, householder? If that man who first climbed the tree does not descend very quickly, as that tree is falling, might it not break his hand or his foot or some other major or minor limb, so that from that cause he might come to death or to suffering like unto death?”

“Evaṃ, bhante”.

“It is so, venerable sir.”

“Evameva kho, gahapati, ariyasāvako iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘rukkhaphalūpamā kāmā vuttā bhagavatā bahudukkhā bahupāyāsā, ādīnavo ettha bhiyyo’ti. Evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya disvā yāyaṃ upekkhā nānattā nānattasitā taṃ abhinivajjetvā yāyaṃ upekkhā ekattā ekattasitā yattha sabbaso lokāmisūpādānā aparisesā nirujjhanti tamevūpekkhaṃ bhāveti.

Just so, householder, a noble disciple reflects thus: ‘Sensual pleasures have been declared by the Blessed One to be like the fruit of a tree—of much suffering, of much tribulation; the danger in them is greater.’ Having seen this as it truly is with right wisdom, and having turned away from that equanimity which is of diversity, based on diversity, he develops that equanimity which is of unity, based on unity, where all grasping for worldly allurements ceases without remainder.

49. “Sa [V 2.0033] kho so, gahapati, ariyasāvako imaṃyeva anuttaraṃ upekkhāsatipārisuddhiṃ āgamma anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati, seyyathidaṃ [T 2.0046] – ekampi jātiṃ dvepi jātiyo…pe… iti sākāraṃ sauddesaṃ anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati.

49. Householder, that noble disciple, relying on this very unsurpassed purity of mindfulness due to equanimity, recollects his manifold past abodes, that is to say: one birth, two births... Thus he recollects his manifold past abodes with their aspects and details.

“Sa kho so, gahapati, ariyasāvako imaṃyeva anuttaraṃ upekkhāsatipārisuddhiṃ āgamma dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena satte passati cavamāne upapajjamāne hīne paṇīte suvaṇṇe dubbaṇṇe sugate duggate…pe… yathākammūpage satte pajānāti.

Householder, that noble disciple, relying on this very unsurpassed purity of mindfulness due to equanimity, with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, sees beings passing away and reappearing—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate... and he understands beings as faring according to their kamma.

“Sa kho so, gahapati, ariyasāvako imaṃyeva anuttaraṃ upekkhāsatipārisuddhiṃ āgamma āsavānaṃ khayā anāsavaṃ cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharati. Ettāvatā kho, gahapati, ariyassa vinaye sabbena sabbaṃ sabbathā sabbaṃ vohārasamucchedo hoti.

Householder, that noble disciple, relying on this very unsurpassed purity of mindfulness due to equanimity, through the destruction of the taints, in this very life realizes for himself with direct knowledge the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, and having attained it, dwells therein. To this extent, householder, in the discipline of the Noble One, there is a complete and utter cutting off of conventional designation in every way.

50. “Taṃ [M 2.0031] kiṃ maññasi, gahapati, yathā ariyassa vinaye sabbena sabbaṃ sabbathā sabbaṃ vohārasamucchedo hoti, api nu tvaṃ evarūpaṃ vohārasamucchedaṃ attani samanupassasī”ti? “Ko cāhaṃ, bhante, ko ca ariyassa vinaye sabbena sabbaṃ sabbathā sabbaṃ vohārasamucchedo! Ārakā ahaṃ, bhante, ariyassa vinaye sabbena sabbaṃ sabbathā sabbaṃ vohārasamucchedā. Mayañhi, bhante, pubbe aññatitthiye paribbājake anājānīyeva samāne ājānīyāti amaññimha, anājānīyeva samāne ājānīyabhojanaṃ bhojimha, anājānīyeva samāne ājānīyaṭhāne ṭhapimha; bhikkhū pana mayaṃ, bhante, ājānīyeva samāne anājānīyāti amaññimha, ājānīyeva [T 2.0047] samāne anājānīyabhojanaṃ bhojimha, ājānīyeva samāne anājānīyaṭhāne ṭhapimha; idāni pana mayaṃ, bhante, aññatitthiye [P 1.0368] paribbājake anājānīyeva samāne anājānīyāti jānissāma, anājānīyeva samāne anājānīyabhojanaṃ bhojessāma, anājānīyeva samāne anājānīyaṭhāne ṭhapessāma. Bhikkhū pana mayaṃ, bhante, ājānīyeva samāne ājānīyāti jānissāma ājānīyeva samāne ājānīyabhojanaṃ bhojessāma, ājānīyeva samāne ājānīyaṭhāne ṭhapessāma. Ajanesi vata me, bhante, bhagavā samaṇesu samaṇappemaṃ, samaṇesu samaṇappasādaṃ, samaṇesu samaṇagāravaṃ. Abhikkantaṃ, bhante, abhikkantaṃ, bhante[V 2.0034]! Seyyathāpi, bhante, nikkujjitaṃ vā ukkujjeyya, paṭicchannaṃ vā vivareyya, mūḷhassa vā maggaṃ ācikkheyya, andhakāre vā telapajjotaṃ dhāreyya, cakkhumanto rūpāni dakkhantīti; evamevaṃ kho, bhante, bhagavatā anekapariyāyena dhammo pakāsito. Esāhaṃ, bhante, bhagavantaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi dhammañca bhikkhusaṅghañca. Upāsakaṃ maṃ bhagavā dhāretu ajjatagge pāṇupetaṃ saraṇaṃ gata”nti.

50. “What do you think, householder? In the Noble One’s Discipline, where conventional designation is completely and utterly cut off in every way and in every respect, do you see such a cutting off of conventional designation in yourself?” “Who am I, venerable sir, and what is the complete and utter cutting off of all conventional designation in the Noble One’s Discipline! I am far, venerable sir, from the complete and utter cutting off of all conventional designation in the Noble One’s Discipline. For previously, venerable sir, we regarded other sectarian wanderers, who were not thoroughbreds, as thoroughbreds; we gave food for thoroughbreds to those who were not thoroughbreds; we placed those who were not thoroughbreds in the position of thoroughbreds. But we regarded the monks, who were thoroughbreds, as not thoroughbreds; we gave food for non-thoroughbreds to those who were thoroughbreds; we placed those who were thoroughbreds in the position of non-thoroughbreds. Now, however, venerable sir, we will recognize other sectarian wanderers, who are not thoroughbreds, as not thoroughbreds; we will give food for non-thoroughbreds to those who are not thoroughbreds; we will place those who are not thoroughbreds in the position of non-thoroughbreds. And we will recognize the monks, who are thoroughbreds, as thoroughbreds; we will give food for thoroughbreds to those who are thoroughbreds; we will place those who are thoroughbreds in the position of thoroughbreds. Truly, venerable sir, the Blessed One has generated in me love for recluses, confidence in recluses, and reverence for recluses. Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir! Just as one might set upright what was overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or hold up an oil lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes could see forms—so too has the Dhamma been made clear in many ways by the Blessed One. I, venerable sir, go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Bhikkhu Saṅgha. May the Blessed One remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.”

Potaliyasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ catutthaṃ.

The Potaliya Sutta, the fourth, is concluded.

5. Jīvakasuttaṃ

5. The Jīvaka Sutta

51. Evaṃ [T 2.0048][V 2.0035] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā rājagahe viharati jīvakassa komārabhaccassa ambavane. Atha kho jīvako komārabhacco yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi[M 2.0032]. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho jīvako komārabhacco bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “sutaṃ metaṃ, bhante – ‘samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ uddissa pāṇaṃ ārabhanti ārambhanti (ka.), taṃ samaṇo gotamo jānaṃ uddissakataṃ uddissakaṭaṃ (sī. pī.) maṃsaṃ paribhuñjati paṭiccakamma’nti. Ye te, bhante, evamāhaṃsu – ‘samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ uddissa pāṇaṃ ārabhanti, taṃ samaṇo gotamo jānaṃ uddissakataṃ maṃsaṃ paribhuñjati paṭiccakamma’nti, kacci te, bhante, bhagavato vuttavādino, na ca bhagavantaṃ abhūtena abbhācikkhanti, dhammassa cānudhammaṃ byākaronti, na ca koci sahadhammiko vādānuvādo gārayhaṃ ṭhānaṃ āgacchatī”ti?

51. Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the mango grove of Jīvaka Komārabhacca. Then Jīvaka Komārabhacca approached the Blessed One, and after paying homage to him, sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Jīvaka Komārabhacca said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, I have heard this: ‘They kill living beings for the ascetic Gotama; the ascetic Gotama knowingly eats meat prepared on his account and from an intentional act.’ Venerable sir, those who say: ‘They kill living beings for the ascetic Gotama; the ascetic Gotama knowingly eats meat prepared on his account and from an intentional act’—are they reporting the Blessed One’s actual words and not misrepresenting the Blessed One with what is untrue? Do they declare in accordance with the Dhamma, so that no legitimate grounds for criticism, following from this line of reasoning, can be found?”

52. “Ye [P 1.0369] te, jīvaka, evamāhaṃsu – ‘samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ uddissa pāṇaṃ ārabhanti, taṃ samaṇo gotamo jānaṃ uddissakataṃ maṃsaṃ paribhuñjati paṭiccakamma’nti na me te vuttavādino, abbhācikkhanti ca maṃ te asatā abhūtena. Tīhi kho ahaṃ, jīvaka, ṭhānehi maṃsaṃ aparibhoganti vadāmi. Diṭṭhaṃ, sutaṃ, parisaṅkitaṃ – imehi kho ahaṃ, jīvaka[T 2.0049], tīhi ṭhānehi maṃsaṃ aparibhoganti vadāmi. Tīhi kho ahaṃ, jīvaka, ṭhānehi maṃsaṃ paribhoganti vadāmi. Adiṭṭhaṃ, asutaṃ, aparisaṅkitaṃ – imehi kho ahaṃ, jīvaka, tīhi ṭhānehi maṃsaṃ paribhoganti vadāmi.

52. “Jīvaka, those who say this: ‘They kill living beings for the ascetic Gotama; the ascetic Gotama knowingly eats meat prepared on his account and from an intentional act,’ are not reporting my actual words; they are misrepresenting me with what is false and untrue. Jīvaka, I say that meat is not to be consumed on three grounds: when it is seen, heard, or suspected. On these three grounds, Jīvaka, I say that meat is not to be consumed. Jīvaka, I say that meat is to be consumed on three grounds: when it is not seen, not heard, and not suspected. On these three grounds, Jīvaka, I say that meat is to be consumed.”

53. “Idha, jīvaka, bhikkhu aññataraṃ gāmaṃ vā nigamaṃ vā upanissāya viharati. So mettāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharati, tathā dutiyaṃ, tathā tatiyaṃ, tathā catutthaṃ. Iti uddhamadho tiriyaṃ sabbadhi sabbattatāya sabbāvantaṃ lokaṃ mettāsahagatena cetasā vipulena mahaggatena appamāṇena averena abyābajjhena pharitvā viharati. Tamenaṃ gahapati vā gahapatiputto vā upasaṅkamitvā svātanāya bhattena nimanteti. Ākaṅkhamānova ākaṅkhamāno (syā. kaṃ.), jīvaka, bhikkhu adhivāseti[V 2.0036]. So tassā rattiyā accayena pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya yena tassa gahapatissa vā gahapatiputtassa vā nivesanaṃ tenupasaṅkamati; upasaṅkamitvā paññatte āsane nisīdati. Tamenaṃ so gahapati vā gahapatiputto vā paṇītena piṇḍapātena parivisati. Tassa na evaṃ hoti – ‘sādhu vata māyaṃ maṃ + ayaṃ = māyaṃ gahapati vā gahapatiputto vā paṇītena piṇḍapātena [M 2.0033] pariviseyyāti! Aho vata māyaṃ gahapati vā gahapatiputto vā āyatimpi evarūpena paṇītena piṇḍapātena pariviseyyā’ti – evampissa na hoti. So taṃ piṇḍapātaṃ agathito agadhito (syā. kaṃ. ka.) amucchito anajjhopanno anajjhāpanno (syā. kaṃ. ka.) ādīnavadassāvī nissaraṇapañño paribhuñjati. Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, jīvaka[T 2.0050], api nu so bhikkhu tasmiṃ samaye attabyābādhāya vā ceteti, parabyābādhāya vā ceteti, ubhayabyābādhāya vā cetetī”ti?

53. “Jīvaka, in this Dispensation, a bhikkhu dwells depending on a certain village or town. He abides pervading one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, likewise the second, likewise the third, and likewise the fourth. Thus above, below, and across, everywhere, identifying himself with all, he abides pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness—extensive, exalted, immeasurable, without enmity, and without affliction. Then a householder or a householder’s son approaches him and invites him for the next day’s meal. Jīvaka, if the bhikkhu so wishes, he accepts. When the night has passed, in the morning, he dresses, takes his bowl and outer robe, and goes to the residence of that householder or householder’s son. Having arrived, he sits down on the prepared seat. Then that householder or householder’s son serves him with choice almsfood. It does not occur to him: ‘Indeed, it would be good if this householder or householder’s son were to serve me with choice almsfood!’ Nor does it occur to him: ‘Oh, that this householder or householder’s son would serve me with such choice almsfood in the future, too!’ He partakes of that almsfood without being greedy, without being infatuated, and without being attached, seeing the danger in it and with the wisdom of escape. What do you think, Jīvaka? At that time, does that bhikkhu intend for his own affliction, for the affliction of others, or for the affliction of both?”

“No hetaṃ, bhante”.

“No, venerable sir.”

“Nanu so, jīvaka, bhikkhu tasmiṃ samaye anavajjaṃyeva āhāraṃ āhāretī”ti?

“Jīvaka, does not that bhikkhu at that time partake of only blameless food?”

“Evaṃ, bhante. Sutaṃ metaṃ, bhante – ‘brahmā mettāvihārī’ti. Taṃ me idaṃ, bhante, bhagavā sakkhidiṭṭho; bhagavā hi, bhante, mettāvihārī”ti. “Yena kho, jīvaka, rāgena yena dosena [P 1.0370] yena mohena byāpādavā assa so rāgo so doso so moho tathāgatassa pahīno ucchinnamūlo tālāvatthukato anabhāvaṃkato anabhāvakato (sī. pī.), anabhāvaṃgato (syā. kaṃ.) āyatiṃ anuppādadhammo. Sace kho te, jīvaka, idaṃ sandhāya bhāsitaṃ anujānāmi te eta”nti. “Etadeva kho pana me, bhante, sandhāya bhāsitaṃ” bhāsitanti (syā.).

“So it is, venerable sir. I have heard this, venerable sir: ‘Brahmā is an abider in loving-kindness.’ This, venerable sir, is that Brahmā seen by me in person, namely the Blessed One; for the Blessed One, venerable sir, is an abider in loving-kindness.” “Jīvaka, that greed, that hatred, and that delusion by which one would have affliction—that greed, that hatred, and that delusion have been abandoned by the Tathāgata, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, brought to non-existence, and are of a nature not to arise again in the future. If, Jīvaka, it was with reference to this that you spoke, I grant you that.” “Venerable sir, it was indeed with reference to this that I spoke.”

54. “Idha, jīvaka, bhikkhu aññataraṃ gāmaṃ vā nigamaṃ vā upanissāya viharati. So karuṇāsahagatena cetasā…pe… muditāsahagatena cetasā…pe… upekkhāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharati, tathā dutiyaṃ, tathā tatiyaṃ, tathā catutthaṃ. Iti uddhamadho tiriyaṃ sabbadhi sabbattatāya sabbāvantaṃ lokaṃ upekkhāsahagatena cetasā vipulena mahaggatena appamāṇena averena abyābajjhena pharitvā viharati. Tamenaṃ gahapati vā gahapatiputto vā upasaṅkamitvā svātanāya bhattena nimanteti. Ākaṅkhamānova, jīvaka, bhikkhu adhivāseti. So [V 2.0037] tassā rattiyā accayena pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya [T 2.0051] yena gahapatissa vā gahapatiputtassa vā nivesanaṃ tenupasaṅkamati; upasaṅkamitvā paññatte āsane nisīdati. Tamenaṃ so gahapati vā gahapatiputto vā paṇītena piṇḍapātena parivisati. Tassa na evaṃ hoti – ‘sādhu vata māyaṃ gahapati vā gahapatiputto vā paṇītena piṇḍapātena pariviseyyāti! Aho vata māyaṃ gahapati vā gahapatiputto vā āyatimpi [M 2.0034] evarūpena paṇītena piṇḍapātena pariviseyyā’ti – evampissa na hoti. So taṃ piṇḍapātaṃ agathito amucchito anajjhopanno ādīnavadassāvī nissaraṇapañño paribhuñjati. Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, jīvaka, api nu so bhikkhu tasmiṃ samaye attabyābādhāya vā ceteti, parabyābādhāya vā ceteti, ubhayabyābādhāya vā cetetī”ti?

54. “Jīvaka, in this Dispensation, a bhikkhu dwells depending on a certain village or town. He abides pervading one direction with a mind imbued with compassion... with sympathetic joy... with equanimity, likewise the second, likewise the third, and likewise the fourth. Thus above, below, and across, everywhere, identifying himself with all, he abides pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with equanimity—extensive, exalted, immeasurable, without enmity, and without affliction. Then a householder or a householder’s son approaches him and invites him for the next day’s meal. Jīvaka, if the bhikkhu so wishes, he accepts. When the night has passed, in the morning, he dresses, takes his bowl and outer robe, and goes to the residence of that householder or householder’s son. Having arrived, he sits down on the prepared seat. Then that householder or householder’s son serves him with choice almsfood. It does not occur to him: ‘Indeed, it would be good if this householder or householder’s son were to serve me with choice almsfood!’ Nor does it occur to him: ‘Oh, that this householder or householder’s son would serve me with such choice almsfood in the future, too!’ He partakes of that almsfood without being greedy, without being infatuated, and without being attached, seeing the danger in it and with the wisdom of escape. What do you think, Jīvaka? At that time, does that bhikkhu intend for his own affliction, for the affliction of others, or for the affliction of both?”

“No hetaṃ, bhante”.

“No, venerable sir.”

“Nanu so, jīvaka, bhikkhu tasmiṃ samaye anavajjaṃyeva āhāraṃ āhāretī”ti?

“Jīvaka, does not that bhikkhu at that time partake of only blameless food?”

“Evaṃ, bhante. Sutaṃ metaṃ, bhante – ‘brahmā upekkhāvihārī’ti. Taṃ me idaṃ, bhante, bhagavā sakkhidiṭṭho; bhagavā hi, bhante, upekkhāvihārī”ti. “Yena kho, jīvaka, rāgena yena dosena yena mohena vihesavā assa arativā assa paṭighavā assa so rāgo so doso so moho tathāgatassa pahīno ucchinnamūlo tālāvatthukato anabhāvaṃkato āyatiṃ anuppādadhammo. Sace kho te, jīvaka, idaṃ sandhāya bhāsitaṃ, anujānāmi te [P 1.0371] eta”nti. “Etadeva kho pana me, bhante, sandhāya bhāsitaṃ”.

“So it is, venerable sir. I have heard this, venerable sir: ‘Brahmā is an abider in equanimity.’ This, venerable sir, is that Brahmā seen by me in person, namely the Blessed One; for the Blessed One, venerable sir, is an abider in equanimity.” “Jīvaka, that greed, that hatred, and that delusion by which one would have vexation, or discontent, or resentment—that greed, that hatred, and that delusion have been abandoned by the Tathāgata, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, brought to non-existence, and are of a nature not to arise again in the future. If, Jīvaka, it was with reference to this that you spoke, I grant you that.” “Venerable sir, it was indeed with reference to this that I spoke.”

55. “Yo [T 2.0052] kho, jīvaka, tathāgataṃ vā tathāgatasāvakaṃ vā uddissa pāṇaṃ ārabhati so pañcahi ṭhānehi bahuṃ apuññaṃ pasavati. Yampi so, gahapati, evamāha – ‘gacchatha, amukaṃ nāma pāṇaṃ ānethā’ti, iminā paṭhamena ṭhānena bahuṃ apuññaṃ pasavati. Yampi so pāṇo galappaveṭhakena galappavedhakena (bahūsu) ānīyamāno dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti, iminā dutiyena ṭhānena bahuṃ apuññaṃ pasavati. Yampi so evamāha – ‘gacchatha imaṃ pāṇaṃ ārabhathā’ti, iminā tatiyena ṭhānena bahuṃ apuññaṃ pasavati. Yampi so pāṇo ārabhiyamāno dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti[V 2.0038], iminā catutthena ṭhānena bahuṃ apuññaṃ pasavati. Yampi so tathāgataṃ vā tathāgatasāvakaṃ vā akappiyena āsādeti, iminā pañcamena ṭhānena bahuṃ apuññaṃ pasavati. Yo kho, jīvaka, tathāgataṃ vā tathāgatasāvakaṃ vā uddissa pāṇaṃ ārabhati so imehi pañcahi ṭhānehi bahuṃ apuññaṃ pasavatī”ti.

55. “Jīvaka, whoever slaughters a living being for the sake of the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata generates much demerit in five instances. Firstly, when that person says, ‘Go, fetch such-and-such a living being,’ by this first instance he generates much demerit. Secondly, when that living being, being led with a rope around its neck, experiences pain and distress, by this second instance he generates much demerit. Thirdly, when he says, ‘Go, slaughter this living being,’ by this third instance he generates much demerit. Fourthly, when that living being, while being slaughtered, experiences pain and distress, by this fourth instance he generates much demerit. Fifthly, when he serves the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata with what is unallowable, by this fifth instance he generates much demerit. Jīvaka, whoever slaughters a living being for the sake of the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata generates much demerit in these five instances.”

Evaṃ vutte, jīvako komārabhacco bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “acchariyaṃ, bhante, abbhutaṃ, bhante! Kappiyaṃ vata, bhante, bhikkhū āhāraṃ āhārenti[M 2.0035]; anavajjaṃ vata, bhante, bhikkhū āhāraṃ āhārenti. Abhikkantaṃ, bhante, abhikkantaṃ, bhante…pe… [T 2.0053] upāsakaṃ maṃ bhagavā dhāretu ajjatagge pāṇupetaṃ saraṇaṃ gata”nti.

When this was said, Jīvaka Komārabhacca said this to the Blessed One: “It is wonderful, venerable sir! It is amazing, venerable sir! Indeed, venerable sir, the bhikkhus consume allowable food; indeed, venerable sir, the bhikkhus consume blameless food. Excellent, venerable sir! Excellent, venerable sir! … From this day forth, may the Blessed One remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

Jīvakasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ pañcamaṃ.

The Jīvaka Sutta, the fifth, is concluded.

6. Upālisuttaṃ

6. The Upāli Sutta

56. Evaṃ [V 2.0039] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā nāḷandāyaṃ viharati pāvārikambavane. Tena kho pana samayena nigaṇṭho nāṭaputto nāthaputto (sī.), nātaputto (pī.) nāḷandāyaṃ paṭivasati mahatiyā nigaṇṭhaparisāya saddhiṃ. Atha kho dīghatapassī nigaṇṭho nāḷandāyaṃ piṇḍāya caritvā pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto yena pāvārikambavanaṃ yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā [P 1.0372] bhagavatā saddhiṃ sammodi. Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Ekamantaṃ ṭhitaṃ kho dīghatapassiṃ nigaṇṭhaṃ bhagavā etadavoca – “saṃvijjanti kho, tapassi dīghatapassi (syā. kaṃ. ka.), āsanāni; sace ākaṅkhasi nisīdā”ti. Evaṃ vutte, dīghatapassī nigaṇṭho aññataraṃ nīcaṃ āsanaṃ gahetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinnaṃ kho dīghatapassiṃ nigaṇṭhaṃ bhagavā etadavoca – “kati pana, tapassi, nigaṇṭho nāṭaputto kammāni paññapeti pāpassa kammassa kiriyāya pāpassa kammassa pavattiyā”ti?

56. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Nāḷandā in Pāvārika's mango grove. Now at that time, the Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta was residing at Nāḷandā with a large assembly of Nigaṇṭhas. Then the Nigaṇṭha Dīgha Tapassī, having wandered for alms in Nāḷandā and returned from his alms-round after the meal, approached Pāvārika's mango grove where the Blessed One was. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. Having exchanged courteous and memorable greetings, he stood to one side. The Blessed One said this to the Nigaṇṭha Dīgha Tapassī as he was standing to one side: “There are seats available, Tapassī; if you wish, sit down.” When this was said, the Nigaṇṭha Dīgha Tapassī took a low seat and sat down to one side. The Blessed One said this to the Nigaṇṭha Dīgha Tapassī as he was sitting to one side: “How many actions, Tapassī, does the Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta declare for the performance of an evil action and for the undertaking of an evil action?”

“Na kho, āvuso gotama, āciṇṇaṃ nigaṇṭhassa nāṭaputtassa ‘kammaṃ, kamma’nti paññapetuṃ; ‘daṇḍaṃ, daṇḍa’nti kho, āvuso gotama, āciṇṇaṃ nigaṇṭhassa nāṭaputtassa paññapetu”nti.

“Friend Gotama, it is not the custom of the Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta to declare it as ‘action, action’; rather, friend Gotama, it is the custom of the Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta to declare it as ‘rod, rod’.”

“Kati pana, tapassi, nigaṇṭho nāṭaputto daṇḍāni paññapeti pāpassa kammassa kiriyāya pāpassa kammassa pavattiyā”ti?

“How many rods, Tapassī, does the Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta declare for the performance of an evil action and for the undertaking of an evil action?”

“Tīṇi kho, āvuso gotama, nigaṇṭho [T 2.0055] nāṭaputto daṇḍāni paññapeti pāpassa kammassa kiriyāya pāpassa kammassa pavattiyāti, seyyathidaṃ – kāyadaṇḍaṃ, vacīdaṇḍaṃ, manodaṇḍa”nti.

“Friend Gotama, the Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta declares three rods for the performance of an evil action and for the undertaking of an evil action, namely: the bodily rod, the verbal rod, and the mental rod.”

“Kiṃ pana, tapassi, aññadeva kāyadaṇḍaṃ, aññaṃ vacīdaṇḍaṃ, aññaṃ manodaṇḍa”nti?

“But, Tapassī, is the bodily rod one thing, the verbal rod another, and the mental rod another?”

“Aññadeva[V 2.0040], āvuso gotama, kāyadaṇḍaṃ, aññaṃ vacīdaṇḍaṃ, aññaṃ manodaṇḍa”nti.

“Indeed, friend Gotama, the bodily rod is one thing, the verbal rod is another, and the mental rod is another.”

“Imesaṃ pana, tapassi, tiṇṇaṃ daṇḍānaṃ evaṃ paṭivibhattānaṃ evaṃ paṭivisiṭṭhānaṃ katamaṃ daṇḍaṃ nigaṇṭho nāṭaputto mahāsāvajjataraṃ paññapeti pāpassa kammassa kiriyāya pāpassa kammassa pavattiyā[M 2.0036], yadi vā kāyadaṇḍaṃ, yadi vā vacīdaṇḍaṃ, yadi vā manodaṇḍa”nti?

“Among these three rods, Tapassī, thus distinguished and thus differentiated, which rod does the Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta declare to be more blameworthy for the performance of an evil action and for the undertaking of an evil action: the bodily rod, the verbal rod, or the mental rod?”

“Imesaṃ kho, āvuso gotama, tiṇṇaṃ daṇḍānaṃ evaṃ paṭivibhattānaṃ evaṃ paṭivisiṭṭhānaṃ kāyadaṇḍaṃ nigaṇṭho nāṭaputto mahāsāvajjataraṃ paññapeti pāpassa kammassa kiriyāya pāpassa kammassa pavattiyā, no tathā vacīdaṇḍaṃ, no tathā manodaṇḍa”nti.

“Among these three rods, friend Gotama, thus distinguished and thus differentiated, the Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta declares the bodily rod to be more blameworthy for the performance of an evil action and for the undertaking of an evil action; not so the verbal rod, not so the mental rod.”

“Kāyadaṇḍanti, tapassi, vadesi”?

“So you say it is the bodily rod, Tapassī?”

“Kāyadaṇḍanti, āvuso gotama, vadāmi”.

“I say it is the bodily rod, friend Gotama.”

“Kāyadaṇḍanti, tapassi, vadesi”?

“So you say it is the bodily rod, Tapassī?”

“Kāyadaṇḍanti, āvuso gotama, vadāmi”.

“I say it is the bodily rod, friend Gotama.”

“Kāyadaṇḍanti, tapassi, vadesi”?

“So you say it is the bodily rod, Tapassī?”

“Kāyadaṇḍanti, āvuso gotama, vadāmī”ti.

“I say it is the bodily rod, friend Gotama.”

Itiha bhagavā dīghatapassiṃ nigaṇṭhaṃ imasmiṃ kathāvatthusmiṃ yāvatatiyakaṃ patiṭṭhāpesi.

Thus the Blessed One made the Nigaṇṭha Dīgha Tapassī stand by his statement on this point of discussion for a third time.

57. Evaṃ [P 1.0373] vutte, dīghatapassī nigaṇṭho bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “tvaṃ panāvuso gotama, kati daṇḍāni paññapesi pāpassa kammassa kiriyāya [T 2.0056] pāpassa kammassa pavattiyā”ti?

57. When this was said, the Nigaṇṭha Dīgha Tapassī said this to the Blessed One: “But you, friend Gotama, how many rods do you declare for the performance of an evil action and for the undertaking of an evil action?”

“Na [V 2.0041] kho, tapassi, āciṇṇaṃ tathāgatassa ‘daṇḍaṃ, daṇḍa’nti paññapetuṃ; ‘kammaṃ, kamma’nti kho, tapassi, āciṇṇaṃ tathāgatassa paññapetu”nti?

“Tapassī, it is not the custom of the Tathāgata to declare it as ‘rod, rod.’ Rather, Tapassī, it is the custom of the Tathāgata to declare it as ‘action, action’.”

“Tvaṃ panāvuso gotama, kati kammāni paññapesi pāpassa kammassa kiriyāya pāpassa kammassa pavattiyā”ti?

“But you, friend Gotama, how many actions do you declare for the performance of an evil action and for the undertaking of an evil action?”

“Tīṇi kho ahaṃ, tapassi, kammāni paññapemi pāpassa kammassa kiriyāya pāpassa kammassa pavattiyā, seyyathidaṃ – kāyakammaṃ, vacīkammaṃ, manokamma”nti.

“I, Tapassī, declare three actions for the performance of an evil action and for the undertaking of an evil action, namely: bodily action, verbal action, and mental action.”

“Kiṃ panāvuso gotama, aññadeva kāyakammaṃ, aññaṃ vacīkammaṃ, aññaṃ manokamma”nti?

“But, friend Gotama, is bodily kamma one thing, verbal kamma another, and mental kamma yet another?”

“Aññadeva, tapassi, kāyakammaṃ, aññaṃ vacīkammaṃ, aññaṃ manokamma”nti.

“Indeed, Tapassī, bodily kamma is one thing, verbal kamma another, and mental kamma yet another.”

“Imesaṃ panāvuso gotama, tiṇṇaṃ kammānaṃ evaṃ paṭivibhattānaṃ evaṃ paṭivisiṭṭhānaṃ katamaṃ kammaṃ mahāsāvajjataraṃ paññapesi pāpassa kammassa kiriyāya pāpassa kammassa pavattiyā, yadi vā kāyakammaṃ, yadi vā vacīkammaṃ, yadi vā manokamma”nti?

“Now, friend Gotama, among these three kammas, thus distinguished and differentiated, which kamma do you declare to be the most blameworthy for the doing of evil kamma and the occurrence of evil kamma—whether bodily kamma, verbal kamma, or mental kamma?”

“Imesaṃ kho ahaṃ, tapassi, tiṇṇaṃ kammānaṃ evaṃ paṭivibhattānaṃ evaṃ paṭivisiṭṭhānaṃ manokammaṃ mahāsāvajjataraṃ paññapemi pāpassa kammassa kiriyāya pāpassa kammassa pavattiyā, no tathā kāyakammaṃ, no tathā vacīkamma”nti.

“Among these three kammas, Tapassī, thus distinguished and differentiated, I declare mental kamma to be the most blameworthy for the doing of evil kamma and the occurrence of evil kamma—not so bodily kamma, not so verbal kamma.”

“Manokammanti, āvuso gotama, vadesi”?

“Do you say mental kamma, friend Gotama?”

“Manokammanti, tapassi, vadāmi”.

“I say mental kamma, Tapassī.”

“Manokammanti, āvuso gotama, vadesi”?

“Do you say mental kamma, friend Gotama?”

“Manokammanti, tapassi, vadāmi”.

“I say mental kamma, Tapassī.”

“Manokammanti[V 2.0042], āvuso gotama, vadesi”?

“Do you say mental kamma, friend Gotama?”

“Manokammanti, tapassi, vadāmī”ti.

“I say mental kamma, Tapassī.”

Itiha dīghatapassī nigaṇṭho bhagavantaṃ imasmiṃ kathāvatthusmiṃ yāvatatiyakaṃ patiṭṭhāpetvā uṭṭhāyāsanā [T 2.0057] yena nigaṇṭho nāṭaputto tenupasaṅkami.

Thus, Dīghatapassī the Nigaṇṭha, having established the Blessed One in this topic of discussion up to the third time, rose from his seat and approached Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta.

58. Tena [M 2.0037] kho pana samayena nigaṇṭho nāṭaputto mahatiyā gihiparisāya saddhiṃ nisinno hoti bālakiniyā parisāya upālipamukhāya. Addasā kho nigaṇṭho nāṭaputto dīghatapassiṃ nigaṇṭhaṃ dūratova āgacchantaṃ; disvāna dīghatapassiṃ nigaṇṭhaṃ etadavoca – “handa, kuto nu tvaṃ, tapassi, āgacchasi divā divassā”ti? “Ito hi kho ahaṃ, bhante, āgacchāmi samaṇassa gotamassa santikā”ti. “Ahu pana te, tapassi, samaṇena gotamena saddhiṃ kocideva kathāsallāpo”ti[P 1.0374]? “Ahu kho me, bhante, samaṇena gotamena saddhiṃ kocideva kathāsallāpo”ti. “Yathā kathaṃ pana te, tapassi, ahu samaṇena gotamena saddhiṃ kocideva kathāsallāpo”ti? Atha kho dīghatapassī nigaṇṭho yāvatako ahosi bhagavatā saddhiṃ kathāsallāpo taṃ sabbaṃ nigaṇṭhassa nāṭaputtassa ārocesi. Evaṃ vutte, nigaṇṭho nāṭaputto dīghatapassiṃ nigaṇṭhaṃ etadavoca – “sādhu sādhu, tapassi! Yathā taṃ sutavatā sāvakena sammadeva satthusāsanaṃ ājānantena evameva dīghatapassinā nigaṇṭhena samaṇassa gotamassa byākataṃ. Kiñhi sobhati chavo manodaṇḍo imassa evaṃ oḷārikassa kāyadaṇḍassa upanidhāya! Atha kho kāyadaṇḍova mahāsāvajjataro pāpassa kammassa kiriyāya pāpassa kammassa pavattiyā, no tathā vacīdaṇḍo, no tathā manodaṇḍo”ti.

58. At that time, Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta was seated with a large assembly of householders, the assembly from Bālakinī headed by Upāli. Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta saw Dīghatapassī the Nigaṇṭha coming from afar. Upon seeing him, he said to Dīghatapassī the Nigaṇṭha: “Well then, from where do you come, Tapassī, in the middle of the day?” “I come, venerable sir, from the presence of the ascetic Gotama.” “Did you have any conversation at all, Tapassī, with the ascetic Gotama?” “I did, venerable sir, have some conversation with the ascetic Gotama.” “And what, Tapassī, was your conversation with the ascetic Gotama like?” Then Dīghatapassī the Nigaṇṭha recounted to Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta the entire conversation he had had with the Blessed One. When this was said, Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta said to Dīghatapassī the Nigaṇṭha: “Good, good, Tapassī! Just as a learned disciple, knowing the Teacher’s instruction well, should explain it, so too has Dīghatapassī the Nigaṇṭha explained it to the ascetic Gotama. For how can the wretched mental rod be of any account when compared to this gross bodily rod! Indeed, the bodily rod is far more blameworthy for the doing of evil kamma and the occurrence of evil kamma; not so the verbal rod, nor the mental rod.”

59. Evaṃ [T 2.0058] vutte, upāli gahapati nigaṇṭhaṃ nāṭaputtaṃ etadavoca – “sādhu sādhu, bhante dīghatapassī tapassī (sī. pī.)! Yathā taṃ sutavatā sāvakena sammadeva satthusāsanaṃ ājānantena evamevaṃ bhadantena tapassinā samaṇassa gotamassa byākataṃ. Kiñhi sobhati chavo manodaṇḍo imassa evaṃ oḷārikassa kāyadaṇḍassa upanidhāya! Atha kho kāyadaṇḍova mahāsāvajjataro pāpassa kammassa kiriyāya pāpassa kammassa pavattiyā, no tathā vacīdaṇḍo, no tathā manodaṇḍo. Handa [V 2.0043] cāhaṃ, bhante, gacchāmi samaṇassa gotamassa imasmiṃ kathāvatthusmiṃ vādaṃ āropessāmi. Sace me samaṇo gotamo tathā patiṭṭhahissati yathā bhadantena tapassinā patiṭṭhāpitaṃ; seyyathāpi nāma balavā puriso dīghalomikaṃ eḷakaṃ lomesu gahetvā ākaḍḍheyya parikaḍḍheyya samparikaḍḍheyya, evamevāhaṃ samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ vādena vādaṃ ākaḍḍhissāmi parikaḍḍhissāmi samparikaḍḍhissāmi[M 2.0038]. Seyyathāpi nāma balavā soṇḍikākammakāro mahantaṃ soṇḍikākilañjaṃ gambhīre udakarahade pakkhipitvā kaṇṇe gahetvā ākaḍḍheyya parikaḍḍheyya samparikaḍḍheyya, evamevāhaṃ samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ vādena vādaṃ ākaḍḍhissāmi parikaḍḍhissāmi samparikaḍḍhissāmi. Seyyathāpi nāma balavā soṇḍikādhutto vālaṃ thālaṃ (ka.) kaṇṇe gahetvā odhuneyya niddhuneyya nipphoṭeyya nicchādeyya (sī. pī. ka.), niccoṭeyya (ka.), nippoṭheyya (syā. kaṃ.), evamevāhaṃ samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ vādena vādaṃ odhunissāmi [P 1.0375] niddhunissāmi nipphoṭessāmi[T 2.0059]. Seyyathāpi nāma kuñjaro saṭṭhihāyano gambhīraṃ pokkharaṇiṃ ogāhetvā sāṇadhovikaṃ nāma kīḷitajātaṃ kīḷati, evamevāhaṃ samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ sāṇadhovikaṃ maññe kīḷitajātaṃ kīḷissāmi. Handa cāhaṃ, bhante, gacchāmi samaṇassa gotamassa imasmiṃ kathāvatthusmiṃ vādaṃ āropessāmī”ti. “Gaccha tvaṃ, gahapati, samaṇassa gotamassa imasmiṃ kathāvatthusmiṃ vādaṃ āropehi. Ahaṃ vā hi, gahapati, samaṇassa gotamassa vādaṃ āropeyyaṃ, dīghatapassī vā nigaṇṭho, tvaṃ vā”ti.

59. When this was said, the householder Upāli said to Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta: “Excellent, excellent, venerable sir! The venerable ascetic Dīghatapassī has explained it to the ascetic Gotama just as a learned disciple who rightly understands the Teacher’s instruction would. For how can the wretched mental rod be of any account when compared to this gross bodily rod! Indeed, the bodily rod is far more blameworthy for the doing of evil kamma and the occurrence of evil kamma; not so the verbal rod, nor the mental rod. Come now, venerable sir, I will go and refute the doctrine of the ascetic Gotama on this point. If the ascetic Gotama holds to the same position that the venerable ascetic has established, then just as a strong man might seize a long-fleeced goat by its fleece and drag it back and forth and all around, so too will I, with my argument, drag the ascetic Gotama back and forth and all around. Just as a strong brewer’s worker might plunge a large brewer’s mat into a deep pool of water and, taking it by the corner, drag it back and forth and all around, so too will I, with my argument, drag the ascetic Gotama back and forth and all around. Just as a strong drunkard might take a cup by the rim and shake it down, shake it up, and shake it out, so too will I, with my argument, shake the ascetic Gotama down, shake him up, and shake him out. Just as a sixty-year-old elephant might plunge into a deep lotus pond and play the game called ‘the hemp-washing game,’ so too, I think, will I play the ‘hemp-washing game’ with the ascetic Gotama.
