Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho abhayo rājakumāro bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “bhāseyya nu kho, bhante, tathāgato taṃ vācaṃ yā sā vācā paresaṃ appiyā amanāpā”ti? “Na khvettha, rājakumāra, ekaṃsenā”ti. “Ettha, bhante, anassuṃ nigaṇṭhā”ti. “Kiṃ pana tvaṃ, rājakumāra, evaṃ vadesi – ‘ettha[P 1.0394], bhante, anassuṃ nigaṇṭhā’”ti? “Idhāhaṃ, bhante, yena nigaṇṭho nāṭaputto tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā nigaṇṭhaṃ nāṭaputtaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃ. Ekamantaṃ nisinnaṃ kho maṃ, bhante, nigaṇṭho nāṭaputto etadavoca – ‘ehi tvaṃ, rājakumāra, samaṇassa gotamassa vādaṃ āropehi. Evaṃ te kalyāṇo kittisaddo abbhuggacchissati – abhayena rājakumārena samaṇassa gotamassa evaṃ mahiddhikassa evaṃ mahānubhāvassa vādo āropito’ti. Evaṃ vutte, ahaṃ, bhante, nigaṇṭhaṃ nāṭaputtaṃ etadavocaṃ – ‘yathā kathaṃ panāhaṃ[T 2.0090], bhante, samaṇassa gotamassa evaṃ mahiddhikassa evaṃ mahānubhāvassa vādaṃ āropessāmī’ti? ‘Ehi tvaṃ, rājakumāra, yena samaṇo gotamo tenupasaṅkama; upasaṅkamitvā samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ evaṃ vadehi – bhāseyya nu kho, bhante, tathāgato taṃ vācaṃ yā sā vācā paresaṃ appiyā amanāpāti? Sace te samaṇo gotamo evaṃ puṭṭho evaṃ byākaroti – bhāseyya, rājakumāra, tathāgato taṃ vācaṃ yā sā vācā paresaṃ appiyā amanāpāti, tamenaṃ tvaṃ evaṃ vadeyyāsi – atha kiñcarahi te, bhante, puthujjanena nānākaraṇaṃ? Puthujjanopi hi taṃ vācaṃ bhāseyya [M 2.0057] yā sā vācā paresaṃ appiyā amanāpāti. Sace pana te samaṇo gotamo evaṃ puṭṭho evaṃ byākaroti – na, rājakumāra, tathāgato taṃ vācaṃ bhāseyya yā sā [V 2.0064] vācā paresaṃ appiyā amanāpāti, tamenaṃ tvaṃ evaṃ vadeyyāsi – atha kiñcarahi te, bhante, devadatto byākato – āpāyiko devadatto, nerayiko devadatto, kappaṭṭho devadatto, atekiccho devadattoti? Tāya ca pana te vācāya devadatto kupito ahosi anattamanoti. Imaṃ kho te, rājakumāra, samaṇo gotamo ubhatokoṭikaṃ pañhaṃ puṭṭho samāno [T 2.0091] neva sakkhiti uggilituṃ na sakkhiti ogilituṃ. Seyyathāpi nāma purisassa ayosiṅghāṭakaṃ kaṇṭhe vilaggaṃ, so neva sakkuṇeyya uggilituṃ na sakkuṇeyya ogilituṃ; evameva kho te, rājakumāra, samaṇo gotamo imaṃ ubhatokoṭikaṃ pañhaṃ puṭṭho samāno neva sakkhiti uggilituṃ na sakkhiti ogilitu’”nti.

85. Prince Abhaya, who was sitting to one side, said to the Blessed One: 'Venerable sir, would the Tathāgata speak words that are disagreeable and unpleasant to others?' 'Prince, in this matter, there is no categorical answer.' 'On this point, venerable sir, the Nigaṇṭhas are lost.' 'But why, Prince, do you say: “On this point, venerable sir, the Nigaṇṭhas are lost”?' 'Once, venerable sir, I approached the Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta; having approached, I paid homage to him and sat down to one side. Venerable sir, as I was sitting to one side, the Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta said this to me: “Come, Prince, bring an accusation against the ascetic Gotama. In this way, a good report of your fame will spread: ‘An accusation has been brought by Prince Abhaya against the ascetic Gotama, so mighty and so powerful!’” When this was said, venerable sir, I replied to the Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta: “But how, venerable sir, can I bring an accusation against the ascetic Gotama, so mighty and so powerful?” “Come, Prince, approach the ascetic Gotama and say this to him: ‘Venerable sir, would the Tathāgata speak words that are disagreeable and unpleasant to others?’ If the ascetic Gotama, when asked this by you, answers: ‘Prince, the Tathāgata would speak such words,’ then you should say to him: ‘Then, venerable sir, what is the difference between you and an ordinary person? For an ordinary person also speaks words that are disagreeable and unpleasant to others.’ But if the ascetic Gotama, when asked this by you, answers: ‘No, Prince, the Tathāgata would not speak words that are disagreeable and unpleasant to others,’ then you should say to him: ‘Then why, venerable sir, was Devadatta declared by you: “Devadatta is bound for the states of deprivation, Devadatta is destined for hell, Devadatta will remain there for an aeon, Devadatta is incorrigible”? And by those words of yours, Devadatta was angered and displeased.’ Prince, the ascetic Gotama, when asked this two-edged question by you, will be able neither to spit it out nor to swallow it. Just as if an iron hook were stuck in a man’s throat, and he would be able neither to spit it out nor to swallow it; even so, Prince, the ascetic Gotama, when asked this two-edged question by you, will be able neither to spit it out nor to swallow it.”'

86. Tena kho pana samayena daharo kumāro mando uttānaseyyako abhayassa rājakumārassa aṅke nisinno hoti. Atha kho bhagavā abhayaṃ rājakumāraṃ etadavoca – “taṃ kiṃ [P 1.0395] maññasi, rājakumāra, sacāyaṃ kumāro tuyhaṃ vā pamādamanvāya dhātiyā vā pamādamanvāya kaṭṭhaṃ vā kaṭhalaṃ kathalaṃ (ka.) vā mukhe āhareyya, kinti naṃ kareyyāsī”ti? “Āhareyyassāhaṃ, bhante. Sace, bhante, na sakkuṇeyyaṃ ādikeneva āhattuṃ āharituṃ (syā. kaṃ.), vāmena hatthena sīsaṃ pariggahetvā paggahetvā (sī.) dakkhiṇena hatthena vaṅkaṅguliṃ karitvā salohitampi āhareyyaṃ. Taṃ kissa hetu? Atthi me, bhante, kumāre anukampā”ti. “Evameva kho, rājakumāra, yaṃ tathāgato vācaṃ jānāti abhūtaṃ atacchaṃ anatthasaṃhitaṃ sā ca paresaṃ appiyā amanāpā, na taṃ tathāgato vācaṃ bhāsati. Yampi tathāgato vācaṃ jānāti bhūtaṃ tacchaṃ anatthasaṃhitaṃ sā ca paresaṃ appiyā amanāpā, tampi tathāgato vācaṃ na bhāsati. Yañca kho tathāgato vācaṃ jānāti bhūtaṃ tacchaṃ atthasaṃhitaṃ sā ca paresaṃ appiyā amanāpā, tatra kālaññū tathāgato hoti tassā vācāya veyyākaraṇāya. Yaṃ tathāgato vācaṃ jānāti abhūtaṃ atacchaṃ [M 2.0058] anatthasaṃhitaṃ sā ca paresaṃ piyā manāpā, na taṃ tathāgato vācaṃ bhāsati. Yampi tathāgato vācaṃ jānāti bhūtaṃ tacchaṃ anatthasaṃhitaṃ sā ca paresaṃ piyā manāpā tampi tathāgato vācaṃ na bhāsati. Yañca tathāgato vācaṃ jānāti bhūtaṃ tacchaṃ atthasaṃhitaṃ sā [T 2.0092] ca paresaṃ piyā manāpā, tatra kālaññū tathāgato hoti tassā vācāya veyyākaraṇāya. Taṃ kissa hetu? Atthi, rājakumāra, tathāgatassa sattesu anukampā”ti.

86. Now at that time a young, simple, infant boy, lying on his back, was seated on Prince Abhaya's lap. Then the Blessed One said to Prince Abhaya: "What do you think, Prince? If this boy, through your carelessness or the nurse's carelessness, were to put a stick or a potsherd in his mouth, what would you do to him?" "I would remove it, venerable sir. If, venerable sir, I could not remove it at the very first attempt, I would hold his head with my left hand and, making my right finger crooked, I would remove it even if it meant drawing blood. Why is that? Because I have compassion for the boy, venerable sir." "Just so, Prince, the Tathāgata knows speech that is untrue, incorrect, and unbeneficial, and that is disagreeable and unpleasant to others—such speech the Tathāgata does not utter. The Tathāgata also knows speech that is true, correct, but unbeneficial, and that is disagreeable and unpleasant to others—such speech the Tathāgata does not utter. But the Tathāgata knows speech that is true, correct, and beneficial, though it is disagreeable and unpleasant to others—in that case, the Tathāgata is one who knows the right time for speaking such words. The Tathāgata knows speech that is untrue, incorrect, and unbeneficial, but that is agreeable and pleasant to others—such speech the Tathāgata does not utter. The Tathāgata also knows speech that is true, correct, but unbeneficial, and that is agreeable and pleasant to others—such speech the Tathāgata does not utter. But the Tathāgata knows speech that is true, correct, and beneficial, and that is agreeable and pleasant to others—in that case, the Tathāgata is one who knows the right time for speaking such words. Why is that? Because, Prince, the Tathāgata has compassion for beings."

87. “Yeme, bhante, khattiyapaṇḍitāpi brāhmaṇapaṇḍitāpi gahapatipaṇḍitāpi samaṇapaṇḍitāpi pañhaṃ abhisaṅkharitvā tathāgataṃ upasaṅkamitvā pucchanti, pubbeva nu kho, etaṃ, bhante[V 2.0065], bhagavato cetaso parivitakkitaṃ hoti ‘ye maṃ upasaṅkamitvā evaṃ pucchissanti tesāhaṃ evaṃ puṭṭho evaṃ byākarissāmī’ti, udāhu ṭhānasovetaṃ tathāgataṃ paṭibhātī”ti?

87. “Venerable sir, when those wise khattiyas, wise brahmins, wise householders, and wise ascetics formulate a question and approach the Tathāgata to ask it, has this, venerable sir, already been considered in the Blessed One's mind: ‘When they approach me and ask thus, I, being asked thus, will answer them thus’? Or does it occur to the Tathāgata on the spot?”

“Tena hi, rājakumāra, taññevettha paṭipucchissāmi, yathā te khameyya tathā naṃ byākareyyāsi. Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, rājakumāra, kusalo tvaṃ rathassa aṅgapaccaṅgāna”nti?

“In that case, Prince, I will ask you a counter-question on this very point. Answer as you see fit. What do you think, Prince, are you skilled in the various parts of a chariot?”

“Evaṃ, bhante, kusalo ahaṃ rathassa aṅgapaccaṅgāna”nti.

“Yes, venerable sir, I am skilled in the various parts of a chariot.”

“Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, rājakumāra, ye taṃ upasaṅkamitvā evaṃ puccheyyuṃ – ‘kiṃ nāmidaṃ rathassa aṅgapaccaṅga’nti? Pubbeva nu kho te etaṃ cetaso parivitakkitaṃ [P 1.0396] assa ‘ye maṃ upasaṅkamitvā evaṃ pucchissanti tesāhaṃ evaṃ puṭṭho evaṃ byākarissāmī’ti, udāhu ṭhānasovetaṃ paṭibhāseyyā”ti?

“What do you think, Prince? If those who approached you were to ask, ‘What is the name of this part of the chariot?’ would you have previously thought in your mind: ‘When they approach me and ask thus, I, being asked thus, will answer them thus,’ or would it occur to you on the spot?”

“Ahañhi, bhante, rathiko saññāto kusalo rathassa aṅgapaccaṅgānaṃ. Sabbāni me rathassa aṅgapaccaṅgāni suviditāni. Ṭhānasovetaṃ maṃ paṭibhāseyyā”ti[T 2.0093].

“Venerable sir, I am a renowned charioteer, skilled in the various parts of a chariot. All the various parts of a chariot are well-known to me. It would occur to me on the spot.”

“Evameva kho, rājakumāra, ye te khattiyapaṇḍitāpi brāhmaṇapaṇḍitāpi gahapatipaṇḍitāpi samaṇapaṇḍitāpi pañhaṃ abhisaṅkharitvā tathāgataṃ upasaṅkamitvā pucchanti, ṭhānasovetaṃ tathāgataṃ paṭibhāti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Sā hi, rājakumāra, tathāgatassa dhammadhātu suppaṭividdhā yassā dhammadhātuyā suppaṭividdhattā ṭhānasovetaṃ tathāgataṃ paṭibhātī”ti.

“In the same way, Prince, when those wise khattiyas, wise brahmins, wise householders, or wise ascetics formulate a question and approach the Tathāgata to ask, it occurs to the Tathāgata on the spot. Why is that? Because, Prince, that Dhamma-element has been thoroughly penetrated by the Tathāgata. Because that Dhamma-element has been thoroughly penetrated, it occurs to the Tathāgata on the spot.”

Evaṃ vutte, abhayo rājakumāro bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “abhikkantaṃ, bhante, abhikkantaṃ, bhante…pe… ajjatagge pāṇupetaṃ saraṇaṃ gata”nti.

When this was said, Prince Abhaya said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir! ... From this day forth, may the Blessed One remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

Abhayarājakumārasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ.

The Discourse to Prince Abhaya, the eighth, is concluded.

9. Bahuvedanīyasuttaṃ

9. The Discourse on Many Kinds of Feeling

88. Evaṃ [T 2.0094][M 2.0059][V 2.0066] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme. Atha kho pañcakaṅgo thapati yenāyasmā udāyī tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmantaṃ udāyiṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho pañcakaṅgo thapati āyasmantaṃ udāyiṃ etadavoca – “kati nu kho, bhante udāyi, vedanā vuttā bhagavatā”ti? “Tisso kho, thapati gahapati (syā. kaṃ. pī.), vedanā vuttā bhagavatā. Sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā – imā [P 1.0397] kho, thapati, tisso vedanā vuttā bhagavatā”ti. Evaṃ vutte, pañcakaṅgo thapati āyasmantaṃ udāyiṃ etadavoca – “na kho, bhante udāyi, tisso vedanā vuttā bhagavatā; dve vedanā vuttā bhagavatā – sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā. Yāyaṃ, bhante, adukkhamasukhā vedanā santasmiṃ esā paṇīte sukhe vuttā bhagavatā”ti. Dutiyampi kho āyasmā udāyī pañcakaṅgaṃ thapatiṃ etadavoca – “na kho, gahapati, dve vedanā vuttā bhagavatā; tisso vedanā vuttā bhagavatā. Sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā – imā kho, thapati, tisso vedanā vuttā bhagavatā”ti. Dutiyampi kho pañcakaṅgo thapati āyasmantaṃ udāyiṃ etadavoca – “na kho, bhante udāyi, tisso vedanā vuttā bhagavatā; dve vedanā vuttā bhagavatā – sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā. Yāyaṃ, bhante[T 2.0095], adukkhamasukhā vedanā santasmiṃ esā paṇīte sukhe vuttā bhagavatā”ti. Tatiyampi kho āyasmā udāyī pañcakaṅgaṃ thapatiṃ etadavoca – “na kho, thapati, dve vedanā vuttā bhagavatā; tisso vedanā vuttā bhagavatā. Sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā – imā kho, thapati, tisso vedanā vuttā bhagavatā”ti. Tatiyampi kho pañcakaṅgo thapati āyasmantaṃ udāyiṃ etadavoca – “na kho, bhante udāyi, tisso vedanā vuttā bhagavatā, dve vedanā vuttā bhagavatā – sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā. Yāyaṃ, bhante, adukkhamasukhā vedanā santasmiṃ esā paṇīte sukhe vuttā bhagavatā”ti. Neva kho sakkhi āyasmā udāyī pañcakaṅgaṃ thapatiṃ saññāpetuṃ na panāsakkhi pañcakaṅgo thapati āyasmantaṃ udāyiṃ saññāpetuṃ.

88. Thus have I heard. At one time, the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī, in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Then Pañcakaṅga the carpenter approached the Venerable Udāyī; having approached, he paid homage to the Venerable Udāyī and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Pañcakaṅga the carpenter said to the Venerable Udāyī: “Venerable Udāyī, how many feelings have been declared by the Blessed One?” “Indeed, carpenter, three feelings have been declared by the Blessed One: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. These, carpenter, are the three feelings declared by the Blessed One.” When this was said, Pañcakaṅga the carpenter said to the Venerable Udāyī: “Venerable Udāyī, not three feelings have been declared by the Blessed One; two feelings have been declared by the Blessed One—pleasant feeling and painful feeling. That neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, venerable sir, has been declared by the Blessed One as included in peaceful, sublime pleasure.” For a second time, the Venerable Udāyī said to Pañcakaṅga the carpenter: “No, householder, two feelings have not been declared by the Blessed One; three feelings have been declared by the Blessed One: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. These, carpenter, are the three feelings declared by the Blessed One.” For a second time, Pañcakaṅga the carpenter said to the Venerable Udāyī: “Venerable Udāyī, not three feelings have been declared by the Blessed One; two feelings have been declared by the Blessed One—pleasant feeling and painful feeling. That neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, venerable sir, has been declared by the Blessed One as included in peaceful, sublime pleasure.” For a third time, the Venerable Udāyī said to Pañcakaṅga the carpenter: “No, carpenter, two feelings have not been declared by the Blessed One; three feelings have been declared by the Blessed One: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. These, carpenter, are the three feelings declared by the Blessed One.” For a third time, Pañcakaṅga the carpenter said to the Venerable Udāyī: “Venerable Udāyī, not three feelings have been declared by the Blessed One; two feelings have been declared by the Blessed One—pleasant feeling and painful feeling. That neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, venerable sir, has been declared by the Blessed One as included in peaceful, sublime pleasure.” The Venerable Udāyī was not able to convince Pañcakaṅga the carpenter, nor was Pañcakaṅga the carpenter able to convince the Venerable Udāyī.

89. Assosi [V 2.0067] kho āyasmā ānando āyasmato udāyissa pañcakaṅgena thapatinā saddhiṃ imaṃ kathāsallāpaṃ. Atha kho āyasmā ānando [M 2.0060] yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho āyasmā ānando yāvatako ahosi āyasmato udāyissa pañcakaṅgena thapatinā saddhiṃ kathāsallāpo taṃ sabbaṃ bhagavato ārocesi. Evaṃ vutte, bhagavā āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ etadavoca – “santaññeva kho, ānanda, pariyāyaṃ pañcakaṅgo thapati udāyissa nābbhanumodi, santaññeva [T 2.0096] ca pana pariyāyaṃ udāyī pañcakaṅgassa thapatissa nābbhanumodi. Dvepānanda, vedanā vuttā mayā pariyāyena[P 1.0398], tissopi vedanā vuttā mayā pariyāyena, pañcapi vedanā vuttā mayā pariyāyena, chapi vedanā vuttā mayā pariyāyena, aṭṭhārasapi vedanā vuttā mayā pariyāyena, chattiṃsapi vedanā vuttā mayā pariyāyena, aṭṭhasatampi vedanā vuttā mayā pariyāyena. Evaṃ pariyāyadesito kho, ānanda, mayā dhammo. Evaṃ pariyāyadesite kho, ānanda, mayā dhamme ye aññamaññassa subhāsitaṃ sulapitaṃ na samanujānissanti na samanumaññissanti na samanumodissanti tesametaṃ pāṭikaṅkhaṃ – bhaṇḍanajātā kalahajātā vivādāpannā aññamaññaṃ mukhasattīhi vitudantā viharissanti. Evaṃ pariyāyadesito kho, ānanda, mayā dhammo. Evaṃ pariyāyadesite kho, ānanda, mayā dhamme ye aññamaññassa subhāsitaṃ sulapitaṃ samanujānissanti samanumaññissanti samanumodissanti tesametaṃ pāṭikaṅkhaṃ – samaggā sammodamānā avivadamānā khīrodakībhūtā aññamaññaṃ piyacakkhūhi sampassantā viharissanti”.

89. The Venerable Ānanda heard this conversation between the Venerable Udāyī and Pañcakaṅga the carpenter. Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the Venerable Ānanda reported to the Blessed One the entire conversation that had taken place between the Venerable Udāyī and Pañcakaṅga the carpenter. When this was said, the Blessed One said to the Venerable Ānanda: “Indeed, Ānanda, from one valid perspective, Pañcakaṅga the carpenter did not approve of what Udāyī said, and from another valid perspective, Udāyī did not approve of what Pañcakaṅga the carpenter said. Ānanda, by way of exposition, I have declared two feelings; by way of exposition, I have declared three feelings; by way of exposition, I have declared five feelings; by way of exposition, I have declared six feelings; by way of exposition, I have declared eighteen feelings; by way of exposition, I have declared thirty-six feelings; and by way of exposition, I have declared one hundred and eight feelings. Thus, Ānanda, the Dhamma has been taught by me with exposition. When the Dhamma has been taught by me with such exposition, for those who will not understand, acknowledge, or approve of what is well-spoken and well-said by one another—this can be expected of them: they will live having given rise to quarrels, given rise to disputes, and fallen into contention, piercing each other with verbal spears. Thus, Ānanda, the Dhamma has been taught by me with exposition. When the Dhamma has been taught by me with such exposition, for those who will understand, acknowledge, and approve of what is well-spoken and well-said by one another—this can be expected of them: they will live in concord, rejoicing together, without contention, having become like milk and water mixed, regarding one another with loving eyes.”

90. “Pañca kho ime, ānanda, kāmaguṇā. Katame pañca? Cakkhuviññeyyā rūpā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā rajanīyā, sotaviññeyyā saddā…pe… ghānaviññeyyā gandhā…pe… jivhāviññeyyā rasā…pe… kāyaviññeyyā phoṭṭhabbā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā [T 2.0097] piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā rajanīyā – ime kho, ānanda, pañca kāmaguṇā. Yaṃ kho, ānanda, ime pañca kāmaguṇe paṭicca uppajjati sukhaṃ somanassaṃ idaṃ vuccati kāmasukhaṃ.

90. “Ānanda, there are these five strands of sensual pleasure. Which five? Forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, pleasing, agreeable, of a lovely form, connected with sensual desire, and enticing; sounds cognizable by the ear... smells cognizable by the nose... tastes cognizable by the tongue... tactile objects cognizable by the body that are desirable, pleasing, agreeable, of a lovely form, connected with sensual desire, and enticing—these, Ānanda, are the five strands of sensual pleasure. Ānanda, whatever pleasure and mental joy arises in dependence on these five strands of sensual pleasure, this is called sensual pleasure.”

“Yo kho, ānanda, evaṃ vadeyya – ‘etaparamaṃ sattā sukhaṃ somanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedentī’ti, idamassa nānujānāmi. Taṃ kissa hetu? Atthānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṃ [V 2.0068] sukhaṃ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca. Katamañcānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṃ sukhaṃ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca? Idhānanda, bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati[M 2.0061]. Idaṃ kho, ānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṃ sukhaṃ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca.

“Ānanda, if anyone were to say, ‘This is the ultimate happiness and joy that beings experience,’ I do not approve of that. For what reason? Because, Ānanda, there is another happiness more excellent and more sublime than this happiness. And what, Ānanda, is that other happiness more excellent and more sublime than this happiness? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. This, Ānanda, is that other happiness more excellent and more sublime than this happiness.”

“Yo kho, ānanda, evaṃ vadeyya – ‘etaparamaṃ sattā sukhaṃ somanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedentī’ti, idamassa nānujānāmi. Taṃ [P 1.0399] kissa hetu? Atthānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṃ sukhaṃ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca. Katamañcānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṃ sukhaṃ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca? Idhānanda, bhikkhu vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā…pe… dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Idaṃ kho, ānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṃ sukhaṃ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca.

“Ānanda, if anyone were to say, ‘This is the ultimate happiness and joy that beings experience,’ I do not approve of that. For what reason? Because, Ānanda, there is another happiness more excellent and more sublime than this happiness. And what, Ānanda, is that other happiness more excellent and more sublime than this happiness? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, with the stilling of applied thought and sustained thought… enters and dwells in the second jhāna. This, Ānanda, is that other happiness more excellent and more sublime than this happiness.”

“Yo kho, ānanda, evaṃ vadeyya…pe…. Katamañcānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṃ sukhaṃ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca? Idhānanda, bhikkhu pītiyā ca virāgā…pe… tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Idaṃ kho, ānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṃ sukhaṃ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca.

“Ānanda, if anyone were to say… and what, Ānanda, is that other happiness more excellent and more sublime than this happiness? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, with the fading away of rapture… enters and dwells in the third jhāna. This, Ānanda, is that other happiness more excellent and more sublime than this happiness.”

“Yo kho, ānanda, evaṃ vadeyya…pe…. Katamañcānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṃ sukhaṃ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca? Idhānanda, bhikkhu sukhassa ca pahānā…pe… catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Idaṃ kho, ānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṃ sukhaṃ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca.

“Ānanda, if anyone were to say… and what, Ānanda, is that other happiness more excellent and more sublime than this happiness? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, with the abandoning of pleasure… enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna. This, Ānanda, is that other happiness more excellent and more sublime than this happiness.”

“Yo kho, ānanda, evaṃ vadeyya…pe…. Katamañcānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṃ sukhaṃ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca[T 2.0098]? Idhānanda, bhikkhu sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ samatikkamā, paṭighasaññānaṃ [V 2.0069] atthaṅgamā, nānattasaññānaṃ amanasikārā ‘ananto ākāso’ti ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati. Idaṃ kho, ānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṃ sukhaṃ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca.

“Ānanda, if anyone were to say… and what, Ānanda, is that other happiness more excellent and more sublime than this happiness? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, with the complete transcending of perceptions of form, with the passing away of perceptions of resistance, not attending to perceptions of diversity, thinking ‘space is infinite,’ enters and dwells in the base of infinite space. This, Ānanda, is that other happiness more excellent and more sublime than this happiness.”

“Yo kho, ānanda, evaṃ vadeyya…pe…. Katamañcānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṃ sukhaṃ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca? Idhānanda, bhikkhu sabbaso ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma ‘anantaṃ viññāṇa’nti viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati. Idaṃ kho, ānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṃ sukhaṃ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca.

“Ānanda, if anyone were to say… and what, Ānanda, is that other happiness more excellent and more sublime than this happiness? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, with the complete transcending of the base of infinite space, thinking, ‘consciousness is infinite,’ enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness. This, Ānanda, is that other happiness more excellent and more sublime than this happiness.”

“Yo kho, ānanda, evaṃ vadeyya…pe…. Katamañcānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṃ sukhaṃ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca? Idhānanda, bhikkhu sabbaso viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma ‘natthi kiñcī’ti ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati. Idaṃ kho, ānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṃ sukhaṃ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca.

“Ānanda, if anyone were to say… and what, Ānanda, is that other happiness more excellent and more sublime than this happiness? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, with the complete transcending of the base of infinite consciousness, thinking, ‘There is nothing,’ enters and dwells in the base of nothingness. This, Ānanda, is that other happiness more excellent and more sublime than this happiness.”

“Yo [M 2.0062][P 1.0400] kho, ānanda, evaṃ vadeyya…pe…. Katamañcānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṃ sukhaṃ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca? Idhānanda, bhikkhu sabbaso ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ samatikkamma nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati. Idaṃ kho, ānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṃ sukhaṃ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca.

“Ānanda, if anyone were to say… and what, Ānanda, is that other happiness more excellent and more sublime than this happiness? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, having completely transcended the base of nothingness, enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. This, Ānanda, is that other happiness more excellent and more sublime than this happiness.”

“Yo kho, ānanda, evaṃ vadeyya – ‘etaparamaṃ sattā sukhaṃ somanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedentī’ti, idamassa nānujānāmi. Taṃ kissa hetu? Atthānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṃ sukhaṃ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca. Katamañcānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṃ sukhaṃ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca? Idhānanda, bhikkhu sabbaso nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ [T 2.0099] samatikkamma saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ upasampajja viharati. Idaṃ kho, ānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṃ sukhaṃ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca.

“Ānanda, if anyone were to say, ‘This is the ultimate happiness and joy that beings experience,’ I do not approve of that. For what reason? Because, Ānanda, there is another happiness more excellent and more sublime than this happiness. And what, Ānanda, is that other happiness more excellent and more sublime than this happiness? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, having entirely transcended the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling. This, Ānanda, is that other happiness more excellent and more sublime than this happiness.”

91. “Ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ, ānanda, vijjati yaṃ aññatitthiyā paribbājakā evaṃ vadeyyuṃ [V 2.0070] – ‘saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ samaṇo gotamo āha; tañca sukhasmiṃ paññapeti. Tayidaṃ kiṃsu, tayidaṃ kathaṃsū’ti? Evaṃvādino, ānanda, aññatitthiyā paribbājakā evamassu vacanīyā – ‘na kho, āvuso, bhagavā sukhaṃyeva vedanaṃ sandhāya sukhasmiṃ paññapeti; api ca, āvuso, yattha yattha sukhaṃ upalabbhati yahiṃ yahiṃ taṃ taṃ tathāgato sukhasmiṃ paññapetī’”ti.

91. “It is possible, Ānanda, that wanderers of other sects might say this: ‘The ascetic Gotama speaks of the cessation of perception and feeling, and he designates it as happiness. What is this, and how is this?’ When wanderers of other sects speak thus, Ānanda, they should be told this: ‘Friends, the Blessed One does not designate as happiness only pleasant feeling; but rather, friends, wherever and in whatever way happiness is found, the Tathāgata designates that as happiness.’”

Idamavoca bhagavā. Attamano āyasmā ānando bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandīti.

The Blessed One said this. The Venerable Ānanda, gratified, rejoiced in the Blessed One's words.

Bahuvedanīyasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ navamaṃ.

The Discourse on Many Kinds of Feeling, the ninth, is concluded.

10. Apaṇṇakasuttaṃ

10. The Apaṇṇaka Sutta

92. Evaṃ [T 2.0100][V 2.0071] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā kosalesu cārikaṃ caramāno mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ yena sālā nāma kosalānaṃ brāhmaṇagāmo tadavasari. Assosuṃ kho sāleyyakā brāhmaṇagahapatikā – “samaṇo khalu bho gotamo sakyaputto sakyakulā pabbajito kosalesu cārikaṃ caramāno mahatā [P 1.0401] bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ sālaṃ [M 2.0063] anuppatto. Taṃ kho pana bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ evaṃ kalyāṇo kittisaddo abbhuggato – ‘itipi so bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho vijjācaraṇasampanno sugato lokavidū anuttaro purisadammasārathi satthā devamanussānaṃ buddho bhagavā’ti. So imaṃ lokaṃ sadevakaṃ samārakaṃ sabrahmakaṃ sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiṃ pajaṃ sadevamanussaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā pavedeti. So dhammaṃ deseti ādikalyāṇaṃ majjhekalyāṇaṃ pariyosānakalyāṇaṃ sātthaṃ sabyañjanaṃ, kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ parisuddhaṃ brahmacariyaṃ pakāseti. Sādhu kho pana tathārūpānaṃ arahataṃ dassanaṃ hotī”ti. Atha kho sāleyyakā brāhmaṇagahapatikā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā appekacce bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Appekacce bhagavatā saddhiṃ sammodiṃsu; sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Appekacce yena bhagavā tenañjaliṃ paṇāmetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Appekacce [T 2.0101] bhagavato santike nāmagottaṃ sāvetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Appekacce tuṇhībhūtā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu.

92. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was wandering on tour among the Kosalans with a great community of monks, and he arrived at Sālā, a Kosalan brahmin village. The brahmin householders of Sālā heard: “The ascetic Gotama, the son of the Sakyans, who went forth from the Sakyan clan, has arrived at Sālā while wandering on tour among the Kosalans with a great community of monks. Now a good report of that Master Gotama has spread thus: ‘That Blessed One is an Arahant, a perfectly enlightened one, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, the Well-farer, knower of the world, unsurpassed trainer of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One.’ He has realized with his own direct knowledge and makes known this world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans. He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with its meaning and phrasing, and he reveals a holy life that is utterly complete and pure. It is good indeed to see such Arahants.” Then the brahmin householders of Sālā approached the Blessed One. Having approached, some paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Some exchanged greetings with the Blessed One and, when the courteous and memorable talk was concluded, sat down to one side. Some raised their hands in reverential salutation toward the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Some announced their name and clan in the presence of the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Some remained silent and sat down to one side.

93. Ekamantaṃ nisinne kho sāleyyake brāhmaṇagahapatike bhagavā etadavoca – “atthi pana vo, gahapatayo, koci manāpo satthā yasmiṃ vo ākāravatī saddhā paṭiladdhā”ti? “Natthi kho no, bhante, koci manāpo satthā yasmiṃ no ākāravatī saddhā paṭiladdhā”ti. “Manāpaṃ vo, gahapatayo, satthāraṃ alabhantehi ayaṃ apaṇṇako dhammo samādāya vattitabbo. Apaṇṇako hi, gahapatayo, dhammo samatto samādinno, so vo bhavissati dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāya. Katamo ca, gahapatayo, apaṇṇako dhammo”?

93. When the brahmin householders of Sālā were seated to one side, the Blessed One said this to them: “Householders, is there for you any agreeable teacher in whom you have acquired faith that is based on reason?” “No, venerable sir, there is no agreeable teacher for us in whom we have acquired faith that is based on reason.” “Householders, since you have not found an agreeable teacher, this infallible teaching should be undertaken and practiced. For, householders, an infallible teaching, when completely undertaken, will be for your long-term welfare and happiness. And what, householders, is the infallible teaching?”

94. “Santi[V 2.0072], gahapatayo, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘natthi dinnaṃ, natthi yiṭṭhaṃ, natthi hutaṃ; natthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ sukaṭadukkaṭānaṃ (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko, natthi ayaṃ loko, natthi paro loko; natthi mātā, natthi pitā; natthi sattā opapātikā; natthi loke samaṇabrāhmaṇā sammaggatā samaggatā (ka.) sammā paṭipannā ye imañca lokaṃ parañca lokaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā pavedentī’ti. Tesaṃyeva kho, gahapatayo, samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ [M 2.0064] eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā [P 1.0402] ujuvipaccanīkavādā. Te evamāhaṃsu – ‘atthi dinnaṃ, atthi yiṭṭhaṃ, atthi hutaṃ; atthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko; atthi ayaṃ loko, atthi paro loko; atthi mātā, atthi pitā; atthi sattā [T 2.0102] opapātikā; atthi loke samaṇabrāhmaṇā sammaggatā sammā paṭipannā ye imañca lokaṃ parañca lokaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā pavedentī’ti. Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, gahapatayo – ‘nanume samaṇabrāhmaṇā aññamaññassa ujuvipaccanīkavādā’”ti? “Evaṃ, bhante”.

94. “Householders, there are some ascetics and brahmins who are of such a doctrine and view: ‘There is no fruit of giving, no fruit of great sacrifice, no fruit of offerings; there is no fruit or result of good and bad actions; there is no this world, no other world; there is no mother, no father; there are no spontaneously arisen beings; there are in the world no ascetics and brahmins who are well-gone, well-practiced, and who, having realized this world and the other world for themselves with direct knowledge, make them known.’ But, householders, there are other ascetics and brahmins whose doctrines are directly contrary to those. They say: ‘There is fruit of giving, there is fruit of great sacrifice, there is fruit of offerings; there is fruit and result of good and bad actions; there is this world, there is the other world; there is mother, there is father; there are spontaneously arisen beings; there are in the world ascetics and brahmins who are well-gone, well-practiced, and who, having realized this world and the other world for themselves with direct knowledge, make them known.’ What do you think, householders? Are not these ascetics and brahmins directly opposed to one another in their views?” “So it is, venerable sir.”

95. “Tatra, gahapatayo, ye te samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘natthi dinnaṃ, natthi yiṭṭhaṃ…pe… ye imañca lokaṃ parañca lokaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā pavedentī’ti tesametaṃ pāṭikaṅkhaṃ? Yamidaṃ yadidaṃ (ka.) kāyasucaritaṃ, vacīsucaritaṃ, manosucaritaṃ – ime tayo kusale dhamme abhinivajjetvā abhinibbajjetvā (syā. kaṃ.), abhinibbijjitvā (ka.) yamidaṃ yadidaṃ (ka.) kāyaduccaritaṃ, vacīduccaritaṃ, manoduccaritaṃ – ime tayo akusale dhamme samādāya vattissanti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Na hi te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā passanti akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ ādīnavaṃ okāraṃ saṃkilesaṃ, kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ nekkhamme ānisaṃsaṃ vodānapakkhaṃ. Santaṃyeva pana paraṃ lokaṃ ‘natthi paro loko’ tissa diṭṭhi hoti; sāssa hoti micchādiṭṭhi. Santaṃyeva kho pana paraṃ lokaṃ ‘natthi paro loko’ti saṅkappeti; svāssa hoti micchāsaṅkappo. Santaṃyeva kho pana paraṃ lokaṃ ‘natthi paro loko’ti vācaṃ bhāsati; sāssa hoti micchāvācā. Santaṃyeva kho pana paraṃ lokaṃ ‘natthi paro loko’ti āha; ye te arahanto paralokaviduno tesamayaṃ paccanīkaṃ karoti. Santaṃyeva kho pana paraṃ lokaṃ ‘natthi paro loko’ti paraṃ [T 2.0103] saññāpeti paññāpeti (ka.); sāssa hoti asaddhammasaññatti assaddhammapaññatti (ka.). Tāya ca pana asaddhammasaññattiyā attānukkaṃseti, paraṃ vambheti. Iti pubbeva kho panassa susīlyaṃ pahīnaṃ hoti, dussīlyaṃ paccupaṭṭhitaṃ – ayañca micchādiṭṭhi micchāsaṅkappo micchāvācā ariyānaṃ paccanīkatā asaddhammasaññatti attukkaṃsanā paravambhanā. Evamassime evaṃ’si’me’ (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) aneke pāpakā akusalā dhammā sambhavanti micchādiṭṭhipaccayā.

95. “In this regard, householders, concerning those ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and view: ‘There is no fruit of giving... who, having realized this world and the other world for themselves with direct knowledge, make them known’—this is to be expected of them: having rejected these three wholesome things—good bodily conduct, good verbal conduct, and good mental conduct—they will undertake and practice these three unwholesome things—bad bodily conduct, bad verbal conduct, and bad mental conduct. For what reason? Because those venerable ascetics and brahmins do not see the danger, the inferiority, and the defilement of unwholesome states, nor the benefit in renunciation and the aspect of purification of wholesome states. Though there really is another world, their view is: ‘There is no other world.’ This is their wrong view. Though there really is another world, they form the intention: ‘There is no other world.’ This is their wrong intention. Though there really is another world, they speak the words: ‘There is no other world.’ This is their wrong speech. Though there really is another world, they say: ‘There is no other world,’ thereby opposing those Arahants who know the other world. Though there really is another world, they persuade others that: ‘There is no other world.’ This is their teaching of false doctrine. And by means of that teaching of false doctrine, they praise themselves and disparage others. Thus, their good virtue was already abandoned beforehand, and their lack of virtue is established—this wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, opposition to the noble ones, teaching of false doctrine, self-praise, and disparagement of others. In this way, for them, these many evil, unwholesome states arise conditioned by wrong view.

“Tatra[M 2.0065][V 2.0073][P 1.0403], gahapatayo, viññū puriso iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘sace kho natthi paro loko evamayaṃ bhavaṃ purisapuggalo kāyassa bhedā sotthimattānaṃ karissati; sace kho atthi paro loko evamayaṃ bhavaṃ purisapuggalo kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjissati. Kāmaṃ kho pana māhu paro loko, hotu nesaṃ bhavataṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ saccaṃ vacanaṃ; atha ca panāyaṃ bhavaṃ purisapuggalo diṭṭheva dhamme viññūnaṃ gārayho – dussīlo purisapuggalo micchādiṭṭhi natthikavādo’ti. Sace kho attheva paro loko, evaṃ imassa bhoto purisapuggalassa ubhayattha kaliggaho – yañca diṭṭheva dhamme viññūnaṃ gārayho, yañca kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjissati. Evamassāyaṃ apaṇṇako dhammo dussamatto samādinno, ekaṃsaṃ pharitvā tiṭṭhati, riñcati kusalaṃ ṭhānaṃ.

“Householders, therein a wise man reflects thus: ‘If, indeed, there is no other world, then this venerable person, with the breakup of the body, will make himself safe. If, indeed, there is another world, then this venerable person, with the breakup of the body, after death, will be reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a place of ruin, in hell. Let it be, indeed, that there is no other world; let the words of those venerable samaṇas and brāhmaṇas be true. And yet, this venerable person is censured by the wise in this very life as an immoral person, of wrong view, a nihilist.’ If, indeed, there really is another world, then for this venerable person there is a losing throw in both cases: in that he is censured by the wise in this very life, and in that, with the breakup of the body, after death, he will be reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a place of ruin, in hell. Thus, for him, this incontrovertible teaching is badly grasped and badly undertaken; it stands pervading only one side, and it forsakes the wholesome position.”

96. “Tatra[T 2.0104], gahapatayo, ye te samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘atthi dinnaṃ…pe… ye imañca lokaṃ parañca lokaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā pavedentī’ti tesametaṃ pāṭikaṅkhaṃ? Yamidaṃ kāyaduccaritaṃ, vacīduccaritaṃ, manoduccaritaṃ – ime tayo akusale dhamme abhinivajjetvā yamidaṃ kāyasucaritaṃ, vacīsucaritaṃ, manosucaritaṃ – ime tayo kusale dhamme samādāya vattissanti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Passanti hi te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ ādīnavaṃ okāraṃ saṃkilesaṃ, kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ nekkhamme ānisaṃsaṃ vodānapakkhaṃ. Santaṃyeva kho pana paraṃ lokaṃ ‘atthi paro loko’ tissa diṭṭhi hoti; sāssa hoti sammādiṭṭhi. Santaṃyeva kho pana paraṃ lokaṃ ‘atthi paro loko’ti saṅkappeti; svāssa hoti sammāsaṅkappo. Santaṃyeva kho pana paraṃ lokaṃ ‘atthi paro loko’ti vācaṃ bhāsati; sāssa hoti sammāvācā. Santaṃyeva kho pana paraṃ lokaṃ ‘atthi paro loko’ti āha; ye te arahanto paralokaviduno tesamayaṃ na paccanīkaṃ karoti. Santaṃyeva kho pana paraṃ lokaṃ ‘atthi paro loko’ti paraṃ [P 1.0404] saññāpeti; sāssa hoti saddhammasaññatti. Tāya ca pana saddhammasaññattiyā nevattānukkaṃseti, na paraṃ vambheti. Iti pubbeva kho panassa dussīlyaṃ pahīnaṃ hoti, susīlyaṃ paccupaṭṭhitaṃ – ayañca sammādiṭṭhi sammāsaṅkappo sammāvācā ariyānaṃ apaccanīkatā saddhammasaññatti anattukkaṃsanā [T 2.0105][M 2.0066] aparavambhanā. Evamassime aneke kusalā dhammā sambhavanti sammādiṭṭhipaccayā.

96. Householders, therein, for those samaṇas and brāhmaṇas who speak thus and hold such a view—‘There is what is given… who, having realized it for themselves by direct knowledge, make known this world and the next’—this is to be expected: that they will avoid these three unwholesome states—misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind—and, having undertaken these three wholesome states—good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind—they will so conduct themselves. For what reason? Because those venerable samaṇas and brāhmaṇas see the danger, inferiority, and defilement of unwholesome states, and they see the benefit in renunciation, the aspect of purification, of wholesome states. Since there really is another world, his view is ‘There is another world’; that is his right view. Since there really is another world, he thinks ‘There is another world’; that is his right thought. Since there really is another world, he speaks the words ‘There is another world’; that is his right speech. Since there really is another world, he says ‘There is another world’; he does not act in opposition to those Arahants who know the other world. Since there really is another world, he makes it known to others that ‘There is another world’; that is for him a making known of the true Dhamma. And by that making known of the true Dhamma, he neither extols himself nor disparages others. Thus, even beforehand, his immorality is abandoned and morality is established. And this right view, right thought, right speech, non-opposition to the noble ones, making known of the true Dhamma, not extolling oneself, and not disparaging others—in this way, for him, these many wholesome states arise conditioned by right view.

“Tatra, gahapatayo, viññū puriso iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘sace kho atthi paro loko[V 2.0074], evamayaṃ bhavaṃ purisapuggalo kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjissati. Kāmaṃ kho pana māhu paro loko, hotu nesaṃ bhavataṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ saccaṃ vacanaṃ; atha ca panāyaṃ bhavaṃ purisapuggalo diṭṭheva dhamme viññūnaṃ pāsaṃso – sīlavā purisapuggalo sammādiṭṭhi atthikavādo’ti. Sace kho attheva paro loko, evaṃ imassa bhoto purisapuggalassa ubhayattha kaṭaggaho – yañca diṭṭheva dhamme viññūnaṃ pāsaṃso, yañca kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjissati. Evamassāyaṃ apaṇṇako dhammo susamatto samādinno, ubhayaṃsaṃ pharitvā tiṭṭhati, riñcati akusalaṃ ṭhānaṃ.

Householders, therein a wise man reflects thus: ‘If, indeed, there is another world, then this venerable person, with the breakup of the body, after death, will be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. Let it be, indeed, that there is no other world; let the words of those venerable samaṇas and brāhmaṇas be true. And yet, this venerable person is praised by the wise in this very life as a virtuous person, of right view, an affirmationist.’ If, indeed, there really is another world, then for this venerable person there is a winning throw in both cases: in that he is praised by the wise in this very life, and in that, with the breakup of the body, after death, he will be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. Thus, for him, this incontrovertible teaching is well-grasped and well-undertaken; it stands pervading both sides, and it forsakes the unwholesome position.

97. “Santi, gahapatayo, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘karoto kārayato, chindato chedāpayato, pacato pācāpayato, socayato socāpayato, kilamato kilamāpayato, phandato phandāpayato, pāṇamatipātayato pāṇamatimāpayato (sī. pī.), pāṇamatipātāpayato (syā. kaṃ.), pāṇamatipāpayato (ka.), adinnaṃ ādiyato, sandhiṃ chindato, nillopaṃ harato, ekāgārikaṃ karoto, paripanthe tiṭṭhato, paradāraṃ gacchato, musā [T 2.0106] bhaṇato; karoto na karīyati pāpaṃ. Khurapariyantena cepi cakkena yo imissā pathaviyā pāṇe ekaṃ maṃsakhalaṃ ekaṃ maṃsapuñjaṃ kareyya, natthi tatonidānaṃ pāpaṃ, natthi pāpassa āgamo. Dakkhiṇañcepi gaṅgāya tīraṃ gaccheyya hananto ghātento, chindanto chedāpento, pacanto pācento; natthi tatonidānaṃ pāpaṃ, natthi pāpassa āgamo. Uttarañcepi gaṅgāya tīraṃ gaccheyya dadanto dāpento, yajanto yajāpento; natthi tatonidānaṃ puññaṃ, natthi puññassa āgamo. Dānena damena saṃyamena saccavajjena saccavācena (ka.) natthi puññaṃ, natthi puññassa āgamo’ti. Tesaṃyeva kho, gahapatayo, samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā ujuvipaccanīkavādā [P 1.0405] te evamāhaṃsu – ‘karoto kārayato, chindato chedāpayato, pacato pācāpayato, socayato [M 2.0067] socāpayato, kilamato kilamāpayato, phandato phandāpayato, pāṇamatipātayato, adinnaṃ ādiyato, sandhiṃ chindato, nillopaṃ harato, ekāgārikaṃ karoto, paripanthe tiṭṭhato, paradāraṃ gacchato, musā bhaṇato; karoto karīyati pāpaṃ. Khurapariyantena cepi cakkena yo imissā pathaviyā pāṇe ekaṃ maṃsakhalaṃ ekaṃ maṃsapuñjaṃ kareyya, atthi tatonidānaṃ pāpaṃ, atthi pāpassa āgamo. Dakkhiṇañcepi gaṅgāya tīraṃ gaccheyya hananto ghātento, chindanto chedāpento, pacanto pācento; atthi tatonidānaṃ pāpaṃ, atthi pāpassa āgamo. Uttarañcepi gaṅgāya tīraṃ gaccheyya dadanto dāpento, yajanto [T 2.0107] yajāpento; atthi tatonidānaṃ puññaṃ, atthi puññassa āgamo. Dānena [V 2.0075] damena saṃyamena saccavajjena atthi puññaṃ, atthi puññassa āgamo’ti. Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, gahapatayo, nanume samaṇabrāhmaṇā aññamaññassa ujuvipaccanīkavādā”ti? “Evaṃ, bhante”.

97. Householders, there are some ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and are of such a view: ‘For one who acts or causes another to act, who cuts or causes another to cut, who torments or causes another to torment, who causes grief or causes another to grieve, who wearies or causes another to weary, who agitates or causes another to agitate, who takes the life of a living being, who takes what is not given, who breaks into a house, who plunders, who commits robbery in a single house, who stands on the highway, who goes to another’s wife, who speaks falsely—for one who does so, no evil is done. Even if one were to make the living beings on this earth into one mass of flesh, one heap of flesh, with a razor-edged wheel, from that cause there is no evil, there is no accrual of evil. If one were to go along the southern bank of the Ganges killing and causing to kill, cutting and causing to cut, tormenting and causing to torment, from that cause there is no evil, there is no accrual of evil. If one were to go along the northern bank of the Ganges giving and causing to give, sacrificing and causing to sacrifice, from that cause there is no merit, there is no accrual of merit. Through giving, through taming, through restraint, through truthful speech, there is no merit, there is no accrual of merit.’ Now, householders, among those very ascetics and brahmins, there are some ascetics and brahmins who hold a directly opposing view. They speak thus: ‘For one who acts or causes another to act, who cuts or causes another to cut, who torments or causes another to torment, who causes grief or causes another to grieve, who wearies or causes another to weary, who agitates or causes another to agitate, who takes the life of a living being, who takes what is not given, who breaks into a house, who plunders, who commits robbery in a single house, who stands on the highway, who goes to another’s wife, who speaks falsely—for one who does so, evil is done. Even if one were to make the living beings on this earth into one mass of flesh, one heap of flesh, with a razor-edged wheel, from that cause there is evil, there is an accrual of evil. If one were to go along the southern bank of the Ganges killing and causing to kill, cutting and causing to cut, tormenting and causing to torment, from that cause there is evil, there is an accrual of evil. If one were to go along the northern bank of the Ganges giving and causing to give, sacrificing and causing to sacrifice, from that cause there is merit, there is an accrual of merit. Through giving, through taming, through restraint, through truthful speech, there is merit, there is an accrual of merit.’ What do you think, householders? Are not these ascetics and brahmins of a directly opposing view to one another?” “It is so, venerable sir.”

98. “Tatra, gahapatayo, ye te samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘karoto kārayato, chindato chedāpayato, pacato pācāpayato, socayato socāpayato, kilamato kilamāpayato, phandato phandāpayato, pāṇamatipātayato, adinnaṃ ādiyato, sandhiṃ chindato, nillopaṃ harato, ekāgārikaṃ karoto, paripanthe tiṭṭhato, paradāraṃ gacchato, musā bhaṇato; karoto na karīyati pāpaṃ. Khurapariyantena cepi cakkena yo imissā pathaviyā pāṇe ekaṃ maṃsakhalaṃ ekaṃ maṃsapuñjaṃ kareyya, natthi tatonidānaṃ pāpaṃ, natthi pāpassa āgamo. Dakkhiṇañcepi gaṅgāya tīraṃ gaccheyya hananto ghātento…pe… dānena damena saṃyamena saccavajjena natthi puññaṃ, natthi puññassa āgamo’ti tesametaṃ pāṭikaṅkhaṃ? Yamidaṃ kāyasucaritaṃ, vacīsucaritaṃ, manosucaritaṃ – ime tayo kusale dhamme abhinivajjetvā yamidaṃ kāyaduccaritaṃ, vacīduccaritaṃ, manoduccaritaṃ – ime tayo akusale dhamme samādāya vattissanti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Na hi te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā passanti akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ ādīnavaṃ okāraṃ saṃkilesaṃ, kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ nekkhamme [T 2.0108] ānisaṃsaṃ vodānapakkhaṃ. Santaṃyeva kho pana kiriyaṃ ‘natthi kiriyā’ tissa diṭṭhi hoti; sāssa hoti micchādiṭṭhi. Santaṃyeva kho pana kiriyaṃ ‘natthi kiriyā’ti saṅkappeti; svāssa hoti [M 2.0068] micchāsaṅkappo. Santaṃyeva kho pana kiriyaṃ ‘natthi kiriyā’ti vācaṃ bhāsati; sāssa hoti micchāvācā. Santaṃyeva kho pana kiriyaṃ ‘natthi kiriyā’ti āha, ye te arahanto kiriyavādā tesamayaṃ paccanīkaṃ karoti. Santaṃyeva kho pana kiriyaṃ ‘natthi kiriyā’ti paraṃ saññāpeti; sāssa hoti asaddhammasaññatti. Tāya ca pana asaddhammasaññattiyā attānukkaṃseti, paraṃ vambheti. Iti pubbeva kho panassa susīlyaṃ pahīnaṃ hoti, dussīlyaṃ paccupaṭṭhitaṃ – ayañca [P 1.0406] micchādiṭṭhi micchāsaṅkappo micchāvācā ariyānaṃ paccanīkatā asaddhammasaññatti attukkaṃsanā paravambhanā. Evamassime aneke pāpakā akusalā dhammā sambhavanti micchādiṭṭhipaccayā.

98. Householders, in that regard, for those ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and are of such a view: ‘For one who acts or causes another to act… who speaks falsely—for one who does so, no evil is done… Through giving, through taming, through restraint, through truthful speech, there is no merit, there is no accrual of merit’—this is to be expected of them: they will abandon these three wholesome states—good bodily conduct, good verbal conduct, and good mental conduct—and will undertake and practice these three unwholesome states—misconduct in body, misconduct in speech, and misconduct in mind. For what reason? Because those venerable ascetics and brahmins do not see the danger, the inferiority, and the defilement of unwholesome states, nor do they see the benefit in renunciation and the aspect of purity of wholesome states. Indeed, though action truly exists, his view is, ‘There is no action’; this is his wrong view. Indeed, though action truly exists, he thinks, ‘There is no action’; this is his wrong thought. Indeed, though action truly exists, he speaks the words, ‘There is no action’; this is his wrong speech. When he says, ‘There is no action,’ he opposes those Arahants who are proponents of action. He convinces another that ‘There is no action’; this is his instruction contrary to the true Dhamma. And by means of that instruction contrary to the true Dhamma, he extols himself and disparages others. Thus, for him, good virtue was already abandoned before, and bad virtue has become established. And there is this wrong view, this wrong thought, this wrong speech, this opposition to the noble ones, this instruction contrary to the true Dhamma, and this self-exaltation and disparagement of others. In this way, for him, these many evil, unwholesome states arise conditioned by wrong view.

“Tatra, gahapatayo, viññū puriso iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘sace kho natthi kiriyā, evamayaṃ bhavaṃ purisapuggalo kāyassa bhedā sotthimattānaṃ karissati; sace kho atthi kiriyā evamayaṃ [V 2.0076] bhavaṃ purisapuggalo kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjissati. Kāmaṃ kho pana māhu kiriyā, hotu nesaṃ bhavataṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ saccaṃ vacanaṃ; atha ca panāyaṃ bhavaṃ purisapuggalo diṭṭheva dhamme viññūnaṃ gārayho – dussīlo purisapuggalo [T 2.0109] micchādiṭṭhi akiriyavādo’ti. Sace kho attheva kiriyā, evaṃ imassa bhoto purisapuggalassa ubhayattha kaliggaho – yañca diṭṭheva dhamme viññūnaṃ gārayho, yañca kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjissati. Evamassāyaṃ apaṇṇako dhammo dussamatto samādinno, ekaṃsaṃ pharitvā tiṭṭhati, riñcati kusalaṃ ṭhānaṃ.

Here, householders, a wise person reflects thus: ‘If indeed there is no action, then this venerable individual will make himself safe on the breakup of the body. But if indeed there is action, then this venerable individual, on the breakup of the body, after death, will be reborn in a state of loss, a bad destination, a place of ruin, in hell. Let there indeed be no action, let the words of those venerable ascetics and brahmins be true; and yet this venerable individual is censured by the wise in this very life as: “An immoral individual, of wrong view, a proponent of non-action.”’ If indeed there is action, then for this venerable individual there is a losing throw in both cases: in that he is censured by the wise in this very life, and in that on the breakup of the body, after death, he will be reborn in a state of loss, a bad destination, a place of ruin, in hell. Thus, for him, this incontrovertible teaching is wrongly taken up and wrongly undertaken; it stands covering one side, abandoning the wholesome position.

99. “Tatra, gahapatayo, ye te samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘karoto kārayato, chindato chedāpayato, pacato pācāpayato, socayato socāpayato, kilamato kilamāpayato, phandato phandāpayato, pāṇamatipātayato, adinnaṃ ādiyato, sandhiṃ chindato, nillopaṃ harato, ekāgārikaṃ karoto, paripanthe tiṭṭhato, paradāraṃ gacchato, musā bhaṇato; karoto karīyati pāpaṃ. Khurapariyantena cepi cakkena yo imissā pathaviyā pāṇe ekaṃ maṃsakhalaṃ ekaṃ maṃsapuñjaṃ kareyya, atthi tatonidānaṃ pāpaṃ, atthi pāpassa āgamo. Dakkhiṇañcepi gaṅgāya tīraṃ gaccheyya hananto ghātento, chindanto [M 2.0069] chedāpento, pacanto pācento, atthi tatonidānaṃ pāpaṃ, atthi pāpassa āgamo. Uttarañcepi gaṅgāya tīraṃ gaccheyya dadanto dāpento, yajanto yajāpento, atthi tatonidānaṃ puññaṃ, atthi puññassa āgamo. Dānena damena saṃyamena saccavajjena atthi puññaṃ, atthi puññassa āgamo’ti tesametaṃ pāṭikaṅkhaṃ? Yamidaṃ kāyaduccaritaṃ, vacīduccaritaṃ[T 2.0110], manoduccaritaṃ – ime tayo akusale dhamme abhinivajjetvā yamidaṃ kāyasucaritaṃ, vacīsucaritaṃ, manosucaritaṃ – ime tayo kusale dhamme samādāya vattissanti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Passanti hi te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ ādīnavaṃ okāraṃ saṃkilesaṃ, kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ nekkhamme ānisaṃsaṃ vodānapakkhaṃ. Santaṃyeva kho pana kiriyaṃ ‘atthi kiriyā’ tissa diṭṭhi hoti; sāssa hoti sammādiṭṭhi. Santaṃyeva kho pana kiriyaṃ ‘atthi kiriyā’ti saṅkappeti; svāssa hoti sammāsaṅkappo. Santaṃyeva kho pana kiriyaṃ ‘atthi kiriyā’ti vācaṃ bhāsati; sāssa hoti sammāvācā. Santaṃyeva kho pana kiriyaṃ ‘atthi kiriyā’ti āha; ye te arahanto kiriyavādā tesamayaṃ na paccanīkaṃ karoti. Santaṃyeva kho pana kiriyaṃ ‘atthi kiriyā’ti paraṃ saññāpeti; sāssa [V 2.0077] hoti saddhammasaññatti. Tāya [P 1.0407] ca pana saddhammasaññattiyā nevattānukkaṃseti, na paraṃ vambheti. Iti pubbeva kho panassa dussīlyaṃ pahīnaṃ hoti, susīlyaṃ paccupaṭṭhitaṃ – ayañca sammādiṭṭhi sammāsaṅkappo sammāvācā ariyānaṃ apaccanīkatā saddhammasaññatti anattukkaṃsanā aparavambhanā. Evamassime aneke kusalā dhammā sambhavanti sammādiṭṭhipaccayā.

99. Here, householders, among them, those ascetics and brahmins who have such a saying, such a view: ‘For one who acts or causes another to act, for one who cuts or causes another to cut, for one who torments or causes another to be tormented, for one who causes grief or causes another to grieve, for one who becomes fatigued or causes another to be fatigued, for one who trembles or causes another to tremble, for one who takes life, who takes what is not given, who commits burglary, who commits plunder, who robs a single house, who stands in ambush, who goes to another’s wife, who speaks falsely; for one who acts, evil is done. Even if one were to make the living beings on this earth into a single heap of flesh, a single mass of flesh, with a razor-rimmed wheel, there is evil from that cause, there is an influx of evil. Even if one were to go to the southern bank of the Ganges, killing and causing to kill, cutting and causing to cut, tormenting and causing to torment, there is evil from that cause, there is an influx of evil. Even if one were to go to the northern bank of the Ganges, giving and causing to give, sacrificing and causing to sacrifice, there is merit from that cause, there is an influx of merit. Through giving, through taming, through restraint, through truthful speech, there is merit, there is an influx of merit’—is it to be expected of them that they, having rejected these three unwholesome states—bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct—will live having undertaken these three wholesome states—bodily good conduct, verbal good conduct, and mental good conduct? For what reason? Because those venerable ascetics and brahmins see the danger, the inferiority, and the defilement of unwholesome states, and they see the benefit in renunciation and the aspect of purification in wholesome states. When action indeed exists, his view is: ‘There is action.’ That is his right view. When action indeed exists, he resolves: ‘There is action.’ That is his right resolve. When action indeed exists, he speaks the words: ‘There is action.’ That is his right speech. When action indeed exists, he says: ‘There is action.’ He does not act contrary to those Arahants who are proponents of action. When action indeed exists, he instructs another: ‘There is action.’ That is his instruction in the true Dhamma. And by that instruction in the true Dhamma, he neither extols himself nor disparages others. Thus, indeed, his former immorality is abandoned, and morality is established for him—and this right view, right resolve, right speech, non-opposition to the noble ones, instruction in the true Dhamma, non-self-exaltation, and non-disparagement of others. In this way, for him, these many wholesome states arise conditioned by right view.

“Tatra, gahapatayo, viññū puriso iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘sace kho atthi kiriyā, evamayaṃ bhavaṃ purisapuggalo kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjissati. Kāmaṃ kho pana māhu [T 2.0111] kiriyā, hotu nesaṃ bhavataṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ saccaṃ vacanaṃ; atha ca panāyaṃ bhavaṃ purisapuggalo diṭṭheva dhamme viññūnaṃ pāsaṃso – sīlavā purisapuggalo sammādiṭṭhi kiriyavādo’ti. Sace kho attheva kiriyā, evaṃ imassa bhoto purisapuggalassa ubhayattha kaṭaggaho – yañca diṭṭheva dhamme viññūnaṃ pāsaṃso, yañca kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjissati. Evamassāyaṃ apaṇṇako dhammo susamatto samādinno, ubhayaṃsaṃ pharitvā tiṭṭhati, riñcati akusalaṃ ṭhānaṃ.

Here, householders, a wise person reflects thus: ‘If indeed there is action, then this venerable individual, on the breakup of the body, after death, will be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. Let there indeed be no action, let the words of those venerable ascetics and brahmins be true; and yet this venerable individual is praised by the wise in this very life as: “A moral individual, of right view, a proponent of action.”’ If indeed there is action, then for this venerable individual there is a winning throw in both cases: in that he is praised by the wise in this very life, and in that on the breakup of the body, after death, he will be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. Thus, for him, this incontrovertible teaching is well taken up and well undertaken; it stands covering both sides, abandoning the unwholesome position.

100. “Santi[M 2.0070], gahapatayo, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘natthi hetu, natthi paccayo sattānaṃ saṃkilesāya; ahetū appaccayā sattā saṃkilissanti. Natthi hetu, natthi paccayo sattānaṃ visuddhiyā; ahetū appaccayā sattā visujjhanti. Natthi balaṃ, natthi vīriyaṃ viriyaṃ (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.), natthi purisathāmo, natthi purisaparakkamo; sabbe sattā sabbe pāṇā sabbe bhūtā sabbe jīvā avasā abalā avīriyā niyatisaṃgatibhāvapariṇatā chasvevābhijātīsu sukhadukkhaṃ paṭisaṃvedentī’ti. Tesaṃyeva kho, gahapatayo, samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā ujuvipaccanīkavādā. Te evamāhaṃsu – ‘atthi hetu, atthi paccayo sattānaṃ saṃkilesāya; sahetū sappaccayā sattā saṃkilissanti. Atthi hetu, atthi paccayo sattānaṃ visuddhiyā; sahetū sappaccayā sattā visujjhanti. Atthi balaṃ, atthi vīriyaṃ, atthi [T 2.0112] purisathāmo, atthi purisaparakkamo; na sabbe sattā sabbe pāṇā sabbe bhūtā sabbe jīvā avasā abalā avīriyā atthi purisaparakkamo, sabbe sattā… savasā sabalā savīriyā (syā. kaṃ. ka.) niyatisaṃgatibhāvapariṇatā chasvevābhijātīsu sukhadukkhaṃ paṭisaṃvedentī’ti. Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, gahapatayo, nanume [P 1.0408] samaṇabrāhmaṇā aññamaññassa ujuvipaccanīkavādā’ti? ‘Evaṃ, bhante’.

100. Householders, there are some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and view: ‘There is no cause, no condition for the defilement of beings; without cause, without condition, beings are defiled. There is no cause, no condition for the purification of beings; without cause, without condition, beings are purified. There is no strength, there is no energy, there is no manly stamina, there is no manly effort; all beings, all that breathe, all creatures, all that live are without power, without strength, without energy, developed by destiny, association, and nature, and experience pleasure and pain in the six classes of birth alone.’ And, householders, among those very ascetics and brahmins, some ascetics and brahmins hold a directly opposing doctrine. They speak thus: ‘There is a cause, there is a condition for the defilement of beings; with cause, with condition, beings are defiled. There is a cause, there is a condition for the purification of beings; with cause, with condition, beings are purified. There is strength, there is energy, there is manly stamina, there is manly effort; not all beings, all that breathe, all creatures, all that live are without power, without strength, without energy, developed by destiny, association, and nature, experiencing pleasure and pain in the six classes of birth alone.’ What do you think, householders? Are not these ascetics and brahmins of a directly opposing doctrine to one another?” “So it is, Venerable Sir.”

101. “Tatra[V 2.0078], gahapatayo, ye te samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘natthi hetu, natthi paccayo sattānaṃ saṃkilesāya; ahetū appaccayā sattā saṃkilissanti. Natthi hetu, natthi paccayo sattānaṃ visuddhiyā; ahetū appaccayā sattā visujjhanti. Natthi balaṃ, natthi vīriyaṃ, natthi purisathāmo, natthi purisaparakkamo; sabbe sattā sabbe pāṇā sabbe bhūtā sabbe jīvā avasā abalā avīriyā niyatisaṃgatibhāvapariṇatā chasvevābhijātīsu sukhadukkhaṃ paṭisaṃvedentī’ti tesametaṃ pāṭikaṅkhaṃ? Yamidaṃ kāyasucaritaṃ, vacīsucaritaṃ, manosucaritaṃ – ime tayo kusale dhamme abhinivajjetvā yamidaṃ kāyaduccaritaṃ, vacīduccaritaṃ, manoduccaritaṃ – ime tayo akusale dhamme samādāya vattissanti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Na hi te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā passanti akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ ādīnavaṃ okāraṃ saṃkilesaṃ, kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ nekkhamme ānisaṃsaṃ vodānapakkhaṃ. Santaṃyeva kho pana hetuṃ ‘natthi [M 2.0071] hetū’ tissa diṭṭhi hoti; sāssa hoti micchādiṭṭhi. Santaṃyeva kho pana hetuṃ ‘natthi hetū’ti saṅkappeti[T 2.0113]; svāssa hoti micchāsaṅkappo. Santaṃyeva kho pana hetuṃ ‘natthi hetū’ti vācaṃ bhāsati; sāssa hoti micchāvācā. Santaṃyeva kho pana hetuṃ ‘natthi hetū’ti āha; ye te arahanto hetuvādā tesamayaṃ paccanīkaṃ karoti. Santaṃyeva kho pana hetuṃ ‘natthi hetū’ti paraṃ saññāpeti; sāssa hoti asaddhammasaññatti. Tāya ca pana asaddhammasaññattiyā attānukkaṃseti, paraṃ vambheti. Iti pubbeva kho panassa susīlyaṃ pahīnaṃ hoti, dussīlyaṃ paccupaṭṭhitaṃ – ayañca micchādiṭṭhi micchāsaṅkappo micchāvācā ariyānaṃ paccanīkatā asaddhammasaññatti attānukkaṃsanā paravambhanā. Evamassime aneke pāpakā akusalā dhammā sambhavanti micchādiṭṭhipaccayā.

101. Householders, in this matter, for those ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and view: ‘There is no cause, no condition for the defilement of beings… they experience pleasure and pain in the six classes of birth alone’—this is to be expected of them: having rejected these three wholesome states, namely, good bodily conduct, good verbal conduct, and good mental conduct, they will undertake and practice these three unwholesome states, namely, bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct. For what reason? Because those venerable ascetics and brahmins do not see the danger, depravity, and defilement of unwholesome states, nor the benefit in renunciation and the aspect of purification of wholesome states. When there is in fact a cause, his view is: ‘There is no cause.’ This is his wrong view. When there is in fact a cause, he forms the intention: ‘There is no cause.’ This is his wrong intention. When there is in fact a cause, he speaks the words: ‘There is no cause.’ This is his wrong speech. When there is in fact a cause, he says: ‘There is no cause.’ He thereby opposes those Arahants who are proponents of cause. When there is in fact a cause, he convinces another: ‘There is no cause.’ This is his teaching of a false doctrine. And by that teaching of a false doctrine, he extols himself and disparages others. Thus, his former good conduct is already abandoned, and his bad conduct is established. And this wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, opposition to the noble ones, teaching of a false doctrine, self-exaltation, and disparaging of others—in this way, for him, these many evil, unwholesome states arise conditioned by wrong view.

“Tatra, gahapatayo, viññū puriso iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘sace kho natthi hetu, evamayaṃ bhavaṃ purisapuggalo kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sotthimattānaṃ karissati; sace kho atthi hetu, evamayaṃ bhavaṃ purisapuggalo kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjissati. Kāmaṃ kho pana māhu hetu, hotu nesaṃ bhavataṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ saccaṃ vacanaṃ; atha ca panāyaṃ bhavaṃ purisapuggalo diṭṭheva dhamme viññūnaṃ gārayho – dussīlo purisapuggalo micchādiṭṭhi ahetukavādo’ti. Sace kho attheva hetu, evaṃ imassa bhoto purisapuggalassa ubhayattha kaliggaho [P 1.0409] – yañca diṭṭheva dhamme viññūnaṃ gārayho, yañca kāyassa bhedā [V 2.0079] paraṃ [T 2.0114] maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjissati. Evamassāyaṃ apaṇṇako dhammo dussamatto samādinno, ekaṃsaṃ pharitvā tiṭṭhati, riñcati kusalaṃ ṭhānaṃ.

Householders, in this matter, a wise person reflects thus: ‘If indeed there is no cause, then this venerable individual, with the breakup of the body, after death, will make himself safe. But if indeed there is a cause, then this venerable individual, with the breakup of the body, after death, will be reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a place of ruin, in hell. Let there indeed be no cause, and let the words of those venerable ascetics and brahmins be true; yet still this venerable individual is censured by the wise in this very life as an immoral person, one of wrong view, a proponent of no-cause.’ If indeed there is a cause, then for this venerable individual there is a losing throw in both cases: in that he is censured by the wise in this very life, and in that, with the breakup of the body, after death, he will be reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a place of ruin, in hell. Thus, for him, this incontrovertible doctrine is badly grasped and badly undertaken; it stands pervading only one side, and forsakes the wholesome position.

102. “Tatra, gahapatayo, ye te samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘atthi hetu, atthi paccayo sattānaṃ saṃkilesāya; sahetū sappaccayā sattā saṃkilissanti. Atthi hetu, atthi paccayo sattānaṃ visuddhiyā; sahetū sappaccayā sattā visujjhanti. Atthi balaṃ, atthi vīriyaṃ, atthi purisathāmo, atthi purisaparakkamo; na sabbe sattā sabbe pāṇā sabbe bhūtā sabbe jīvā avasā abalā avīriyā niyatisaṃgatibhāvapariṇatā chasvevābhijātīsu sukhadukkhaṃ paṭisaṃvedentī’ti tesametaṃ pāṭikaṅkhaṃ? Yamidaṃ kāyaduccaritaṃ, vacīduccaritaṃ, manoduccaritaṃ – ime tayo [M 2.0072] akusale dhamme abhinivajjetvā yamidaṃ kāyasucaritaṃ, vacīsucaritaṃ, manosucaritaṃ – ime tayo kusale dhamme samādāya vattissanti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Passanti hi te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ ādīnavaṃ okāraṃ saṃkilesaṃ, kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ nekkhamme ānisaṃsaṃ vodānapakkhaṃ. Santaṃyeva kho pana hetuṃ ‘atthi hetū’ tissa diṭṭhi hoti; sāssa hoti sammādiṭṭhi. Santaṃyeva kho pana hetuṃ ‘atthi hetū’ti saṅkappeti; svāssa hoti sammāsaṅkappo. Santaṃyeva kho pana hetuṃ ‘atthi hetū’ti vācaṃ bhāsati; sāssa hoti sammāvācā. Santaṃyeva kho pana hetuṃ [T 2.0115] ‘atthi hetū’ti āha, ye te arahanto hetuvādā tesamayaṃ na paccanīkaṃ karoti. Santaṃyeva kho pana hetuṃ ‘atthi hetū’ti paraṃ saññāpeti; sāssa hoti saddhammasaññatti. Tāya ca pana saddhammasaññattiyā nevattānukkaṃseti, na paraṃ vambheti. Iti pubbeva kho panassa dussīlyaṃ pahīnaṃ hoti, susīlyaṃ paccupaṭṭhitaṃ – ayañca sammādiṭṭhi sammāsaṅkappo sammāvācā ariyānaṃ apaccanīkatā saddhammasaññatti anattukkaṃsanā aparavambhanā. Evamassime aneke kusalā dhammā sambhavanti sammādiṭṭhipaccayā.

102. Householders, among these, as to those ascetics and brahmins who are of such a doctrine and such a view: ‘There is a cause, there is a condition for the defilement of beings; with cause and with condition, beings are defiled. There is a cause, there is a condition for the purification of beings; with cause and with condition, beings are purified. There is strength, there is energy, there is human strength, there is human exertion; it is not the case that all beings, all living things, all creatures, and all souls are without power, without strength, without energy, transformed by a nature of fixed destiny and circumstance, experiencing pleasure and pain only in the six classes of birth’—it is to be expected of them that, shunning these three unwholesome states—misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind—and undertaking these three wholesome states—good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind—they will live accordingly. For what reason? Because those venerable ascetics and brahmins see the danger, the degradation, and the defilement in unwholesome states, and they see the benefit in renunciation and the aspect of purification in wholesome states. Since a cause truly exists, the view arises for him, ‘There is a cause’; that is his right view. Since a cause truly exists, he resolves, ‘There is a cause’; that is his right resolve. Since a cause truly exists, he speaks the words, ‘There is a cause’; that is his right speech. Since a cause truly exists, he says, ‘There is a cause’; in this, he does not act in opposition to those Arahants who are proponents of cause. Since a cause truly exists, he instructs others, ‘There is a cause’; that is his instruction in the true Dhamma. And by that instruction in the true Dhamma, he neither exalts himself nor disparages others. Thus, for him, immorality is already abandoned and morality is established. And this right view, right resolve, right speech, non-opposition to the noble ones, instruction in the true Dhamma, non-self-exaltation, and non-disparagement of others—in this way, for him, these many wholesome states arise conditioned by right view.

“Tatra, gahapatayo, viññū puriso iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘sace kho atthi hetu, evamayaṃ bhavaṃ purisapuggalo kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjissati. Kāmaṃ kho pana māhu hetu, hotu nesaṃ bhavataṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ saccaṃ vacanaṃ; atha ca panāyaṃ bhavaṃ purisapuggalo diṭṭheva dhamme viññūnaṃ pāsaṃso – sīlavā purisapuggalo sammādiṭṭhi hetuvādo’ti. Sace kho atthi hetu[P 1.0410], evaṃ imassa bhoto purisapuggalassa ubhayattha kaṭaggaho [V 2.0080] – yañca diṭṭheva dhamme viññūnaṃ pāsaṃso, yañca kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjissati. Evamassāyaṃ apaṇṇako dhammo susamatto samādinno, ubhayaṃsaṃ pharitvā tiṭṭhati, riñcati akusalaṃ ṭhānaṃ.

Herein, householders, a wise person reflects thus: ‘If there is indeed a cause, then this venerable person, with the breakup of the body, after death, will be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. Suppose there is no cause, and let the word of those venerable ascetics and brahmins be true; even so, this venerable person is praised by the wise in this very life as: “A virtuous person, one of right view, a proponent of cause.” If there is indeed a cause, then for this venerable person there is a victory on both counts: in that he is praised by the wise in this very life, and in that, with the breakup of the body, after death, he will be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. Thus this is for him an unerring Dhamma, well-grasped and well-undertaken; it stands pervading both sides and forsakes the unwholesome state.

103. “Santi, gahapatayo, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino [T 2.0116] – ‘natthi sabbaso āruppā’ti. Tesaṃyeva kho, gahapatayo, samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā ujuvipaccanīkavādā. Te evamāhaṃsu – ‘atthi sabbaso āruppā’ti. Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, gahapatayo, nanume samaṇabrāhmaṇā aññamaññassa ujuvipaccanīkavādā”ti? “Evaṃ, bhante”. “Tatra[M 2.0073], gahapatayo, viññū puriso iti paṭisañcikkhati – ye kho te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘natthi sabbaso āruppā’ti, idaṃ me adiṭṭhaṃ; yepi te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘atthi sabbaso āruppā’ti, idaṃ me aviditaṃ. Ahañceva ahañce (?) kho pana ajānanto apassanto ekaṃsena ādāya vohareyyaṃ – idameva saccaṃ, moghamaññanti, na metaṃ assa patirūpaṃ. Ye kho te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘natthi sabbaso āruppā’ti, sace tesaṃ bhavataṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ saccaṃ vacanaṃ, ṭhānametaṃ vijjati – ye te devā rūpino manomayā, apaṇṇakaṃ me tatrūpapatti bhavissati. Ye pana te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘atthi sabbaso āruppā’ti, sace tesaṃ bhavataṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ saccaṃ vacanaṃ, ṭhānametaṃ vijjati – ye te devā arūpino saññāmayā, apaṇṇakaṃ me tatrūpapatti bhavissati. Dissanti kho pana rūpādhikaraṇaṃ rūpakāraṇā (ka.) daṇḍādāna-satthādāna-kalaha-viggaha-vivāda-tuvaṃtuvaṃ-pesuñña-musāvādā. ‘Natthi kho panetaṃ sabbaso arūpe’”ti. So iti [T 2.0117] paṭisaṅkhāya rūpānaṃyeva nibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya paṭipanno hoti.

103. Householders, there are some ascetics and brahmins who are of such a doctrine and such a view: ‘In every respect, there are no formless realms.’ And, householders, there are other ascetics and brahmins who hold a directly opposing view to them. They say thus: ‘In every respect, there are formless realms.’ What do you think, householders? Are not these ascetics and brahmins of a directly opposing view to one another?” “Indeed, venerable sir.” “Therein, householders, a wise person reflects thus: ‘Those venerable ascetics and brahmins who are of such a doctrine and such a view, “In every respect, there are no formless realms”—this I have not seen. And those venerable ascetics and brahmins who are of such a doctrine and such a view, “In every respect, there are formless realms”—this I do not know. If I, not knowing and not seeing, were to take a side and declare, “This alone is true, the other is false,” that would not be fitting for me. As to those venerable ascetics and brahmins who are of such a doctrine and such a view, “In every respect, there are no formless realms”—if the word of those venerable ones were true, this possibility exists: that I will be reborn among those devas who are possessed of form and are mind-made; it is certain that my rebirth will be there. And as to those venerable ascetics and brahmins who are of such a doctrine and such a view, “In every respect, there are formless realms”—if the word of those venerable ones were true, this possibility exists: that I will be reborn among those devas who are formless and are perception-made; it is certain that my rebirth will be there. Now, on account of form, the taking up of rods, the taking up of weapons, quarrels, strife, disputes, recriminations, slander, and false speech are seen. But in the formless, none of this exists in any respect.’ He, having reflected thus, practices for disenchantment with, dispassion for, and cessation of forms.

104. “Santi, gahapatayo, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘natthi sabbaso bhavanirodho’ti. Tesaṃyeva kho, gahapatayo, samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā ujuvipaccanīkavādā. Te evamāhaṃsu – ‘atthi sabbaso [P 1.0411] bhavanirodho’ti. Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, gahapatayo, nanume samaṇabrāhmaṇā aññamaññassa ujuvipaccanīkavādā”ti? “Evaṃ, bhante”. “Tatra, gahapatayo, viññū puriso iti paṭisañcikkhati – ye kho te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘natthi sabbaso bhavanirodho’ti, idaṃ me adiṭṭhaṃ; yepi te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā [V 2.0081] evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘atthi sabbaso bhavanirodho’ti, idaṃ me aviditaṃ. Ahañceva kho pana ajānanto apassanto ekaṃsena ādāya vohareyyaṃ – idameva saccaṃ, moghamaññanti, na metaṃ assa patirūpaṃ. Ye kho te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘natthi sabbaso bhavanirodho’ti, sace tesaṃ bhavataṃ [M 2.0074] samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ saccaṃ vacanaṃ, ṭhānametaṃ vijjati – ye te devā arūpino saññāmayā apaṇṇakaṃ me tatrūpapatti bhavissati. Ye pana te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘atthi sabbaso bhavanirodho’ti, sace tesaṃ bhavataṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ saccaṃ vacanaṃ, ṭhānametaṃ vijjati – yaṃ diṭṭheva dhamme parinibbāyissāmi[T 2.0118]. Ye kho te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘natthi sabbaso bhavanirodho’ti, tesamayaṃ diṭṭhi sārāgāya sarāgāya (syā. kaṃ.) santike, saṃyogāya santike, abhinandanāya santike, ajjhosānāya santike, upādānāya santike. Ye pana te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘atthi sabbaso bhavanirodho’ti, tesamayaṃ diṭṭhi asārāgāya santike, asaṃyogāya santike, anabhinandanāya santike, anajjhosānāya santike, anupādānāya santike’”ti. So iti paṭisaṅkhāya bhavānaṃyeva nibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya paṭipanno hoti.

104.
