So evaṃ vadeyya – ‘na tāvāhaṃ imaṃ [V 2.0100] sallaṃ āharissāmi yāva na taṃ purisaṃ jānāmi yenamhi viddho, khattiyo vā brāhmaṇo vā vesso vā suddo vā’ti; so evaṃ vadeyya – ‘na tāvāhaṃ imaṃ sallaṃ āharissāmi yāva na taṃ purisaṃ jānāmi yenamhi viddho, evaṃnāmo evaṃgotto iti vā’ti; so evaṃ vadeyya – ‘na tāvāhaṃ imaṃ sallaṃ āharissāmi yāva na taṃ purisaṃ jānāmi yenamhi viddho, dīgho vā rasso vā majjhimo vā’ti; so evaṃ vadeyya – ‘na tāvāhaṃ imaṃ sallaṃ āharissāmi yāva na taṃ purisaṃ jānāmi yenamhi viddho, kāḷo vā sāmo vā maṅguracchavī vā’ti; so evaṃ vadeyya – ‘na tāvāhaṃ imaṃ sallaṃ āharissāmi yāva na taṃ purisaṃ jānāmi yenamhi viddho, amukasmiṃ gāme [M 2.0093] vā nigame vā nagare vā’ti; so evaṃ vadeyya – ‘na tāvāhaṃ imaṃ sallaṃ āharissāmi yāva na taṃ dhanuṃ jānāmi yenamhi viddho, yadi vā cāpo yadi vā kodaṇḍo’ti; so evaṃ vadeyya – ‘na tāvāhaṃ imaṃ sallaṃ āharissāmi yāva na taṃ jiyaṃ jānāmi yāyamhi viddho[T 2.0149], yadi vā akkassa yadi vā saṇhassa saṇṭhassa (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) yadi vā nhārussa yadi vā maruvāya yadi vā khīrapaṇṇino’ti; so evaṃ vadeyya – ‘na tāvāhaṃ imaṃ sallaṃ āharissāmi yāva na taṃ kaṇḍaṃ jānāmi yenamhi viddho, yadi vā gacchaṃ yadi vā ropima’nti; so evaṃ vadeyya – ‘na tāvāhaṃ imaṃ sallaṃ āharissāmi yāva na taṃ kaṇḍaṃ jānāmi yenamhi viddho, yassa pattehi vājitaṃ vākhittaṃ (ka.) yadi vā gijjhassa yadi vā kaṅkassa yadi vā kulalassa yadi vā morassa yadi vā sithilahanuno’ti; so evaṃ vadeyya – ‘na tāvāhaṃ imaṃ sallaṃ āharissāmi yāva na taṃ kaṇḍaṃ jānāmi yenamhi viddho, yassa nhārunā parikkhittaṃ yadi vā gavassa yadi vā mahiṃsassa yadi vā bheravassa roruvassa (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) yadi vā semhārassā’ti; so evaṃ vadeyya – ‘na tāvāhaṃ imaṃ sallaṃ āharissāmi yāva na taṃ sallaṃ jānāmi yenamhi viddho, yadi vā sallaṃ yadi vā khurappaṃ yadi vā vekaṇḍaṃ yadi vā nārācaṃ yadi vā vacchadantaṃ yadi vā karavīrapatta’nti [P 1.0430] – aññātameva taṃ, mālukyaputta, tena purisena assa, atha so puriso kālaṃ kareyya. Evameva kho, mālukyaputta, yo evaṃ vadeyya – ‘na tāvāhaṃ bhagavati brahmacariyaṃ carissāmi yāva me bhagavā na byākarissati – “sassato loko”ti vā “asassato loko”ti [T 2.0150] vā…pe… “neva hoti na na hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā”ti vāti – abyākatameva taṃ, mālukyaputta, tathāgatena assa, atha so puggalo kālaṅkareyya.

126. “Mālukyaputta, should anyone say thus: ‘I will not practice the holy life under the Blessed One so long as the Blessed One does not declare to me whether “the world is eternal” or “the world is not eternal”… or whether “a Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death,”’—that matter would remain undeclared by the Tathāgata, Mālukyaputta, and in the meantime that person would die. Suppose, Mālukyaputta, a man were pierced by an arrow thickly smeared with poison. His friends and companions, his kinsmen and relatives, would provide a surgeon to remove the arrow. But the man would say: ‘I will not have this arrow removed until I know whether the man who shot me was a khattiya, a brahmin, a vessa, or a sudda.’ He would say: ‘I will not have this arrow removed until I know the name and clan of the man who shot me.’ He would say: ‘I will not have this arrow removed until I know whether the man who shot me was tall, short, or of medium height.’ He would say: ‘I will not have this arrow removed until I know whether the man who shot me was dark, brown, or golden-skinned.’ He would say: ‘I will not have this arrow removed until I know whether the man who shot me was from such and such a village, market town, or city.’ He would say: ‘I will not have this arrow removed until I know whether the bow that wounded me was a longbow or a crossbow.’ He would say: ‘I will not have this arrow removed until I know whether the bowstring was made of swallow-wort, or of hemp, or of sinew, or of sansevieria, or of a milk-creeper.’ He would say: ‘I will not have this arrow removed until I know whether the arrow shaft was from a wild or a cultivated plant.’ He would say: ‘I will not have this arrow removed until I know with what kind of feathers the arrow shaft was fletched—whether of a vulture, a heron, a hawk, a peacock, or a stork.’ He would say: ‘I will not have this arrow removed until I know with what kind of sinew the arrow shaft was wrapped—whether of an ox, a buffalo, a black lion, or a monkey.’ He would say: ‘I will not have this arrow removed until I know what kind of arrowhead it was—whether an ordinary one, a razor-arrow, a barbed arrow, an iron-tipped arrow, a calf’s-tooth arrow, or an oleander-leaf arrow.’—Mālukyaputta, that would remain unknown to the man, and in the meantime that man would die. In the same way, Mālukyaputta, should anyone say thus: ‘I will not practice the holy life under the Blessed One so long as the Blessed One does not declare to me whether “the world is eternal” or “the world is not eternal”… or whether “a Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death,”’—that matter would remain undeclared by the Tathāgata, Mālukyaputta, and in the meantime that person would die.”

127. “‘Sassato loko’ti, mālukyaputta, diṭṭhiyā sati brahmacariyavāso abhavissāti[V 2.0101], evaṃ ‘no asassato loko’ti, mālukyaputta, diṭṭhiyā sati brahmacariyavāso abhavissāti, evampi ‘no sassato loko’ti vā, mālukyaputta, diṭṭhiyā sati, ‘asassato loko’ti vā diṭṭhiyā sati attheva jāti, atthi jarā, atthi maraṇaṃ, santi sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā; yesāhaṃ diṭṭheva dhamme nighātaṃ paññapemi[M 2.0094]. ‘Antavā loko’ti, mālukyaputta, diṭṭhiyā sati brahmacariyavāso abhavissāti, evaṃ ‘no anantavā loko’ti, mālukyaputta, diṭṭhiyā sati brahmacariyavāso abhavissāti, evampi ‘no antavā loko’ti vā, mālukyaputta, diṭṭhiyā sati, ‘anantavā loko’ti vā diṭṭhiyā sati attheva jāti, atthi jarā, atthi maraṇaṃ, santi sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā; yesāhaṃ diṭṭheva dhamme nighātaṃ paññapemi. ‘Taṃ jīvaṃ taṃ sarīra’nti, mālukyaputta, diṭṭhiyā sati brahmacariyavāso [T 2.0151] abhavissāti, evaṃ ‘no aññaṃ jīvaṃ aññaṃ sarīra’nti, mālukyaputta, diṭṭhiyā sati brahmacariyavāso abhavissāti, evampi ‘no taṃ jīvaṃ taṃ sarīra’nti vā, mālukyaputta, diṭṭhiyā sati, ‘aññaṃ jīvaṃ aññaṃ sarīra’nti vā diṭṭhiyā sati attheva jāti…pe… nighātaṃ paññapemi. ‘Hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā’ti, mālukyaputta, diṭṭhiyā sati brahmacariyavāso abhavissāti, evaṃ ‘no na hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā’ti, mālukyaputta, diṭṭhiyā sati brahmacariyavāso abhavissāti, evampi ‘no hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā’ti vā, mālukyaputta, diṭṭhiyā sati, ‘na hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā’ti vā diṭṭhiyā sati attheva jāti…pe… [P 1.0431] yesāhaṃ diṭṭheva dhamme nighātaṃ paññapemi. ‘Hoti ca na ca hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā’ti, mālukyaputta, diṭṭhiyā sati brahmacariyavāso abhavissāti, evaṃ ‘no neva hoti na na hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā’ti, mālukyaputta, diṭṭhiyā sati brahmacariyavāso abhavissāti, evampi ‘no hoti ca na ca hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā’ti, mālukyaputta, diṭṭhiyā sati, ‘neva hoti na na hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā’ti vā diṭṭhiyā sati attheva jāti…pe… yesāhaṃ diṭṭheva dhamme nighātaṃ paññapemi.

127. Mālukyaputta, if there were the view, 'the world is eternal,' it is not on that account that the holy life would be lived. If there were the view, 'the world is not eternal,' it is not on that account that the holy life would be lived. For whether there is the view, 'the world is eternal,' or the view, 'the world is not eternal,' there is still birth, there is aging, there is death, there are sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, for which I declare the destruction in this very life. Mālukyaputta, if there were the view, 'the world is finite,' it is not on that account that the holy life would be lived. If there were the view, 'the world is infinite,' it is not on that account that the holy life would be lived. For whether there is the view, 'the world is finite,' or the view, 'the world is infinite,' there is still birth, there is aging, there is death, there are sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, for which I declare the destruction in this very life. Mālukyaputta, if there were the view, 'the life principle and the body are the same,' it is not on that account that the holy life would be lived. If there were the view, 'the life principle is one thing and the body another,' it is not on that account that the holy life would be lived. For whether there is the view, 'the life principle and the body are the same,' or the view, 'the life principle is one thing and the body another,' there is still birth... for which I declare the destruction in this very life. Mālukyaputta, if there were the view, 'a being exists after death,' it is not on that account that the holy life would be lived. If there were the view, 'a being does not exist after death,' it is not on that account that the holy life would be lived. For whether there is the view, 'a being exists after death,' or the view, 'a being does not exist after death,' there is still birth... for which I declare the destruction in this very life. Mālukyaputta, if there were the view, 'a being both exists and does not exist after death,' it is not on that account that the holy life would be lived. If there were the view, 'a being neither exists nor does not exist after death,' it is not on that account that the holy life would be lived. For whether there is the view, 'a being both exists and does not exist after death,' or the view, 'a being neither exists nor does not exist after death,' there is still birth... for which I declare the destruction in this very life.

128. “Tasmātiha, mālukyaputta, abyākatañca me abyākatato [T 2.0152] dhāretha; byākatañca me byākatato dhāretha. Kiñca, mālukyaputta, mayā abyākataṃ? ‘Sassato loko’ti mālukyaputta, mayā abyākataṃ; ‘asassato loko’ti – mayā abyākataṃ; ‘antavā loko’ti – mayā abyākataṃ; ‘anantavā loko’ti – mayā abyākataṃ; ‘taṃ jīvaṃ taṃ sarīra’nti [V 2.0102] – mayā abyākataṃ; ‘aññaṃ jīvaṃ aññaṃ sarīra’nti – mayā abyākataṃ; ‘hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā’ti – mayā abyākataṃ; ‘na hoti tathāgato paraṃ [M 2.0095] maraṇā’ti – mayā abyākataṃ; ‘hoti ca na ca hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā’ti – mayā abyākataṃ; ‘neva hoti na na hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā’ti – mayā abyākataṃ. Kasmā cetaṃ, mālukyaputta, mayā abyākataṃ? Na hetaṃ, mālukyaputta, atthasaṃhitaṃ na ādibrahmacariyakaṃ na netaṃ (sī.) nibbidāya na virāgāya na nirodhāya na upasamāya na abhiññāya na sambodhāya na nibbānāya saṃvattati. Tasmā taṃ mayā abyākataṃ. Kiñca, mālukyaputta, mayā byākataṃ? ‘Idaṃ dukkha’nti, mālukyaputta, mayā byākataṃ; ‘ayaṃ dukkhasamudayo’ti – mayā byākataṃ; ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodho’ti – mayā byākataṃ; ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti – mayā byākataṃ. Kasmā cetaṃ, mālukyaputta, mayā byākataṃ? Etañhi, mālukyaputta, atthasaṃhitaṃ etaṃ ādibrahmacariyakaṃ nibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya upasamāya abhiññāya sambodhāya nibbānāya saṃvattati. Tasmā taṃ mayā byākataṃ. Tasmātiha, mālukyaputta[P 1.0432], abyākatañca me [T 2.0153] abyākatato dhāretha; byākatañca me byākatato dhārethā”ti.

128. Therefore, Mālukyaputta, remember what I have not declared as undeclared, and what I have declared as declared. And what, Mālukyaputta, have I not declared? ‘The world is eternal’—this I have not declared. ‘The world is not eternal’—this I have not declared. ‘The world is finite’—this I have not declared. ‘The world is infinite’—this I have not declared. ‘The life principle and the body are the same’—this I have not declared. ‘The life principle is one thing and the body another’—this I have not declared. ‘After death a being exists’—this I have not declared. ‘After death a being does not exist’—this I have not declared. ‘After death a being both exists and does not exist’—this I have not declared. ‘After death a being neither exists nor does not exist’—this I have not declared. And why, Mālukyaputta, have I not declared this? Because it is not connected with the goal, it is not fundamental to the holy life, it does not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to Nibbāna. Therefore I have not declared it. And what, Mālukyaputta, have I declared? ‘This is suffering’—this I have declared. ‘This is the origin of suffering’—this I have declared. ‘This is the cessation of suffering’—this I have declared. ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering’—this I have declared. And why, Mālukyaputta, have I declared this? Because it is connected with the goal, it is fundamental to the holy life, it leads to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to Nibbāna. Therefore I have declared it. Therefore, Mālukyaputta, remember what I have not declared as undeclared, and what I have declared as declared.

Idamavoca bhagavā. Attamano āyasmā mālukyaputto bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandīti.

The Blessed One said this. The Venerable Mālukyaputta, pleased, rejoiced at the Blessed One's words.

Cūḷamālukyasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ tatiyaṃ.

The Shorter Discourse to Mālukyaputta, the third, is concluded.

4. Mahāmālukyasuttaṃ

4. The Greater Discourse to Mālukya

129. Evaṃ [T 2.0154][V 2.0103] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme. Tatra kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi – “bhikkhavo”ti. “Bhadante”ti te bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosuṃ. Bhagavā etadavoca – “dhāretha no tumhe, bhikkhave, mayā desitāni pañcorambhāgiyāni saṃyojanānī”ti?

129. Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!” “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, do you bear in mind the five lower fetters taught by me?”

Evaṃ vutte, āyasmā mālukyaputto bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “ahaṃ kho, bhante, dhāremi bhagavatā desitāni pañcorambhāgiyāni saṃyojanānī”ti. “Yathā kathaṃ pana tvaṃ, mālukyaputta, dhāresi mayā desitāni pañcorambhāgiyāni saṃyojanānī”ti? “Sakkāyadiṭṭhiṃ kho ahaṃ, bhante, bhagavatā orambhāgiyaṃ [M 2.0096] saṃyojanaṃ desitaṃ dhāremi; vicikicchaṃ kho ahaṃ, bhante, bhagavatā orambhāgiyaṃ saṃyojanaṃ desitaṃ dhāremi; sīlabbataparāmāsaṃ kho ahaṃ, bhante, bhagavatā orambhāgiyaṃ saṃyojanaṃ desitaṃ dhāremi; kāmacchandaṃ kho ahaṃ, bhante, bhagavatā orambhāgiyaṃ saṃyojanaṃ desitaṃ dhāremi; byāpādaṃ kho ahaṃ, bhante, bhagavatā orambhāgiyaṃ saṃyojanaṃ desitaṃ dhāremi. Evaṃ kho ahaṃ, bhante, dhāremi bhagavatā desitāni pañcorambhāgiyāni saṃyojanānī”ti.

When this was said, the Venerable Mālukyaputta said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, I bear in mind the five lower fetters taught by the Blessed One.” “But how, Mālukyaputta, do you bear in mind the five lower fetters taught by me?” “Venerable sir, I bear in mind identity view as a lower fetter taught by the Blessed One; I bear in mind doubt as a lower fetter taught by the Blessed One; I bear in mind clinging to rules and observances as a lower fetter taught by the Blessed One; I bear in mind sensual desire as a lower fetter taught by the Blessed One; I bear in mind ill will as a lower fetter taught by the Blessed One. Thus, venerable sir, I bear in mind the five lower fetters taught by the Blessed One.”

“Kassa kho nāma tvaṃ, mālukyaputta, imāni evaṃ pañcorambhāgiyāni saṃyojanāni desitāni dhāresi? Nanu, mālukyaputta[T 2.0155], aññatitthiyā paribbājakā iminā taruṇūpamena upārambhena upārambhissanti? Daharassa hi, mālukyaputta, kumārassa mandassa uttānaseyyakassa sakkāyotipi na hoti, kuto [P 1.0433] panassa uppajjissati sakkāyadiṭṭhi? Anusetvevassa anuseti tvevassa (sī. pī.) sakkāyadiṭṭhānusayo. Daharassa hi, mālukyaputta, kumārassa mandassa uttānaseyyakassa dhammātipi na hoti, kuto panassa uppajjissati dhammesu vicikicchā? Anusetvevassa vicikicchānusayo. Daharassa hi, mālukyaputta, kumārassa mandassa uttānaseyyakassa sīlātipi na hoti, kuto panassa uppajjissati sīlesu sīlabbataparāmāso? Anusetvevassa sīlabbataparāmāsānusayo[V 2.0104]. Daharassa hi, mālukyaputta, kumārassa mandassa uttānaseyyakassa kāmātipi na hoti, kuto panassa uppajjissati kāmesu kāmacchando? Anusetvevassa kāmarāgānusayo. Daharassa hi, mālukyaputta, kumārassa mandassa uttānaseyyakassa sattātipi na hoti, kuto panassa uppajjissati sattesu byāpādo? Anusetvevassa byāpādānusayo. Nanu, mālukyaputta, aññatitthiyā paribbājakā iminā taruṇūpamena upārambhena upārambhissantī”ti? Evaṃ vutte, āyasmā ānando bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “etassa, bhagavā, kālo, etassa, sugata, kālo yaṃ bhagavā pañcorambhāgiyāni saṃyojanāni deseyya. Bhagavato sutvā bhikkhū dhāressantī”ti. “Tena hānanda, suṇāhi, sādhukaṃ manasi karohi; bhāsissāmī”ti. “Evaṃ, bhante”ti kho āyasmā [T 2.0156] ānando bhagavato paccassosi. Bhagavā etadavoca –

“Mālukyaputta, from whom do you bear in mind these five lower fetters as having been taught in this way? Will not the wanderers of other sects reproach you with this analogy of the tender infant? For, Mālukyaputta, a young, tender infant lying on its back does not even have the notion of ‘identity,’ so how could identity view arise in him? Yet the underlying tendency to identity view lies latent in him. A young, tender infant lying on its back does not even have the notion of ‘phenomena,’ so how could doubt about phenomena arise in him? Yet the underlying tendency to doubt lies latent in him. A young, tender infant lying on its back does not even have the notion of ‘precepts,’ so how could clinging to rules and observances regarding precepts arise in him? Yet the underlying tendency to clinging to rules and observances lies latent in him. A young, tender infant lying on its back does not even have the notion of ‘sensual pleasures,’ so how could sensual desire for sensual pleasures arise in him? Yet the underlying tendency to sensual lust lies latent in him. A young, tender infant lying on its back does not even have the notion of ‘beings,’ so how could ill will towards beings arise in him? Yet the underlying tendency to ill will lies latent in him. Will not the wanderers of other sects, Mālukyaputta, reproach you with this analogy of the tender infant?” When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, this is the time! Sugata, this is the time for the Blessed One to teach the five lower fetters. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will bear it in mind.” “Then, Ānanda, listen and attend carefully. I will speak.” “Yes, venerable sir,” the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:

130. “Idhānanda[M 2.0097], assutavā puthujjano ariyānaṃ adassāvī ariyadhammassa akovido ariyadhamme avinīto, sappurisānaṃ adassāvī sappurisadhammassa akovido sappurisadhamme avinīto sakkāyadiṭṭhipariyuṭṭhitena cetasā viharati sakkāyadiṭṭhiparetena; uppannāya ca sakkāyadiṭṭhiyā nissaraṇaṃ yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti. Tassa sā sakkāyadiṭṭhi thāmagatā appaṭivinītā orambhāgiyaṃ saṃyojanaṃ. Vicikicchāpariyuṭṭhitena cetasā viharati vicikicchāparetena; uppannāya ca vicikicchāya nissaraṇaṃ yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti. Tassa sā vicikicchā thāmagatā appaṭivinītā orambhāgiyaṃ saṃyojanaṃ. Sīlabbataparāmāsapariyuṭṭhitena cetasā viharati sīlabbataparāmāsaparetena; uppannassa ca sīlabbataparāmāsassa nissaraṇaṃ yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti. Tassa so sīlabbataparāmāso thāmagato appaṭivinīto orambhāgiyaṃ saṃyojanaṃ. Kāmarāgapariyuṭṭhitena cetasā viharati kāmarāgaparetena[P 1.0434]; uppannassa ca kāmarāgassa nissaraṇaṃ yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti. Tassa so kāmarāgo thāmagato appaṭivinīto orambhāgiyaṃ saṃyojanaṃ. Byāpādapariyuṭṭhitena cetasā viharati byāpādaparetena; uppannassa ca byāpādassa nissaraṇaṃ yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti. Tassa so byāpādo thāmagato appaṭivinīto orambhāgiyaṃ saṃyojanaṃ.

130. “Here, Ānanda, an uninstructed ordinary person, who has not seen the noble ones, is unskilled in the Noble Dhamma, and undisciplined in the Noble Dhamma; who has not seen the true persons, is unskilled in the Dhamma of the true persons, and undisciplined in the Dhamma of the true persons, dwells with a mind obsessed and pervaded by identity view; and he does not understand as it truly is the escape from the arisen identity view. That identity view of his, having become strong and not removed, is a lower fetter. He dwells with a mind obsessed and pervaded by doubt; and he does not understand as it truly is the escape from arisen doubt. That doubt of his, having become strong and not removed, is a lower fetter. He dwells with a mind obsessed and pervaded by clinging to rules and observances; and he does not understand as it truly is the escape from arisen clinging to rules and observances. That clinging to rules and observances of his, having become strong and not removed, is a lower fetter. He dwells with a mind obsessed and pervaded by sensual lust; and he does not understand as it truly is the escape from arisen sensual lust. That sensual lust of his, having become strong and not removed, is a lower fetter. He dwells with a mind obsessed and pervaded by ill will; and he does not understand as it truly is the escape from arisen ill will. That ill will of his, having become strong and not removed, is a lower fetter.”

131. “Sutavā ca kho, ānanda, ariyasāvako [T 2.0157] ariyānaṃ dassāvī ariyadhammassa kovido [V 2.0105] ariyadhamme suvinīto, sappurisānaṃ dassāvī sappurisadhammassa kovido sappurisadhamme suvinīto na sakkāyadiṭṭhipariyuṭṭhitena cetasā viharati na sakkāyadiṭṭhiparetena; uppannāya ca sakkāyadiṭṭhiyā nissaraṇaṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Tassa sā sakkāyadiṭṭhi sānusayā pahīyati. Na vicikicchāpariyuṭṭhitena cetasā viharati na vicikicchāparetena; uppannāya ca vicikicchāya nissaraṇaṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Tassa sā vicikicchā sānusayā pahīyati. Na sīlabbataparāmāsapariyuṭṭhitena cetasā viharati na sīlabbataparāmāsaparetena; uppannassa ca sīlabbataparāmāsassa nissaraṇaṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Tassa so sīlabbataparāmāso sānusayo pahīyati. Na kāmarāgapariyuṭṭhitena cetasā viharati na kāmarāgaparetena; uppannassa ca kāmarāgassa nissaraṇaṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Tassa so kāmarāgo sānusayo pahīyati[M 2.0098]. Na byāpādapariyuṭṭhitena cetasā viharati na byāpādaparetena; uppannassa ca byāpādassa nissaraṇaṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Tassa so byāpādo sānusayo pahīyati.

131. Indeed, Ānanda, a learned noble disciple—who is accustomed to seeing the noble ones, is skilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones, and well-trained in the Dhamma of the noble ones; who is accustomed to seeing true persons, is skilled in the Dhamma of true persons, and well-trained in the Dhamma of true persons—does not dwell with a mind beset and overcome by identity view; and he understands as it really is the escape from an arisen identity view. That identity view of his is abandoned along with its underlying tendency. He does not dwell with a mind beset and overcome by doubt; and he understands as it really is the escape from an arisen doubt. That doubt of his is abandoned along with its underlying tendency. He does not dwell with a mind beset and overcome by clinging to rules and observances; and he understands as it really is the escape from an arisen clinging to rules and observances. That clinging to rules and observances of his is abandoned along with its underlying tendency. He does not dwell with a mind beset and overcome by sensual lust; and he understands as it really is the escape from an arisen sensual lust. That sensual lust of his is abandoned along with its underlying tendency. He does not dwell with a mind beset and overcome by ill will; and he understands as it really is the escape from an arisen ill will. That ill will of his is abandoned along with its underlying tendency.

132. “Yo, ānanda, maggo yā paṭipadā pañcannaṃ orambhāgiyānaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ pahānāya taṃ maggaṃ taṃ paṭipadaṃ anāgamma pañcorambhāgiyāni saṃyojanāni ñassati vā dakkhati vā pajahissati vāti – netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Seyyathāpi, ānanda, mahato rukkhassa tiṭṭhato [T 2.0158] sāravato tacaṃ acchetvā phegguṃ acchetvā sāracchedo bhavissatīti – netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati; evameva kho, ānanda, yo maggo yā paṭipadā pañcannaṃ orambhāgiyānaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ pahānāya taṃ maggaṃ taṃ paṭipadaṃ anāgamma pañcorambhāgiyāni saṃyojanāni ñassati vā dakkhati vā pajahissati vāti – netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati.

132. Ānanda, that one might know, see, or abandon the five lower fetters without having approached the path and the practice for the abandoning of the five lower fetters—this is not possible. Just as, Ānanda, for a great, standing, heartwood-possessing tree, that a cutting of the heartwood would occur without cutting the bark and without cutting the sapwood—this is not possible; even so, Ānanda, that one might know, see, or abandon the five lower fetters without having approached the path and the practice for the abandoning of the five lower fetters—this is not possible.

“Yo ca kho, ānanda, maggo yā paṭipadā pañcannaṃ orambhāgiyānaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ pahānāya taṃ [P 1.0435] maggaṃ taṃ paṭipadaṃ āgamma pañcorambhāgiyāni saṃyojanāni ñassati vā dakkhati vā pajahissati vāti – ṭhānametaṃ vijjati. Seyyathāpi, ānanda, mahato rukkhassa tiṭṭhato sāravato tacaṃ chetvā phegguṃ chetvā sāracchedo bhavissatīti – ṭhānametaṃ vijjati; evameva kho, ānanda, yo maggo yā paṭipadā pañcannaṃ orambhāgiyānaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ pahānāya taṃ maggaṃ taṃ paṭipadaṃ āgamma pañcorambhāgiyāni saṃyojanāni ñassati vā dakkhati vā pajahissati vāti – ṭhānametaṃ vijjati. Seyyathāpi, ānanda, gaṅgā nadī pūrā udakassa samatittikā [V 2.0106] kākapeyyā. Atha dubbalako puriso āgaccheyya – ‘ahaṃ imissā gaṅgāya nadiyā tiriyaṃ bāhāya sotaṃ chetvā sotthinā pāraṃ gacchissāmī’ti gacchāmīti (sī. pī.); so na sakkuṇeyya gaṅgāya nadiyā tiriyaṃ bāhāya sotaṃ chetvā sotthinā pāraṃ gantuṃ. Evameva kho, ānanda, yesaṃ kesañci yassa kassaci (sabbattha) sakkāyanirodhāya dhamme desiyamāne cittaṃ na pakkhandati nappasīdati na santiṭṭhati na vimuccati; seyyathāpi [T 2.0159] so dubbalako puriso evamete daṭṭhabbā. Seyyathāpi, ānanda, gaṅgā nadī pūrā udakassa samatittikā kākapeyyā. Atha balavā puriso āgaccheyya – ‘ahaṃ imissā gaṅgāya nadiyā tiriyaṃ bāhāya [M 2.0099] sotaṃ chetvā sotthinā pāraṃ gacchissāmī’ti; so sakkuṇeyya gaṅgāya nadiyā tiriyaṃ bāhāya sotaṃ chetvā sotthinā pāraṃ gantuṃ. Evameva kho, ānanda, yesaṃ kesañci sakkāyanirodhāya dhamme desiyamāne cittaṃ pakkhandati pasīdati santiṭṭhati vimuccati; seyyathāpi so balavā puriso evamete daṭṭhabbā.

And indeed, Ānanda, that by approaching the path and the practice for the abandoning of the five lower fetters, one might know, see, or abandon the five lower fetters—this is possible. Just as, Ānanda, for a great, standing, heartwood-possessing tree, that a cutting of the heartwood will occur after cutting the bark and cutting the sapwood—this is possible; even so, Ānanda, that by approaching the path and the practice for the abandoning of the five lower fetters, one might know, see, or abandon the five lower fetters—this is possible. Suppose, Ānanda, the river Ganges were full of water, level with its banks, so that a crow could drink from it. Then a weak man were to come, saying: ‘By cutting the current across with my arms, I will cross this river Ganges and safely reach the other shore.’ He would not be able to cut the current of the river Ganges across with his arms and safely get to the other shore. Even so, Ānanda, when the Dhamma is being taught for the cessation of identity, there are some whose minds do not leap forward, do not become clear, do not settle, and are not released; they should be regarded like that weak man. Suppose, Ānanda, the river Ganges were full of water, level with its banks, so that a crow could drink from it. Then a strong man were to come, saying: ‘By cutting the current across with my arms, I will cross this river Ganges and safely reach the other shore.’ He would be able to cut the current of the river Ganges across with his arms and safely get to the other shore. Even so, Ānanda, when the Dhamma is being taught for the cessation of identity, there are some whose minds leap forward, become clear, settle, and are released; they should be regarded like that strong man.

133. “Katamo cānanda, maggo, katamā paṭipadā pañcannaṃ orambhāgiyānaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ pahānāya? Idhānanda, bhikkhu upadhivivekā akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānā sabbaso kāyaduṭṭhullānaṃ paṭippassaddhiyā vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. So yadeva tattha hoti rūpagataṃ vedanāgataṃ saññāgataṃ saṅkhāragataṃ viññāṇagataṃ te dhamme aniccato dukkhato rogato gaṇḍato sallato aghato ābādhato parato palokato suññato anattato samanupassati. So tehi dhammehi cittaṃ paṭivāpeti paṭipāpeti (syā.), patiṭṭhāpeti (ka.). So tehi dhammehi cittaṃ paṭivāpetvā amatāya dhātuyā [P 1.0436] cittaṃ upasaṃharati – ‘etaṃ santaṃ etaṃ paṇītaṃ yadidaṃ sabbasaṅkhārasamatho sabbūpadhipaṭinissaggo [T 2.0160] taṇhākkhayo virāgo nirodho nibbāna’nti. So tattha ṭhito āsavānaṃ khayaṃ pāpuṇāti; no ce āsavānaṃ khayaṃ pāpuṇāti teneva dhammarāgena tāya dhammanandiyā pañcannaṃ orambhāgiyānaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ parikkhayā opapātiko hoti, tattha parinibbāyī, anāvattidhammo tasmā lokā. Ayampi kho, ānanda, maggo ayaṃ paṭipadā pañcannaṃ orambhāgiyānaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ pahānāya.

133. “And what, Ānanda, is the path, what is the practice for the abandoning of the five lower fetters? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, due to seclusion from the substrates of existence, for the abandoning of unwholesome states, for the complete calming of bodily inertia, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. He regards whatever phenomena there that pertain to form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a boil, as a dart, as a calamity, as an affliction, as other, as perishable, as empty, as not-self. He turns his mind away from those phenomena. Having turned his mind away from those phenomena, he directs it to the deathless element: ‘This is peaceful, this is sublime, that is, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all substrates, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.’ Established therein, he attains the destruction of the taints. But if he does not attain the destruction of the taints, then through that very delight in the Dhamma, that joy in the Dhamma, with the utter destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one who is spontaneously reborn, and there he attains final Nibbāna, being of the nature of not returning from that world. This, Ānanda, is indeed the path, this is the practice for the abandoning of the five lower fetters.”

“Puna caparaṃ, ānanda, bhikkhu vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā…pe… [T 2.0161] dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati… [V 2.0107] tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ… catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. So yadeva tattha hoti rūpagataṃ vedanāgataṃ saññāgataṃ saṅkhāragataṃ viññāṇagataṃ… anāvattidhammo tasmā lokā. Ayampi kho, ānanda, maggo ayaṃ paṭipadā pañcannaṃ orambhāgiyānaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ pahānāya.

“Furthermore, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, with the calming of thought and examination… enters and dwells in the second jhāna… the third jhāna… the fourth jhāna. He regards whatever phenomena there that pertain to form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness… he is of the nature of not returning from that world. This too, Ānanda, is indeed the path, this is the practice for the abandoning of the five lower fetters.”

“Puna caparaṃ, ānanda, bhikkhu sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ samatikkamā paṭighasaññānaṃ atthaṅgamā nānattasaññānaṃ amanasikārā ‘ananto ākāso’ti ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati. So yadeva tattha hoti vedanāgataṃ [M 2.0100] saññāgataṃ saṅkhāragataṃ viññāṇagataṃ…pe… [T 2.0162] anāvattidhammo tasmā lokā. Ayampi kho, ānanda, maggo ayaṃ paṭipadā pañcannaṃ orambhāgiyānaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ pahānāya.

“Furthermore, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, with the complete transcending of perceptions of form, with the cessation of perceptions of resistance, and by not attending to perceptions of diversity, aware that ‘space is infinite,’ enters and dwells in the base of the infinity of space. He regards whatever phenomena there that pertain to feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness… he is of the nature of not returning from that world. This too, Ānanda, is indeed the path, this is the practice for the abandoning of the five lower fetters.”

“Puna caparaṃ, ānanda, bhikkhu sabbaso ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma ‘anantaṃ viññāṇa’nti viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati. So yadeva tattha hoti vedanāgataṃ saññāgataṃ saṅkhāragataṃ viññāṇagataṃ…pe… [V 2.0108] anāvattidhammo tasmā lokā. Ayampi kho, ānanda, maggo ayaṃ paṭipadā pañcannaṃ orambhāgiyānaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ pahānāya.

“Furthermore, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, by completely transcending the base of the infinity of space, aware that ‘consciousness is infinite,’ enters and dwells in the base of the infinity of consciousness. He regards whatever phenomena there that pertain to feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness… he is of the nature of not returning from that world. This too, Ānanda, is indeed the path, this is the practice for the abandoning of the five lower fetters.”

“Puna caparaṃ, ānanda, bhikkhu sabbaso viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma ‘natthi kiñcī’ti ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati. So yadeva tattha hoti vedanāgataṃ saññāgataṃ saṅkhāragataṃ viññāṇagataṃ…pe… [P 1.0437] anāvattidhammo tasmā lokā. Ayampi kho, ānanda, maggo ayaṃ paṭipadā pañcannaṃ orambhāgiyānaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ pahānāyā”ti.

“Furthermore, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, by completely transcending the base of the infinity of consciousness, aware that ‘there is nothing,’ enters and dwells in the base of nothingness. He regards whatever phenomena there that pertain to feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness… he is of the nature of not returning from that world. This too, Ānanda, is indeed the path, this is the practice for the abandoning of the five lower fetters.”

“Eso ce, bhante, maggo esā paṭipadā pañcannaṃ orambhāgiyānaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ pahānāya, atha kiñcarahi idhekacce bhikkhū cetovimuttino ekacce bhikkhū paññāvimuttino”ti? “Ettha kho panesāhaṃ ettha kho tesāhaṃ (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.), ānanda, indriyavemattataṃ vadāmī”ti.

“Venerable sir, if this is the path and this is the practice for the abandoning of the five lower fetters, then why is it that here some bhikkhus are liberated through mind, while some bhikkhus are liberated through wisdom?” “In this regard, Ānanda, I declare that there is a diversity of faculties.”

Idamavoca bhagavā. Attamano āyasmā ānando bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandīti.

The Blessed One said this. The Venerable Ānanda, gratified, rejoiced at the Blessed One’s words.

Mahāmālukyasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ catutthaṃ.

The Great Discourse to Mālukya, the fourth, is concluded.

5. Bhaddālisuttaṃ

5. The Bhaddāli Sutta

134. Evaṃ [T 2.0163][V 2.0109] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme. Tatra kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi – “bhikkhavo”ti. “Bhadante”ti te bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosuṃ. Bhagavā etadavoca – “ahaṃ kho, bhikkhave, ekāsanabhojanaṃ bhuñjāmi; ekāsanabhojanaṃ kho, ahaṃ, bhikkhave, bhuñjamāno appābādhatañca sañjānāmi [M 2.0101] appātaṅkatañca lahuṭṭhānañca balañca phāsuvihārañca. Etha, tumhepi, bhikkhave, ekāsanabhojanaṃ bhuñjatha; ekāsanabhojanaṃ kho, bhikkhave, tumhepi bhuñjamānā appābādhatañca sañjānissatha appātaṅkatañca lahuṭṭhānañca balañca phāsuvihārañcā”ti. Evaṃ vutte, āyasmā bhaddāli bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “ahaṃ kho, bhante, na ussahāmi ekāsanabhojanaṃ bhuñjituṃ; ekāsanabhojanañhi me, bhante, bhuñjato siyā kukkuccaṃ, siyā vippaṭisāro”ti. “Tena hi tvaṃ, bhaddāli, yattha nimantito assasi tattha ekadesaṃ bhuñjitvā ekadesaṃ nīharitvāpi bhuñjeyyāsi. Evampi kho [P 1.0438] tvaṃ, bhaddāli, bhuñjamāno ekāsano yāpessasī”ti bhuñjamāno yāpessasīti (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.). “Evampi kho ahaṃ, bhante, na ussahāmi bhuñjituṃ; evampi hi me, bhante, bhuñjato siyā kukkuccaṃ, siyā vippaṭisāro”ti. Atha kho āyasmā bhaddāli bhagavatā sikkhāpade paññāpiyamāne bhikkhusaṅghe sikkhaṃ samādiyamāne anussāhaṃ pavedesi. Atha [T 2.0164] kho āyasmā bhaddāli sabbaṃ taṃ temāsaṃ na bhagavato sammukhībhāvaṃ adāsi, yathā taṃ satthusāsane sikkhāya aparipūrakārī.

134. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks!" "Venerable sir," those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: "Monks, I eat a one-sitting meal; eating a one-sitting meal, I know freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, lightness, strength, and a comfortable abiding. Come, monks, you too eat a one-sitting meal; eating a one-sitting meal, you too will know freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, lightness, strength, and a comfortable abiding." When this was said, the Venerable Bhaddāli said to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, I am unable to eat a one-sitting meal. For if I were to eat a one-sitting meal, I might have scruples and remorse." "Then, Bhaddāli, when you are invited somewhere, you may eat part of it there and, having carried a portion away, eat it also. Even eating in this way, Bhaddāli, you will carry on as one who eats in a single session." "Even in this way, Venerable sir, I am unable to eat. Even eating like this, I might have scruples and remorse." Then, when the Blessed One was laying down a training rule and the Saṅgha of monks was undertaking the training, the Venerable Bhaddāli declared his unwillingness. And so, for that entire three-month period, the Venerable Bhaddāli did not present himself before the Blessed One, just like one who does not fulfill the training in the Teacher's dispensation.

135. Tena kho pana samayena sambahulā bhikkhū bhagavato cīvarakammaṃ karonti – niṭṭhitacīvaro bhagavā temāsaccayena cārikaṃ pakkamissatīti. Atha kho āyasmā bhaddāli yena te bhikkhū tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā tehi bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ sammodi. Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinnaṃ kho āyasmantaṃ bhaddāliṃ te bhikkhū etadavocuṃ – “idaṃ kho, āvuso bhaddāli, bhagavato cīvarakammaṃ karīyati karaṇīyaṃ (ka.). Niṭṭhitacīvaro bhagavā temāsaccayena cārikaṃ pakkamissati. Iṅghāvuso bhaddāli, etaṃ dosakaṃ sādhukaṃ manasi karohi, mā te pacchā dukkarataraṃ ahosī”ti. “Evamāvuso”ti kho āyasmā [V 2.0110] bhaddāli tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ paṭissutvā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho āyasmā bhaddāli bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “accayo maṃ, bhante, accagamā yathābālaṃ yathāmūḷhaṃ yathāakusalaṃ, yohaṃ bhagavatā sikkhāpade paññāpiyamāne bhikkhusaṅghe sikkhaṃ samādiyamāne anussāhaṃ pavedesiṃ. Tassa me, bhante, bhagavā accayaṃ accayato paṭiggaṇhātu āyatiṃ saṃvarāyā”ti.

135. At that time, many monks were making robes for the Blessed One, thinking, "When the robes are finished, the Blessed One will set out on a journey after the three months have passed." Then the Venerable Bhaddāli approached those monks; having approached, he exchanged courteous greetings with them. After concluding the cordial and memorable talk, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting to one side, those monks said this to the Venerable Bhaddāli: "Friend Bhaddāli, this robe-making is being done for the Blessed One. When the robes are finished, the Blessed One will set out on a journey after the three months have passed. Come, friend Bhaddāli, reflect well on this fault, lest it become more difficult for you later." "So be it, friends," the Venerable Bhaddāli replied to those monks, and then he approached the Blessed One. Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Bhaddāli said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, an offense has overcome me, as befits a fool, as befits a deluded one, as befits an unskillful one, in that when the Blessed One was laying down a training rule and the Saṅgha of monks was undertaking the training, I declared my unwillingness. Venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept that offense of mine as an offense, for the sake of restraint in the future."

“Taggha [M 2.0102] tvaṃ, bhaddāli, accayo accagamā yathābālaṃ yathāmūḷhaṃ [T 2.0165] yathāakusalaṃ, yaṃ tvaṃ mayā sikkhāpade paññāpiyamāne bhikkhusaṅghe sikkhaṃ samādiyamāne anussāhaṃ pavedesi. Samayopi kho te, bhaddāli, appaṭividdho ahosi – ‘bhagavā kho sāvatthiyaṃ viharati, bhagavāpi maṃ jānissati – bhaddāli nāma bhikkhu satthusāsane sikkhāya aparipūrakārī’ti. Ayampi kho te, bhaddāli, samayo appaṭividdho ahosi. Samayopi kho te, bhaddāli, appaṭividdho ahosi – ‘sambahulā kho [P 1.0439] bhikkhu sāvatthiyaṃ vassaṃ upagatā, tepi maṃ jānissanti – bhaddāli nāma bhikkhu satthusāsane sikkhāya aparipūrakārī’ti. Ayampi kho te, bhaddāli, samayo appaṭividdho ahosi. Samayopi kho te, bhaddāli, appaṭividdho ahosi – ‘sambahulā kho bhikkhuniyo sāvatthiyaṃ vassaṃ upagatā, tāpi maṃ jānissanti – bhaddāli nāma bhikkhu satthusāsane sikkhāya aparipūrakārī’ti. Ayampi kho te, bhaddāli, samayo appaṭividdho ahosi. Samayopi kho te, bhaddāli, appaṭividdho ahosi – ‘sambahulā kho upāsakā sāvatthiyaṃ paṭivasanti, tepi maṃ jānissanti – bhaddāli nāma bhikkhu satthusāsane sikkhāya aparipūrakārī’ti. Ayampi kho te, bhaddāli, samayo appaṭividdho ahosi. Samayopi kho te, bhaddāli, appaṭividdho ahosi – ‘sambahulā kho upāsikā sāvatthiyaṃ paṭivasanti, tāpi maṃ jānissanti – bhaddāli nāma bhikkhu satthusāsane sikkhāya aparipūrakārī’ti. Ayampi kho te, bhaddāli[T 2.0166], samayo appaṭividdho ahosi. Samayopi kho te, bhaddāli, appaṭividdho ahosi – ‘sambahulā kho nānātitthiyā samaṇabrāhmaṇā sāvatthiyaṃ vassaṃ upagatā, tepi maṃ jānissanti – bhaddāli nāma bhikkhu samaṇassa gotamassa sāvako theraññataro bhikkhu sāsane sikkhāya aparipūrakārī’ti. Ayampi kho te, bhaddāli, samayo appaṭividdho ahosī”ti.

“Indeed, Bhaddāli, an offense has overcome you, as befits a fool, as befits a deluded one, as befits an unskillful one, in that when I was laying down a training rule and the Saṅgha of monks was undertaking the training, you declared your unwillingness. A reason, Bhaddāli, was not penetrated by you: ‘The Blessed One is dwelling at Sāvatthī. The Blessed One will know of me: “The monk named Bhaddāli is one who does not fulfill the training in the Teacher’s dispensation.”’ This reason also, Bhaddāli, was not penetrated by you. A reason, Bhaddāli, was not penetrated by you: ‘Many monks have entered the rains-residence at Sāvatthī. They too will know of me: “The monk named Bhaddāli is one who does not fulfill the training in the Teacher’s dispensation.”’ This reason also, Bhaddāli, was not penetrated by you. A reason, Bhaddāli, was not penetrated by you: ‘Many nuns have entered the rains-residence at Sāvatthī. They too will know of me: “The monk named Bhaddāli is one who does not fulfill the training in the Teacher’s dispensation.”’ This reason also, Bhaddāli, was not penetrated by you. A reason, Bhaddāli, was not penetrated by you: ‘Many laymen reside at Sāvatthī. They too will know of me: “The monk named Bhaddāli is one who does not fulfill the training in the Teacher’s dispensation.”’ This reason also, Bhaddāli, was not penetrated by you. A reason, Bhaddāli, was not penetrated by you: ‘Many laywomen reside at Sāvatthī. They too will know of me: “The monk named Bhaddāli is one who does not fulfill the training in the Teacher’s dispensation.”’ This reason also, Bhaddāli, was not penetrated by you. A reason, Bhaddāli, was not penetrated by you: ‘Many ascetics and brahmins of other sects have entered the rains-residence at Sāvatthī. They too will know of me: “The monk named Bhaddāli, a disciple of the ascetic Gotama, a certain elder monk, is one who does not fulfill the training in the Teacher’s dispensation.”’ This reason also, Bhaddāli, was not penetrated by you.”

“Accayo [V 2.0111] maṃ, bhante, accagamā yathābālaṃ yathāmūḷhaṃ yathāakusalaṃ, yohaṃ bhagavatā sikkhāpade paññāpiyamāne bhikkhusaṅghe sikkhaṃ samādiyamāne anussāhaṃ pavedesiṃ. Tassa me, bhante, bhagavā accayaṃ accayato paṭiggaṇhātu āyatiṃ saṃvarāyā”ti. “Taggha tvaṃ, bhaddāli, accayo accagamā yathābālaṃ yathāmūḷhaṃ yathāakusalaṃ, yaṃ tvaṃ mayā sikkhāpade [M 2.0103] paññāpiyamāne bhikkhusaṅghe sikkhaṃ samādiyamāne anussāhaṃ pavedesi”.

“Venerable sir, a transgression has overcome me, foolish, deluded, and unskillful as I am, in that when the Blessed One was laying down a training rule and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus was undertaking the training, I declared my lack of enthusiasm. Venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept that transgression of mine as a transgression for the sake of future restraint.” “Indeed, Bhaddāli, a transgression has overcome you, foolish, deluded, and unskillful as you are, in that when I was laying down a training rule and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus was undertaking the training, you declared your lack of enthusiasm.”

136. “Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, bhaddāli, idhassa bhikkhu ubhatobhāgavimutto, tamahaṃ evaṃ vadeyyaṃ – ‘ehi me tvaṃ, bhikkhu, paṅke saṅkamo hohī’ti, api nu kho so saṅkameyya vā aññena vā kāyaṃ sannāmeyya, ‘no’ti vā vadeyyā”ti?

136. “What do you think, Bhaddāli? Suppose there were a bhikkhu here who is liberated in both ways, and I were to say to him: ‘Come, bhikkhu, be a causeway for me in the mud.’ Would he act as a causeway, or would he turn his body aside, or would he say ‘no’?”

“No hetaṃ, bhante”.

“Certainly not, venerable sir.”

“Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, bhaddāli, idhassa bhikkhu paññāvimutto… kāyasakkhi… diṭṭhippatto… saddhāvimutto… dhammānusārī… saddhānusārī, tamahaṃ evaṃ vadeyyaṃ – ‘ehi me tvaṃ, bhikkhu, paṅke saṅkamo hohī’ti, api nu kho so saṅkameyya vā aññena vā kāyaṃ sannāmeyya, ‘no’ti vā vadeyyā”ti?

“What do you think, Bhaddāli? Suppose there were a bhikkhu here who is liberated by wisdom… a body-witness… one attained to view… liberated by faith… a Dhamma-follower… a faith-follower. If I were to say to him, ‘Come, bhikkhu, be a causeway for me in the mud,’ would he act as a causeway, or would he turn his body aside, or would he say ‘no’?”

“No hetaṃ, bhante”.

“Certainly not, venerable sir.”

“Taṃ kiṃ [T 2.0167] maññasi, bhaddāli, api nu tvaṃ, bhaddāli, tasmiṃ samaye ubhatobhāgavimutto vā hosi paññāvimutto [P 1.0440] vā kāyasakkhi vā diṭṭhippatto vā saddhāvimutto vā dhammānusārī vā saddhānusārī vā”ti?

“What do you think, Bhaddāli? At that time, were you liberated in both ways, or liberated by wisdom, or a body-witness, or one attained to view, or liberated by faith, or a Dhamma-follower, or a faith-follower?”

“No hetaṃ, bhante”.

“Certainly not, venerable sir.”

“Nanu tvaṃ, bhaddāli, tasmiṃ samaye ritto tuccho aparaddho”ti?

“Bhaddāli, were you not at that time empty, hollow, and at fault?”

“Evaṃ[V 2.0112], bhante. Accayo maṃ, bhante, accagamā yathābālaṃ yathāmūḷhaṃ yathāakusalaṃ, yohaṃ bhagavatā sikkhāpade paññāpiyamāne bhikkhusaṅghe sikkhaṃ samādiyamāne anussāhaṃ pavedesiṃ. Tassa me, bhante, bhagavā accayaṃ accayato paṭiggaṇhātu āyatiṃ saṃvarāyā”ti. “Taggha tvaṃ, bhaddāli, accayo accagamā yathābālaṃ yathāmūḷhaṃ yathāakusalaṃ, yaṃ tvaṃ mayā sikkhāpade paññāpiyamāne bhikkhusaṅghe sikkhaṃ samādiyamāne anussāhaṃ pavedesi. Yato ca kho tvaṃ, bhaddāli, accayaṃ accayato disvā yathādhammaṃ paṭikarosi, taṃ te mayaṃ paṭiggaṇhāma. Vuddhihesā, bhaddāli, ariyassa vinaye yo accayaṃ accayato disvā yathādhammaṃ paṭikaroti, āyatiṃ saṃvaraṃ āpajjati”.

“So it is, venerable sir. Venerable sir, a transgression has overcome me, foolish, deluded, and unskillful as I am, in that when the Blessed One was laying down a training rule and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus was undertaking the training, I declared my lack of enthusiasm. Venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept that transgression of mine as a transgression for the sake of future restraint.” “Indeed, Bhaddāli, a transgression has overcome you, foolish, deluded, and unskillful as you are, in that when I was laying down a training rule and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus was undertaking the training, you declared your lack of enthusiasm. And since you, Bhaddāli, having seen the transgression as a transgression, make amends in accordance with the Dhamma, we accept it of you. For this, Bhaddāli, is growth in the discipline of the Noble One: that one, having seen a transgression as a transgression, makes amends in accordance with the Dhamma and undertakes future restraint.”

137. “Idha, bhaddāli, ekacco bhikkhu satthusāsane sikkhāya aparipūrakārī hoti. Tassa evaṃ hoti – ‘yaṃnūnāhaṃ vivittaṃ senāsanaṃ bhajeyyaṃ araññaṃ rukkhamūlaṃ pabbataṃ kandaraṃ giriguhaṃ susānaṃ vanapatthaṃ abbhokāsaṃ [T 2.0168] palālapuñjaṃ. Appeva nāmāhaṃ uttari uttariṃ (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) manussadhammā alamariyañāṇadassanavisesaṃ sacchikareyya’nti. So vivittaṃ senāsanaṃ bhajati araññaṃ rukkhamūlaṃ pabbataṃ [M 2.0104] kandaraṃ giriguhaṃ susānaṃ vanapatthaṃ abbhokāsaṃ palālapuñjaṃ. Tassa tathāvūpakaṭṭhassa viharato satthāpi upavadati, anuviccapi viññū sabrahmacārī upavadanti, devatāpi upavadanti, attāpi attānaṃ upavadati. So satthārāpi upavadito, anuviccapi viññūhi sabrahmacārīhi upavadito, devatāhipi upavadito, attanāpi attānaṃ upavadito na uttari manussadhammā alamariyañāṇadassanavisesaṃ sacchikaroti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Evañhi taṃ, bhaddāli, hoti yathā taṃ satthusāsane sikkhāya aparipūrakārissa.

137. “Here, Bhaddāli, a certain bhikkhu is one who does not fulfill the training in the Teacher’s Dispensation. It occurs to him: ‘What if I were to frequent a secluded lodging: a forest, the root of a tree, a mountain, a ravine, a mountain cave, a charnel ground, a forest grove, an open space, or a heap of straw? Perhaps I might realize a state superior to the human state, a special state of noble knowledge and vision.’ He frequents a secluded lodging: a forest, the root of a tree, a mountain, a ravine, a mountain cave, a charnel ground, a forest grove, an open space, or a heap of straw. While he is dwelling thus secluded, the Teacher reproaches him; discerning fellows in the holy life, having investigated, reproach him; deities reproach him; and he reproaches himself. That bhikkhu, being reproached by the Teacher, reproached by discerning fellows in the holy life after investigation, reproached by deities, and reproached by himself, does not realize a state superior to the human state, a special state of noble knowledge and vision. For what reason? Because, Bhaddāli, so it is for one who does not fulfill the training in the Teacher’s Dispensation.

138. “Idha pana, bhaddāli, ekacco bhikkhu satthusāsane sikkhāya paripūrakārī hoti. Tassa evaṃ hoti – ‘yaṃnūnāhaṃ vivittaṃ senāsanaṃ bhajeyyaṃ araññaṃ rukkhamūlaṃ pabbataṃ kandaraṃ giriguhaṃ susānaṃ vanapatthaṃ abbhokāsaṃ [P 1.0441] palālapuñjaṃ. Appeva nāmāhaṃ uttari manussadhammā alamariyañāṇadassanavisesaṃ sacchikareyya’nti. So vivittaṃ senāsanaṃ bhajati araññaṃ rukkhamūlaṃ pabbataṃ kandaraṃ giriguhaṃ susānaṃ vanapatthaṃ abbhokāsaṃ palālapuñjaṃ. Tassa tathāvūpakaṭṭhassa viharato satthāpi na upavadati, anuviccapi viññū sabrahmacārī na upavadanti, devatāpi na upavadanti, attāpi attānaṃ na upavadati. So satthārāpi anupavadito[V 2.0113], anuviccapi viññūhi sabrahmacārīhi anupavadito, devatāhipi anupavadito, attanāpi attānaṃ anupavadito uttari manussadhammā alamariyañāṇadassanavisesaṃ sacchikaroti. So vivicceva kāmehi vivicca [T 2.0169] akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Taṃ kissa hetu? Evañhi taṃ, bhaddāli, hoti yathā taṃ satthusāsane sikkhāya paripūrakārissa.

138. “But here, Bhaddāli, a certain bhikkhu is one who fulfills the training in the Teacher’s Dispensation. It occurs to him: ‘What if I were to frequent a secluded lodging: a forest, the root of a tree, a mountain, a ravine, a mountain cave, a charnel ground, a forest grove, an open space, or a heap of straw? Perhaps I might realize a state superior to the human state, a special state of noble knowledge and vision.’ He frequents a secluded lodging: a forest, the root of a tree, a mountain, a ravine, a mountain cave, a charnel ground, a forest grove, an open space, or a heap of straw. While he is dwelling thus secluded, the Teacher does not reproach him; discerning fellows in the holy life, having investigated, do not reproach him; deities do not reproach him; and he does not reproach himself. That bhikkhu, not being reproached by the Teacher, not reproached by discerning fellows in the holy life after investigation, not reproached by deities, and not reproached by himself, realizes a state superior to the human state, a special state of noble knowledge and vision. Quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. For what reason? Because, Bhaddāli, so it is for one who fulfills the training in the Teacher’s Dispensation.”

139. “Puna caparaṃ, bhaddāli, bhikkhu vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā ajjhattaṃ sampasādanaṃ cetaso ekodibhāvaṃ avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ samādhijaṃ pītisukhaṃ dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Taṃ kissa hetu? Evañhi taṃ, bhaddāli, hoti yathā taṃ satthusāsane sikkhāya paripūrakārissa.

139. Furthermore, Bhaddāli, with the stilling of thought and examination, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without thought and examination, and has rapture and happiness born of concentration. For what reason? Because, Bhaddāli, that is how it is for one who is a fulfiller of the training in the Teacher’s Dispensation.

“Puna caparaṃ, bhaddāli, bhikkhu pītiyā ca virāgā upekkhako ca viharati, sato ca sampajāno sukhañca kāyena paṭisaṃvedeti, yaṃ taṃ ariyā ācikkhanti – ‘upekkhako satimā sukhavihārī’ti tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ [M 2.0105] upasampajja viharati. Taṃ kissa hetu? Evañhi taṃ, bhaddāli, hoti yathā taṃ satthusāsane sikkhāya paripūrakārissa.

Furthermore, Bhaddāli, with the fading away of rapture, a bhikkhu dwells equanimously, mindful, and clearly comprehending, and experiences happiness with the body; he enters and dwells in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare: ‘Equanimous and mindful, he dwells happily.’ For what reason? Because, Bhaddāli, that is how it is for one who is a fulfiller of the training in the Teacher’s Dispensation.

“Puna caparaṃ, bhaddāli, bhikkhu sukhassa ca pahānā dukkhassa ca pahānā pubbeva somanassadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamā adukkhamasukhaṃ upekkhāsatipārisuddhiṃ catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Taṃ kissa hetu? Evañhi taṃ, bhaddāli, hoti yathā taṃ satthusāsane sikkhāya paripūrakārissa.

Furthermore, Bhaddāli, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the prior passing away of joy and sorrow, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. For what reason? Because, Bhaddāli, that is how it is for one who is a fulfiller of the training in the Teacher’s Dispensation.

“So evaṃ samāhite citte parisuddhe pariyodāte anaṅgaṇe vigatūpakkilese mudubhūte kammaniye ṭhite āneñjappatte pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇāya cittaṃ abhininnāmeti. So anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati, seyyathidaṃ – ekampi jātiṃ dvepi jātiyo…pe… iti sākāraṃ sauddesaṃ anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati. Taṃ kissa hetu? Evañhi [P 1.0442] taṃ, bhaddāli, hoti yathā taṃ satthusāsane sikkhāya paripūrakārissa.

When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, spotless, rid of defilements, malleable, wieldy, firm, and attained to imperturbability, he directs his mind to the knowledge of the recollection of past lives. He recollects his many kinds of past lives, that is, one birth, two births… thus with their aspects and details he recollects his many kinds of past lives. For what reason? Because, Bhaddāli, that is how it is for one who is a fulfiller of the training in the Teacher’s Dispensation.

“So evaṃ samāhite citte parisuddhe pariyodāte anaṅgaṇe [T 2.0170] vigatūpakkilese mudubhūte kammaniye ṭhite āneñjappatte sattānaṃ cutūpapātañāṇāya cittaṃ abhininnāmeti. So dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena satte passati cavamāne upapajjamāne hīne paṇīte suvaṇṇe dubbaṇṇe sugate duggate yathākammūpage satte pajānāti – ‘ime vata bhonto sattā kāyaduccaritena samannāgatā…pe… vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapannā; ime vā pana bhonto sattā kāyasucaritena samannāgatā…pe… sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapannā’ti iti dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena…pe… yathākammūpage satte pajānāti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Evañhi taṃ, bhaddāli, hoti yathā taṃ satthusāsane sikkhāya paripūrakārissa.

When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, spotless, rid of defilements, malleable, wieldy, firm, and attained to imperturbability, he directs his mind to the knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings. With the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, he sees beings passing away and reappearing—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate. He understands beings as they fare on according to their kamma: ‘These beings, who were endowed with misconduct of body… have reappeared in a plane of misery, a bad destination, a lower realm, in hell. But these beings, who were endowed with good conduct of body… have reappeared in a good destination, in a heavenly world.’ Thus, with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human… he understands beings as they fare on according to their kamma. For what reason? Because, Bhaddāli, that is how it is for one who is a fulfiller of the training in the Teacher’s Dispensation.

“So [V 2.0114] evaṃ samāhite citte parisuddhe pariyodāte anaṅgaṇe vigatūpakkilese mudubhūte kammaniye ṭhite āneñjappatte āsavānaṃ khayañāṇāya cittaṃ abhininnāmeti. So ‘idaṃ dukkha’nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, ‘ayaṃ dukkhasamudayo’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodho’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti; ‘ime āsavā’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, ‘ayaṃ [M 2.0106] āsavasamudayo’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, ‘ayaṃ āsavanirodho’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, ‘ayaṃ āsavanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Tassa evaṃ jānato evaṃ passato kāmāsavāpi cittaṃ vimuccati, bhavāsavāpi cittaṃ vimuccati, avijjāsavāpi cittaṃ vimuccati. Vimuttasmiṃ vimuttamiti ñāṇaṃ hoti. ‘Khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ [T 2.0171] brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti pajānāti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Evañhi taṃ, bhaddāli, hoti yathā taṃ satthusāsane sikkhāya paripūrakārissā”ti.

When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, spotless, rid of defilements, malleable, wieldy, firm, and attained to imperturbability, he directs his mind to the knowledge of the destruction of the taints. He understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering.’ He understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering.’ He understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering.’ He understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.’ He understands as it really is: ‘These are the taints.’ He understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of the taints.’ He understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of the taints.’ He understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of the taints.’ As he knows and sees thus, his mind is liberated from the taint of sensual desire, from the taint of existence, and from the taint of ignorance. When it is liberated, the knowledge arises: ‘It is liberated.’ He understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.’ For what reason? Because, Bhaddāli, that is how it is for one who is a fulfiller of the training in the Teacher’s Dispensation.

140. Evaṃ vutte, āyasmā bhaddāli bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “ko nu kho, bhante, hetu, ko paccayo yena midhekaccaṃ bhikkhuṃ pasayha pasayha pavayha pavayha (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) kāraṇaṃ karonti? Ko pana, bhante, hetu, ko paccayo yena midhekaccaṃ bhikkhuṃ no tathā pasayha pasayha kāraṇaṃ karontī”ti? “Idha, bhaddāli, ekacco bhikkhu abhiṇhāpattiko hoti āpattibahulo. So bhikkhūhi vuccamāno aññenaññaṃ paṭicarati, bahiddhā kathaṃ apanāmeti, kopañca dosañca appaccayañca pātukaroti, na sammā vattati, na lomaṃ pāteti, na netthāraṃ vattati, ‘yena saṅgho attamano hoti taṃ karomī’ti nāha. Tatra, bhaddāli, bhikkhūnaṃ evaṃ hoti – ayaṃ kho, āvuso, bhikkhu [V 2.0115] abhiṇhāpattiko āpattibahulo. So bhikkhūhi vuccamāno aññenaññaṃ paṭicarati, bahiddhā kathaṃ apanāmeti, kopañca dosañca appaccayañca pātukaroti, na sammā vattati, na lomaṃ pāteti, na netthāraṃ vattati, ‘yena saṅgho attamano hoti [P 1.0443] taṃ karomī’ti nāha. Sādhu vatāyasmanto imassa bhikkhuno tathā tathā upaparikkhatha yathāssidaṃ yathayidaṃ (syā. kaṃ. ka.) adhikaraṇaṃ na khippameva vūpasameyyāti. Tassa kho evaṃ, bhaddāli, bhikkhuno bhikkhū [T 2.0172] tathā tathā upaparikkhanti yathāssidaṃ adhikaraṇaṃ na khippameva vūpasammati.

140. When this was said, the Venerable Bhaddāli said to the Blessed One: “What, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the reason, why here a certain bhikkhu is repeatedly and forcefully subjected to disciplinary action? And what, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the reason, why here a certain bhikkhu is not repeatedly and forcefully subjected to disciplinary action in that way?” “Here, Bhaddāli, a certain bhikkhu is a constant offender, abounding in offenses. When spoken to by the bhikkhus, he evades the issue, diverts the discussion to external matters, and displays anger, ill will, and displeasure. He does not conduct himself properly, does not humble himself, does not act for his release, and does not say, ‘I will do what pleases the Saṅgha.’ In that case, Bhaddāli, it occurs to the bhikkhus: ‘Friends, this bhikkhu is a constant offender, abounding in offenses. When spoken to by the bhikkhus, he evades the issue, diverts the discussion to external matters, and displays anger, ill will, and displeasure. He does not conduct himself properly, does not humble himself, does not act for his release, and does not say, “I will do what pleases the Saṅgha.” It would be good, sirs, if you were to investigate this bhikkhu in such a way that this legal issue is not quickly settled.’ Thus, Bhaddāli, the bhikkhus investigate that bhikkhu in such a way that this legal issue is not quickly settled.

141. “Idha pana, bhaddāli, ekacco bhikkhu abhiṇhāpattiko hoti āpattibahulo. So bhikkhūhi vuccamāno nāññenaññaṃ paṭicarati, bahiddhā kathaṃ na apanāmeti, na kopañca dosañca appaccayañca pātukaroti, sammā vattati, lomaṃ pāteti, netthāraṃ vattati, ‘yena saṅgho attamano [M 2.0107] hoti taṃ karomī’ti āha. Tatra, bhaddāli, bhikkhūnaṃ evaṃ hoti – ayaṃ kho, āvuso, bhikkhu abhiṇhāpattiko āpattibahulo. So bhikkhūhi vuccamāno nāññenaññaṃ paṭicarati, bahiddhā kathaṃ na apanāmeti, na kopañca dosañca appaccayañca pātukaroti, sammā vattati, lomaṃ pāteti, netthāraṃ vattati, ‘yena saṅgho attamano hoti taṃ karomī’ti āha. Sādhu vatāyasmanto, imassa bhikkhuno tathā tathā upaparikkhatha yathāssidaṃ adhikaraṇaṃ khippameva vūpasameyyāti. Tassa kho evaṃ, bhaddāli, bhikkhuno bhikkhū tathā tathā upaparikkhanti yathāssidaṃ adhikaraṇaṃ khippameva vūpasammati.

141. Furthermore, Bhaddāli, in this Teaching, a certain monk is one who constantly commits offenses, one who is full of offenses. When admonished by the monks, he does not conceal one matter with another, does not divert the talk to external matters, and does not manifest anger, ill will, or displeasure. He conducts himself properly, lets his pride fall, and practices for his deliverance from the penalty. He says, ‘I will do that by which the Saṅgha is pleased.’ In that case, Bhaddāli, it occurs to the monks thus: ‘Friends, this monk is one who constantly commits offenses, one who is full of offenses. When admonished by the monks, he does not conceal one matter with another, does not divert the talk to external matters, does not manifest anger, ill will, or displeasure, conducts himself properly, lets his pride fall, practices for his deliverance from the penalty, and says, “I will do that by which the Saṅgha is pleased.” It would be good, venerable sirs, if you would investigate this monk in such a way that this legal issue might be settled very quickly.’ And so, Bhaddāli, the monks investigate that monk in such a way that this legal issue is settled very quickly.

142. “Idha, bhaddāli, ekacco bhikkhu adhiccāpattiko hoti anāpattibahulo. So bhikkhūhi vuccamāno aññenaññaṃ paṭicarati, bahiddhā kathaṃ apanāmeti, kopañca dosañca appaccayañca pātukaroti, na sammā vattati, na lomaṃ pāteti, na netthāraṃ vattati, ‘yena saṅgho attamano hoti taṃ karomī’ti nāha. Tatra, bhaddāli, bhikkhūnaṃ evaṃ hoti – ayaṃ kho, āvuso, bhikkhu adhiccāpattiko anāpattibahulo[T 2.0173]. So bhikkhūhi vuccamāno aññenaññaṃ paṭicarati, bahiddhā kathaṃ apanāmeti, kopañca dosañca appaccayañca pātukaroti, na sammā vattati, na lomaṃ pāteti, na netthāraṃ vattati, ‘yena saṅgho attamano hoti taṃ karomī’ti nāha. Sādhu vatāyasmanto, imassa bhikkhuno tathā tathā upaparikkhatha yathāssidaṃ [V 2.0116] adhikaraṇaṃ na khippameva vūpasameyyāti. Tassa kho evaṃ, bhaddāli, bhikkhuno bhikkhū tathā tathā upaparikkhanti yathāssidaṃ adhikaraṇaṃ [P 1.0444] na khippameva vūpasammati.

142. Here, Bhaddāli, a certain monk is one who occasionally commits offenses and is not one with many offenses. When admonished by the monks, he conceals one matter with another, diverts the talk to external matters, and manifests anger, ill will, and displeasure. He does not conduct himself properly, does not let his pride fall, does not practice for his deliverance from the penalty, and does not say, ‘I will do that by which the Saṅgha is pleased.’ In that case, Bhaddāli, it occurs to the monks thus: ‘Friends, this monk is one who occasionally commits offenses and is not one with many offenses. When admonished by the monks, he conceals one matter with another, diverts the talk to external matters, manifests anger, ill will, and displeasure, does not conduct himself properly, does not let his pride fall, does not practice for his deliverance from the penalty, and does not say, “I will do that by which the Saṅgha is pleased.” It would be good, venerable sirs, if you would investigate this monk in such a way that this legal issue might not be settled very quickly.’ And so, Bhaddāli, the monks investigate that monk in such a way that this legal issue is not settled very quickly.

143. “Idha pana, bhaddāli, ekacco bhikkhu adhiccāpattiko hoti anāpattibahulo. So bhikkhūhi vuccamāno nāññenaññaṃ paṭicarati, na bahiddhā kathaṃ apanāmeti, na kopañca dosañca appaccayañca pātukaroti, sammā vattati, lomaṃ pāteti, netthāraṃ vattati, ‘yena saṅgho attamano hoti taṃ karomī’ti āha. Tatra, bhaddāli, bhikkhūnaṃ evaṃ hoti – ayaṃ kho, āvuso, bhikkhu adhiccāpattiko anāpattibahulo. So bhikkhūhi vuccamāno nāññenaññaṃ paṭicarati, na bahiddhā kathaṃ apanāmeti, na kopañca dosañca appaccayañca pātukaroti, sammā vattati, lomaṃ pāteti, netthāraṃ vattati, ‘yena saṅgho [M 2.0108] attamano hoti taṃ karomī’ti āha. Sādhu vatāyasmanto, imassa bhikkhuno tathā tathā upaparikkhatha yathāssidaṃ adhikaraṇaṃ khippameva vūpasameyyāti. Tassa kho evaṃ, bhaddāli, bhikkhuno bhikkhū tathā tathā upaparikkhanti yathāssidaṃ adhikaraṇaṃ khippameva vūpasammati.

143. Furthermore, Bhaddāli, in this Teaching, a certain monk is one who occasionally commits offenses and is not one with many offenses. When admonished by the monks, he does not conceal one matter with another, does not divert the talk to external matters, and does not manifest anger, ill will, or displeasure. He conducts himself properly, lets his pride fall, and practices for his deliverance from the penalty. He says, ‘I will do that by which the Saṅgha is pleased.’ In that case, Bhaddāli, it occurs to the monks thus: ‘Friends, this monk is one who occasionally commits offenses and is not one with many offenses. When admonished by the monks, he does not conceal one matter with another, does not divert the talk to external matters, does not manifest anger, ill will, or displeasure, conducts himself properly, lets his pride fall, practices for his deliverance from the penalty, and says, “I will do that by which the Saṅgha is pleased.” It would be good, venerable sirs, if you would investigate this monk in such a way that this legal issue might be settled very quickly.’ And so, Bhaddāli, the monks investigate that monk in such a way that this legal issue is settled very quickly.

144. “Idha[T 2.0174], bhaddāli, ekacco bhikkhu saddhāmattakena vahati pemamattakena. Tatra, bhaddāli, bhikkhūnaṃ evaṃ hoti – ‘ayaṃ kho, āvuso, bhikkhu saddhāmattakena vahati pemamattakena. Sace mayaṃ imaṃ bhikkhuṃ pasayha pasayha kāraṇaṃ karissāma – mā yampissa taṃ saddhāmattakaṃ pemamattakaṃ tamhāpi parihāyī’ti. Seyyathāpi, bhaddāli, purisassa ekaṃ cakkhuṃ, tassa mittāmaccā ñātisālohitā taṃ ekaṃ cakkhuṃ rakkheyyuṃ – ‘mā yampissa taṃ ekaṃ cakkhuṃ tamhāpi parihāyī’ti; evameva kho, bhaddāli, idhekacco bhikkhu saddhāmattakena vahati pemamattakena. Tatra, bhaddāli, bhikkhūnaṃ evaṃ hoti – ‘ayaṃ kho, āvuso, bhikkhu saddhāmattakena vahati pemamattakena. Sace mayaṃ imaṃ bhikkhuṃ pasayha pasayha kāraṇaṃ karissāma – mā yampissa taṃ saddhāmattakaṃ pemamattakaṃ tamhāpi parihāyī’ti. Ayaṃ kho, bhaddāli, hetu ayaṃ paccayo yena midhekaccaṃ bhikkhuṃ pasayha pasayha kāraṇaṃ karonti. Ayaṃ pana, bhaddāli, hetu ayaṃ paccayo, yena midhekaccaṃ bhikkhuṃ no tathā pasayha pasayha kāraṇaṃ karontī”ti.

144. Here, Bhaddāli, a certain monk carries on through mere faith, through mere affection. In that case, Bhaddāli, it occurs to the monks thus: ‘Friends, this monk carries on through mere faith, through mere affection. If we were to deal with this monk very forcefully, that mere faith and mere affection which he has might be lost.’ It is just as if, Bhaddāli, a man had only one eye, and his friends, companions, relatives, and kin would guard that one eye, thinking: ‘Let him not lose even this one eye that he has.’ In the same way, Bhaddāli, here a certain monk carries on through mere faith, through mere affection. In that case, Bhaddāli, it occurs to the monks thus: ‘Friends, this monk carries on through mere faith, through mere affection. If we were to deal with this monk very forcefully, that mere faith and mere affection which he has might be lost.’ This, Bhaddāli, is the reason, this is the cause, why here some monks are dealt with very forcefully. And this, Bhaddāli, is the reason, this is the cause, why here some monks are not dealt with so very forcefully.

145. “‘Ko [V 2.0117] nu kho, bhante, hetu, ko paccayo yena pubbe appatarāni [P 1.0445] ceva sikkhāpadāni ahesuṃ bahutarā ca bhikkhū aññāya saṇṭhahiṃsu? Ko pana, bhante, hetu, ko paccayo yena etarahi bahutarāni ceva sikkhāpadāni honti appatarā ca bhikkhū aññāya saṇṭhahantī’ti? “Evametaṃ, bhaddāli, hoti sattesu hāyamānesu, saddhamme [T 2.0175] antaradhāyamāne, bahutarāni ceva sikkhāpadāni honti appatarā ca bhikkhū aññāya saṇṭhahantīti. Na tāva, bhaddāli, satthā sāvakānaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paññāpeti yāva na idhekacce āsavaṭṭhānīyā dhammā saṅghe pātubhavanti. Yato ca kho, bhaddāli, idhekacce āsavaṭṭhānīyā dhammā saṅghe pātubhavanti, atha satthā sāvakānaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paññāpeti tesaṃyeva āsavaṭṭhānīyānaṃ dhammānaṃ paṭighātāya. Na tāva, bhaddāli, idhekacce āsavaṭṭhānīyā dhammā saṅghe pātubhavanti yāva na saṅgho mahattaṃ patto hoti. Yato ca kho, bhaddāli, saṅgho mahattaṃ patto hoti, atha idhekacce [M 2.0109] āsavaṭṭhānīyā dhammā saṅghe pātubhavanti. Atha satthā sāvakānaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paññāpeti tesaṃyeva āsavaṭṭhānīyānaṃ dhammānaṃ paṭighātāya. Na tāva, bhaddāli, idhekacce āsavaṭṭhānīyā dhammā saṅghe pātubhavanti yāva na saṅgho lābhaggaṃ patto hoti, yasaggaṃ patto hoti, bāhusaccaṃ patto hoti, rattaññutaṃ patto hoti. Yato ca kho, bhaddāli, saṅgho rattaññutaṃ patto hoti, atha idhekacce āsavaṭṭhānīyā dhammā saṅghe pātubhavanti, atha satthā sāvakānaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paññāpeti tesaṃyeva āsavaṭṭhānīyānaṃ dhammānaṃ paṭighātāya.

145. ‘Venerable Sir, what is the cause, what is the reason that formerly there were fewer training rules and more monks were established in final knowledge? And Venerable Sir, what is the cause, what is the reason that now there are more training rules and fewer monks are established in final knowledge?’ ‘It is so, Bhaddāli. When beings are declining, when the true Dhamma is disappearing, there are more training rules and fewer monks are established in final knowledge. Bhaddāli, the Teacher does not lay down a training rule for the disciples as long as certain conditions that are a basis for the taints have not arisen in the Saṅgha. But when certain conditions that are a basis for the taints arise in the Saṅgha, then the Teacher lays down a training rule for the disciples to counteract those very conditions that are a basis for the taints. Bhaddāli, certain conditions that are a basis for the taints do not arise in the Saṅgha as long as the Saṅgha has not reached great size. But when the Saṅgha has reached great size, then certain conditions that are a basis for the taints arise in the Saṅgha. Then the Teacher lays down a training rule for the disciples to counteract those very conditions that are a basis for the taints. Bhaddāli, certain conditions that are a basis for the taints do not arise in the Saṅgha as long as the Saṅgha has not reached the peak of gains, the peak of fame, the peak of learning, or the peak of seniority. But when the Saṅgha has reached the peak of seniority, then certain conditions that are a basis for the taints arise in the Saṅgha. Then the Teacher lays down a training rule for the disciples to counteract those very conditions that are a basis for the taints.’

146. “Appakā kho tumhe, bhaddāli, tena samayena ahuvattha yadā vo ahaṃ ājānīyasusūpamaṃ dhammapariyāyaṃ desesiṃ. Taṃ sarasi sarasi tvaṃ (sī. pī.), sarasi taṃ (?) bhaddālī”ti[T 2.0176]?

146. “You were few indeed, Bhaddāli, at that time when I taught you the Dhamma exposition with the simile of the young thoroughbred horse. Do you remember that, Bhaddāli?”

“No hetaṃ, bhante”.

“No, Venerable Sir.”

“Tatra, bhaddāli, kaṃ hetuṃ paccesī”ti?

“In that case, Bhaddāli, what do you take to be the reason?”

“So hi nūnāhaṃ, bhante, dīgharattaṃ satthusāsane sikkhāya aparipūrakārī ahosi”nti.

“Indeed, Venerable Sir, it must be that for a long time I have been one who did not fulfill the training in the Teacher's dispensation.”

“Na kho, bhaddāli, eseva hetu, esa paccayo. Api ca me tvaṃ, bhaddāli, dīgharattaṃ cetasā [V 2.0118] cetoparicca vidito – ‘na cāyaṃ moghapuriso mayā dhamme desiyamāne aṭṭhiṃ katvā manasi katvā sabbacetaso sabbaṃ cetaso (ka.) samannāharitvā ohitasoto dhammaṃ suṇātī’ti. Api ca te ahaṃ, bhaddāli, ājānīyasusūpamaṃ dhammapariyāyaṃ desessāmi. Taṃ suṇāhi, sādhukaṃ manasi karohi[P 1.0446]; bhāsissāmī”ti. “Evaṃ, bhante”ti kho āyasmā bhaddāli bhagavato paccassosi. Bhagavā etadavoca –

“That is not the only cause, Bhaddāli, not the only reason. Moreover, Bhaddāli, for a long time you have been known to me, as I have encompassed your mind with my mind: ‘This worthless man, when the Dhamma is being taught by me, does not treat it as essential, does not apply his mind, does not bring his whole heart to bear, nor listen with an attentive ear to the Dhamma.’ Nevertheless, Bhaddāli, I will teach you the Dhamma exposition with the simile of the young thoroughbred horse. Listen to it and attend carefully; I will speak.” “Yes, Venerable Sir,” replied Venerable Bhaddāli to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:

147. “Seyyathāpi, bhaddāli, dakkho assadamako bhadraṃ assājānīyaṃ labhitvā paṭhameneva mukhādhāne kāraṇaṃ kāreti. Tassa mukhādhāne kāraṇaṃ kāriyamānassa hontiyeva visūkāyitāni visevitāni vipphanditāni kānici kānici, yathā taṃ akāritapubbaṃ kāraṇaṃ kāriyamānassa. So abhiṇhakāraṇā anupubbakāraṇā tasmiṃ ṭhāne parinibbāyati. Yato kho, bhaddāli, bhadro assājānīyo abhiṇhakāraṇā anupubbakāraṇā tasmiṃ ṭhāne parinibbuto hoti, tamenaṃ assadamako uttari kāraṇaṃ kāreti yugādhāne. Tassa yugādhāne kāraṇaṃ kāriyamānassa hontiyeva visūkāyitāni visevitāni vipphanditāni kānici kānici, yathā taṃ akāritapubbaṃ kāraṇaṃ kāriyamānassa. So abhiṇhakāraṇā anupubbakāraṇā tasmiṃ [T 2.0177] ṭhāne parinibbāyati[M 2.0110]. Yato kho, bhaddāli, bhadro assājānīyo abhiṇhakāraṇā anupubbakāraṇā tasmiṃ ṭhāne parinibbuto hoti, tamenaṃ assadamako uttari kāraṇaṃ kāreti anukkame maṇḍale khurakāse khurakāye (sī. pī.) dhāve davatte ravatthe (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) rājaguṇe rājavaṃse uttame jave uttame haye uttame sākhalye. Tassa uttame jave uttame haye uttame sākhalye kāraṇaṃ kāriyamānassa hontiyeva visūkāyitāni visevitāni vipphanditāni kānici kānici, yathā taṃ akāritapubbaṃ kāraṇaṃ kāriyamānassa. So abhiṇhakāraṇā anupubbakāraṇā tasmiṃ ṭhāne parinibbāyati. Yato kho, bhaddāli, bhadro assājānīyo abhiṇhakāraṇā anupubbakāraṇā tasmiṃ ṭhāne parinibbuto hoti, tamenaṃ assadamako uttari vaṇṇiyañca pāṇiyañca valiyañca (sī. pī.), baliyañca (syā. kaṃ.) anuppavecchati. Imehi kho, bhaddāli, dasahaṅgehi samannāgato bhadro assājānīyo rājāraho hoti rājabhoggo rañño aṅganteva saṅkhyaṃ gacchati.

147. “Just as, Bhaddāli, a skilled horse trainer, having obtained a fine thoroughbred horse, first subjects it to the discipline of accepting the bridle. While being subjected to the discipline of accepting the bridle, it has some struggles, squirmings, and thrashings, as is the case when being subjected to a discipline not undergone before. But through repeated and gradual discipline, it becomes settled in that practice. When, Bhaddāli, the fine thoroughbred horse has become settled in that practice through repeated and gradual discipline, the horse trainer then subjects it to the further discipline of accepting the yoke. While being subjected to the discipline of accepting the yoke, it has some struggles, squirmings, and thrashings, as is the case when being subjected to a discipline not undergone before. But through repeated and gradual discipline, it becomes settled in that practice. When, Bhaddāli, the fine thoroughbred horse has become settled in that practice through repeated and gradual discipline, the horse trainer then subjects it to the further discipline of pacing, circling, hoof-play, galloping, playfulness, royal qualities, noble lineage, supreme speed, supreme horsemanship, and supreme docility. While being subjected to the discipline of supreme speed, supreme horsemanship, and supreme docility, it has some struggles, squirmings, and thrashings, as is the case when being subjected to a discipline not undergone before. But through repeated and gradual discipline, it becomes settled in that practice. When, Bhaddāli, the fine thoroughbred horse has become settled in that practice through repeated and gradual discipline, the horse trainer then further provides it with choice fodder and drink. Endowed with these ten qualities, Bhaddāli, a fine thoroughbred horse becomes worthy of a king, fit for a king’s use, and is reckoned as a very limb of the king.”

“Evameva kho, bhaddāli, dasahi dhammehi samannāgato bhikkhu āhuneyyo hoti pāhuneyyo dakkhiṇeyyo añjalikaraṇīyo anuttaraṃ puññakkhettaṃ lokassa. Katamehi dasahi? Idha, bhaddāli, bhikkhu asekhāya sammādiṭṭhiyā samannāgato hoti, asekhena sammāsaṅkappena samannāgato hoti, asekhāya [V 2.0119] sammāvācāya samannāgato hoti, asekhena sammākammantena samannāgato hoti, asekhena sammāājīvena samannāgato hoti, asekhena sammāvāyāmena samannāgato hoti[T 2.0178], asekhāya sammāsatiyā [P 1.0447] samannāgato hoti, asekhena sammāsamādhinā samannāgato hoti, asekhena sammāñāṇena samannāgato hoti, asekhāya sammāvimuttiyā samannāgato hoti – imehi kho, bhaddāli, dasahi dhammehi samannāgato bhikkhu āhuneyyo hoti pāhuneyyo dakkhiṇeyyo añjalikaraṇīyo anuttaraṃ puññakkhettaṃ lokassā”ti.

Just so, Bhaddāli, a bhikkhu endowed with ten qualities is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. With what ten?
