Here, Bhaddāli, a bhikkhu is endowed with the right view of one beyond training, endowed with the right intention of one beyond training, endowed with the right speech of one beyond training, endowed with the right action of one beyond training, endowed with the right livelihood of one beyond training, endowed with the right effort of one beyond training, endowed with the right mindfulness of one beyond training, endowed with the right concentration of one beyond training, endowed with the right knowledge of one beyond training, and endowed with the right liberation of one beyond training. Indeed, Bhaddāli, a bhikkhu endowed with these ten qualities is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.

Idamavoca bhagavā. Attamano āyasmā bhaddāli bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandīti.

The Blessed One said this. The Venerable Bhaddāli, being pleased, rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words.

Bhaddālisuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ pañcamaṃ.

The Bhaddāli Sutta, the fifth, is concluded.

6. Laṭukikopamasuttaṃ

6. The Discourse with the Simile of the Quail

148. Evaṃ [T 2.0179][M 2.0111][V 2.0120] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā aṅguttarāpesu viharati āpaṇaṃ nāma aṅguttarāpānaṃ nigamo. Atha kho bhagavā pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya āpaṇaṃ piṇḍāya pāvisi. Āpaṇe piṇḍāya caritvā pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto yenaññataro vanasaṇḍo tenupasaṅkami divāvihārāya. Taṃ vanasaṇḍaṃ ajjhogāhetvā aññatarasmiṃ rukkhamūle divāvihāraṃ nisīdi. Āyasmāpi kho udāyī pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya āpaṇaṃ piṇḍāya pāvisi. Āpaṇe piṇḍāya caritvā pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto yena so vanasaṇḍo tenupasaṅkami divāvihārāya. Taṃ vanasaṇḍaṃ ajjhogāhetvā aññatarasmiṃ rukkhamūle divāvihāraṃ nisīdi. Atha kho āyasmato udāyissa rahogatassa paṭisallīnassa evaṃ cetaso parivitakko udapādi – “bahūnaṃ bahunnaṃ (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) evamīdise aviññāṇakappakaraṇe vata no bhagavā dukkhadhammānaṃ apahattā, bahūnaṃ vata no bhagavā sukhadhammānaṃ upahattā; bahūnaṃ vata no bhagavā akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ apahattā, bahūnaṃ vata no bhagavā kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ upahattā”ti. Atha kho āyasmā udāyī sāyanhasamayaṃ paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi[P 1.0448].

148. Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Aṅguttarāpas, in a market-town of the Aṅguttarāpas named Āpaṇa. Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, and taking his bowl and outer robe, entered Āpaṇa for alms. Having gone for alms in Āpaṇa and returned from the alms round after his meal, he approached a certain woodland for the day's abiding. Having entered that woodland, he sat down at the foot of a certain tree for the day's abiding. The Venerable Udāyī also, in the morning, dressed, and taking his bowl and outer robe, entered Āpaṇa for alms. Having gone for alms in Āpaṇa and returned from the alms round after his meal, he approached that same woodland for the day's abiding. Having entered that woodland, he sat down at the foot of a certain tree for the day's abiding. Then, while the Venerable Udāyī was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in his mind: ‘Truly, the Blessed One is for us the remover of many painful states, the bringer of many pleasant states; truly, the Blessed One is for us the remover of many unwholesome states, the bringer of many wholesome states.’ Then, in the evening, the Venerable Udāyī arose from seclusion and approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side.

149. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho āyasmā udāyī bhagavantaṃ etadavoca [T 2.0180] – “idha mayhaṃ, bhante, rahogatassa paṭisallīnassa evaṃ cetaso parivitakko udapādi – ‘bahūnaṃ vata no bhagavā dukkhadhammānaṃ apahattā, bahūnaṃ vata no bhagavā sukhadhammānaṃ upahattā; bahūnaṃ vata no bhagavā akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ apahattā, bahūnaṃ vata no bhagavā kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ upahattā’ti. Mayañhi, bhante, pubbe sāyañceva bhuñjāma pāto ca divā ca vikāle. Ahu kho so, bhante, samayo yaṃ bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi – ‘iṅgha tumhe, bhikkhave, etaṃ divāvikālabhojanaṃ pajahathā’ti. Tassa mayhaṃ, bhante, ahudeva aññathattaṃ, ahudeva ahu (sī. pī.) domanassaṃ – ‘yampi no saddhā gahapatikā divā vikāle paṇītaṃ khādanīyaṃ bhojanīyaṃ denti tassapi no bhagavā pahānamāha, tassapi no sugato paṭinissaggamāhā’ti. Te [M 2.0112] mayaṃ, bhante, bhagavati pemañca gāravañca hiriñca ottappañca sampassamānā [V 2.0121] evaṃ taṃ divāvikālabhojanaṃ pajahimhā. Te mayaṃ, bhante, sāyañceva bhuñjāma pāto ca. Ahu kho so, bhante, samayo yaṃ bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi – ‘iṅgha tumhe, bhikkhave, etaṃ rattiṃvikālabhojanaṃ pajahathā’ti. Tassa mayhaṃ, bhante, ahudeva aññathattaṃ ahudeva domanassaṃ – ‘yampi no imesaṃ dvinnaṃ bhattānaṃ paṇītasaṅkhātataraṃ tassapi no bhagavā pahānamāha, tassapi no sugato paṭinissaggamāhā’ti. Bhūtapubbaṃ, bhante, aññataro puriso divā sūpeyyaṃ labhitvā evamāha – ‘handa ca imaṃ nikkhipatha, sāyaṃ sabbeva samaggā [T 2.0181] bhuñjissāmā’ti. Yā kāci, bhante, saṅkhatiyo sabbā tā rattiṃ, appā divā. Te mayaṃ, bhante, bhagavati pemañca gāravañca hiriñca ottappañca sampassamānā evaṃ taṃ rattiṃvikālabhojanaṃ pajahimhā. Bhūtapubbaṃ, bhante, bhikkhū rattandhakāratimisāyaṃ piṇḍāya carantā candanikampi pavisanti, oligallepi papatanti, kaṇṭakāvāṭampi kaṇṭakavattampi (sī. pī.), kaṇṭakarājimpi (syā. kaṃ.) ārohanti, suttampi gāviṃ ārohanti, māṇavehipi samāgacchanti katakammehipi akatakammehipi, mātugāmopi te tena (ka.) asaddhammena nimanteti. Bhūtapubbāhaṃ, bhante, rattandhakāratimisāyaṃ piṇḍāya carāmi. Addasā kho maṃ, bhante, aññatarā itthī vijjantarikāya bhājanaṃ dhovantī. Disvā maṃ bhītā vissaramakāsi – ‘abhumme abbhumme (sī. pī.) pisāco vata ma’nti! Evaṃ vutte, ahaṃ, bhante, taṃ itthiṃ etadavocaṃ – ‘nāhaṃ, bhagini, pisāco; bhikkhu piṇḍāya [P 1.0449] ṭhito’ti. ‘Bhikkhussa ātumārī, bhikkhussa mātumārī ṭhito’ti. bhikkhussa ātumātumārī (ka.)! Varaṃ te, bhikkhu, tiṇhena govikantanena kucchi parikanto, na tveva varaṃ yaṃ na tveva yā (sī. pī.) rattandhakāratimisāyaṃ kucchihetu piṇḍāya carasī’ti carasāti (sī. pī.). Tassa mayhaṃ, bhante, tadanussarato evaṃ hoti – ‘bahūnaṃ vata no bhagavā dukkhadhammānaṃ apahattā, bahūnaṃ vata no bhagavā sukhadhammānaṃ upahattā; bahūnaṃ vata no bhagavā akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ apahattā, bahūnaṃ vata no bhagavā kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ upahattā’”ti.

149. Then, the Venerable Udāyī, having sat down to one side, said this to the Blessed One: 'Here, venerable sir, while I was alone in seclusion, this thought arose in my mind: ‘Indeed, the Blessed One has removed many states of suffering for us; indeed, the Blessed One has brought many states of happiness for us. Indeed, the Blessed One has removed many unwholesome states for us; indeed, the Blessed One has brought many wholesome states for us.’ For, venerable sir, in the past we used to eat in the evening, in the morning, and during the day at the wrong time. There came a time, venerable sir, when the Blessed One addressed the monks: ‘Come, monks, abandon this daytime meal at the wrong time.’ Then, venerable sir, I felt dismay and sorrow: ‘The faithful householders give us delicious food during the day at the wrong time, yet the Blessed One tells us to abandon it, the Fortunate One advises us to relinquish it.’ But, venerable sir, out of love, respect, shame, and fear of wrongdoing toward the Blessed One, we abandoned that daytime meal at the wrong time. Then, venerable sir, we ate only in the evening and in the morning. There came another time, venerable sir, when the Blessed One addressed the monks: ‘Come, monks, abandon this nighttime meal at the wrong time.’ Then, venerable sir, I felt dismay and sorrow: ‘The Blessed One tells us to abandon even the one considered more delicious of these two meals, the Fortunate One advises us to relinquish it.’ Once, venerable sir, a certain man obtained relish during the day and said: ‘Come, set this aside, and in the evening we will all eat it together.’ Indeed, venerable sir, whatever delicacies are prepared are all for the nighttime; few are for the daytime. But, venerable sir, out of love, respect, shame, and fear of wrongdoing toward the Blessed One, we abandoned that nighttime meal at the wrong time. Once, venerable sir, monks wandering for alms in the pitch-black darkness of night entered a sewer, fell into a cesspit, climbed over a thorny fence, stepped on a sleeping cow, and encountered thieves, both those who had already committed a crime and those who had not. A woman even invited them to misconduct. Once, venerable sir, I was wandering for alms in the pitch-black darkness of night. A certain woman saw me by a flash of lightning while washing a pot and, frightened, screamed: ‘Woe is me! A goblin is upon me!’ When she said this, I told her: ‘Sister, I am not a goblin; I am a monk standing for alms.’ She replied: ‘May your father die, monk! May your mother die! Better for you, monk, that your belly be slit open with a sharp butcher’s knife than to wander for alms in the pitch-black darkness of night for the sake of your belly!’ Recalling this, venerable sir, I think: ‘Indeed, the Blessed One has removed many states of suffering for us; indeed, the Blessed One has brought many states of happiness for us. Indeed, the Blessed One has removed many unwholesome states for us; indeed, the Blessed One has brought many wholesome states for us.’”

150. “Evameva panudāyi, idhekacce moghapurisā ‘idaṃ pajahathā’ti mayā [T 2.0182] vuccamānā te evamāhaṃsu – ‘kiṃ panimassa appamattakassa oramattakassa adhisallikhatevāyaṃ samaṇo’ti. Te tañceva nappajahanti, mayi [M 2.0113] ca appaccayaṃ upaṭṭhāpenti. Ye ca bhikkhū sikkhākāmā tesaṃ taṃ, udāyi, hoti balavaṃ bandhanaṃ, daḷhaṃ bandhanaṃ, thiraṃ bandhanaṃ, apūtikaṃ bandhanaṃ, thūlo, kaliṅgaro – seyyathāpi, udāyi, laṭukikā sakuṇikā pūtilatāya bandhanena baddhā tattheva vadhaṃ vā bandhaṃ vā maraṇaṃ vā āgameti. Yo nu kho, udāyi, evaṃ vadeyya – ‘yena sā laṭukikā sakuṇikā pūtilatāya bandhanena baddhā tattheva vadhaṃ vā bandhaṃ vā maraṇaṃ vā āgameti, tañhi tassā abalaṃ bandhanaṃ[V 2.0122], dubbalaṃ bandhanaṃ, pūtikaṃ bandhanaṃ, asārakaṃ bandhana’nti; sammā nu kho so, udāyi, vadamāno vadeyyā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante. Yena sā, bhante, laṭukikā sakuṇikā pūtilatāya bandhanena baddhā tattheva vadhaṃ vā bandhaṃ vā maraṇaṃ vā āgameti, tañhi tassā balavaṃ bandhanaṃ, daḷhaṃ bandhanaṃ, thiraṃ bandhanaṃ apūtikaṃ bandhanaṃ, thūlo, kaliṅgaro”ti. “Evameva kho, udāyi, idhekacce moghapurisā ‘idaṃ pajahathā’ti mayā vuccamānā te evamāhaṃsu – ‘kiṃ panimassa appamattakassa oramattakassa adhisallikhatevāyaṃ samaṇo’ti? Te tañceva nappajahanti, mayi ca appaccayaṃ upaṭṭhāpenti. Ye ca bhikkhū sikkhākāmā tesaṃ taṃ, udāyi, hoti balavaṃ bandhanaṃ, daḷhaṃ bandhanaṃ, thiraṃ bandhanaṃ, apūtikaṃ bandhanaṃ, thūlo, kaliṅgaro”.

150. In the same way, Udāyī, some foolish men here, when told by me, ‘Give this up,’ say, ‘Why is this ascetic so excessively scrupulous about this trifling, petty thing?’ They do not give it up, and they establish displeasure in me and in those monks who are desirous of the training. For those foolish men, Udāyī, that becomes a strong bond, a firm bond, a lasting bond, an unrotten bond, a thick log. Just as, Udāyī, a small quail bound by a rotten creeper meets with slaughter, bondage, or death right there. If someone were to say, ‘That by which this small quail, bound by a rotten creeper, meets with slaughter, bondage, or death right there—that is for her a weak bond, a feeble bond, a rotten bond, a worthless bond’—would he be speaking rightly, Udāyī?" "No, venerable sir. That by which this small quail, bound by a rotten creeper, meets with slaughter, bondage, or death right there—that is for her a strong bond, a firm bond, a lasting bond, an unrotten bond, a thick log." "Just so, Udāyī, some foolish men here, when told by me, ‘Give this up,’ say, ‘Why is this ascetic so excessively scrupulous about this trifling, petty thing?’ They do not give it up, and they establish displeasure in me and in those monks who are desirous of the training. For those foolish men, Udāyī, that becomes a strong bond, a firm bond, a lasting bond, an unrotten bond, a thick log.

151. “Idha [T 2.0183] panudāyi, ekacce kulaputtā ‘idaṃ pajahathā’ti mayā [P 1.0450] vuccamānā te evamāhaṃsu – ‘kiṃ panimassa appamattakassa oramattakassa pahātabbassa yassa no bhagavā pahānamāha, yassa no sugato paṭinissaggamāhā’ti? Te tañceva pajahanti, mayi ca na appaccayaṃ upaṭṭhāpenti. Ye ca bhikkhū sikkhākāmā te taṃ pahāya appossukkā pannalomā paradattavuttā paradavuttā (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) migabhūtena cetasā viharanti. Tesaṃ taṃ, udāyi, hoti abalaṃ bandhanaṃ, dubbalaṃ bandhanaṃ, pūtikaṃ bandhanaṃ, asārakaṃ bandhanaṃ – seyyathāpi, udāyi, rañño nāgo īsādanto urūḷhavā abhijāto saṅgāmāvacaro daḷhehi varattehi bandhanehi baddho īsakaṃyeva kāyaṃ sannāmetvā tāni bandhanāni saṃchinditvā saṃpadāletvā yena kāmaṃ pakkamati. Yo nu kho, udāyi, evaṃ vadeyya – ‘yehi so rañño nāgo īsādanto urūḷhavā abhijāto saṅgāmāvacaro daḷhehi varattehi bandhanehi baddho īsakaṃyeva kāyaṃ sannāmetvā tāni bandhanāni saṃchinditvā saṃpadāletvā yena kāmaṃ pakkamati, tañhi tassa balavaṃ bandhanaṃ, daḷhaṃ bandhanaṃ, thiraṃ bandhanaṃ, apūtikaṃ [M 2.0114] bandhanaṃ, thūlo, kaliṅgaro’ti; sammā nu kho so, udāyi, vadamāno vadeyyā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante. Yehi so, bhante, rañño nāgo īsādanto urūḷhavā abhijāto saṅgāmāvacaro daḷhehi varattehi bandhanehi baddho īsakaṃyeva kāyaṃ sannāmetvā tāni bandhanāni saṃchinditvā [T 2.0184] saṃpadāletvā yena kāmaṃ pakkamati, tañhi tassa abalaṃ bandhanaṃ…pe… asārakaṃ bandhana”nti. “Evameva kho, udāyi, idhekacce kulaputtā ‘idaṃ pajahathā’ti mayā vuccamānā te evamāhaṃsu – ‘kiṃ panimassa appamattakassa oramattakassa pahātabbassa yassa no bhagavā pahānamāha, yassa no sugato paṭinissaggamāhā’ti? Te tañceva pajahanti, mayi ca na appaccayaṃ upaṭṭhāpenti. Ye ca bhikkhū sikkhākāmā te taṃ [V 2.0123] pahāya appossukkā pannalomā paradattavuttā migabhūtena cetasā viharanti. Tesaṃ taṃ, udāyi, hoti abalaṃ bandhanaṃ, dubbalaṃ bandhanaṃ, pūtikaṃ bandhanaṃ, asārakaṃ bandhanaṃ”.

151. Herein, Udāyī, some clansmen, when told by me, ‘Abandon this,’ say thus: ‘What is this trifling, insignificant thing to be abandoned, that our Blessed One speaks of its abandonment, that our Sugata speaks of its relinquishment?’ They abandon that very thing and do not arouse displeasure towards me, nor towards those monks who are desirous of training. They, having abandoned that, dwell without anxiety, with pride cast down, living on what is given by others, with a mind that has become like a deer's. For them, Udāyī, that is a weak fetter, a feeble fetter, a rotten fetter, a sapless fetter. Suppose, Udāyī, a king's elephant with tusks like a chariot-pole, well-proportioned, of noble breed, a battle-goer, were bound with strong leather straps. Bending its body just a little, it would cut and break those bonds and depart wherever it wished. Now, Udāyī, if someone were to say: ‘Those bonds with which the king's elephant with tusks like a chariot-pole, well-proportioned, of noble breed, a battle-goer, was bound, which it cut and broke by bending its body just a little and departed wherever it wished—for it that was a strong fetter, a firm fetter, an enduring fetter, an unrotting fetter, a thick wooden fetter’—would that person be speaking rightly?" "Certainly not, venerable sir. Those bonds with which the king's elephant... departed wherever it wished—for it that was a weak fetter... a sapless fetter." "Even so, Udāyī, some clansmen here, when told by me, ‘Abandon this,’ say thus: ‘What is this trifling, insignificant thing to be abandoned, that our Blessed One speaks of its abandonment, that our Sugata speaks of its relinquishment?’ They abandon that very thing and do not arouse displeasure towards me, nor towards those monks who are desirous of training. They, having abandoned that, dwell without anxiety, with pride cast down, living on what is given by others, with a mind that has become like a deer's. For them, Udāyī, that is a weak fetter, a feeble fetter, a rotten fetter, a sapless fetter.

152. “Seyyathāpi, udāyi, puriso daliddo assako anāḷhiyo; tassa’ssa ekaṃ agārakaṃ oluggaviluggaṃ kākātidāyiṃ kākātiḍāyiṃ (?) naparamarūpaṃ, ekā khaṭopikā kaḷopikā (ka.) oluggaviluggā naparamarūpā, ekissā kumbhiyā [P 1.0451] dhaññasamavāpakaṃ naparamarūpaṃ, ekā jāyikā naparamarūpā. So ārāmagataṃ bhikkhuṃ passeyya sudhotahatthapādaṃ manuññaṃ bhojanaṃ bhuttāviṃ sītāya chāyāya nisinnaṃ adhicitte yuttaṃ. Tassa evamassa – ‘sukhaṃ vata, bho, sāmaññaṃ, ārogyaṃ vata, bho, sāmaññaṃ! So vatassaṃ so vatassa (ka.) yohaṃ kesamassuṃ ohāretvā kāsāyāni vatthāni acchādetvā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajeyya’nti. So na sakkuṇeyya ekaṃ agārakaṃ oluggaviluggaṃ kākātidāyiṃ naparamarūpaṃ pahāya, ekaṃ khaṭopikaṃ [T 2.0185] oluggaviluggaṃ naparamarūpaṃ pahāya, ekissā kumbhiyā dhaññasamavāpakaṃ naparamarūpaṃ pahāya, ekaṃ jāyikaṃ naparamarūpaṃ pahāya kesamassuṃ ohāretvā kāsāyāni vatthāni acchādetvā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajituṃ. Yo nu kho, udāyi, evaṃ vadeyya – ‘yehi so puriso bandhanehi baddho na sakkoti ekaṃ agārakaṃ oluggaviluggaṃ kākātidāyiṃ naparamarūpaṃ pahāya, ekaṃ khaṭopikaṃ oluggaviluggaṃ naparamarūpaṃ pahāya, ekissā kumbhiyā dhaññasamavāpakaṃ naparamarūpaṃ pahāya, ekaṃ jāyikaṃ naparamarūpaṃ pahāya kesamassuṃ [M 2.0115] ohāretvā kāsāyāni vatthāni acchādetvā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajituṃ; tañhi tassa abalaṃ bandhanaṃ, dubbalaṃ bandhanaṃ, pūtikaṃ bandhanaṃ, asārakaṃ bandhana’nti; sammā nu kho so, udāyi, vadamāno vadeyyā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante. Yehi so, bhante, puriso bandhanehi baddho, na sakkoti ekaṃ agārakaṃ oluggaviluggaṃ kākātidāyiṃ naparamarūpaṃ pahāya, ekaṃ khaṭopikaṃ oluggaviluggaṃ naparamarūpaṃ pahāya, ekissā kumbhiyā dhaññasamavāpakaṃ naparamarūpaṃ pahāya, ekaṃ jāyikaṃ naparamarūpaṃ pahāya kesamassuṃ ohāretvā kāsāyāni vatthāni acchādetvā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajituṃ; tañhi tassa balavaṃ bandhanaṃ, daḷhaṃ bandhanaṃ, thiraṃ bandhanaṃ, apūtikaṃ bandhanaṃ, thūlo, kaliṅgaro”ti. “Evameva kho, udāyi, idhekacce moghapurisā ‘idaṃ pajahathā’ti mayā vuccamānā te evamāhaṃsu – ‘kiṃ panimassa appamattakassa oramattakassa [T 2.0186] adhisallikhatevāyaṃ samaṇo’ti? Te tañceva nappajahanti, mayi ca appaccayaṃ upaṭṭhāpenti. Ye ca bhikkhū sikkhākāmā tesaṃ taṃ, udāyi, hoti balavaṃ bandhanaṃ, daḷhaṃ bandhanaṃ, thiraṃ bandhanaṃ, apūtikaṃ bandhanaṃ, thūlo, kaliṅgaro”.

152. Suppose, Udāyī, there is a man who is poor, without possessions, and destitute. He might have a single hut, dilapidated and ruined, exposed to crows, not of the best quality; a single cot, dilapidated and ruined, not of the best quality; a single pot with a collection of grains, not of the best quality; and a single wife, not of the best quality. He might see a monk in a monastery, with hands and feet well washed, having eaten a delightful meal, sitting in the cool shade, devoted to the higher mind. It might occur to him: ‘Ah, how pleasant is the state of a recluse! Ah, how healthy is the state of a recluse! If only I were to shave off my hair and beard, put on the ochre robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness!’ But he would be unable to abandon his single dilapidated hut... his single wife... to shave off his hair and beard, put on the ochre robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness. Now, Udāyī, if someone were to say: ‘Those bonds by which that man is bound, such that he is unable to abandon his single dilapidated hut... and go forth... for him that is a weak fetter, a feeble fetter, a rotten fetter, a sapless fetter’—would that person be speaking rightly?" "Certainly not, venerable sir. Those bonds by which that man is bound... for him that is a strong fetter, a firm fetter, an enduring fetter, an unrotting fetter, a thick wooden fetter." "Even so, Udāyī, some worthless men here, when told by me, ‘Abandon this,’ say thus: ‘What is there to this trifling, insignificant thing? This ascetic is just being over-scrupulous.’ They do not abandon that very thing, and they arouse displeasure towards me and towards those monks who are desirous of training. For them, Udāyī, that becomes a strong fetter, a firm fetter, an enduring fetter, an unrotting fetter, a thick wooden fetter.

153. “Seyyathāpi[V 2.0124], udāyi, gahapati vā gahapatiputto vā aḍḍho mahaddhano [P 1.0452] mahābhogo, nekānaṃ nikkhagaṇānaṃ cayo, nekānaṃ dhaññagaṇānaṃ cayo, nekānaṃ khettagaṇānaṃ cayo, nekānaṃ vatthugaṇānaṃ cayo, nekānaṃ bhariyagaṇānaṃ cayo, nekānaṃ dāsagaṇānaṃ cayo, nekānaṃ dāsigaṇānaṃ cayo; so ārāmagataṃ bhikkhuṃ passeyya sudhotahatthapādaṃ manuññaṃ bhojanaṃ bhuttāviṃ sītāya chāyāya nisinnaṃ adhicitte yuttaṃ. Tassa evamassa – ‘sukhaṃ vata, bho, sāmaññaṃ, ārogyaṃ vata, bho, sāmaññaṃ! So vatassaṃ yohaṃ kesamassuṃ ohāretvā kāsāyāni vatthāni acchādetvā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajeyya’nti. So sakkuṇeyya nekāni nikkhagaṇāni pahāya, nekāni dhaññagaṇāni pahāya, nekāni khettagaṇāni pahāya, nekāni vatthugaṇāni pahāya, nekāni bhariyagaṇāni pahāya, nekāni dāsagaṇāni pahāya, nekāni dāsigaṇāni pahāya kesamassuṃ ohāretvā kāsāyāni vatthāni acchādetvā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajituṃ. Yo nu kho, udāyi, evaṃ vadeyya – ‘yehi so gahapati vā gahapatiputto vā bandhanehi baddho, sakkoti nekāni nikkhagaṇāni pahāya, nekāni dhaññagaṇāni pahāya, nekāni [M 2.0116] khettagaṇāni pahāya, nekāni vatthugaṇāni pahāya, nekāni bhariyagaṇāni pahāya, nekāni dāsagaṇāni pahāya, nekāni dāsigaṇāni pahāya kesamassuṃ ohāretvā kāsāyāni vatthāni acchādetvā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajituṃ, tañhi tassa balavaṃ bandhanaṃ, daḷhaṃ bandhanaṃ, thiraṃ bandhanaṃ, apūtikaṃ bandhanaṃ, thūlo, kaliṅgaro’ti; sammā nu kho so, udāyi, vadamāno vadeyyā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante. Yehi so, bhante, gahapati vā gahapatiputto vā bandhanehi baddho, sakkoti nekāni nikkhagaṇāni pahāya, nekāni dhaññagaṇāni pahāya, nekāni [T 2.0187] khettagaṇāni pahāya, nekāni vatthugaṇāni pahāya, nekāni bhariyagaṇāni pahāya, nekāni dāsagaṇāni pahāya, nekāni dāsigaṇāni pahāya kesamassuṃ ohāretvā kāsāyāni vatthāni acchādetvā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajituṃ; tañhi tassa abalaṃ bandhanaṃ, dubbalaṃ bandhanaṃ, pūtikaṃ bandhanaṃ, asārakaṃ bandhana”nti. “Evameva kho, udāyi, idhekacce kulaputtā ‘idaṃ pajahathā’ti mayā vuccamānā te evamāhaṃsu – ‘kiṃ panimassa appamattakassa oramattakassa pahātabbassa yassa no bhagavā pahānamāha yassa, no sugato paṭinissaggamāhā’ti? Te tañceva pajahanti, mayi ca na appaccayaṃ upaṭṭhāpenti. Ye ca bhikkhū sikkhākāmā te taṃ pahāya [P 1.0453] appossukkā pannalomā paradattavuttā migabhūtena cetasā viharanti. Tesaṃ taṃ, udāyi, hoti abalaṃ bandhanaṃ, dubbalaṃ bandhanaṃ, pūtikaṃ bandhanaṃ, asārakaṃ bandhanaṃ”.

153. “For example, Udāyi, a householder or a householder’s son is wealthy, with great riches and possessions: a collection of many groups of gold coins, a collection of many groups of grain, a collection of many groups of fields, a collection of many groups of properties, a collection of many groups of wives, a collection of many groups of male slaves, and a collection of many groups of female slaves. He might see a monk in a monastery who has washed his hands and feet well, has eaten a delightful meal, and is sitting in the cool shade, engaged in the higher mind. To him this thought might occur: ‘Oh, how happy is the state of a recluse! Oh, how healthy is the state of a recluse! It would be good if I were to shave off my hair and beard, put on the ochre-dyed robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness!’ And he would be able to abandon his many groups of gold coins, many groups of grain, many groups of fields, many groups of properties, many groups of wives, many groups of male slaves, and many groups of female slaves, to shave off his hair and beard, put on the ochre-dyed robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness. Now, Udāyi, if someone were to say: ‘The bonds by which that householder or householder’s son is bound, such that he is able to abandon his many groups of gold coins, many groups of grain, many groups of fields, many groups of properties, many groups of wives, many groups of male slaves, and many groups of female slaves, to shave off his hair and beard, put on the ochre-dyed robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness—surely, that bond for him is powerful, firm, solid, unrotting, a thick log-fetter!’—would that person be speaking rightly, Udāyi?” “No, venerable sir. The bonds by which that householder or householder’s son is bound, such that he is able to abandon his many groups of gold coins, many groups of grain, many groups of fields, many groups of properties, many groups of wives, many groups of male slaves, and many groups of female slaves, to shave off his hair and beard, put on the ochre-dyed robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness—surely, that bond for him is powerless, weak, rotting, and without substance.” “Just so, Udāyi, when I say to some clansmen here, ‘Abandon this,’ they say: ‘What is this trifling, inferior thing to be abandoned, for which the Blessed One speaks of abandoning, for which the Well-farer speaks of relinquishing?’ They do abandon just that, and they do not establish displeasure towards me, nor towards those monks who desire the training. Having abandoned that, those clansmen dwell without anxiety, with hair laid low, living on what is given by others, with a mind like a deer's. For them, Udāyi, that bond is powerless, weak, rotting, and without substance.”

154. “Cattārome[V 2.0125], udāyi, puggalā santo saṃvijjamānā lokasmiṃ. Katame [T 2.0188] cattāro? Idhudāyi, ekacco puggalo upadhipahānāya paṭipanno hoti upadhipaṭinissaggāya. Tamenaṃ upadhipahānāya paṭipannaṃ upadhipaṭinissaggāya upadhipaṭisaṃyuttā sarasaṅkappā samudācaranti. So te adhivāseti, nappajahati, na vinodeti, na byantīkaroti, na anabhāvaṃ gameti. Imaṃ kho ahaṃ, udāyi, puggalaṃ ‘saṃyutto’ti vadāmi no ‘visaṃyutto’. Taṃ kissa hetu? Indriyavemattatā hi me, udāyi, imasmiṃ puggale viditā.

154. “Udāyi, these four persons are found existing in the world. Which four? Here, Udāyi, a certain person is practicing for the abandoning of the substrates of existence, for their relinquishing. While he is practicing for the abandoning and relinquishing of the substrates of existence, thoughts connected with the substrates of existence assail him. He consents to them; he does not abandon them, does not dispel them, does not bring them to an end, and does not cause them to cease. This person, Udāyi, I call ‘fettered,’ not ‘unfettered.’ For what reason? Because the diversity of faculties in this person is known to me, Udāyi.”

“Idha panudāyi, ekacco puggalo upadhipahānāya paṭipanno hoti upadhipaṭinissaggāya. Tamenaṃ upadhipahānāya paṭipannaṃ upadhipaṭinissaggāya upadhipaṭisaṃyuttā sarasaṅkappā samudācaranti. So te nādhivāseti, pajahati, vinodeti, byantīkaroti, anabhāvaṃ gameti. Imampi kho ahaṃ, udāyi[M 2.0117], puggalaṃ ‘saṃyutto’ti vadāmi no ‘visaṃyutto’. Taṃ kissa hetu? Indriyavemattatā hi me, udāyi, imasmiṃ puggale viditā.

“Furthermore, Udāyi, a certain person here is practicing for the abandoning of the substrates of existence, for their relinquishing. While he is practicing for the abandoning and relinquishing of the substrates of existence, thoughts connected with the substrates of existence assail him. He does not consent to them; he abandons them, dispels them, brings them to an end, and causes them to cease. This person too, Udāyi, I call ‘fettered,’ not ‘unfettered.’ For what reason? Because the diversity of faculties in this person is known to me, Udāyi.”

“Idha panudāyi, ekacco puggalo upadhipahānāya paṭipanno hoti upadhipaṭinissaggāya. Tamenaṃ upadhipahānāya paṭipannaṃ upadhipaṭinissaggāya kadāci karahaci satisammosā upadhipaṭisaṃyuttā sarasaṅkappā samudācaranti; dandho, udāyi, satuppādo. Atha kho naṃ khippameva pajahati, vinodeti, byantīkaroti, anabhāvaṃ gameti. Seyyathāpi, udāyi, puriso divasaṃsantatte divasasantatte (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) ayokaṭāhe dve vā tīṇi vā udakaphusitāni nipāteyya; dandho, udāyi, udakaphusitānaṃ nipāto. Atha kho naṃ khippameva parikkhayaṃ pariyādānaṃ gaccheyya. Evameva kho, udāyi, idhekacco [T 2.0189] puggalo upadhipahānāya paṭipanno hoti upadhipaṭinissaggāya. Tamenaṃ upadhipahānāya paṭipannaṃ upadhipaṭinissaggāya kadāci karahaci satisammosā upadhipaṭisaṃyuttā sarasaṅkappā samudācaranti; dandho, udāyi, satuppādo. Atha kho naṃ khippameva pajahati, vinodeti, byantīkaroti, anabhāvaṃ gameti. Imampi kho ahaṃ, udāyi, puggalaṃ ‘saṃyutto’ti vadāmi no ‘visaṃyutto’. Taṃ [P 1.0454] kissa hetu? Indriyavemattatā hi me, udāyi, imasmiṃ puggale viditā.

Here, Udāyi, a certain person has entered upon the path for the abandoning of attachments, for the relinquishing of attachments. While he has entered upon the path for the abandoning of attachments and the relinquishing of attachments, occasionally, due to a lapse in mindfulness, thoughts connected with attachments assail him; slow, Udāyi, is the arising of mindfulness. Yet he quickly abandons them, dispels them, eliminates them, and brings them to non-existence. Just as, Udāyi, if a man were to drop two or three drops of water onto an iron pan heated all day—slow, Udāyi, would be the falling of those drops. Yet they would quickly go to exhaustion and utter disappearance. In the same way, Udāyi, here a certain person has entered upon the path for the abandoning of attachments, for the relinquishing of attachments. While he has entered upon the path for the abandoning of attachments and the relinquishing of attachments, occasionally, due to a lapse in mindfulness, thoughts connected with attachments assail him; slow, Udāyi, is the arising of mindfulness. Yet he quickly abandons them, dispels them, eliminates them, and brings them to non-existence. This person too, Udāyi, I call ‘conjoined,’ not ‘unconjoined.’ For what reason? Because the variation of faculties in this person is known to me, Udāyi.

“Idha panudāyi, ekacco puggalo ‘upadhi dukkhassa mūla’nti – iti viditvā nirupadhi hoti, upadhisaṅkhaye vimutto. Imaṃ kho ahaṃ, udāyi, puggalaṃ ‘visaṃyutto’ti vadāmi no ‘saṃyutto’ti[V 2.0126]. Taṃ kissa hetu? Indriyavemattatā hi me, udāyi, imasmiṃ puggale viditā. Ime kho, udāyi, cattāro puggalā santo saṃvijjamānā lokasmiṃ.

Here, Udāyi, a certain person, having known thus, ‘Attachment is the root of suffering,’ becomes without attachment, liberated in the destruction of attachment. This person, Udāyi, I call ‘unconjoined,’ not ‘conjoined.’ For what reason? Because the variation of faculties in this person is known to me, Udāyi. These, Udāyi, are the four persons who exist and are found in the world.

155. “Pañca kho ime, udāyi, kāmaguṇā. Katame pañca? Cakkhuviññeyyā rūpā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā rajanīyā, sotaviññeyyā saddā…pe… ghānaviññeyyā gandhā… jivhāviññeyyā rasā… kāyaviññeyyā phoṭṭhabbā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā rajanīyā. Ime kho, udāyi, pañca kāmaguṇā. Yaṃ kho, udāyi, ime pañca kāmaguṇe paṭicca uppajjati sukhaṃ somanassaṃ idaṃ vuccati kāmasukhaṃ miḷhasukhaṃ mīḷhasukhaṃ (sī. pī.) puthujjanasukhaṃ anariyasukhaṃ, na sevitabbaṃ, na bhāvetabbaṃ, na bahulīkātabbaṃ; ‘bhāyitabbaṃ [T 2.0190] etassa sukhassā’ti vadāmi.

155. Udāyi, there are these five strands of sensual pleasure. Which five? Forms cognizable by the eye—desirable, pleasing, agreeable, of a lovely form, connected with sensual desire, and enticing; sounds cognizable by the ear… smells cognizable by the nose… tastes cognizable by the tongue… tangible objects cognizable by the body—desirable, pleasing, agreeable, of a lovely form, connected with sensual desire, and enticing. These, Udāyi, are the five strands of sensual pleasure. The pleasure and joy that arise dependent on these five strands of sensual pleasure—this is called sensual pleasure, filthy pleasure, the pleasure of an ordinary person, ignoble pleasure. It should not be pursued, should not be developed, should not be cultivated. I say that one should fear this pleasure.

156. “Idhudāyi[M 2.0118], bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehi…pe… paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati, vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā… dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati, pītiyā ca virāgā… tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati, sukhassa ca pahānā… catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Idaṃ vuccati nekkhammasukhaṃ pavivekasukhaṃ upasamasukhaṃ sambodhasukhaṃ, āsevitabbaṃ, bhāvetabbaṃ, bahulīkātabbaṃ; ‘na bhāyitabbaṃ etassa sukhassā’ti vadāmi.

156. Here, Udāyi, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures… enters and dwells in the first jhāna. With the stilling of applied and sustained thought… he enters and dwells in the second jhāna. With the fading away of rapture… he enters and dwells in the third jhāna. With the abandoning of pleasure… he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna. This is called the pleasure of renunciation, the pleasure of seclusion, the pleasure of peace, the pleasure of awakening. It should be pursued, developed, and cultivated. I say, ‘One should not fear this pleasure.’

“Idhudāyi, bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehi…pe… paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati; idaṃ kho ahaṃ, udāyi, iñjitasmiṃ vadāmi. Kiñca tattha iñjitasmiṃ? Yadeva tattha vitakkavicārā aniruddhā honti idaṃ tattha iñjitasmiṃ. Idhudāyi, bhikkhu vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā…pe… dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati; idampi kho ahaṃ, udāyi, iñjitasmiṃ vadāmi. Kiñca tattha iñjitasmiṃ? Yadeva tattha pītisukhaṃ aniruddhaṃ hoti idaṃ tattha iñjitasmiṃ. Idhudāyi, bhikkhu pītiyā ca virāgā…pe… [V 2.0127] tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati; idampi kho ahaṃ, udāyi, iñjitasmiṃ vadāmi. Kiñca tattha iñjitasmiṃ? Yadeva tattha upekkhāsukhaṃ [P 1.0455] aniruddhaṃ hoti idaṃ tattha iñjitasmiṃ. Idhudāyi, bhikkhu sukhassa ca pahānā…pe… catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati; idaṃ kho ahaṃ, udāyi, aniñjitasmiṃ vadāmi.

Here, Udāyi, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures… enters and dwells in the first jhāna; this, Udāyi, I say is an agitated state. And what is agitated therein? The fact that applied and sustained thought have not ceased therein—this is what is agitated therein. Here, Udāyi, a bhikkhu, with the stilling of applied and sustained thought… enters and dwells in the second jhāna; this too, Udāyi, I say is an agitated state. And what is agitated therein? The fact that rapture and pleasure have not ceased therein—this is what is agitated therein. Here, Udāyi, a bhikkhu, with the fading away of rapture… enters and dwells in the third jhāna; this too, Udāyi, I say is an agitated state. And what is agitated therein? The fact that the pleasure of equanimity has not ceased therein—this is what is agitated therein. Here, Udāyi, a bhikkhu, with the abandoning of pleasure… enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna; this, Udāyi, I say is an unagitated state.

“Idhudāyi[T 2.0191], bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehi…pe… paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati; idaṃ kho ahaṃ, udāyi, ‘anala’nti vadāmi, ‘pajahathā’ti vadāmi, ‘samatikkamathā’ti vadāmi. Ko ca tassa samatikkamo? Idhudāyi, bhikkhu vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā… dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati, ayaṃ tassa samatikkamo; idampi kho ahaṃ, udāyi, ‘anala’nti vadāmi, ‘pajahathā’ti vadāmi, ‘samatikkamathā’ti vadāmi. Ko ca tassa samatikkamo? Idhudāyi, bhikkhu pītiyā ca virāgā… tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati, ayaṃ tassa samatikkamo; idampi kho ahaṃ, udāyi, ‘anala’nti vadāmi, ‘pajahathā’ti vadāmi, ‘samatikkamathā’ti vadāmi. Ko ca tassa samatikkamo? Idhudāyi, bhikkhu sukhassa ca pahānā… catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati, ayaṃ tassa samatikkamo; idampi kho ahaṃ, udāyi, ‘anala’nti vadāmi, ‘pajahathā’ti vadāmi, ‘samatikkamathā’ti vadāmi. Ko ca tassa samatikkamo? Idhudāyi, bhikkhu sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ samatikkamā paṭighasaññānaṃ atthaṅgamā nānattasaññānaṃ amanasikārā ‘ananto ākāso’ti ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati, ayaṃ tassa samatikkamo; idampi kho ahaṃ, udāyi, ‘anala’nti [M 2.0119] vadāmi, ‘pajahathā’ti vadāmi, ‘samatikkamathā’ti vadāmi. Ko ca tassa samatikkamo? Idhudāyi, bhikkhu sabbaso ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma ‘anantaṃ viññāṇa’nti viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati, ayaṃ tassa samatikkamo[T 2.0192]; idampi kho ahaṃ, udāyi, ‘anala’nti vadāmi, ‘pajahathā’ti vadāmi, ‘samatikkamathā’ti vadāmi. Ko ca [V 2.0128] tassa samatikkamo? Idhudāyi, bhikkhu sabbaso viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma ‘natthi kiñcī’ti ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati, ayaṃ tassa samatikkamo; idampi kho ahaṃ, udāyi, ‘anala’nti vadāmi, ‘pajahathā’ti vadāmi, ‘samatikkamathā’ti vadāmi. Ko ca tassa samatikkamo? Idhudāyi, bhikkhu sabbaso ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ samatikkamma nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ upasampajja [P 1.0456] viharati, ayaṃ tassa samatikkamo; idampi kho ahaṃ, udāyi, ‘anala’nti vadāmi, ‘pajahathā’ti vadāmi, ‘samatikkamathā’ti vadāmi. Ko ca tassa samatikkamo? Idhudāyi, bhikkhu sabbaso nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ samatikkamma saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ upasampajja viharati, ayaṃ tassa samatikkamo; iti kho ahaṃ, udāyi, nevasaññānāsaññāyatanassapi pahānaṃ vadāmi. Passasi no tvaṃ, udāyi, taṃ saṃyojanaṃ aṇuṃ vā thūlaṃ vā yassāhaṃ no pahānaṃ vadāmī”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”ti.

“Here, Udāyi, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures… enters and dwells in the first jhāna. This, Udāyi, I declare is ‘not sufficient.’ I declare, ‘Abandon it.’ I declare, ‘Transcend it.’ And what is the means of transcending it? Here, Udāyi, a bhikkhu, with the stilling of applied and sustained thought… enters and dwells in the second jhāna. This is the means of transcending it. This too, Udāyi, I declare is ‘not sufficient.’ I declare, ‘Abandon it.’ I declare, ‘Transcend it.’ And what is the means of transcending it? Here, Udāyi, a bhikkhu, with the fading away of rapture… enters and dwells in the third jhāna. This is the means of transcending it. This too, Udāyi, I declare is ‘not sufficient.’ I declare, ‘Abandon it.’ I declare, ‘Transcend it.’ And what is the means of transcending it? Here, Udāyi, a bhikkhu, with the abandoning of pleasure… enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna. This is the means of transcending it. This too, Udāyi, I declare is ‘not sufficient.’ I declare, ‘Abandon it.’ I declare, ‘Transcend it.’ And what is the means of transcending it? Here, Udāyi, a bhikkhu, by completely transcending perceptions of form, with the cessation of perceptions of resistance, by not attending to perceptions of diversity, meditating ‘Space is infinite,’ enters and dwells in the sphere of infinite space. This is the means of transcending it. This too, Udāyi, I declare is ‘not sufficient.’ I declare, ‘Abandon it.’ I declare, ‘Transcend it.’ And what is the means of transcending it? Here, Udāyi, a bhikkhu, by completely transcending the sphere of infinite space, meditating ‘Consciousness is infinite,’ enters and dwells in the sphere of infinite consciousness. This is the means of transcending it. This too, Udāyi, I declare is ‘not sufficient.’ I declare, ‘Abandon it.’ I declare, ‘Transcend it.’ And what is the means of transcending it? Here, Udāyi, a bhikkhu, by completely transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, meditating ‘There is nothing,’ enters and dwells in the sphere of nothingness. This is the means of transcending it. This too, Udāyi, I declare is ‘not sufficient.’ I declare, ‘Abandon it.’ I declare, ‘Transcend it.’ And what is the means of transcending it? Here, Udāyi, a bhikkhu, by completely transcending the sphere of nothingness, enters and dwells in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. This is the means of transcending it. This too, Udāyi, I declare is ‘not sufficient.’ I declare, ‘Abandon it.’ I declare, ‘Transcend it.’ And what is the means of transcending it? Here, Udāyi, a bhikkhu, by completely transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling. This is the means of transcending it. Thus, Udāyi, I declare the abandoning even of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Do you, Udāyi, see any fetter, subtle or gross, of which I do not declare the abandoning?” “Indeed not, venerable sir.”

Idamavoca bhagavā. Attamano āyasmā udāyī bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandīti.

The Blessed One said this. Delighted, the venerable Udāyī rejoiced in the Blessed One's utterance.

Laṭukikopamasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ chaṭṭhaṃ.

The Laṭukikopama Sutta, the sixth, is concluded.

7. Cātumasuttaṃ

7. The Cātuma Sutta

157. Evaṃ [T 2.0193][V 2.0129] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā cātumāyaṃ viharati āmalakīvane. Tena kho pana samayena sāriputtamoggallānappamukhāni pañcamattāni bhikkhusatāni cātumaṃ anuppattāni honti bhagavantaṃ dassanāya. Te ca āgantukā bhikkhū nevāsikehi bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ paṭisammodamānā senāsanāni paññāpayamānā pattacīvarāni paṭisāmayamānā uccāsaddā mahāsaddā ahesuṃ. Atha kho bhagavā āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ āmantesi – “ke panete, ānanda, uccāsaddā mahāsaddā, kevaṭṭā maññe macchavilope”ti? “Etāni, bhante, sāriputtamoggallānappamukhāni pañcamattāni bhikkhusatāni cātumaṃ [M 2.0120] anuppattāni bhagavantaṃ dassanāya. Te āgantukā bhikkhū nevāsikehi bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ paṭisammodamānā senāsanāni paññāpayamānā pattacīvarāni paṭisāmayamānā uccāsaddā mahāsaddā”ti. “Tenahānanda, mama vacanena te bhikkhū āmantehi – ‘satthā āyasmante āmantetī’”ti. “Evaṃ, bhante”ti kho āyasmā ānando bhagavato paṭissutvā yena te bhikkhū tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā te bhikkhū etadavoca – “satthā āyasmante āmantetī”ti. “Evamāvuso”ti kho te bhikkhū [P 1.0457] āyasmato ānandassa paṭissutvā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Ekamantaṃ nisinne kho te [T 2.0194] bhikkhū bhagavā etadavoca – “kiṃ nu tumhe, bhikkhave, uccāsaddā mahāsaddā, kevaṭṭā maññe macchavilope”ti? “Imāni, bhante, sāriputtamoggallānappamukhāni pañcamattāni bhikkhusatāni cātumaṃ anuppattāni bhagavantaṃ dassanāya. Teme āgantukā bhikkhū nevāsikehi bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ paṭisammodamānā senāsanāni paññāpayamānā pattacīvarāni paṭisāmayamānā uccāsaddā mahāsaddā”ti. “Gacchatha, bhikkhave, paṇāmemi vo, na vo mama santike vatthabba”nti. “Evaṃ, bhante”ti kho te bhikkhū bhagavato paṭissutvā uṭṭhāyāsanā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā senāsanaṃ saṃsāmetvā pattacīvaramādāya pakkamiṃsu.

157. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Cātumā in the Āmalakīvana. Now at that time, five hundred bhikkhus headed by Sāriputta and Moggallāna had arrived at Cātumā to see the Blessed One. And those visiting bhikkhus, while exchanging greetings with the resident bhikkhus, preparing their lodgings, and putting away their bowls and robes, became loud and made a great noise. Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “What, Ānanda, are these loud and great noises, like those of fishermen, I think, at a fish-haul?” “Venerable Sir, these five hundred bhikkhus headed by Sāriputta and Moggallāna have arrived at Cātumā to see the Blessed One. These visiting bhikkhus, while exchanging greetings with the resident bhikkhus, preparing their lodgings, and putting away their bowls and robes, are loud and make a great noise.” “In that case, Ānanda, address those bhikkhus in my name, saying: ‘The Teacher summons the venerable ones.’” “Yes, Venerable Sir,” the Venerable Ānanda replied, and having assented to the Blessed One, he went to those bhikkhus and said to them: “The Teacher summons the venerable ones.” “Yes, friend,” those bhikkhus replied, and having assented to the Venerable Ānanda, they went to the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. When they were seated to one side, the Blessed One said to those bhikkhus: “Why, bhikkhus, are you loud and making a great noise, like fishermen, I think, at a fish-haul?” “Venerable Sir, these five hundred bhikkhus headed by Sāriputta and Moggallāna have arrived at Cātumā to see the Blessed One. These visiting bhikkhus, while exchanging greetings with the resident bhikkhus, preparing their lodgings, and putting away their bowls and robes, have become loud and are making a great noise.” “Go, bhikkhus, I dismiss you. You are not to stay in my presence.” “Yes, Venerable Sir,” those bhikkhus replied, and having assented to the Blessed One, they rose from their seats, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping their right side towards him, set their lodgings in order, took their bowls and robes, and departed.

158. Tena kho pana samayena cātumeyyakā sakyā santhāgāre sandhāgāre (ka.) sannipatitā honti kenacideva [V 2.0130] karaṇīyena. Addasaṃsu kho cātumeyyakā sakyā te bhikkhū dūratova āgacchante; disvāna yena te bhikkhū tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā te bhikkhū etadavocuṃ – “handa, kahaṃ pana tumhe āyasmanto gacchathā”ti? “Bhagavatā kho, āvuso, bhikkhusaṅgho paṇāmito”ti. “Tenahāyasmanto muhuttaṃ nisīdatha, appeva nāma mayaṃ sakkuṇeyyāma bhagavantaṃ pasādetu”nti. “Evamāvuso”ti kho te bhikkhū cātumeyyakānaṃ sakyānaṃ paccassosuṃ. Atha kho cātumeyyakā sakyā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ [T 2.0195] abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Ekamantaṃ nisinnā kho cātumeyyakā sakyā bhagavantaṃ etadavocuṃ – “abhinandatu, bhante, bhagavā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ; abhivadatu, bhante, bhagavā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ. Seyyathāpi, bhante[M 2.0121], bhagavatā pubbe bhikkhusaṅgho anuggahito, evameva bhagavā etarahi anuggaṇhātu bhikkhusaṅghaṃ. Santettha, bhante, bhikkhū navā acirapabbajitā adhunāgatā imaṃ dhammavinayaṃ. Tesaṃ bhagavantaṃ dassanāya alabhantānaṃ siyā aññathattaṃ, siyā vipariṇāmo. Seyyathāpi, bhante, bījānaṃ taruṇānaṃ udakaṃ alabhantānaṃ siyā aññathattaṃ siyā vipariṇāmo; evameva kho, bhante, santettha bhikkhū [P 1.0458] navā acirapabbajitā adhunāgatā imaṃ dhammavinayaṃ, tesaṃ bhagavantaṃ dassanāya alabhantānaṃ siyā aññathattaṃ, siyā vipariṇāmo. Seyyathāpi, bhante, vacchassa taruṇassa mātaraṃ apassantassa siyā aññathattaṃ, siyā vipariṇāmo; evameva kho, bhante, santettha bhikkhū navā acirapabbajitā adhunāgatā imaṃ dhammavinayaṃ, tesaṃ bhagavantaṃ apassantānaṃ siyā aññathattaṃ, siyā vipariṇāmo. Abhinandatu, bhante, bhagavā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ; abhivadatu, bhante, bhagavā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ. Seyyathāpi, bhante, bhagavatā pubbe bhikkhusaṅgho anuggahito; evameva bhagavā etarahi anuggaṇhātu bhikkhusaṅgha”nti.

158. Now at that time the Cātumā Sakyans were gathered in the assembly hall for some business or other. The Cātumā Sakyans saw those bhikkhus coming from afar. Seeing them, they approached the bhikkhus and said: “Pray, venerable sirs, where are you going?” “Friends, the Saṅgha of bhikkhus has been dismissed by the Blessed One.” “Then, venerable sirs, please sit for a moment. Perhaps we may be able to appease the Blessed One.” “Yes, friends,” those bhikkhus replied, assenting to the Cātumā Sakyans. Then the Cātumā Sakyans approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, they said to the Blessed One: “Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One be pleased with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus; may the Blessed One address the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. Just as the Blessed One has formerly supported the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, so too may the Blessed One now support the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. There are, Venerable Sir, new bhikkhus here, not long ordained, who have recently come to this Dhamma and Discipline. Not getting to see the Blessed One, there might be a change in them, there might be a deviation. Just as, Venerable Sir, young seeds that do not get water might change or deviate; even so, Venerable Sir, there are new bhikkhus here, not long ordained, who have recently come to this Dhamma and Discipline. Not getting to see the Blessed One, there might be a change in them, there might be a deviation. Just as, Venerable Sir, a young calf that does not see its mother might change or deviate; even so, Venerable Sir, there are new bhikkhus here, not long ordained, who have recently come to this Dhamma and Discipline. Not seeing the Blessed One, there might be a change in them, there might be a deviation. May the Blessed One be pleased with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus; may the Blessed One address the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. Just as the Blessed One has formerly supported the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, so too may the Blessed One now support the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.”

159. Atha kho brahmā sahampati bhagavato cetasā cetoparivitakkamaññāya – seyyathāpi nāma balavā puriso samiñjitaṃ sammiñjitaṃ (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) vā bāhaṃ pasāreyya, pasāritaṃ vā bāhaṃ samiñjeyya, evameva – brahmaloke [T 2.0196] antarahito bhagavato purato pāturahosi. Atha kho brahmā sahampati ekaṃsaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ karitvā yena bhagavā tenañjaliṃ paṇāmetvā bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “abhinandatu, bhante, bhagavā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ; abhivadatu, bhante, bhagavā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ. Seyyathāpi, bhante, bhagavatā pubbe bhikkhusaṅgho anuggahito; evameva bhagavā etarahi anuggaṇhātu bhikkhusaṅghaṃ. Santettha, bhante, bhikkhū navā acirapabbajitā adhunāgatā imaṃ dhammavinayaṃ, tesaṃ bhagavantaṃ [V 2.0131] dassanāya alabhantānaṃ siyā aññathattaṃ, siyā vipariṇāmo. Seyyathāpi, bhante, bījānaṃ taruṇānaṃ udakaṃ alabhantānaṃ siyā aññathattaṃ, siyā vipariṇāmo; evameva kho, bhante, santettha bhikkhū navā acirapabbajitā adhunāgatā imaṃ dhammavinayaṃ, tesaṃ bhagavantaṃ dassanāya alabhantānaṃ siyā aññathattaṃ, siyā vipariṇāmo. Seyyathāpi bhante, vacchassa taruṇassa mātaraṃ apassantassa siyā aññathattaṃ, siyā vipariṇāmo; evameva kho, bhante, santettha bhikkhū navā [M 2.0122] acirapabbajitā adhunāgatā imaṃ dhammavinayaṃ, tesaṃ bhagavantaṃ apassantānaṃ siyā aññathattaṃ, siyā vipariṇāmo. Abhinandatu, bhante, bhagavā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ; abhivadatu, bhante, bhagavā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ. Seyyathāpi, bhante, bhagavatā pubbe bhikkhusaṅgho [P 1.0459] anuggahito; evameva bhagavā etarahi anuggaṇhātu bhikkhusaṅgha”nti.

159. Then Brahmā Sahampati, having known with his mind the thought in the Blessed One's mind—just as a strong man might extend his bent arm or bend his extended arm, in the same way—disappeared from the Brahmā world and reappeared before the Blessed One. Then Brahmā Sahampati, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder and extended his joined palms towards the Blessed One, said this to the Blessed One: 'Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One rejoice in the Saṅgha of bhikkhus; Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One address the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. Just as, Venerable Sir, the Saṅgha of bhikkhus was formerly favored by the Blessed One, in the same way, may the Blessed One now favor the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. There are here, Venerable Sir, new bhikkhus, not long gone forth, who have recently come to this Dhamma and Discipline. For them, not getting to see the Blessed One, there might be an alteration, there might be a change. Just as, Venerable Sir, for young seeds not receiving water, there might be an alteration, there might be a change; in the same way, Venerable Sir, there are here new bhikkhus, not long gone forth, who have recently come to this Dhamma and Discipline. For them, not getting to see the Blessed One, there might be an alteration, there might be a change. Just as, Venerable Sir, for a young calf not seeing its mother, there might be an alteration, there might be a change; in the same way, Venerable Sir, there are here new bhikkhus, not long gone forth, who have recently come to this Dhamma and Discipline. For them, not seeing the Blessed One, there might be an alteration, there might be a change. Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One rejoice in the Saṅgha of bhikkhus; Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One address the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. Just as, Venerable Sir, the Saṅgha of bhikkhus was formerly favored by the Blessed One, in the same way, may the Blessed One now favor the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.'

160. Asakkhiṃsu kho cātumeyyakā ca sakyā brahmā ca sahampati bhagavantaṃ pasādetuṃ bījūpamena ca taruṇūpamena ca. Atha [T 2.0197] kho āyasmā mahāmoggallāno bhikkhū āmantesi – “uṭṭhethāvuso, gaṇhatha pattacīvaraṃ. Pasādito bhagavā cātumeyyakehi ca sakyehi brahmunā ca sahampatinā bījūpamena ca taruṇūpamena cā”ti. “Evamāvuso”ti kho te bhikkhū āyasmato mahāmoggallānassa paṭissutvā uṭṭhāyāsanā pattacīvaramādāya yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Ekamantaṃ nisinnaṃ kho āyasmantaṃ sāriputtaṃ bhagavā etadavoca – “kinti te, sāriputta, ahosi mayā bhikkhusaṅghe paṇāmite”ti? “Evaṃ kho me, bhante, ahosi – ‘bhagavatā bhikkhusaṅgho paṇāmito. Appossukko dāni bhagavā diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāraṃ anuyutto viharissati, mayampi dāni appossukkā diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāramanuyuttā viharissāmā’”ti. “Āgamehi tvaṃ, sāriputta, āgamehi tvaṃ, sāriputta, diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra”nti. Atha kho bhagavā āyasmantaṃ mahāmoggallānaṃ āmantesi – “kinti te, moggallāna, ahosi mayā bhikkhusaṅghe paṇāmite”ti? “Evaṃ kho me, bhante, ahosi – ‘bhagavatā bhikkhusaṅgho paṇāmito. Appossukko dāni bhagavā diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāraṃ anuyutto viharissati, ahañca dāni āyasmā ca sāriputto bhikkhusaṅghaṃ pariharissāmā’”ti. “Sādhu sādhu, moggallāna! Ahaṃ vā hi, moggallāna[T 2.0198], bhikkhusaṅghaṃ parihareyyaṃ sāriputtamoggallānā vā”ti.

160. The Sakyans of Cātumā and Brahmā Sahampati were indeed able to appease the Blessed One with the simile of the young seeds and the simile of the young calf. Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna addressed the bhikkhus: 'Arise, friends, take your bowls and robes. The Blessed One has been appeased by the Sakyans of Cātumā and Brahmā Sahampati with the simile of the young seeds and the simile of the young calf.' 'Yes, friend,' those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, and rising from their seats and taking their bowls and robes, they approached the Blessed One. Having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. The Blessed One said this to the Venerable Sāriputta who was seated to one side: 'What did you think, Sāriputta, when the Saṅgha of bhikkhus was dismissed by me?' 'This is what I thought, Venerable Sir: "The Saṅgha of bhikkhus has been dismissed by the Blessed One. Now the Blessed One, being free from care, will dwell devoted to abiding in bliss in the present life. We too, now being free from care, will dwell devoted to abiding in bliss in the present life."' 'Wait, Sāriputta. Postpone for now, Sāriputta, this abiding in bliss in the present life.' Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna: 'What did you think, Moggallāna, when the Saṅgha of bhikkhus was dismissed by me?' 'This is what I thought, Venerable Sir: "The Saṅgha of bhikkhus has been dismissed by the Blessed One. Now the Blessed One, being free from care, will dwell devoted to abiding in bliss in the present life. And now the Venerable Sāriputta and I will look after the Saṅgha of bhikkhus."' 'Good, good, Moggallāna! Indeed, Moggallāna, either I should look after the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, or Sāriputta and Moggallāna should.'

161. Atha [V 2.0132] kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi – “cattārimāni, bhikkhave, bhayāni udakorohante pāṭikaṅkhitabbāni. Katamāni cattāri? Ūmibhayaṃ ummībhayaṃ (syā. kaṃ.), kumbhīlabhayaṃ, āvaṭṭabhayaṃ, susukābhayaṃ – imāni, bhikkhave, cattāri bhayāni udakorohante pāṭikaṅkhitabbāni. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, cattārimāni bhayāni [M 2.0123] idhekacce puggale imasmiṃ dhammavinaye agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajite pāṭikaṅkhitabbāni. Katamāni [P 1.0460] cattāri? Ūmibhayaṃ, kumbhīlabhayaṃ, āvaṭṭabhayaṃ, susukābhayaṃ.

161. Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: 'Bhikkhus, these four dangers are to be expected by one descending into the water. What four? The danger of waves, the danger of crocodiles, the danger of whirlpools, and the danger of monstrous fish. These, bhikkhus, are the four dangers to be expected by one descending into the water. In the same way, bhikkhus, these four dangers are to be expected for a certain individual here who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness in this Dhamma and Discipline. What four? The danger of waves, the danger of crocodiles, the danger of whirlpools, and the danger of monstrous fish.'

162. “Katamañca, bhikkhave, ūmibhayaṃ? Idha, bhikkhave, ekacco kulaputto saddhā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajito hoti – ‘otiṇṇomhi jātiyā jarāya maraṇena sokehi paridevehi dukkhehi domanassehi upāyāsehi dukkhotiṇṇo dukkhapareto; appeva nāma imassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa antakiriyā paññāyethā’ti. Tamenaṃ tathā pabbajitaṃ samānaṃ sabrahmacārī ovadanti, anusāsanti – ‘evaṃ te abhikkamitabbaṃ, evaṃ te paṭikkamitabbaṃ, evaṃ te ālokitabbaṃ, evaṃ te vilokitabbaṃ, evaṃ te samiñjitabbaṃ, evaṃ te pasāritabbaṃ, evaṃ te saṅghāṭipattacīvaraṃ dhāretabba’nti. Tassa evaṃ hoti – ‘mayaṃ kho pubbe agāriyabhūtā samānā aññe ovadāma, anusāsāma ovadāmapi anusāsāmapi (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.). Ime panamhākaṃ puttamattā maññe, nattamattā maññe, amhe evaṃ (ka.) ovaditabbaṃ [T 2.0199] anusāsitabbaṃ maññantī’ti. So sikkhaṃ paccakkhāya hīnāyāvattati. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, ūmibhayassa bhīto sikkhaṃ paccakkhāya hīnāyāvatto. ‘Ūmibhaya’nti kho, bhikkhave, kodhupāyāsassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ.

162. And what, bhikkhus, is the danger of waves? Here, bhikkhus, some clansman, out of faith, goes forth from the household life into homelessness, thinking: ‘I am beset by birth, aging, and death, by sorrows, lamentations, pains, griefs, and despairs; beset by suffering, afflicted by suffering. Perhaps an end to this entire mass of suffering might be discerned.’ Having thus gone forth, his companions in the holy life advise and instruct him: ‘You should step forward thus, you should step back thus, you should look ahead thus, you should look aside thus, you should bend thus, you should stretch thus, you should carry your double-layered robe, bowl, and outer robe thus.’ It occurs to him: ‘Formerly, when we were householders, we advised and instructed others. But these, who seem to me like my own sons and grandsons, think they should advise and instruct us.’ So he renounces the training and reverts to the lower life. This, bhikkhus, is called one who, afraid of the danger of waves, renounces the training and reverts to the lower life. ‘The danger of waves,’ bhikkhus, is a designation for anger and vexation.

163. “Katamañca, bhikkhave, kumbhīlabhayaṃ? Idha, bhikkhave, ekacco kulaputto saddhā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajito hoti – ‘otiṇṇomhi jātiyā jarāya maraṇena sokehi paridevehi dukkhehi domanassehi upāyāsehi dukkhotiṇṇo dukkhapareto; appeva nāma imassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa antakiriyā paññāyethā’ti. Tamenaṃ tathā pabbajitaṃ samānaṃ sabrahmacārī ovadanti anusāsanti – ‘idaṃ te khāditabbaṃ, idaṃ te na khāditabbaṃ; idaṃ te bhuñjitabbaṃ, idaṃ te na bhuñjitabbaṃ; idaṃ te sāyitabbaṃ, idaṃ te na sāyitabbaṃ; idaṃ te pātabbaṃ, idaṃ te na pātabbaṃ; kappiyaṃ te khāditabbaṃ, akappiyaṃ te na khāditabbaṃ; kappiyaṃ te bhuñjitabbaṃ, akappiyaṃ te na bhuñjitabbaṃ; kappiyaṃ te sāyitabbaṃ, akappiyaṃ te na sāyitabbaṃ[V 2.0133]; kappiyaṃ te pātabbaṃ, akappiyaṃ te na pātabbaṃ; kāle te khāditabbaṃ, vikāle te na khāditabbaṃ; kāle te bhuñjitabbaṃ, vikāle te [M 2.0124] na bhuñjitabbaṃ; kāle te sāyitabbaṃ, vikāle te na sāyitabbaṃ; kāle te pātabbaṃ, vikāle te na pātabba’nti. Tassa evaṃ [P 1.0461] hoti – ‘mayaṃ kho pubbe agāriyabhūtā samānā yaṃ icchāma taṃ khādāma, yaṃ na icchāma na taṃ khādāma; yaṃ icchāma taṃ bhuñjāma, yaṃ [T 2.0200] na icchāma na taṃ bhuñjāma; yaṃ icchāma taṃ sāyāma, yaṃ na icchāma na taṃ sāyāma; yaṃ icchāma taṃ pivāma pipāma (sī. pī.), yaṃ na icchāma na taṃ pivāma; kappiyampi khādāma, akappiyampi khādāma; kappiyampi bhuñjāma, akappiyampi bhuñjāma; kappiyampi sāyāma, akappiyampi sāyāma; kappiyampi pivāma, akappiyampi pivāma; kālepi khādāma, vikālepi khādāma; kālepi bhuñjāma vikālepi bhuñjāma; kālepi sāyāma, vikālepi sāyāma; kālepi pivāma, vikālepi pivāma. Yampi no saddhā gahapatikā divā vikāle paṇītaṃ khādanīyaṃ bhojanīyaṃ denti tatthapime mukhāvaraṇaṃ maññe karontī’ti. So sikkhaṃ paccakkhāya hīnāyāvattati. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, kumbhīlabhayassa bhīto sikkhaṃ paccakkhāya hīnāyāvatto. ‘Kumbhīlabhaya’nti kho, bhikkhave, odarikattassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ.

163. And what, bhikkhus, is the danger of crocodiles? Here, bhikkhus, some clansman, out of faith, goes forth from the household life into homelessness, thinking: ‘I am beset by birth, aging, and death, by sorrows, lamentations, pains, griefs, and despairs; beset by suffering, afflicted by suffering. Perhaps an end to this entire mass of suffering might be discerned.’ Having thus gone forth, his companions in the holy life advise and instruct him: ‘You should eat this, you should not eat that; you should consume this, you should not consume that; you should savor this, you should not savor that; you should drink this, you should not drink that; you should eat what is allowable, you should not eat what is not allowable; you should consume what is allowable, you should not consume what is not allowable; you should savor what is allowable, you should not savor what is not allowable; you should drink what is allowable, you should not drink what is not allowable; you should eat at the proper time, you should not eat at the wrong time; you should consume at the proper time, you should not consume at the wrong time; you should savor at the proper time, you should not savor at the wrong time; you should drink at the proper time, you should not drink at the wrong time.’ It occurs to him: ‘Formerly, when we were householders, we ate what we wanted and did not eat what we did not want; we consumed what we wanted and did not consume what we did not want; we savored what we wanted and did not savor what we did not want; we drank what we wanted and did not drink what we did not want. We ate both what was allowable and what was not allowable; we consumed both what was allowable and what was not allowable; we savored both what was allowable and what was not allowable; we drank both what was allowable and what was not allowable. We ate both at the proper time and at the wrong time; we consumed both at the proper time and at the wrong time; we savored both at the proper time and at the wrong time; we drank both at the proper time and at the wrong time. And when faithful householders give us excellent hard and soft food during the day but at the wrong time, it seems to me they are placing a restraint upon my mouth.’ So he renounces the training and reverts to the lower life. This, bhikkhus, is called one who, afraid of the danger of crocodiles, renounces the training and reverts to the lower life. ‘The danger of crocodiles,’ bhikkhus, is a designation for gluttony.

164. “Katamañca, bhikkhave, āvaṭṭabhayaṃ? Idha, bhikkhave, ekacco kulaputto saddhā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajito hoti – ‘otiṇṇomhi jātiyā jarāya maraṇena sokehi paridevehi dukkhehi domanassehi upāyāsehi dukkhotiṇṇo dukkhapareto; appeva nāma imassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa antakiriyā paññāyethā’ti. So evaṃ pabbajito samāno pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya gāmaṃ vā nigamaṃ vā piṇḍāya pavisati. Arakkhiteneva kāyena arakkhitāya [T 2.0201] vācāya anupaṭṭhitāya satiyā asaṃvutehi indriyehi so tattha passati gahapatiṃ vā gahapatiputtaṃ vā pañcahi kāmaguṇehi samappitaṃ samaṅgībhūtaṃ paricārayamānaṃ paricāriyamānaṃ (syā. kaṃ. ka.). Tassa evaṃ hoti – ‘mayaṃ kho pubbe agāriyabhūtā samānā pañcahi kāmaguṇehi samappitā samaṅgībhūtā paricārimhā. Saṃvijjanti kho pana me kule saṃvijjanti kho kule (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) bhogā. Sakkā bhoge ca bhuñjituṃ puññāni ca kātu’nti. So sikkhaṃ paccakkhāya hīnāyāvattati. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, āvaṭṭabhayassa bhīto sikkhaṃ paccakkhāya hīnāyāvatto. ‘Āvaṭṭabhaya’nti kho, bhikkhave, pañcannetaṃ kāmaguṇānaṃ adhivacanaṃ.

164. And what, bhikkhus, is the danger of whirlpools? Here, bhikkhus, some clansman, out of faith, goes forth from the household life into homelessness, thinking: ‘I am beset by birth, aging, and death, by sorrows, lamentations, pains, griefs, and despairs; beset by suffering, afflicted by suffering. Perhaps an end to this entire mass of suffering might be discerned.’ He, having thus gone forth, in the morning, having dressed and taken his bowl and outer robe, enters a village or town for alms with his body unguarded, his speech unguarded, his mindfulness unestablished, and his sense faculties unrestrained. He sees there a householder or a householder’s son provided with, endowed with, and enjoying the five strands of sensual pleasure. It occurs to him: ‘Formerly, when we were householders, we too were provided with, endowed with, and enjoyed the five strands of sensual pleasure. There is wealth in my family. It is possible both to enjoy that wealth and to make merit.’ So he renounces the training and reverts to the lower life. This, bhikkhus, is called one who, afraid of the danger of whirlpools, renounces the training and reverts to the lower life. ‘The danger of whirlpools,’ bhikkhus, is a designation for the five strands of sensual pleasure.

165. “Katamañca[M 2.0125][V 2.0134], bhikkhave, susukābhayaṃ? Idha, bhikkhave, ekacco [P 1.0462] kulaputto saddhā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajito hoti – ‘otiṇṇomhi jātiyā jarāya maraṇena sokehi paridevehi dukkhehi domanassehi upāyāsehi dukkhotiṇṇo dukkhapareto; appeva nāma imassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa antakiriyā paññāyethā’ti. So evaṃ pabbajito samāno pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya gāmaṃ vā nigamaṃ vā piṇḍāya pavisati. Arakkhiteneva kāyena arakkhitāya vācāya anupaṭṭhitāya satiyā asaṃvutehi indriyehi so tattha passati mātugāmaṃ dunnivatthaṃ vā duppārutaṃ vā. Tassa mātugāmaṃ disvā dunnivatthaṃ vā duppārutaṃ vā rāgo cittaṃ anuddhaṃseti. So rāgānuddhaṃsena anuddhastena (sī. pī.) cittena sikkhaṃ paccakkhāya hīnāyāvattati[T 2.0202]. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, susukābhayassa bhīto sikkhaṃ paccakkhāya hīnāyāvatto. ‘Susukābhaya’nti kho, bhikkhave, mātugāmassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Imāni kho, bhikkhave, cattāri bhayāni, idhekacce puggale imasmiṃ dhammavinaye agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajite pāṭikaṅkhitabbānī”ti.

165. “And what, bhikkhus, is the danger of the shark? Here, bhikkhus, some clansman, out of faith, goes forth from the household life into homelessness, thinking: ‘I am beset by birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; beset by suffering, afflicted by suffering. Perhaps an end to this entire mass of suffering might be discerned.’ Having thus gone forth, in the morning, having dressed, taking his bowl and outer robe, he enters a village or a town for alms. With his body unguarded, his speech unguarded, his mindfulness unestablished, and his sense faculties unrestrained, he sees there a woman improperly dressed or improperly clad. Upon seeing a woman improperly dressed or improperly clad, lust corrupts his mind. With his mind corrupted by lust, he gives up the training and reverts to the lower life. This one, bhikkhus, is said to be afraid of the danger of the shark, to have given up the training, and to have reverted to the lower life. ‘The danger of the shark,’ bhikkhus, is a designation for a woman. These, bhikkhus, are the four dangers that are to be expected for a certain person in this Dhamma and Discipline who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness.”

Idamavoca bhagavā. Attamanā te bhikkhū bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandunti.

The Blessed One said this. Those bhikkhus, delighted, rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words.

Cātumasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ sattamaṃ.

The Cātuma Sutta, the seventh, is concluded.

8. Naḷakapānasuttaṃ

8. The Naḷakapāna Sutta

166. Evaṃ [T 2.0203][V 2.0135] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā kosalesu viharati naḷakapāne palāsavane. Tena kho pana samayena sambahulā abhiññātā abhiññātā kulaputtā bhagavantaṃ uddissa saddhā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajitā honti – āyasmā ca anuruddho, āyasmā ca bhaddiyo nandiyo (sī. pī.) vinaye ca ma. ni. 1 cūḷagosiṅge ca, āyasmā ca kimilo kimbilo (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.), āyasmā ca bhagu, āyasmā ca koṇḍañño kuṇḍadhāno (sī. pī.), āyasmā ca revato, āyasmā ca ānando, aññe ca abhiññātā abhiññātā kulaputtā. Tena kho pana samayena bhagavā bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto [P 1.0463] abbhokāse nisinno hoti. Atha kho bhagavā te kulaputte [M 2.0126] ārabbha bhikkhū āmantesi – “ye te, bhikkhave, kulaputtā mamaṃ uddissa saddhā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajitā, kacci te, bhikkhave, bhikkhū abhiratā brahmacariye”ti? Evaṃ vutte, te bhikkhū tuṇhī ahesuṃ. Dutiyampi kho bhagavā te kulaputte ārabbha bhikkhū āmantesi – “ye te, bhikkhave, kulaputtā mamaṃ uddissa saddhā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajitā, kacci te, bhikkhave, bhikkhū abhiratā brahmacariye”ti? Dutiyampi kho te bhikkhū tuṇhī ahesuṃ. Tatiyampi kho bhagavā te kulaputte ārabbha bhikkhū āmantesi – “ye te, bhikkhave, kulaputtā mamaṃ uddissa saddhā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajitā[T 2.0204], kacci te, bhikkhave, bhikkhū abhiratā brahmacariye”ti? Tatiyampi kho te bhikkhū tuṇhī ahesuṃ.

166. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Kosalans at Naḷakapāna in the Palāsa Grove. Now at that time, many very well-known, very well-known clansmen had gone forth from the household life into homelessness out of faith, for the sake of the Blessed One: the Venerable Anuruddha, the Venerable Bhaddiya, the Venerable Kimbila, the Venerable Bhagu, the Venerable Koṇḍañña, the Venerable Revata, the Venerable Ānanda, and other very well-known, very well-known clansmen. At that time the Blessed One was sitting in the open air, surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. Then the Blessed One, concerning those clansmen, addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, those clansmen who have gone forth from the household life into homelessness out of faith for my sake—are those bhikkhus, I ask, delighting in the holy life?” When this was said, those bhikkhus were silent. A second time the Blessed One, concerning those clansmen, addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, those clansmen who have gone forth from the household life into homelessness out of faith for my sake—are those bhikkhus, I ask, delighting in the holy life?” A second time, those bhikkhus were silent. A third time the Blessed One, concerning those clansmen, addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, those clansmen who have gone forth from the household life into homelessness out of faith for my sake—are those bhikkhus, I ask, delighting in the holy life?” A third time, those bhikkhus were silent.

167. Atha kho bhagavato etadahosi – “yaṃnūnāhaṃ te kulaputte puccheyya”nti! Atha kho bhagavā āyasmantaṃ anuruddhaṃ āmantesi – “kacci tumhe, anuruddhā, abhiratā brahmacariye”ti? “Taggha mayaṃ, bhante, abhiratā brahmacariye”ti. “Sādhu sādhu, anuruddhā! Etaṃ kho, anuruddhā, tumhākaṃ patirūpaṃ kulaputtānaṃ saddhā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajitānaṃ yaṃ tumhe abhirameyyātha brahmacariye. Yena tumhe anuruddhā, bhadrena yobbanena samannāgatā paṭhamena vayasā susukāḷakesā kāme paribhuñjeyyātha tena tumhe, anuruddhā, bhadrenapi yobbanena samannāgatā paṭhamena vayasā susukāḷakesā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajitā. Te ca kho pana tumhe, anuruddhā, neva rājābhinītā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajitā, na corābhinītā agārasmā [V 2.0136] anagāriyaṃ pabbajitā, na iṇaṭṭā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajitā, na bhayaṭṭā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajitā, nājīvikāpakatā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajitā. Api ca khomhi otiṇṇo jātiyā jarāya maraṇena sokehi paridevehi dukkhehi domanassehi upāyāsehi, dukkhotiṇṇo dukkhapareto; appeva nāma imassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa antakiriyā paññāyethāti – nanu tumhe, anuruddhā, evaṃ saddhā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajitā”ti? “Evaṃ, bhante”. “Evaṃ [T 2.0205] pabbajitena ca pana, anuruddhā, kulaputtena kimassa karaṇīyaṃ? Vivekaṃ, anuruddhā, kāmehi vivekaṃ akusalehi dhammehi pītisukhaṃ nādhigacchati aññaṃ vā aññaṃ ca (ka.) tato santataraṃ, tassa abhijjhāpi cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhati, byāpādopi cittaṃ [M 2.0127] pariyādāya tiṭṭhati, thīnamiddhampi thīnamiddhampi (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhati uddhaccakukkuccampi cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhati, vicikicchāpi cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhati, aratīpi [P 1.0464] cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhati, tandīpi cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhati. Vivekaṃ, anuruddhā, kāmehi vivekaṃ akusalehi dhammehi pītisukhaṃ nādhigacchati aññaṃ vā tato santataraṃ”.

167. Then this thought occurred to the Blessed One: “What if I were to question those clansmen?” Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Anuruddha: “Anuruddhas, are you, I ask, delighting in the holy life?” “Indeed, venerable sir, we are delighting in the holy life.” “Good, good, Anuruddhas! It is indeed fitting for you clansmen who have gone forth from the household life into homelessness out of faith that you should delight in the holy life. You, Anuruddhas, who are endowed with fine youth, in the first stage of life, very young with black hair, could be enjoying sensual pleasures. Yet you, Anuruddhas, endowed with that fine youth, in the first stage of life, very young with black hair, have gone forth from the household life into homelessness. And you, Anuruddhas, did not go forth from the household life into homelessness because you were oppressed by kings, nor oppressed by thieves, nor due to debt, nor due to fear, nor because your livelihood was ruined. But rather, thinking: ‘I am beset by birth, aging, death, sorrows, lamentations, pains, griefs, and despairs; beset by suffering, afflicted by suffering. Perhaps an end to this entire mass of suffering might be discerned.’ Is it not so, Anuruddhas, that you went forth from the household life into homelessness out of such faith?” “Even so, venerable sir.” “And for a clansman who has so gone forth, Anuruddhas, what is to be done? If, Anuruddhas, one does not attain the joy and pleasure of seclusion from sensual pleasures and seclusion from unwholesome qualities, or something even more peaceful than that, then covetousness takes possession of the mind and remains, ill will takes possession of the mind and remains, sloth and torpor take possession of the mind and remain, restlessness and remorse take possession of the mind and remain, doubt takes possession of the mind and remains, discontent takes possession of the mind and remains, and languor takes possession of the mind and remains. If, Anuruddhas, one does not attain the joy and pleasure of seclusion from sensual pleasures and seclusion from unwholesome qualities, or something even more peaceful than that.”

“Vivekaṃ, anuruddhā, kāmehi vivekaṃ akusalehi dhammehi pītisukhaṃ adhigacchati aññaṃ vā tato santataraṃ, tassa abhijjhāpi cittaṃ na pariyādāya tiṭṭhati, byāpādopi cittaṃ na pariyādāya tiṭṭhati, thīnamiddhampi cittaṃ na pariyādāya tiṭṭhati, uddhaccakukkuccampi cittaṃ na pariyādāya tiṭṭhati, vicikicchāpi cittaṃ na pariyādāya tiṭṭhati, aratīpi cittaṃ na pariyādāya tiṭṭhati, tandīpi cittaṃ na pariyādāya tiṭṭhati. Vivekaṃ, anuruddhā, kāmehi vivekaṃ akusalehi dhammehi pītisukhaṃ adhigacchati aññaṃ vā tato santataraṃ.

Anuruddhas, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, one attains rapture and happiness, or another state more peaceful than that. Covetousness does not overpower the mind and remain; ill will does not overpower the mind and remain; sloth and torpor do not overpower the mind and remain; restlessness and remorse do not overpower the mind and remain; doubt does not overpower the mind and remain; discontent does not overpower the mind and remain; and languor does not overpower the mind and remain. Anuruddhas, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, one attains rapture and happiness, or another state more peaceful than that.

168. “Kinti vo, anuruddhā, mayi hoti – ‘ye āsavā saṃkilesikā ponobbhavikā ponobhavikā (sī. pī.) sadarā dukkhavipākā āyatiṃ jātijarāmaraṇiyā, appahīnā te tathāgatassa; tasmā tathāgato saṅkhāyekaṃ paṭisevati, saṅkhāyekaṃ adhivāseti, saṅkhāyekaṃ parivajjeti, saṅkhāyekaṃ vinodetī’”ti? “Na kho [T 2.0206] no, bhante, bhagavati evaṃ hoti – ‘ye āsavā saṃkilesikā ponobbhavikā sadarā dukkhavipākā āyatiṃ jātijarāmaraṇiyā, appahīnā te tathāgatassa; tasmā tathāgato saṅkhāyekaṃ paṭisevati, saṅkhāyekaṃ adhivāseti, saṅkhāyekaṃ parivajjeti, saṅkhāyekaṃ vinodetī’ti. Evaṃ kho no, bhante, bhagavati hoti – ‘ye āsavā saṃkilesikā ponobbhavikā [V 2.0137] sadarā dukkhavipākā āyatiṃ jātijarāmaraṇiyā, pahīnā te tathāgatassa; tasmā tathāgato saṅkhāyekaṃ paṭisevati, saṅkhāyekaṃ adhivāseti, saṅkhāyekaṃ parivajjeti, saṅkhāyekaṃ vinodetī’”ti. “Sādhu sādhu, anuruddhā! Tathāgatassa, anuruddhā, ye āsavā saṃkilesikā ponobbhavikā sadarā dukkhavipākā āyatiṃ jātijarāmaraṇiyā, pahīnā te ucchinnamūlā tālāvatthukatā anabhāvaṃkatā āyatiṃ anuppādadhammā. Seyyathāpi, anuruddhā, tālo matthakacchinno abhabbo punavirūḷhiyā; evameva kho, anuruddhā[M 2.0128], tathāgatassa ye āsavā saṃkilesikā ponobbhavikā sadarā dukkhavipākā āyatiṃ jātijarāmaraṇiyā, pahīnā te ucchinnamūlā tālāvatthukatā anabhāvaṃkatā āyatiṃ anuppādadhammā; tasmā tathāgato saṅkhāyekaṃ paṭisevati, saṅkhāyekaṃ adhivāseti, saṅkhāyekaṃ parivajjeti, saṅkhāyekaṃ vinodeti”.

168. What thought occurs to you, Anuruddhas, concerning me: ‘Those taints that are defiling, that lead to renewed existence, are accompanied by distress, result in suffering, and lead to future birth, aging, and death, have not been abandoned by the Tathāgata; therefore, the Tathāgata, having discerned, makes use of a certain thing, having discerned, endures a certain thing, having discerned, avoids a certain thing, and having discerned, dispels a certain thing’?” “No, venerable sir, this thought does not occur to us concerning the Blessed One. Rather, venerable sir, this thought occurs to us concerning the Blessed One: ‘Those taints that are defiling, that lead to renewed existence, are accompanied by distress, result in suffering, and lead to future birth, aging, and death, have been abandoned by the Tathāgata; therefore, the Tathāgata, having discerned, makes use of a certain thing, having discerned, endures a certain thing, having discerned, avoids a certain thing, and having discerned, dispels a certain thing.’” “Good, good, Anuruddhas! For the Tathāgata, Anuruddhas, those taints that are defiling, that lead to renewed existence, are accompanied by distress, result in suffering, and lead to future birth, aging, and death, have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, brought to non-existence, and are of a nature not to arise in the future. Just as, Anuruddhas, a palm tree with its crown cut off is incapable of further growth; even so, Anuruddhas, for the Tathāgata those taints that are defiling, that lead to renewed existence, are accompanied by distress, result in suffering, and lead to future birth, aging, and death, have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, brought to non-existence, and are of a nature not to arise in the future. Therefore, the Tathāgata, having discerned, makes use of a certain thing, having discerned, endures a certain thing, having discerned, avoids a certain thing, and having discerned, dispels a certain thing.”

“Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, anuruddhā, kaṃ atthavasaṃ sampassamāno tathāgato sāvake abbhatīte kālaṅkate upapattīsu byākaroti – ‘asu amutra upapanno; asu amutra upapanno’”ti? “Bhagavaṃmūlakā [P 1.0465] no, bhante, dhammā bhagavaṃnettikā bhagavaṃpaṭisaraṇā. Sādhu vata, bhante, bhagavantaṃyeva paṭibhātu etassa bhāsitassa attho. Bhagavato sutvā bhikkhū dhāressantī”ti[T 2.0207]. “Na kho, anuruddhā, tathāgato janakuhanatthaṃ na janalapanatthaṃ na lābhasakkārasilokānisaṃsatthaṃ na ‘iti maṃ jano jānātū’ti sāvake abbhatīte kālaṅkate upapattīsu byākaroti – ‘asu amutra upapanno, asu amutra upapanno’ti. Santi ca kho, anuruddhā, kulaputtā saddhā uḷāravedā uḷārapāmojjā. Te taṃ sutvā tadatthāya cittaṃ upasaṃharanti. Tesaṃ taṃ, anuruddhā, hoti dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāya”.

What do you think, Anuruddhas? Seeing what benefit does the Tathāgata make declarations about disciples who have passed on and died, regarding their rebirths: ‘So-and-so has been reborn there; so-and-so has been reborn there’?” “Venerable sir, our teachings have the Blessed One as their root, the Blessed One as their guide, and the Blessed One as their refuge. It would be good, venerable sir, if the meaning of this statement would become clear to the Blessed One himself.
