Tatraggivessana, ye te samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘sabbaṃ me khamatī’ti tattha viññū puriso iti paṭisañcikkhati [T 2.0265] – ‘yā kho me ayaṃ diṭṭhi – sabbaṃ me khamatīti, imañce ahaṃ diṭṭhiṃ thāmasā parāmāsā abhinivissa vohareyyaṃ – idameva saccaṃ moghamaññanti; dvīhi me assa viggaho – yo cāyaṃ samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā evaṃvādī [P 1.0499] evaṃdiṭṭhi – sabbaṃ me nakkhamatīti, yo cāyaṃ samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā evaṃvādī evaṃdiṭṭhi – ekaccaṃ me khamati, ekaccaṃ me nakkhamatīti – imehi assa dvīhi viggaho. Iti viggahe sati vivādo, vivāde sati vighāto, vighāte sati vihesā’. Iti so viggahañca vivādañca vighātañca vihesañca attani sampassamāno tañceva diṭṭhiṃ pajahati aññañca diṭṭhiṃ na upādiyati. Evametāsaṃ diṭṭhīnaṃ pahānaṃ hoti, evametāsaṃ diṭṭhīnaṃ paṭinissaggo hoti.

202. When this was said, the wanderer Dīghanakha said to the Blessed One: 'The venerable Gotama extols my view; the venerable Gotama thoroughly extols my view.' 'Aggivessana, among those ascetics and brahmins who are of such speech and such a view—"Some things are acceptable to me, some things are not acceptable to me"—that view of theirs which is acceptable is close to passion, close to bondage, close to delight, close to attachment, and close to grasping. That view of theirs which is not acceptable is close to dispassion, close to non-bondage, close to non-delight, close to non-attachment, and close to non-grasping. Therein, Aggivessana, among those ascetics and brahmins who are of such speech and such a view—"All things are acceptable to me"—a discerning person reflects thus: "This view of mine, that 'All things are acceptable to me'—if I were to grasp this view tenaciously, adhere to it, and declare, 'This alone is true; all else is false,' I would have a dispute with two persons: with the ascetic or brahmin who is of the speech and view, 'All things are not acceptable to me,' and with the ascetic or brahmin who is of the speech and view, 'Some things are acceptable to me, some things are not acceptable to me.' With these two, there would be a dispute. When there is a dispute, there is contention; when there is contention, there is distress; when there is distress, there is vexation." Thus, seeing within himself dispute, contention, distress, and vexation, he abandons that very view and does not grasp another view. In this way, there is the abandoning of these views; in this way, there is the relinquishment of these views.'

203. “Tatraggivessana, ye te samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘sabbaṃ me nakkhamatī’ti tattha viññū puriso iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘yā kho me ayaṃ diṭṭhi – sabbaṃ me nakkhamatī’ti, imañce ahaṃ diṭṭhiṃ thāmasā parāmāsā abhinivissa vohareyyaṃ – idameva saccaṃ moghamaññanti; dvīhi me assa viggaho – yo cāyaṃ samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā evaṃvādī evaṃdiṭṭhi [M 2.0167] – sabbaṃ me khamatīti, yo cāyaṃ samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā evaṃvādī evaṃdiṭṭhi – ekaccaṃ me khamati ekaccaṃ me nakkhamatīti – imehi assa dvīhi viggaho. Iti viggahe sati vivādo, vivāde sati vighāto, vighāte sati vihesā’. Iti so viggahañca vivādañca [T 2.0266] vighātañca vihesañca attani sampassamāno tañceva diṭṭhiṃ pajahati aññañca diṭṭhiṃ na upādiyati. Evametāsaṃ diṭṭhīnaṃ pahānaṃ hoti, evametāsaṃ diṭṭhīnaṃ paṭinissaggo hoti.

203. 'Therein, Aggivessana, among those ascetics and brahmins who are of such speech and such a view—"All things are not acceptable to me"—a discerning person reflects thus: "This view of mine, that 'All things are not acceptable to me'—if I were to grasp this view tenaciously, adhere to it, and declare, 'This alone is true; all else is false,' I would have a dispute with two persons: with the ascetic or brahmin who is of the speech and view, 'All things are acceptable to me,' and with the ascetic or brahmin who is of the speech and view, 'Some things are acceptable to me, some things are not acceptable to me.' With these two, there would be a dispute. When there is a dispute, there is contention; when there is contention, there is distress; when there is distress, there is vexation." Thus, seeing within himself dispute, contention, distress, and vexation, he abandons that very view and does not grasp another view. In this way, there is the abandoning of these views; in this way, there is the relinquishment of these views.'

204. “Tatraggivessana, ye te samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘ekaccaṃ me khamati, ekaccaṃ me nakkhamatī’ti tattha viññū puriso iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘yā kho me [V 2.0178] ayaṃ diṭṭhi – ekaccaṃ me khamati, ekaccaṃ me nakkhamatīti, imañce ahaṃ diṭṭhiṃ thāmasā parāmāsā abhinivissa vohareyyaṃ – idameva saccaṃ moghamaññanti; dvīhi me assa viggaho – yo cāyaṃ samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā evaṃvādī evaṃdiṭṭhi – sabbaṃ me khamatīti, yo cāyaṃ samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā evaṃvādī evaṃdiṭṭhi – sabbaṃ me nakkhamatīti – imehi assa dvīhi viggaho. Iti viggahe sati vivādo, vivāde sati vighāto, vighāte sati vihesā’. Iti so viggahañca vivādañca vighātañca vihesañca attani sampassamāno tañceva diṭṭhiṃ pajahati aññañca diṭṭhiṃ na upādiyati. Evametāsaṃ diṭṭhīnaṃ pahānaṃ hoti, evametāsaṃ diṭṭhīnaṃ paṭinissaggo hoti.

204. 'Aggivessana, among those ascetics and brahmins who are of such speech and such a view—"Some things are acceptable to me, some things are not acceptable to me"—a discerning person reflects thus: "This view of mine, that 'Some things are acceptable to me, some things are not acceptable to me'—if I were to grasp this view tenaciously, adhere to it, and declare, 'This alone is true; all else is false,' I would have a dispute with two persons: with the ascetic or brahmin who is of the speech and view, 'All things are acceptable to me,' and with the ascetic or brahmin who is of the speech and view, 'All things are not acceptable to me.' With these two, there would be a dispute. When there is a dispute, there is contention; when there is contention, there is distress; when there is distress, there is vexation." Thus, seeing within himself dispute, contention, distress, and vexation, he abandons that very view and does not grasp another view. In this way, there is the abandoning of these views; in this way, there is the relinquishment of these views.'

205. “Ayaṃ [P 1.0500] kho panaggivessana, kāyo rūpī cātumahābhūtiko cātummahābhūtiko (sī. syā.) mātāpettikasambhavo odanakummāsupacayo aniccucchādanaparimaddanabhedanaviddhaṃsanadhammo, aniccato dukkhato rogato gaṇḍato sallato aghato ābādhato parato palokato suññato anattato samanupassitabbo[T 2.0267]. Tassimaṃ kāyaṃ aniccato dukkhato rogato gaṇḍato sallato aghato ābādhato parato palokato suññato anattato samanupassato yo kāyasmiṃ kāyachando kāyasneho kāyanvayatā sā pahīyati.

205. 'Furthermore, Aggivessana, this body has form, is composed of the four great elements, born of mother and father, built up by rice and gruel, and is subject to impermanence, to being anointed and massaged, to breaking up, and to destruction. It should be regarded as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a boil, as a dart, as a calamity, as an affliction, as other, as perishable, as empty, and as not-self. For one who regards this body as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a boil, as a dart, as a calamity, as an affliction, as other, as perishable, as empty, and as not-self, whatever desire for the body, affection for the body, and attachment to the body there is, that is abandoned.'

“Tisso kho imā, aggivessana, vedanā – sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā. Yasmiṃ, aggivessana, samaye sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedeti[M 2.0168], neva tasmiṃ samaye dukkhaṃ vedanaṃ vedeti, na adukkhamasukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedeti; sukhaṃyeva tasmiṃ samaye vedanaṃ vedeti. Yasmiṃ, aggivessana, samaye dukkhaṃ vedanaṃ vedeti, neva tasmiṃ samaye sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedeti, na adukkhamasukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedeti; dukkhaṃyeva tasmiṃ samaye vedanaṃ vedeti. Yasmiṃ, aggivessana, samaye adukkhamasukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedeti, neva tasmiṃ samaye sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedeti, na dukkhaṃ vedanaṃ vedeti; adukkhamasukhaṃyeva tasmiṃ samaye vedanaṃ vedeti. Sukhāpi kho, aggivessana, vedanā aniccā saṅkhatā paṭiccasamuppannā khayadhammā vayadhammā virāgadhammā nirodhadhammā; dukkhāpi kho, aggivessana, vedanā aniccā saṅkhatā paṭiccasamuppannā khayadhammā vayadhammā virāgadhammā nirodhadhammā; adukkhamasukhāpi kho, aggivessana, vedanā aniccā saṅkhatā paṭiccasamuppannā khayadhammā vayadhammā virāgadhammā nirodhadhammā. Evaṃ passaṃ, aggivessana, sutavā ariyasāvako sukhāyapi vedanāya nibbindati, dukkhāyapi vedanāya nibbindati, adukkhamasukhāyapi vedanāya [V 2.0179] nibbindati[T 2.0268]; nibbindaṃ virajjati, virāgā vimuccati. Vimuttasmiṃ, vimuttamiti ñāṇaṃ hoti. ‘Khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti pajānāti. Evaṃ vimuttacitto kho, aggivessana, bhikkhu na kenaci saṃvadati, na kenaci vivadati, yañca loke vuttaṃ tena voharati, aparāmasa”nti.

Aggivessana, there are these three feelings: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Aggivessana, at the time when one experiences a pleasant feeling, at that time one does not experience a painful feeling, nor a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling; at that time one experiences only a pleasant feeling. Aggivessana, at the time when one experiences a painful feeling, at that time one does not experience a pleasant feeling, nor a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling; at that time one experiences only a painful feeling. Aggivessana, at the time when one experiences a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, at that time one does not experience a pleasant feeling, nor a painful feeling; at that time one experiences only a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Aggivessana, a pleasant feeling is also impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation. Aggivessana, a painful feeling is also impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation. Aggivessana, a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is also impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation. Seeing thus, Aggivessana, the instructed noble disciple becomes disenchanted with pleasant feeling, disenchanted with painful feeling, and disenchanted with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. When he is liberated, the knowledge arises: ‘I am liberated.’ He understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.’ Aggivessana, a bhikkhu with a mind thus liberated does not enter into discussion with anyone, nor does he dispute with anyone; he makes use of the conventional speech of the world without misapprehending it.

206. Tena kho pana samayena āyasmā sāriputto bhagavato piṭṭhito [P 1.0501] ṭhito hoti bhagavantaṃ bījayamāno vījayamāno (sī. pī.). Atha kho āyasmato sāriputtassa etadahosi – “tesaṃ tesaṃ kira no bhagavā dhammānaṃ abhiññā pahānamāha, tesaṃ tesaṃ kira no sugato dhammānaṃ abhiññā paṭinissaggamāhā”ti. Iti hidaṃ āyasmato sāriputtassa paṭisañcikkhato anupādāya āsavehi cittaṃ vimucci. Dīghanakhassa pana paribbājakassa virajaṃ vītamalaṃ dhammacakkhuṃ udapādi – “yaṃ kiñci samudayadhammaṃ sabbaṃ taṃ nirodhadhamma”nti. Atha kho dīghanakho paribbājako diṭṭhadhammo pattadhammo viditadhammo pariyogāḷhadhammo tiṇṇavicikiccho vigatakathaṃkatho vesārajjappatto aparappaccayo satthusāsane bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “abhikkantaṃ, bho gotama, abhikkantaṃ, bho gotama! Seyyathāpi, bho gotama, nikkujjitaṃ vā ukkujjeyya, paṭicchannaṃ vā vivareyya, mūḷhassa vā maggaṃ [M 2.0169] ācikkheyya, andhakāre vā telapajjotaṃ dhāreyya – cakkhumanto rūpāni dakkhantīti – evameva kho bhotā gotamena anekapariyāyena [T 2.0269] dhammo pakāsito. Esāhaṃ bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi dhammañca bhikkhusaṅghañca. Upāsakaṃ maṃ bhavaṃ gotamo dhāretu ajjatagge pāṇupetaṃ saraṇaṃ gata”nti.

206. Now at that time, the Venerable Sāriputta was standing behind the Blessed One, fanning him. Then this thought occurred to the Venerable Sāriputta: ‘Indeed, our Blessed One teaches the abandoning of these various things through direct knowledge; indeed, our Sugata teaches the relinquishment of these various things through direct knowledge.’ As the Venerable Sāriputta reflected thus, his mind was liberated from the taints without clinging. For the wanderer Dīghanakha, the dust-free, stainless Dhamma-eye arose: ‘Whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease.’ Then the wanderer Dīghanakha, having seen the Dhamma, attained the Dhamma, understood the Dhamma, plunged into the Dhamma, having crossed beyond doubt, having become free from perplexity, having gained assurance, and being independent of others in the Teacher’s dispensation, said to the Blessed One: ‘Excellent, Master Gotama, excellent! Just as, Master Gotama, one might set upright what was overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or hold up an oil lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes could see forms—in the very same way, the Dhamma has been made clear in many ways by Master Gotama. I go for refuge to Master Gotama, to the Dhamma, and to the Bhikkhu Saṅgha. May Master Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.’

Dīghanakhasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ catutthaṃ.

The Dīghanakha Sutta, the fourth, is concluded.

5. Māgaṇḍiyasuttaṃ

5. The Māgaṇḍiya Sutta

207. Evaṃ [V 2.0180] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā kurūsu viharati kammāsadhammaṃ nāma kurūnaṃ nigamo, bhāradvājagottassa brāhmaṇassa agyāgāre tiṇasanthārake tiṇasantharake (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.). Atha kho bhagavā pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya kammāsadhammaṃ piṇḍāya pāvisi. Kammāsadhammaṃ piṇḍāya caritvā pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto yena aññataro vanasaṇḍo tenupasaṅkami divāvihārāya. Taṃ vanasaṇḍaṃ ajjhogāhetvā aññatarasmiṃ rukkhamūle divāvihāraṃ nisīdi. Atha [P 1.0502] kho māgaṇḍiyo māgandiyo (sī. pī.) paribbājako jaṅghāvihāraṃ anucaṅkamamāno anuvicaramāno yena bhāradvājagottassa brāhmaṇassa agyāgāraṃ tenupasaṅkami. Addasā kho māgaṇḍiyo paribbājako bhāradvājagottassa brāhmaṇassa agyāgāre tiṇasanthārakaṃ paññattaṃ. Disvāna bhāradvājagottaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ etadavoca – “kassa nvayaṃ bhoto bhāradvājassa agyāgāre tiṇasanthārako paññatto, samaṇaseyyānurūpaṃ samaṇaseyyārūpaṃ (sī. pī.) maññe”ti? “Atthi, bho māgaṇḍiya, samaṇo gotamo sakyaputto sakyakulā pabbajito. Taṃ kho pana bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ evaṃ kalyāṇo kittisaddo abbhuggato – ‘itipi so bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho vijjācaraṇasampanno sugato lokavidū anuttaro purisadammasārathi [T 2.0271] satthā devamanussānaṃ buddho bhagavā’ti. Tassesā bhoto gotamassa seyyā paññattā”ti. “Duddiṭṭhaṃ vata, bho bhāradvāja, addasāma; duddiṭṭhaṃ vata, bho bhāradvāja, addasāma! Ye mayaṃ tassa bhoto gotamassa bhūnahuno bhūnahanassa (syā. kaṃ.) seyyaṃ addasāmā”ti. “Rakkhassetaṃ, māgaṇḍiya, vācaṃ; rakkhassetaṃ[M 2.0170], māgaṇḍiya, vācaṃ. Bahū hi tassa bhoto gotamassa khattiyapaṇḍitāpi brāhmaṇapaṇḍitāpi gahapatipaṇḍitāpi samaṇapaṇḍitāpi abhippasannā vinītā ariye ñāye dhamme kusale”ti. “Sammukhā cepi mayaṃ, bho bhāradvāja, taṃ bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ passeyyāma, sammukhāpi naṃ vadeyyāma – ‘bhūnahu bhūnahano (syā. kaṃ.) samaṇo gotamo’ti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Evañhi no sutte ocaratī”ti. “Sace taṃ bhoto māgaṇḍiyassa agaru āroceyyāmi taṃ āroceyyametaṃ (sī. pī.), ārocessāmi tassa (syā. kaṃ.) samaṇassa gotamassā”ti. “Appossukko bhavaṃ bhāradvājo vuttova naṃ vadeyyā”ti.

207. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Kurus, at Kammāsadhamma, a market town of the Kurus, in the fire-worship hut of the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan, on a spread of grass. Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Kammāsadhamma for alms. Having gone for alms in Kammāsadhamma and returned from the alms round after his meal, he went to a certain grove for his day’s abiding. Having entered that grove, he sat down at the foot of a certain tree for his day’s abiding. Now, the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya, while walking and wandering for exercise, approached the fire-worship hut of the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan. The wanderer Māgaṇḍiya saw the spread of grass prepared in the fire-worship hut of the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan. Seeing it, he said to the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan: ‘For whom, venerable Bhāradvāja, is this grass spread prepared in your fire-worship hut? It seems fit for a recluse’s bed.’ ‘There is, venerable Māgaṇḍiya, the recluse Gotama, a Sakyan son who has gone forth from the Sakyan clan. A good report about that venerable Gotama has spread thus: “That Blessed One is an Arahant, a perfectly enlightened one, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, a fortunate one, knower of the world, an unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, an enlightened one, a blessed one.” This bed is prepared for that venerable Gotama.’ ‘It is a bad sight we have seen, venerable Bhāradvāja; a bad sight we have seen! We who have seen the bed of that venerable Gotama, the destroyer of growth!’ ‘Guard your speech, Māgaṇḍiya; guard your speech! Many wise khattiyas, wise brahmins, wise householders, and wise recluses have deep confidence in that venerable Gotama, and are trained in the noble principle, the Dhamma, which is wholesome.’ ‘Even if we were to see that venerable Gotama face to face, venerable Bhāradvāja, we would say to him face to face: “The recluse Gotama is a destroyer of growth.” Why is that? For so it is handed down in our scripture.’ ‘If it is not burdensome to you, venerable Māgaṇḍiya, I will report this to the recluse Gotama.’ ‘Be at ease, venerable Bhāradvāja. You may say just what has been said.’

208. Assosi kho bhagavā dibbāya sotadhātuyā visuddhāya atikkantamānusikāya bhāradvājagottassa [V 2.0181] brāhmaṇassa māgaṇḍiyena paribbājakena saddhiṃ imaṃ kathāsallāpaṃ. Atha kho bhagavā sāyanhasamayaṃ paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito yena bhāradvājagottassa brāhmaṇassa agyāgāraṃ tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā nisīdi bhagavā paññatte tiṇasanthārake. Atha kho bhāradvājagotto brāhmaṇo yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavatā saddhiṃ sammodi. Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā [T 2.0272] ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinnaṃ kho bhāradvājagottaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ bhagavā etadavoca – “ahu pana te, bhāradvāja, māgaṇḍiyena paribbājakena saddhiṃ [P 1.0503] imaṃyeva tiṇasanthārakaṃ ārabbha kocideva kathāsallāpo”ti? Evaṃ vutte, bhāradvājagotto brāhmaṇo saṃviggo lomahaṭṭhajāto bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “etadeva kho pana mayaṃ bhoto gotamassa ārocetukāmā. Atha ca pana bhavaṃ gotamo anakkhātaṃyeva akkhāsī”ti. Ayañca hi ayañca hidaṃ (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) bhagavato bhāradvājagottena brāhmaṇena saddhiṃ antarākathā vippakatā hoti. Atha kho māgaṇḍiyo paribbājako jaṅghāvihāraṃ anucaṅkamamāno anuvicaramāno yena bhāradvājagottassa brāhmaṇassa agyāgāraṃ yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavatā saddhiṃ sammodi. Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinnaṃ kho māgaṇḍiyaṃ paribbājakaṃ bhagavā etadavoca –

208. The Blessed One heard with his divine ear element, purified and surpassing the human, this conversation between the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan and the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya. Then, in the evening, the Blessed One arose from seclusion and went to the fire-worship hut of the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan. Having gone there, he sat down on the prepared grass spread. Then the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he exchanged courteous greetings with the Blessed One. When this courteous and memorable talk was finished, he sat down to one side. When the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan was seated to one side, the Blessed One said to him: 'Bhāradvāja, was there some conversation between you and the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya concerning this very grass spread?' When this was said, the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan, agitated and with his hair standing on end, said to the Blessed One: 'Indeed, we were just about to report this to venerable Gotama. And yet, venerable Gotama has already spoken what was unspoken!' Now, while this conversation between the Blessed One and the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan was still unfinished, the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya, while walking and wandering for exercise, approached the fire-worship hut of the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan, where the Blessed One was. Having approached, he exchanged courteous greetings with the Blessed One. When this courteous and memorable talk was finished, he sat down to one side. When the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya was seated to one side, the Blessed One said to him:

209. “Cakkhuṃ [M 2.0171] kho, māgaṇḍiya, rūpārāmaṃ rūparataṃ rūpasammuditaṃ. Taṃ tathāgatassa dantaṃ guttaṃ rakkhitaṃ saṃvutaṃ, tassa ca saṃvarāya dhammaṃ deseti. Idaṃ nu te etaṃ, māgaṇḍiya, sandhāya bhāsitaṃ – ‘bhūnahu samaṇo gotamo’”ti? “Etadeva kho pana me, bho gotama, sandhāya bhāsitaṃ – ‘bhūnahu samaṇo gotamo’ti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Evañhi no sutte ocaratī”ti. “Sotaṃ kho, māgaṇḍiya, saddārāmaṃ…pe… ghānaṃ [T 2.0273] kho, māgaṇḍiya gandhārāmaṃ… jivhā kho, māgaṇḍiya, rasārāmā rasaratā rasasammuditā. Sā tathāgatassa dantā guttā rakkhitā saṃvutā, tassā ca saṃvarāya dhammaṃ deseti. Idaṃ nu te etaṃ, māgaṇḍiya, sandhāya bhāsitaṃ – ‘bhūnahu samaṇo gotamo’”ti? “Etadeva kho pana me, bho gotama, sandhāya bhāsitaṃ – ‘bhūnahu samaṇo gotamo’ti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Evañhi no sutte ocaratī”ti. “Kāyo kho, māgaṇḍiya, phoṭṭhabbārāmo phoṭṭhabbarato…pe… mano kho, māgaṇḍiya, dhammārāmo dhammarato dhammasammudito. So tathāgatassa danto gutto rakkhito saṃvuto, tassa ca saṃvarāya dhammaṃ deseti. Idaṃ nu te etaṃ, māgaṇḍiya, sandhāya bhāsitaṃ – ‘bhūnahu samaṇo gotamo’”ti? “Etadeva kho pana me, bho [V 2.0182] gotama, sandhāya bhāsitaṃ – ‘bhūnahu samaṇo gotamo’ti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Evañhi no sutte ocaratī”ti.

209. “The eye, Māgaṇḍiya, delights in forms, takes pleasure in forms, and rejoices in forms. That eye of the Tathāgata is tamed, guarded, protected, and restrained, and he teaches the Dhamma for its restraint. Is it with reference to this, Māgaṇḍiya, that you said: ‘The ascetic Gotama is a destroyer of growth’?” “Indeed, Master Gotama, it is with reference to this very thing that I said: ‘The ascetic Gotama is a destroyer of growth.’ For what reason? Because this is what is found in our scripture.” “The ear, Māgaṇḍiya, delights in sounds… The nose, Māgaṇḍiya, delights in odors… The tongue, Māgaṇḍiya, delights in flavors, takes pleasure in flavors, and rejoices in flavors. That tongue of the Tathāgata is tamed, guarded, protected, and restrained, and he teaches the Dhamma for its restraint. Is it with reference to this, Māgaṇḍiya, that you said: ‘The ascetic Gotama is a destroyer of growth’?” “Indeed, Master Gotama, it is with reference to this very thing that I said: ‘The ascetic Gotama is a destroyer of growth.’ For what reason? Because this is what is found in our scripture.” “The body, Māgaṇḍiya, delights in tactile sensations… The mind, Māgaṇḍiya, delights in mental phenomena, takes pleasure in mental phenomena, and rejoices in mental phenomena. That mind of the Tathāgata is tamed, guarded, protected, and restrained, and he teaches the Dhamma for its restraint. Is it with reference to this, Māgaṇḍiya, that you said: ‘The ascetic Gotama is a destroyer of growth’?” “Indeed, Master Gotama, it is with reference to this very thing that I said: ‘The ascetic Gotama is a destroyer of growth.’ For what reason? Because this is what is found in our scripture.”

210. “Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, māgaṇḍiya – ‘idhekacco cakkhuviññeyyehi [P 1.0504] rūpehi paricāritapubbo assa iṭṭhehi kantehi manāpehi piyarūpehi kāmūpasaṃhitehi rajanīyehi, so aparena samayena rūpānaṃyeva samudayañca atthaṅgamañca assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ viditvā rūpataṇhaṃ pahāya rūpapariḷāhaṃ paṭivinodetvā vigatapipāso ajjhattaṃ vūpasantacitto vihareyya. Imassa pana te, māgaṇḍiya, kimassa vacanīya’”nti? “Na kiñci, bho gotama”. “Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, māgaṇḍiya – ‘idhekacco sotaviññeyyehi saddehi…pe… ghānaviññeyyehi [T 2.0274] gandhehi… jivhāviññeyyehi rasehi… kāyaviññeyyehi phoṭṭhabbehi paricāritapubbo assa iṭṭhehi kantehi manāpehi piyarūpehi kāmūpasaṃhitehi rajanīyehi, so aparena samayena phoṭṭhabbānaṃyeva samudayañca atthaṅgamañca assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ viditvā phoṭṭhabbataṇhaṃ pahāya phoṭṭhabbapariḷāhaṃ paṭivinodetvā vigatapipāso ajjhattaṃ vūpasantacitto vihareyya. Imassa pana te, māgaṇḍiya, kimassa vacanīya’”nti? “Na kiñci, bho gotama”.

210. “What do you think, Māgaṇḍiya? Suppose someone here had previously indulged in forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, pleasing, endearing, connected with sensual pleasure, and arousing passion. Then, at a later time, having known as it really is the arising, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding those very forms, they would abandon craving for forms, dispel the fever for forms, and dwell free from thirst, their mind inwardly pacified. What would you have to say about this person, Māgaṇḍiya?” “Nothing, Master Gotama.” “What do you think, Māgaṇḍiya? Suppose someone here had previously indulged in sounds cognizable by the ear… odors cognizable by the nose… flavors cognizable by the tongue… tactile sensations cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, pleasing, endearing, connected with sensual pleasure, and arousing passion. Then, at a later time, having known as it really is the arising, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding those very tactile sensations, they would abandon craving for tactile sensations, dispel the fever for tactile sensations, and dwell free from thirst, their mind inwardly pacified. What would you have to say about this person, Māgaṇḍiya?” “Nothing, Master Gotama.”

211. “Ahaṃ [M 2.0172] kho pana, māgaṇḍiya, pubbe agāriyabhūto samāno pañcahi kāmaguṇehi samappito samaṅgībhūto paricāresiṃ cakkhuviññeyyehi rūpehi iṭṭhehi kantehi manāpehi piyarūpehi kāmūpasaṃhitehi rajanīyehi, sotaviññeyyehi saddehi…pe… ghānaviññeyyehi gandhehi… jivhāviññeyyehi rasehi… kāyaviññeyyehi phoṭṭhabbehi iṭṭhehi kantehi manāpehi piyarūpehi kāmūpasaṃhitehi rajanīyehi. Tassa mayhaṃ, māgaṇḍiya, tayo pāsādā ahesuṃ – eko vassiko, eko hemantiko, eko gimhiko. So kho ahaṃ, māgaṇḍiya, vassike pāsāde vassike cattāro vassike pāsāde cattāro (syā. kaṃ.) māse nippurisehi tūriyehi turiyehi (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) paricārayamāno paricāriyamāno (sabbattha) na heṭṭhāpāsādaṃ orohāmi. So aparena samayena kāmānaṃyeva samudayañca atthaṅgamañca assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ viditvā kāmataṇhaṃ pahāya kāmapariḷāhaṃ paṭivinodetvā vigatapipāso [T 2.0275] ajjhattaṃ vūpasantacitto viharāmi. So aññe satte passāmi kāmesu avītarāge kāmataṇhāhi khajjamāne kāmapariḷāhena pariḍayhamāne kāme paṭisevante. So tesaṃ na pihemi, na tattha abhiramāmi[V 2.0183]. Taṃ kissa hetu? Yāhayaṃ, māgaṇḍiya, rati, aññatreva kāmehi aññatra akusalehi dhammehi – api dibbaṃ sukhaṃ [P 1.0505] samadhigayha tiṭṭhati – tāya ratiyā ramamāno hīnassa na pihemi, na tattha abhiramāmi.

211. “I, Māgaṇḍiya, in the past, when I was a householder, was furnished and endowed with, and indulged in, the five strands of sensual pleasure: with forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, pleasing, endearing, connected with sensual pleasure, and arousing passion; with sounds cognizable by the ear… with odors cognizable by the nose… with flavors cognizable by the tongue… with tactile sensations cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, pleasing, endearing, connected with sensual pleasure, and arousing passion. I had three palaces, Māgaṇḍiya—one for the rainy season, one for the winter, and one for the summer. In the rainy-season palace, Māgaṇḍiya, for the four months of the rainy season, I was entertained by musicians with no men present, and I did not descend to the lower part of the palace. Then, at a later time, having known as it really is the arising, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding sensual pleasures, I abandoned craving for sensual pleasures, dispelled the fever for sensual pleasures, and now dwell free from thirst, my mind inwardly pacified. I see other beings who are not free from passion for sensual pleasures, being devoured by craving for sensual pleasures, burning with the fever of sensual pleasures, indulging in sensual pleasures. I do not envy them, nor do I delight in that. For what reason? Because, Māgaṇḍiya, there is a delight apart from sensual pleasures, apart from unwholesome states—which stands surpassing even divine happiness. Delighting in that delight, I do not envy what is inferior, nor do I take pleasure in it.”

212. “Seyyathāpi, māgaṇḍiya, gahapati vā gahapatiputto vā aḍḍho mahaddhano mahābhogo pañcahi kāmaguṇehi samappito samaṅgībhūto paricāreyya cakkhuviññeyyehi rūpehi…pe… phoṭṭhabbehi iṭṭhehi kantehi manāpehi piyarūpehi kāmūpasaṃhitehi rajanīyehi. So kāyena sucaritaṃ caritvā vācāya sucaritaṃ caritvā manasā sucaritaṃ caritvā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjeyya devānaṃ tāvatiṃsānaṃ sahabyataṃ. So tattha nandane vane accharāsaṅghaparivuto dibbehi pañcahi kāmaguṇehi samappito samaṅgībhūto paricāreyya. So passeyya gahapatiṃ vā gahapatiputtaṃ vā pañcahi kāmaguṇehi samappitaṃ samaṅgībhūtaṃ paricārayamānaṃ.

212. “Suppose, Māgaṇḍiya, a householder or a householder's son—wealthy, of great wealth, and of great possessions—might be furnished and endowed with, and indulge in, the five strands of sensual pleasure: with forms cognizable by the eye… with tactile sensations that are desirable, lovely, pleasing, endearing, connected with sensual pleasure, and arousing passion. Having practiced good conduct by body, speech, and mind, on the breaking up of the body, after death, he would be reborn in a good destination, the heavenly world, in the company of the Tāvatiṃsa devas. There, in the Nandana Grove, surrounded by a host of celestial nymphs, he would be furnished and endowed with, and indulge in, the five divine strands of sensual pleasure. And he might see a householder or a householder's son being furnished and endowed with, and indulging in, the five strands of sensual pleasure.”

“Taṃ [M 2.0173] kiṃ maññasi, māgaṇḍiya, api nu so devaputto nandane vane accharāsaṅghaparivuto dibbehi pañcahi kāmaguṇehi [T 2.0276] samappito samaṅgībhūto paricārayamāno amussa gahapatissa vā gahapatiputtassa vā piheyya, mānusakānaṃ vā pañcannaṃ kāmaguṇānaṃ mānusakehi vā kāmehi āvaṭṭeyyā”ti? “No hidaṃ, bho gotama”. Taṃ kissa hetu? Mānusakehi, bho gotama, kāmehi dibbakāmā abhikkantatarā ca paṇītatarā cā”ti. “Evameva kho ahaṃ, māgaṇḍiya, pubbe agāriyabhūto samāno pañcahi kāmaguṇehi samappito samaṅgībhūto paricāresiṃ cakkhuviññeyyehi rūpehi iṭṭhehi kantehi manāpehi piyarūpehi kāmūpasaṃhitehi rajanīyehi, sotaviññeyyehi saddehi…pe… ghānaviññeyyehi gandhehi… jivhāviññeyyehi rasehi… kāyaviññeyyehi phoṭṭhabbehi iṭṭhehi kantehi manāpehi piyarūpehi kāmūpasaṃhitehi rajanīyehi. So aparena samayena kāmānaṃyeva samudayañca atthaṅgamañca assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ viditvā kāmataṇhaṃ pahāya kāmapariḷāhaṃ paṭivinodetvā vigatapipāso ajjhattaṃ vūpasantacitto viharāmi. So aññe satte passāmi kāmesu avītarāge kāmataṇhāhi khajjamāne kāmapariḷāhena pariḍayhamāne [P 1.0506] kāme paṭisevante, so tesaṃ na pihemi, na tattha abhiramāmi. Taṃ kissa hetu? Yāhayaṃ, māgaṇḍiya, rati aññatreva kāmehi aññatra akusalehi [V 2.0184] dhammehi – api dibbaṃ sukhaṃ samadhigayha tiṭṭhati – tāya ratiyā ramamāno hīnassa na pihemi, na tattha abhiramāmi.

“What do you think, Māgaṇḍiya? Would that son of a deva, in the Nandana Grove, surrounded by a host of celestial nymphs, satisfied and endowed with the five divine strands of sensual pleasure, being attended to, envy that householder or householder’s son, or would he return on account of human sensual pleasures?” “No, Master Gotama. For what reason? Because, Master Gotama, divine sensual pleasures are more excellent and more sublime than human sensual pleasures.” “Even so, Māgaṇḍiya, in the past, when I was a householder, I was satisfied and endowed with, and enjoyed, the five strands of sensual pleasure: with forms cognizable by the eye that are wished for, desired, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual pleasure, and arousing passion; with sounds cognizable by the ear… with odors cognizable by the nose… with tastes cognizable by the tongue… with tangibles cognizable by the body that are wished for, desired, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual pleasure, and arousing passion. Then I, at a later time, having understood as it really is the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of sensual pleasures, having abandoned craving for sensual pleasures, having dispelled the fever for sensual pleasures, I dwell free from thirst, with a mind inwardly pacified. I see other beings who are not free from lust for sensual pleasures, being devoured by craving for sensual pleasures, burning with the fever for sensual pleasures, indulging in sensual pleasures. I do not envy them, nor do I delight in that. For what reason? There is, Māgaṇḍiya, this delight which is apart from sensual pleasures, apart from unwholesome states—it stands surpassing even divine bliss. Delighting in that delight, I do not yearn for what is inferior, nor do I delight in it.”

213. “Seyyathāpi[T 2.0277], māgaṇḍiya, kuṭṭhī puriso arugatto pakkagatto kimīhi khajjamāno nakhehi vaṇamukhāni vippatacchamāno aṅgārakāsuyā kāyaṃ paritāpeyya. Tassa mittāmaccā ñātisālohitā bhisakkaṃ sallakattaṃ upaṭṭhāpeyyuṃ. Tassa so bhisakko sallakatto bhesajjaṃ kareyya. So taṃ bhesajjaṃ āgamma kuṭṭhehi parimucceyya, arogo assa sukhī serī sayaṃvasī yena kāmaṃ gamo. So aññaṃ kuṭṭhiṃ purisaṃ passeyya arugattaṃ pakkagattaṃ kimīhi khajjamānaṃ nakhehi vaṇamukhāni vippatacchamānaṃ aṅgārakāsuyā kāyaṃ paritāpentaṃ.

213. “Suppose, Māgaṇḍiya, there was a man afflicted with leprosy, his body covered with sores and festering lesions, being devoured by worms, scratching the openings of his wounds with his nails, and heating his body over a pit of glowing embers. His friends, companions, and relatives would bring a physician-surgeon to treat him. The physician-surgeon would prepare medicine for him. By means of that medicine, he would be freed from the leprosy, becoming healthy, happy, independent, his own master, and free to go where he pleased. Then he might see another man afflicted with leprosy, his body covered with sores and festering lesions, being devoured by worms, scratching the openings of his wounds with his nails, and heating his body over a pit of glowing embers.”

“Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, māgaṇḍiya, api nu so puriso amussa kuṭṭhissa purisassa piheyya aṅgārakāsuyā vā bhesajjaṃ paṭisevanāya vā”ti? “No [M 2.0174] hidaṃ, bho gotama. Taṃ kissa hetu? Roge hi, bho gotama, sati bhesajjena karaṇīyaṃ hoti, roge asati na bhesajjena karaṇīyaṃ hotī”ti. “Evameva kho ahaṃ, māgaṇḍiya, pubbe agāriyabhūto samāno pañcahi kāmaguṇehi samappito samaṅgībhūto paricāresiṃ, cakkhuviññeyyehi rūpehi iṭṭhehi kantehi manāpehi piyarūpehi kāmūpasaṃhitehi rajanīyehi, sotaviññeyyehi saddehi…pe… ghānaviññeyyehi gandhehi… jivhāviññeyyehi rasehi… kāyaviññeyyehi phoṭṭhabbehi iṭṭhehi kantehi manāpehi piyarūpehi kāmūpasaṃhitehi rajanīyehi. So aparena samayena kāmānaṃyeva samudayañca atthaṅgamañca assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ viditvā kāmataṇhaṃ pahāya kāmapariḷāhaṃ [T 2.0278] paṭivinodetvā vigatapipāso ajjhattaṃ vūpasantacitto viharāmi. So aññe satte passāmi kāmesu avītarāge kāmataṇhāhi khajjamāne kāmapariḷāhena pariḍayhamāne kāme paṭisevante. So tesaṃ na pihemi, na tattha abhiramāmi. Taṃ kissa hetu? Yāhayaṃ, māgaṇḍiya, rati, aññatreva kāmehi aññatra akusalehi dhammehi – api dibbaṃ sukhaṃ samadhigayha tiṭṭhati – tāya ratiyā ramamāno hīnassa na pihemi, na tattha abhiramāmi.

“What do you think, Māgaṇḍiya? Would that man envy that leper for his pit of glowing embers or for his partaking of medicine?” “No, Master Gotama. For what reason? Because, Master Gotama, when there is a disease, medicine is needed, but when there is no disease, medicine is not needed.” “Even so, Māgaṇḍiya, in the past, when I was a householder, I was satisfied and endowed with, and enjoyed, the five strands of sensual pleasure: with forms cognizable by the eye that are wished for, desired, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual pleasure, and arousing passion; with sounds cognizable by the ear… with odors cognizable by the nose… with tastes cognizable by the tongue… with tangibles cognizable by the body that are wished for, desired, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual pleasure, and arousing passion. Then I, at a later time, having understood as it really is the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of sensual pleasures, having abandoned craving for sensual pleasures, having dispelled the fever for sensual pleasures, I dwell free from thirst, with a mind inwardly pacified. I see other beings who are not free from lust for sensual pleasures, being devoured by craving for sensual pleasures, burning with the fever for sensual pleasures, indulging in sensual pleasures. I do not envy them, nor do I delight in that. For what reason? There is, Māgaṇḍiya, this delight which is apart from sensual pleasures, apart from unwholesome states—it stands surpassing even divine bliss. Delighting in that delight, I do not yearn for what is inferior, nor do I delight in it.”

214. “Seyyathāpi[P 1.0507], māgaṇḍiya, kuṭṭhī puriso arugatto pakkagatto kimīhi khajjamāno nakhehi vaṇamukhāni vippatacchamāno aṅgārakāsuyā kāyaṃ paritāpeyya. Tassa mittāmaccā [V 2.0185] ñātisālohitā bhisakkaṃ sallakattaṃ upaṭṭhāpeyyuṃ. Tassa so bhisakko sallakatto bhesajjaṃ kareyya. So taṃ bhesajjaṃ āgamma kuṭṭhehi parimucceyya, arogo assa sukhī serī sayaṃvasī yena kāmaṃ gamo. Tamenaṃ dve balavanto purisā nānābāhāsu gahetvā aṅgārakāsuṃ upakaḍḍheyyuṃ.

214. “Suppose, Māgaṇḍiya, a man afflicted with leprosy, his body covered with sores and festering lesions, being devoured by worms, were to scratch the openings of his wounds with his nails and heat his body over a pit of glowing embers. His friends, companions, and relatives would arrange for a physician and surgeon for him. That physician and surgeon would prepare medicine for him. By resorting to that medicine, he would be freed from his leprosy, becoming healthy, happy, independent, his own master, and free to go where he pleases. Then two strong men would seize him by both arms and drag him toward a pit of glowing embers.”

“Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, māgaṇḍiya, api nu so puriso iti citiceva kāyaṃ sannāmeyyā”ti? “Evaṃ, bho gotama”. “Taṃ kissa hetu”? “Asu hi, bho gotama, aggi dukkhasamphasso ceva mahābhitāpo ca mahāpariḷāho cā”ti. “Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, māgaṇḍiya, idāneva nu kho so aggi dukkhasamphasso ceva mahābhitāpo ca mahāpariḷāho ca udāhu pubbepi so aggi dukkhasamphasso ceva mahābhitāpo ca mahāpariḷāho cā”ti[T 2.0279]? “Idāni ceva, bho gotama, so aggi dukkhasamphasso ceva mahābhitāpo [M 2.0175] ca mahāpariḷāho ca, pubbepi so aggi dukkhasamphasso ceva mahābhitāpo ca mahāpariḷāho ca. Asu ca asu hi ca (sī. pī.), bho gotama, kuṭṭhī puriso arugatto pakkagatto kimīhi khajjamāno nakhehi vaṇamukhāni vippatacchamāno upahatindriyo dukkhasamphasseyeva aggismiṃ sukhamiti viparītasaññaṃ paccalatthā”ti. “Evameva kho, māgaṇḍiya, atītampi addhānaṃ kāmā dukkhasamphassā ceva mahābhitāpā ca mahāpariḷāhā ca, anāgatampi addhānaṃ kāmā dukkhasamphassā ceva mahābhitāpā ca mahāpariḷāhā ca, etarahipi paccuppannaṃ addhānaṃ kāmā dukkhasamphassā ceva mahābhitāpā ca mahāpariḷāhā ca. Ime ca, māgaṇḍiya, sattā kāmesu avītarāgā kāmataṇhāhi khajjamānā kāmapariḷāhena pariḍayhamānā upahatindriyā dukkhasamphassesuyeva kāmesu sukhamiti viparītasaññaṃ paccalatthuṃ.

“What do you think, Māgaṇḍiya, would that man bend his body this way and that?” “Yes, venerable Gotama.” “For what reason?” “Because, venerable Gotama, that fire is of painful contact, of great heat, and of great torment.” “What do you think, Māgaṇḍiya, is that fire of painful contact, of great heat, and of great torment only now, or was that fire also in the past of painful contact, of great heat, and of great torment?” “Both now, venerable Gotama, that fire is of painful contact, of great heat, and of great torment; and in the past also that fire was of painful contact, of great heat, and of great torment. And, venerable Gotama, that man with leprosy, with a body full of sores and festering, being eaten by worms, scratching the openings of his wounds with his nails, with impaired faculties, would obtain the distorted perception of ‘pleasure’ in the fire which is indeed of painful contact.” “Even so, Māgaṇḍiya, in the past, sensual pleasures were of painful contact, of great heat, and of great torment. In the future, sensual pleasures will be of painful contact, of great heat, and of great torment. And now, in the present, sensual pleasures are of painful contact, of great heat, and of great torment. And these beings, Māgaṇḍiya, not free from passion for sensual pleasures, being eaten by craving for sensual pleasures, being burned by the torment of sensual pleasures, with impaired faculties, have obtained the distorted perception of ‘pleasure’ in sensual pleasures which are indeed of painful contact.”

215. “Seyyathāpi, māgaṇḍiya, kuṭṭhī puriso arugatto pakkagatto kimīhi khajjamāno nakhehi vaṇamukhāni vippatacchamāno aṅgārakāsuyā kāyaṃ paritāpeti. Yathā yathā kho, māgaṇḍiya, asu kuṭṭhī puriso arugatto pakkagatto kimīhi khajjamāno nakhehi vaṇamukhāni vippatacchamāno aṅgārakāsuyā kāyaṃ paritāpeti tathā tathā’ssa tathā tathā tasseva (syā. kaṃ. ka.) tāni vaṇamukhāni asucitarāni [P 1.0508] ceva honti duggandhatarāni ca pūtikatarāni ca[T 2.0280], hoti ceva kāci sātamattā assādamattā – yadidaṃ vaṇamukhānaṃ kaṇḍūvanahetu; evameva kho, māgaṇḍiya, sattā kāmesu avītarāgā [V 2.0186] kāmataṇhāhi khajjamānā kāmapariḷāhena ca pariḍayhamānā kāme paṭisevanti. Yathā yathā kho, māgaṇḍiya, sattā kāmesu avītarāgā kāmataṇhāhi khajjamānā kāmapariḷāhena ca pariḍayhamānā kāme paṭisevanti tathā tathā tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ kāmataṇhā ceva pavaḍḍhati, kāmapariḷāhena ca pariḍayhanti, hoti ceva sātamattā assādamattā – yadidaṃ pañcakāmaguṇe paṭicca.

215. “Suppose, Māgaṇḍiya, a man with leprosy, his body covered with sores and festering, being eaten by worms, scratching the openings of his wounds with his nails, were to warm his body over a pit of embers. The more, Māgaṇḍiya, that man with leprosy, with a body full of sores and festering, being eaten by worms, scratching the openings of his wounds with his nails, warms his body over a pit of embers, the more those openings of his wounds become even more impure, more foul-smelling, and more putrid. And there is a certain measure of gratification, a measure of satisfaction, on account of the itching of the openings of the wounds. Even so, Māgaṇḍiya, beings not free from passion for sensual pleasures, being eaten by craving for sensual pleasures and being burned by the torment of sensual pleasures, indulge in sensual pleasures. The more, Māgaṇḍiya, that beings not free from passion for sensual pleasures, being eaten by craving for sensual pleasures and being burned by the torment of sensual pleasures, indulge in sensual pleasures, the more their craving for sensual pleasures increases, and they are burned by the torment of sensual pleasures. And there is a certain measure of gratification, a measure of satisfaction, dependent on the five cords of sensual pleasure.”

“Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, māgaṇḍiya, api nu te diṭṭho vā suto vā rājā vā rājamahāmatto vā pañcahi kāmaguṇehi samappito samaṅgībhūto paricārayamāno kāmataṇhaṃ appahāya kāmapariḷāhaṃ appaṭivinodetvā vigatapipāso ajjhattaṃ vūpasantacitto vihāsi vā viharati vā viharissati vā”ti[M 2.0176]? “No hidaṃ, bho gotama”. “Sādhu, māgaṇḍiya! Mayāpi kho etaṃ, māgaṇḍiya, neva diṭṭhaṃ na sutaṃ rājā vā rājamahāmatto vā pañcahi kāmaguṇehi samappito samaṅgībhūto paricārayamāno kāmataṇhaṃ appahāya kāmapariḷāhaṃ appaṭivinodetvā vigatapipāso ajjhattaṃ vūpasantacitto vihāsi vā viharati vā viharissati vā. Atha kho, māgaṇḍiya, ye hi keci samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā vigatapipāsā ajjhattaṃ vūpasantacittā vihāsuṃ vā viharanti vā viharissanti vā sabbe te kāmānaṃyeva samudayañca [T 2.0281] atthaṅgamañca assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ viditvā kāmataṇhaṃ pahāya kāmapariḷāhaṃ paṭivinodetvā vigatapipāsā ajjhattaṃ vūpasantacittā vihāsuṃ vā viharanti vā viharissanti vā”ti. Atha kho bhagavā tāyaṃ velāyaṃ imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi –

“What do you think, Māgaṇḍiya? Have you ever seen or heard of a king or a royal minister who, furnished with, endowed with, and enjoying the five cords of sensual pleasure, without having abandoned craving for sensual pleasures, without having dispelled the torment of sensual pleasures, has dwelt, dwells, or will dwell free from thirst, with a mind inwardly pacified?” “Certainly not, venerable Gotama.” “Good, Māgaṇḍiya! I too have neither seen nor heard of a king or a royal minister who, furnished with, endowed with, and enjoying the five cords of sensual pleasure, without having abandoned craving for sensual pleasures, without having dispelled the torment of sensual pleasures, has dwelt, dwells, or will dwell free from thirst, with a mind inwardly pacified. But, Māgaṇḍiya, whatever ascetics or brahmins have dwelt, dwell, or will dwell free from thirst, with minds inwardly pacified—all of them, having understood as it really is the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to sensual pleasures, and having abandoned craving for sensual pleasures and dispelled the torment of sensual pleasures, have dwelt, dwell, or will dwell free from thirst, with minds inwardly pacified.” Then, on that occasion, the Blessed One uttered this inspired utterance:

“Ārogyaparamā lābhā, nibbānaṃ paramaṃ sukhaṃ;

Aṭṭhaṅgiko ca maggānaṃ, khemaṃ amatagāmina”nti.

“Health is the supreme gain, Nibbāna the supreme happiness; Of paths leading to the Deathless, the Eightfold is the secure one.”

216. Evaṃ vutte, māgaṇḍiyo paribbājako bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “acchariyaṃ, bho gotama, abbhutaṃ, bho gotama! Yāva subhāsitaṃ cidaṃ bhotā gotamena – ‘ārogyaparamā [P 1.0509] lābhā, nibbānaṃ paramaṃ sukha’nti. Mayāpi kho etaṃ, bho gotama, sutaṃ pubbakānaṃ paribbājakānaṃ ācariyapācariyānaṃ bhāsamānānaṃ – ‘ārogyaparamā lābhā, nibbānaṃ paramaṃ sukha’nti; tayidaṃ, bho gotama, sametī”ti. “Yaṃ pana te etaṃ, māgaṇḍiya, sutaṃ pubbakānaṃ paribbājakānaṃ [V 2.0187] ācariyapācariyānaṃ bhāsamānānaṃ – ‘ārogyaparamā lābhā, nibbānaṃ paramaṃ sukha’nti, katamaṃ taṃ ārogyaṃ, katamaṃ taṃ nibbāna”nti? Evaṃ vutte, māgaṇḍiyo paribbājako sakāneva sudaṃ gattāni pāṇinā anomajjati – “idantaṃ, bho gotama, ārogyaṃ, idantaṃ nibbānaṃ. Ahañhi, bho gotama, etarahi arogo sukhī, na maṃ kiñci ābādhatī”ti.

216. When this was said, the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya said to the Blessed One: “It is wonderful, venerable Gotama, it is marvelous, venerable Gotama! How well this has been spoken by the venerable Gotama: ‘Health is the supreme gain, Nibbāna the supreme happiness.’ I too, venerable Gotama, have heard this from former wanderers, teachers and teachers of teachers, when they were speaking: ‘Health is the supreme gain, Nibbāna the supreme happiness.’ This of yours accords with that.” “But, Māgaṇḍiya, as to that which you have heard from former wanderers, teachers and teachers of teachers, when they were speaking: ‘Health is the supreme gain, Nibbāna the supreme happiness,’ what is that health, and what is that Nibbāna?” When this was said, the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya stroked his own limbs with his hand and said: “This, venerable Gotama, is that health; this is that Nibbāna. For I am now healthy and happy, and no affliction troubles me.”

217. “Seyyathāpi, māgaṇḍiya, jaccandho puriso; so na passeyya [T 2.0282] kaṇhasukkāni rūpāni, na passeyya nīlakāni rūpāni, na passeyya pītakāni rūpāni, na passeyya lohitakāni rūpāni, na passeyya mañjiṭṭhakāni mañjeṭṭhikāni (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.), mañjeṭṭhakāni (ka.) rūpāni, na passeyya samavisamaṃ, na passeyya tārakarūpāni, na passeyya candimasūriye. So suṇeyya cakkhumato bhāsamānassa – ‘chekaṃ vata, bho[M 2.0177], odātaṃ vatthaṃ abhirūpaṃ nimmalaṃ sucī’ti! So odātapariyesanaṃ careyya. Tamenaṃ aññataro puriso telamalikatena sāhuḷicīrena telamasikatena sāhuḷacīvarena (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) vañceyya – ‘idaṃ te, ambho purisa, odātaṃ vatthaṃ abhirūpaṃ nimmalaṃ sucī’ti. So taṃ paṭiggaṇheyya, paṭiggahetvā pārupeyya, pārupetvā attamano attamanavācaṃ nicchāreyya – ‘chekaṃ vata, bho, odātaṃ vatthaṃ abhirūpaṃ nimmalaṃ sucī’ti!

217. “Suppose, Māgaṇḍiya, there was a man blind from birth; he would not see black and white forms, nor would he see blue forms, yellow forms, red forms, or crimson forms. He would not see the even and the uneven, nor the forms of the stars, nor the moon and sun. He might hear a person with sight saying, ‘Indeed, sirs, this white cloth is excellent, beautiful, spotless, and clean!’ Then he would go in search of a white cloth. A certain man might deceive him with an oil-grimed, coarse woolen garment, saying, ‘Here, good man, is a white cloth for you, beautiful, spotless, and clean!’ He would accept it and put it on. Having put it on, delighted, he might utter words of delight, ‘Indeed, sirs, this white cloth is excellent, beautiful, spotless, and clean!’”

“Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, māgaṇḍiya, api nu so jaccandho puriso jānanto passanto amuṃ telamalikataṃ sāhuḷicīraṃ paṭiggaṇheyya, paṭiggahetvā pārupeyya, pārupetvā attamano attamanavācaṃ nicchāreyya – ‘chekaṃ vata, bho, odātaṃ vatthaṃ abhirūpaṃ nimmalaṃ sucī’ti udāhu cakkhumato saddhāyā”ti? “Ajānanto hi, bho gotama, apassanto so jaccandho puriso amuṃ telamalikataṃ sāhuḷicīraṃ paṭiggaṇheyya, paṭiggahetvā pārupeyya, pārupetvā attamano attamanavācaṃ nicchāreyya – ‘chekaṃ [P 1.0510] vata, bho, odātaṃ vatthaṃ abhirūpaṃ nimmalaṃ sucī’ti, cakkhumato saddhāyā”ti. “Evameva kho, māgaṇḍiya, aññatitthiyā paribbājakā andhā acakkhukā ajānantā ārogyaṃ, apassantā nibbānaṃ[T 2.0283], atha ca panimaṃ gāthaṃ bhāsanti – ‘ārogyaparamā lābhā, nibbānaṃ paramaṃ sukha’nti. Pubbakehesā, māgaṇḍiya, arahantehi sammāsambuddhehi gāthā bhāsitā –

“What do you think, Māgaṇḍiya? Would that man blind from birth, knowing and seeing, accept that oil-grimed, coarse woolen garment, and having accepted it, wear it, and having worn it, being delighted, utter words of delight: ‘Indeed, sirs, this white cloth is excellent, beautiful, spotless, and clean’—or would he do so out of faith in the one with sight?” “Not knowing, Venerable Gotama, not seeing, that man blind from birth would accept that oil-grimed, coarse woolen garment, and having accepted it, would wear it, and having worn it, being delighted, would utter words of delight: ‘Indeed, sirs, this white cloth is excellent, beautiful, spotless, and clean’—out of faith in the one with sight.” “Just so, Māgaṇḍiya, the wanderers of other sects are blind and without vision; not knowing health, not seeing Nibbāna, they nevertheless recite this verse: ‘Health is the highest gain, Nibbāna is the supreme happiness.’ This verse, Māgaṇḍiya, was spoken by the former Arahants, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones:

‘Ārogyaparamā [V 2.0188] lābhā, nibbānaṃ paramaṃ sukhaṃ;

Aṭṭhaṅgiko ca maggānaṃ, khemaṃ amatagāmina’nti.

“‘Health is the highest of gains, Nibbāna is the supreme happiness; and of paths, the Eightfold Path is the secure one, leading to the Deathless.’”

218. “Sā etarahi anupubbena puthujjanagāthā puthujjanagatā (sī. pī.). Ayaṃ kho pana, māgaṇḍiya, kāyo rogabhūto gaṇḍabhūto sallabhūto aghabhūto ābādhabhūto, so tvaṃ imaṃ kāyaṃ rogabhūtaṃ gaṇḍabhūtaṃ sallabhūtaṃ aghabhūtaṃ ābādhabhūtaṃ – ‘idantaṃ, bho gotama, ārogyaṃ, idantaṃ nibbāna’nti vadesi. Tañhi te, māgaṇḍiya, ariyaṃ cakkhuṃ natthi yena tvaṃ ariyena cakkhunā ārogyaṃ jāneyyāsi, nibbānaṃ passeyyāsī”ti. “Evaṃ pasanno ahaṃ bhoto gotamassa! Pahoti me bhavaṃ gotamo tathā dhammaṃ desetuṃ yathāhaṃ ārogyaṃ jāneyyaṃ, nibbānaṃ passeyya”nti.

218. “That verse has now, in due course, become a verse of ordinary people. This body, Māgaṇḍiya, is a disease, a tumor, a dart, a calamity, an affliction. And you, regarding this body—which is a disease, a tumor, a dart, a calamity, an affliction—say: ‘This, Venerable Gotama, is that health; this is that Nibbāna.’ For you, Māgaṇḍiya, do not have that noble eye by which you might know health and see Nibbāna.” “I am so confident in the Venerable Gotama! The Venerable Gotama is able to teach me the Dhamma in such a way that I may know health and see Nibbāna.”

219. “Seyyathāpi[M 2.0178], māgaṇḍiya, jaccandho puriso; so na passeyya kaṇhasukkāni rūpāni, na passeyya nīlakāni rūpāni, na passeyya pītakāni rūpāni, na passeyya lohitakāni rūpāni, na passeyya mañjiṭṭhakāni rūpāni, na passeyya samavisamaṃ, na passeyya tārakarūpāni, na passeyya candimasūriye. Tassa mittāmaccā ñātisālohitā bhisakkaṃ sallakattaṃ upaṭṭhāpeyyuṃ. Tassa so bhisakko sallakatto bhesajjaṃ kareyya. So taṃ bhesajjaṃ āgamma na cakkhūni uppādeyya, na [T 2.0284] cakkhūni visodheyya. Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, māgaṇḍiya, nanu so vejjo yāvadeva kilamathassa vighātassa bhāgī assā”ti? “Evaṃ, bho gotama”. “Evameva kho, māgaṇḍiya, ahañce te dhammaṃ deseyyaṃ – ‘idantaṃ ārogyaṃ, idantaṃ nibbāna’nti, so tvaṃ ārogyaṃ na jāneyyāsi, nibbānaṃ na passeyyāsi. So mamassa kilamatho, sā mamassa vihesā”ti. “Evaṃ [P 1.0511] pasanno ahaṃ bhoto gotamassa. Pahoti me bhavaṃ gotamo tathā dhammaṃ desetuṃ yathāhaṃ ārogyaṃ jāneyyaṃ, nibbānaṃ passeyya”nti.

219. “Suppose, Māgaṇḍiya, there was a man blind from birth. He would not see black and white forms, nor would he see blue forms, yellow forms, red forms, or crimson forms. He would not see the even and the uneven, nor the forms of the stars, nor the moon and sun. His friends, companions, relatives, and kinsmen might bring a physician and surgeon to him. That physician and surgeon might prepare medicine for him. But by means of that medicine, he would not be able to produce eyes or clarify his vision. What do you think, Māgaṇḍiya? Would that physician not just reap weariness and vexation?” “So it is, Venerable Gotama.” “Just so, Māgaṇḍiya, if I were to teach you the Dhamma, saying, ‘This is that health, this is that Nibbāna,’ you would not know health and you would not see Nibbāna. That would be weariness for me; that would be vexation for me.” “I am so confident in the Venerable Gotama. The Venerable Gotama is able to teach me the Dhamma in such a way that I may know health and see Nibbāna.”

220. “Seyyathāpi, māgaṇḍiya, jaccandho puriso; so na passeyya kaṇhasukkāni rūpāni, na passeyya nīlakāni rūpāni, na passeyya pītakāni rūpāni, na passeyya lohitakāni rūpāni, na passeyya mañjiṭṭhakāni rūpāni, na passeyya samavisamaṃ, na passeyya tārakarūpāni, na passeyya candimasūriye. So suṇeyya cakkhumato bhāsamānassa – ‘chekaṃ vata, bho, odātaṃ vatthaṃ abhirūpaṃ nimmalaṃ sucī’ti! So odātapariyesanaṃ careyya. Tamenaṃ aññataro [V 2.0189] puriso telamalikatena sāhuḷicīrena vañceyya – ‘idaṃ te, ambho purisa, odātaṃ vatthaṃ abhirūpaṃ nimmalaṃ sucī’ti. So taṃ paṭiggaṇheyya, paṭiggahetvā pārupeyya. Tassa mittāmaccā ñātisālohitā bhisakkaṃ sallakattaṃ upaṭṭhāpeyyuṃ. Tassa so bhisakko sallakatto bhesajjaṃ kareyya – uddhaṃvirecanaṃ adhovirecanaṃ añjanaṃ paccañjanaṃ natthukammaṃ. So taṃ bhesajjaṃ [T 2.0285] āgamma cakkhūni uppādeyya, cakkhūni visodheyya. Tassa saha cakkhuppādā yo amusmiṃ telamalikate sāhuḷicīre chandarāgo so pahīyetha. Tañca naṃ purisaṃ amittatopi daheyya, paccatthikatopi daheyya, api ca jīvitā voropetabbaṃ maññeyya – ‘dīgharattaṃ vata, bho, ahaṃ iminā purisena telamalikatena sāhuḷicīrena nikato vañcito paluddho – idaṃ te, ambho purisa, odātaṃ vatthaṃ [M 2.0179] abhirūpaṃ nimmalaṃ sucī’ti. Evameva kho, māgaṇḍiya, ahañce te dhammaṃ deseyyaṃ – ‘idantaṃ ārogyaṃ, idantaṃ nibbāna’nti. So tvaṃ ārogyaṃ jāneyyāsi, nibbānaṃ passeyyāsi. Tassa te saha cakkhuppādā yo pañcasupādānakkhandhesu chandarāgo so pahīyetha; api ca te evamassa – ‘dīgharattaṃ vata, bho, ahaṃ iminā cittena nikato vañcito paluddho paladdho (sī. pī.). Ahañhi rūpaṃyeva upādiyamāno upādiyiṃ, vedanaṃyeva upādiyamāno upādiyiṃ, saññaṃyeva upādiyamāno upādiyiṃ, saṅkhāreyeva upādiyamāno upādiyiṃ, viññāṇaṃyeva upādiyamāno upādiyiṃ. Tassa me upādānapaccayā bhavo, bhavapaccayā jāti, jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇaṃ sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā [P 1.0512] sambhavanti; evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa samudayo hotī’”ti. “Evaṃ pasanno ahaṃ bhoto gotamassa! Pahoti me bhavaṃ gotamo tathā dhammaṃ desetuṃ yathāhaṃ imamhā āsanā anandho vuṭṭhaheyya”nti.

220. “Suppose, Māgaṇḍiya, there was a man blind from birth who could not see black and white forms, could not see blue forms, could not see yellow forms, could not see red forms, or crimson forms. He could not see what was even or uneven, nor the stars, nor the sun and moon. He might hear someone with good eyesight saying, ‘How excellent, sir, is this white cloth, beautiful, spotless, and clean!’ He would then go in search of a white cloth. But someone might deceive him with a coarse garment smeared with oily grime, saying, ‘Here, good man, is a white cloth for you, beautiful, spotless, and clean!’ He would accept it and put it on. His friends, companions, and kinsmen would then have a physician, a surgeon, attend to him. That physician, the surgeon, would prepare medicine for him—an emetic, a purgative, an eye-ointment, a counter-ointment, and a nasal treatment. By means of that medicine, his eyes would be generated and cleansed. With the arising of his eyes, his desire and lust for that coarse garment smeared with oily grime would be abandoned. He would regard that man as an enemy and a foe, and would even think he should be deprived of life, thinking: ‘For a long time, indeed, I have been cheated, deceived, and defrauded by this man with his coarse garment smeared with oily grime, who said, “Here, good man, is a white cloth for you, beautiful, spotless, and clean!”’ In the very same way, Māgaṇḍiya, if I were to teach you the Dhamma, saying, ‘This is that health, this is that Nibbāna,’ you would know health and see Nibbāna. With the arising of your vision, your desire and lust for the five aggregates of clinging would be abandoned. And it might occur to you: ‘For a long time, indeed, I have been cheated, deceived, and defrauded by this mind. For it was by clinging that I clung to form, by clinging that I clung to feeling, by clinging that I clung to perception, by clinging that I clung to formations, by clinging that I clung to consciousness. For me, with clinging as condition, becoming comes to be; with becoming as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come to be. Thus is the origin of this whole mass of suffering!’” “I have such faith in the venerable Gotama! The venerable Gotama is capable of teaching me the Dhamma in such a way that I might rise from this seat no longer blind.”

221. “Tena hi tvaṃ, māgaṇḍiya, sappurise bhajeyyāsi. Yato kho [T 2.0286] tvaṃ, māgaṇḍiya, sappurise bhajissasi tato tvaṃ, māgaṇḍiya, saddhammaṃ sossasi; yato kho tvaṃ, māgaṇḍiya, saddhammaṃ sossasi tato tvaṃ, māgaṇḍiya, dhammānudhammaṃ paṭipajjissasi; yato kho tvaṃ, māgaṇḍiya, dhammānudhammaṃ paṭipajjissasi tato tvaṃ, māgaṇḍiya, sāmaṃyeva ñassasi, sāmaṃ dakkhissasi – ime rogā gaṇḍā sallā; idha rogā gaṇḍā sallā aparisesā nirujjhanti. Tassa me upādānanirodhā bhavanirodho, bhavanirodhā jātinirodho, jātinirodhā jarāmaraṇaṃ sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā nirujjhanti; evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa nirodho hotī”ti.

221. “Then, Māgaṇḍiya, you should associate with true persons. When you associate with true persons, Māgaṇḍiya, you will hear the true Dhamma. When you hear the true Dhamma, Māgaṇḍiya, you will practice in accordance with the Dhamma. When you practice in accordance with the Dhamma, Māgaṇḍiya, you will know for yourself, you will see for yourself: ‘These are diseases, these are tumors, these are darts. Here these diseases, tumors, and darts cease without remainder. For me, with the cessation of clinging comes the cessation of becoming; with the cessation of becoming comes the cessation of birth; with the cessation of birth, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease. Thus is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.’”

222. Evaṃ [V 2.0190] vutte, māgaṇḍiyo paribbājako bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “abhikkantaṃ, bho gotama, abhikkantaṃ, bho gotama! Seyyathāpi, bho gotama, nikkujjitaṃ vā ukkujjeyya, paṭicchannaṃ vā vivareyya, mūḷhassa vā maggaṃ ācikkheyya, andhakāre vā telapajjotaṃ dhāreyya – cakkhumanto rūpāni dakkhantīti; evamevaṃ bhotā gotamena anekapariyāyena dhammo pakāsito. Esāhaṃ bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi dhammañca bhikkhusaṅghañca[M 2.0180]. Labheyyāhaṃ bhoto gotamassa santike pabbajjaṃ, labheyyaṃ upasampada”nti. “Yo kho, māgaṇḍiya, aññatitthiyapubbo imasmiṃ dhammavinaye ākaṅkhati pabbajjaṃ, ākaṅkhati upasampadaṃ, so cattāro māse parivasati; catunnaṃ māsānaṃ accayena āraddhacittā bhikkhū pabbājenti[T 2.0287], upasampādenti bhikkhubhāvāya. Api ca mettha puggalavemattatā viditā”ti. “Sace, bhante, aññatitthiyapubbā imasmiṃ dhammavinaye ākaṅkhantā pabbajjaṃ, ākaṅkhantā upasampadaṃ cattāro māse parivasanti, catunnaṃ māsānaṃ accayena āraddhacittā bhikkhū pabbājenti upasampādenti bhikkhubhāvāya; ahaṃ cattāri vassāni parivasissāmi, catunnaṃ vassānaṃ accayena āraddhacittā bhikkhū pabbājentu, upasampādentu bhikkhubhāvāyā”ti[P 1.0513]. Alattha kho māgaṇḍiyo paribbājako bhagavato santike pabbajjaṃ, alattha upasampadaṃ. Acirūpasampanno kho panāyasmā māgaṇḍiyo eko vūpakaṭṭho appamatto ātāpī pahitatto viharanto nacirasseva – yassatthāya kulaputtā sammadeva agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajanti tadanuttaraṃ – brahmacariyapariyosānaṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja vihāsi. ‘Khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti abbhaññāsi. Aññataro kho panāyasmā māgaṇḍiyo arahataṃ ahosīti.

222. When this was said, the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya said to the Blessed One: “Excellent, Master Gotama, excellent! Just as, Master Gotama, one might set upright what was overturned, reveal what was hidden, show the path to one who is lost, or hold up an oil lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—in the same way the Dhamma has been made clear by Master Gotama in many ways. I go to Master Gotama for refuge, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May I receive the going forth in Master Gotama’s presence, may I receive the higher ordination.” “Whoever, Māgaṇḍiya, having previously belonged to another sect, desires the going forth and the higher ordination in this Dhamma and Discipline, must first undergo probation for four months. At the end of four months, if the bhikkhus are satisfied, they may give him the going forth and the higher ordination into the state of a bhikkhu. However, individual differences are known to me in this matter.” “If, venerable sir, those who previously belonged to another sect and desire the going forth and the higher ordination in this Dhamma and Discipline must undergo probation for four months, and at the end of four months, if the bhikkhus are satisfied, they give them the going forth and the higher ordination into the state of a bhikkhu—then I will undergo probation for four years. At the end of four years, if the bhikkhus are satisfied, let them give me the going forth and the higher ordination into the state of a bhikkhu.” The wanderer Māgaṇḍiya received the going forth in the Blessed One’s presence; he received the higher ordination. And soon after his higher ordination, the Venerable Māgaṇḍiya, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, realized for himself with direct knowledge, here and now, that unsurpassed consummation of the holy life for which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness. He understood: “Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.” And the Venerable Māgaṇḍiya became one of the arahants.

Māgaṇḍiyasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ pañcamaṃ.

The Māgaṇḍiya Sutta, the fifth, is concluded.

6. Sandakasuttaṃ

6. The Sandaka Sutta

223. Evaṃ [T 2.0288][V 2.0191] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā kosambiyaṃ viharati ghositārāme. Tena kho pana samayena sandako paribbājako pilakkhaguhāyaṃ paṭivasati mahatiyā paribbājakaparisāya saddhiṃ pañcamattehi paribbājakasatehi. Atha kho āyasmā ānando sāyanhasamayaṃ paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito bhikkhū āmantesi – “āyāmāvuso, yena devakatasobbho tenupasaṅkamissāma guhādassanāyā”ti. “Evamāvuso”ti kho te bhikkhū āyasmato ānandassa paccassosuṃ. Atha kho āyasmā ānando sambahulehi bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ yena devakatasobbho tenupasaṅkami. Tena kho pana samayena sandako paribbājako mahatiyā [M 2.0181] paribbājakaparisāya saddhiṃ nisinno hoti unnādiniyā uccāsaddamahāsaddāya anekavihitaṃ tiracchānakathaṃ kathentiyā, seyyathidaṃ – rājakathaṃ corakathaṃ mahāmattakathaṃ senākathaṃ bhayakathaṃ yuddhakathaṃ annakathaṃ pānakathaṃ vatthakathaṃ sayanakathaṃ mālākathaṃ gandhakathaṃ ñātikathaṃ yānakathaṃ gāmakathaṃ nigamakathaṃ nagarakathaṃ janapadakathaṃ itthikathaṃ sūrakathaṃ visikhākathaṃ kumbhaṭṭhānakathaṃ pubbapetakathaṃ nānattakathaṃ lokakkhāyikaṃ samuddakkhāyikaṃ [P 1.0514] itibhavābhavakathaṃ iti vā. Addasā kho sandako paribbājako āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ dūratova āgacchantaṃ. Disvāna sakaṃ parisaṃ saṇṭhāpesi [T 2.0289] – “appasaddā bhonto hontu, mā bhonto saddamakattha; ayaṃ samaṇassa gotamassa sāvako āgacchati samaṇo ānando. Yāvatā kho pana samaṇassa gotamassa sāvakā kosambiyaṃ paṭivasanti, ayaṃ tesaṃ aññataro samaṇo ānando. Appasaddakāmā kho pana te āyasmanto appasaddavinītā appasaddassa vaṇṇavādino; appeva nāma appasaddaṃ parisaṃ viditvā upasaṅkamitabbaṃ maññeyyā”ti. Atha kho te paribbājakā tuṇhī ahesuṃ.

223. Thus have I heard: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Kosambī, in Ghosita’s Park. Now at that time the wanderer Sandaka was staying in the Pilakkha cave together with a large assembly of wanderers, about five hundred in number. Then in the evening, the Venerable Ānanda arose from seclusion and addressed the bhikkhus: "Come, friends, let us go to the Devakata Pool to see the cave." "Yes, friend," those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Ānanda. Then the Venerable Ānanda, together with a number of bhikkhus, went to the Devakata Pool. At that time, the wanderer Sandaka was seated with his large assembly of wanderers, making a loud, great noise, an uproar, while telling many kinds of base talk—such as talk about kings, robbers, chief ministers, armies, dangers, battles, food, drink, clothes, beds, garlands, perfumes, relatives, vehicles, villages, towns, cities, countries, women, men, heroes, streets, wells, the departed, various kinds of talk, speculation about the world, speculation about the ocean, and talk about being and non-being. The wanderer Sandaka saw the Venerable Ānanda coming from afar. Upon seeing him, he quieted his own assembly: "Be quiet, sirs, do not make a sound. This ascetic Ānanda, a disciple of the ascetic Gotama, is coming. Of all the disciples of the ascetic Gotama dwelling in Kosambī, this ascetic Ānanda is one of them. These venerable ones love quiet, are trained in quiet, and praise quiet. Perhaps, upon seeing a quiet assembly, he might think it worthwhile to approach." Then those wanderers fell silent.

224. Atha kho āyasmā ānando yena sandako paribbājako tenupasaṅkami. Atha kho sandako paribbājako āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ etadavoca – “etu kho bhavaṃ ānando, svāgataṃ bhoto ānandassa. Cirassaṃ kho bhavaṃ ānando imaṃ pariyāyamakāsi yadidaṃ idhāgamanāya. Nisīdatu bhavaṃ ānando, idamāsanaṃ paññatta”nti. Nisīdi kho āyasmā ānando [V 2.0192] paññatte āsane. Sandakopi kho paribbājako aññataraṃ nīcaṃ āsanaṃ gahetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinnaṃ kho sandakaṃ paribbājakaṃ āyasmā ānando etadavoca – “kāyanuttha, sandaka, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā, kā ca pana vo antarākathā vippakatā”ti? “Tiṭṭhatesā, bho ānanda, kathā yāya mayaṃ etarahi kathāya sannisinnā. Nesā bhoto ānandassa kathā dullabhā bhavissati pacchāpi savanāya. Sādhu vata bhavantaṃyeva ānandaṃ paṭibhātu sake ācariyake dhammīkathā”ti. “Tena hi, sandaka, suṇāhi[T 2.0290], sādhukaṃ manasi karohi, bhāsissāmī”ti. “Evaṃ bho”ti kho sandako paribbājako āyasmato ānandassa paccassosi. Āyasmā ānando etadavoca – “cattārome[M 2.0182], sandaka, tena bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā sammāsambuddhena abrahmacariyavāsā akkhātā cattāri ca anassāsikāni brahmacariyāni akkhātāni, yattha viññū puriso sasakkaṃ brahmacariyaṃ na vaseyya, vasanto ca vasanto vā (sī. pī.) evamuparipi anārādhanapakkhe nārādheyya ñāyaṃ dhammaṃ kusala”nti. “Katame pana te, bho ānanda, tena bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā sammāsambuddhena cattāro abrahmacariyavāsā akkhātā, yattha viññū [P 1.0515] puriso sasakkaṃ brahmacariyaṃ na vaseyya, vasanto ca nārādheyya ñāyaṃ dhammaṃ kusala”nti?

224. Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the wanderer Sandaka. The wanderer Sandaka then said this to the Venerable Ānanda: 'May the Venerable Ānanda come; welcome to the Venerable Ānanda. It has been a long time, indeed, since the Venerable Ānanda made this occasion to come here. May the Venerable Ānanda be seated; this seat is prepared.' The Venerable Ānanda sat down on the prepared seat. The wanderer Sandaka also took a certain low seat and sat down to one side. To the wanderer Sandaka, who was seated to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this: 'For what talk, Sandaka, are you now assembled? And what was the unfinished talk among you?' 'Let that talk be, Venerable Ānanda, for which we are now assembled. That talk will not be difficult for the Venerable Ānanda to hear later on. It would be good, venerable sir, if a Dhamma talk concerning your own teacher's doctrine would occur to the Venerable Ānanda himself.' 'In that case, Sandaka, listen and apply your mind well; I will speak.' 'Yes, venerable sir,' the wanderer Sandaka replied to the Venerable Ānanda. The Venerable Ānanda said this: 'Sandaka, these four ways of life that are not the holy life have been declared by that Blessed One who knows, who sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, and four uncomforting holy lives have been declared, wherein a wise person would certainly not live the holy life, and living it, would not accomplish the right, wholesome Dhamma.' 'But which, Venerable Ānanda, are those four ways of life that are not the holy life declared by that Blessed One who knows, who sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, wherein a wise person would certainly not live the holy life, and living it, would not accomplish the right, wholesome Dhamma?'

225. “Idha, sandaka, ekacco satthā evaṃvādī hoti evaṃdiṭṭhi – ‘natthi dinnaṃ, natthi yiṭṭhaṃ, natthi hutaṃ, natthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko, natthi ayaṃ loko, natthi paroloko, natthi mātā, natthi pitā, natthi sattā opapātikā, natthi loke samaṇabrāhmaṇā sammaggatā sammāpaṭipannā ye imañca lokaṃ parañca lokaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā pavedenti. Cātumahābhūtiko ayaṃ puriso yadā kālaṅkaroti, pathavī pathavīkāyaṃ anupeti anupagacchati, āpo āpokāyaṃ anupeti anupagacchati, tejo tejokāyaṃ anupeti anupagacchati, vāyo vāyokāyaṃ anupeti anupagacchati[T 2.0291], ākāsaṃ indriyāni saṅkamanti. Āsandipañcamā purisā mataṃ ādāya gacchanti, yāvāḷāhanā padāni paññāyanti. Kāpotakāni aṭṭhīni bhavanti. Bhassantā āhutiyo; dattupaññattaṃ yadidaṃ dānaṃ. Tesaṃ tucchā musā vilāpo ye keci atthikavādaṃ vadanti. Bāle ca paṇḍite ca kāyassa bhedā ucchijjanti vinassanti na honti paraṃ maraṇā’ti.

225. 'Here, Sandaka, a certain teacher has such a saying, such a view: "There is nothing given, nothing offered, nothing sacrificed. There is no fruit or result of good and bad actions. There is no this world, no other world. There is no mother, no father. There are no spontaneously arisen beings. There are in the world no recluses and brahmins who are rightly directed, rightly practiced, who, having realized for themselves by direct knowledge this world and the other world, make it known. This person is composed of the four great elements. When one dies, the earth element returns to and merges with the external earth-body, the water element returns to and merges with the external water-body, the fire element returns to and merges with the external fire-body, the air element returns to and merges with the external air-body, and the faculties pass into space. Men with the bier as their fifth carry the dead away; their footprints are seen as far as the charnel ground. The bones become pigeon-colored. Offerings end in ashes. This which is called giving is a doctrine of fools. Of those who profess an affirmationist doctrine, their speech is empty, false, and mere babble. Both the foolish and the wise, with the breakup of the body, are annihilated and perish; they do not exist after death."'"

“Tatra[V 2.0193], sandaka, viññū puriso iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘ayaṃ kho bhavaṃ satthā evaṃvādī evaṃdiṭṭhi – natthi dinnaṃ, natthi yiṭṭhaṃ, natthi hutaṃ, natthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko, natthi ayaṃ loko, natthi paroloko, natthi mātā, natthi pitā, natthi sattā opapātikā, natthi loke samaṇabrāhmaṇā sammaggatā sammāpaṭipannā ye imañca lokaṃ parañca lokaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā pavedenti. Cātumahābhūtiko ayaṃ puriso yadā kālaṅkaroti, pathavī pathavīkāyaṃ anupeti anupagacchati, āpo āpokāyaṃ [M 2.0183] anupeti anupagacchati, tejo tejokāyaṃ anupeti anupagacchati, vāyo vāyokāyaṃ anupeti anupagacchati, ākāsaṃ indriyāni saṅkamanti. Āsandipañcamā purisā mataṃ ādāya gacchanti, yāvāḷāhanā padāni paññāyanti. Kāpotakāni aṭṭhīni bhavanti. Bhassantā āhutiyo; dattupaññattaṃ yadidaṃ dānaṃ. Tesaṃ tucchā musā vilāpo ye keci atthikavādaṃ vadanti. Bāle ca paṇḍite ca kāyassa bhedā ucchijjanti [T 2.0292] vinassanti na honti paraṃ maraṇā’ti. Sace imassa bhoto satthuno saccaṃ vacanaṃ, akatena me ettha kataṃ, avusitena me ettha vusitaṃ. Ubhopi mayaṃ ettha samasamā sāmaññaṃ pattā, yo cāhaṃ na vadāmi ‘ubho kāyassa bhedā ucchijjissāma, vinassissāma, na bhavissāma paraṃ maraṇā’ti. Atirekaṃ kho panimassa bhoto satthuno naggiyaṃ muṇḍiyaṃ ukkuṭikappadhānaṃ kesamassulocanaṃ yohaṃ puttasambādhasayanaṃ puttasambādhavasanaṃ (sī.) ajjhāvasanto kāsikacandanaṃ paccanubhonto mālāgandhavilepanaṃ dhārento jātarūparajataṃ sādiyanto iminā bhotā satthārā samasamagatiko bhavissāmi. Abhisamparāyaṃ sohaṃ kiṃ jānanto kiṃ passanto imasmiṃ satthari brahmacariyaṃ carissāmi? ‘So abrahmacariyavāso aya’nti – iti viditvā tasmā brahmacariyā nibbijja pakkamati nibbijjāpakkamati (sī.). Ayaṃ kho, sandaka, tena bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā sammāsambuddhena paṭhamo abrahmacariyavāso akkhāto yattha viññū puriso sasakkaṃ brahmacariyaṃ [P 1.0516] na vaseyya, vasanto ca nārādheyya ñāyaṃ dhammaṃ kusalaṃ.

Therein, Sandaka, a wise person reflects thus: 'This venerable teacher speaks thus and holds this view: “There is nothing given, nothing sacrificed, nothing offered. There is no fruit or result of good and bad deeds. There is no this world, no other world. There is no mother, no father. There are no spontaneously arisen beings. There are no ascetics or brahmins in the world who are well-gone and well-practiced, who, having realized it for themselves through direct knowledge, make known this world and the other world. This person is composed of the four great elements. When they die, earth returns to the earth element, water to the water element, fire to the fire element, air to the air element, and the faculties pass into space. Men, with the bier as the fifth, carry away the dead; their praises are known only as far as the charnel ground. The bones become the color of a dove. Offerings end in ashes. This giving is a teaching prescribed by fools. The speech of those who profess a doctrine of ‘there is’ is empty, false, and mere babble. Both the foolish and the wise, with the breakup of the body, are annihilated and perish; they do not exist after death.” If this venerable teacher’s word is true, then for me in this teaching, what is undone is done, and what is unlived is lived. We both have reached the same state of sameness, even I who do not declare: ‘We both, with the breakup of the body, will be annihilated, will perish, and will not exist after death.’ Excessive indeed are this venerable teacher’s practices of nakedness, shaven-headedness, squatting, and plucking out hair and beard, while I dwell in a home crowded with children, enjoying sandalwood from Kasi, wearing garlands, scents, and unguents, and accepting gold and silver. I will have the very same future destiny as this venerable teacher! Knowing what, seeing what of a future life, should I live the holy life under this teacher?’ Realizing, ‘This is a life devoid of the holy life,’ they become disgusted with that holy life and depart. This, Sandaka, is the first life devoid of the holy life declared by the Blessed One—who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One—wherein a wise person would certainly not live the holy life, and if they did, they would not accomplish the methodical, wholesome Dhamma.

226. “Puna caparaṃ, sandaka, idhekacco satthā evaṃvādī hoti evaṃdiṭṭhi – ‘karoto kārayato chindato chedāpayato pacato pācāpayato socayato socāpayato kilamato kilamāpayato phandato phandāpayato pāṇamatipātayato adinnaṃ ādiyato sandhiṃ chindato nillopaṃ harato ekāgārikaṃ karoto paripanthe tiṭṭhato paradāraṃ gacchato musā bhaṇato [T 2.0293] karoto na [V 2.0194] karīyati pāpaṃ. Khurapariyantena cepi cakkena yo imissā pathaviyā pāṇe ekaṃ maṃsakhalaṃ ekaṃ maṃsapuñjaṃ kareyya, natthi tatonidānaṃ pāpaṃ, natthi pāpassa āgamo. Dakkhiṇañcepi gaṅgāya tīraṃ gaccheyya hananto ghātento chindanto chedāpento pacanto pacāpento, natthi tatonidānaṃ pāpaṃ, natthi [M 2.0184] pāpassa āgamo. Uttarañcepi gaṅgāya tīraṃ gaccheyya dadanto dāpento yajanto yajāpento, natthi tatonidānaṃ puññaṃ, natthi puññassa āgamo. Dānena damena saṃyamena saccavajjena natthi puññaṃ, natthi puññassa āgamo’ti.

226. Furthermore, Sandaka, there is another teacher who speaks thus, holds such a view: 'For one who acts or causes another to act, who cuts or causes another to cut, who torments or causes another to torment, who causes grief or causes another to cause grief, who becomes weary or causes another to become weary, who trembles or causes another to tremble, who destroys life, takes what is not given, breaks into a house, plunders, burglarizes a single house, commits highway robbery, commits adultery, or speaks falsely—for one who acts thus, no evil is done. Even if with a razor-edged wheel one were to make all the living beings on this earth into a single mass of flesh, a single heap of flesh, from that there is no evil, no inflow of evil. Even if one were to go along the southern bank of the Ganges killing and causing to kill, cutting and causing to cut, tormenting and causing to torment, from that there is no evil, no inflow of evil. Even if one were to go along the northern bank of the Ganges giving and causing to give, sacrificing and causing to sacrifice, from that there is no merit, no inflow of merit. Through giving, taming, restraint, and truthful speech, there is no merit, no inflow of merit.'

“Tatra, sandaka, viññū puriso iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘ayaṃ kho bhavaṃ satthā evaṃvādī evaṃdiṭṭhi – karoto kārayato chindato chedāpayato pacato pācāpayato socato socāpayato kilamato kilamāpayato phandato phandāpayato pāṇamatipātayato adinnaṃ ādiyato sandhiṃ chindato nillopaṃ harato ekāgārikaṃ karoto paripanthe tiṭṭhato paradāraṃ gacchato musā bhaṇato karoto na karīyati pāpaṃ khurapariyantena cepi cakkena yo imissā pathaviyā pāṇe ekaṃ maṃsakhalaṃ ekaṃ maṃsapuñjaṃ kareyya, natthi tatonidānaṃ pāpaṃ, natthi pāpassa āgamo. Dakkhiṇañcepi gaṅgāya tīraṃ gaccheyya hananto ghātento chindanto chedāpento pacanto pacāpento, natthi tatonidānaṃ pāpaṃ, natthi pāpassa āgamo.
