Uttarañcepi gaṅgāya tīraṃ [T 2.0294] gaccheyya dadanto dāpento yajanto yajāpento, natthi tatonidānaṃ puññaṃ, natthi puññassa āgamo. Dānena damena saṃyamena saccavajjena natthi puññaṃ, natthi puññassa āgamo’ti. Sace imassa bhoto satthuno saccaṃ vacanaṃ, akatena me ettha kataṃ, avusitena me ettha vusitaṃ. Ubhopi mayaṃ ettha samasamā sāmaññaṃ pattā, yo cāhaṃ na vadāmi ‘ubhinnaṃ kurutaṃ na karīyati pāpa’nti. Atirekaṃ kho panimassa bhoto satthuno naggiyaṃ muṇḍiyaṃ ukkuṭikappadhānaṃ kesamassulocanaṃ yohaṃ puttasambādhasayanaṃ ajjhāvasanto kāsikacandanaṃ paccanubhonto mālāgandhavilepanaṃ dhārento jātarūparajataṃ sādiyanto iminā bhotā satthārā samasamagatiko bhavissāmi. Abhisamparāyaṃ sohaṃ kiṃ jānanto kiṃ passanto imasmiṃ satthari brahmacariyaṃ carissāmi? ‘So abrahmacariyavāso aya’nti iti viditvā tasmā brahmacariyā nibbijja pakkamati. Ayaṃ kho, sandaka, tena bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā sammāsambuddhena dutiyo abrahmacariyavāso akkhāto yattha viññū puriso sasakkaṃ brahmacariyaṃ na vaseyya, vasanto ca nārādheyya ñāyaṃ dhammaṃ kusalaṃ.

“In this case, Sandaka, a wise person reflects thus: ‘This venerable teacher has such a view and holds such an opinion: “For one who acts or causes another to act, who mutilates or causes another to mutilate, who tortures or causes another to torture, who grieves or causes another to grieve, who oppresses or causes another to oppress, who disturbs or causes another to disturb, who kills, who takes what is not given, who breaks into houses, who plunders, who commits burglary, who waits in ambush on the highway, who commits adultery, who speaks lies—no evil is done by the doer. Even if one were to make the living beings on this earth into a single heap of flesh, a single mass of flesh, with a razor-edged wheel, there is no evil because of that, no coming of evil. If one were to go to the south bank of the Ganges killing, slaughtering, mutilating, causing another to mutilate, torturing, causing another to torture, there is no evil because of that, no coming of evil. If one were to go to the north bank of the Ganges giving, causing others to give, sacrificing, causing others to sacrifice, there is no merit because of that, no coming of merit. Through giving, self-control, restraint, and truthful speech, there is no merit, no coming of merit.” If this venerable teacher’s word is true, then for me, who have not done these things, it is as if it is done. We are both exactly equal here, having reached the same state, even though I do not say: “For both of us who act, no evil is done.” Furthermore, this venerable teacher’s nakedness, shaven-headedness, effort in the squatting posture, and plucking out of hair and beard are superfluous, since I—who live in a home crowded with children, enjoying sandalwood from Kāsi, wearing garlands, perfumes, and ointments, and accepting gold and silver—will have the very same destination in the next life as this venerable teacher. Knowing what, seeing what, should I live the holy life under this teacher?’ Having realized, ‘This is a way of life that is not the holy life,’ he becomes disillusioned and departs from that holy life. This, Sandaka, is the second way of life that is not the holy life, declared by the Blessed One, who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, wherein a wise person would certainly not live the holy life; and if they were to live it, they would not achieve the right and wholesome Dhamma.”

227. “Puna caparaṃ, sandaka, idhekacco satthā evaṃvādī hoti evaṃdiṭṭhi – ‘natthi hetu, natthi paccayo sattānaṃ saṃkilesāya; ahetū appaccayā sattā [M 2.0185] saṃkilissanti; natthi hetu, natthi paccayo [V 2.0195] sattānaṃ visuddhiyā; ahetū appaccayā sattā visujjhanti; natthi balaṃ, natthi [T 2.0295] vīriyaṃ, natthi purisathāmo[P 1.0517], natthi purisaparakkamo; sabbe sattā sabbe pāṇā sabbe bhūtā sabbe jīvā avasā abalā avīriyā niyatisaṅgatibhāvapariṇatā chasvevābhijātīsu sukhadukkhaṃ paṭisaṃvedentī’ti.

227. Furthermore, Sandaka, some teacher here is one who speaks thus, who holds such a view: ‘There is no cause, no condition for the defilement of beings; beings are defiled without cause and without condition. There is no cause, no condition for the purification of beings; beings are purified without cause and without condition. There is no strength, there is no energy, there is no human stamina, there is no human exertion. All beings, all living things, all creatures, all souls are without mastery, without strength, without energy, determined by destiny, circumstance, and nature, and they experience pleasure and pain in the six classes of birth alone.’

“Tatra, sandaka, viññū puriso iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘ayaṃ kho bhavaṃ satthā evaṃvādī evaṃdiṭṭhi – natthi hetu, natthi paccayo sattānaṃ saṃkilesāya, ahetū appaccayā sattā saṃkilissanti. Natthi hetu natthi paccayo sattānaṃ visuddhiyā, ahetū appaccayā sattā visujjhanti. Natthi balaṃ, natthi vīriyaṃ, natthi purisathāmo, natthi purisaparakkamo, sabbe sattā sabbe pāṇā sabbe bhūtā sabbe jīvā avasā abalā avīriyā niyatisaṅgatibhāvapariṇatā chasvevābhijātīsu sukhadukkhaṃ paṭisaṃvedentī’ti. Sace imassa bhoto satthuno saccaṃ vacanaṃ, akatena me ettha kataṃ, avusitena me ettha vusitaṃ. Ubhopi mayaṃ ettha samasamā sāmaññaṃ pattā, yo cāhaṃ na vadāmi ‘ubho ahetū appaccayā visujjhissāmā’ti. Atirekaṃ kho panimassa bhoto satthuno naggiyaṃ muṇḍiyaṃ ukkuṭikappadhānaṃ kesamassulocanaṃ yohaṃ puttasambādhasayanaṃ ajjhāvasanto kāsikacandanaṃ paccanubhonto mālāgandhavilepanaṃ dhārento jātarūparajataṃ sādiyanto iminā bhotā satthārā samasamagatiko bhavissāmi. Abhisamparāyaṃ sohaṃ kiṃ jānanto kiṃ passanto imasmiṃ satthari brahmacariyaṃ carissāmi? ‘So abrahmacariyavāso aya’nti – iti viditvā tasmā [T 2.0296] brahmacariyā nibbijja pakkamati. Ayaṃ kho, sandaka, tena bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā sammāsambuddhena tatiyo abrahmacariyavāso akkhāto yattha viññū puriso sasakkaṃ brahmacariyaṃ na vaseyya, vasanto ca nārādheyya ñāyaṃ dhammaṃ kusalaṃ.

In that case, Sandaka, a wise person reflects thus: 'This venerable teacher is one who speaks thus, who holds such a view: “There is no cause, no condition for the defilement of beings; beings are defiled without cause and without condition. There is no cause, no condition for the purification of beings; beings are purified without cause and without condition. There is no strength, there is no energy, there is no human stamina, there is no human exertion. All beings, all living things, all creatures, all souls are without mastery, without strength, without energy, determined by destiny, circumstance, and nature, and they experience pleasure and pain in the six classes of birth alone.” If this venerable teacher’s word is true, then for me, in this teaching, what is not done is as good as done, and the life not lived is as good as lived. We are both exactly equal here, having attained the same state, even I who do not say, “We both will be purified without cause and without condition.” Indeed, this venerable teacher’s nakedness, shaven-headedness, squatting posture, and plucking out of hair and beard are then superfluous, since I—who dwell in a home crowded with children, enjoying Kāsi sandalwood, wearing garlands, perfumes, and ointments, and accepting gold and silver—will have the very same destination in the next life as this venerable teacher. So I, knowing what, seeing what, shall I live the holy life under this teacher? Realizing, “This is a way of life that is not the holy life,” and having understood this, becoming disgusted with that holy life, he departs. This, Sandaka, is the third way of life that is not the holy life, declared by the Blessed One, who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, wherein a wise person would certainly not live the holy life; and if they were to live it, they would not accomplish the right and wholesome Dhamma.

228. “Puna caparaṃ, sandaka, idhekacco satthā evaṃvādī hoti evaṃdiṭṭhi – ‘sattime kāyā akaṭā akaṭavidhā animmitā animmātā vañjhā kūṭaṭṭhā esikaṭṭhāyiṭṭhitā, te na iñjanti na vipariṇamanti na aññamaññaṃ byābādhenti nālaṃ aññamaññassa sukhāya vā dukkhāya vā sukhadukkhāya vā. Katame satta? Pathavīkāyo āpokāyo tejokāyo vāyokāyo sukhe dukkhe jīve sattame – ime sattakāyā akaṭā akaṭavidhā animmitā [M 2.0186] animmātā [V 2.0196] vañjhā kūṭaṭṭhā esikaṭṭhāyiṭṭhitā. Te na iñjanti na vipariṇamanti na aññamaññaṃ byābādhenti. Nālaṃ aññamaññassa sukhāya vā dukkhāya vā sukhadukkhāya vā. Tattha natthi hantā vā ghātetā vā sotā vā sāvetā vā viññātā vā viññāpetā vā. Yopi tiṇhena satthena sīsaṃ chindati, na koci kañci kiñci (ka.) jīvitā voropeti. Sattannaṃtveva kāyānamantarena satthaṃ vivaramanupatati. Cuddasa kho panimāni yonipamukhasatasahassāni saṭṭhi ca satāni cha ca satāni pañca ca kammuno satāni pañca ca kammāni tīṇi [T 2.0297] ca kammāni, kamme ca aḍḍhakamme ca, dvaṭṭhipaṭipadā, dvaṭṭhantarakappā, chaḷābhijātiyo, aṭṭha purisabhūmiyo, ekūnapaññāsa ājīvakasate, ekūnapaññāsa paribbājakasate, ekūnapaññāsa [P 1.0518] nāgāvāsasate, vīse indriyasate, tiṃse nirayasate, chattiṃsa rajodhātuyo, satta saññīgabbhā, satta asaññīgabbhā, satta nigaṇṭhigabbhā, satta devā, satta mānusā, satta pesācā, satta sarā, satta pavuṭā, satta papātā, satta papātasatāni, satta supinā, satta supinasatāni, cullāsīti cūḷāsīti (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) mahākappino mahākappuno (sī. pī.) satasahassāni, yāni bāle ca paṇḍite ca sandhāvitvā saṃsaritvā dukkhassantaṃ karissanti. Tattha natthi imināhaṃ sīlena vā vatena vā tapena vā brahmacariyena vā aparipakkaṃ vā kammaṃ paripācessāmi, paripakkaṃ vā kammaṃ phussa phussa byantiṃ karissāmīti. Hevaṃ natthi doṇamite sukhadukkhe pariyantakate saṃsāre, natthi hāyanavaḍḍhane, natthi ukkaṃsāvakaṃse. Seyyathāpi nāma suttaguḷe khitte nibbeṭhiyamānameva paleti, evameva bāle ca paṇḍite ca sandhāvitvā saṃsaritvā dukkhassantaṃ karissantī’ti.

228. Furthermore, Sandaka, there is a certain teacher who holds this doctrine and view: ‘There are these seven bodies, unmade, unfashioned, uncreated, not caused to be created, barren, standing firm as a mountain peak, standing firm like a pillar. They do not move, do not change, do not harm one another, nor are they capable of causing one another pleasure, pain, or both pleasure and pain. Which seven? The earth-body, the water-body, the fire-body, the wind-body, pleasure, pain, and the life-principle as the seventh—these seven bodies are unmade, unfashioned, uncreated, not caused to be created, barren, standing firm as a mountain peak, standing firm like a pillar. They do not move, do not change, do not harm one another, nor are they capable of causing one another pleasure, pain, or both pleasure and pain. Here, there is no killer, no instigator of killing, no hearer, no proclaimer, no knower, no instructor. Even if one were to cut off someone’s head with a sharp sword, no one would be depriving anyone of life. The sword merely passes through the space between these seven bodies. There are one million four hundred thousand principal wombs, and six thousand, and six hundred; five hundred actions, and five actions, and three actions, and an action and a half-action; sixty-two paths, sixty-two intermediate aeons, six classes of high birth, eight stages of human existence, forty-nine hundred Ājīvakas, forty-nine hundred wanderers, forty-nine hundred Nāga abodes, two thousand faculties, three thousand hells, thirty-six realms of dust, seven sentient conceptions, seven non-sentient conceptions, seven knot-conceptions, many devas, countless humans, many demons, seven great lakes, seven great knots, seven great precipices, seven hundred precipices, seven great dreams, seven hundred lesser dreams, and eighty-four hundred thousand great aeons—through which fools and the wise alike will wander and transmigrate until they make an end of suffering. There is no such thing as: "By this morality, observance, austerity, or holy life, I will ripen unripened kamma or exhaust ripened kamma by experiencing it again and again." Pleasure and pain are measured out, the round of rebirth is limited; there is no decrease or increase, no rise or fall. Just as a ball of thread, when thrown, unwinds until it is exhausted, so too fools and the wise alike will wander and transmigrate until they make an end of suffering.’

“Tatra, sandaka, viññū puriso iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘ayaṃ kho bhavaṃ satthā evaṃvādī evaṃdiṭṭhi – sattime kāyā akaṭā akaṭavidhā animmitā animmātā vañjhā kūṭaṭṭhā esikaṭṭhāyiṭṭhitā. Te na iñjanti na vipariṇamanti na aññamaññaṃ byābādhenti. Nālaṃ aññamaññassa sukhāya vā dukkhāya vā sukhadukkhāya vā. Katame satta[T 2.0298]? Pathavīkāyo āpokāyo tejokāyo vāyokāyo sukhe dukkhe jīve sattame – ime satta kāyā akaṭā akaṭavidhā animmitā animmātā vañjhā kūṭaṭṭhā esikaṭṭhāyiṭṭhitā. Te na iñjanti na vipariṇamanti na aññamaññaṃ byābādhenti. Nālaṃ aññamaññassa sukhāya vā dukkhāya vā sukhadukkhāya vā. Tattha natthi hantā vā [M 2.0187] ghātetā vā sotā vā sāvetā vā viññātā vā viññāpetā vā. Yopi tiṇhena satthena sīsaṃ chindati, na koci kañci jīvitā voropeti[V 2.0197]. Sattannaṃtveva kāyānamantarena satthaṃ vivaramanupatati. Cuddasa kho panimāni yonipamukhasatasahassāni saṭṭhi ca satāni cha ca satāni pañca ca kammuno satāni pañca ca kammāni tīṇi ca kammāni, kamme ca aḍḍhakamme ca, dvaṭṭhipaṭipadā, dvaṭṭhantarakappā, chaḷābhijātiyo, aṭṭha purisabhūmiyo, ekūnapaññāsa ājīvakasate, ekūnapaññāsa paribbājakasate, ekūnapaññāsa nāgāvāsasate, vīse indriyasate, tiṃse nirayasate, chattiṃsa rajodhātuyo, satta saññīgabbhā, satta asaññīgabbhā, satta nigaṇṭhigabbhā, satta devā, satta mānusā, satta pesācā, satta sarā, satta pavuṭā, satta papātā, satta papātasatāni, satta supinā, satta supinasatāni, cullāsīti mahākappino satasahassāni, yāni bāle ca paṇḍite ca sandhāvitvā saṃsaritvā dukkhassantaṃ karissanti. Tattha natthi imināhaṃ sīlena vā vatena vā tapena vā brahmacariyena vā aparipakkaṃ [T 2.0299] vā kammaṃ paripācessāmi, paripakkaṃ vā kammaṃ phussa phussa byantiṃ karissāmīti, hevaṃ natthi doṇamite sukhadukkhe pariyantakate saṃsāre, natthi hāyanavaḍḍhane, natthi ukkaṃsāvakaṃse. Seyyathāpi nāma suttaguḷe khitte nibbeṭhiyamānameva paleti, evameva bāle ca paṇḍite ca sandhāvitvā saṃsaritvā dukkhassantaṃ karissantī’ti. Sace pana imassa bhoto satthuno saccaṃ vacanaṃ, akatena me ettha kataṃ, avusitena me ettha vusitaṃ. Ubhopi mayaṃ ettha samasamā sāmaññaṃ pattā, yo cāhaṃ na vadāmi. ‘Ubho sandhāvitvā saṃsaritvā dukkhassantaṃ karissāmā’ti. Atirekaṃ kho panimassa bhoto satthuno naggiyaṃ muṇḍiyaṃ ukkuṭikappadhānaṃ kesamassulocanaṃ yohaṃ puttasambādhasayanaṃ ajjhāvasanto kāsikacandanaṃ paccanubhonto mālāgandhavilepanaṃ dhārento jātarūparajataṃ sādiyanto iminā bhotā satthārā samasamagatiko bhavissāmi. Abhisamparāyaṃ sohaṃ kiṃ jānanto kiṃ passanto imasmiṃ satthari brahmacariyaṃ carissāmi? ‘So abrahmacariyavāso aya’nti – iti viditvā tasmā brahmacariyā nibbijja pakkamati. Ayaṃ kho, sandaka, tena bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā sammāsambuddhena catuttho abrahmacariyavāso akkhāto yattha viññū puriso sasakkaṃ brahmacariyaṃ na vaseyya, vasanto ca nārādheyya ñāyaṃ dhammaṃ kusalaṃ.

In that doctrine, Sandaka, a wise person reflects thus: 'This venerable teacher holds such a view and doctrine: “There are these seven bodies, unmade, unfashioned, uncreated, not caused to be created, barren, stable like a mountain peak, firmly established like a pillar. They do not move, do not alter, do not affect one another. They are incapable of causing one another pleasure, pain, or both pleasure and pain. Which seven? The earth-body, the water-body, the fire-body, the air-body, pleasure, pain, and the life-faculty as the seventh—these seven bodies are unmade, unfashioned, uncreated, not caused to be created, barren, stable like a mountain peak, firmly established like a pillar. They do not move, do not alter, do not affect one another. They are incapable of causing one another pleasure, pain, or both pleasure and pain. Herein, there is no killer, no causer of killing, no hearer, no one who causes to hear, no knower, no one who causes to know. Even if one cuts off another’s head with a sharp sword, no one deprives anyone of life. The sword merely passes through the space between the seven bodies. There are fourteen hundred thousand primary wombs, sixty-six hundred, five hundred kammas, five kammas, three kammas, kamma and half-kamma, sixty-two paths, sixty-two intermediate aeons, six classes of birth, eight stages of human existence, forty-nine hundred kinds of Ājīvakas, forty-nine hundred kinds of wanderers, forty-nine hundred kinds of Nāga abodes, twenty hundred faculties, thirty hundred hells, thirty-six dust elements, seven perceptive wombs, seven non-perceptive wombs, seven knot-wombs, seven gods, seven humans, seven goblins, seven lakes, seven great knots, seven precipices, seven hundred precipices, seven dreams, and seven hundred dreams, and eighty-four hundred thousand great aeons through which fools and the wise, having wandered and transmigrated, will make an end of suffering. Herein, there is no such thing as: ‘By this virtue, observance, austerity, or holy life, I will ripen unripened kamma or eradicate ripened kamma by repeatedly experiencing it.’ There is no such thing as pleasure and pain being measured out, or saṃsāra having a fixed end. There is no decrease or increase, no low or high. Just as a ball of thread, when thrown, unwinds to its full extent, so too fools and the wise, having wandered and transmigrated, will make an end of suffering.” If this venerable teacher’s words were true, then for me, what is not done is done, and what is not lived is lived. Both of us here have attained the same state, the state of being the same—I who do not hold this view, and he who does. Indeed, the practices of this venerable teacher are superfluous—the nakedness, shaven head, squatting posture, and plucking of hair and beard—if I, who live at home crowded with children, enjoy sandalwood from Kasi, wear garlands, perfumes, and ointments, and accept gold and silver, am to have the same destination in the next life as this venerable teacher. Knowing and seeing what, would I then practice the holy life under this teacher? Knowing, ‘This is a non-holy life,’ he becomes disgusted with that holy life and departs. This, Sandaka, is the fourth non-holy life declared by the Blessed One, who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, wherein a wise person would certainly not live the holy life, or living it, would not attain the proper, wholesome Dhamma.

“Ime [M 2.0188] kho te, sandaka, tena bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā sammāsambuddhena cattāro abrahmacariyavāsā [T 2.0300] akkhātā yattha [P 1.0519] viññū puriso sasakkaṃ brahmacariyaṃ na vaseyya, vasanto ca nārādheyya ñāyaṃ dhammaṃ kusala”nti.

These, Sandaka, are the four non-holy lives declared by that Blessed One, who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, wherein a wise person would certainly not live the holy life, or living it, would not attain the proper, wholesome Dhamma.

“Acchariyaṃ[V 2.0198], bho ānanda, abbhutaṃ, bho ānanda! Yāvañcidaṃ tena bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā sammāsambuddhena cattāro abrahmacariyavāsāva samānā ‘abrahmacariyavāsā’ti akkhātā yattha viññū puriso sasakkaṃ brahmacariyaṃ na vaseyya, vasanto ca nārādheyya ñāyaṃ dhammaṃ kusalanti. Katamāni pana tāni, bho ānanda, tena bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā sammāsambuddhena cattāri anassāsikāni brahmacariyāni akkhātāni yattha viññū puriso sasakkaṃ brahmacariyaṃ na vaseyya, vasanto ca nārādheyya ñāyaṃ dhammaṃ kusala”nti?

Wonderful, Venerable Ānanda, amazing, Venerable Ānanda! To such an extent has the Blessed One, who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, declared these four non-holy lives to be 'non-holy lives', wherein a wise person would certainly not live the holy life, or living it, would not attain the proper, wholesome Dhamma. But what, Venerable Ānanda, are those four unreliable holy lives declared by the Blessed One, who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, wherein a wise person would certainly not live the holy life, or living it, would not attain the proper, wholesome Dhamma?

229. “Idha, sandaka, ekacco satthā sabbaññū sabbadassāvī aparisesaṃ ñāṇadassanaṃ paṭijānāti – ‘carato ca me tiṭṭhato ca suttassa ca jāgarassa ca satataṃ samitaṃ ñāṇadassanaṃ paccupaṭṭhita’nti. So suññampi agāraṃ pavisati, piṇḍampi na labhati, kukkuropi ḍaṃsati, caṇḍenapi hatthinā samāgacchati, caṇḍenapi assena samāgacchati, caṇḍenapi goṇena samāgacchati, itthiyāpi purisassapi nāmampi gottampi pucchati, gāmassapi nigamassapi nāmampi maggampi pucchati. So ‘kimida’nti puṭṭho samāno ‘suññaṃ me agāraṃ pavisitabbaṃ ahosi’, tena pāvisiṃ; ‘piṇḍampi aladdhabbaṃ ahosi’, tena nālatthaṃ[T 2.0301]; ‘kukkurena ḍaṃsitabbaṃ ahosi’, tenamhi tena (ka.), tenāsiṃ (?) daṭṭho; ‘caṇḍena hatthinā samāgantabbaṃ ahosi’, tena samāgamiṃ; ‘caṇḍena assena samāgantabbaṃ ahosi’, tena samāgamiṃ; ‘caṇḍena goṇena samāgantabbaṃ ahosi’, tena samāgamiṃ; ‘itthiyāpi purisassapi nāmampi gottampi pucchitabbaṃ ahosi’, tena pucchiṃ; ‘gāmassapi nigamassapi nāmampi maggampi pucchitabbaṃ ahosi’, tena pucchinti. Tatra, sandaka, viññū puriso iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘ayaṃ kho bhavaṃ satthā sabbaññū sabbadassāvī aparisesaṃ ñāṇadassanaṃ paṭijānāti…pe… [T 2.0302] ‘gāmassapi nigamassapi nāmampi maggampi pucchitabbaṃ ahosi, tena pucchi’nti[M 2.0189]. So ‘anassāsikaṃ idaṃ brahmacariya’nti – iti viditvā tasmā brahmacariyā nibbijja pakkamati. Idaṃ kho, sandaka, tena bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā sammāsambuddhena paṭhamaṃ anassāsikaṃ brahmacariyaṃ akkhātaṃ [P 1.0520] yattha viññū puriso sasakkaṃ brahmacariyaṃ na vaseyya, vasanto ca nārādheyya ñāyaṃ dhammaṃ kusalaṃ.

229. Here, Sandaka, a certain teacher professes to be all-knowing, all-seeing, and claims complete knowledge and vision, saying: ‘Whether I am walking, standing, sleeping, or awake, knowledge and vision are constantly and continuously present to me.’ Yet he enters an empty house, does not receive alms-food, is bitten by a dog, encounters a fierce elephant, a fierce horse, and a fierce bull. He asks the name and clan of a woman and a man, and asks the name of a village and a town, and the path. When asked, ‘What is this?’, he replies: ‘It was to be that I would enter an empty house, so I entered. It was to be that I would not obtain alms-food, so I did not obtain it. It was to be that I would be bitten by a dog, so I was bitten. It was to be that I would encounter a fierce elephant, so I did. It was to be that I would encounter a fierce horse, so I did. It was to be that I would encounter a fierce bull, so I did. It was to be that I would ask the name and clan of a woman and a man, so I asked. It was to be that I would ask the name of a village and a town, and the path, so I asked.’ Therein, Sandaka, an intelligent man reflects thus: ‘This venerable teacher professes to be all-knowing, all-seeing, and claims complete knowledge and vision… and yet he says, “It was to be that I would ask the name of a village and a town, and the path, so I asked.”’ Having understood, ‘This holy life is unconsoling,’ he becomes disenchanted with that holy life and departs. This, Sandaka, is the first unconsoling holy life declared by that Blessed One who is knowing, seeing, an Arahant, a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, wherein an intelligent man would certainly not live the holy life, and living it, would not accomplish the right and wholesome Dhamma.

230. “Puna caparaṃ, sandaka, idhekacco satthā anussaviko hoti anussavasacco. So anussavena itihitihaparamparāya piṭakasampadāya dhammaṃ deseti. Anussavikassa kho pana, sandaka[V 2.0199], satthuno anussavasaccassa sussutampi hoti dussutampi hoti tathāpi hoti aññathāpi hoti. Tatra, sandaka, viññū puriso iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘ayaṃ kho bhavaṃ satthā anussaviko anussavasacco so anussavena itihitihaparamparāya piṭakasampadāya dhammaṃ deseti. Anussavikassa kho pana satthuno anussavasaccassa sussutampi hoti dussutampi hoti tathāpi hoti aññathāpi hoti’. So ‘anassāsikaṃ idaṃ brahmacariya’nti – iti viditvā tasmā brahmacariyā nibbijja pakkamati. Idaṃ kho, sandaka, tena bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā sammāsambuddhena dutiyaṃ anassāsikaṃ brahmacariyaṃ akkhātaṃ yattha viññū puriso sasakkaṃ brahmacariyaṃ na vaseyya, vasanto ca nārādheyya ñāyaṃ dhammaṃ kusalaṃ.

230. Furthermore, Sandaka, here a certain teacher is one who relies on oral tradition, who holds that tradition as truth. He teaches the Dhamma based on oral tradition, on what has been handed down in a lineage, on the authority of the scriptures. But, Sandaka, for a teacher who relies on oral tradition and holds that tradition as truth, what he teaches may be well-heard or badly-heard; it may be so or it may be otherwise. Therein, Sandaka, an intelligent man reflects thus: ‘This venerable teacher relies on oral tradition and holds that tradition as truth… what he teaches may be well-heard or badly-heard; it may be so or it may be otherwise.’ Having understood, ‘This holy life is unconsoling,’ he becomes disenchanted with that holy life and departs. This, Sandaka, is the second unconsoling holy life declared by that Blessed One who is knowing, seeing, an Arahant, a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, wherein an intelligent man would certainly not live the holy life, and living it, would not accomplish the right and wholesome Dhamma.

231. “Puna [T 2.0303] caparaṃ, sandaka, idhekacco satthā takkī hoti vīmaṃsī. So takkapariyāhataṃ vīmaṃsānucaritaṃ sayaṃpaṭibhānaṃ dhammaṃ deseti. Takkissa kho pana, sandaka, satthuno vīmaṃsissa sutakkitampi hoti duttakkitampi hoti tathāpi hoti aññathāpi hoti. Tatra, sandaka, viññū puriso iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘ayaṃ kho bhavaṃ satthā takkī vīmaṃsī. So takkapariyāhataṃ vīmaṃsānucaritaṃ sayaṃpaṭibhānaṃ dhammaṃ deseti. Takkissa kho pana satthuno vīmaṃsissa sutakkitampi hoti duttakkitampi hoti tathāpi hoti aññathāpi hoti’. So ‘anassāsikaṃ idaṃ brahmacariya’nti – iti viditvā tasmā brahmacariyā nibbijja pakkamati. Idaṃ kho, sandaka, tena bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā sammāsambuddhena tatiyaṃ anassāsikaṃ brahmacariyaṃ akkhātaṃ yattha viññū puriso sasakkaṃ brahmacariyaṃ na vaseyya, vasanto ca nārādheyya ñāyaṃ dhammaṃ kusalaṃ.

231. Furthermore, Sandaka, here a certain teacher is a reasoner, an investigator. He teaches a Dhamma hammered out by reasoning, followed out by investigation, of his own invention. But, Sandaka, for a teacher who is a reasoner and an investigator, his reasoning may be well-reasoned or badly-reasoned; it may be so or it may be otherwise. Therein, Sandaka, an intelligent man reflects thus: ‘This venerable teacher is a reasoner and an investigator. He teaches a Dhamma hammered out by reasoning, followed out by investigation, of his own invention. For a teacher who is a reasoner and an investigator, his reasoning may be well-reasoned or badly-reasoned; it may be so or it may be otherwise.’ Having understood, ‘This holy life is unconsoling,’ he becomes disenchanted with that holy life and departs. This, Sandaka, is the third unconsoling holy life declared by that Blessed One who is knowing, seeing, an Arahant, a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, wherein an intelligent man would certainly not live the holy life, and living it, would not accomplish the right and wholesome Dhamma.

232. “Puna [M 2.0190] caparaṃ, sandaka, idhekacco satthā mando hoti momūho. So mandattā momūhattā tattha tattha tathā tathā (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) pañhaṃ puṭṭho [P 1.0521] samāno vācāvikkhepaṃ āpajjati amarāvikkhepaṃ – ‘evantipi evampi (sī. pī.) me no, tathātipi tathāpi (sī. pī.) me no, aññathātipi aññathāpi (sī. pī.) ( ) sabbattha natthi me no, notipi me no, no notipi me no’ti. Tatra, sandaka, viññū puriso iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘ayaṃ kho bhavaṃ satthā mando momūho. So mandattā momūhattā tattha tattha pañhaṃ puṭṭho samāno vācāvikkhepaṃ āpajjati amarāvikkhepaṃ [T 2.0304] – evantipi me no, tathātipi me no, aññathātipi me no, notipi me no, no notipi me no’ti. So ‘anassāsikaṃ idaṃ brahmacariya’nti – iti viditvā [V 2.0200] tasmā brahmacariyā nibbijja pakkamati. Idaṃ kho, sandaka, tena bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā sammāsambuddhena catutthaṃ anassāsikaṃ brahmacariyaṃ akkhātaṃ yattha viññū puriso sasakkaṃ brahmacariyaṃ na vaseyya, vasanto ca nārādheyya ñāyaṃ dhammaṃ kusalaṃ.

232. Furthermore, Sandaka, here a certain teacher is dull, utterly bewildered. Due to his dullness and utter bewilderment, when asked a question on this or that point, he resorts to verbal evasion and eel-wriggling, saying: ‘I do not hold that it is so. I do not hold that it is thus. I do not hold that it is otherwise. I do not hold that it is not. I do not hold that it is not not.’ Therein, Sandaka, an intelligent man reflects thus: ‘This venerable teacher is dull, utterly bewildered. Due to his dullness and utter bewilderment, when asked a question on this or that point, he resorts to verbal evasion and eel-wriggling, saying: “I do not hold that it is so. I do not hold that it is thus. I do not hold that it is otherwise. I do not hold that it is not. I do not hold that it is not not.”’ Having understood, ‘This holy life is unconsoling,’ he becomes disenchanted with that holy life and departs. This, Sandaka, is the fourth unconsoling holy life declared by that Blessed One who is knowing, seeing, an Arahant, a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, wherein an intelligent man would certainly not live the holy life, and living it, would not accomplish the right and wholesome Dhamma.

“Imāni kho, (tāni sandaka, tena bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā sammāsambuddhena cattāri anassāsikāni brahmacariyāni akkhātāni yattha viññū puriso sasakkaṃ brahmacariyaṃ na vaseyya, vasanto ca nārādheyya ñāyaṃ dhammaṃ kusala”nti.

Sandaka, these indeed are the four comfortless holy lives declared by that Blessed One—who knows, who sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One—wherein a wise person should certainly not live the holy life, and, while living it, would not accomplish the right, wholesome Dhamma.

“Acchariyaṃ, bho ānanda, abbhutaṃ, bho ānanda! Yāvañcidaṃ tena bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā sammāsambuddhena cattāri anassāsikāneva brahmacariyāni anassāsikāni brahmacariyānīti akkhātāni yattha viññū puriso sasakkaṃ brahmacariyaṃ na vaseyya, vasanto ca nārādheyya ñāyaṃ dhammaṃ kusalaṃ. So pana, bho ānanda, satthā kiṃ vādī kiṃ akkhāyī yattha viññū puriso sasakkaṃ brahmacariyaṃ vaseyya, vasanto ca ārādheyya ñāyaṃ dhammaṃ kusala”nti.

Wonderful, venerable Ānanda! Marvelous, venerable Ānanda! How well have the four comfortless holy lives been declared as comfortless holy lives by that Blessed One who knows, who sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One—wherein a wise person should certainly not live the holy life, and, while living it, would not accomplish the right, wholesome Dhamma. But, venerable Ānanda, what is the doctrine and what is the teaching of that teacher wherein a wise person should certainly live the holy life, and, while living it, would accomplish the right, wholesome Dhamma?

233. “Idha, sandaka, tathāgato loke uppajjati arahaṃ sammāsambuddho vijjācaraṇasampanno sugato lokavidū anuttaro purisadammasārathi satthā devamanussānaṃ buddho bhagavā…pe… vitthāro ma. ni. 2.9-10 kandarakasutte so ime [T 2.0305] pañca nīvaraṇe pahāya cetaso upakkilese paññāya dubbalīkaraṇe vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi [M 2.0191] dhammehi savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Yasmiṃ kho yasmiṃ kho pana (syā. kaṃ. ka.), sandaka, satthari sāvako evarūpaṃ uḷāravisesaṃ adhigacchati tattha [P 1.0522] viññū puriso sasakkaṃ brahmacariyaṃ vaseyya, vasanto ca ārādheyya ñāyaṃ dhammaṃ kusalaṃ.

233. Here, Sandaka, a Tathāgata arises in the world, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, perfect in knowledge and conduct, the Well-farer, the Knower of worlds, the unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, the Teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. … He, having abandoned these five hindrances, which are defilements of the mind and weaken wisdom, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and abides in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. Sandaka, in the case of a teacher under whom a disciple attains such a sublime distinction, there a wise person should certainly live the holy life, and, while living it, would accomplish the right, wholesome Dhamma.

“Puna caparaṃ, sandaka, bhikkhu vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā…pe... dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Yasmiṃ kho, sandaka, satthari sāvako evarūpaṃ uḷāravisesaṃ adhigacchati tattha viññū puriso sasakkaṃ brahmacariyaṃ vaseyya, vasanto ca ārādheyya ñāyaṃ dhammaṃ kusalaṃ.

Furthermore, Sandaka, with the stilling of applied and sustained thought, a bhikkhu enters and abides in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without applied and sustained thought, and has rapture and pleasure born of concentration. Sandaka, in the case of a teacher under whom a disciple attains such a sublime distinction, there a wise person should certainly live the holy life, and, while living it, would accomplish the right, wholesome Dhamma.

“Puna [V 2.0201] caparaṃ, sandaka, bhikkhu pītiyā ca virāgā upekkhako ca viharati…pe… tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Yasmiṃ kho, sandaka, satthari sāvako evarūpaṃ uḷāravisesaṃ adhigacchati tattha viññū puriso sasakkaṃ brahmacariyaṃ vaseyya, vasanto ca ārādheyya ñāyaṃ dhammaṃ kusalaṃ.

Furthermore, Sandaka, with the fading away of rapture, a bhikkhu abides in equanimity, mindful and fully aware, and experiences pleasure with the body. He enters and abides in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare, ‘Equanimous and mindful, he has a pleasant abiding.’ Sandaka, in the case of a teacher under whom a disciple attains such a sublime distinction, there a wise person should certainly live the holy life, and, while living it, would accomplish the right, wholesome Dhamma.

“Puna caparaṃ, sandaka, bhikkhu sukhassa ca pahānā…pe… catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Yasmiṃ kho, sandaka, satthari sāvako evarūpaṃ uḷāravisesaṃ adhigacchati tattha viññū puriso sasakkaṃ brahmacariyaṃ vaseyya, vasanto ca ārādheyya ñāyaṃ dhammaṃ kusalaṃ.

Furthermore, Sandaka, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain—and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief—a bhikkhu enters and abides in the fourth jhāna, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. Sandaka, in the case of a teacher under whom a disciple attains such a sublime distinction, there a wise person should certainly live the holy life, and, while living it, would accomplish the right, wholesome Dhamma.

“So evaṃ samāhite citte parisuddhe pariyodāte anaṅgaṇe [T 2.0306] vigatūpakkilese mudubhūte kammaniye ṭhite āneñjappatte pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇāya cittaṃ abhininnāmeti. So anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati, seyyathidaṃ – ekampi jātiṃ dvepi jātiyo…pe… iti sākāraṃ sauddesaṃ anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati. Yasmiṃ kho, sandaka, satthari sāvako evarūpaṃ uḷāravisesaṃ adhigacchati tattha viññū puriso sasakkaṃ brahmacariyaṃ vaseyya, vasanto ca ārādheyya ñāyaṃ dhammaṃ kusalaṃ.

When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of defilements, malleable, workable, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs and inclines his mind to the knowledge of recollecting past lives. He recollects his manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births… Thus he recollects his manifold past lives with their aspects and details. Sandaka, in the case of a teacher under whom a disciple attains such a sublime distinction, there a wise person should certainly live the holy life, and, while living it, would accomplish the right, wholesome Dhamma.

“So evaṃ samāhite citte parisuddhe pariyodāte anaṅgaṇe vigatūpakkilese mudubhūte kammaniye ṭhite āneñjappatte sattānaṃ cutūpapātañāṇāya cittaṃ abhininnāmeti. So dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena satte passati cavamāne upapajjamāne hīne paṇīte suvaṇṇe dubbaṇṇe sugate duggate…pe… yathākammūpage satte pajānāti. Yasmiṃ kho, sandaka, satthari sāvako evarūpaṃ uḷāravisesaṃ adhigacchati [M 2.0192] tattha viññū puriso sasakkaṃ brahmacariyaṃ vaseyya, vasanto ca ārādheyya ñāyaṃ dhammaṃ kusalaṃ.

When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of defilements, malleable, workable, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs and inclines his mind to the knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings. With the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, he sees beings passing away and reappearing—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate. He understands how beings fare in accordance with their kamma. Sandaka, in the case of a teacher under whom a disciple attains such a sublime distinction, there a wise person should certainly live the holy life, and, while living it, would accomplish the right, wholesome Dhamma.

“So evaṃ samāhite citte parisuddhe pariyodāte anaṅgaṇe vigatūpakkilese mudubhūte kammaniye ṭhite āneñjappatte āsavānaṃ khayañāṇāya cittaṃ abhininnāmeti. So ‘idaṃ dukkha’nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, ‘ayaṃ dukkhasamudayo’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodho’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti; ‘ime āsavā’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, ‘ayaṃ āsavasamudayo’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, ‘ayaṃ āsavanirodho’ti yathābhūtaṃ [V 2.0202] pajānāti, ‘ayaṃ āsavanirodhagāminī [T 2.0307] paṭipadā’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Tassa evaṃ jānato evaṃ passato kāmāsavāpi cittaṃ vimuccati, bhavāsavāpi cittaṃ vimuccati, avijjāsavāpi cittaṃ vimuccati. Vimuttasmiṃ vimuttamiti ñāṇaṃ hoti. ‘Khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti pajānāti. Yasmiṃ kho, sandaka, satthari sāvako evarūpaṃ uḷāravisesaṃ adhigacchati tattha viññū puriso sasakkaṃ brahmacariyaṃ vaseyya, vasanto ca ārādheyya ñāyaṃ dhammaṃ kusala”nti.

When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of defilements, malleable, workable, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs and inclines his mind to the knowledge of the destruction of the taints. He understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering.’ He understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering.’ He understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering.’ He understands as it really is: ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.’ He understands as it really is: ‘These are the taints.’ He understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of the taints.’ He understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of the taints.’ He understands as it really is: ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of the taints.’ Knowing and seeing thus, his mind is liberated from the taint of sensual desire, from the taint of existence, and from the taint of ignorance. When it is liberated, the knowledge arises: ‘It is liberated.’ He understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.’ Sandaka, in the case of a teacher under whom a disciple attains such a sublime distinction, there a wise person should certainly live the holy life, and, while living it, would accomplish the right, wholesome Dhamma.

234. “Yo pana so, bho ānanda, bhikkhu arahaṃ khīṇāsavo vusitavā katakaraṇīyo ohitabhāro anuppattasadattho parikkhīṇabhavasaṃyojano sammadaññā vimutto paribhuñjeyya [P 1.0523] so kāme”ti? “Yo so, sandaka, bhikkhu arahaṃ khīṇāsavo vusitavā katakaraṇīyo ohitabhāro anuppattasadattho parikkhīṇabhavasaṃyojano sammadaññā vimutto abhabbo so pañcaṭṭhānāni ajjhācarituṃ. Abhabbo khīṇāsavo bhikkhu sañcicca pāṇaṃ jīvitā voropetuṃ, abhabbo khīṇāsavo bhikkhu adinnaṃ theyyasaṅkhātaṃ ādātuṃ, abhabbo khīṇāsavo bhikkhu methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevetuṃ, abhabbo khīṇāsavo bhikkhu sampajānamusā bhāsituṃ, abhabbo khīṇāsavo bhikkhu sannidhikārakaṃ kāme paribhuñjituṃ, seyyathāpi pubbe agāriyabhūto. Yo so, sandaka, bhikkhu arahaṃ khīṇāsavo vusitavā katakaraṇīyo ohitabhāro anuppattasadattho parikkhīṇabhavasaṃyojano sammadaññā vimutto abhabbo so [T 2.0308] imāni pañcaṭṭhānāni ajjhācaritu”nti.

234. “But, Venerable Ānanda, would that bhikkhu who is an Arahant, whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained his own welfare, whose fetters of existence are completely destroyed, and is liberated by perfect knowledge—would such a one enjoy sensual pleasures?” “Sandaka, that bhikkhu who is an Arahant, whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained his own welfare, whose fetters of existence are completely destroyed, and is liberated by perfect knowledge—such a one is incapable of transgressing five points. A bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is incapable of intentionally depriving a living being of life. A bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is incapable of taking what is not given, which is reckoned as theft. A bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is incapable of engaging in sexual intercourse. A bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is incapable of knowingly speaking falsehood. A bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is incapable of enjoying sensual pleasures by storing them up, as he did formerly as a householder. Sandaka, that bhikkhu who is an Arahant, whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained his own welfare, whose fetters of existence are completely destroyed, and is liberated by perfect knowledge—such a one is incapable of transgressing these five points.”

235. “Yo [M 2.0193] pana so, bho ānanda, bhikkhu arahaṃ khīṇāsavo vusitavā katakaraṇīyo ohitabhāro anuppattasadattho parikkhīṇabhavasaṃyojano sammadaññā vimutto tassa carato ceva tiṭṭhato ca suttassa ca jāgarassa ca satataṃ samitaṃ ñāṇadassanaṃ paccupaṭṭhitaṃ – ‘khīṇā me āsavā’”ti? “Tena hi, sandaka, upamaṃ te karissāmi; upamāyapidhekacce viññū purisā bhāsitassa atthaṃ ājānanti. Seyyathāpi, sandaka, purisassa hatthapādā chinnā; tassa carato ceva tiṭṭhato ca suttassa ca jāgarassa ca satataṃ samitaṃ (jānāti – ‘chinnā me hatthapādā’ti, udāhu paccavekkhamāno jānāti – ‘chinnā me hatthapādā’”ti? “Na kho, bho ānanda, so puriso satataṃ samitaṃ jānāti – ‘chinnā me hatthapādā’ ti.) (chinnāva hatthapādā,) (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) Api ca kho pana naṃ paccavekkhamāno jānāti – ‘chinnā me hatthapādā’”ti. “Evameva kho, sandaka, yo so [V 2.0203] bhikkhu arahaṃ khīṇāsavo vusitavā katakaraṇīyo ohitabhāro anuppattasadattho parikkhīṇabhavasaṃyojano sammadaññā vimutto tassa carato ceva tiṭṭhato ca suttassa ca jāgarassa ca satataṃ samitaṃ (ñāṇadassanaṃ na paccupaṭṭhitaṃ – ‘khīṇā me āsavā’ti;) (khīṇāva āsavā,) (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) api ca kho pana naṃ paccavekkhamāno jānāti – ‘khīṇā me āsavā’”ti.

235. “But, Venerable Ānanda, for that bhikkhu who is an Arahant, whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained his own welfare, whose fetters of existence are completely destroyed, and is liberated by perfect knowledge—is the knowledge and vision ‘My taints are destroyed’ constantly and continuously present to him while he is walking, standing, sleeping, or awake?” “Well then, Sandaka, I shall make a comparison for you; for by means of a comparison, some wise persons here understand the meaning of what is said. Suppose, Sandaka, a man’s hands and feet were cut off. For that man, while walking, standing, sleeping, or awake, does he constantly and continuously know, ‘My hands and feet are cut off,’ or does he know it when he reflects upon it?” “No, Venerable Ānanda, that man does not constantly and continuously know, ‘My hands and feet are cut off.’ Rather, he knows it when he reflects upon it.” “In the same way, Sandaka, for that bhikkhu who is an Arahant, whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained his own welfare, whose fetters of existence are completely destroyed, and is liberated by perfect knowledge—the knowledge and vision ‘My taints are destroyed’ is not constantly and continuously present to him while he is walking, standing, sleeping, or awake; rather, he knows it when he reflects upon it.”

236. “Kīvabahukā pana, bho ānanda, imasmiṃ dhammavinaye niyyātāro”ti? “Na kho, sandaka, ekaṃyeva sataṃ na dve satāni na tīṇi satāni na cattāri satāni na pañca satāni, atha kho bhiyyova ye imasmiṃ dhammavinaye niyyātāro”ti. “Acchariyaṃ, bho ānanda, abbhutaṃ, bho ānanda! Na ca nāma sadhammokkaṃsanā bhavissati, na [T 2.0309] paradhammavambhanā, āyatane ca dhammadesanā tāva bahukā [P 1.0524] ca niyyātāro paññāyissanti. Ime panājīvakā puttamatāya puttā attānañceva ukkaṃsenti, pare ca vambhenti tayo ceva niyyātāro paññapenti, seyyathidaṃ – nandaṃ vacchaṃ, kisaṃ saṃkiccaṃ, makkhaliṃ gosāla”nti. Atha kho sandako paribbājako sakaṃ parisaṃ āmantesi – “carantu bhonto samaṇe gotame brahmacariyavāso. Na dāni sukaraṃ amhehi lābhasakkārasiloke pariccajitu”nti. Iti hidaṃ sandako paribbājako sakaṃ parisaṃ uyyojesi bhagavati brahmacariyeti.

236. “But, Venerable Ānanda, how many are there who find deliverance in this Dhamma and Discipline?” “Not just one hundred, Sandaka, nor two hundred, nor three hundred, nor four hundred, nor five hundred, but indeed many more are those who find deliverance in this Dhamma and Discipline.” “It is wonderful, Venerable Ānanda, it is marvelous! There is no praising of one's own teaching and no disparaging of others', and the teaching of the Dhamma is given at length, whereby so many who find deliverance are made known. But these Ājīvakas, like the sons of a mother whose son has died, praise themselves and disparage others, and they make known only three who find deliverance, namely: Nanda Vaccha, Kisa Saṅkicca, and Makkhali Gosāla.” Then the wanderer Sandaka addressed his own assembly: “Go, venerable sirs, live the holy life under the ascetic Gotama. It is not easy for us now to abandon gain, honor, and renown.” Thus the wanderer Sandaka dispatched his own assembly to the holy life under the Blessed One.

Sandakasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ chaṭṭhaṃ.

The Sandaka Sutta, the sixth, is concluded.

7. Mahāsakuludāyisuttaṃ

7. The Greater Sakuludāyī Sutta

237. Evaṃ [T 2.0310][M 2.0194][V 2.0204][P 2.0001] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā rājagahe viharati veḷuvane kalandakanivāpe. Tena kho pana samayena sambahulā abhiññātā abhiññātā paribbājakā moranivāpe paribbājakārāme paṭivasanti, seyyathidaṃ – annabhāro varadharo sakuludāyī ca paribbājako aññe ca abhiññātā abhiññātā paribbājakā. Atha kho bhagavā pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya rājagahaṃ piṇḍāya pāvisi. Atha kho bhagavato etadahosi – “atippago kho tāva rājagahe piṇḍāya carituṃ. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ yena moranivāpo paribbājakārāmo yena sakuludāyī paribbājako tenupasaṅkameyya”nti. Atha kho bhagavā yena moranivāpo paribbājakārāmo tenupasaṅkami. Tena kho pana samayena sakuludāyī paribbājako mahatiyā paribbājakaparisāya saddhiṃ nisinno hoti unnādiniyā uccāsaddamahāsaddāya anekavihitaṃ tiracchānakathaṃ kathentiyā, seyyathidaṃ – rājakathaṃ corakathaṃ mahāmattakathaṃ senākathaṃ bhayakathaṃ yuddhakathaṃ annakathaṃ pānakathaṃ vatthakathaṃ sayanakathaṃ mālākathaṃ gandhakathaṃ ñātikathaṃ yānakathaṃ gāmakathaṃ nigamakathaṃ nagarakathaṃ janapadakathaṃ itthikathaṃ sūrakathaṃ visikhākathaṃ kumbhaṭṭhānakathaṃ pubbapetakathaṃ [P 2.0002] nānattakathaṃ lokakkhāyikaṃ samuddakkhāyikaṃ itibhavābhavakathaṃ [T 2.0311] iti vā. Addasā kho sakuludāyī paribbājako bhagavantaṃ dūratova āgacchantaṃ. Disvāna sakaṃ parisaṃ saṇṭhāpeti – “appasaddā bhonto hontu; mā bhonto saddamakattha. Ayaṃ samaṇo gotamo āgacchati; appasaddakāmo kho pana so āyasmā appasaddassa vaṇṇavādī. Appeva nāma appasaddaṃ parisaṃ viditvā upasaṅkamitabbaṃ maññeyyā”ti. Atha kho te paribbājakā tuṇhī ahesuṃ. Atha kho bhagavā yena sakuludāyī paribbājako tenupasaṅkami. Atha kho sakuludāyī paribbājako bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “etu kho, bhante, bhagavā. Svāgataṃ, bhante, bhagavato. Cirassaṃ kho, bhante, bhagavā imaṃ pariyāyamakāsi yadidaṃ idhāgamanāya. Nisīdatu, bhante, bhagavā; idamāsanaṃ paññatta”nti. Nisīdi bhagavā paññatte āsane. Sakuludāyīpi kho paribbājako aññataraṃ nīcaṃ āsanaṃ gahetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinnaṃ kho sakuludāyiṃ paribbājakaṃ bhagavā etadavoca –

237. Thus have I heard: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha, in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Sanctuary. Now at that time, many well-known wanderers were staying at the Peacocks’ Feeding Ground, the wanderers’ park—namely, Annabhāra, Varadhara, the wanderer Sakuludāyī, and other well-known wanderers. Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning, took his bowl and robe and entered Rājagaha for alms. Then it occurred to the Blessed One: "It is still too early to walk for alms in Rājagaha. Why don’t I go to the Peacocks’ Feeding Ground, the wanderers’ park, where Sakuludāyī the wanderer is staying?" So the Blessed One went to the Peacocks’ Feeding Ground, the wanderers’ park. Now at that time, Sakuludāyī the wanderer was sitting with a large assembly of wanderers, making a loud, boisterous noise, engaged in various kinds of worldly talk—such as talk about kings, robbers, ministers, armies, dangers, battles, food, drink, clothes, beds, garlands, perfumes, relatives, vehicles, villages, towns, cities, countries, women, heroes, streets, watering places, the departed, miscellaneous tales, speculations about the world and the ocean, and talk about being or not being. Sakuludāyī the wanderer saw the Blessed One approaching from afar. Upon seeing him, he quieted his own assembly, saying: "Be quiet, sirs, do not make a noise. This ascetic Gotama is coming; he appreciates quiet and speaks in praise of quiet. Perhaps, knowing that our assembly is quiet, he may think to approach us." Then those wanderers fell silent. The Blessed One approached Sakuludāyī the wanderer. Sakuludāyī then said to the Blessed One: "Come, Venerable Sir, Blessed One! Welcome, Venerable Blessed One! It has been a long time since the Blessed One found an opportunity to come here. Please, Venerable Sir, sit down. This seat has been prepared." The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat. Sakuludāyī the wanderer also took a low seat and sat to one side. When Sakuludāyī the wanderer was seated to one side, the Blessed One said to him:

238. “Kāyanuttha[M 2.0195][V 2.0205], udāyi, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā, kā ca pana vo antarākathā vippakatā”ti? “Tiṭṭhatesā, bhante, kathā yāya mayaṃ etarahi kathāya sannisinnā. Nesā, bhante, kathā bhagavato dullabhā bhavissati pacchāpi savanāya. Purimāni, bhante, divasāni purimatarāni nānātitthiyānaṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ kutūhalasālāyaṃ sannisinnānaṃ sannipatitānaṃ ayamantarākathā [T 2.0312] udapādi – ‘lābhā vata, bho, aṅgamagadhānaṃ, suladdhalābhā vata, bho, aṅgamagadhānaṃ! Tatrime yatthime (sī.) samaṇabrāhmaṇā saṅghino gaṇino gaṇācariyā ñātā yasassino titthakarā sādhusammatā bahujanassa rājagahaṃ vassāvāsaṃ osaṭā. Ayampi kho pūraṇo kassapo saṅghī ceva gaṇī ca gaṇācariyo ca ñāto yasassī titthakaro sādhusammato bahujanassa; sopi rājagahaṃ vassāvāsaṃ osaṭo. Ayampi kho makkhali gosālo…pe… ajito kesakambalo… pakudho kaccāyano… sañjayo belaṭṭhaputto… nigaṇṭho nāṭaputto saṅghī ceva gaṇī ca gaṇācariyo ca ñāto [P 2.0003] yasassī titthakaro sādhusammato bahujanassa; sopi rājagahaṃ vassāvāsaṃ osaṭo. Ayampi kho samaṇo gotamo saṅghī ceva gaṇī ca gaṇācariyo ca ñāto yasassī titthakaro sādhusammato bahujanassa; sopi rājagahaṃ vassāvāsaṃ osaṭo. Ko nu kho imesaṃ bhavataṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ saṅghīnaṃ gaṇīnaṃ gaṇācariyānaṃ ñātānaṃ yasassīnaṃ titthakarānaṃ sādhusammatānaṃ bahujanassa sāvakānaṃ sakkato garukato mānito pūjito, kañca pana sāvakā sakkatvā garuṃ katvā garukatvā (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) upanissāya viharantī’”ti?

238. "For what talk, Udāyī, were you sitting together just now? And what was this unfinished conversation of yours?" "Venerable sir, let that conversation for which we were sitting together just now be. That conversation will not be difficult for the Blessed One to hear later. Venerable sir, some days ago, quite some time ago, when ascetics and brahmins of various sects were sitting together, gathered together in the debating hall, this discussion arose among them: ‘Truly, good sirs, it is a gain for the people of Aṅga and Magadha, a great gain indeed for the people of Aṅga and Magadha, that these ascetics and brahmins—leaders of communities, leaders of groups, teachers of groups, well-known, famous, founders of schools, esteemed as good by many people—have come to spend the rains in Rājagaha. This Pūraṇa Kassapa is a leader of a community, a leader of a group, a teacher of a group, well-known, famous, a founder of a school, esteemed as good by many people; he too has come to spend the rains in Rājagaha. This Makkhali Gosāla… Ajita Kesakambala… Pakudha Kaccāyana… Sañjaya Belaṭṭhaputta… Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta is a leader of a community, a leader of a group, a teacher of a group, well-known, famous, a founder of a school, esteemed as good by many people; he too has come to spend the rains in Rājagaha. This ascetic Gotama is a leader of a community, a leader of a group, a teacher of a group, well-known, famous, a founder of a school, esteemed as good by many people; he too has come to spend the rains in Rājagaha. Now, which of these venerable ascetics and brahmins—leaders of communities, leaders of groups, teachers of groups, well-known, famous, founders of schools, esteemed as good by many people—is honored, respected, revered, and venerated by his disciples, and whom do his disciples live in dependence on, honoring and respecting him?’"

239. “Tatrekacce evamāhaṃsu – ‘ayaṃ kho pūraṇo kassapo saṅghī ceva gaṇī ca gaṇācariyo ca ñāto yasassī titthakaro sādhusammato bahujanassa; so ca kho sāvakānaṃ na sakkato na garukato na mānito na [T 2.0313] pūjito, na ca pana pūraṇaṃ kassapaṃ sāvakā sakkatvā garuṃ katvā upanissāya viharanti. Bhūtapubbaṃ pūraṇo kassapo anekasatāya parisāya dhammaṃ deseti. Tatraññataro pūraṇassa kassapassa sāvako saddamakāsi – “mā bhonto pūraṇaṃ kassapaṃ etamatthaṃ pucchittha; neso etaṃ jānāti; mayametaṃ jānāma, amhe etamatthaṃ pucchatha; mayametaṃ bhavantānaṃ byākarissāmā”ti. Bhūtapubbaṃ pūraṇo kassapo [M 2.0196] bāhā paggayha kandanto na labhati – “appasaddā bhonto hontu, mā bhonto saddamakattha. Nete, bhavante, pucchanti, amhe ete pucchanti; mayametesaṃ byākarissāmā”ti. Bahū kho pana pūraṇassa kassapassa sāvakā vādaṃ āropetvā apakkantā – “na tvaṃ imaṃ dhammavinayaṃ ājānāsi, ahaṃ imaṃ dhammavinayaṃ ājānāmi[V 2.0206], kiṃ tvaṃ imaṃ dhammavinayaṃ ājānissasi? Micchāpaṭipanno tvamasi, ahamasmi sammāpaṭipanno, sahitaṃ me, asahitaṃ te, purevacanīyaṃ pacchā avaca, pacchāvacanīyaṃ pure avaca, adhiciṇṇaṃ te viparāvattaṃ, āropito te vādo, niggahitosi, cara vādappamokkhāya, nibbeṭhehi vā sace pahosī”ti. Iti pūraṇo kassapo sāvakānaṃ na sakkato na garukato na mānito na pūjito, na ca pana pūraṇaṃ kassapaṃ sāvakā sakkatvā garuṃ katvā upanissāya viharanti. Akkuṭṭho ca pana pūraṇo kassapo dhammakkosenā’”ti.

239. Therein, some said thus: 'Indeed, this Pūraṇa Kassapa has a company and a group, is a teacher of a group, is well-known, has a large retinue, is a founder of a doctrine, and is considered a good person by the great multitude. Yet he is not respected, revered, esteemed, or worshipped by his disciples; nor do the disciples live in dependence on Pūraṇa Kassapa, having respected and revered him. Formerly, Pūraṇa Kassapa was teaching the Dhamma to an assembly of many hundreds. Therein, a certain disciple of Pūraṇa Kassapa made a sound, saying: “Sirs, do not ask Pūraṇa Kassapa about this matter; he does not know it. We know it. Ask us about this matter; we will explain it to you.” Formerly, Pūraṇa Kassapa, with arms upraised and weeping, could not restrain them, saying: “Sirs, be quiet! Sirs, do not make a sound! They are not asking you; they are asking us. We will explain it to them.” Indeed, many of Pūraṇa Kassapa’s disciples, having leveled a charge against his doctrine, departed, saying: “You do not know this Dhamma and Discipline; I know this Dhamma and Discipline. How could you know this Dhamma and Discipline? You are one who has practiced wrongly; I am one who has practiced rightly. My statement is beneficial; yours is not beneficial. What should have been said before, you said after; what should have been said after, you said before. Your long-practiced teaching is overturned. A charge has been leveled against your doctrine; you are censured. Go, for the sake of freedom from this charge, or disentangle it if you are able!” Thus, Pūraṇa Kassapa is not respected, revered, esteemed, or worshipped by his disciples; nor do the disciples live in dependence on Pūraṇa Kassapa, having respected and revered him. And Pūraṇa Kassapa is reviled with a just reviling.'

“Ekacce [P 2.0004] evamāhaṃsu – ‘ayampi kho makkhali gosālo…pe… ajito kesakambalo… pakudho kaccāyano… sañjayo [T 2.0314] belaṭṭhaputto… nigaṇṭho nāṭaputto saṅghī ceva gaṇī ca gaṇācariyo ca ñāto yasassī titthakaro sādhusammato bahujanassa; so ca kho sāvakānaṃ na sakkato na garukato na mānito na pūjito, na ca pana nigaṇṭhaṃ nāṭaputtaṃ sāvakā sakkatvā garuṃ katvā upanissāya viharanti. Bhūtapubbaṃ nigaṇṭho nāṭaputto anekasatāya parisāya dhammaṃ deseti. Tatraññataro nigaṇṭhassa nāṭaputtassa sāvako saddamakāsi – mā bhonto nigaṇṭhaṃ nāṭaputtaṃ etamatthaṃ pucchittha; neso etaṃ jānāti; mayametaṃ jānāma, amhe etamatthaṃ pucchatha; mayametaṃ bhavantānaṃ byākarissāmāti. Bhūtapubbaṃ nigaṇṭho nāṭaputto bāhā paggayha kandanto na labhati – “appasaddā bhonto hontu, mā bhonto saddamakattha. Nete bhavante pucchanti, amhe ete pucchanti; mayametesaṃ byākarissāmā”ti. Bahū kho pana nigaṇṭhassa nāṭaputtassa sāvakā vādaṃ āropetvā apakkantā – “na tvaṃ imaṃ dhammavinayaṃ ājānāsi, ahaṃ imaṃ dhammavinayaṃ ājānāmi. Kiṃ tvaṃ imaṃ dhammavinayaṃ ājānissasi? Micchāpaṭipanno tvamasi. Ahamasmi sammāpaṭipanno. Sahitaṃ me asahitaṃ te, purevacanīyaṃ pacchā avaca, pacchāvacanīyaṃ pure avaca, adhiciṇṇaṃ te viparāvattaṃ, āropito te vādo, niggahitosi, cara vādappamokkhāya, nibbeṭhehi [M 2.0197] vā sace pahosī”ti. Iti nigaṇṭho nāṭaputto sāvakānaṃ na sakkato na garukato na mānito na pūjito, na ca pana nigaṇṭhaṃ nāṭaputtaṃ [T 2.0315] sāvakā sakkatvā garuṃ katvā upanissāya viharanti. Akkuṭṭho ca pana nigaṇṭho nāṭaputto dhammakkosenā’”ti.

Some said thus: 'This Makkhali Gosāla... Ajita Kesakambala... Pakudha Kaccāyana... Sañjaya Belaṭṭhaputta... and this Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta has a company and a group, is a teacher of a group, is well-known, has a large retinue, is a founder of a doctrine, and is considered a good person by the great multitude. Yet he is not respected, revered, esteemed, or worshipped by his disciples; nor do the disciples live in dependence on Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta, having respected and revered him. Formerly, Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta was teaching the Dhamma to an assembly of many hundreds. Therein, a certain disciple of Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta made a sound, saying: “Sirs, do not ask Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta about this matter; he does not know it. We know it. Ask us about this matter; we will explain it to you.” Formerly, Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta, with arms upraised and weeping, could not restrain them, saying: “Sirs, be quiet! Sirs, do not make a sound! They are not asking you; they are asking us. We will explain it to them.” Indeed, many of Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta’s disciples, having leveled a charge against his doctrine, departed, saying: “You do not know this Dhamma and Discipline; I know this Dhamma and Discipline. How could you know this Dhamma and Discipline? You are one who has practiced wrongly; I am one who has practiced rightly. My statement is beneficial; yours is not beneficial. What should have been said before, you said after; what should have been said after, you said before. Your long-practiced teaching is overturned. A charge has been leveled against your doctrine; you are censured. Go, for the sake of freedom from this charge, or disentangle it if you are able!” Thus, Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta is not respected, revered, esteemed, or worshipped by his disciples; nor do the disciples live in dependence on Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta, having respected and revered him. And Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta is reviled with a just reviling.'

240. “Ekacce evamāhaṃsu – ‘ayampi kho samaṇo gotamo saṅghī ceva gaṇī ca gaṇācariyo [V 2.0207] ca ñāto yasassī titthakaro sādhusammato bahujanassa; so ca kho sāvakānaṃ sakkato garukato mānito pūjito, samaṇañca pana gotamaṃ sāvakā sakkatvā garuṃ katvā upanissāya viharanti. Bhūtapubbaṃ samaṇo gotamo anekasatāya parisāya dhammaṃ desesi. Tatraññataro samaṇassa gotamassa sāvako ukkāsi. Tamenāññataro sabrahmacārī jaṇṇukena jaṇṇuke (sī.) ghaṭṭesi – “appasaddo āyasmā [P 2.0005] hotu, māyasmā saddamakāsi, satthā no bhagavā dhammaṃ desesī”ti. Yasmiṃ samaye samaṇo gotamo anekasatāya parisāya dhammaṃ deseti, neva tasmiṃ samaye samaṇassa gotamassa sāvakānaṃ khipitasaddo vā hoti ukkāsitasaddo vā. Tamenaṃ mahājanakāyo paccāsīsamānarūpo paccāsiṃ samānarūpo (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) paccupaṭṭhito hoti – “yaṃ no bhagavā dhammaṃ bhāsissati taṃ no sossāmā”ti. Seyyathāpi nāma puriso cātummahāpathe khuddamadhuṃ khuddaṃ madhuṃ (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) anelakaṃ pīḷeyya uppīḷeyya (sī.). Tamenaṃ mahājanakāyo paccāsīsamānarūpo paccupaṭṭhito assa. Evameva yasmiṃ samaye samaṇo gotamo anekasatāya parisāya dhammaṃ deseti, neva tasmiṃ samaye samaṇassa gotamassa sāvakānaṃ khipitasaddo vā hoti ukkāsitasaddo vā. Tamenaṃ mahājanakāyo paccāsīsamānarūpo paccupaṭṭhito hoti [T 2.0316] – “yaṃ no bhagavā dhammaṃ bhāsissati taṃ no sossāmā”ti. Yepi samaṇassa gotamassa sāvakā sabrahmacārīhi sampayojetvā sikkhaṃ paccakkhāya hīnāyāvattanti tepi satthu ceva vaṇṇavādino honti, dhammassa ca vaṇṇavādino honti, saṅghassa ca vaṇṇavādino honti, attagarahinoyeva honti anaññagarahino, “mayamevamhā alakkhikā mayaṃ appapuññā te mayaṃ evaṃ svākkhāte dhammavinaye pabbajitvā nāsakkhimhā yāvajīvaṃ [M 2.0198] paripuṇṇaṃ parisuddhaṃ brahmacariyaṃ caritu”nti. Te ārāmikabhūtā vā upāsakabhūtā vā pañcasikkhāpade samādāya vattanti. Iti samaṇo gotamo sāvakānaṃ sakkato garukato mānito pūjito, samaṇañca pana gotamaṃ sāvakā sakkatvā garuṃ katvā upanissāya viharantī’”ti.

240. Some have said thus: 'This recluse Gotama is possessed of a community, possessed of a group, and a teacher of a group; he is well-known, has a large following, is a founder of a school of thought, and is considered a good person by many people. And he is respected, revered, esteemed, and venerated by his disciples; and the disciples, having respected and revered the recluse Gotama, dwell in dependence upon him. Formerly, the recluse Gotama was teaching the Dhamma to an assembly of many hundreds. There, a certain disciple of the recluse Gotama coughed. Then a certain fellow in the holy life nudged him with his knee, saying: “Venerable one, be silent; let the venerable one not make a sound. Our Teacher, the Blessed One, is teaching the Dhamma.” At the time when the recluse Gotama teaches the Dhamma to an assembly of many hundreds, at that time there is neither the sound of his disciples sneezing nor the sound of coughing. The great multitude is present before him, expectant, thinking: “Whatever Dhamma the Blessed One will speak, that we shall hear.” Just as if a man at a crossroads of four great highways were to squeeze out flawless honey from small bees, and the great multitude would be present before him, expectant; even so, at the time when the recluse Gotama teaches the Dhamma to an assembly of many hundreds, at that time there is neither the sound of his disciples sneezing nor the sound of coughing. The great multitude is present before him, expectant, thinking: “Whatever Dhamma the Blessed One will speak, that we shall hear.” Even those disciples of the recluse Gotama who, having disputed with their fellows in the holy life, renounce the training and return to the lower life, they too become speakers of praise for the Teacher, speakers of praise for the Dhamma, and speakers of praise for the Saṅgha. They are self-reproaching, not reproaching others, saying: “We indeed were unfortunate, we were of little merit; we who, having gone forth in such a well-expounded Dhamma and Discipline, were unable to practice the complete and pure holy life for our entire lives.” Having become monastery attendants or lay followers, they live undertaking the five training rules. Thus, the recluse Gotama is respected, revered, esteemed, and venerated by his disciples; and the disciples, having respected and revered the recluse Gotama, dwell in dependence upon him.'

241. “Kati pana tvaṃ, udāyi, mayi dhamme samanupassasi, yehi mamaṃ mama (sabbattha) sāvakā sakkaronti garuṃ karonti garukaronti (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) mānenti pūjenti, sakkatvā garuṃ katvā upanissāya viharantī”ti? “Pañca kho ahaṃ, bhante, bhagavati dhamme samanupassāmi yehi bhagavantaṃ sāvakā sakkaronti garuṃ karonti mānenti pūjenti, sakkatvā garuṃ katvā upanissāya viharanti. Katame pañca? Bhagavā hi, bhante, appāhāro, appāhāratāya ca vaṇṇavādī. Yampi, bhante, bhagavā appāhāro, appāhāratāya ca vaṇṇavādī imaṃ kho ahaṃ, bhante, bhagavati [V 2.0208] paṭhamaṃ dhammaṃ samanupassāmi yena bhagavantaṃ sāvakā sakkaronti garuṃ karonti mānenti pūjenti, sakkatvā garuṃ katvā [T 2.0317] upanissāya viharanti.

241. “Udāyi, how many qualities do you see in me, on account of which my disciples respect, revere, esteem, and venerate me, and having respected and revered me, dwell in dependence upon me?” “Venerable sir, I see five qualities in the Blessed One, on account of which his disciples respect, revere, esteem, and venerate the Blessed One, and having respected and revered him, dwell in dependence upon him. What are the five? Venerable sir, the Blessed One eats little and is a speaker of praise for eating little. That the Blessed One, venerable sir, eats little and is a speaker of praise for eating little—this, venerable sir, is the first quality I see in the Blessed One, on account of which his disciples respect, revere, esteem, and venerate him, and having respected and revered him, dwell in dependence upon him.

“Puna [P 2.0006] caparaṃ, bhante, bhagavā santuṭṭho itarītarena cīvarena, itarītaracīvarasantuṭṭhiyā ca vaṇṇavādī. Yampi, bhante, bhagavā santuṭṭho itarītarena cīvarena, itarītaracīvarasantuṭṭhiyā ca vaṇṇavādī, imaṃ kho ahaṃ, bhante, bhagavati dutiyaṃ dhammaṃ samanupassāmi yena bhagavantaṃ sāvakā sakkaronti garuṃ karonti mānenti pūjenti, sakkatvā garuṃ katvā upanissāya viharanti.

“Furthermore, venerable sir, the Blessed One is content with whatever robe and is a speaker of praise for contentment with whatever robe. That the Blessed One, venerable sir, is content with whatever robe and is a speaker of praise for contentment with whatever robe—this, venerable sir, is the second quality I see in the Blessed One, on account of which his disciples respect, revere, esteem, and venerate him, and having respected and revered him, dwell in dependence upon him.

“Puna caparaṃ, bhante, bhagavā santuṭṭho itarītarena piṇḍapātena, itarītarapiṇḍapātasantuṭṭhiyā ca vaṇṇavādī. Yampi, bhante, bhagavā santuṭṭho itarītarena piṇḍapātena, itarītarapiṇḍapātasantuṭṭhiyā ca vaṇṇavādī, imaṃ kho ahaṃ, bhante, bhagavati tatiyaṃ dhammaṃ samanupassāmi yena bhagavantaṃ sāvakā sakkaronti garuṃ karonti mānenti pūjenti, sakkatvā garuṃ katvā upanissāya viharanti.

“Furthermore, venerable sir, the Blessed One is content with whatever almsfood and is a speaker of praise for contentment with whatever almsfood. That the Blessed One, venerable sir, is content with whatever almsfood and is a speaker of praise for contentment with whatever almsfood—this, venerable sir, is the third quality I see in the Blessed One, on account of which his disciples respect, revere, esteem, and venerate him, and having respected and revered him, dwell in dependence upon him.

“Puna caparaṃ, bhante, bhagavā santuṭṭho itarītarena senāsanena, itarītarasenāsanasantuṭṭhiyā ca vaṇṇavādī. Yampi, bhante, bhagavā santuṭṭho itarītarena senāsanena, itarītarasenāsanasantuṭṭhiyā ca vaṇṇavādī, imaṃ [M 2.0199] kho ahaṃ, bhante, bhagavati catutthaṃ dhammaṃ samanupassāmi yena bhagavantaṃ sāvakā sakkaronti garuṃ karonti mānenti pūjenti, sakkatvā garuṃ katvā upanissāya viharanti.

“Furthermore, venerable sir, the Blessed One is content with whatever lodging and is a speaker of praise for contentment with whatever lodging. That the Blessed One, venerable sir, is content with whatever lodging and is a speaker of praise for contentment with whatever lodging—this, venerable sir, is the fourth quality I see in the Blessed One, on account of which his disciples respect, revere, esteem, and venerate him, and having respected and revered him, dwell in dependence upon him.

“Puna caparaṃ, bhante, bhagavā pavivitto, pavivekassa ca vaṇṇavādī[T 2.0318]. Yampi, bhante, bhagavā pavivitto, pavivekassa ca vaṇṇavādī, imaṃ kho ahaṃ, bhante, bhagavati pañcamaṃ dhammaṃ samanupassāmi yena bhagavantaṃ sāvakā sakkaronti garuṃ karonti mānenti pūjenti, sakkatvā garuṃ katvā upanissāya viharanti.

“Furthermore, venerable sir, the Blessed One is secluded and is a speaker of praise for seclusion. That the Blessed One, venerable sir, is secluded and is a speaker of praise for seclusion—this, venerable sir, is the fifth quality I see in the Blessed One, on account of which his disciples respect, revere, esteem, and venerate him, and having respected and revered him, dwell in dependence upon him.

“Ime kho ahaṃ, bhante, bhagavati pañca dhamme samanupassāmi yehi bhagavantaṃ sāvakā sakkaronti [V 2.0209] garuṃ karonti mānenti pūjenti, sakkatvā garuṃ katvā upanissāya viharantī”ti.

“Venerable sir, I see in the Blessed One these five qualities because of which his disciples honor, respect, revere, and venerate the Blessed One, and having honored and respected him, live in dependence on him.”

242. “‘Appāhāro samaṇo gotamo, appāhāratāya ca vaṇṇavādī’ti, iti ce maṃ, udāyi, sāvakā sakkareyyuṃ garuṃ kareyyuṃ māneyyuṃ pūjeyyuṃ, sakkatvā garuṃ katvā upanissāya vihareyyuṃ, santi kho pana me, udāyi, sāvakā kosakāhārāpi aḍḍhakosakāhārāpi beluvāhārāpi aḍḍhabeluvāhārāpi. Ahaṃ [P 2.0007] kho pana, udāyi, appekadā iminā pattena samatittikampi bhuñjāmi bhiyyopi bhuñjāmi. ‘Appāhāro samaṇo gotamo, appāhāratāya ca vaṇṇavādī’ti, iti ce maṃ, udāyi, sāvakā sakkareyyuṃ garuṃ kareyyuṃ māneyyuṃ pūjeyyuṃ, sakkatvā garuṃ katvā upanissāya vihareyyuṃ, ye te, udāyi, mama sāvakā kosakāhārāpi aḍḍhakosakāhārāpi beluvāhārāpi aḍḍhabeluvāhārāpi na maṃ te iminā dhammena sakkareyyuṃ garuṃ kareyyuṃ māneyyuṃ pūjeyyuṃ, sakkatvā garuṃ katvā upanissāya vihareyyuṃ.

242. “Udāyi, if my disciples were to honor, respect, esteem, and venerate me, and having honored and respected me, were to live in dependence on me for this reason: ‘The recluse Gotama eats little and speaks in praise of eating little’—well, Udāyi, there are disciples of mine who eat a kosaka-measure of food, half a kosaka-measure, a bilva-fruit-measure, or half a bilva-fruit-measure. And I, Udāyi, sometimes eat from this bowl filling it level with the rim, and I eat even more. If my disciples were to honor, respect, esteem, and venerate me for this reason: ‘The recluse Gotama eats little and speaks in praise of eating little,’ and having honored and respected me, were to live in dependence on me—then, Udāyi, those disciples of mine who eat a kosaka-measure of food, half a kosaka-measure, a bilva-fruit-measure, or half a bilva-fruit-measure would not, on account of this quality, honor, respect, esteem, or venerate me, nor would they, having honored and respected me, live in dependence on me.

“‘Santuṭṭho samaṇo gotamo itarītarena cīvarena, itarītaracīvarasantuṭṭhiyā [T 2.0319] ca vaṇṇavādī’ti, iti ce maṃ, udāyi, sāvakā sakkareyyuṃ garuṃ kareyyuṃ māneyyuṃ pūjeyyuṃ, sakkatvā garuṃ katvā upanissāya vihareyyuṃ, santi kho pana me, udāyi, sāvakā paṃsukūlikā lūkhacīvaradharā te susānā vā saṅkārakūṭā vā pāpaṇikā vā nantakāni pāpaṇikāni vā nantakāni vā (sī.) uccinitvā ucchinditvā (ka.) saṅghāṭiṃ karitvā dhārenti. Ahaṃ kho panudāyi, appekadā gahapaticīvarāni dhāremi [M 2.0200] daḷhāni satthalūkhāni alābulomasāni. ‘Santuṭṭho samaṇo gotamo itarītarena cīvarena, itarītaracīvarasantuṭṭhiyā ca vaṇṇavādī’ti, iti ce maṃ, udāyi, sāvakā sakkareyyuṃ garuṃ kareyyuṃ māneyyuṃ pūjeyyuṃ, sakkatvā garuṃ katvā upanissāya vihareyyuṃ, ye te, udāyi, mama sāvakā paṃsukūlikā lūkhacīvaradharā te susānā vā saṅkārakūṭā vā pāpaṇikā vā nantakāni uccinitvā saṅghāṭiṃ karitvā dhārenti, na maṃ te iminā dhammena sakkareyyuṃ garuṃ kareyyuṃ māneyyuṃ pūjeyyuṃ, sakkatvā garuṃ katvā upanissāya vihareyyuṃ.

“‘The recluse Gotama is content with whatever kind of robe, and speaks in praise of contentment with whatever kind of robe.’ If, Udāyi, my disciples were to honor, respect, esteem, and venerate me for this, and, having honored and respected me, were to live in dependence on me—well, Udāyi, there are disciples of mine who are wearers of rag-robes, who wear coarse robes. They pick up rags from a charnel ground, a rubbish heap, or a shop, make them into an outer robe, and wear them. But I, Udāyi, sometimes wear robes given by householders—strong, smooth, and soft as gourd-down. ‘The recluse Gotama is content with whatever kind of robe, and speaks in praise of contentment with whatever kind of robe.’ If, Udāyi, my disciples were to honor, respect, esteem, and venerate me for this, and, having honored and respected me, were to live in dependence on me—then those disciples of mine who are wearers of rag-robes, who wear coarse robes, who pick up rags from a charnel ground, a rubbish heap, or a shop, make them into an outer robe, and wear them, would not, on account of this quality, honor, respect, esteem, or venerate me, nor would they, having honored and respected me, live in dependence on me.

“‘Santuṭṭho samaṇo gotamo itarītarena piṇḍapātena, itarītarapiṇḍapātasantuṭṭhiyā ca vaṇṇavādī’ti, iti ce maṃ, udāyi, sāvakā sakkareyyuṃ garuṃ kareyyuṃ māneyyuṃ pūjeyyuṃ, sakkatvā [V 2.0210] garuṃ katvā upanissāya vihareyyuṃ, santi kho pana me, udāyi, sāvakā piṇḍapātikā sapadānacārino uñchāsake vate ratā, te antaragharaṃ paviṭṭhā samānā āsanenapi nimantiyamānā na sādiyanti. Ahaṃ kho panudāyi, appekadā nimantanepi nimantanassāpi (ka.) bhuñjāmi sālīnaṃ odanaṃ vicitakāḷakaṃ [T 2.0320][P 2.0008] anekasūpaṃ anekabyañjanaṃ. ‘Santuṭṭho samaṇo gotamo itarītarena piṇḍapātena, itarītarapiṇḍapātasantuṭṭhiyā ca vaṇṇavādī’ti, iti ce maṃ, udāyi, sāvakā sakkareyyuṃ garuṃ kareyyuṃ māneyyuṃ pūjeyyuṃ, sakkatvā garuṃ katvā upanissāya vihareyyuṃ, ye te, udāyi, mama sāvakā piṇḍapātikā sapadānacārino uñchāsake vate ratā te antaragharaṃ paviṭṭhā samānā āsanenapi nimantiyamānā na sādiyanti, na maṃ te iminā dhammena sakkareyyuṃ garuṃ kareyyuṃ māneyyuṃ pūjeyyuṃ, sakkatvā garuṃ katvā upanissāya vihareyyuṃ.

“‘The recluse Gotama is content with whatever kind of almsfood, and speaks in praise of contentment with whatever kind of almsfood.’ If, Udāyi, my disciples were to honor, respect, esteem, and venerate me for this, and, having honored and respected me, were to live in dependence on me—well, Udāyi, there are disciples of mine who are alms-gatherers, who go on continuous alms-rounds, who delight in the practice of gleaning. When they have gone among the houses, they do not consent even when invited with a seat. But I, Udāyi, sometimes eat by invitation, partaking of fine rice with the black grains picked out, with many soups and many curries. ‘The recluse Gotama is content with whatever kind of almsfood, and speaks in praise of contentment with whatever kind of almsfood.’ If, Udāyi, my disciples were to honor, respect, esteem, and venerate me for this, and, having honored and respected me, were to live in dependence on me—then those disciples of mine who are alms-gatherers, who go on continuous alms-rounds, who delight in the practice of gleaning, who, when they have gone among the houses, do not consent even when invited with a seat, would not, on account of this quality, honor, respect, esteem, or venerate me, nor would they, having honored and respected me, live in dependence on me.

“‘Santuṭṭho samaṇo gotamo itarītarena senāsanena, itarītarasenāsanasantuṭṭhiyā ca vaṇṇavādī’ti, iti ce maṃ, udāyi, sāvakā sakkareyyuṃ garuṃ kareyyuṃ māneyyuṃ pūjeyyuṃ, sakkatvā garuṃ katvā upanissāya vihareyyuṃ, santi kho pana me, udāyi, sāvakā rukkhamūlikā abbhokāsikā, te aṭṭhamāse channaṃ na upenti. Ahaṃ kho panudāyi, appekadā kūṭāgāresupi viharāmi ullittāvalittesu nivātesu phusitaggaḷesu phussitaggaḷesu (sī. pī.) pihitavātapānesu. ‘Santuṭṭho samaṇo gotamo itarītarena [M 2.0201] senāsanena, itarītarasenāsanasantuṭṭhiyā ca vaṇṇavādī’ti, iti ce maṃ, udāyi, sāvakā sakkareyyuṃ garuṃ kareyyuṃ māneyyuṃ pūjeyyuṃ, sakkatvā garuṃ katvā upanissāya vihareyyuṃ, ye te, udāyi, mama sāvakā rukkhamūlikā abbhokāsikā te aṭṭhamāse channaṃ na upenti, na maṃ te iminā dhammena sakkareyyuṃ garuṃ kareyyuṃ māneyyuṃ pūjeyyuṃ, sakkatvā [T 2.0321] garuṃ katvā upanissāya vihareyyuṃ.

“‘The recluse Gotama is content with whatever kind of lodging, and speaks in praise of contentment with whatever kind of lodging.’ If, Udāyi, my disciples were to honor, respect, esteem, and venerate me for this, and, having honored and respected me, were to live in dependence on me—well, Udāyi, there are disciples of mine who are tree-root-dwellers and open-air-dwellers; for eight months, they do not approach a roofed dwelling. But I, Udāyi, sometimes dwell in gabled monasteries that are plastered inside and out, sheltered from the wind, with fastened bolts and closed windows. ‘The recluse Gotama is content with whatever kind of lodging, and speaks in praise of contentment with whatever kind of lodging.’ If, Udāyi, my disciples were to honor, respect, esteem, and venerate me for this, and, having honored and respected me, were to live in dependence on me—then those disciples of mine who are tree-root-dwellers and open-air-dwellers, who for eight months do not approach a roofed dwelling, would not, on account of this quality, honor, respect, esteem, or venerate me, nor would they, having honored and respected me, live in dependence on me.

“‘Pavivitto samaṇo gotamo, pavivekassa ca vaṇṇavādī’ti, iti ce maṃ, udāyi, sāvakā sakkareyyuṃ garuṃ kareyyuṃ māneyyuṃ pūjeyyuṃ, sakkatvā garuṃ katvā upanissāya vihareyyuṃ, santi kho pana me, udāyi, sāvakā āraññikā pantasenāsanā araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni ajjhogāhetvā viharanti, te anvaddhamāsaṃ saṅghamajjhe osaranti pātimokkhuddesāya. Ahaṃ kho panudāyi, appekadā ākiṇṇo viharāmi bhikkhūhi bhikkhunīhi [V 2.0211] upāsakehi upāsikāhi raññā rājamahāmattehi titthiyehi titthiyasāvakehi. ‘Pavivitto samaṇo gotamo, pavivekassa ca vaṇṇavādī’ti, iti ce [P 2.0009] maṃ, udāyi, sāvakā sakkareyyuṃ garuṃ kareyyuṃ māneyyuṃ pūjeyyuṃ, sakkatvā garuṃ katvā upanissāya vihareyyuṃ, ye te, udāyi, mama sāvakā āraññakā pantasenāsanā araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni ajjhogāhetvā viharanti te anvaddhamāsaṃ saṅghamajjhe osaranti pātimokkhuddesāya, na maṃ te iminā dhammena sakkareyyuṃ garuṃ kareyyuṃ māneyyuṃ pūjeyyuṃ, sakkatvā garuṃ katvā upanissāya vihareyyuṃ.

“‘The recluse Gotama is secluded and speaks in praise of seclusion.’ If for this reason, Udāyi, my disciples were to respect me, esteem me, revere me, and venerate me, and, having respected and esteemed me, were to live in dependence on me—indeed, Udāyi, there are disciples of mine who are forest-dwellers, living in remote lodgings, who dwell having entered remote lodgings in the great forest groves. They descend into the midst of the Saṅgha every half-month for the recitation of the Pātimokkha.
