But I, Udāyi, sometimes dwell crowded with monks, nuns, male lay followers, female lay followers, kings, royal ministers, sectarians, and the disciples of sectarians. ‘The recluse Gotama is secluded and speaks in praise of seclusion.’ If for this reason, Udāyi, my disciples were to respect me, esteem me, revere me, and venerate me, and, having respected and esteemed me, were to live in dependence on me—those disciples of mine, Udāyi, who are forest-dwellers, living in remote lodgings, who dwell having entered remote lodgings in the great forest groves, and who descend into the midst of the Saṅgha every half-month for the recitation of the Pātimokkha—they would not, for this quality, respect me, esteem me, revere me, or venerate me; nor, having respected and esteemed me, would they live in dependence on me.”

“Iti kho, udāyi, na mamaṃ sāvakā imehi pañcahi dhammehi sakkaronti garuṃ karonti mānenti pūjenti, sakkatvā garuṃ katvā upanissāya viharanti.

“Thus indeed, Udāyi, it is not for these five qualities that my disciples respect me, esteem me, revere me, and venerate me; nor, having respected and esteemed me, do they live in dependence on me.

243. “Atthi kho, udāyi, aññe ca pañca dhammā yehi pañcahi dhammehi mamaṃ sāvakā sakkaronti garuṃ karonti mānenti pūjenti[T 2.0322], sakkatvā garuṃ katvā upanissāya viharanti. Katame pañca? Idhudāyi, mamaṃ sāvakā adhisīle sambhāventi – ‘sīlavā samaṇo gotamo paramena sīlakkhandhena samannāgato’ti. Yampudāyi yamudāyi (syā. ka.), mamaṃ sāvakā adhisīle sambhāventi – ‘sīlavā samaṇo gotamo paramena sīlakkhandhena samannāgato’ti, ayaṃ kho, udāyi[M 2.0202], paṭhamo dhammo yena mamaṃ sāvakā sakkaronti garuṃ karonti mānenti pūjenti, sakkatvā garuṃ katvā upanissāya viharanti.

243. “Indeed, Udāyi, there are five other qualities for which my disciples respect me, esteem me, revere me, and venerate me, and, having respected and esteemed me, live in dependence on me. What are the five? Here, Udāyi, my disciples praise me for superior virtue: ‘The recluse Gotama is virtuous, endowed with the supreme aggregate of virtue.’ That my disciples praise me for superior virtue, Udāyi—‘The recluse Gotama is virtuous, endowed with the supreme aggregate of virtue’—this, Udāyi, is the first quality for which my disciples respect me, esteem me, revere me, and venerate me, and, having respected and esteemed me, live in dependence on me.

244. “Puna caparaṃ, udāyi, mamaṃ sāvakā abhikkante ñāṇadassane sambhāventi – ‘jānaṃyevāha samaṇo gotamo – jānāmīti, passaṃyevāha samaṇo gotamo – passāmīti; abhiññāya samaṇo gotamo dhammaṃ deseti no anabhiññāya; sanidānaṃ samaṇo gotamo dhammaṃ deseti no anidānaṃ; sappāṭihāriyaṃ samaṇo gotamo dhammaṃ deseti no appāṭihāriya’nti. Yampudāyi, mamaṃ sāvakā abhikkante ñāṇadassane sambhāventi – ‘jānaṃyevāha samaṇo gotamo – jānāmīti, passaṃyevāha samaṇo gotamo – passāmīti; abhiññāya samaṇo gotamo dhammaṃ deseti no anabhiññāya; sanidānaṃ samaṇo gotamo dhammaṃ deseti no anidānaṃ; sappāṭihāriyaṃ samaṇo gotamo dhammaṃ deseti no appāṭihāriya’nti, ayaṃ kho, udāyi, dutiyo dhammo yena mamaṃ sāvakā [V 2.0212][P 2.0010] sakkaronti garuṃ karonti mānenti pūjenti, sakkatvā garuṃ katvā upanissāya viharanti.

244. “Furthermore, Udāyi, my disciples praise me for excellent knowledge and vision: ‘The recluse Gotama says, “I know,” only when he indeed knows; the recluse Gotama says, “I see,” only when he indeed sees. The recluse Gotama teaches the Dhamma having directly known it, not without having directly known it. The recluse Gotama teaches the Dhamma with its basis, not without its basis. The recluse Gotama teaches the Dhamma with demonstration, not without demonstration.’ That my disciples praise me for excellent knowledge and vision, Udāyi: ‘The recluse Gotama says, “I know,” only when he indeed knows… not without demonstration,’ this, Udāyi, is the second quality for which my disciples respect me, esteem me, revere me, and venerate me, and, having respected and esteemed me, live in dependence on me.

245. “Puna [T 2.0323] caparaṃ, udāyi, mamaṃ sāvakā adhipaññāya sambhāventi – ‘paññavā samaṇo gotamo paramena paññākkhandhena samannāgato; taṃ vata anāgataṃ vādapathaṃ na dakkhati, uppannaṃ vā parappavādaṃ na sahadhammena suniggahitaṃ niggaṇhissatīti – netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati’. Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, udāyi, api nu me sāvakā evaṃ jānantā evaṃ passantā antarantarā kathaṃ opāteyyu”nti?

245. “Furthermore, Udāyi, my disciples praise me for superior wisdom: ‘The recluse Gotama is wise, endowed with the supreme aggregate of wisdom. That he would not see a future line of argument, or that he would not, with reason, well refute a rival doctrine that has arisen—this situation does not exist.’ What do you think, Udāyi? Would my disciples, knowing thus and seeing thus, interrupt my speech from time to time?”

“No hetaṃ, bhante”.

“Certainly not, venerable sir.”

“Na kho panāhaṃ, udāyi, sāvakesu anusāsaniṃ paccāsīsāmi paccāsiṃsāmi (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.); aññadatthu mamayeva sāvakā anusāsaniṃ paccāsīsanti.

“Indeed, Udāyi, I do not expect instruction from my disciples; on the contrary, it is my disciples who expect instruction from me.

“Yampudāyi, mamaṃ sāvakā adhipaññāya sambhāventi – ‘paññavā samaṇo gotamo paramena paññākkhandhena samannāgato; taṃ vata anāgataṃ vādapathaṃ na dakkhati, uppannaṃ vā parappavādaṃ na sahadhammena niggahitaṃ niggaṇhissatīti – netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati’. Ayaṃ kho, udāyi, tatiyo dhammo yena mamaṃ sāvakā sakkaronti garuṃ karonti mānenti pūjenti, sakkatvā garuṃ katvā upanissāya viharanti.

“That my disciples praise me for superior wisdom, Udāyi: ‘The recluse Gotama is wise, endowed with the supreme aggregate of wisdom. That he would not see a future line of argument, or that he would not, with reason, refute a rival doctrine that has arisen—this situation does not exist.’ This, Udāyi, is the third quality for which my disciples respect me, esteem me, revere me, and venerate me, and, having respected and esteemed me, live in dependence on me.

246. “Puna [M 2.0203] caparaṃ, udāyi, mama sāvakā yena dukkhena dukkhotiṇṇā dukkhaparetā te maṃ upasaṅkamitvā dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ pucchanti, tesāhaṃ dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ puṭṭho byākaromi, tesāhaṃ cittaṃ ārādhemi pañhassa veyyākaraṇena; te maṃ dukkhasamudayaṃ… dukkhanirodhaṃ… dukkhanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ ariyasaccaṃ pucchanti, tesāhaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ ariyasaccaṃ puṭṭho byākaromi[T 2.0324], tesāhaṃ cittaṃ ārādhemi pañhassa veyyākaraṇena. Yampudāyi, mama sāvakā yena dukkhena dukkhotiṇṇā dukkhaparetā te maṃ upasaṅkamitvā dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ pucchanti, tesāhaṃ dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ puṭṭho byākaromi, tesāhaṃ cittaṃ ārādhemi pañhassa veyyākaraṇena. Te maṃ dukkhasamudayaṃ [V 2.0213]… dukkhanirodhaṃ… dukkhanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ ariyasaccaṃ pucchanti. Tesāhaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ ariyasaccaṃ puṭṭho byākaromi. Tesāhaṃ cittaṃ ārādhemi pañhassa veyyākaraṇena. Ayaṃ kho, udāyi, catuttho dhammo yena [P 2.0011] mamaṃ sāvakā sakkaronti garuṃ karonti mānenti pūjenti, sakkatvā garuṃ katvā upanissāya viharanti.

246. Furthermore, Udāyī, my disciples who are beset by suffering, overcome by suffering, approach me and ask about the Noble Truth of Suffering. When asked, I explain the Noble Truth of Suffering to them, and by means of explaining the question, I satisfy their minds. They ask me about the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering… the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering… the Noble Truth of the Path leading to the Cessation of Suffering. When asked, I explain the Noble Truth of the Path leading to the Cessation of Suffering to them, and by means of explaining the question, I satisfy their minds. Indeed, Udāyī, my disciples who are beset by suffering, overcome by suffering, approach me and ask about the Noble Truth of Suffering. When asked, I explain the Noble Truth of Suffering to them, and by means of explaining the question, I satisfy their minds. They ask me about the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering… the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering… the Noble Truth of the Path leading to the Cessation of Suffering. When asked, I explain the Noble Truth of the Path leading to the Cessation of Suffering to them, and by means of explaining the question, I satisfy their minds. This, Udāyī, is the fourth reason for which my disciples respect, revere, esteem, and venerate me; and having respected and revered me, they dwell in dependence on me.

247. “Puna caparaṃ, udāyi, akkhātā mayā sāvakānaṃ paṭipadā, yathāpaṭipannā me sāvakā cattāro satipaṭṭhāne bhāventi. Idhudāyi, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ; vedanāsu vedanānupassī viharati… citte cittānupassī viharati… dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Tatra ca pana me sāvakā bahū abhiññāvosānapāramippattā viharanti.

247. Furthermore, Udāyī, I have declared a practice to my disciples, by practicing in which manner my disciples develop the four foundations of mindfulness. Here, Udāyī, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having subdued covetousness and displeasure in the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings… he dwells contemplating the mind in the mind… he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having subdued covetousness and displeasure in the world. And in that practice, many of my disciples dwell, having reached the culmination and perfection of direct knowledge.

“Puna caparaṃ, udāyi, akkhātā mayā sāvakānaṃ paṭipadā, yathāpaṭipannā me sāvakā cattāro sammappadhāne bhāventi. Idhudāyi[T 2.0325], bhikkhu anuppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ anuppādāya chandaṃ janeti, vāyamati, vīriyaṃ ārabhati, cittaṃ paggaṇhāti, padahati; uppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānāya chandaṃ janeti, vāyamati, vīriyaṃ ārabhati, cittaṃ paggaṇhāti, padahati; anuppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ uppādāya chandaṃ janeti, vāyamati, vīriyaṃ ārabhati, cittaṃ paggaṇhāti, padahati; uppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ ṭhitiyā asammosāya bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā chandaṃ janeti, vāyamati, vīriyaṃ ārabhati, cittaṃ paggaṇhāti, padahati. Tatra ca pana me sāvakā bahū abhiññāvosānapāramippattā viharanti.

Furthermore, Udāyī, I have declared a practice to my disciples, by practicing in which manner my disciples develop the four right exertions. Here, Udāyī, for the non-arising of unarisen, evil, unwholesome states, a monk generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives. For the abandoning of arisen, evil, unwholesome states, he generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives. For the arising of unarisen wholesome states, he generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives. For the maintenance, non-confusion, increase, abundance, development, and fulfillment of arisen wholesome states, he generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives. And in that practice, many of my disciples dwell, having reached the culmination and perfection of direct knowledge.

“Puna [M 2.0204] caparaṃ, udāyi, akkhātā mayā sāvakānaṃ paṭipadā, yathāpaṭipannā me sāvakā cattāro iddhipāde bhāventi. Idhudāyi, bhikkhu chandasamādhipadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ iddhipādaṃ bhāveti, vīriyasamādhipadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ iddhipādaṃ bhāveti, cittasamādhipadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ iddhipādaṃ bhāveti, vīmaṃsāsamādhipadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ iddhipādaṃ bhāveti. Tatra ca pana me sāvakā bahū abhiññāvosānapāramippattā viharanti.

Furthermore, Udāyī, I have declared a practice to my disciples, by practicing in which manner my disciples develop the four bases of spiritual power. Here, Udāyī, a monk develops the basis of spiritual power that is endowed with concentration due to desire and the formations of striving; he develops the basis of spiritual power that is endowed with concentration due to energy and the formations of striving; he develops the basis of spiritual power that is endowed with concentration due to mind and the formations of striving; he develops the basis of spiritual power that is endowed with concentration due to investigation and the formations of striving. And in that practice, many of my disciples dwell, having reached the culmination and perfection of direct knowledge.

“Puna [V 2.0214] caparaṃ, udāyi, akkhātā mayā sāvakānaṃ paṭipadā, yathāpaṭipannā me sāvakā pañcindriyāni bhāventi. Idhudāyi[P 2.0012], bhikkhu saddhindriyaṃ bhāveti upasamagāmiṃ sambodhagāmiṃ; vīriyindriyaṃ bhāveti…pe… satindriyaṃ bhāveti… samādhindriyaṃ bhāveti… paññindriyaṃ bhāveti [T 2.0326] upasamagāmiṃ sambodhagāmiṃ. Tatra ca pana me sāvakā bahū abhiññāvosānapāramippattā viharanti.

Furthermore, Udāyī, I have declared a practice to my disciples, by practicing in which manner my disciples develop the five faculties. Here, Udāyī, a monk develops the faculty of faith, which leads to peace and to awakening; he develops the faculty of energy… the faculty of mindfulness… the faculty of concentration… he develops the faculty of wisdom, which leads to peace and to awakening. And in that practice, many of my disciples dwell, having reached the culmination and perfection of direct knowledge.

“Puna caparaṃ, udāyi, akkhātā mayā sāvakānaṃ paṭipadā, yathāpaṭipannā me sāvakā pañca balāni bhāventi. Idhudāyi, bhikkhu saddhābalaṃ bhāveti upasamagāmiṃ sambodhagāmiṃ; vīriyabalaṃ bhāveti…pe… satibalaṃ bhāveti… samādhibalaṃ bhāveti… paññābalaṃ bhāveti upasamagāmiṃ sambodhagāmiṃ. Tatra ca pana me sāvakā bahū abhiññāvosānapāramippattā viharanti.

Furthermore, Udāyī, I have declared a practice to my disciples, by practicing in which manner my disciples develop the five powers. Here, Udāyī, a monk develops the power of faith, which leads to peace and to awakening; he develops the power of energy… the power of mindfulness… the power of concentration… he develops the power of wisdom, which leads to peace and to awakening. And in that practice, many of my disciples dwell, having reached the culmination and perfection of direct knowledge.

“Puna caparaṃ, udāyi, akkhātā mayā sāvakānaṃ paṭipadā, yathāpaṭipannā me sāvakā sattabojjhaṅge bhāventi. Idhudāyi, bhikkhu satisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti vivekanissitaṃ virāganissitaṃ nirodhanissitaṃ vossaggapariṇāmiṃ; dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti…pe… vīriyasambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti… pītisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti… passaddhisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti… samādhisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti… upekkhāsambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti vivekanissitaṃ virāganissitaṃ nirodhanissitaṃ vossaggapariṇāmiṃ. Tatra ca pana me sāvakā bahū abhiññāvosānapāramippattā viharanti.

Furthermore, Udāyī, I have declared a practice to my disciples, by practicing in which manner my disciples develop the seven factors of enlightenment. Here, Udāyī, a monk develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and matures in relinquishment; he develops the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena… the enlightenment factor of energy… the enlightenment factor of rapture… the enlightenment factor of tranquility… the enlightenment factor of concentration… he develops the enlightenment factor of equanimity, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and matures in relinquishment. And in that practice, many of my disciples dwell, having reached the culmination and perfection of direct knowledge.

“Puna caparaṃ, udāyi, akkhātā mayā sāvakānaṃ paṭipadā, yathāpaṭipannā me sāvakā ariyaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ bhāventi. Idhudāyi, bhikkhu sammādiṭṭhiṃ bhāveti, sammāsaṅkappaṃ bhāveti, sammāvācaṃ bhāveti[T 2.0327], sammākammantaṃ bhāveti, sammāājīvaṃ bhāveti, sammāvāyāmaṃ bhāveti, sammāsatiṃ [M 2.0205] bhāveti, sammāsamādhiṃ bhāveti. Tatra ca pana me sāvakā bahū abhiññāvosānapāramippattā viharanti.

Furthermore, Udāyī, I have declared to my disciples the practice, practicing in accordance with which my disciples develop the noble eightfold path. Here, Udāyī, a bhikkhu develops right view, develops right intention, develops right speech, develops right action, develops right livelihood, develops right effort, develops right mindfulness, and develops right concentration. And in that, many of my disciples dwell, having reached the perfection that is the culmination of direct knowledge.

248. “Puna [V 2.0215] caparaṃ, udāyi, akkhātā mayā sāvakānaṃ paṭipadā, yathāpaṭipannā me sāvakā aṭṭha vimokkhe bhāventi. Rūpī rūpāni passati, ayaṃ paṭhamo vimokkho; ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī bahiddhā rūpāni passati, ayaṃ dutiyo vimokkho; subhanteva adhimutto hoti, ayaṃ tatiyo vimokkho; sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ [P 2.0013] samatikkamā paṭighasaññānaṃ atthaṅgamā nānattasaññānaṃ amanasikārā ‘ananto ākāso’ti ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati, ayaṃ catuttho vimokkho; sabbaso ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma ‘anantaṃ viññāṇa’nti viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati, ayaṃ pañcamo vimokkho; sabbaso viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma ‘natthi kiñcī’ti ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati, ayaṃ chaṭṭho vimokkho; sabbaso ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ samatikkamma nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati, ayaṃ sattamo vimokkho; sabbaso nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ samatikkamma saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ upasampajja viharati, ayaṃ aṭṭhamo vimokkho. Tatra ca pana me sāvakā bahū abhiññāvosānapāramippattā viharanti.

248. Furthermore, Udāyī, I have declared to my disciples the practice, practicing in accordance with which my disciples develop the eight liberations. One with form sees forms; this is the first liberation. Internally perceiving no form, one sees forms externally; this is the second liberation. One is intent only on 'it is beautiful'; this is the third liberation. By completely transcending perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, by not attending to perceptions of diversity, considering 'space is infinite,' one enters and dwells in the sphere of infinite space; this is the fourth liberation. By completely transcending the sphere of infinite space, considering 'consciousness is infinite,' one enters and dwells in the sphere of infinite consciousness; this is the fifth liberation. By completely transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, considering 'there is nothing,' one enters and dwells in the sphere of nothingness; this is the sixth liberation. By completely transcending the sphere of nothingness, one enters and dwells in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; this is the seventh liberation. By completely transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling; this is the eighth liberation. And in that, many of my disciples dwell, having reached the perfection that is the culmination of direct knowledge.

249. “Puna caparaṃ, udāyi, akkhātā mayā sāvakānaṃ paṭipadā, yathāpaṭipannā [T 2.0328] me sāvakā aṭṭha abhibhāyatanāni bhāventi. Ajjhattaṃ rūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati parittāni suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇāni. ‘Tāni abhibhuyya jānāmi, passāmī’ti evaṃ saññī hoti. Idaṃ paṭhamaṃ abhibhāyatanaṃ.

249. Furthermore, Udāyī, I have declared to my disciples the practice, practicing in accordance with which my disciples develop the eight bases of mastery. A certain person, perceiving form internally, sees forms externally that are limited, of good and bad color. He is one who perceives thus: 'Having mastered them, I know, I see.' This is the first base of mastery.

“Ajjhattaṃ rūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati appamāṇāni suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇāni. ‘Tāni abhibhuyya jānāmi, passāmī’ti evaṃ saññī hoti. Idaṃ dutiyaṃ abhibhāyatanaṃ.

A certain person, perceiving form internally, sees forms externally that are measureless, of good and bad color. He is one who perceives thus: 'Having mastered them, I know, I see.' This is the second base of mastery.

“Ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati parittāni suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇāni. ‘Tāni abhibhuyya jānāmi, passāmī’ti evaṃ saññī hoti. Idaṃ tatiyaṃ abhibhāyatanaṃ.

A certain person, perceiving no form internally, sees forms externally that are limited, of good and bad color. He is one who perceives thus: 'Having mastered them, I know, I see.' This is the third base of mastery.

“Ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati appamāṇāni suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇāni. ‘Tāni abhibhuyya jānāmi, passāmī’ti evaṃ saññī hoti. Idaṃ catutthaṃ abhibhāyatanaṃ.

A certain person, perceiving no form internally, sees forms externally that are measureless, of good and bad color. He is one who perceives thus: 'Having mastered them, I know, I see.' This is the fourth base of mastery.

“Ajjhattaṃ [M 2.0206][V 2.0216] arūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati nīlāni nīlavaṇṇāni nīlanidassanāni nīlanibhāsāni. Seyyathāpi nāma umāpupphaṃ nīlaṃ nīlavaṇṇaṃ nīlanidassanaṃ nīlanibhāsaṃ, seyyathāpi vā pana taṃ vatthaṃ bārāṇaseyyakaṃ ubhatobhāgavimaṭṭhaṃ nīlaṃ nīlavaṇṇaṃ nīlanidassanaṃ nīlanibhāsaṃ; evameva ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati nīlāni nīlavaṇṇāni nīlanidassanāni nīlanibhāsāni. ‘Tāni abhibhuyya jānāmi, passāmī’ti evaṃ saññī hoti. Idaṃ pañcamaṃ abhibhāyatanaṃ[P 2.0014].

A certain person, perceiving no form internally, sees forms externally that are blue, of blue color, seen as blue, with a blue radiance. Just as the flax flower is blue, of blue color, seen as blue, with a blue radiance; or just as that cloth from Bārāṇasī, smooth on both sides, is blue, of blue color, seen as blue, with a blue radiance; in the very same way, a certain person, perceiving no form internally, sees forms externally that are blue, of blue color, seen as blue, with a blue radiance. He is one who perceives thus: 'Having mastered them, I know, I see.' This is the fifth base of mastery.

“Ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati pītāni pītavaṇṇāni pītanidassanāni pītanibhāsāni. Seyyathāpi nāma kaṇikārapupphaṃ [T 2.0329] pītaṃ pītavaṇṇaṃ pītanidassanaṃ pītanibhāsaṃ, seyyathāpi vā pana taṃ vatthaṃ bārāṇaseyyakaṃ ubhatobhāgavimaṭṭhaṃ pītaṃ pītavaṇṇaṃ pītanidassanaṃ pītanibhāsaṃ; evameva ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati pītāni pītavaṇṇāni pītanidassanāni pītanibhāsāni. ‘Tāni abhibhuyya jānāmi, passāmī’ti evaṃ saññī hoti. Idaṃ chaṭṭhaṃ abhibhāyatanaṃ.

A certain person, perceiving no form internally, sees forms externally that are yellow, of yellow color, seen as yellow, with a yellow radiance. Just as the kaṇikāra flower is yellow, of yellow color, seen as yellow, with a yellow radiance; or just as that cloth from Bārāṇasī, smooth on both sides, is yellow, of yellow color, seen as yellow, with a yellow radiance; in the very same way, a certain person, perceiving no form internally, sees forms externally that are yellow, of yellow color, seen as yellow, with a yellow radiance. He is one who perceives thus: 'Having mastered them, I know, I see.' This is the sixth base of mastery.

“Ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati lohitakāni lohitakavaṇṇāni lohitakanidassanāni lohitakanibhāsāni. Seyyathāpi nāma bandhujīvakapupphaṃ lohitakaṃ lohitakavaṇṇaṃ lohitakanidassanaṃ lohitakanibhāsaṃ, seyyathāpi vā pana taṃ vatthaṃ bārāṇaseyyakaṃ ubhatobhāgavimaṭṭhaṃ lohitakaṃ lohitakavaṇṇaṃ lohitakanidassanaṃ lohitakanibhāsaṃ; evameva ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati lohitakāni lohitakavaṇṇāni lohitakanidassanāni lohitakanibhāsāni. ‘Tāni abhibhuyya jānāmi, passāmī’ti evaṃ saññī hoti. Idaṃ sattamaṃ abhibhāyatanaṃ.

A certain person, perceiving no form internally, sees forms externally that are red, of red color, seen as red, with a red radiance. Just as the bandhujīvaka flower is red, of red color, seen as red, with a red radiance; or just as that cloth from Bārāṇasī, smooth on both sides, is red, of red color, seen as red, with a red radiance; in the very same way, a certain person, perceiving no form internally, sees forms externally that are red, of red color, seen as red, with a red radiance. He is one who perceives thus: 'Having mastered them, I know, I see.' This is the seventh base of mastery.

“Ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati odātāni odātavaṇṇāni odātanidassanāni odātanibhāsāni. Seyyathāpi nāma osadhitārakā odātā odātavaṇṇā odātanidassanā odātanibhāsā, seyyathāpi vā pana taṃ vatthaṃ bārāṇaseyyakaṃ ubhatobhāgavimaṭṭhaṃ odātaṃ odātavaṇṇaṃ odātanidassanaṃ odātanibhāsaṃ; evameva ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati odātāni odātavaṇṇāni odātanidassanāni odātanibhāsāni[T 2.0330][V 2.0217]. ‘Tāni abhibhuyya jānāmi[M 2.0207], passāmī’ti evaṃsaññī hoti. Idaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ abhibhāyatanaṃ. Tatra ca pana me sāvakā bahū abhiññāvosānapāramippattā viharanti.

One who perceives no form internally sees forms externally, white, white in color, seen as white, and with a white radiance. Just as the morning star is white, white in color, seen as white, and with a white radiance, or like Benares cloth, smooth on both sides, white, white in color, seen as white, and with a white radiance—just so, one who perceives no form internally sees forms externally, white, white in color, seen as white, and with a white radiance. ‘Having mastered them, I shall know, I shall see’—thus he is percipient. This is the eighth base of mastery. And many of my disciples dwell having attained the ultimate perfection of direct knowledge.

250. “Puna caparaṃ, udāyi, akkhātā mayā sāvakānaṃ paṭipadā, yathāpaṭipannā me sāvakā dasa kasiṇāyatanāni bhāventi. Pathavīkasiṇameko sañjānāti uddhamadho tiriyaṃ advayaṃ appamāṇaṃ; āpokasiṇameko sañjānāti…pe… tejokasiṇameko sañjānāti… vāyokasiṇameko sañjānāti… nīlakasiṇameko sañjānāti… pītakasiṇameko sañjānāti… lohitakasiṇameko sañjānāti… odātakasiṇameko sañjānāti… ākāsakasiṇameko sañjānāti [P 2.0015]… viññāṇakasiṇameko sañjānāti uddhamadho tiriyaṃ advayaṃ appamāṇaṃ. Tatra ca pana me sāvakā bahū abhiññāvosānapāramippattā viharanti.

250. Furthermore, Udāyi, I have declared to my disciples the practice by which, having undertaken it, my disciples develop the ten kasiṇa-bases. One cognizes the earth kasiṇa above, below, across, as non-dual, as limitless. One cognizes the water kasiṇa... the fire kasiṇa... the air kasiṇa... the blue kasiṇa... the yellow kasiṇa... the red kasiṇa... the white kasiṇa... the space kasiṇa... One cognizes the consciousness kasiṇa above, below, across, as non-dual, as limitless. And there, many of my disciples dwell having attained the ultimate perfection of direct knowledge.

251. “Puna caparaṃ, udāyi, akkhātā mayā sāvakānaṃ paṭipadā, yathāpaṭipannā me sāvakā cattāri jhānāni bhāventi. Idhudāyi, bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. So imameva kāyaṃ vivekajena pītisukhena abhisandeti parisandeti paripūreti parippharati, nāssa kiñci sabbāvato kāyassa vivekajena pītisukhena apphuṭaṃ hoti. Seyyathāpi, udāyi, dakkho nhāpako nahāpako (sī. pī.) vā nhāpakantevāsī [T 2.0331] vā kaṃsathāle nhānīyacuṇṇāni nahānīyacuṇṇāni (sī. pī.) ākiritvā udakena paripphosakaṃ paripphosakaṃ sanneyya, sāyaṃ nhānīyapiṇḍi sāssa nahānīyapiṇḍī (sī. syā. kaṃ.) snehānugatā snehapareto santarabāhirā phuṭā snehena na ca pagghariṇī; evameva kho, udāyi, bhikkhu imameva kāyaṃ vivekajena pītisukhena abhisandeti parisandeti paripūreti parippharati, nāssa kiñci sabbāvato kāyassa vivekajena pītisukhena apphuṭaṃ hoti.

251. Furthermore, Udāyi, I have declared to my disciples the practice by which, having undertaken it, my disciples develop the four jhānas. Here, Udāyi, a bhikkhu, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by initial and sustained thought, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. He drenches, permeates, fills, and suffuses this very body with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion, so that there is no part of his entire body unpervaded by the rapture and happiness born of seclusion. Just as, Udāyi, a skilled bath attendant or his apprentice, having poured bath powder into a bronze vessel, would knead it while sprinkling it again and again with water, so that the ball of bath powder is followed by moisture, suffused by moisture, pervaded by moisture inside and out, yet does not drip—so too, Udāyi, a bhikkhu drenches, permeates, fills, and suffuses this very body with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion, so that there is no part of his entire body unpervaded by the rapture and happiness born of seclusion.

“Puna caparaṃ, udāyi, bhikkhu vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā ajjhattaṃ sampasādanaṃ…pe… dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. So imameva kāyaṃ samādhijena pītisukhena abhisandeti parisandeti paripūreti parippharati, nāssa kiñci sabbāvato kāyassa samādhijena pītisukhena apphuṭaṃ hoti[M 2.0208]. Seyyathāpi, udāyi, udakarahado gambhīro ubbhidodako ubbhitodako (syā. kaṃ. ka.). Tassa nevassa puratthimāya disāya udakassa āyamukhaṃ[V 2.0218], na pacchimāya disāya udakassa āyamukhaṃ, na uttarāya disāya udakassa āyamukhaṃ, na dakkhiṇāya disāya udakassa [P 2.0016] āyamukhaṃ, devo ca na kālena kālaṃ sammā dhāraṃ anuppaveccheyya; atha kho tamhāva udakarahadā sītā vāridhārā ubbhijjitvā tameva udakarahadaṃ sītena vārinā abhisandeyya parisandeyya paripūreyya paripphareyya, nāssa na nesaṃ (sī.) kiñci sabbāvato udakarahadassa sītena vārinā apphuṭaṃ assa. Evameva kho, udāyi, bhikkhu imameva kāyaṃ samādhijena pītisukhena abhisandeti parisandeti paripūreti parippharati, nāssa kiñci sabbāvato [T 2.0332] kāyassa samādhijena pītisukhena apphuṭaṃ hoti.

Furthermore, Udāyi, with the stilling of initial and sustained thought, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal tranquility and unification of mind, is without initial and sustained thought, and is with rapture and happiness born of concentration. He drenches, permeates, fills, and suffuses this very body with the rapture and happiness born of concentration, so that there is no part of his entire body unpervaded by the rapture and happiness born of concentration. Just as, Udāyi, there might be a deep lake with water welling up, with no inlet for water from the east, west, north, or south, and the sky would not from time to time send down proper showers, yet a cool spring of water, having welled up from that lake, would drench, permeate, fill, and suffuse that very lake with cool water, so that there would be no part of the entire lake unpervaded by the cool water—so too, Udāyi, a bhikkhu drenches, permeates, fills, and suffuses this very body with the rapture and happiness born of concentration, so that there is no part of his entire body unpervaded by the rapture and happiness born of concentration.

“Puna caparaṃ, udāyi, bhikkhu pītiyā ca virāgā…pe… tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. So imameva kāyaṃ nippītikena sukhena abhisandeti parisandeti paripūreti parippharati, nāssa kiñci sabbāvato kāyassa nippītikena sukhena apphuṭaṃ hoti. Seyyathāpi, udāyi, uppaliniyaṃ vā paduminiyaṃ vā puṇḍarīkiniyaṃ vā appekaccāni uppalāni vā padumāni vā puṇḍarīkāni vā udake jātāni udake saṃvaḍḍhāni udakānuggatāni anto nimuggaposīni, tāni yāva caggā yāva ca mūlā sītena vārinā abhisannāni parisannāni paripūrāni paripphuṭāni, nāssa kiñci sabbāvataṃ, uppalānaṃ vā padumānaṃ vā puṇḍarīkānaṃ vā sītena vārinā apphuṭaṃ assa; evameva kho, udāyi, bhikkhu imameva kāyaṃ nippītikena sukhena abhisandeti parisandeti paripūreti parippharati, nāssa kiñci sabbāvato kāyassa nippītikena sukhena apphuṭaṃ hoti.

Furthermore, Udāyi, with the fading away of rapture, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the third jhāna. He drenches, permeates, fills, and suffuses this very body with happiness devoid of rapture, so that there is no part of his entire body unpervaded by happiness devoid of rapture. Just as, Udāyi, in a pond of blue lotuses, or red lotuses, or white lotuses, some blue lotuses, red lotuses, or white lotuses are born in the water, grown in the water, remain in the water, and are nourished submerged within the water; they are, from their tips to their roots, drenched, permeated, filled, and suffused with cool water, so that there is no part of all those blue, red, or white lotuses unpervaded by cool water—so too, Udāyi, a bhikkhu drenches, permeates, fills, and suffuses this very body with happiness devoid of rapture, so that there is no part of his entire body unpervaded by happiness devoid of rapture.

“Puna caparaṃ, udāyi, bhikkhu sukhassa ca pahānā dukkhassa ca pahānā pubbeva somanassadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamā adukkhamasukhaṃ upekkhāsatipārisuddhiṃ catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. So imameva kāyaṃ parisuddhena cetasā pariyodātena pharitvā nisinno hoti, nāssa kiñci sabbāvato kāyassa parisuddhena cetasā pariyodātena apphuṭaṃ hoti. Seyyathāpi, udāyi, puriso odātena vatthena sasīsaṃ pārupitvā nisinno assa, nāssa kiñci sabbāvato kāyassa odātena vatthena [M 2.0209] apphuṭaṃ assa; evameva kho, udāyi, bhikkhu imameva kāyaṃ [V 2.0219] parisuddhena cetasā pariyodātena pharitvā nisinno hoti, nāssa kiñci sabbāvato kāyassa parisuddhena [P 2.0017] cetasā pariyodātena apphuṭaṃ hoti. Tatra ca pana me sāvakā bahū abhiññāvosānapāramippattā viharanti.

“Furthermore, Udāyi, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and has a purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. He sits having pervaded this very body with a pure, bright mind, so that there is no part of his entire body unpervaded by the pure, bright mind. Just as, Udāyi, a man might sit wrapped from head to foot in a white cloth, so that there is no part of his entire body untouched by the white cloth; even so, Udāyi, a bhikkhu sits, having pervaded this very body with a pure, bright mind, so that there is no part of his entire body unpervaded by the pure, bright mind. And in that respect, many of my disciples dwell having reached the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge.”

252. “Puna caparaṃ, udāyi, akkhātā mayā sāvakānaṃ paṭipadā, yathāpaṭipannā me sāvakā evaṃ pajānanti – ‘ayaṃ kho me kāyo rūpī cātumahābhūtiko mātāpettikasambhavo odanakummāsūpacayo aniccucchādanaparimaddanabhedanaviddhaṃsanadhammo; idañca pana me viññāṇaṃ ettha sitaṃ ettha paṭibaddhaṃ’. Seyyathāpi, udāyi, maṇi veḷuriyo subho jātimā aṭṭhaṃso suparikammakato accho vippasanno sabbākārasampanno; tatridaṃ suttaṃ āvutaṃ nīlaṃ vā pītaṃ vā lohitaṃ vā odātaṃ vā paṇḍusuttaṃ vā. Tamenaṃ cakkhumā puriso hatthe karitvā paccavekkheyya – ‘ayaṃ kho maṇi veḷuriyo subho jātimā aṭṭhaṃso suparikammakato accho vippasanno sabbākārasampanno; tatridaṃ suttaṃ āvutaṃ nīlaṃ vā pītaṃ vā lohitaṃ vā odātaṃ vā paṇḍusuttaṃ vā’ti. Evameva kho, udāyi, akkhātā mayā sāvakānaṃ paṭipadā, yathāpaṭipannā me sāvakā evaṃ pajānanti – ‘ayaṃ kho me kāyo rūpī cātumahābhūtiko mātāpettikasambhavo odanakummāsūpacayo aniccucchādanaparimaddanabhedanaviddhaṃsanadhammo; idañca [T 2.0334] pana me viññāṇaṃ ettha sitaṃ ettha paṭibaddha’nti. Tatra ca pana me sāvakā bahū abhiññāvosānapāramippattā viharanti.

252. Furthermore, Udāyi, I have declared a practice to my disciples, and by practicing accordingly, my disciples understand thus: ‘This body of mine is material, composed of the four great elements, born of mother and father, nourished by rice and gruel, subject to impermanence, rubbing, massaging, breaking up, and dissolution; and this consciousness of mine is dependent on it, bound to it.’ Just as, Udāyi, there might be a beryl gem—fine, of good stock, eight-faceted, well-fashioned, clear, exceptionally clear, and endowed with all excellent qualities; and through it is threaded a blue, or yellow, or red, or white, or pale-yellow thread. A man with good eyesight, taking it in his hand, would examine it thus: ‘This is a beryl gem—fine, of good stock, eight-faceted, well-fashioned, clear, exceptionally clear, and endowed with all excellent qualities; and through it is threaded this blue, or yellow, or red, or white, or pale-yellow thread.’ Even so, Udāyi, I have declared a practice to my disciples, and by practicing accordingly, my disciples understand thus: ‘This body of mine is material, composed of the four great elements, born of mother and father, nourished by rice and gruel, subject to impermanence, rubbing, massaging, breaking up, and dissolution; and this consciousness of mine is dependent on it, bound to it.’ And in that respect, many of my disciples dwell having reached the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge.

253. “Puna caparaṃ, udāyi, akkhātā mayā sāvakānaṃ paṭipadā, yathāpaṭipannā me sāvakā imamhā kāyā aññaṃ kāyaṃ abhinimminanti rūpiṃ manomayaṃ sabbaṅgapaccaṅgiṃ ahīnindriyaṃ. Seyyathāpi, udāyi, puriso muñjamhā īsikaṃ pabbāheyya; tassa evamassa – ‘ayaṃ muñjo, ayaṃ īsikā; añño muñjo, aññā īsikā; muñjamhātveva īsikā pabbāḷhā’ti. Seyyathā vā panudāyi, puriso asiṃ kosiyā pabbāheyya; tassa evamassa – ‘ayaṃ asi, ayaṃ kosi; añño asi aññā kosi; kosiyātveva asi pabbāḷho’ti. Seyyathā vā, panudāyi[P 2.0018], puriso ahiṃ karaṇḍā uddhareyya; tassa evamassa – ‘ayaṃ ahi, ayaṃ karaṇḍo; añño [M 2.0210] ahi, añño karaṇḍo; karaṇḍātveva ahi ubbhato’ti. Evameva kho, udāyi, akkhātā mayā sāvakānaṃ paṭipadā, yathāpaṭipannā me sāvakā imamhā kāyā aññaṃ kāyaṃ [V 2.0220] abhinimminanti rūpiṃ manomayaṃ sabbaṅgapaccaṅgiṃ ahīnindriyaṃ. Tatra ca pana me sāvakā bahū abhiññāvosānapāramippattā viharanti.

253. Furthermore, Udāyi, I have declared a practice to my disciples, and by practicing accordingly, my disciples create from this body another body—material, mind-made, complete with all its major and minor limbs, with no deficient faculties. Just as, Udāyi, a man might draw a reed from muñja grass; he would think: ‘This is the muñja grass, this is the reed; the muñja grass is one thing, the reed another; it is from the muñja grass that the reed has been drawn out.’ Or as, Udāyi, a man might draw a sword from its scabbard; he would think: ‘This is the sword, this is the scabbard; the sword is one thing, the scabbard another; it is from the scabbard that the sword has been drawn out.’ Or as, Udāyi, a man might draw a snake from a basket; he would think: ‘This is the snake, this is the basket; the snake is one thing, the basket another; it is from the basket that the snake has been drawn out.’ Even so, Udāyi, I have declared a practice to my disciples, and by practicing accordingly, my disciples create from this body another body—material, mind-made, complete with all its major and minor limbs, with no deficient faculties. And in that respect, many of my disciples dwell having reached the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge.

254. “Puna caparaṃ, udāyi, akkhātā mayā sāvakānaṃ paṭipadā, yathāpaṭipannā me sāvakā anekavihitaṃ iddhividhaṃ paccanubhonti – ekopi [T 2.0335] hutvā bahudhā honti, bahudhāpi hutvā eko hoti; āvibhāvaṃ, tirobhāvaṃ; tirokuṭṭaṃ tiropākāraṃ tiropabbataṃ asajjamānā gacchanti, seyyathāpi ākāse; pathaviyāpi ummujjanimujjaṃ karonti, seyyathāpi udake; udakepi abhijjamāne abhijjamānā (ka.) gacchanti, seyyathāpi pathaviyaṃ; ākāsepi pallaṅkena kamanti, seyyathāpi pakkhī sakuṇo; imepi candimasūriye evaṃmahiddhike evaṃmahānubhāve pāṇinā parimasanti parimajjanti, yāva brahmalokāpi kāyena vasaṃ vattenti. Seyyathāpi, udāyi, dakkho kumbhakāro vā kumbhakārantevāsī vā suparikammakatāya mattikāya yaṃ yadeva bhājanavikatiṃ ākaṅkheyya taṃ tadeva kareyya abhinipphādeyya; seyyathā vā panudāyi, dakkho dantakāro vā dantakārantevāsī vā suparikammakatasmiṃ dantasmiṃ yaṃ yadeva dantavikatiṃ ākaṅkheyya taṃ tadeva kareyya abhinipphādeyya; seyyathā vā panudāyi, dakkho suvaṇṇakāro vā suvaṇṇakārantevāsī vā suparikammakatasmiṃ suvaṇṇasmiṃ yaṃ yadeva suvaṇṇavikatiṃ ākaṅkheyya taṃ tadeva kareyya abhinipphādeyya. Evameva kho, udāyi, akkhātā mayā sāvakānaṃ paṭipadā, yathāpaṭipannā me sāvakā anekavihitaṃ iddhividhaṃ paccanubhonti – ekopi hutvā bahudhā honti, bahudhāpi hutvā eko hoti; āvibhāvaṃ, tirobhāvaṃ; tirokuṭṭaṃ tiropākāraṃ tiropabbataṃ asajjamānā gacchanti, seyyathāpi ākāse; pathaviyāpi ummujjanimujjaṃ karonti, seyyathāpi udake; udakepi abhijjamāne gacchanti[T 2.0336], seyyathāpi pathaviyaṃ; ākāsepi pallaṅkena kamanti, seyyathāpi pakkhī [P 2.0019] sakuṇo; imepi candimasūriye evaṃmahiddhike evaṃmahānubhāve pāṇinā parimasanti parimajjanti, yāva brahmalokāpi kāyena [M 2.0211] vasaṃ vattenti. Tatra ca pana me sāvakā bahū abhiññāvosānapāramippattā viharanti.

254. Furthermore, Udāyi, I have declared to my disciples a path of practice. Following that path, my disciples experience manifold kinds of psychic power: being one, they become many; being many, they become one; they appear and disappear; they pass through walls, ramparts, and mountains unhindered as if through space; they dive in and out of the earth as if it were water; they walk on water without sinking as if on land; they travel cross-legged through the sky like a winged bird; they touch and stroke with their hand even the sun and moon, so mighty and powerful; they wield bodily mastery as far as the Brahma-world. Just as, Udāyi, a skilled potter or his apprentice could shape any kind of vessel he desires from well-prepared clay; or as a skilled ivory-worker or his apprentice could craft any ivory piece he desires from well-prepared ivory; or as a skilled goldsmith or his apprentice could fashion any gold ornament he desires from well-prepared gold—so too, Udāyi, I have declared to my disciples a path of practice. Following that path, my disciples experience manifold kinds of psychic power: being one, they become many; being many, they become one; they appear and disappear; they pass through walls, ramparts, and mountains unhindered as if through space; they dive in and out of the earth as if it were water; they walk on water without sinking as if on land; they travel cross-legged through the sky like a winged bird; they touch and stroke with their hand even the sun and moon, so mighty and powerful; they wield bodily mastery as far as the Brahma-world. And many of my disciples dwell having reached the perfection of the culmination of direct knowledge.

255. “Puna caparaṃ, udāyi, akkhātā mayā sāvakānaṃ paṭipadā, yathāpaṭipannā me sāvakā dibbāya sotadhātuyā visuddhāya atikkantamānusikāya ubho sadde suṇanti – dibbe ca mānuse ca, ye dūre santike ca. Seyyathāpi, udāyi, balavā saṅkhadhamo appakasireneva cātuddisā viññāpeyya; evameva kho, udāyi, akkhātā mayā sāvakānaṃ paṭipadā, yathāpaṭipannā [V 2.0221] me sāvakā dibbāya sotadhātuyā visuddhāya atikkantamānusikāya ubho sadde suṇanti – dibbe ca mānuse ca, ye dūre santike ca. Tatra ca pana me sāvakā bahū abhiññāvosānapāramippattā viharanti.

255. Furthermore, Udāyi, I have declared to my disciples a path of practice, and following that path my disciples, with the divine ear element, purified and surpassing the human, hear both kinds of sounds, divine and human, those that are far and near. Just as, Udāyi, a strong conch-blower could effortlessly make himself heard in the four directions; so too, Udāyi, I have declared to my disciples a path of practice, and following that path my disciples, with the divine ear element, purified and surpassing the human, hear both kinds of sounds, divine and human, those that are far and near. And many of my disciples dwell having reached the perfection of the culmination of direct knowledge.

256. “Puna caparaṃ, udāyi, akkhātā mayā sāvakānaṃ paṭipadā, yathāpaṭipannā me sāvakā parasattānaṃ parapuggalānaṃ cetasā ceto paricca pajānanti – sarāgaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘sarāgaṃ citta’nti pajānanti, vītarāgaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘vītarāgaṃ citta’nti pajānanti; sadosaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘sadosaṃ citta’nti pajānanti, vītadosaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘vītadosaṃ citta’nti pajānanti; samohaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘samohaṃ citta’nti [T 2.0337] pajānanti, vītamohaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘vītamohaṃ citta’nti pajānanti; saṃkhittaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘saṅkhittaṃ citta’nti pajānanti, vikkhittaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘vikkhittaṃ citta’nti pajānanti; mahaggataṃ vā cittaṃ ‘mahaggataṃ citta’nti pajānanti, amahaggataṃ vā cittaṃ ‘amahaggataṃ citta’nti pajānanti; sauttaraṃ vā cittaṃ ‘sauttaraṃ citta’nti pajānanti, anuttaraṃ vā cittaṃ ‘anuttaraṃ citta’nti pajānanti; samāhitaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘samāhitaṃ citta’nti pajānanti, asamāhitaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘asamāhitaṃ citta’nti pajānanti; vimuttaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘vimuttaṃ citta’nti pajānanti, avimuttaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘avimuttaṃ citta’nti pajānanti. Seyyathāpi, udāyi, itthī vā puriso vā daharo yuvā maṇḍanakajātiko ādāse vā parisuddhe pariyodāte acche vā udakapatte sakaṃ mukhanimittaṃ paccavekkhamāno sakaṇikaṃ vā ‘sakaṇika’nti sakaṇikaṅgaṃ vā sakaṇikaṅganti (sī.) jāneyya[P 2.0020], akaṇikaṃ vā ‘akaṇika’nti akaṇikaṅgaṃ vā akaṇikaṅganti (sī.) jāneyya; evameva kho, udāyi, akkhātā mayā sāvakānaṃ paṭipadā, yathāpaṭipannā me sāvakā parasattānaṃ parapuggalānaṃ cetasā ceto paricca pajānanti – sarāgaṃ [M 2.0212] vā cittaṃ ‘sarāgaṃ citta’nti pajānanti, vītarāgaṃ vā cittaṃ…pe… sadosaṃ vā cittaṃ… vītadosaṃ vā cittaṃ… samohaṃ vā cittaṃ… vītamohaṃ vā cittaṃ… saṅkhittaṃ vā cittaṃ… vikkhittaṃ vā cittaṃ… mahaggataṃ vā [T 2.0338] cittaṃ… amahaggataṃ vā cittaṃ… sauttaraṃ vā cittaṃ… anuttaraṃ vā cittaṃ… samāhitaṃ vā cittaṃ… asamāhitaṃ vā cittaṃ… vimuttaṃ vā cittaṃ… avimuttaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘avimuttaṃ citta’nti pajānanti. Tatra ca pana me sāvakā bahū abhiññāvosānapāramippattā viharanti.

256. Furthermore, Udāyi, I have declared to my disciples the path by which, when my disciples have followed it, they know the mind of other beings, of other persons, having encompassed it with their own mind: they know a mind with lust as 'a mind with lust,' and a mind without lust as 'a mind without lust'; they know a mind with aversion as 'a mind with aversion,' and a mind without aversion as 'a mind without aversion'; they know a mind with delusion as 'a mind with delusion,' and a mind without delusion as 'a mind without delusion'; they know a contracted mind as 'a contracted mind,' and a distracted mind as 'a distracted mind'; they know an exalted mind as 'an exalted mind,' and an unexalted mind as 'an unexalted mind'; they know a surpassable mind as 'a surpassable mind,' and an unsurpassable mind as 'an unsurpassable mind'; they know a concentrated mind as 'a concentrated mind,' and an unconcentrated mind as 'an unconcentrated mind'; they know a liberated mind as 'a liberated mind,' and an unliberated mind as 'an unliberated mind.' Just as, Udāyi, a woman or a man—young, youthful, fond of adornment—would examine their own facial reflection in a clean, bright mirror or in a bowl of clear water, knowing 'it has a blemish' if there is a blemish, or 'it has no blemish' if there is none; in the same way, Udāyi, I have declared to my disciples the path by which, when my disciples have followed it, they know the mind of other beings, of other persons, having encompassed it with their own mind: they know a mind with lust as 'a mind with lust,' a mind without lust... and so on... a mind with aversion... a mind without aversion... a mind with delusion... a mind without delusion... a contracted mind... a distracted mind... an exalted mind... an unexalted mind... a surpassable mind... an unsurpassable mind... a concentrated mind... an unconcentrated mind... a liberated mind... they know an unliberated mind as 'an unliberated mind.' And in this, many of my disciples abide, having attained the ultimate perfection of direct knowledge.

257. “Puna caparaṃ, udāyi, akkhātā mayā sāvakānaṃ paṭipadā, yathāpaṭipannā me sāvakā [V 2.0222] anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussaranti, seyyathidaṃ – ekampi jātiṃ dvepi jātiyo tissopi jātiyo catassopi jātiyo pañcapi jātiyo dasapi jātiyo vīsampi jātiyo tiṃsampi jātiyo cattālīsampi jātiyo paññāsampi jātiyo jātisatampi jātisahassampi jātisatasahassampi, anekepi saṃvaṭṭakappe anekepi vivaṭṭakappe anekepi saṃvaṭṭavivaṭṭakappe – ‘amutrāsiṃ evaṃnāmo evaṃgotto evaṃvaṇṇo evamāhāro evaṃsukhadukkhappaṭisaṃvedī evamāyupariyanto, so tato cuto amutra udapādiṃ; tatrāpāsiṃ evaṃnāmo evaṃgotto evaṃvaṇṇo evamāhāro evaṃsukhadukkhappaṭisaṃvedī evamāyupariyanto, so tato cuto idhūpapanno’ti. Iti sākāraṃ sauddesaṃ anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati. Seyyathāpi, udāyi, puriso sakamhā gāmā aññaṃ gāmaṃ gaccheyya, tamhāpi gāmā aññaṃ gāmaṃ gaccheyya; so tamhā gāmā sakaṃyeva gāmaṃ paccāgaccheyya; tassa evamassa – ‘ahaṃ kho sakamhā gāmā aññaṃ gāmaṃ [T 2.0339] agacchiṃ, tatra evaṃ aṭṭhāsiṃ evaṃ nisīdiṃ evaṃ abhāsiṃ evaṃ tuṇhī ahosiṃ; tamhāpi gāmā amuṃ gāmaṃ agacchiṃ, tatrāpi evaṃ aṭṭhāsiṃ [P 2.0021] evaṃ nisīdiṃ evaṃ abhāsiṃ evaṃ tuṇhī ahosiṃ, somhi tamhā gāmā sakaṃyeva gāmaṃ paccāgato’ti. Evameva kho, udāyi, akkhātā mayā sāvakānaṃ paṭipadā, yathāpaṭipannā me sāvakā anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussaranti, seyyathidaṃ – ekampi jātiṃ…pe… iti sākāraṃ sauddesaṃ anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussaranti. Tatra ca pana me sāvakā bahū abhiññāvosānapāramippattā viharanti.

257. Furthermore, Udāyi, I have declared to my disciples the path by which, when my disciples have followed it, they recollect their manifold past lives—that is, one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many eons of world-contraction, many eons of world-expansion, many eons of world-contraction and expansion: 'There I was, of such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, experiencing such pleasure and pain, with such a lifespan. Passing away from there, I arose elsewhere. There too I was of such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, experiencing such pleasure and pain, with such a lifespan. Passing away from there, I was reborn here.' Thus they recollect their manifold past lives with their aspects and details. Just as, Udāyi, a man might go from his own village to another village, and from that village to yet another village, and then return from that village back to his own village. He would think: 'I went from my own village to another village, where I stood thus, sat thus, spoke thus, and was silent thus. From that village, I went to that other village, where I also stood thus, sat thus, spoke thus, and was silent thus. I am he who has returned from that village to my own village.' In the same way, Udāyi, I have declared to my disciples the path by which, when my disciples have followed it, they recollect their manifold past lives—that is, one birth... and so on... Thus they recollect their manifold past lives with their aspects and details. And in this, many of my disciples abide, having attained the ultimate perfection of direct knowledge.

258. “Puna caparaṃ, udāyi, akkhātā mayā sāvakānaṃ paṭipadā, yathāpaṭipannā me sāvakā dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena satte [M 2.0213] passanti cavamāne upapajjamāne hīne paṇīte suvaṇṇe dubbaṇṇe sugate duggate yathākammūpage satte pajānanti – ‘ime vata bhonto sattā kāyaduccaritena samannāgatā vacīduccaritena samannāgatā manoduccaritena samannāgatā ariyānaṃ upavādakā micchādiṭṭhikā micchādiṭṭhikammasamādānā, te kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapannā; ime vā pana bhonto sattā kāyasucaritena samannāgatā vacīsucaritena samannāgatā manosucaritena samannāgatā ariyānaṃ anupavādakā sammādiṭṭhikā sammādiṭṭhikammasamādānā, te kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ [T 2.0340] upapannā’ti. Iti dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena satte passanti cavamāne upapajjamāne hīne paṇīte suvaṇṇe dubbaṇṇe sugate duggate yathākammūpage [V 2.0223] satte pajānanti. Seyyathāpi, udāyi, dve agārā sadvārā sannadvārā (ka.). Tatra cakkhumā puriso majjhe ṭhito passeyya manusse gehaṃ pavisantepi nikkhamantepi anucaṅkamantepi anuvicarantepi; evameva kho, udāyi, akkhātā mayā sāvakānaṃ paṭipadā, yathāpaṭipannā me sāvakā dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena satte passanti cavamāne upapajjamāne hīne paṇīte suvaṇṇe dubbaṇṇe sugate duggate yathākammūpage satte pajānanti…pe… tatra ca pa me sāvakā bahū abhiññāvosānapāramippattā viharanti.

258. Furthermore, Udāyi, I have declared to my disciples the path by which, when my disciples have followed it, they with the divine eye—purified and surpassing the human—see beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and understand how beings fare according to their actions: ‘Indeed, these beings who engaged in misconduct of body, speech, and mind, who were revilers of the noble ones, held wrong views, and undertook actions based on wrong views—after the breakup of the body, after death, have been reborn in a state of loss, a bad destination, the lower realms, even hell. But these beings who engaged in good conduct of body, speech, and mind, who were not revilers of the noble ones, held right views, and undertook actions based on right views—after the breakup of the body, after death, have been reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world.’ Thus, with the divine eye—purified and surpassing the human—they see beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and understand how beings fare according to their actions. Just as, Udāyi, if there were two houses with doors, and a man with good sight standing in the middle could see people entering the house, exiting from the house, walking to and fro, and moving about; in the same way, Udāyi, I have declared to my disciples the path by which, when my disciples have followed it, they with the divine eye—purified and surpassing the human—see beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and understand how beings fare according to their actions. And in this matter, many of my disciples abide having attained the ultimate perfection in direct knowledge.

259. “Puna [P 2.0022] caparaṃ, udāyi, akkhātā mayā sāvakānaṃ paṭipadā, yathāpaṭipannā me sāvakā āsavānaṃ khayā anāsavaṃ cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharanti. Seyyathāpi, udāyi, pabbatasaṅkhepe udakarahado accho vippasanno anāvilo, tattha cakkhumā puriso tīre ṭhito passeyya sippisambukampi sippikasambukampi (syā. kaṃ. ka.) sakkharakaṭhalampi macchagumbampi carantampi tiṭṭhantampi. Tassa evamassa – ‘ayaṃ kho udakarahado accho vippasanno anāvilo, tatrime sippisambukāpi sakkharakaṭhalāpi macchagumbāpi carantipi tiṭṭhantipī’ti. Evameva kho, udāyi, akkhātā mayā sāvakānaṃ paṭipadā, yathāpaṭipannā [T 2.0341] me sāvakā āsavānaṃ khayā anāsavaṃ cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharanti. Tatra ca pana me [M 2.0214] sāvakā bahū abhiññāvosānapāramippattā viharanti. Ayaṃ kho, udāyi, pañcamo dhammo yena mama sāvakā sakkaronti garuṃ karonti mānenti pūjenti, sakkatvā garuṃ katvā upanissāya viharanti.

259. Furthermore, Udāyi, I have declared to my disciples the path by which, when my disciples have followed it, through the destruction of the taints, they dwell having attained the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, having realized it for themselves with direct knowledge in this very life. Just as, Udāyi, in a mountain gorge there is a pool of water, clear, limpid, undisturbed, and a man with good sight standing on the bank would see oysters and snails, gravel and potsherds, and schools of fish moving about or staying still. He would think: ‘This pool is clear, limpid, undisturbed, and here are these oysters and snails, gravel and potsherds, and schools of fish moving about or staying still.’ In the same way, Udāyi, I have declared to my disciples the path by which, when my disciples have followed it, through the destruction of the taints, they dwell having attained the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, having realized it for themselves with direct knowledge in this very life. And in this matter, many of my disciples abide having attained the ultimate perfection in direct knowledge. This, Udāyi, is the fifth quality on account of which my disciples honor, respect, revere, and venerate me, and having honored and respected me, they dwell in dependence on me.

“Ime kho, udāyi, pañca dhammā yehi mamaṃ sāvakā sakkaronti garuṃ karonti mānenti pūjenti, sakkatvā garuṃ katvā upanissāya viharantī”ti.

These, Udāyi, are the five qualities on account of which my disciples honor, respect, revere, and venerate me; and having honored and respected me, they dwell in dependence on me.

Idamavoca bhagavā. Attamano sakuludāyī paribbājako bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandīti.

Thus spoke the Blessed One. The wanderer Sakuludāyī, delighted, rejoiced at the Blessed One's words.

Mahāsakuludāyisuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ sattamaṃ.

The Great Discourse to Sakuludāyī, the seventh, is concluded.

8. Samaṇamuṇḍikasuttaṃ

8. The Discourse to Samaṇamuṇḍika

260. Evaṃ [T 2.0342][V 2.0224] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme. Tena kho pana samayena uggāhamāno paribbājako samaṇamuṇḍikāputto samaṇamaṇḍikāputto (sī. pī.) samayappavādake tindukācīre ekasālake mallikāya ārāme paṭivasati [P 2.0023] mahatiyā paribbājakaparisāya saddhiṃ pañcamattehi paribbājakasatehi. Atha kho pañcakaṅgo thapati sāvatthiyā nikkhami divā divassa bhagavantaṃ dassanāya. Atha kho pañcakaṅgassa thapatissa etadahosi – “akālo kho tāva bhagavantaṃ dassanāya; paṭisallīno bhagavā. Manobhāvaniyānampi bhikkhūnaṃ asamayo dassanāya; paṭisallīnā manobhāvaniyā bhikkhū. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ yena samayappavādako tindukācīro ekasālako mallikāya ārāmo yena uggāhamāno paribbājako samaṇamuṇḍikāputto tenupasaṅkameyya”nti. Atha kho pañcakaṅgo thapati yena samayappavādako tindukācīro ekasālako mallikāya ārāmo yena uggāhamāno paribbājako samaṇamuṇḍikāputto tenupasaṅkami.

260. Thus have I heard. At one time, the Blessed One was dwelling in Sāvatthī, in the Jeta Grove, at the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍika. Now at that time, the wanderer Uggāhamāna, son of Samaṇamuṇḍikā, was dwelling in Mallikā’s Park at the Tindukācīra, the single-halled place for debates, together with a great assembly of wanderers, with about five hundred wanderers. Then the carpenter Pañcakaṅga departed from Sāvatthī during the day to see the Blessed One. Then this thought occurred to the carpenter Pañcakaṅga: 'It is now an inopportune time to see the Blessed One; the Blessed One is in seclusion. It is also an inopportune time to see the monks who are developing the mind; the monks who are developing the mind are in seclusion. Suppose I were to go to Mallikā’s Park, to the Tindukācīra, the single-halled place for debates, where the wanderer Uggāhamāna, son of Samaṇamuṇḍikā, is staying?' Then the carpenter Pañcakaṅga went to Mallikā’s Park, to the Tindukācīra, the single-halled place for debates, where the wanderer Uggāhamāna, son of Samaṇamuṇḍikā, was staying.

Tena kho pana samayena uggāhamāno paribbājako samaṇamuṇḍikāputto mahatiyā paribbājakaparisāya saddhiṃ nisinno hoti unnādiniyā uccāsaddamahāsaddāya anekavihitaṃ tiracchānakathaṃ kathentiyā, seyyathidaṃ – rājakathaṃ corakathaṃ mahāmattakathaṃ senākathaṃ bhayakathaṃ [T 2.0343] yuddhakathaṃ [M 2.0215] annakathaṃ pānakathaṃ vatthakathaṃ sayanakathaṃ mālākathaṃ gandhakathaṃ ñātikathaṃ yānakathaṃ gāmakathaṃ nigamakathaṃ nagarakathaṃ janapadakathaṃ itthikathaṃ sūrakathaṃ visikhākathaṃ kumbhaṭṭhānakathaṃ pubbapetakathaṃ nānattakathaṃ lokakkhāyikaṃ samuddakkhāyikaṃ itibhavābhavakathaṃ iti vā.

Now at that time, the wanderer Uggāhamāna, son of Samaṇamuṇḍikā, was sitting together with a great assembly of wanderers, who were making a loud and great noise, a resounding clamor, and speaking various kinds of worldly talk. That is to say: talk of kings, talk of thieves, talk of great ministers, talk of armies, talk of dangers, talk of battles, talk of food, talk of drink, talk of clothes, talk of beds, talk of garlands, talk of perfumes, talk of relatives, talk of vehicles, talk of villages, talk of market towns, talk of cities, talk of countries, talk of women, talk of heroes, talk of streets, talk of the potters' place, talk of departed ancestors, miscellaneous talk, speculation about the world, speculation about the sea, and talk of prosperity and decline.

Addasā kho uggāhamāno paribbājako samaṇamuṇḍikāputto pañcakaṅgaṃ thapatiṃ dūratova āgacchantaṃ. Disvāna sakaṃ parisaṃ saṇṭhāpesi – “appasaddā bhonto hontu, mā bhonto saddamakattha; ayaṃ samaṇassa gotamassa sāvako āgacchati pañcakaṅgo thapati. Yāvatā kho pana samaṇassa gotamassa sāvakā gihī odātavasanā sāvatthiyaṃ paṭivasanti ayaṃ tesaṃ aññataro [V 2.0225] pañcakaṅgo thapati. Appasaddakāmā kho pana te āyasmanto appasaddavinītā appasaddassa vaṇṇavādino; appeva nāma appasaddaṃ parisaṃ viditvā upasaṅkamitabbaṃ maññeyyā”ti. Atha kho te paribbājakā tuṇhī ahesuṃ.

The wanderer Uggāhamāna, son of Samaṇamuṇḍikā, saw the carpenter Pañcakaṅga coming from afar. Having seen him, he quieted his own assembly, saying: 'Sirs, be of little sound; sirs, do not make a sound. This disciple of the ascetic Gotama, the carpenter Pañcakaṅga, is approaching. Insofar as there are lay disciples of the ascetic Gotama, clad in white, who dwell in Sāvatthī, this carpenter Pañcakaṅga is one among them. Indeed, those venerable ones desire little sound, are trained in little sound, and are speakers of praise for little sound. Perhaps, upon seeing that the assembly has little sound, he might think it fit to approach.' Then those wanderers became silent.

261. Atha kho pañcakaṅgo thapati yena uggāhamāno paribbājako samaṇamuṇḍikāputto tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā uggāhamānena paribbājakena samaṇamuṇḍikāputtena saddhiṃ sammodi[P 2.0024]. Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinnaṃ kho pañcakaṅgaṃ thapatiṃ uggāhamāno paribbājako samaṇamuṇḍikāputto etadavoca – “catūhi kho ahaṃ, gahapati, dhammehi samannāgataṃ purisapuggalaṃ paññapemi sampannakusalaṃ paramakusalaṃ [T 2.0344] uttamapattipattaṃ samaṇaṃ ayojjhaṃ. Katamehi catūhi? Idha, gahapati, na kāyena pāpakammaṃ karoti, na pāpakaṃ vācaṃ bhāsati, na pāpakaṃ saṅkappaṃ saṅkappeti, na pāpakaṃ ājīvaṃ ājīvati – imehi kho ahaṃ, gahapati, catūhi dhammehi samannāgataṃ purisapuggalaṃ paññapemi sampannakusalaṃ paramakusalaṃ uttamapattipattaṃ samaṇaṃ ayojjha”nti.

261. Then the carpenter Pañcakaṅga approached the wanderer Uggāhamāna, son of Samaṇamuṇḍikā. Having approached, he exchanged courteous greetings with the wanderer Uggāhamāna, son of Samaṇamuṇḍikā. After concluding this courteous and memorable talk, he sat down to one side. To the carpenter Pañcakaṅga, so seated, the wanderer Uggāhamāna, son of Samaṇamuṇḍikā, said this: 'Householder, I declare a person who is endowed with four qualities to be one accomplished in the wholesome, one of supreme wholesomeness, one who has attained the highest attainment, an invincible ascetic. With which four? Here, householder, one does no evil action with the body, one speaks no evil speech, one conceives no evil intention, and one does not live by an evil livelihood. Householder, it is a person endowed with these four qualities that I declare to be one accomplished in the wholesome, one of supreme wholesomeness, one who has attained the highest attainment, an invincible ascetic.'

Atha kho pañcakaṅgo thapati uggāhamānassa paribbājakassa samaṇamuṇḍikāputtassa bhāsitaṃ neva abhinandi nappaṭikkosi. Anabhinanditvā appaṭikkositvā uṭṭhāyāsanā pakkāmi – “bhagavato santike etassa bhāsitassa atthaṃ ājānissāmī”ti. Atha kho pañcakaṅgo thapati yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho pañcakaṅgo thapati yāvatako ahosi uggāhamānena [M 2.0216] paribbājakena samaṇamuṇḍikāputtena saddhiṃ kathāsallāpo taṃ sabbaṃ bhagavato ārocesi.

Then the carpenter Pañcakaṅga neither delighted in nor scorned the statement of the wanderer Uggāhamāna, son of Samaṇamuṇḍikā. Without delighting in it or scorning it, he rose from his seat and departed, thinking: 'In the presence of the Blessed One, I will come to know the meaning of this statement.' Then the carpenter Pañcakaṅga approached the Blessed One, and having paid homage to him, sat down to one side. Seated to one side, he reported to the Blessed One the entire conversation he had with the wanderer Uggāhamāna, son of Samaṇamuṇḍikā.

262. Evaṃ vutte, bhagavā pañcakaṅgaṃ thapatiṃ etadavoca – “evaṃ sante kho, thapati, daharo kumāro mando uttānaseyyako sampannakusalo bhavissati paramakusalo uttamapattipatto samaṇo ayojjho, yathā uggāhamānassa paribbājakassa samaṇamuṇḍikāputtassa vacanaṃ. Daharassa hi, thapati, kumārassa mandassa uttānaseyyakassa kāyotipi na hoti, kuto pana kāyena pāpakammaṃ karissati, aññatra phanditamattā! Daharassa hi, thapati, kumārassa mandassa uttānaseyyakassa [T 2.0345] vācātipi na hoti, kuto pana pāpakaṃ vācaṃ bhāsissati, aññatra roditamattā[V 2.0226]! Daharassa hi, thapati, kumārassa mandassa uttānaseyyakassa saṅkappotipi na hoti, kuto pana pāpakaṃ saṅkappaṃ saṅkappissati, aññatra vikūjitamattā vikujjitamattā (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.)! Daharassa hi, thapati, kumārassa mandassa uttānaseyyakassa ājīvotipi na hoti, kuto pana pāpakaṃ [P 2.0025] ājīvaṃ ājīvissati, aññatra mātuthaññā! Evaṃ sante kho, thapati, daharo kumāro mando uttānaseyyako sampannakusalo bhavissati paramakusalo uttamapattipatto samaṇo ayojjho, yathā uggāhamānassa paribbājakassa samaṇamuṇḍikāputtassa vacanaṃ.

262. When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the carpenter Pañcakaṅga: 'If that were so, carpenter, then according to the words of the wanderer Uggāhamāna, son of Samaṇamuṇḍikā, a young boy, slow, lying on his back, would be an ascetic accomplished in the wholesome, supremely wholesome, one who has attained the highest attainment, and invincible. For, carpenter, a young boy, slow, lying on his back, does not yet have the concept of 'body'; how then could he perform an evil action with the body, other than merely twitching? For, carpenter, a young boy, slow, lying on his back, does not yet have the concept of 'speech'; how then could he speak an evil word, other than merely crying? For, carpenter, a young boy, slow, lying on his back, does not yet have the concept of 'intention'; how then could he conceive an evil intention, other than merely whimpering? For, carpenter, a young boy, slow, lying on his back, does not yet have the concept of 'livelihood'; how then could he live by an evil livelihood, other than by suckling at his mother's breast? If that were so, carpenter, then according to the words of the wanderer Uggāhamāna, son of Samaṇamuṇḍikā, a young boy, slow, lying on his back, would be an ascetic accomplished in the wholesome, supremely wholesome, one who has attained the highest attainment, and invincible.'

263. “Catūhi kho ahaṃ, thapati, dhammehi samannāgataṃ purisapuggalaṃ paññapemi na ceva sampannakusalaṃ na paramakusalaṃ na uttamapattipattaṃ samaṇaṃ ayojjhaṃ, api cimaṃ daharaṃ kumāraṃ mandaṃ uttānaseyyakaṃ samadhigayha tiṭṭhati. Katamehi catūhi? Idha, thapati, na kāyena pāpakammaṃ karoti, na pāpakaṃ vācaṃ bhāsati, na pāpakaṃ saṅkappaṃ saṅkappeti, na pāpakaṃ ājīvaṃ ājīvati – imehi kho ahaṃ, thapati, catūhi dhammehi samannāgataṃ purisapuggalaṃ paññapemi na ceva sampannakusalaṃ na paramakusalaṃ na uttamapattipattaṃ samaṇaṃ ayojjhaṃ, api cimaṃ daharaṃ kumāraṃ mandaṃ uttānaseyyakaṃ samadhigayha tiṭṭhati.

263. Carpenter, I do not declare a person endowed with four qualities to be accomplished in the wholesome, nor supremely wholesome, nor one who has attained the highest attainment, nor an invincible ascetic; and yet, he stands having surpassed this young, slow boy lying on his back. With which four? Here, carpenter, one does not perform an evil action with the body, does not speak an evil word, does not conceive an evil intention, and does not live by an evil livelihood. Carpenter, I do not declare a person endowed with these four qualities to be accomplished in the wholesome, nor supremely wholesome, nor one who has attained the highest attainment, nor an invincible ascetic; and yet, he stands having surpassed this young, slow boy lying on his back.

“Dasahi [T 2.0346] kho ahaṃ, thapati, dhammehi samannāgataṃ purisapuggalaṃ paññapemi sampannakusalaṃ paramakusalaṃ uttamapattipattaṃ samaṇaṃ ayojjhaṃ. Ime akusalā sīlā; tamahaṃ kahaṃ (sī.), tahaṃ (pī.), thapati, veditabbanti vadāmi. Itosamuṭṭhānā akusalā [M 2.0217] sīlā; tamahaṃ, thapati, veditabbanti vadāmi. Idha akusalā sīlā aparisesā nirujjhanti; tamahaṃ, thapati, veditabbanti vadāmi. Evaṃ paṭipanno akusalānaṃ sīlānaṃ nirodhāya paṭipanno hoti; tamahaṃ, thapati, veditabbanti vadāmi.

Carpenter, I declare a person endowed with ten qualities to be accomplished in the wholesome, supremely wholesome, one who has attained the highest attainment, and an invincible ascetic. 'These are unwholesome moralities'; this, carpenter, I say is to be known. 'Unwholesome moralities arise from this source'; this, carpenter, I say is to be known. 'Here, unwholesome moralities cease without remainder'; this, carpenter, I say is to be known. 'One who practices thus is practicing for the cessation of unwholesome moralities'; this, carpenter, I say is to be known.

“Ime kusalā sīlā; tamahaṃ, thapati, veditabbanti vadāmi. Itosamuṭṭhānā kusalā sīlā; tamahaṃ, thapati, veditabbanti vadāmi. Idha kusalā sīlā aparisesā nirujjhanti; tamahaṃ, thapati, veditabbanti vadāmi. Evaṃ paṭipanno kusalānaṃ sīlānaṃ nirodhāya paṭipanno hoti; tamahaṃ, thapati, veditabbanti vadāmi.

There are these wholesome moralities; this, carpenter, I say is to be known. There are wholesome moralities that arise from this source; this, carpenter, I say is to be known. Here, wholesome moralities cease without remainder; this, carpenter, I say is to be known. One who practices thus is one who practices for the cessation of wholesome moralities; this, carpenter, I say is to be known.

“Ime akusalā saṅkappā; tamahaṃ, thapati, veditabbanti vadāmi. Itosamuṭṭhānā akusalā saṅkappā[V 2.0227]; tamahaṃ, thapati, veditabbanti vadāmi. Idha akusalā [P 2.0026] saṅkappā aparisesā nirujjhanti; tamahaṃ, thapati, veditabbanti vadāmi. Evaṃ paṭipanno akusalānaṃ saṅkappānaṃ nirodhāya paṭipanno hoti; tamahaṃ, thapati, veditabbanti vadāmi.

There are these unwholesome thoughts; this, carpenter, I say is to be known. There are unwholesome thoughts that arise from this source; this, carpenter, I say is to be known. Here, unwholesome thoughts cease without remainder; this, carpenter, I say is to be known. One who practices thus is one who practices for the cessation of unwholesome thoughts; this, carpenter, I say is to be known.

“Ime kusalā saṅkappā; tamahaṃ, thapati, veditabbanti vadāmi. Itosamuṭṭhānā kusalā saṅkappā[T 2.0347]; tamahaṃ, thapati, veditabbanti vadāmi. Idha kusalā saṅkappā aparisesā nirujjhanti; tamahaṃ, thapati, veditabbanti vadāmi. Evaṃ paṭipanno kusalānaṃ saṅkappānaṃ nirodhāya paṭipanno hoti; tamahaṃ, thapati, veditabbanti vadāmi.

There are these wholesome thoughts; this, carpenter, I say is to be known. There are wholesome thoughts that arise from this source; this, carpenter, I say is to be known. Here, wholesome thoughts cease without remainder; this, carpenter, I say is to be known. One who practices thus is one who practices for the cessation of wholesome thoughts; this, carpenter, I say is to be known.

264. “Katame ca, thapati, akusalā sīlā? Akusalaṃ kāyakammaṃ, akusalaṃ vacīkammaṃ, pāpako ājīvo – ime vuccanti, thapati, akusalā sīlā.

264. And what, carpenter, are the unwholesome moralities? Unwholesome bodily action, unwholesome verbal action, and evil livelihood—these, carpenter, are called the unwholesome moralities.

“Ime ca, thapati, akusalā sīlā kiṃsamuṭṭhānā? Samuṭṭhānampi nesaṃ vuttaṃ. ‘Cittasamuṭṭhānā’tissa vacanīyaṃ. Katamaṃ cittaṃ? Cittampi hi bahuṃ anekavidhaṃ nānappakārakaṃ. Yaṃ cittaṃ sarāgaṃ sadosaṃ samohaṃ, itosamuṭṭhānā akusalā sīlā.

And these unwholesome moralities, carpenter, from what do they arise? Their origin has also been stated. It should be said: 'They arise from the mind.' What mind? For the mind is indeed manifold, of many kinds, of various sorts. The mind that is with greed, with hatred, with delusion—from this, the unwholesome moralities arise.

“Ime ca, thapati, akusalā sīlā kuhiṃ aparisesā nirujjhanti? Nirodhopi nesaṃ vutto. Idha, thapati, bhikkhu kāyaduccaritaṃ pahāya kāyasucaritaṃ [M 2.0218] bhāveti, vacīduccaritaṃ pahāya vacīsucaritaṃ bhāveti, manoduccaritaṃ pahāya manosucaritaṃ bhāveti, micchājīvaṃ pahāya sammājīvena jīvitaṃ kappeti – etthete akusalā sīlā aparisesā nirujjhanti.

And where, carpenter, do these unwholesome moralities cease without remainder? Their cessation has also been stated. Here, carpenter, a monk, having abandoned bodily misconduct, cultivates wholesome bodily conduct; having abandoned verbal misconduct, cultivates wholesome verbal conduct; having abandoned mental misconduct, cultivates wholesome mental conduct; having abandoned wrong livelihood, he makes his living by right livelihood. It is here that these unwholesome moralities cease without remainder.

“Kathaṃ paṭipanno, thapati, akusalānaṃ sīlānaṃ nirodhāya paṭipanno hoti? Idha, thapati, bhikkhu anuppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ anuppādāya chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati; uppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānāya chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati; anuppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ uppādāya chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati; uppannānaṃ [T 2.0348] kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ ṭhitiyā asammosāya bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā chandaṃ janeti [V 2.0228] vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati. Evaṃ paṭipanno [P 2.0027] kho, thapati, akusalānaṃ sīlānaṃ nirodhāya paṭipanno hoti.

And how, carpenter, does one practice for the cessation of unwholesome moralities? Here, carpenter, a bhikkhu generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states. He generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives for the abandoning of arisen evil, unwholesome states. He generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives for the arising of unarisen wholesome states. He generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives for the maintenance, non-fading, increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of arisen wholesome states. Practicing in this way, carpenter, one practices for the cessation of unwholesome moralities.

265. “Katame ca, thapati, kusalā sīlā? Kusalaṃ kāyakammaṃ, kusalaṃ vacīkammaṃ, ājīvaparisuddhampi kho ahaṃ, thapati, sīlasmiṃ vadāmi. Ime vuccanti, thapati, kusalā sīlā.

265. And what, carpenter, are wholesome moralities? Wholesome bodily action, wholesome verbal action; and I declare, carpenter, that purity of livelihood is included in morality. These, carpenter, are called wholesome moralities.

“Ime ca, thapati, kusalā sīlā kiṃsamuṭṭhānā? Samuṭṭhānampi nesaṃ vuttaṃ. ‘Cittasamuṭṭhānā’tissa vacanīyaṃ. Katamaṃ cittaṃ? Cittampi hi bahuṃ anekavidhaṃ nānappakārakaṃ. Yaṃ cittaṃ vītarāgaṃ vītadosaṃ vītamohaṃ, itosamuṭṭhānā kusalā sīlā.

And these wholesome moralities, carpenter, from what do they arise? Their origin has also been stated. It should be said, ‘They arise from the mind.’ What mind? For the mind is indeed manifold, of many kinds, of various sorts. Wholesome moralities arise from that mind which is free from greed, free from hatred, free from delusion.

“Ime ca, thapati, kusalā sīlā kuhiṃ aparisesā nirujjhanti? Nirodhopi nesaṃ vutto. Idha, thapati, bhikkhu sīlavā hoti no ca sīlamayo, tañca cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti; yatthassa te kusalā sīlā aparisesā nirujjhanti.

And where, carpenter, do these wholesome moralities cease without remainder? Their cessation has also been stated. Here, carpenter, a bhikkhu is virtuous but is not made of virtue, and he understands as it truly is the liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those wholesome moralities of his cease without remainder.

“Kathaṃ paṭipanno ca, thapati, kusalānaṃ sīlānaṃ nirodhāya paṭipanno hoti? Idha, thapati, bhikkhu anuppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ anuppādāya chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati[M 2.0219]; uppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānāya…pe… anuppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ uppādāya…pe… uppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ [T 2.0349] ṭhitiyā asammosāya bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati. Evaṃ paṭipanno kho, thapati, kusalānaṃ sīlānaṃ nirodhāya paṭipanno hoti.

And how, carpenter, does one practice for the cessation of wholesome moralities? Here, carpenter, a bhikkhu—for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states; for the abandoning of arisen evil, unwholesome states... for the arising of unarisen wholesome states... for the maintenance, non-fading, increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of arisen wholesome states—generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives. Practicing in this way, carpenter, one practices for the cessation of wholesome moralities.

266. “Katame ca, thapati, akusalā saṅkappā? Kāmasaṅkappo, byāpādasaṅkappo, vihiṃsāsaṅkappo – ime vuccanti, thapati, akusalā saṅkappā.

266. And what, carpenter, are unwholesome thoughts? The thought of sensual pleasure, the thought of ill will, the thought of cruelty—these, carpenter, are called unwholesome thoughts.

“Ime ca, thapati, akusalā saṅkappā kiṃsamuṭṭhānā? Samuṭṭhānampi nesaṃ vuttaṃ. ‘Saññāsamuṭṭhānā’tissa [V 2.0229] vacanīyaṃ. Katamā saññā? Saññāpi hi bahū anekavidhā nānappakārakā. Kāmasaññā, byāpādasaññā, vihiṃsāsaññā – itosamuṭṭhānā akusalā saṅkappā.

And these unwholesome thoughts, carpenter, from what do they arise? Their origin has also been stated. It should be said, ‘They arise from perception.’ What perception? For perception is indeed manifold, of many kinds, of various sorts. The perception of sensual pleasure, the perception of ill will, the perception of cruelty—from these arise unwholesome thoughts.

“Ime ca, thapati, akusalā saṅkappā kuhiṃ aparisesā nirujjhanti? Nirodhopi nesaṃ vutto. Idha, thapati, bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehi…pe… paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ [P 2.0028] upasampajja viharati; etthete akusalā saṅkappā aparisesā nirujjhanti.

“And these unwholesome thoughts, master builder, where do they cease without remainder? Their cessation has also been stated. Here, master builder, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures… enters and abides in the first jhāna; it is here that these unwholesome thoughts cease without remainder.”

“Kathaṃ paṭipanno ca, thapati, akusalānaṃ saṅkappānaṃ nirodhāya paṭipanno hoti? Idha, thapati, bhikkhu anuppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ anuppādāya chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati; uppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānāya…pe… anuppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ uppādāya…pe… uppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ ṭhitiyā asammosāya [T 2.0350] bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati. Evaṃ paṭipanno kho, thapati, akusalānaṃ saṅkappānaṃ nirodhāya paṭipanno hoti.

“And how, master builder, does one practice for the cessation of unwholesome thoughts? Here, master builder, a bhikkhu generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states; for the abandoning of arisen evil, unwholesome states… for the arising of unarisen wholesome states… for the maintenance, non-fading, increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of arisen wholesome states, he generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives. Practicing in this way, master builder, one practices for the cessation of unwholesome thoughts.”

267. “Katame ca, thapati, kusalā saṅkappā? Nekkhammasaṅkappo, abyāpādasaṅkappo, avihiṃsāsaṅkappo – ime vuccanti, thapati, kusalā saṅkappā.

267. “And what, master builder, are wholesome thoughts? The thought of renunciation, the thought of non-ill will, the thought of non-cruelty—these, master builder, are called wholesome thoughts.”
