Atha kho ahameva taṃ vedanaṃ vediyāmī”ti. “Idaṃ kho taṃ, mahārāja, tena bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā sammāsambuddhena sandhāya bhāsitaṃ – ‘atāṇo loko anabhissaro’ti, yamahaṃ ñatvā ca disvā sutvā ca agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajito”ti. “Acchariyaṃ, bho raṭṭhapāla, abbhutaṃ, bho raṭṭhapāla! Yāva subhāsitaṃ cidaṃ tena bhagavatā jānatā [T 2.0409] passatā arahatā sammāsambuddhena – ‘atāṇo loko anabhissaro’ti. Atāṇo hi, bho raṭṭhapāla, loko anabhissaro.

“There are, Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, in this royal family, elephant corps, cavalry corps, chariot corps, and infantry corps, which exist for our defense in times of danger. But the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla says, ‘The world is without refuge, without a protector.’ How, Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, should the meaning of this statement be understood?” “What do you think, great king? Do you have any chronic ailment?” “I do, Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, have a chronic ailment. Sometimes, Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, my friends and ministers, my kinsmen and relatives, stand surrounding me, thinking, ‘Now King Koravya will pass away, now King Koravya will pass away.’” “What do you think, great king? Are you able to say to your friends and ministers, your kinsmen and relatives: ‘Come, my good friends and ministers, kinsmen and relatives, let all who are present share this feeling, so that I might feel a lighter feeling’? Or is it you alone who must experience that feeling?” “I am not able, Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, to say to my friends and ministers, my kinsmen and relatives: ‘Come, my good friends and ministers, kinsmen and relatives, let all who are present share this feeling, so that I might feel a lighter feeling.’ Rather, it is I alone who experience that feeling.” “It was with reference to this, great king, that the Blessed One, who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, said: ‘The world is without refuge, without a protector.’ It was after knowing, seeing, and hearing this that I went forth from the household life into homelessness.” “It is wonderful, Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, it is marvelous, Venerable Raṭṭhapāla! How well-spoken indeed was this by the Blessed One, who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One: ‘The world is without refuge, without a protector.’ For indeed, Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, the world is without refuge and without a protector.”

“Saṃvijjati kho, bho raṭṭhapāla, imasmiṃ rājakule pahūtaṃ hiraññasuvaṇṇaṃ bhūmigatañca vehāsagatañca. ‘Assako loko, sabbaṃ pahāya gamanīya’nti – bhavaṃ raṭṭhapālo āha. Imassa pana, bho raṭṭhapāla, bhāsitassa kathaṃ attho daṭṭhabbo”ti? “Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, mahārāja, yathā tvaṃ etarahi pañcahi kāmaguṇehi [P 2.0071] samappito samaṅgībhūto paricāresi, lacchasi tvaṃ paratthāpi – ‘evamevāhaṃ imeheva pañcahi kāmaguṇehi samappito samaṅgībhūto paricāremī’ti, udāhu aññe imaṃ bhogaṃ paṭipajjissanti, tvaṃ pana yathākammaṃ gamissasī”ti? “Yathāhaṃ, bho raṭṭhapāla, etarahi pañcahi kāmaguṇehi samappito samaṅgībhūto paricāremi, nāhaṃ lacchāmi paratthāpi – ‘evameva imeheva pañcahi kāmaguṇehi samappito samaṅgībhūto paricāremī’ti. Atha kho aññe imaṃ bhogaṃ paṭipajjissanti; ahaṃ pana yathākammaṃ gamissāmī”ti. “Idaṃ kho taṃ, mahārāja, tena bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā sammāsambuddhena sandhāya bhāsitaṃ – ‘assako loko, sabbaṃ pahāya gamanīya’nti, yamahaṃ ñatvā ca disvā ca sutvā ca agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajito”ti. “Acchariyaṃ, bho raṭṭhapāla, abbhutaṃ, bho raṭṭhapāla! Yāva subhāsitaṃ cidaṃ tena bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā [V 2.0268] sammāsambuddhena – ‘assako loko[T 2.0410], sabbaṃ pahāya gamanīya’nti[M 2.0259]. Assako hi, bho raṭṭhapāla, loko sabbaṃ pahāya gamanīyaṃ.

“Indeed, Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, in this royal household there is abundant gold and silver, both buried in the ground and stored above. But the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla says, ‘The world is ownerless; one must go, having left everything behind.’ How, Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, should the meaning of this statement be understood?” “What do you think, great king? Just as you now enjoy yourself, endowed and possessed of the five cords of sensual pleasure, will you in the next world also be able to say, ‘In this same way I will enjoy myself, endowed and possessed of these same five cords of sensual pleasure’? Or will others take possession of this wealth, while you will go according to your kamma?” “Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, just as I now enjoy myself, endowed and possessed of the five cords of sensual pleasure, I will not in the next world be able to say, ‘In this same way I will enjoy myself, endowed and possessed of these same five cords of sensual pleasure.’ Instead, others will take possession of this wealth, while I will go according to my kamma.” “This, great king, is what the Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One—was referring to when he said, ‘The world is ownerless; one must go, having left everything behind.’ It was after knowing, seeing, and hearing this that I went forth from the household life into homelessness.” “It is wonderful, Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, it is marvelous, Venerable Raṭṭhapāla! How well-spoken this is by that Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One: ‘The world is ownerless; one must go, having left everything behind.’ Indeed, Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, the world is ownerless; one must go, having left everything behind.”

“‘Ūno loko atitto taṇhādāso’ti – bhavaṃ raṭṭhapālo āha. Imassa, bho raṭṭhapāla, bhāsitassa kathaṃ attho daṭṭhabbo”ti? “Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, mahārāja, phītaṃ kuruṃ ajjhāvasasī”ti? “Evaṃ, bho raṭṭhapāla, phītaṃ kuruṃ ajjhāvasāmī”ti. “Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, mahārāja, idha puriso āgaccheyya puratthimāya disāya saddhāyiko paccayiko. So taṃ upasaṅkamitvā evaṃ vadeyya – ‘yagghe, mahārāja, jāneyyāsi, ahaṃ āgacchāmi puratthimāya disāya? Tatthaddasaṃ mahantaṃ janapadaṃ iddhañceva phītañca bahujanaṃ ākiṇṇamanussaṃ. Bahū tattha hatthikāyā assakāyā rathakāyā pattikāyā; bahu tattha dhanadhaññaṃ dantājinaṃ (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.); bahu tattha hiraññasuvaṇṇaṃ akatañceva katañca; bahu tattha itthipariggaho. Sakkā ca tāvatakeneva balamattena balatthena (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.), bahalatthena (ka.) abhivijinituṃ. Abhivijina, mahārājā’ti, kinti naṃ kareyyāsī”ti? “Tampi [P 2.0072] mayaṃ, bho raṭṭhapāla, abhivijiya ajjhāvaseyyāmā”ti. “Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, mahārāja, idha puriso āgaccheyya pacchimāya disāya… uttarāya disāya… dakkhiṇāya disāya… parasamuddato saddhāyiko paccayiko. So taṃ upasaṅkamitvā evaṃ vadeyya – ‘yagghe, mahārāja, jāneyyāsi, ahaṃ āgacchāmi parasamuddato? Tatthaddasaṃ mahantaṃ janapadaṃ iddhañceva phītañca bahujanaṃ ākiṇṇamanussaṃ. Bahū tattha hatthikāyā assakāyā rathakāyā [T 2.0411] pattikāyā; bahu tattha dhanadhaññaṃ; bahu tattha hiraññasuvaṇṇaṃ akatañceva katañca; bahu tattha itthipariggaho. Sakkā ca tāvatakeneva balamattena abhivijinituṃ. Abhivijina, mahārājā’ti, kinti naṃ kareyyāsī”ti? “Tampi mayaṃ, bho raṭṭhapāla, abhivijiya ajjhāvaseyyāmā”ti. “Idaṃ kho taṃ, mahārāja, tena bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā sammāsambuddhena sandhāya bhāsitaṃ – ‘ūno loko atitto taṇhādāso’ti, yamahaṃ ñatvā ca disvā sutvā ca agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajito”ti. “Acchariyaṃ, bho raṭṭhapāla, abbhutaṃ, bho raṭṭhapāla! Yāva subhāsitaṃ cidaṃ tena bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā sammāsambuddhena – ‘ūno loko atitto taṇhādāso’ti. Ūno hi, bho raṭṭhapāla, loko atitto taṇhādāso”ti.

“‘The world is deficient, insatiable, a slave to craving’—so said the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla. How, Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, should the meaning of this statement be understood?” “What do you think, great king? Do you rule over the prosperous Kuru country?” “Yes, Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, I rule over the prosperous Kuru country.” “What do you think, great king? Suppose a trustworthy and reliable man were to come from the eastern direction. He would approach you and say: ‘If it pleases you, great king, you should know that I come from the eastern direction. There I saw a great country, prosperous and thriving, with many people, crowded with humans. There were many corps of elephants, corps of cavalry, corps of chariots, and corps of infantry; much wealth and grain; much gold and silver, both unworked and worked; and many women to be taken. It can be conquered with just such a force as you have. Conquer it, great king!’ What would you do about it?” “We too, Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, would conquer it and rule over it.” “What do you think, great king? Suppose a trustworthy and reliable man were to come from the western direction… from the northern direction… from the southern direction… from across the ocean. He would approach you and say: ‘If it pleases you, great king, you should know that I come from across the ocean. There I saw a great country, prosperous and thriving, with many people, crowded with humans. There were many corps of elephants, corps of cavalry, corps of chariots, and corps of infantry; much wealth and grain; much gold and silver, both unworked and worked; and many women to be taken. It can be conquered with just such a force as you have. Conquer it, great king!’ What would you do about it?” “We too, Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, would conquer it and rule over it.” “This, great king, is what the Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One—was referring to when he said: ‘The world is deficient, insatiable, a slave to craving.’ It was after knowing, seeing, and hearing this that I went forth from the household life into homelessness.” “It is wonderful, Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, it is marvelous, Venerable Raṭṭhapāla! How well-spoken this is by that Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One: ‘The world is deficient, insatiable, a slave to craving.’ Indeed, Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, the world is deficient, insatiable, a slave to craving.”

Idamavoca [M 2.0260][V 2.0269] āyasmā raṭṭhapālo. Idaṃ vatvā athāparaṃ etadavoca –

The Venerable Raṭṭhapāla said this. Having said this, he then said further:

307. “Passāmi loke sadhane manusse,

307. “I see in the world people with wealth,

Laddhāna vittaṃ na dadanti mohā;

Luddhā dhanaṃ laddhā dhanaṃ (ka.) sannicayaṃ karonti,

Bhiyyova kāme abhipatthayanti.

Having obtained wealth, out of delusion they do not give; greedy, they accumulate riches and desire sensual pleasures even more.

“Rājā pasayhā pathaviṃ vijitvā,

Sasāgarantaṃ mahimāvasanto mahiyā vasanto (sī. ka.);

Oraṃ samuddassa atittarūpo,

Pāraṃ [T 2.0412] samuddassapi patthayetha.

“A king, having conquered the earth by force, ruling over the land to the ocean's shore, unsatisfied with this side of the ocean, would still desire the other side.

“Rājā [P 2.0073] ca aññe ca bahū manussā,

Avītataṇhā atittataṇhā (ka.) maraṇaṃ upenti;

Ūnāva hutvāna jahanti dehaṃ,

Kāmehi lokamhi na hatthi titti.

“The king and many other people, with craving unquenched, approach death; still deficient, they abandon the body. In the world, there is no satisfaction from sensual pleasures.

“Kandanti naṃ ñātī pakiriya kese,

Ahovatā no amarāti cāhu;

Vatthena naṃ pārutaṃ nīharitvā,

Citaṃ samādāya samādhāya (sī.) tatoḍahanti.

“His relatives lament, with hair disheveled, crying, ‘Oh, would that our relative were immortal!’; having wrapped him in a cloth, they carry him out, then place him on a pyre and burn him.

“So ḍayhati sūlehi tujjamāno,

Ekena vatthena pahāya bhoge;

Na mīyamānassa bhavanti tāṇā,

Ñātīdha mittā atha vā sahāyā.

“He is burned, prodded by stakes, with a single cloth, having abandoned his possessions; for one who is dying, there are no protectors—not relatives, friends, or companions here.

“Dāyādakā [V 2.0270] tassa dhanaṃ haranti,

Satto pana gacchati yena kammaṃ;

Na mīyamānaṃ dhanamanveti kiñci,

Puttā ca dārā ca dhanañca raṭṭhaṃ.

“His heirs take his wealth, but the being goes according to his kamma. Nothing whatsoever follows the one who is dying—not sons, nor wife, nor wealth, nor kingdom.”

“Na [M 2.0261] dīghamāyuṃ labhate dhanena, na cāpi vittena jaraṃ vihanti;

Appaṃ hidaṃ jīvitamāhu dhīrā, asassataṃ [T 2.0413] vippariṇāmadhammaṃ.

Not by wealth is long life obtained, nor by riches is old age warded off; short indeed is this life, say the wise—impermanent, subject to change.

“Aḍḍhā daliddā ca phusanti phassaṃ,

Bālo ca dhīro ca tatheva phuṭṭho;

Bālo ca bālyā vadhitova seti,

Dhīro ca dhīrova (ka.) na vedhati phassaphuṭṭho.

The rich and the poor experience contact; the fool and the wise are touched in the very same way. The fool, on account of his foolishness, lies down trembling; but the wise one, though touched by contact, does not tremble.

“Tasmā hi paññāva dhanena seyyo,

Yāya vosānamidhādhigacchati;

Abyositattā asositattā (sī. pī.) hi bhavābhavesu,

Pāpāni kammāni karonti mohā.

Therefore, wisdom is indeed better than wealth, by which one attains the culmination here. For, not having reached the culmination, they commit evil deeds in various existences out of delusion.

“Upeti gabbhañca parañca lokaṃ,

Saṃsāramāpajja paramparāya;

Tassappapañño abhisaddahanto,

Upeti gabbhañca parañca lokaṃ.

One goes to a womb and to the next world, entering the cycle of rebirth successively. The one of little wisdom, placing faith in such a person, goes to a womb and to the next world.

“Coro [P 2.0074] yathā sandhimukhe gahito,

Sakammunā haññati pāpadhammo;

Evaṃ pajā pecca paramhi loke,

Sakammunā haññati pāpadhammo.

Just as a thief of evil conduct, caught at a break-in, is afflicted by his own deed; even so, after passing away, a person of evil conduct is afflicted in the next world by their own deed.

“Kāmāhi [V 2.0271] citrā madhurā manoramā,

Virūparūpena mathenti cittaṃ;

Ādīnavaṃ kāmaguṇesu disvā,

Tasmā [T 2.0414] ahaṃ pabbajitomhi rāja.

Sensual pleasures are indeed varied, sweet, and delightful; by their diverse forms, they churn the mind. Having seen the danger in the strands of sensual pleasure, therefore, O king, I have gone forth.

“Dumapphalāneva patanti māṇavā,

Daharā ca vuḍḍhā ca sarīrabhedā;

Etampi disvā evampi disvā (sī.), etaṃ viditvā (syā. kaṃ.) pabbajitomhi rāja,

Apaṇṇakaṃ sāmaññameva seyyo”ti.

Just as fruits fall from a tree, so do people fall—the young and the old—at the breakup of the body. Having seen this as well, O king, I have gone forth. The ascetic life itself is unquestionably superior.

Raṭṭhapālasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ dutiyaṃ.

The Raṭṭhapāla Sutta, the second, is concluded.

3. Maghadevasuttaṃ

3. The Maghadeva Sutta

308. Evaṃ [T 2.0415][M 2.0262][V 2.0272] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā mithilāyaṃ viharati maghadevaambavane makhādevaambavane (sī. pī.), magghadevaambavane (ka.). Atha kho bhagavā aññatarasmiṃ padese sitaṃ pātvākāsi. Atha kho āyasmato ānandassa etadahosi – “ko nu kho hetu, ko paccayo bhagavato sitassa pātukammāya? Na akāraṇena tathāgatā sitaṃ pātukarontī”ti. Atha kho āyasmā ānando ekaṃsaṃ cīvaraṃ katvā yena bhagavā tenañjaliṃ paṇāmetvā bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “ko nu kho, bhante, hetu, ko paccayo bhagavato sitassa pātukammāya? Na akāraṇena tathāgatā sitaṃ pātukarontī”ti. “Bhūtapubbaṃ, ānanda, imissāyeva mithilāyaṃ rājā ahosi maghadevo nāma dhammiko dhammarājā dhamme ṭhito mahārājā; dhammaṃ carati brāhmaṇagahapatikesu negamesu ceva jānapadesu ca; uposathañca upavasati cātuddasiṃ pañcadasiṃ [P 2.0075] aṭṭhamiñca pakkhassa. Atha kho, ānanda, rājā maghadevo bahūnaṃ vassānaṃ bahūnaṃ vassasatānaṃ bahūnaṃ vassasahassānaṃ accayena kappakaṃ āmantesi – ‘yadā me, samma kappaka, passeyyāsi sirasmiṃ palitāni jātāni, atha me āroceyyāsī’ti. ‘Evaṃ, devā’ti kho, ānanda, kappako rañño maghadevassa paccassosi. Addasā kho, ānanda, kappako bahūnaṃ vassānaṃ [T 2.0416] bahūnaṃ vassasatānaṃ bahūnaṃ vassasahassānaṃ accayena rañño maghadevassa sirasmiṃ palitāni jātāni. Disvāna rājānaṃ maghadevaṃ etadavoca – ‘pātubhūtā kho devassa devadūtā, dissanti sirasmiṃ palitāni jātānī’ti. ‘Tena hi, samma kappaka, tāni palitāni sādhukaṃ saṇḍāsena uddharitvā mama añjalismiṃ patiṭṭhāpehī’ti. ‘Evaṃ, devā’ti kho, ānanda, kappako rañño maghadevassa paṭissutvā tāni palitāni sādhukaṃ saṇḍāsena uddharitvā rañño maghadevassa añjalismiṃ patiṭṭhāpesi.

308. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling in Mithilā, in the Maghadeva Mango Grove. Then the Blessed One revealed a smile in a certain place. Then it occurred to the Venerable Ānanda: “What is the cause, what is the reason for the Blessed One’s revealing a smile? Tathāgatas do not reveal a smile without a reason.” Then the Venerable Ānanda arranged his robe over one shoulder, raised his joined hands in salutation towards the Blessed One, and said this to the Blessed One: “What, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the reason for the Blessed One’s revealing a smile? Tathāgatas do not reveal a smile without a reason.” “Once upon a time, Ānanda, in this very Mithilā, there was a king named Maghadeva, a righteous king, a king of Dhamma, a great king established in the Dhamma. He practiced the Dhamma among brahmins and householders, and among townspeople and country folk. And he observed the Uposatha on the fourteenth, fifteenth, and eighth days of the lunar fortnight. Then, Ānanda, after many years, many hundreds of years, many thousands of years had passed, King Maghadeva addressed his barber: ‘When, my dear barber, you see grey hairs that have appeared on my head, you should then inform me.’ ‘Yes, Your Majesty,’ Ānanda, the barber replied in assent to King Maghadeva. Then, Ānanda, after many years, many hundreds of years, many thousands of years had passed, the barber saw grey hairs that had appeared on King Maghadeva’s head. Having seen them, he said this to King Maghadeva: ‘The divine messengers have appeared, Your Majesty; grey hairs that have appeared on your head are seen.’ ‘In that case, my dear barber, carefully pluck out those grey hairs with tweezers and place them in my cupped hands.’ ‘Yes, Your Majesty,’ Ānanda, the barber replied to King Maghadeva, and having obeyed his word, he carefully plucked out those grey hairs with tweezers and placed them in King Maghadeva’s cupped hands.

309. “Atha kho, ānanda, rājā maghadevo kappakassa gāmavaraṃ datvā jeṭṭhaputtaṃ kumāraṃ āmantāpetvā etadavoca – ‘pātubhūtā kho me, tāta kumāra, devadūtā; dissanti sirasmiṃ palitāni jātāni; bhuttā kho pana me mānusakā kāmā; samayo dibbe kāme pariyesituṃ. Ehi [M 2.0263][V 2.0273] tvaṃ, tāta kumāra, imaṃ rajjaṃ paṭipajja. Ahaṃ pana kesamassuṃ ohāretvā kāsāyāni vatthāni acchādetvā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajissāmi. Tena hi, tāta kumāra, yadā tvampi passeyyāsi sirasmiṃ palitāni jātāni, atha kappakassa gāmavaraṃ datvā jeṭṭhaputtaṃ kumāraṃ sādhukaṃ rajje samanusāsitvā kesamassuṃ ohāretvā kāsāyāni vatthāni acchādetvā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajeyyāsi. Yena me idaṃ kalyāṇaṃ vattaṃ nihitaṃ anuppavatteyyāsi, mā kho me tvaṃ antimapuriso ahosi. Yasmiṃ kho, tāta kumāra, purisayuge vattamāne evarūpassa kalyāṇassa vattassa [T 2.0417] samucchedo hoti so tesaṃ antimapuriso hoti. Taṃ tāhaṃ, tāta kumāra, evaṃ vadāmi – yena me idaṃ kalyāṇaṃ vattaṃ [P 2.0076] nihitaṃ anuppavatteyyāsi, mā kho me tvaṃ antimapuriso ahosī’ti. Atha kho, ānanda, rājā maghadevo kappakassa gāmavaraṃ datvā jeṭṭhaputtaṃ kumāraṃ sādhukaṃ rajje samanusāsitvā imasmiṃyeva maghadevaambavane kesamassuṃ ohāretvā kāsāyāni vatthāni acchādetvā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbaji. So mettāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā vihāsi, tathā dutiyaṃ, tathā tatiyaṃ, tathā catutthaṃ; iti uddhamadho tiriyaṃ sabbadhi sabbattatāya sabbāvantaṃ lokaṃ mettāsahagatena cetasā vipulena mahaggatena appamāṇena averena abyābajjhena abyāpajjhena (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.), abyāpajjena (ka.) pharitvā vihāsi. Karuṇāsahagatena cetasā… muditāsahagatena cetasā… upekkhāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā vihāsi, tathā dutiyaṃ, tathā tatiyaṃ, tathā catutthaṃ; iti uddhamadho tiriyaṃ sabbadhi sabbattatāya sabbāvantaṃ lokaṃ upekkhāsahagatena cetasā vipulena mahaggatena appamāṇena averena abyābajjhena pharitvā vihāsi.

309. Then, Ānanda, King Maghadeva, having given a choice village to the barber, had his eldest son, the prince, summoned and said this: ‘Dear prince, the divine messengers have appeared to me; grey hairs are seen to have grown on my head. I have enjoyed human sensual pleasures; it is time to seek divine sensual pleasures. Come, dear prince, take up this kingdom. As for me, having shaved off my hair and beard, having put on the ochre robes, I will go forth from the household life into homelessness. Therefore, dear prince, when you too see grey hairs that have grown on your head, then, having given a choice village to the barber and having properly instructed your eldest son, the prince, in the kingdom, you should shave off your hair and beard, put on the ochre robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness. You should continue this good practice that I have established; do not be the last man of my line. For, dear prince, in whatever generation of men this good practice is cut off, he is the last man among them. Therefore, dear prince, I say this to you: you should continue this good practice that I have established; do not be the last man of my line.’ Then, Ānanda, King Maghadeva, having given a choice village to the barber and having properly instructed his eldest son, the prince, in the kingdom, in this very Maghadeva Mango Grove, shaved off his hair and beard, put on the ochre robes, and went forth from the household life into homelessness. He dwelt pervading one direction with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth; thus above, below, and across, everywhere, for all, he dwelt pervading the entire world with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness—vast, exalted, immeasurable, without enmity, and without affliction. With a mind accompanied by compassion… with a mind accompanied by appreciative joy… with a mind accompanied by equanimity, he dwelt pervading one direction, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth; thus above, below, and across, everywhere, for all, he dwelt pervading the entire world with a mind accompanied by equanimity—vast, exalted, immeasurable, without enmity, and without affliction.

“Rājā kho panānanda, maghadevo caturāsītivassasahassāni kumārakīḷitaṃ kīḷi, caturāsītivassasahassāni oparajjaṃ kāresi, caturāsītivassasahassāni rajjaṃ kāresi, caturāsītivassasahassāni imasmiṃyeva maghadevaambavane agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajito brahmacariyamacari. So cattāro brahmavihāre bhāvetvā [T 2.0418] kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā brahmalokūpago ahosi.

Indeed, Ānanda, King Maghadeva played children’s games for eighty-four thousand years, acted as viceroy for eighty-four thousand years, and ruled the kingdom for eighty-four thousand years. For eighty-four thousand years, in this very Maghadeva Mango Grove, having gone forth from the household life into homelessness, he practiced the holy life. He, having developed the four divine abidings, with the breakup of the body, after death, was reborn in the Brahma world.

310. “Atha [M 2.0264] kho rañño, ānanda, maghadevassa putto bahūnaṃ vassānaṃ bahūnaṃ vassasatānaṃ bahūnaṃ vassasahassānaṃ accayena kappakaṃ āmantesi – ‘yadā me, samma kappaka, passeyyāsi [V 2.0274] sirasmiṃ palitāni jātāni, atha kho āroceyyāsī’ti. ‘Evaṃ, devā’ti kho, ānanda, kappako rañño maghadevassa puttassa paccassosi. Addasā kho, ānanda, kappako bahūnaṃ vassānaṃ bahūnaṃ vassasatānaṃ bahūnaṃ vassasahassānaṃ accayena rañño maghadevassa puttassa sirasmiṃ palitāni jātāni. Disvāna rañño maghadevassa puttaṃ etadavoca – ‘pātubhūtā kho devassa devadūtā; dissanti sirasmiṃ palitāni [P 2.0077] jātānī’ti. ‘Tena hi, samma kappaka, tāni palitāni sādhukaṃ saṇḍāsena uddharitvā mama añjalismiṃ patiṭṭhāpehī’ti. ‘Evaṃ, devā’ti kho, ānanda, kappako rañño maghadevassa puttassa paṭissutvā tāni palitāni sādhukaṃ saṇḍāsena uddharitvā rañño maghadevassa puttassa añjalismiṃ patiṭṭhāpesi.

310. Then, Ānanda, after the passing of many years, many hundreds of years, many thousands of years, the son of King Maghadeva addressed the barber: ‘Friend barber, when you see grey hairs that have grown on my head, then you should inform me.’ ‘So be it, Your Majesty,’ Ānanda, the barber replied to the son of King Maghadeva. Ānanda, after the passing of many years, many hundreds of years, many thousands of years, the barber saw grey hairs that had grown on the head of the son of King Maghadeva. Having seen them, he said this to the son of King Maghadeva: ‘The divine messengers have appeared to Your Majesty; grey hairs are seen to have grown on your head.’ ‘In that case, friend barber, carefully pluck out those grey hairs with tweezers and place them in my cupped hands.’ ‘So be it, Your Majesty,’ Ānanda, the barber, having assented to the son of King Maghadeva, carefully plucked out those grey hairs with tweezers and placed them in the cupped hands of the son of King Maghadeva.

“Atha kho, ānanda, rañño maghadevassa putto kappakassa gāmavaraṃ datvā jeṭṭhaputtaṃ kumāraṃ āmantāpetvā etadavoca – ‘pātubhūtā kho, me, tāta kumāra, devadūtā; dissanti sirasmiṃ palitāni jātāni; bhuttā kho pana me mānusakā kāmā; samayo dibbe kāme pariyesituṃ. Ehi tvaṃ, tāta kumāra, imaṃ rajjaṃ paṭipajja. Ahaṃ pana kesamassuṃ ohāretvā kāsāyāni vatthāni [T 2.0419] acchādetvā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajissāmi. Tena hi, tāta kumāra, yadā tvampi passeyyāsi sirasmiṃ palitāni jātāni, atha kappakassa gāmavaraṃ datvā jeṭṭhaputtaṃ kumāraṃ sādhukaṃ rajje samanusāsitvā kesamassuṃ ohāretvā kāsāyāni vatthāni acchādetvā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajeyyāsi. Yena me idaṃ kalyāṇaṃ vattaṃ nihitaṃ anuppavatteyyāsi, mā kho me tvaṃ antimapuriso ahosi. Yasmiṃ kho, tāta kumāra, purisayuge vattamāne evarūpassa kalyāṇassa vattassa samucchedo hoti so tesaṃ antimapuriso hoti. Taṃ tāhaṃ, tāta kumāra, evaṃ vadāmi – yena me idaṃ kalyāṇaṃ vattaṃ nihitaṃ anuppavatteyyāsi, mā kho me tvaṃ antimapuriso ahosī’ti. Atha kho, ānanda, rañño maghadevassa putto kappakassa gāmavaraṃ datvā jeṭṭhaputtaṃ kumāraṃ sādhukaṃ rajje samanusāsitvā imasmiṃyeva maghadevaambavane kesamassuṃ ohāretvā kāsāyāni [M 2.0265] vatthāni acchādetvā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbaji. So mettāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā vihāsi, tathā dutiyaṃ, tathā tatiyaṃ, tathā catutthaṃ; iti uddhamadho tiriyaṃ sabbadhi sabbattatāya sabbāvantaṃ lokaṃ mettāsahagatena cetasā vipulena mahaggatena appamāṇena averena abyābajjhena pharitvā vihāsi. Karuṇāsahagatena cetasā… muditāsahagatena cetasā… upekkhāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ [T 2.0420][V 2.0275] disaṃ pharitvā vihāsi, tathā dutiyaṃ, tathā tatiyaṃ, tathā catutthaṃ; iti uddhamadho tiriyaṃ sabbadhi sabbattatāya sabbāvantaṃ lokaṃ upekkhāsahagatena cetasā vipulena mahaggatena appamāṇena averena abyābajjhena pharitvā [P 2.0078] vihāsi. Rañño kho panānanda, maghadevassa putto caturāsītivassasahassāni kumārakīḷitaṃ kīḷi, caturāsītivassasahassāni oparajjaṃ kāresi, caturāsītivassasahassāni rajjaṃ kāresi, caturāsītivassasahassāni imasmiṃyeva maghadevaambavane agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajito brahmacariyamacari. So cattāro brahmavihāre bhāvetvā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā brahmalokūpago ahosi.

Then, Ānanda, King Maghadeva’s son, having given an excellent village to the barber, summoned his eldest son, the prince, and said this: ‘My dear prince, the divine messengers have appeared to me; grey hairs are seen to have arisen on my head. I have enjoyed human sensual pleasures; it is time to seek divine sensual pleasures. Come, dear prince, take up this kingship. As for me, I will shave off my hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness. Therefore, dear prince, when you too see grey hairs that have arisen on your head, then after giving an excellent village to the barber and properly instructing your eldest son, the prince, in kingship, you should shave off your hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness. In this way, you should continue this noble practice established by me; do not be the last man of my line. For, dear prince, in whatever generation of men this noble practice is discontinued, that one becomes the last man among them. Therefore, dear prince, I say this to you: in this way, you should continue this noble practice established by me; do not be the last man of my line.’

Then, Ānanda, King Maghadeva’s son, having given an excellent village to the barber and properly instructing his eldest son, the prince, in kingship, shaved off his hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and went forth from the household life into homelessness in this very Maghadeva mango grove. He dwelled pervading one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth; thus above, below, and across, everywhere, recognizing all as himself, he dwelled pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness—vast, sublime, immeasurable, without enmity, and without ill will. With a mind imbued with compassion… with a mind imbued with sympathetic joy… he dwelled pervading one direction with a mind imbued with equanimity, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth; thus above, below, and across, everywhere, recognizing all as himself, he dwelled pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with equanimity—vast, sublime, immeasurable, without enmity, and without ill will.

Now, Ānanda, King Maghadeva’s son played as a prince for eighty-four thousand years, served as viceroy for eighty-four thousand years, and reigned as king for eighty-four thousand years. For eighty-four thousand years, having gone forth from the household life into homelessness in this very Maghadeva mango grove, he practiced the holy life. Having developed the four divine abidings, with the breakup of the body, after death, he was reborn in the Brahma-world.

311. “Rañño kho panānanda, maghadevassa puttapaputtakā tassa paramparā caturāsītirājasahassāni caturāsītikhattiyasahassāni (sī. pī.), caturāsītisahassāni (syā. kaṃ.) imasmiṃyeva maghadevaambavane kesamassuṃ ohāretvā kāsāyāni vatthāni acchādetvā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajiṃsu. Te mettāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā vihariṃsu, tathā dutiyaṃ, tathā tatiyaṃ, tathā catutthaṃ; iti uddhamadho tiriyaṃ sabbadhi sabbattatāya sabbāvantaṃ lokaṃ mettāsahagatena cetasā vipulena mahaggatena appamāṇena averena abyābajjhena pharitvā vihariṃsu. Karuṇāsahagatena cetasā… muditāsahagatena cetasā… upekkhāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā vihariṃsu, tathā dutiyaṃ, tathā tatiyaṃ, tathā catutthaṃ; iti uddhamadho tiriyaṃ sabbadhi sabbattatāya sabbāvantaṃ lokaṃ upekkhāsahagatena cetasā vipulena [T 2.0421] mahaggatena appamāṇena averena abyābajjhena pharitvā vihariṃsu. Caturāsītivassasahassāni kumārakīḷitaṃ kīḷiṃsu, caturāsītivassasahassāni oparajjaṃ kāresuṃ, caturāsītivassasahassāni rajjaṃ kāresuṃ, caturāsītivassasahassāni imasmiṃyeva maghadevaambavane agārasmā [M 2.0266] anagāriyaṃ pabbajitā brahmacariyamacariṃsu. Te cattāro brahmavihāre bhāvetvā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā brahmalokūpagā ahesuṃ. Nimi tesaṃ rājā rājānaṃ (sī. pī.) pacchimako ahosi dhammiko dhammarājā dhamme ṭhito mahārājā; dhammaṃ carati brāhmaṇagahapatikesu negamesu ceva jānapadesu ca; uposathañca upavasati cātuddasiṃ pañcadasiṃ aṭṭhamiñca pakkhassa.

311. Furthermore, Ānanda, the sons and grandsons of King Maghadeva, a lineage of eighty-four thousand kings, in this very Maghadeva mango grove, shaved off their hair and beards, donned the saffron robes, and went forth from the household life into homelessness. They dwelled pervading one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth; thus above, below, and across, everywhere, recognizing all as themselves, they dwelled pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness—vast, sublime, immeasurable, without enmity, and without ill will. With a mind imbued with compassion… with a mind imbued with sympathetic joy… they dwelled pervading one direction with a mind imbued with equanimity, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth; thus above, below, and across, everywhere, recognizing all as themselves, they dwelled pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with equanimity—vast, sublime, immeasurable, without enmity, and without ill will. For eighty-four thousand years they played as princes, for eighty-four thousand years they served as viceroys, and for eighty-four thousand years they reigned as kings. For eighty-four thousand years, having gone forth from the household life into homelessness in this very Maghadeva mango grove, they practiced the holy life. Having developed the four divine abidings, with the breakup of the body, after death, they were reborn in the Brahma-world. King Nimi was the last of them. He was a righteous king, a king of righteousness, a great king established in the Dhamma. He acted righteously towards brahmins and householders, towards the people of the towns and the countryside. And he observed the Uposatha on the fourteenth, fifteenth, and eighth days of the lunar fortnight.

312. “Bhūtapubbaṃ, ānanda, devānaṃ tāvatiṃsānaṃ sudhammāyaṃ [P 2.0079] sabhāyaṃ sannisinnānaṃ sannipatitānaṃ ayamantarākathā udapādi – ‘lābhā vata, bho, videhānaṃ, suladdhaṃ vata, bho, videhānaṃ, yesaṃ nimi rājā dhammiko dhammarājā dhamme ṭhito mahārājā; dhammaṃ carati brāhmaṇagahapatikesu [V 2.0276] negamesu ceva jānapadesu ca; uposathañca upavasati cātuddasiṃ pañcadasiṃ aṭṭhamiñca pakkhassā’ti. Atha kho, ānanda, sakko devānamindo deve tāvatiṃse āmantesi – ‘iccheyyātha no tumhe, mārisā, nimiṃ rājānaṃ daṭṭhu’nti? ‘Icchāma mayaṃ, mārisa, nimiṃ rājānaṃ daṭṭhu’nti. Tena kho pana, ānanda, samayena nimi rājā tadahuposathe pannarase sīsaṃnhāto sasīsaṃ nahāto (sī.), sīsanhāto (syā. kaṃ.) uposathiko uparipāsādavaragato [T 2.0422] nisinno hoti. Atha kho, ānanda, sakko devānamindo – seyyathāpi nāma balavā puriso samiñjitaṃ vā bāhaṃ pasāreyya, pasāritaṃ vā bāhaṃ samiñjeyya, evameva – devesu tāvatiṃsesu antarahito nimissa rañño pamukhe pāturahosi. Atha kho, ānanda, sakko devānamindo nimiṃ rājānaṃ etadavoca – ‘lābhā te, mahārāja, suladdhaṃ te, mahārāja. Devā, mahārāja, tāvatiṃsā sudhammāyaṃ sabhāyaṃ kittayamānarūpā sannisinnā – “lābhā vata, bho, videhānaṃ, suladdhaṃ vata, bho, videhānaṃ, yesaṃ nimi rājā dhammiko dhammarājā dhamme ṭhito mahārājā; dhammaṃ carati brāhmaṇagahapatikesu negamesu ceva jānapadesu ca; uposathañca upavasati cātuddasiṃ pañcadasiṃ aṭṭhamiñca pakkhassā”ti. Devā te, mahārāja, tāvatiṃsā dassanakāmā. Tassa te ahaṃ, mahārāja, sahassayuttaṃ ājaññarathaṃ pahiṇissāmi; abhiruheyyāsi, mahārāja, dibbaṃ yānaṃ avikampamāno’ti. Adhivāsesi kho, ānanda, nimi rājā tuṇhībhāvena.

312. Once upon a time, Ānanda, while the Tāvatiṃsa devas were sitting together, assembled in the Sudhammā assembly hall, this conversation arose among them: ‘Sirs, it is a gain for the Videhans, it is a great gain for the Videhans, for whom King Nimi is a righteous king, a king of righteousness, a great king established in the Dhamma; he practices the Dhamma among brahmins and householders, and among the people of the towns and countryside; and he observes the Uposatha on the fourteenth, fifteenth, and eighth days of the fortnight.’ Then, Ānanda, Sakka, lord of the devas, addressed the Tāvatiṃsa devas: ‘Sirs, would you wish to see King Nimi?’ ‘Sir, we wish to see King Nimi.’ Now at that time, Ānanda, on that Uposatha day, the fifteenth of the fortnight, King Nimi, having bathed his head and observing the Uposatha, was seated on the excellent upper floor of his palace. Then, Ānanda, Sakka, lord of the devas—just as a strong man might extend his flexed arm or flex his extended arm, even so—disappeared from among the Tāvatiṃsa devas and appeared in the presence of King Nimi. Then, Ānanda, Sakka, lord of the devas, said this to King Nimi: ‘It is a gain for you, great king, it is a great gain for you, great king. The Tāvatiṃsa devas, great king, are seated together in the Sudhammā assembly hall, singing your praises, saying: “Sirs, it is a gain for the Videhans, it is a great gain for the Videhans, for whom King Nimi is a righteous king, a king of righteousness, a great king established in the Dhamma; he practices the Dhamma among brahmins and householders, and among the people of the towns and countryside; and he observes the Uposatha on the fourteenth, fifteenth, and eighth days of the fortnight.” The Tāvatiṃsa devas, great king, are desirous of seeing you. For your sake, great king, I will send a chariot of thoroughbreds yoked with a thousand horses; you should mount the divine vehicle without wavering, great king.’ And, Ānanda, King Nimi consented by his silence.

313. “Atha [M 2.0267] kho, ānanda, sakko devānamindo nimissa rañño adhivāsanaṃ viditvā – seyyathāpi nāma balavā puriso samiñjitaṃ vā bāhaṃ pasāreyya, pasāritaṃ vā bāhaṃ samiñjeyya, evameva – nimissa rañño pamukhe antarahito devesu tāvatiṃsesu pāturahosi. Atha kho, ānanda, sakko devānamindo mātaliṃ saṅgāhakaṃ āmantesi – ‘ehi tvaṃ, samma mātali, sahassayuttaṃ ājaññarathaṃ yojetvā [T 2.0423] nimiṃ rājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā evaṃ vadehi – ayaṃ te, mahārāja, sahassayutto ājaññaratho sakkena devānamindena pesito; abhiruheyyāsi, mahārāja, dibbaṃ yānaṃ [P 2.0080] avikampamāno’ti. ‘Evaṃ, bhaddantavā’ti kho, ānanda, mātali saṅgāhako sakkassa devānamindassa paṭissutvā sahassayuttaṃ ājaññarathaṃ yojetvā nimiṃ rājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā etadavoca – ‘ayaṃ te, mahārāja, sahassayutto ājaññaratho sakkena devānamindena pesito; abhiruha, mahārāja, dibbaṃ yānaṃ avikampamāno. Api ca, mahārāja, katamena taṃ nemi, yena vā pāpakammā pāpakānaṃ kammānaṃ [V 2.0277] vipākaṃ paṭisaṃvedenti, yena vā kalyāṇakammā kalyāṇakammānaṃ vipākaṃ paṭisaṃvedentī’ti? ‘Ubhayeneva maṃ, mātali, nehī’ti. Sampavesesi sampāpesi (sī. pī.) kho, ānanda, mātali, saṅgāhako nimiṃ rājānaṃ sudhammaṃ sabhaṃ. Addasā kho, ānanda, sakko devānamindo nimiṃ rājānaṃ dūratova āgacchantaṃ. Disvāna nimiṃ rājānaṃ etadavoca – ‘ehi kho, mahārāja. Svāgataṃ, mahārāja. Devā te dassanakāmā, mahārāja, tāvatiṃsā sudhammāyaṃ sabhāyaṃ kittayamānarūpā sannisinnā – “lābhā vata, bho, videhānaṃ, suladdhaṃ vata, bho, videhānaṃ, yesaṃ nimi rājā dhammiko dhammarājā dhamme ṭhito mahārājā; dhammaṃ carati brāhmaṇagahapatikesu negamesu ceva jānapadesu ca; uposathañca upavasati cātuddasiṃ pañcadasiṃ aṭṭhamiñca pakkhassā”ti. Devā te, mahārāja, tāvatiṃsā dassanakāmā[T 2.0424]. Abhirama, mahārāja, devesu devānubhāvenā’ti. ‘Alaṃ, mārisa, tattheva maṃ mithilaṃ paṭinetu. Tathāhaṃ dhammaṃ carissāmi brāhmaṇagahapatikesu negamesu ceva jānapadesu ca; uposathañca upavasāmi cātuddasiṃ pañcadasiṃ aṭṭhamiñca pakkhassā’ti.

313. Then, Ānanda, Sakka, lord of the devas, knowing King Nimi’s consent—just as a strong man might extend his flexed arm or flex his extended arm, even so—vanished from the presence of King Nimi and reappeared among the Tāvatiṃsa devas. Then, Ānanda, Sakka, lord of the devas, addressed Mātali the Supporter: ‘Come, friend Mātali, yoke the chariot of thoroughbreds with a thousand horses, approach King Nimi, and say this: “Great king, this chariot of thoroughbreds yoked with a thousand horses has been sent by Sakka, lord of the devas. You should mount the divine vehicle without wavering, great king.”’ ‘So be it, good sir,’ Mātali the Supporter assented to Sakka, lord of the devas. Having yoked the chariot of thoroughbreds with a thousand horses, he approached King Nimi and said this: ‘Great king, this chariot of thoroughbreds yoked with a thousand horses has been sent by Sakka, lord of the devas. Mount the divine vehicle without wavering, great king. Moreover, great king, by which path shall I lead you: the one by which evil-doers experience the result of their evil deeds, or the one by which doers of good deeds experience the result of their good deeds?’ ‘Mātali, lead me by both paths.’ Then, Ānanda, Mātali the Supporter led King Nimi into the Sudhammā assembly. Ānanda, Sakka, lord of the devas, saw King Nimi coming from afar. Seeing him, he said this to King Nimi: ‘Come, great king. Welcome, great king. The Tāvatiṃsa devas are desirous of seeing you, great king, and are seated together in the Sudhammā assembly hall, singing your praises: “Sirs, it is a gain for the Videhans, it is a great gain for the Videhans, for whom King Nimi is a righteous king, a king of righteousness, a great king established in the Dhamma; he practices the Dhamma among brahmins and householders, and among the people of the towns and countryside; and he observes the Uposatha on the fourteenth, fifteenth, and eighth days of the fortnight.” The Tāvatiṃsa devas, great king, are desirous of seeing you. Delight, great king, among the devas with their divine majesty.’ ‘Enough, sir. Lead me back to that very Mithilā. There I shall continue to practice the Dhamma among brahmins and householders, and among the people of the towns and countryside; and I shall continue to observe the Uposatha on the fourteenth, fifteenth, and eighth days of the fortnight.’

314. “Atha kho, ānanda, sakko devānamindo mātaliṃ saṅgāhakaṃ āmantesi – ‘ehi tvaṃ, samma mātali, sahassayuttaṃ ājaññarathaṃ yojetvā nimiṃ [M 2.0268] rājānaṃ tattheva mithilaṃ paṭinehī’ti. ‘Evaṃ, bhaddantavā’ti kho, ānanda, mātali saṅgāhako sakkassa devānamindassa paṭissutvā sahassayuttaṃ ājaññarathaṃ yojetvā nimiṃ rājānaṃ tattheva mithilaṃ paṭinesi. Tatra sudaṃ, ānanda, nimi rājā dhammaṃ carati brāhmaṇagahapatikesu negamesu ceva jānapadesu ca, uposathañca [P 2.0081] upavasati cātuddasiṃ pañcadasiṃ aṭṭhamiñca pakkhassāti. Atha kho, ānanda, nimi rājā bahūnaṃ vassānaṃ bahūnaṃ vassasatānaṃ bahūnaṃ vassasahassānaṃ accayena kappakaṃ āmantesi – ‘yadā me, samma kappaka, passeyyāsi sirasmiṃ palitāni jātāni, atha me āroceyyāsī’ti. ‘Evaṃ, devā’ti kho, ānanda, kappako nimissa rañño paccassosi. Addasā kho, ānanda, kappako bahūnaṃ vassānaṃ bahūnaṃ vassasatānaṃ bahūnaṃ vassasahassānaṃ accayena nimissa rañño sirasmiṃ palitāni jātāni. Disvāna nimiṃ rājānaṃ etadavoca – ‘pātubhūtā kho devassa devadūtā; dissanti sirasmiṃ palitāni jātānī’ti. ‘Tena hi, samma kappaka, tāni palitāni sādhukaṃ [T 2.0425] saṇḍāsena uddharitvā mama añjalismiṃ patiṭṭhāpehī’ti. ‘Evaṃ, devā’ti kho, ānanda, kappako nimissa rañño paṭissutvā tāni palitāni sādhukaṃ saṇḍāsena [V 2.0278] uddharitvā nimissa rañño añjalismiṃ patiṭṭhāpesi. Atha kho, ānanda, nimi rājā kappakassa gāmavaraṃ datvā jeṭṭhaputtaṃ kumāraṃ āmantāpetvā etadavoca – ‘pātubhūtā kho me, tāta kumāra, devadūtā; dissanti sirasmiṃ palitāni jātāni; bhuttā kho pana me mānusakā kāmā; samayo dibbe kāme pariyesituṃ. Ehi tvaṃ, tāta kumāra, imaṃ rajjaṃ paṭipajja. Ahaṃ pana kesamassuṃ ohāretvā kāsāyāni vatthāni acchādetvā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajissāmi. Tena hi, tāta kumāra, yadā tvampi passeyyāsi sirasmiṃ palitāni jātāni, atha kappakassa gāmavaraṃ datvā jeṭṭhaputtaṃ kumāraṃ sādhukaṃ rajje samanusāsitvā kesamassuṃ ohāretvā kāsāyāni vatthāni acchādetvā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajeyyāsi. Yena me idaṃ kalyāṇaṃ vattaṃ nihitaṃ anuppavatteyyāsi, mā kho me tvaṃ antimapuriso ahosi. Yasmiṃ kho, tāta kumāra, purisayuge vattamāne evarūpassa kalyāṇassa vattassa samucchedo hoti so tesaṃ antimapuriso hoti. Taṃ tāhaṃ, tāta kumāra, evaṃ vadāmi – ‘yena me idaṃ kalyāṇaṃ vattaṃ nihitaṃ anuppavatteyyāsi, mā kho me tvaṃ antimapuriso ahosī’ti.

314. Then, Ānanda, Sakka, lord of the gods, addressed Mātali the benefactor: ‘Come, good Mātali, harness the chariot of thoroughbreds yoked with a thousand and take King Nimi back to that very Mithilā.’ ‘Very well, Lord,’ Ānanda, replied Mātali the benefactor to Sakka, lord of the gods, and having harnessed the chariot of thoroughbreds yoked with a thousand, he took King Nimi back to that very Mithilā. There, Ānanda, King Nimi practiced the Dhamma among brahmins and householders, and among the people of the towns and the countryside, and he observed the Uposatha on the fourteenth, fifteenth, and eighth days of the lunar fortnight. Then, Ānanda, after many years, many hundreds of years, many thousands of years had passed, King Nimi addressed his barber: ‘When, my good barber, you see that grey hairs have grown on my head, you should then inform me.’ ‘So be it, Your Majesty,’ Ānanda, the barber replied to King Nimi. And, Ānanda, after many years, many hundreds of years, many thousands of years had passed, the barber saw that grey hairs had grown on King Nimi’s head. Having seen them, he said this to King Nimi: ‘The divine messengers have appeared for Your Majesty; grey hairs are seen to have grown on your head.’ ‘In that case, my good barber, carefully pluck out those grey hairs with tweezers and place them in my cupped hands.’ ‘So be it, Your Majesty,’ Ānanda, the barber replied to King Nimi, and having carefully plucked out those grey hairs with tweezers, he placed them in King Nimi’s cupped hands. Then, Ānanda, King Nimi, having given a choice village to the barber, had his eldest son, the prince, summoned and said this: ‘The divine messengers have appeared for me, dear prince; grey hairs are seen to have grown on my head. I have enjoyed human sensual pleasures; it is now time to seek divine sensual pleasures. Come, dear prince, take up this kingdom. As for me, having shaved off my hair and beard and donned the ochre robes, I shall go forth from the household life into homelessness. Therefore, dear prince, when you too see that grey hairs have grown on your head, then, having given a choice village to the barber and having thoroughly instructed your eldest son, the prince, in kingship, you should shave off your hair and beard, don the ochre robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness. You should continue this good tradition established by me; do not be the last man of my line. For, dear prince, in whatever generation of men the cessation of such a good tradition occurs, that one is the last man among them. I say this to you, dear prince: “You should continue this good tradition established by me; do not be the last man of my line.”’

315. “Atha [M 2.0269] kho, ānanda, nimi rājā kappakassa gāmavaraṃ datvā [T 2.0426] jeṭṭhaputtaṃ kumāraṃ sādhukaṃ rajje samanusāsitvā imasmiṃyeva maghadevaambavane kesamassuṃ ohāretvā kāsāyāni vatthāni acchādetvā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbaji. So mettāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā vihāsi, tathā dutiyaṃ[P 2.0082], tathā tatiyaṃ, tathā catutthaṃ; iti uddhamadho tiriyaṃ sabbadhi sabbattatāya sabbāvantaṃ lokaṃ mettāsahagatena cetasā vipulena mahaggatena appamāṇena averena abyābajjhena pharitvā vihāsi. Karuṇāsahagatena cetasā… muditāsahagatena cetasā… upekkhāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā vihāsi, tathā dutiyaṃ, tathā tatiyaṃ, tathā catutthaṃ; iti uddhamadho tiriyaṃ sabbadhi sabbattatāya sabbāvantaṃ lokaṃ upekkhāsahagatena cetasā vipulena mahaggatena appamāṇena averena abyābajjhena pharitvā vihāsi. Nimi kho, panānanda, rājā caturāsītivassasahassāni kumārakīḷitaṃ kīḷi, caturāsītivassasahassāni oparajjaṃ kāresi, caturāsītivassasahassāni rajjaṃ kāresi, caturāsītivassasahassāni imasmiṃyeva maghadevaambavane agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajito brahmacariyamacari. So cattāro brahmavihāre bhāvetvā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā brahmalokūpago ahosi. Nimissa kho panānananda[V 2.0279], rañño kaḷārajanako nāma putto ahosi. Na so agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbaji. So taṃ kalyāṇaṃ vattaṃ samucchindi. So tesaṃ antimapuriso ahosi.

315. Then, Ānanda, King Nimi, having given a choice village to the barber and having thoroughly instructed his eldest son, the prince, in kingship, in that very Maghadeva mango grove shaved off his hair and beard, donned the ochre robes, and went forth from the household life into homelessness. He dwelt pervading one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth. Thus above, below, across, and everywhere, identifying with all, he dwelt pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness—abundant, exalted, immeasurable, without hostility, and without ill will. With a mind imbued with compassion... with a mind imbued with altruistic joy... with a mind imbued with equanimity, he dwelt pervading one direction, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth. Thus above, below, across, and everywhere, identifying with all, he dwelt pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with equanimity—abundant, exalted, immeasurable, without hostility, and without ill will. For, Ānanda, King Nimi played the games of a prince for eighty-four thousand years, acted as viceroy for eighty-four thousand years, and ruled the kingdom for eighty-four thousand years. For eighty-four thousand years, having gone forth from the household life into homelessness in this very Maghadeva mango grove, he lived the spiritual life. Having developed the four divine abodes, at the breaking up of the body, after death, he was reborn in the Brahma world. King Nimi, Ānanda, had a son named Kaḷārajanaka. He did not go forth from the household life into homelessness. He cut off that good tradition. He was the last man among them.

316. “Siyā [T 2.0427] kho pana te, ānanda, evamassa – ‘añño nūna tena samayena rājā maghadevo ahosi, yena taṃ kalyāṇaṃ vattaṃ nihita’nti yo taṃ kalyāṇaṃ vattaṃ nihinīti (sī.). Na kho panetaṃ, ānanda, evaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ahaṃ tena samayena rājā maghadevo ahosiṃ. (Ahaṃ taṃ kalyāṇaṃ vattaṃ nihiniṃ,) ( ) natthi (ka.) mayā taṃ kalyāṇaṃ vattaṃ nihitaṃ; pacchimā janatā anuppavattesi. Taṃ kho panānanda, kalyāṇaṃ vattaṃ na nibbidāya na virāgāya na nirodhāya na upasamāya na abhiññāya na sambodhāya na nibbānāya saṃvattati, yāvadeva brahmalokūpapattiyā. Idaṃ kho panānanda, etarahi mayā kalyāṇaṃ vattaṃ [M 2.0270] nihitaṃ ekantanibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya upasamāya abhiññāya sambodhāya nibbānāya saṃvattati. Katamañcānanda, etarahi mayā kalyāṇaṃ vattaṃ nihitaṃ ekantanibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya upasamāya abhiññāya sambodhāya nibbānāya saṃvattati? Ayameva ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo, seyyathidaṃ – sammādiṭṭhi, sammāsaṅkappo, sammāvācā, sammākammanto, sammāājīvo, sammāvāyāmo[P 2.0083], sammāsati, sammāsamādhi. Idaṃ kho, ānanda, etarahi mayā kalyāṇaṃ vattaṃ nihitaṃ ekantanibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya upasamāya abhiññāya sambodhāya nibbānāya saṃvattati. Taṃ vo ahaṃ, ānanda, evaṃ vadāmi – ‘yena me idaṃ kalyāṇaṃ vattaṃ nihitaṃ anuppavatteyyātha, mā kho me tumhe antimapurisā ahuvattha’. Yasmiṃ kho, ānanda, purisayuge vattamāne evarūpassa kalyāṇassa vattassa [T 2.0428] samucchedo hoti so tesaṃ antimapuriso hoti. Taṃ vo ahaṃ, ānanda, evaṃ vadāmi – ‘yena me idaṃ kalyāṇaṃ vattaṃ nihitaṃ anuppavatteyyātha, mā kho me tumhe antimapurisā ahuvatthā’”ti.

316. “Perhaps, Ānanda, it may occur to you: ‘Surely, at that time, it was another King Maghadeva by whom that good practice was established.’ But it should not be seen thus, Ānanda. I myself was King Maghadeva at that time. That good practice was established by me; the later generation followed it. But, Ānanda, that good practice did not conduce to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to awakening, or to Nibbāna—it conduced only as far as rebirth in the Brahmā world. But now, Ānanda, this good practice established by me conduces solely to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to awakening, and to Nibbāna. And what, Ānanda, is this good practice that I have now established, which conduces solely to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to awakening, and to Nibbāna? It is this very Noble Eightfold Path, namely: Right View, Right Intention, Right Speech, Right Action, Right Livelihood, Right Effort, Right Mindfulness, and Right Concentration. This, Ānanda, is the good practice I have now established, which conduces solely to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to awakening, and to Nibbāna. Therefore, Ānanda, I say this to you: ‘Continue to follow this good practice established by me, and do not be my last men.’ For, Ānanda, in whatever generation of men the cutting off of such a good practice occurs, that one is the last man among them. Therefore, Ānanda, I say this to you: ‘Continue to follow this good practice established by me, and do not be my last men.’”

Idamavoca bhagavā. Attamano āyasmā ānando bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandīti.

The Blessed One said this. The Venerable Ānanda, delighted, greatly rejoiced in the Blessed One's words.

Maghadevasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ tatiyaṃ.

The third Maghadeva Sutta is finished.

4. Madhurasuttaṃ

4. The Madhura Sutta

317. Evaṃ [T 2.0429][V 2.0280] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ āyasmā mahākaccāno madhurāyaṃ viharati gundāvane. Assosi kho rājā mādhuro avantiputto – “samaṇo khalu, bho, kaccāno madhurāyaṃ mathurāyaṃ (ṭīkā) viharati gundāvane. Taṃ kho pana bhavantaṃ kaccānaṃ evaṃ kalyāṇo kittisaddo abbhuggato – ‘paṇḍito viyatto medhāvī bahussuto cittakathī kalyāṇapaṭibhāno vuddho ceva arahā ca’. Sādhu kho pana tathārūpānaṃ arahataṃ dassanaṃ hotī”ti. Atha kho rājā mādhuro avantiputto bhadrāni bhadrāni yānāni yojāpetvā bhadraṃ yānaṃ abhiruhitvā bhadrehi bhadrehi yānehi madhurāya niyyāsi mahaccarājānubhāvena āyasmantaṃ mahākaccānaṃ dassanāya. Yāvatikā yānassa bhūmi yānena gantvā yānā paccorohitvā pattikova yenāyasmā mahākaccāno tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā [M 2.0271] āyasmatā [P 2.0084] mahākaccānena saddhiṃ sammodi. Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho rājā mādhuro avantiputto āyasmantaṃ mahākaccānaṃ etadavoca – “brāhmaṇā, bho kaccāna, evamāhaṃsu – ‘brāhmaṇova seṭṭho vaṇṇo, hīno añño vaṇṇo; brāhmaṇova sukko vaṇṇo, kaṇho añño vaṇṇo; brāhmaṇāva sujjhanti, no abrāhmaṇā; brāhmaṇāva brahmuno puttā orasā mukhato jātā brahmajā brahmanimmitā brahmadāyādā’ti. Idha bhavaṃ kaccāno kimakkhāyī”ti? “Ghosoyeva kho eso, mahārāja, lokasmiṃ – ‘brāhmaṇova seṭṭho vaṇṇo, hīno añño vaṇṇo; brāhmaṇova sukko vaṇṇo, kaṇho añño vaṇṇo; brāhmaṇāva sujjhanti, no abrāhmaṇā; brāhmaṇāva brahmuno puttā orasā mukhato jātā [T 2.0430] brahmajā brahmanimmitā brahmadāyādā’ti. Tadamināpetaṃ, mahārāja, pariyāyena veditabbaṃ yathā ghosoyeveso lokasmiṃ – ‘brāhmaṇova seṭṭho vaṇṇo, hīno añño vaṇṇo…pe… brahmadāyādā’”ti.

317. Thus have I heard. At one time, the Venerable Mahākaccāna was dwelling in Madhurā, in the Gundā Grove. King Mādhura Avantiputta heard: “Sirs, the ascetic Kaccāna is, it seems, dwelling in Madhurā in the Gundā Grove. And of that venerable Kaccāna, this good report has spread: ‘He is wise, accomplished, of keen wisdom, learned, an eloquent speaker, of fine eloquence, an elder, and an Arahant.’ Indeed, it is good to see such Arahants.” Then King Mādhura Avantiputta had fine carriages harnessed, mounted a fine carriage, and set out from Madhurā with great royal splendor to see the Venerable Mahākaccāna. Having gone as far as the ground was passable for a carriage, he dismounted from the carriage and approached the Venerable Mahākaccāna on foot. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Mahākaccāna. After concluding this courteous and memorable conversation, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, King Mādhura Avantiputta said this to the Venerable Mahākaccāna: “Master Kaccāna, the brahmins say this: ‘The brahmin caste is the highest; any other caste is inferior. The brahmin caste is fair; any other caste is dark. Only brahmins are pure, not non-brahmins. Brahmins alone are Brahmā’s sons, his offspring, born from his mouth, born of Brahmā, created by Brahmā, heirs of Brahmā.’ Regarding this, what does the venerable Kaccāna say?” “Great King, this is merely a sound in the world: ‘The brahmin caste is the highest; any other caste is inferior. The brahmin caste is fair; any other caste is dark. Only brahmins are pure, not non-brahmins. Brahmins alone are Brahmā’s sons, his offspring, born from his mouth, born of Brahmā, created by Brahmā, heirs of Brahmā.’ Great King, it should be understood by this line of reasoning that this is merely a sound in the world: ‘The brahmin caste is the highest... heirs of Brahmā.’”

318. “Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, mahārāja, khattiyassa cepi ijjheyya dhanena vā dhaññena vā rajatena vā jātarūpena vā khattiyopissāssa pubbuṭṭhāyī pacchānipātī kiṃkārapaṭissāvī manāpacārī piyavādī… brāhmaṇopissāssa… vessopissāssa… suddopissāssa pubbuṭṭhāyī pacchānipātī [V 2.0281] kiṃkārapaṭissāvī manāpacārī piyavādī”ti? “Khattiyassa cepi, bho kaccāna, ijjheyya dhanena vā dhaññena vā rajatena vā jātarūpena vā khattiyopissāssa pubbuṭṭhāyī pacchānipātī kiṃkārapaṭissāvī manāpacārī piyavādī… brāhmaṇopissāssa… vessopissāssa… suddopissāssa pubbuṭṭhāyī pacchānipātī kiṃkārapaṭissāvī manāpacārī piyavādī”ti.

318. “What do you think of this, great king? If a khattiya were to prosper with wealth, or grain, or silver, or gold, would another khattiya rise before him, retire after him, be attentive to his commands, act agreeably, and speak endearingly to him? Would a brahmin also… a vessa also… a sudda also rise before him, retire after him, be attentive to his commands, act agreeably, and speak endearingly to him?” “Master Kaccāna, if a khattiya were to prosper with wealth, or grain, or silver, or gold, another khattiya would rise before him, retire after him, be attentive to his commands, act agreeably, and speak endearingly to him. A brahmin also… a vessa also… a sudda also would rise before him, retire after him, be attentive to his commands, act agreeably, and speak endearingly to him.”

“Taṃ [T 2.0431] kiṃ maññasi, mahārāja, brāhmaṇassa cepi ijjheyya dhanena vā dhaññena vā rajatena vā jātarūpena vā brāhmaṇopissāssa pubbuṭṭhāyī pacchānipātī kiṃkārapaṭissāvī manāpacārī piyavādī… vessopissāssa… suddopissāssa [P 2.0085]… khattiyopissāssa pubbuṭṭhāyī pacchānipātī kiṃkārapaṭissāvī manāpacārī piyavādī”ti? “Brāhmaṇassa cepi, bho kaccāna, ijjheyya dhanena vā dhaññena vā rajatena vā jātarūpena vā brāhmaṇopissāssa pubbuṭṭhāyī pacchānipātī kiṃkārapaṭissāvī manāpacārī piyavādī… vessopissāssa… suddopissāssa [M 2.0272]… khattiyopissāssa pubbuṭṭhāyī pacchānipātī kiṃkārapaṭissāvī manāpacārī piyavādī”ti.

“What do you think of this, great king? If a brahmin were to prosper with wealth, grain, silver, or gold, would another brahmin rise before him, go to bed after him, be receptive to his orders, act to please him, and speak endearingly? And would a merchant, a commoner, and a noble also rise before him, go to bed after him, be receptive to his orders, act to please him, and speak endearingly?” “If a brahmin were to prosper, Venerable Kaccāna, with wealth, grain, silver, or gold, another brahmin would rise before him, go to bed after him, be receptive to his orders, act to please him, and speak endearingly. So too would a merchant, a commoner, and a noble rise before him, go to bed after him, be receptive to his orders, act to please him, and speak endearingly.”

“Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, mahārāja, vessassa cepi ijjheyya dhanena vā dhaññena vā rajatena vā jātarūpena vā vessopissāssa pubbuṭṭhāyī pacchānipātī kiṃkārapaṭissāvī manāpacārī piyavādī… suddopissāssa… khattiyopissāssa… brāhmaṇopissāssa pubbuṭṭhāyī pacchānipātī kiṃkārapaṭissāvī manāpacārī piyavādī”ti? “Vessassa cepi, bho kaccāna, ijjheyya dhanena vā dhaññena vā rajatena vā jātarūpena vā vessopissāssa pubbuṭṭhāyī pacchānipātī kiṃkārapaṭissāvī manāpacārī piyavādī… suddopissāssa… khattiyopissāssa… brāhmaṇopissāssa pubbuṭṭhāyī pacchānipātī kiṃkārapaṭissāvī manāpacārī piyavādī”ti.

“What do you think of this, great king? If a merchant were to prosper with wealth, grain, silver, or gold, would another merchant rise before him, go to bed after him, be receptive to his orders, act to please him, and speak endearingly? And would a commoner, a noble, and a brahmin also rise before him, go to bed after him, be receptive to his orders, act to please him, and speak endearingly?” “If a merchant were to prosper, Venerable Kaccāna, with wealth, grain, silver, or gold, another merchant would rise before him, go to bed after him, be receptive to his orders, act to please him, and speak endearingly. So too would a commoner, a noble, and a brahmin rise before him, go to bed after him, be receptive to his orders, act to please him, and speak endearingly.”

“Taṃ [T 2.0432] kiṃ maññasi, mahārāja, suddassa cepi ijjheyya dhanena vā dhaññena vā rajatena vā jātarūpena vā suddopissāssa pubbuṭṭhāyī pacchānipātī kiṃkārapaṭissāvī manāpacārī piyavādī… khattiyopissāssa… brāhmaṇopissāssa… vessopissāssa pubbuṭṭhāyī pacchānipātī kiṃkārapaṭissāvī manāpacārī piyavādī”ti? “Suddassa cepi, bho kaccāna, ijjheyya dhanena vā dhaññena vā rajatena vā jātarūpena vā suddopissāssa pubbuṭṭhāyī pacchānipātī kiṃkārapaṭissāvī [V 2.0282] manāpacārī piyavādīti… khattiyopissāssa… brāhmaṇopissāssa… vessopissāssa pubbuṭṭhāyī pacchānipātī kiṃkārapaṭissāvī manāpacārī piyavādī”ti.

“What do you think of this, great king? If a commoner were to prosper with wealth, grain, silver, or gold, would another commoner rise before him, go to bed after him, be receptive to his orders, act to please him, and speak endearingly? And would a noble, a brahmin, and a merchant also rise before him, go to bed after him, be receptive to his orders, act to please him, and speak endearingly?” “If a commoner were to prosper, Venerable Kaccāna, with wealth, grain, silver, or gold, another commoner would rise before him, go to bed after him, be receptive to his orders, act to please him, and speak endearingly. So too would a noble, a brahmin, and a merchant rise before him, go to bed after him, be receptive to his orders, act to please him, and speak endearingly.”

“Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, mahārāja, yadi evaṃ sante, ime cattāro vaṇṇā samasamā honti no vā? Kathaṃ vā te ettha hotī”ti? “Addhā [P 2.0086] kho, bho kaccāna, evaṃ sante, ime cattāro vaṇṇā samasamā honti. Nesaṃ nāsaṃ (sī.), nāhaṃ (syā. kaṃ.) ettha kiñci nānākaraṇaṃ samanupassāmī”ti. “Imināpi kho etaṃ, mahārāja, pariyāyena veditabbaṃ yathā ghoso yeveso lokasmiṃ – ‘brāhmaṇova seṭṭho vaṇṇo, hīno añño vaṇṇo…pe… brahmadāyādā’”ti.

“What do you think of this, great king? This being the case, are these four classes equal or not? What is your view on this matter?” “Certainly, Venerable Kaccāna, this being the case, these four classes are equal. I see no distinction whatsoever among them in this regard.” “By this line of reasoning also, great king, it should be understood how this proclamation in the world—‘The brahmin is the highest class; other classes are inferior... heirs of Brahmā’—is merely a proclamation.”

319. “Taṃ [M 2.0273] kiṃ maññasi, mahārāja, idhassa khattiyo pāṇātipātī adinnādāyī kāmesumicchācārī musāvādī pisuṇavāco pharusavāco samphappalāpī abhijjhālu byāpannacitto micchādiṭṭhi micchādiṭṭhī (sabbattha) kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ [T 2.0433] vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjeyya no vā? Kathaṃ vā te ettha hotī”ti? “Khattiyopi hi, bho kaccāna, pāṇātipātī adinnādāyī kāmesumicchācārī musāvādī pisuṇavāco pharusavāco samphappalāpī abhijjhālu byāpannacitto micchādiṭṭhi kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjeyya. Evaṃ me ettha hoti, evañca pana me etaṃ arahataṃ suta”nti.

319. “What do you think of this, great king? Suppose a noble here were to destroy life, take what is not given, engage in sexual misconduct, speak falsely, speak divisively, speak harshly, engage in frivolous chatter, be covetous, have a mind of ill will, and hold wrong view. With the breakup of the body, after death, would he be reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a place of ruin, in hell—or not? What is your view on this matter?” “A noble, Venerable Kaccāna, who destroys life, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsely, speaks divisively, speaks harshly, engages in frivolous chatter, is covetous, has a mind of ill will, and holds wrong view, with the breakup of the body, after death, would be reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a place of ruin, in hell. This is my view on this matter, and moreover, I have heard this from the Arahants.”

“Sādhu sādhu, mahārāja! Sādhu kho te etaṃ, mahārāja, evaṃ hoti, sādhu ca pana te etaṃ arahataṃ sutaṃ. Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, mahārāja, idhassa brāhmaṇo…pe… idhassa vesso…pe… idhassa suddo pāṇātipātī adinnādāyī…pe… micchādiṭṭhi kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjeyya no vā? Kathaṃ vā te ettha hotī”ti? “Suddopi hi, bho kaccāna, pāṇātipātī adinnādāyī…pe… micchādiṭṭhi kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjeyya. Evaṃ me ettha hoti, evañca pana me etaṃ arahataṃ suta”nti.

“Good, good, great king! It is good, great king, that you hold this view, and it is good that you have heard this from the Arahants. What do you think of this, great king? Suppose a brahmin here… or a merchant… or a commoner were to destroy life, take what is not given… and hold wrong view. With the breakup of the body, after death, would he be reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a place of ruin, in hell—or not? What is your view on this matter?” “A commoner, Venerable Kaccāna, who destroys life, takes what is not given… and holds wrong view, with the breakup of the body, after death, would be reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a place of ruin, in hell. This is my view on this matter, and moreover, I have heard this from the Arahants.”

“Sādhu sādhu, mahārāja! Sādhu kho te etaṃ, mahārāja, evaṃ hoti, sādhu ca pana te etaṃ arahataṃ sutaṃ. Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, mahārāja, yadi evaṃ sante, ime cattāro vaṇṇā samasamā [V 2.0283] honti no vā? Kathaṃ vā te ettha hotī”ti? “Addhā [P 2.0087] kho, bho kaccāna, evaṃ sante, ime cattāro vaṇṇā samasamā honti. Nesaṃ ettha [T 2.0434] kiñci nānākaraṇaṃ samanupassāmī”ti. “Imināpi kho etaṃ, mahārāja, pariyāyena veditabbaṃ yathā ghoso yeveso lokasmiṃ – ‘brāhmaṇova seṭṭho vaṇṇo, hīno añño vaṇṇo…pe… brahmadāyādā’”ti.

“Good, good, great king! It is good, great king, that you hold such a view, and it is good that you have heard this from the Arahants. What do you think, great king? This being the case, are these four classes equal or not? What is your view on this?” “Certainly, Venerable Kaccāna, this being the case, these four classes are equal. I see no difference between them in this regard.” “By this method also, great king, it should be understood how that which is said in the world—‘The brahmin class alone is the best; other classes are inferior... heirs of Brahmā’—is merely a sound.”

320. “Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, mahārāja, idhassa khattiyo pāṇātipātā paṭivirato, adinnādānā paṭivirato, kāmesumicchācārā paṭivirato, musāvādā paṭivirato, pisuṇāya vācāya paṭivirato, pharusāya vācāya paṭivirato, samphappalāpā paṭivirato, anabhijjhālu abyāpannacitto sammādiṭṭhi [M 2.0274] sammādiṭṭhī (syā. kaṃ. pī. ka.) kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjeyya no vā? Kathaṃ vā te ettha hotī”ti? “Khattiyopi hi, bho kaccāna, pāṇātipātā paṭivirato, adinnādānā paṭivirato, kāmesumicchācārā paṭivirato, musāvādā paṭivirato, pisuṇāya vācāya paṭivirato, pharusāya vācāya paṭivirato, samphappalāpā paṭivirato, anabhijjhālu abyāpannacitto sammādiṭṭhi kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjeyya. Evaṃ me ettha hoti, evañca pana me etaṃ arahataṃ suta”nti.

320. “What do you think, great king? Suppose here a noble abstains from killing living beings, from taking what is not given, from sexual misconduct, from false speech, from divisive speech, from harsh speech, and from idle chatter; is not covetous, has a mind free from ill will, and possesses right view. With the breakup of the body, after death, would he be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world—or not? What is your view in this matter?” “Indeed, venerable Kaccāna, a noble who abstains from killing living beings… and possesses right view would, with the breakup of the body, after death, be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. This is my view in this matter, and moreover, this is what I have heard from the arahants.”

“Sādhu sādhu, mahārāja! Sādhu kho te etaṃ, mahārāja, evaṃ hoti, sādhu ca pana te etaṃ arahataṃ sutaṃ. Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, mahārāja, idhassa brāhmaṇo, idhassa vesso, idhassa suddo pāṇātipātā paṭivirato adinnādānā paṭivirato…pe… sammādiṭṭhi kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjeyya no vā? Kathaṃ vā [T 2.0435] te ettha hotī”ti? “Suddopi hi, bho kaccāna, pāṇātipātā paṭivirato, adinnādānā paṭivirato…pe… sammādiṭṭhi kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjeyya. Evaṃ me ettha hoti, evañca pana me etaṃ arahataṃ suta”nti.

“Good, good, great king! It is good, great king, that you have this view, and it is also good that you have heard this from the arahants. What do you think, great king? Suppose here a brahmin… a merchant… or a worker abstains from killing living beings, from taking what is not given… and possesses right view. With the breakup of the body, after death, would he be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world—or not? What is your view in this matter?” “Indeed, venerable Kaccāna, even a worker who abstains from killing living beings, from taking what is not given… and possesses right view would, with the breakup of the body, after death, be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. This is my view in this matter, and moreover, this is what I have heard from the arahants.”

“Sādhu sādhu, mahārāja! Sādhu kho te etaṃ, mahārāja, evaṃ hoti, sādhu ca pana te etaṃ arahataṃ sutaṃ. Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, mahārāja, yadi evaṃ sante, ime cattāro vaṇṇā samasamā honti no vā? Kathaṃ vā te ettha hotī”ti? “Addhā [P 2.0088] kho, bho kaccāna, evaṃ sante, ime cattāro vaṇṇā samasamā honti. Nesaṃ ettha kiñci nānākaraṇaṃ samanupassāmī”ti[V 2.0284]. “Imināpi kho etaṃ, mahārāja, pariyāyena veditabbaṃ yathā ghoso yeveso lokasmiṃ – ‘brāhmaṇova seṭṭho vaṇṇo, hīno añño vaṇṇo…pe… brahmadāyādā’”ti.

“Good, good, great king! It is good, great king, that you have this view, and it is also good that you have heard this from the arahants. What do you think, great king? This being the case, are these four classes equal or not? What is your view in this matter?” “Assuredly, venerable Kaccāna, this being the case, these four classes are equal. I see no distinction whatsoever among them in this regard.” “By this line of reasoning too, great king, it should be understood how this is merely a sound in the world: ‘The brahmin is the highest class, the other classes are inferior… heirs of Brahmā.’”

321. “Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, mahārāja, idha khattiyo sandhiṃ vā chindeyya, nillopaṃ vā hareyya, ekāgārikaṃ vā kareyya, paripanthe vā tiṭṭheyya, paradāraṃ vā gaccheyya, tañce te purisā gahetvā dasseyyuṃ – ‘ayaṃ te, deva, coro āgucārī. Imassa yaṃ icchasi taṃ daṇḍaṃ paṇehī’ti. Kinti [M 2.0275] naṃ kareyyāsī”ti? “Ghāteyyāma vā, bho kaccāna, jāpeyyāma vā pabbājeyyāma vā yathāpaccayaṃ vā kareyyāma. Taṃ kissa hetu? Yā hissa[T 2.0436], bho kaccāna, pubbe ‘khattiyo’ti samaññā sāssa antarahitā; corotveva saṅkhyaṃ saṅkhaṃ (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) gacchatī”ti.

321. “What do you think, great king? Suppose a noble here were to break into a house, commit plunder, burglarize a single house, lie in wait on the highway, or go to another man’s wife. If your men were to seize him and present him to you, saying, ‘Your Majesty, this is a thief and a wrongdoer. Impose upon him whatever punishment you wish.’ What would you do to him?” “Venerable Kaccāna, we would execute him, or burn him, or banish him, or act according to the circumstances. For what reason? Because, venerable Kaccāna, the former designation he had as ‘noble’ has disappeared; he is counted only as a thief.”

“Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, mahārāja, idha brāhmaṇo, idha vesso, idha suddo sandhiṃ vā chindeyya, nillopaṃ vā hareyya, ekāgārikaṃ vā kareyya, paripanthe vā tiṭṭheyya, paradāraṃ vā gaccheyya, tañce te purisā gahetvā dasseyyuṃ – ‘ayaṃ te, deva, coro āgucārī. Imassa yaṃ icchasi taṃ daṇḍaṃ paṇehī’ti. Kinti naṃ kareyyāsī”ti? “Ghāteyyāma vā, bho kaccāna, jāpeyyāma vā pabbājeyyāma vā yathāpaccayaṃ vā kareyyāma. Taṃ kissa hetu? Yā hissa, bho kaccāna, pubbe ‘suddo’ti samaññā sāssa antarahitā; corotveva saṅkhyaṃ gacchatī”ti.

“What do you think, great king? Suppose a brahmin here, a merchant here, or a worker here were to break into a house, commit plunder, burglarize a single house, lie in wait on the highway, or go to another man’s wife. If your men were to seize him and present him to you, saying, ‘Your Majesty, this is a thief and a wrongdoer. Impose upon him whatever punishment you wish.’ What would you do to him?” “Venerable Kaccāna, we would execute him, or burn him, or banish him, or act according to the circumstances. For what reason? Because, venerable Kaccāna, the former designation he had as ‘worker’ has disappeared; he is counted only as a thief.”

“Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, mahārāja, yadi evaṃ sante, ime cattāro vaṇṇā samasamā honti no vā? Kathaṃ vā te ettha hotī”ti? “Addhā kho, bho kaccāna, evaṃ sante, ime cattāro vaṇṇā samasamā honti. Nesaṃ ettha kiñci nānākaraṇaṃ samanupassāmī”ti. “Imināpi kho etaṃ, mahārāja, pariyāyena veditabbaṃ yathā ghoso yeveso lokasmiṃ – ‘brāhmaṇova seṭṭho vaṇṇo, hīno [P 2.0089] añño vaṇṇo…pe… brahmadāyādā’”ti.

“What do you think, great king? This being the case, are these four classes equal or not? What is your view in this matter?” “Assuredly, venerable Kaccāna, this being the case, these four classes are equal. I see no distinction whatsoever among them in this regard.” “By this line of reasoning too, great king, it should be understood how this is merely a sound in the world: ‘The brahmin is the highest class, the other classes are inferior… heirs of Brahmā.’”

322. “Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, mahārāja, idha khattiyo kesamassuṃ ohāretvā kāsāyāni vatthāni acchādetvā [T 2.0437] agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajito assa virato pāṇātipātā, virato adinnādānā, virato musāvādā, rattūparato, ekabhattiko, brahmacārī, sīlavā, kalyāṇadhammo? Kinti naṃ kareyyāsī”ti? “Abhivādeyyāma vā pi (dī. ni. 1.184, 187 sāmaññaphale), bho kaccāna, paccuṭṭheyyāma vā āsanena vā [V 2.0285] nimanteyyāma abhinimanteyyāma vā naṃ cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānappaccayabhesajjaparikkhārehi dhammikaṃ vā assa rakkhāvaraṇaguttiṃ saṃvidaheyyāma. Taṃ kissa hetu? Yā hissa, bho kaccāna, pubbe ‘khattiyo’ti samaññā sāssa antarahitā; samaṇotveva saṅkhyaṃ gacchatī”ti.

322. “What do you think, great king? Suppose a noble here were to shave off his hair and beard, put on ochre robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness; and he were to abstain from killing living beings, from taking what is not given, and from false speech; refraining from eating at night, eating only a single meal, celibate, virtuous, and of excellent character. What would you do to him?” “Venerable Kaccāna, we would pay homage to him, rise up for him, or invite him with a seat. We would also invite him to accept robes, alms-food, lodging, and medicinal requisites for the sick. We would arrange for his lawful protection, shelter, and guard. For what reason? Because, venerable Kaccāna, the former designation he had as ‘noble’ has disappeared; he is counted only as a renunciate.”

“Taṃ [M 2.0276] kiṃ maññasi, mahārāja, idha brāhmaṇo, idha vesso, idha suddo kesamassuṃ ohāretvā kāsāyāni vatthāni acchādetvā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajito assa virato pāṇātipātā, virato adinnādānā virato musāvādā, rattūparato, ekabhattiko, brahmacārī, sīlavā, kalyāṇadhammo? Kinti naṃ kareyyāsī”ti? “Abhivādeyyāma vā, bho kaccāna, paccuṭṭheyyāma vā āsanena vā nimanteyyāma abhinimanteyyāma vā naṃ cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānappaccayabhesajjaparikkhārehi dhammikaṃ vā assa rakkhāvaraṇaguttiṃ saṃvidaheyyāma. Taṃ kissa hetu? Yā hissa, bho kaccāna, pubbe ‘suddo’ti samaññā sāssa antarahitā; samaṇotveva saṅkhyaṃ gacchatī”ti.

“What do you think, great king? Suppose a brahmin, a merchant, or a worker were to shave off his hair and beard, put on saffron robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness; and he were to abstain from killing living beings, from taking what is not given, and from false speech; and he were to refrain from eating at night, eat only one meal a day, be celibate, virtuous, and of good character. What would you do to him?” “Venerable Kaccāna, we would pay homage to him, rise up for him, or invite him with a seat. We would invite him to accept robes, alms-food, lodging, and medicinal requisites for the sick. And we would arrange for him lawful protection, shelter, and security. For what reason? Because, Venerable Kaccāna, whatever former designation he had as a ‘worker,’ that has disappeared; he is reckoned only as a renunciate.”

“Taṃ [T 2.0438] kiṃ maññasi, mahārāja, yadi evaṃ sante, ime cattāro vaṇṇā samasamā honti no vā? Kathaṃ vā te ettha hotī”ti? “Addhā kho, bho kaccāna, evaṃ sante, ime cattāro vaṇṇā samasamā honti. Nesaṃ ettha kiñci nānākaraṇaṃ samanupassāmī”ti. “Imināpi kho etaṃ, mahārāja, pariyāyena veditabbaṃ yathā ghoso yeveso lokasmiṃ – ‘brāhmaṇova seṭṭho vaṇṇo, hīno añño vaṇṇo; brāhmaṇova sukko vaṇṇo, kaṇho añño vaṇṇo; brāhmaṇāva sujjhanti, no abrāhmaṇā; brāhmaṇāva brahmuno puttā orasā mukhato jātā brahmajā brahmanimmitā brahmadāyādā’”ti.

“What do you think, great king? This being so, are these four classes equal or not? Or how does it seem to you in this matter?” “Certainly, Venerable Kaccāna, this being so, these four classes are equal. I do not see any distinction whatsoever among them in this matter.” “By this reasoning too, great king, it should be understood how this is merely a proclamation in the world: ‘The brahmin class is the best class; any other class is inferior. The brahmin class is the fair class; any other class is dark. Only brahmins are purified, not non-brahmins. Only brahmins are Brahmā’s sons, his legitimate heirs, born from his mouth, born of Brahmā, created by Brahmā, and heirs of Brahmā.’”

323. Evaṃ [P 2.0090] vutte, rājā mādhuro avantiputto āyasmantaṃ mahākaccānaṃ etadavoca – “abhikkantaṃ, bho kaccāna, abhikkantaṃ, bho kaccāna! Seyyathāpi, bho kaccāna, nikkujjitaṃ vā ukkujjeyya, paṭicchannaṃ vā vivareyya, mūḷhassa vā maggaṃ ācikkheyya, andhakāre vā telapajjotaṃ dhāreyya – ‘cakkhumanto rūpāni dakkhantī’ti; evamevaṃ bhotā kaccānena anekapariyāyena dhammo pakāsito. Esāhaṃ bhavantaṃ kaccānaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi dhammañca bhikkhusaṅghañca[V 2.0286]. Upāsakaṃ maṃ bhavaṃ kaccāno dhāretu ajjatagge pāṇupetaṃ saraṇaṃ gata”nti. “Mā kho maṃ tvaṃ, mahārāja, saraṇaṃ agamāsi. Tameva tvaṃ [T 2.0439] tametaṃ tvaṃ (syā. kaṃ.), tametaṃ (ka.) bhagavantaṃ saraṇaṃ gaccha yamahaṃ saraṇaṃ gato”ti. “Kahaṃ pana, bho kaccāna, etarahi so [M 2.0277] bhagavā viharati arahaṃ sammāsambuddho”ti? “Parinibbuto kho, mahārāja, etarahi so bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho”ti. “Sacepi mayaṃ, bho kaccāna, suṇeyyāma taṃ bhagavantaṃ dasasu yojanesu, dasapi mayaṃ yojanāni gaccheyyāma taṃ bhagavantaṃ dassanāya arahantaṃ sammāsambuddhaṃ. Sacepi mayaṃ, bho kaccāna, suṇeyyāma taṃ bhagavantaṃ vīsatiyā yojanesu, tiṃsāya yojanesu, cattārīsāya yojanesu, paññāsāya yojanesu, paññāsampi mayaṃ yojanāni gaccheyyāma taṃ bhagavantaṃ dassanāya arahantaṃ sammāsambuddhaṃ. Yojanasate cepi mayaṃ bho kaccāna, suṇeyyāma taṃ bhagavantaṃ, yojanasatampi mayaṃ gaccheyyāma taṃ bhagavantaṃ dassanāya arahantaṃ sammāsambuddhaṃ. Yato ca, bho kaccāna, parinibbuto so bhagavā, parinibbutampi mayaṃ bhagavantaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāma dhammañca bhikkhusaṅghañca. Upāsakaṃ maṃ bhavaṃ kaccāno dhāretu ajjatagge pāṇupetaṃ saraṇaṃ gata”nti.

323. When this was said, King Madhura Avantiputta said this to the Venerable Mahākaccāna: “Excellent, Venerable Kaccāna, excellent! It is as if, Venerable Kaccāna, one were to set upright what was overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or point out the path to one who was lost, or hold an oil lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms. In the very same way, the Dhamma has been made clear in many ways by the Venerable Kaccāna. I go for refuge to the Venerable Kaccāna, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May the Venerable Kaccāna remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forward for as long as life lasts.” “Do not go for refuge to me, great king.
