Go for refuge to that same Blessed One to whom I have gone for refuge.” “But where, Venerable Kaccāna, does that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, now dwell?” “Great king, that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, has now attained final Nibbāna.” “Venerable Kaccāna, if we were to hear that the Blessed One was ten yojanas away, we would travel those ten yojanas to see that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. If we were to hear that the Blessed One was twenty, thirty, forty, or fifty yojanas away, we would travel even fifty yojanas to see that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. And if, Venerable Kaccāna, we were to hear that the Blessed One was a hundred yojanas away, we would travel even a hundred yojanas to see that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. But since, Venerable Kaccāna, that Blessed One has attained final Nibbāna, we go for refuge to that Blessed One even though he has attained final Nibbāna, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May the Venerable Kaccāna remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forward for as long as life lasts.”

Madhurasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ catutthaṃ.

The Madhura Sutta, the fourth, is concluded.

5. Bodhirājakumārasuttaṃ

5. The Discourse to Prince Bodhi

324. Evaṃ [T 2.0440][V 2.0287][P 2.0091] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā bhaggesu viharati susumāragire bhesakaḷāvane migadāye. Tena kho pana samayena bodhissa rājakumārassa kokanado kokanudo (syā. kaṃ. ka.) nāma pāsādo acirakārito hoti anajjhāvuṭṭho samaṇena vā brāhmaṇena vā kenaci vā manussabhūtena. Atha kho bodhi rājakumāro sañjikāputtaṃ māṇavaṃ āmantesi – “ehi tvaṃ, samma sañjikāputta, yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkama; upasaṅkamitvā mama vacanena bhagavato pāde sirasā vanda, appābādhaṃ appātaṅkaṃ lahuṭṭhānaṃ balaṃ phāsuvihāraṃ puccha – ‘bodhi, bhante, rājakumāro bhagavato pāde sirasā vandati, appābādhaṃ appātaṅkaṃ lahuṭṭhānaṃ balaṃ phāsuvihāraṃ pucchatī’ti. Evañca vadehi – ‘adhivāsetu kira, bhante, bhagavā bodhissa rājakumārassa svātanāya bhattaṃ saddhiṃ bhikkhusaṅghenā’”ti. “Evaṃ, bho”ti kho sañjikāputto māṇavo bodhissa rājakumārassa paṭissutvā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavatā saddhiṃ sammodi. Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ [M 2.0278] nisinno kho sañjikāputto māṇavo bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “bodhi kho bodhi bho gotama (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) rājakumāro bhoto gotamassa pāde sirasā [T 2.0441] vandati, appābādhaṃ appātaṅkaṃ lahuṭṭhānaṃ balaṃ phāsuvihāraṃ pucchati. Evañca vadeti – ‘adhivāsetu kira bhavaṃ gotamo bodhissa rājakumārassa svātanāya bhattaṃ saddhiṃ bhikkhusaṅghenā’”ti. Adhivāsesi bhagavā tuṇhībhāvena. Atha kho sañjikāputto māṇavo bhagavato adhivāsanaṃ viditvā uṭṭhāyāsanā yena bodhi rājakumāro tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bodhiṃ rājakumāraṃ etadavoca – “avocumha bhoto vacanena taṃ bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ – ‘bodhi kho rājakumāro bhoto [P 2.0092] gotamassa pāde sirasā vandati, appābādhaṃ appātaṅkaṃ lahuṭṭhānaṃ balaṃ phāsuvihāraṃ pucchati. Evañca vadeti – adhivāsetu kira bhavaṃ gotamo bodhissa rājakumārassa svātanāya bhattaṃ saddhiṃ bhikkhusaṅghenā’ti. Adhivuṭṭhañca pana samaṇena gotamenā”ti.

324. Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Bhaggas, at Susumāragira, in the deer sanctuary at Bhesakaḷā Grove. Now at that time, Prince Bodhi had just finished building a palace named Kokanada, which had not yet been occupied by any ascetic, brahmin, or any human being. Then Prince Bodhi addressed the young man Sañjikāputta: "Come, dear Sañjikāputta, approach the Blessed One. Having approached, pay homage at the Blessed One’s feet with your head on my behalf, and inquire whether he is free from illness and affliction, agile, strong, and dwelling at ease—saying, ‘Venerable sir, Prince Bodhi pays homage at the Blessed One’s feet with his head and inquires whether the Blessed One is free from illness and affliction, agile, strong, and dwelling at ease.’ And say this: ‘Venerable sir, may the Blessed One kindly accept Prince Bodhi’s invitation for tomorrow’s meal together with the Sangha of bhikkhus.’" "Yes, sir," replied the young man Sañjikāputta to Prince Bodhi. He then approached the Blessed One and exchanged courteous greetings with him. When they had concluded their greetings and amiable talk, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the young man Sañjikāputta said to the Blessed One: "Prince Bodhi pays homage at the feet of the venerable Gotama with his head and inquires whether the venerable Gotama is free from illness and affliction, agile, strong, and dwelling at ease. And he says this: ‘May the venerable Gotama kindly accept Prince Bodhi’s invitation for tomorrow’s meal together with the Sangha of bhikkhus.’" The Blessed One consented by silence. Then the young man Sañjikāputta, understanding the Blessed One’s acceptance, rose from his seat, approached Prince Bodhi, and said: "We conveyed your message to the venerable Gotama: ‘Prince Bodhi pays homage at the feet of the venerable Gotama with his head and inquires whether he is free from illness and affliction, agile, strong, and dwelling at ease. And he says this: May the venerable Gotama kindly accept Prince Bodhi’s invitation for tomorrow’s meal together with the Sangha of bhikkhus.’ And the ascetic Gotama has consented."

325. Atha kho bodhi rājakumāro tassā rattiyā accayena sake nivesane paṇītaṃ khādanīyaṃ bhojanīyaṃ paṭiyādāpetvā, kokanadañca pāsādaṃ odātehi dussehi santharāpetvā yāva pacchimasopānakaḷevarā [V 2.0288] kaḷebarā (sī.), sañjikāputtaṃ māṇavaṃ āmantesi – “ehi tvaṃ, samma sañjikāputta, yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkama; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavato kālaṃ ārocehi – ‘kālo, bhante, niṭṭhitaṃ bhatta’”nti. “Evaṃ, bho”ti kho sañjikāputto māṇavo bodhissa rājakumārassa paṭissutvā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavato kālaṃ ārocesi – “kālo, bho gotama, niṭṭhitaṃ bhatta”nti. Atha [T 2.0442] kho bhagavā pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya yena bodhissa rājakumārassa nivesanaṃ tenupasaṅkami. Tena kho pana samayena bodhi rājakumāro bahidvārakoṭṭhake ṭhito hoti bhagavantaṃ āgamayamāno. Addasā kho bodhi rājakumāro bhagavantaṃ dūratova āgacchantaṃ. Disvāna paccuggantvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā purakkhatvā yena kokanado pāsādo tenupasaṅkami. Atha kho bhagavā pacchimaṃ sopānakaḷevaraṃ nissāya aṭṭhāsi. Atha kho bodhi rājakumāro bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “abhiruhatu abhirūhatu (syā. kaṃ. pī.) akkamatu (cūḷava. 268), bhante, bhagavā dussāni, abhiruhatu sugato dussāni; yaṃ mama assa dīgharattaṃ hitāya [M 2.0279] sukhāyā”ti. Evaṃ vutte, bhagavā tuṇhī ahosi. Dutiyampi kho…pe… tatiyampi kho bodhi rājakumāro bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “abhiruhatu, bhante, bhagavā. Dussāni, abhiruhatu sugato dussāni; yaṃ mama assa dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāyā”ti.

325. Then, Prince Bodhi, after the night had passed, had fine hard and soft food prepared in his own residence and had the Kokanada Palace spread with white cloths right down to the last step of the staircase. He then addressed the young man Sañjikāputta: "Come, dear Sañjikāputta, approach the Blessed One. Having approached, announce the time to the Blessed One: 'It is time, venerable sir, the meal is ready.'" "Yes, sir," replied the young man Sañjikāputta to Prince Bodhi. He then approached the Blessed One and announced the time: "It is time, venerable Gotama, the meal is ready." Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and outer robe, went to the residence of Prince Bodhi. At that time, Prince Bodhi was standing at the outer gatehouse, awaiting the Blessed One. Prince Bodhi saw the Blessed One coming from afar. Seeing him, he went out to meet him, paid homage to the Blessed One, and led him to the Kokanada Palace. Then the Blessed One stood at the foot of the staircase. Prince Bodhi then said to the Blessed One: "May the Blessed One ascend upon the cloths, venerable sir; may the Sugata ascend upon the cloths. May that be for my long-term welfare and happiness." When this was said, the Blessed One remained silent. A second time… and a third time, Prince Bodhi said to the Blessed One: "May the Blessed One ascend upon the cloths, venerable sir; may the Sugata ascend upon the cloths. May that be for my long-term welfare and happiness."

326. Atha kho bhagavā āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ apalokesi. Atha kho āyasmā [P 2.0093] ānando bodhiṃ rājakumāraṃ etadavoca – “saṃharatu, rājakumāra, dussāni; na bhagavā celapaṭikaṃ celapattikaṃ (sī. pī.) akkamissati. Pacchimaṃ janataṃ tathāgato anukampatī”ti apaloketīti (sabbattha). Atha kho bodhi rājakumāro dussāni saṃharāpetvā uparikokanadapāsāde uparikokanade pāsāde (sī. pī. vinayeca), uparikokanade (syā. kaṃ.) āsanāni paññapesi. Atha kho bhagavā kokanadaṃ pāsādaṃ [T 2.0443] abhiruhitvā paññatte āsane nisīdi saddhiṃ bhikkhusaṅghena. Atha kho bodhi rājakumāro buddhappamukhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ paṇītena khādanīyena bhojanīyena sahatthā santappesi sampavāresi. Atha kho bodhi rājakumāro bhagavantaṃ bhuttāviṃ onītapattapāṇiṃ aññataraṃ nīcaṃ āsanaṃ gahetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho bodhi rājakumāro bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “mayhaṃ kho, bhante, evaṃ hoti – ‘na kho sukhena sukhaṃ adhigantabbaṃ, dukkhena kho sukhaṃ adhigantabba’”nti.

326. Then the Blessed One glanced at Venerable Ānanda. Then Venerable Ānanda said to Prince Bodhi: "Gather up the cloths, Prince. The Blessed One will not step on the cloth covering. The Tathāgata has compassion for future generations." Then Prince Bodhi had the cloths gathered up and had seats prepared in the upper Kokanada palace. Then the Blessed One ascended the Kokanada palace and sat down on the prepared seat together with the Sangha of bhikkhus. Then Prince Bodhi, with his own hands, served and satisfied the Sangha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha with fine hard and soft food until they indicated they had had enough. When the Blessed One had finished his meal and withdrawn his hand from the bowl, Prince Bodhi took a low seat and sat to one side. Seated to one side, Prince Bodhi said to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, this thought occurs to me: 'Happiness is not to be attained through pleasure; happiness is to be attained through suffering.'"

327. “Mayhampi kho, rājakumāra, pubbeva sambodhā anabhisambuddhassa bodhisattasseva sato [V 2.0289] etadahosi – ‘na kho sukhena sukhaṃ adhigantabbaṃ, dukkhena kho sukhaṃ adhigantabba’nti. So kho ahaṃ, rājakumāra, aparena samayena daharova samāno susukāḷakeso bhadrena yobbanena samannāgato paṭhamena vayasā akāmakānaṃ mātāpitūnaṃ assumukhānaṃ rudantānaṃ kesamassuṃ ohāretvā kāsāyāni vatthāni acchādetvā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajiṃ. So evaṃ pabbajito samāno kiṃkusalagavesī kiṃkusalaṃgavesī (ka.) anuttaraṃ santivarapadaṃ pariyesamāno yena āḷāro kālāmo tenupasaṅkamiṃ; upasaṅkamitvā āḷāraṃ kālāmaṃ etadavocaṃ – ‘icchāmahaṃ, āvuso kālāma, imasmiṃ dhammavinaye brahmacariyaṃ caritu’nti. Evaṃ vutte, rājakumāra, āḷāro kālāmo maṃ etadavoca – ‘viharatāyasmā, tādiso [M 2.0280] ayaṃ dhammo yattha viññū puriso nacirasseva sakaṃ ācariyakaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja vihareyyā’ti. So [T 2.0444] kho ahaṃ, rājakumāra, nacirasseva khippameva taṃ dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇiṃ. So kho ahaṃ, rājakumāra, tāvatakeneva oṭṭhapahatamattena lapitalāpanamattena ñāṇavādañca vadāmi, theravādañca jānāmi passāmīti ca paṭijānāmi, ahañceva aññe ca. Tassa mayhaṃ, rājakumāra, etadahosi – ‘na kho āḷāro kālāmo imaṃ dhammaṃ kevalaṃ saddhāmattakena sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharāmīti pavedeti; addhā āḷāro kālāmo imaṃ dhammaṃ jānaṃ passaṃ viharatī’ti.

327. To me also, prince, before my awakening, when I was still an unawakened Bodhisatta, this thought occurred: ‘Indeed, happiness is not to be attained through ease; happiness is to be attained through hardship.’ So, prince, at a later time, while still a young man with jet-black hair, endowed with blessed youth, in the prime of life, though my mother and father were unwilling and wept with tearful faces, I shaved off my hair and beard, put on the ochre robes, and went forth from the household life into homelessness. Having thus gone forth, seeking what is wholesome, searching for the unsurpassed, supreme state of peace, I approached Āḷāra Kālāma. Having approached, I said this to Āḷāra Kālāma: ‘Friend Kālāma, I wish to lead the holy life in this Dhamma and Discipline.’ When this was said, prince, Āḷāra Kālāma said this to me: ‘Let the venerable one dwell. This Dhamma is such that an intelligent person could, in no long time, realize for himself with direct knowledge his own teacher's doctrine, and having attained it, dwell therein.’ Then, prince, in no long time, very quickly, I mastered that Dhamma. To that extent, prince, with mere lip-service, with mere recitation, I could speak the ‘knowledge-claim’ and the ‘elder’s claim,’ and I professed, ‘I know, I see’—I as well as others. To me, prince, this thought occurred: ‘Āḷāra Kālāma does not declare this Dhamma from mere faith alone, saying, “Having realized it for myself with direct knowledge and attained it, I dwell therein.” Surely, Āḷāra Kālāma dwells knowing and seeing this Dhamma.’

“Atha khvāhaṃ, rājakumāra, yena āḷāro kālāmo tenupasaṅkamiṃ; upasaṅkamitvā āḷāraṃ kālāmaṃ etadavocaṃ – ‘kittāvatā no, āvuso kālāma, imaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharāmīti pavedesī’ti upasampajja pavedesīti (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.)? Evaṃ vutte, rājakumāra, āḷāro kālāmo ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ pavedesi. Tassa mayhaṃ, rājakumāra, etadahosi – ‘na kho āḷārasseva kālāmassa atthi saddhā, mayhaṃpatthi saddhā; na kho āḷārasseva kālāmassa atthi vīriyaṃ…pe… sati… samādhi… paññā, mayhaṃpatthi paññā. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ yaṃ dhammaṃ āḷāro kālāmo sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharāmīti pavedeti tassa dhammassa sacchikiriyāya padaheyya’nti. So kho ahaṃ, rājakumāra, nacirasseva khippameva taṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja vihāsiṃ. Atha [T 2.0445] khvāhaṃ, rājakumāra, yena āḷāro kālāmo tenupasaṅkamiṃ; upasaṅkamitvā āḷāraṃ kālāmaṃ etadavocaṃ – ‘ettāvatā no, āvuso kālāma, imaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja pavedesī’ti? ‘Ettāvatā kho ahaṃ, āvuso, imaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja pavedemī’ti. ‘Ahampi kho, āvuso, ettāvatā imaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharāmī’ti. ‘Lābhā no, āvuso, suladdhaṃ no, āvuso, ye mayaṃ āyasmantaṃ tādisaṃ sabrahmacāriṃ passāma[V 2.0290]. Iti yāhaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja pavedemi, taṃ tvaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharasi. Yaṃ tvaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharasi, tamahaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā [M 2.0281] upasampajja pavedemi. Iti yāhaṃ dhammaṃ jānāmi taṃ tvaṃ dhammaṃ jānāsi; yaṃ tvaṃ dhammaṃ jānāsi tamahaṃ dhammaṃ jānāmi. Iti yādiso ahaṃ, tādiso tuvaṃ; yādiso tuvaṃ tādiso ahaṃ. Ehi dāni, āvuso, ubhova santā imaṃ gaṇaṃ pariharāmā’ti. Iti kho, rājakumāra, āḷāro kālāmo ācariyo me samāno (attano) ( ) natthi (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) antevāsiṃ maṃ samānaṃ attanā attano (sī. pī.) samasamaṃ ṭhapesi, uḷārāya ca maṃ pūjāya pūjesi. Tassa mayhaṃ, rājakumāra, etadahosi – ‘nāyaṃ dhammo nibbidāya na virāgāya na nirodhāya na upasamāya na abhiññāya na sambodhāya na nibbānāya saṃvattati, yāvadeva ākiñcaññāyatanūpapattiyā’ti[T 2.0446]. So kho ahaṃ, rājakumāra, taṃ dhammaṃ analaṅkaritvā tasmā dhammā nibbijja apakkamiṃ.

Then, prince, I approached Āḷāra Kālāma. Having approached, I said this to Āḷāra Kālāma: ‘Friend Kālāma, to what extent do you declare this Dhamma, having realized it for yourself with direct knowledge, and having attained it, you declare that you dwell therein?’ When this was said, prince, Āḷāra Kālāma declared the sphere of nothingness. To me, prince, this thought occurred: ‘It is not that Āḷāra Kālāma alone has faith; I too have faith. It is not that Āḷāra Kālāma alone has energy… mindfulness… concentration… wisdom; I too have wisdom. What if I were to strive for the realization of that Dhamma which Āḷāra Kālāma declares he has realized for himself with direct knowledge, and having attained it, dwells therein?’ Then, prince, in no long time, very quickly, I realized that Dhamma for myself with direct knowledge, and having attained it, dwelt therein. Then, prince, I approached Āḷāra Kālāma. Having approached, I said this to Āḷāra Kālāma: ‘Friend Kālāma, is it to this extent that you declare this Dhamma, having realized it for yourself with direct knowledge and having attained it?’ ‘It is to this extent, friend, that I declare this Dhamma, having realized it for myself with direct knowledge and having attained it.’ ‘I too, friend, to this extent have realized this Dhamma for myself with direct knowledge, and having attained it, dwell therein.’ ‘It is a gain for us, friend, a great gain for us, that we see such a venerable companion in the holy life. The Dhamma that I declare, having realized it for myself with direct knowledge and having attained it, that Dhamma you have realized for yourself with direct knowledge, and having attained it, dwell in. The Dhamma that you have realized for yourself with direct knowledge, and having attained it, dwell in, that Dhamma I declare, having realized it for myself with direct knowledge and having attained it. Thus, the Dhamma I know, you know; the Dhamma you know, I know. As I am, so are you; as you are, so am I. Come now, friend, let us both lead this community.’ Thus, prince, Āḷāra Kālāma, being my teacher, placed me, his student, on an equal footing with himself and honored me with great honor. To me, prince, this thought occurred: ‘This Dhamma does not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to awakening, or to Nibbāna, but only as far as rebirth in the sphere of nothingness.’ So, prince, not being satisfied with that Dhamma, I became disenchanted with it and departed.

328. “So kho ahaṃ, rājakumāra, kiṃkusalagavesī anuttaraṃ santivarapadaṃ pariyesamāno yena udako uddako (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) rāmaputto tenupasaṅkamiṃ; upasaṅkamitvā udakaṃ rāmaputtaṃ etadavocaṃ – ‘icchāmahaṃ, āvuso āvuso rāma (sī. syā. kaṃ. ka.) passa ma. ni. 1.278 pāsarāsisutte, imasmiṃ dhammavinaye brahmacariyaṃ caritu’nti. Evaṃ vutte, rājakumāra, udako rāmaputto maṃ etadavoca – ‘viharatāyasmā, tādiso ayaṃ dhammo yattha viññū puriso nacirasseva sakaṃ ācariyakaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja vihareyyā’ti. So kho ahaṃ, rājakumāra, nacirasseva khippameva taṃ dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇiṃ. So kho ahaṃ, rājakumāra, tāvatakeneva oṭṭhapahatamattena lapitalāpanamattena ñāṇavādañca vadāmi, theravādañca jānāmi passāmīti ca paṭijānāmi, ahañceva aññe ca. Tassa mayhaṃ, rājakumāra, etadahosi – ‘na kho rāmo imaṃ dhammaṃ kevalaṃ saddhāmattakena sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharāmīti pavedesi; addhā rāmo imaṃ dhammaṃ jānaṃ passaṃ vihāsī’ti. Atha khvāhaṃ, rājakumāra, yena udako rāmaputto tenupasaṅkamiṃ; upasaṅkamitvā udakaṃ rāmaputtaṃ etadavocaṃ – ‘kittāvatā no, āvuso, rāmo imaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharāmīti pavedesī’ti? Evaṃ vutte, rājakumāra, udako rāmaputto nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ pavedesi. Tassa [T 2.0447] mayhaṃ, rājakumāra, etadahosi – ‘na kho rāmasseva ahosi saddhā, mayhaṃpatthi saddhā; na kho rāmasseva ahosi vīriyaṃ…pe… sati… samādhi… paññā, mayhaṃpatthi [M 2.0282] paññā. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ yaṃ dhammaṃ rāmo sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharāmīti pavedeti tassa dhammassa sacchikiriyāya padaheyya’nti. So kho ahaṃ, rājakumāra, nacirasseva khippameva taṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja vihāsiṃ.

328. Then, prince, seeking what is wholesome, searching for the unsurpassed, sublime state of peace, I approached Udaka Rāmaputta. Having approached, I said to Udaka Rāmaputta: ‘Friend, I wish to lead the holy life in this Dhamma and Discipline.’ When this was said, prince, Udaka Rāmaputta said to me: ‘Let the venerable one stay. Such is this Dhamma that an intelligent person can, in no long time, realize for himself with higher knowledge his own teacher’s doctrine, and having attained it, abide therein.’ Indeed, prince, in no long time, I quickly learned that Dhamma. Indeed, prince, with just that much, with mere lip-service and recitation, I spoke the doctrine of knowledge and the established teaching, and I claimed, as did others, ‘I know, I see.’ Then, prince, it occurred to me: ‘Rāma did not declare this Dhamma out of mere faith, saying, “Having realized it for myself with higher knowledge, and having attained it, I abide therein.” Surely, Rāma abided knowing and seeing this Dhamma.’ Then, prince, I approached Udaka Rāmaputta. Having approached, I said to Udaka Rāmaputta: ‘Friend, to what extent did Rāma declare this Dhamma, saying, “Having realized it for myself with higher knowledge, and having attained it, I abide therein”?’ When this was said, prince, Udaka Rāmaputta declared the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Then it occurred to me, prince: ‘It was not only Rāma who had faith; I too have faith. It was not only Rāma who had energy... mindfulness... concentration... wisdom; I too have wisdom. What if I were to strive for the realization of that Dhamma which Rāma declared, saying, “Having realized it for myself with higher knowledge, and having attained it, I abide therein”?’ Indeed, prince, in no long time, I quickly realized that Dhamma for myself with higher knowledge, and having attained it, I abided therein.

“Atha [V 2.0291] khvāhaṃ, rājakumāra, yena udako rāmaputto tenupasaṅkamiṃ; upasaṅkamitvā udakaṃ rāmaputtaṃ etadavocaṃ – ‘ettāvatā no, āvuso, rāmo imaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja pavedesī’ti? ‘Ettāvatā kho, āvuso, rāmo imaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja pavedesī’ti. ‘Ahampi kho, āvuso, ettāvatā imaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharāmī’ti. ‘Lābhā no, āvuso, suladdhaṃ no, āvuso, ye mayaṃ āyasmantaṃ tādisaṃ sabrahmacāriṃ passāma. Iti yaṃ dhammaṃ rāmo sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja pavedesi taṃ tvaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharasi. Yaṃ tvaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharasi taṃ dhammaṃ rāmo sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja pavedesi. Iti yaṃ dhammaṃ rāmo abhiññāsi taṃ tvaṃ dhammaṃ jānāsi; yaṃ tvaṃ dhammaṃ jānāsi taṃ dhammaṃ rāmo abhiññāsi. Iti [T 2.0448] yādiso rāmo ahosi tādiso tuvaṃ, yādiso tuvaṃ tādiso rāmo ahosi. Ehi dāni, āvuso, tuvaṃ imaṃ gaṇaṃ pariharā’ti. Iti kho, rājakumāra, udako rāmaputto sabrahmacārī me samāno ācariyaṭṭhāne maṃ ṭhapesi, uḷārāya ca maṃ pūjāya pūjesi. Tassa mayhaṃ, rājakumāra, etadahosi – ‘nāyaṃ dhammo nibbidāya na virāgāya na nirodhāya na upasamāya na abhiññāya na sambodhāya na nibbānāya saṃvattati, yāvadeva nevasaññānāsaññāyatanūpapattiyā’ti. So kho ahaṃ, rājakumāra, taṃ dhammaṃ analaṅkaritvā tasmā dhammā nibbijja apakkamiṃ.

Then, prince, I approached Udaka Rāmaputta. Having approached, I said to Udaka Rāmaputta: ‘Friend, was it to this extent that Rāma declared this Dhamma, having realized it for himself with higher knowledge and having attained it?’ ‘Friend, it was to this extent that Rāma declared this Dhamma, having realized it for himself with higher knowledge and having attained it.’ ‘I too, friend, to this extent have realized this Dhamma for myself with higher knowledge, and having attained it, I abide therein.’ ‘It is a gain for us, friend, a great gain for us, that we see such a venerable companion in the holy life. Thus, the Dhamma that Rāma declared, having realized it for himself with higher knowledge and having attained it—that Dhamma you abide in, having realized it for yourself with higher knowledge and having attained it. The Dhamma that you abide in, having realized it for yourself with higher knowledge and having attained it—that Dhamma Rāma declared, having realized it for himself with higher knowledge and having attained it. Thus, the Dhamma that Rāma directly knew, you know; the Dhamma that you know, Rāma directly knew. Thus, as Rāma was, so are you; as you are, so was Rāma. Come now, friend, you should lead this group.’ In this way, prince, Udaka Rāmaputta, my companion in the holy life, placed me in the position of a teacher and honored me with the highest honor. Then, prince, it occurred to me: ‘This Dhamma does not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to higher knowledge, to enlightenment, or to Nibbāna, but leads only to rebirth in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.’ So, prince, not being satisfied with that Dhamma, I became disenchanted with it and departed.

329. “So kho ahaṃ, rājakumāra, kiṃkusalagavesī anuttaraṃ santivarapadaṃ pariyesamāno, magadhesu anupubbena cārikaṃ caramāno, yena uruvelā senānigamo tadavasariṃ. Tatthaddasaṃ ramaṇīyaṃ bhūmibhāgaṃ, pāsādikañca vanasaṇḍaṃ, nadīñca sandantiṃ setakaṃ supatitthaṃ, ramaṇīyaṃ samantā ca gocaragāmaṃ. Tassa mayhaṃ, rājakumāra, etadahosi – ‘ramaṇīyo vata, bho, bhūmibhāgo, pāsādiko ca vanasaṇḍo, nadiñca sandantiṃ setakā supatitthā[M 2.0283], ramaṇīyā samantā sāmantā (?) purimapiṭṭhepi ca gocaragāmo. Alaṃ vatidaṃ kulaputtassa padhānatthikassa padhānāyā’ti. So kho ahaṃ, rājakumāra, tattheva nisīdiṃ – ‘alamidaṃ padhānāyā’ti. Apissu maṃ, rājakumāra, tisso upamā paṭibhaṃsu anacchariyā pubbe [T 2.0449] assutapubbā.

329. Then, prince, seeking what is wholesome, searching for the unsurpassed, sublime state of peace, I wandered by stages through the Magadhan country and in due course arrived at the army township of Uruvelā. There I saw a delightful stretch of land, a lovely woodland grove, a flowing river with clear water and pleasant fords, and a village for alms-resort nearby. Then, prince, it occurred to me: ‘Truly, this is a delightful stretch of land, a lovely woodland grove, and the river flows, delightful with clear water and pleasant fords, with a village for alms-resort nearby. This is indeed a suitable place for a clansman intent on striving to engage in striving.’ So, prince, I sat down right there, thinking: ‘This is a suitable place for striving.’ And then, prince, three amazing similes occurred to me, which I had never heard before.

“Seyyathāpi, rājakumāra, allaṃ kaṭṭhaṃ sasnehaṃ udake nikkhittaṃ. Atha puriso āgaccheyya uttarāraṇiṃ ādāya – ‘aggiṃ abhinibbattessāmi, tejo pātukarissāmī’ti. Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, rājakumāra, api nu so puriso amuṃ allaṃ kaṭṭhaṃ sasnehaṃ udake nikkhittaṃ uttarāraṇiṃ [V 2.0292] ādāya abhimanthento abhimatthanto (syā. kaṃ. ka.) aggiṃ abhinibbatteyya, tejo pātukareyyā”ti? “No hidaṃ, bhante. Taṃ kissa hetu? Aduñhi, bhante, allaṃ kaṭṭhaṃ sasnehaṃ tañca pana udake nikkhittaṃ, yāvadeva ca pana so puriso kilamathassa vighātassa bhāgī assā”ti. “Evameva kho, rājakumāra, ye hi keci samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā kāyena ceva cittena ca kāmehi avūpakaṭṭhā viharanti, yo ca nesaṃ kāmesu kāmacchando kāmasneho kāmamucchā kāmapipāsā kāmapariḷāho so ca ajjhattaṃ na suppahīno hoti, na suppaṭippassaddho. Opakkamikā cepi te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā dukkhā tibbā kharā kaṭukā vedanā vedayanti, abhabbāva te ñāṇāya dassanāya anuttarāya sambodhāya. No cepi te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā opakkamikā dukkhā tibbā kharā kaṭukā vedanā vedayanti, abhabbāva te ñāṇāya dassanāya anuttarāya sambodhāya. Ayaṃ kho maṃ, rājakumāra, paṭhamā upamā paṭibhāsi anacchariyā pubbe assutapubbā.

Prince, suppose there were a wet, sappy piece of wood placed in water. Then a man would come with an upper fire-stick, thinking, ‘I shall produce fire, I shall make heat appear.’ What do you think, prince? Could that man, by taking the upper fire-stick and rubbing that wet, sappy piece of wood that had been placed in water, produce fire and make heat appear?" "No, venerable sir. For what reason? Because, venerable sir, that piece of wood is wet and sappy, and it has been placed in water. That man would only become a partaker of fatigue and vexation." "So it is, prince, with any ascetics or brahmins who dwell with body and mind not withdrawn from sensual pleasures, and for whom the sensual desire, sensual affection, sensual obsession, sensual thirst, and sensual fever for sensual pleasures have not been well abandoned and well calmed internally. Even if those venerable ascetics and brahmins, through their striving, experience painful, sharp, harsh, and bitter feelings, they are incapable of knowledge, of vision, of unsurpassed enlightenment. And even if those venerable ascetics and brahmins, through their striving, do not experience painful, sharp, harsh, and bitter feelings, they are incapable of knowledge, of vision, of unsurpassed enlightenment. This, prince, is the first simile that occurred to me, extraordinary and unheard of before.

330. “Aparāpi kho maṃ, rājakumāra, dutiyā upamā paṭibhāsi anacchariyā [T 2.0450] pubbe assutapubbā. Seyyathāpi, rājakumāra, allaṃ kaṭṭhaṃ sasnehaṃ ārakā udakā thale nikkhittaṃ. Atha puriso āgaccheyya uttarāraṇiṃ ādāya – ‘aggiṃ abhinibbattessāmi, tejo pātukarissāmī’ti. Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, rājakumāra, api nu so puriso amuṃ allaṃ kaṭṭhaṃ sasnehaṃ ārakā udakā thale nikkhittaṃ uttarāraṇiṃ ādāya abhimanthento aggiṃ abhinibbatteyya[M 2.0284], tejo pātukareyyā”ti? “No hidaṃ, bhante. Taṃ kissa hetu? Aduñhi, bhante, allaṃ kaṭṭhaṃ sasnehaṃ kiñcāpi ārakā udakā thale nikkhittaṃ, yāvadeva ca pana so puriso kilamathassa vighātassa bhāgī assā”ti. “Evameva kho, rājakumāra, ye hi keci samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā kāyena ceva cittena ca kāmehi vūpakaṭṭhā viharanti, yo ca nesaṃ kāmesu kāmacchando kāmasneho kāmamucchā kāmapipāsā kāmapariḷāho so ca ajjhattaṃ na suppahīno hoti, na suppaṭippassaddho. Opakkamikā cepi te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā dukkhā tibbā kharā kaṭukā vedanā vedayanti, abhabbāva te ñāṇāya dassanāya anuttarāya sambodhāya. No cepi te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā opakkamikā dukkhā tibbā kharā kaṭukā vedanā vedayanti, abhabbāva te ñāṇāya dassanāya anuttarāya sambodhāya. Ayaṃ kho maṃ, rājakumāra, dutiyā upamā paṭibhāsi anacchariyā pubbe assutapubbā.

330. Furthermore, prince, a second simile occurred to me, extraordinary and unheard of before. Suppose, prince, there were a wet, sappy piece of wood placed on dry land, far from water. Then a man would come with an upper fire-stick, thinking, ‘I shall produce fire, I shall make heat appear.’ What do you think, prince? Could that man, by taking the upper fire-stick and rubbing that wet, sappy piece of wood that had been placed on dry land far from water, produce fire and make heat appear?" "No, venerable sir. For what reason? Because, venerable sir, although that piece of wood is wet and sappy, and has been placed on dry land far from water, that man would only become a partaker of fatigue and vexation." "So it is, prince, with any ascetics or brahmins who dwell with body and mind withdrawn from sensual pleasures, but for whom the sensual desire, sensual affection, sensual obsession, sensual thirst, and sensual fever for sensual pleasures have not been well abandoned and well calmed internally. Even if those venerable ascetics and brahmins, through their striving, experience painful, sharp, harsh, and bitter feelings, they are incapable of knowledge, of vision, of unsurpassed enlightenment. And even if those venerable ascetics and brahmins, through their striving, do not experience painful, sharp, harsh, and bitter feelings, they are incapable of knowledge, of vision, of unsurpassed enlightenment. This, prince, is the second simile that occurred to me, extraordinary and unheard of before.

331. “Aparāpi [V 2.0293] kho maṃ, rājakumāra, tatiyā upamā paṭibhāsi anacchariyā [T 2.0451] pubbe assutapubbā. Seyyathāpi, rājakumāra, sukkhaṃ kaṭṭhaṃ koḷāpaṃ ārakā udakā thale nikkhittaṃ. Atha puriso āgaccheyya uttarāraṇiṃ ādāya – ‘aggiṃ abhinibbattessāmi, tejo pātukarissāmī’ti. Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, rājakumāra, api nu so puriso amuṃ sukkhaṃ kaṭṭhaṃ koḷāpaṃ ārakā udakā thale nikkhittaṃ uttarāraṇiṃ ādāya abhimanthento aggiṃ abhinibbatteyya, tejo pātukareyyā”ti? “Evaṃ, bhante”. Taṃ kissa hetu? Aduñhi, bhante, sukkhaṃ kaṭṭhaṃ koḷāpaṃ, tañca pana ārakā udakā thale nikkhitta”nti. “Evameva kho, rājakumāra, ye hi keci samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā kāyena ceva cittena ca kāmehi vūpakaṭṭhā viharanti, yo ca nesaṃ kāmesu kāmacchando kāmasneho kāmamucchā kāmapipāsā kāmapariḷāho so ca ajjhattaṃ suppahīno hoti suppaṭippassaddho. Opakkamikā cepi te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā dukkhā tibbā kharā kaṭukā vedanā vedayanti, bhabbāva te ñāṇāya dassanāya anuttarāya sambodhāya. No cepi te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā opakkamikā dukkhā tibbā kharā kaṭukā vedanā [M 2.0285] vedayanti, bhabbāva te ñāṇāya dassanāya anuttarāya sambodhāya. Ayaṃ kho maṃ, rājakumāra, tatiyā upamā paṭibhāsi anacchariyā pubbe assutapubbā. Imā kho maṃ, rājakumāra, tisso upamā paṭibhaṃsu anacchariyā pubbe assutapubbā.

331. Furthermore, prince, a third simile occurred to me, extraordinary and unheard of before. Suppose, prince, there were a dry, sapless piece of wood placed on dry land, far from water. Then a man would come with an upper fire-stick, thinking, ‘I shall produce fire, I shall make heat appear.’ What do you think, prince? Could that man, by taking the upper fire-stick and rubbing that dry, sapless piece of wood that had been placed on dry land far from water, produce fire and make heat appear?" "Yes, venerable sir." "For what reason?" "Because, venerable sir, that piece of wood is dry and sapless, and it has been placed on dry land, far from water." "So it is, prince, with any ascetics or brahmins who dwell with body and mind withdrawn from sensual pleasures, and for whom the sensual desire, sensual affection, sensual obsession, sensual thirst, and sensual fever for sensual pleasures have been well abandoned and well calmed internally. Even if those venerable ascetics and brahmins, through their striving, experience painful, sharp, harsh, and bitter feelings, they are capable of knowledge, of vision, of unsurpassed enlightenment. And even if those venerable ascetics and brahmins, through their striving, do not experience painful, sharp, harsh, and bitter feelings, they are capable of knowledge, of vision, of unsurpassed enlightenment. This, prince, is the third simile that occurred to me, extraordinary and unheard of before. These, prince, are the three similes that occurred to me, extraordinary and unheard of before.

332. “Tassa [T 2.0452] mayhaṃ, rājakumāra, etadahosi – ‘yaṃnūnāhaṃ dantebhidantamādhāya passa ma. ni. 1.220 vitakkasaṇṭhānasutte, jivhāya tāluṃ āhacca, cetasā cittaṃ abhiniggaṇheyyaṃ abhinippīḷeyyaṃ abhisantāpeyya’nti. So kho ahaṃ, rājakumāra, dantebhidantamādhāya, jivhāya tāluṃ āhacca, cetasā cittaṃ abhiniggaṇhāmi abhinippīḷemi abhisantāpemi. Tassa mayhaṃ, rājakumāra, dantebhidantamādhāya, jivhāya tāluṃ āhacca, cetasā cittaṃ abhiniggaṇhato abhinippīḷayato abhisantāpayato kacchehi sedā muccanti. Seyyathāpi, rājakumāra, balavā puriso dubbalataraṃ purisaṃ sīse vā gahetvā khandhe vā gahetvā abhiniggaṇheyya abhinippīḷeyya abhisantāpeyya; evameva kho me, rājakumāra, dantebhidantamādhāya, jivhāya tāluṃ āhacca, cetasā cittaṃ abhiniggaṇhato abhinippīḷayato abhisantāpayato kacchehi sedā muccanti. Āraddhaṃ kho pana me, rājakumāra, vīriyaṃ hoti asallīnaṃ, upaṭṭhitā sati asammuṭṭhā, sāraddho ca pana me kāyo hoti appaṭippassaddho, teneva dukkhappadhānena padhānābhitunnassa sato.

332. To me, O prince, this thought occurred: 'What if I, with teeth clenched and tongue pressed against the palate, should with the mind restrain, crush, and torment the mind?' So, O prince, with teeth clenched and tongue pressed against the palate, I restrained, crushed, and tormented the mind with the mind. As I, O prince, was doing so, sweat flowed from my armpits. Just as, O prince, a strong man, having seized a weaker man by the head or by the shoulders, might restrain, crush, and torment him; even so, O prince, as I was restraining the mind with the mind with teeth clenched and tongue pressed against the palate, sweat flowed from my armpits. Indeed, O prince, my energy was aroused and unshrinking, my mindfulness was established and unconfused; however, my body was agitated and uncalmed, being pierced by that very painful striving.

333. “Tassa [V 2.0294] mayhaṃ, rājakumāra, etadahosi – ‘yaṃnūnāhaṃ appāṇakaṃyeva jhānaṃ jhāyeyya’nti. So kho ahaṃ, rājakumāra, mukhato ca nāsato ca assāsapassāse uparundhiṃ. Tassa mayhaṃ, rājakumāra, mukhato ca nāsato ca assāsapassāsesu uparuddhesu kaṇṇasotehi vātānaṃ [T 2.0453] nikkhamantānaṃ adhimatto saddo hoti. Seyyathāpi nāma kammāragaggariyā dhamamānāya adhimatto saddo hoti, evameva kho me, rājakumāra, mukhato ca nāsato ca assāsapassāsesu uparuddhesu kaṇṇasotehi vātānaṃ nikkhamantānaṃ adhimatto saddo hoti. Āraddhaṃ kho pana me, rājakumāra, vīriyaṃ hoti asallīnaṃ, upaṭṭhitā [M 2.0286] sati asammuṭṭhā, sāraddho ca pana me kāyo hoti appaṭippassaddho, teneva dukkhappadhānena padhānābhitunnassa sato.

333. To me, O prince, this thought occurred: 'What if I were to practice the breathless meditation?' So, O prince, I stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths from the mouth and from the nose. As I, O prince, stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths from the mouth and from the nose, there was an exceedingly loud sound of winds exiting from the orifices of my ears. Just as there is an exceedingly loud sound from a blacksmith's bellows when it is being blown, even so, O prince, when the in-breaths and out-breaths from my mouth and nose were stopped, there was an exceedingly loud sound of winds exiting from the orifices of my ears. Indeed, O prince, my energy was aroused and unshrinking, my mindfulness was established and unconfused; however, my body was agitated and uncalmed, being pierced by that very painful striving.

“Tassa mayhaṃ, rājakumāra, etadahosi – ‘yaṃnūnāhaṃ appāṇakaṃyeva jhānaṃ jhāyeyya’nti. So kho ahaṃ, rājakumāra, mukhato ca nāsato ca kaṇṇato ca assāsapassāse uparundhiṃ. Tassa mayhaṃ, rājakumāra, mukhato ca nāsato ca kaṇṇato ca assāsapassāsesu uparuddhesu adhimattā vātā muddhani ūhananti ūhanti (sī.), ohananti (syā. kaṃ.), uhananti (ka.). Seyyathāpi, rājakumāra, balavā puriso tiṇhena sikharena muddhani abhimattheyya muddhānaṃ abhimantheyya (sī. pī.), muddhānaṃ abhimattheyya (syā. kaṃ.), evameva kho me, rājakumāra, mukhato ca nāsato ca kaṇṇato ca assāsapassāsesu uparuddhesu adhimattā vātā muddhani ūhananti. Āraddhaṃ kho pana me, rājakumāra, vīriyaṃ hoti asallīnaṃ, upaṭṭhitā sati asammuṭṭhā, sāraddho ca pana me kāyo hoti appaṭippassaddho, teneva dukkhappadhānena padhānābhitunnassa sato.

To me, O prince, this thought occurred: 'What if I were to practice the breathless meditation?' So, O prince, I stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths from the mouth, from the nose, and from the ears. As I, O prince, stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths from the mouth, from the nose, and from the ears, excessive winds struck my head. Just as, O prince, a strong man might bore into one's head with a sharp point; even so, O prince, when the in-breaths and out-breaths from my mouth, nose, and ears were stopped, excessive winds struck my head. Indeed, O prince, my energy was aroused and unshrinking, my mindfulness was established and unconfused; however, my body was agitated and uncalmed, being pierced by that very painful striving.

“Tassa [T 2.0454] mayhaṃ, rājakumāra, etadahosi – ‘yaṃnūnāhaṃ appāṇakaṃyeva jhānaṃ jhāyeyya’nti. So kho ahaṃ, rājakumāra, mukhato ca nāsato ca kaṇṇato ca assāsapassāse uparundhiṃ. Tassa mayhaṃ, rājakumāra, mukhato ca nāsato ca kaṇṇato ca assāsapassāsesu uparuddhesu adhimattā sīse sīsavedanā honti. Seyyathāpi, rājakumāra, balavā puriso daḷhena varattakkhaṇḍena varattakabandhanena (sī.) sīse sīsaveṭhaṃ dadeyya; evameva kho me, rājakumāra, mukhato ca nāsato ca kaṇṇato ca assāsapassāsesu uparuddhesu adhimattā sīse sīsavedanā honti. Āraddhaṃ kho pana me, rājakumāra, vīriyaṃ hoti asallīnaṃ, upaṭṭhitā sati asammuṭṭhā, sāraddho ca pana me kāyo hoti appaṭippassaddho, teneva dukkhappadhānena padhānābhitunnassa sato.

To me, O prince, this thought occurred: 'What if I were to practice the breathless meditation?' So, O prince, I stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths from the mouth, from the nose, and from the ears. As I, O prince, stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths from the mouth, from the nose, and from the ears, excessive pains arose in my head. Just as, O prince, a strong man might bind one's head with a strong leather strap as a headband; even so, O prince, when the in-breaths and out-breaths from my mouth, nose, and ears were stopped, excessive pains arose in my head. Indeed, O prince, my energy was aroused and unshrinking, my mindfulness was established and unconfused; however, my body was agitated and uncalmed, being pierced by that very painful striving.

“Tassa mayhaṃ, rājakumāra, etadahosi – ‘yaṃnūnāhaṃ appāṇakaṃyeva jhānaṃ jhāyeyya’nti. So kho ahaṃ, rājakumāra, mukhato ca nāsato ca kaṇṇato ca assāsapassāse uparundhiṃ. Tassa mayhaṃ, rājakumāra, mukhato ca nāsato ca kaṇṇato ca assāsapassāsesu uparuddhesu adhimattā [V 2.0295] vātā kucchiṃ parikantanti. Seyyathāpi, rājakumāra, dakkho goghātako vā goghātakantevāsī vā tiṇhena govikantanena kucchiṃ parikanteyya, evameva kho me, rājakumāra, mukhato ca nāsato ca kaṇṇato ca assāsapassāsesu uparuddhesu adhimattā[T 2.0455], vātā kucchiṃ parikantanti. Āraddhaṃ kho pana me, rājakumāra, vīriyaṃ hoti asallīnaṃ, upaṭṭhitā sati asammuṭṭhā, sāraddho ca pana me kāyo hoti appaṭippassaddho, teneva dukkhappadhānena padhānābhitunnassa sato.

To me, O prince, this thought occurred: 'What if I were to practice the breathless meditation?' So, O prince, I stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths from the mouth, from the nose, and from the ears. As I, O prince, stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths from the mouth, from the nose, and from the ears, excessive winds cut through my belly. Just as, O prince, a skilled butcher or his apprentice might cut through a belly with a sharp butcher's knife; even so, O prince, when the in-breaths and out-breaths from my mouth, nose, and ears were stopped, excessive winds cut through my belly. Indeed, O prince, my energy was aroused and unshrinking, my mindfulness was established and unconfused; however, my body was agitated and uncalmed, being pierced by that very painful striving.

“Tassa mayhaṃ, rājakumāra, etadahosi – ‘yaṃnūnāhaṃ appāṇakaṃyeva jhānaṃ jhāyeyya’nti. So kho ahaṃ, rājakumāra, mukhato ca nāsato ca kaṇṇato ca assāsapassāse uparundhiṃ. Tassa mayhaṃ, rājakumāra, mukhato ca nāsato ca kaṇṇato ca assāsapassāsesu uparuddhesu [M 2.0287] adhimatto kāyasmiṃ ḍāho hoti. Seyyathāpi, rājakumāra, dve balavanto purisā dubbalataraṃ purisaṃ nānābāhāsu gahetvā aṅgārakāsuyā santāpeyyuṃ samparitāpeyyuṃ, evameva kho me, rājakumāra, mukhato ca nāsato ca kaṇṇato ca assāsapassāsesu uparuddhesu adhimatto kāyasmiṃ ḍāho hoti. Āraddhaṃ kho pana me, rājakumāra, vīriyaṃ hoti asallīnaṃ, upaṭṭhitā sati asammuṭṭhā, sāraddho ca pana me kāyo hoti appaṭippassaddho, teneva dukkhappadhānena padhānābhitunnassa sato.

Then, O prince, this thought occurred to me: 'What if I were to practice the jhāna that is entirely without breath?' So, O prince, I restrained the in-breaths and out-breaths through my mouth, nose, and ears. As I restrained the in-breaths and out-breaths through my mouth, nose, and ears, O prince, an excessive burning arose in my body. Just as if, O prince, two strong men were to seize a weaker man by his various arms and roast and scorch him over a pit of embers; even so, O prince, when I restrained the in-breaths and out-breaths through my mouth, nose, and ears, an excessive burning arose in my body. Indeed, O prince, my energy was roused and unflagging, my mindfulness was established and unconfused; however, my body was agitated and uncalmed, being pierced by that painful exertion.

“Apissu maṃ, rājakumāra, devatā disvā evamāhaṃsu – ‘kālaṅkato samaṇo gotamo’ti. Ekaccā devatā evamāhaṃsu – ‘na kālaṅkato samaṇo gotamo, api ca kālaṅkarotī’ti. Ekaccā devatā evamāhaṃsu – ‘na kālaṅkato samaṇo gotamo, nāpi kālaṅkaroti[T 2.0456]. Arahaṃ samaṇo gotamo. Vihārotveva so vihārotveveso (sī.) arahato evarūpo hotī’ti vihārotveveso arahato”ti (?).

Moreover, O prince, some deities, having seen me, said this: ‘The ascetic Gotama is dead.’ Certain deities said this: ‘The ascetic Gotama is not dead, but he is dying.’ Certain other deities said this: ‘The ascetic Gotama is not dead, nor is he dying. The ascetic Gotama is an Arahant. Such, indeed, is the abiding of an Arahant.’

334. “Tassa mayhaṃ, rājakumāra, etadahosi – ‘yaṃnūnāhaṃ sabbaso āhārupacchedāya paṭipajjeyya’nti. Atha kho maṃ, rājakumāra, devatā upasaṅkamitvā [M 2.0288] etadavocuṃ – ‘mā kho tvaṃ, mārisa, sabbaso āhārupacchedāya paṭipajji. Sace kho tvaṃ, mārisa, sabbaso āhārupacchedāya paṭipajjissasi, tassa te mayaṃ dibbaṃ ojaṃ lomakūpehi ajjhohāressāma ajjhoharissāma (syā. kaṃ. pī. ka.), tāya tvaṃ yāpessasī’ti. Tassa mayhaṃ, rājakumāra, etadahosi – ‘ahañceva kho pana sabbaso ajajjitaṃ ajaddhukaṃ (sī. pī.), jaddhukaṃ (syā. kaṃ.) paṭijāneyyaṃ. Imā ca me devatā dibbaṃ ojaṃ lomakūpehi ajjhohāreyyuṃ ajjhohareyyuṃ (syā. kaṃ. pī. ka.), tāya cāhaṃ yāpeyyaṃ, taṃ mamassa musā’ti. So kho ahaṃ, rājakumāra, tā devatā paccācikkhāmi. ‘Hala’nti vadāmi.

334. Then, O prince, this thought occurred to me: 'What if I were to practice the complete cutting off of food?' Then, O prince, deities approached me and said this: 'Do not, good sir, practice the complete cutting off of food. If you, good sir, should practice the complete cutting off of food, we will infuse divine nutriment into the pores of your skin, and by that you will sustain yourself.' Then, O prince, this thought occurred to me: 'If I were to profess complete fasting, and these deities were to infuse divine nutriment into the pores of my skin, and I were to sustain myself by that, it would be a falsehood on my part.' So, O prince, I refused those deities, saying: 'That is not acceptable.'

“Tassa [V 2.0296] mayhaṃ, rājakumāra, etadahosi – ‘yaṃnūnāhaṃ thokaṃ thokaṃ āhāraṃ āhāreyyaṃ pasataṃ pasataṃ, yadi vā muggayūsaṃ yadi vā kulatthayūsaṃ yadi vā kaḷāyayūsaṃ yadi vā hareṇukayūsa’nti. So kho ahaṃ, rājakumāra, thokaṃ thokaṃ āhāraṃ āhāresiṃ pasataṃ pasataṃ, yadi vā muggayūsaṃ yadi vā kulatthayūsaṃ yadi vā kaḷāyayūsaṃ yadi vā hareṇukayūsaṃ. Tassa mayhaṃ, rājakumāra, thokaṃ thokaṃ āhāraṃ āhārayato pasataṃ pasataṃ, yadi vā muggayūsaṃ yadi vā kulatthayūsaṃ [T 2.0457] yadi vā kaḷāyayūsaṃ yadi vā hareṇukayūsaṃ, adhimattakasimānaṃ patto kāyo hoti. Seyyathāpi nāma āsītikapabbāni vā kāḷapabbāni vā, evamevassu me aṅgapaccaṅgāni bhavanti tāyevappāhāratāya. Seyyathāpi nāma oṭṭhapadaṃ, evamevassu me ānisadaṃ hoti tāyevappāhāratāya. Seyyathāpi nāma vaṭṭanāvaḷī, evamevassu me piṭṭhikaṇṭako uṇṇatāvanato hoti tāyevappāhāratāya. Seyyathāpi nāma jarasālāya gopānasiyo oluggaviluggā bhavanti, evamevassu me phāsuḷiyo oluggaviluggā bhavanti tāyevappāhāratāya. Seyyathāpi nāma gambhīre udapāne udakatārakā gambhīragatā okkhāyikā dissanti, evamevassu me akkhikūpesu akkhitārakā gambhīragatā okkhāyikā dissanti tāyevappāhāratāya. Seyyathāpi nāma tittakālābu āmakacchinno vātātapena saṃphuṭito samphusito (syā. kaṃ.), saṃpuṭīto (ka.) saṃphuṭitoti ettha saṅkucitoti attho hoti sammilāto, evamevassu me sīsacchavi saṃphuṭitā hoti sammilātā tāyevappāhāratāya. So kho [M 2.0289] ahaṃ, rājakumāra, ‘udaracchaviṃ parimasissāmī’ti piṭṭhikaṇṭakaṃyeva pariggaṇhāmi, ‘piṭṭhikaṇṭakaṃ parimasissāmī’ti udaracchaviṃyeva pariggaṇhāmi. Yāvassu me, rājakumāra, udaracchavi piṭṭhikaṇṭakaṃ allīnā hoti tāyevappāhāratāya. So kho ahaṃ, rājakumāra, ‘vaccaṃ vā muttaṃ vā karissāmī’ti tattheva avakujjo papatāmi tāyevappāhāratāya. So kho [T 2.0458] ahaṃ, rājakumāra, imameva kāyaṃ assāsento pāṇinā gattāni anumajjāmi. Tassa mayhaṃ, rājakumāra, pāṇinā gattāni anumajjato pūtimūlāni lomāni kāyasmā papatanti tāyevappāhāratāya. Apissu maṃ, rājakumāra, manussā disvā evamāhaṃsu – ‘kāḷo samaṇo gotamo’ti, ekacce manussā evamāhaṃsu – ‘na kāḷo samaṇo gotamo, sāmo samaṇo gotamo’ti. Ekacce manussā evamāhaṃsu – ‘na kāḷo samaṇo gotamo, napi sāmo, maṅguracchavi samaṇo gotamo’ti. Yāvassu me, rājakumāra, tāva parisuddho chavivaṇṇo pariyodāto upahato hoti tāyevappāhāratāya.

Then, O prince, this thought occurred to me: 'What if I were to take only a little food at a time, a hollowed handful at a time, whether of bean soup, horse-gram soup, chickpea soup, or pea soup?' So, O prince, I took only a little food at a time, a hollowed handful at a time, whether of bean soup, horse-gram soup, chickpea soup, or pea soup. As I was taking such little food, O prince, my body reached a state of extreme emaciation. Due to that very lack of food, my limbs became like the joints of an āsītika plant or a kāḷa plant. Due to that very lack of food, my buttocks became like a camel's hoof. Due to that very lack of food, my spine became prominent and sunken like a string of beads. Due to that very lack of food, my ribs jutted out, crooked and broken, like the rafters of a decaying hall. Due to that very lack of food, the pupils of my eyes, sunk deep in their sockets, appeared as reflections of stars in the water of a deep well. Due to that very lack of food, the skin of my scalp became shriveled and withered, like a bitter gourd cut raw and withered by wind and sun. O prince, when I thought, 'I will touch the skin of my belly,' it was my very spine that I took hold of. When I thought, 'I will touch my spine,' it was the skin of my belly that I took hold of. To such an extent, O prince, had the skin of my belly clung to my spine due to that very lack of food. O prince, when I thought, 'I will defecate or urinate,' I would fall down right there on my face due to that very lack of food. O prince, as I was soothing this very body by rubbing my limbs with my hands, the body-hairs, their roots rotted, fell from my body due to that very lack of food. Moreover, O prince, people who saw me said this: 'The ascetic Gotama is black.' Some people said: 'The ascetic Gotama is not black, he is dark-skinned.' Other people said: 'The ascetic Gotama is neither black nor dark-skinned; he has the complexion of a maṅgura fish.' To such an extent, O prince, was my pure and bright skin-complexion ruined due to that very lack of food.

335. “Tassa mayhaṃ, rājakumāra, etadahosi – ‘ye kho keci atītamaddhānaṃ samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā opakkamikā dukkhā tibbā tippā (sī. pī.) kharā kaṭukā vedanā vedayiṃsu, etāvaparamaṃ nayito bhiyyo. Yepi hi keci anāgatamaddhānaṃ samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā opakkamikā dukkhā [V 2.0297] tibbā kharā kaṭukā vedanā vedayissanti, etāvaparamaṃ nayito bhiyyo. Yepi hi keci etarahi samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā opakkamikā dukkhā tibbā kharā kaṭukā vedanā vedayanti, etāvaparamaṃ nayito bhiyyo. Na kho panāhaṃ imāya kaṭukāya dukkarakārikāya adhigacchāmi uttarimanussadhammā alamariyañāṇadassanavisesaṃ; siyā nu kho añño maggo bodhāyā’ti. Tassa mayhaṃ, rājakumāra, etadahosi – ‘abhijānāmi kho panāhaṃ [T 2.0459] pitu sakkassa kammante sītāya jambucchāyāya nisinno vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharitā; siyā nu kho eso maggo bodhāyā’ti. Tassa mayhaṃ, rājakumāra, satānusāri viññāṇaṃ ahosi – ‘eseva maggo bodhāyā’ti. Tassa mayhaṃ, rājakumāra, etadahosi – ‘kiṃ nu kho ahaṃ tassa sukhassa bhāyāmi yaṃ taṃ sukhaṃ aññatreva kāmehi aññatra akusalehi [M 2.0290] dhammehī’ti? Tassa mayhaṃ, rājakumāra, etadahosi – ‘na kho ahaṃ tassa sukhassa bhāyāmi yaṃ taṃ sukhaṃ aññatreva kāmehi aññatra akusalehi dhammehī’ti.

335. Then, prince, this thought occurred to me: ‘Whatever striving ascetics or brahmins in the past experienced painful, sharp, harsh, and bitter feelings, that was their utmost limit; there is nothing beyond this. And whatever striving ascetics or brahmins in the future will experience painful, sharp, harsh, and bitter feelings, that will be their utmost limit; there is nothing beyond this. And whatever striving ascetics or brahmins at present are experiencing painful, sharp, harsh, and bitter feelings, that is their utmost limit; there is nothing beyond this. Yet I, by this bitter and difficult practice, do not attain any state superior to that of ordinary humans, any special knowledge and vision befitting the noble ones. Might there be another path to enlightenment?’ Then, prince, this thought occurred to me: ‘I recall that while my father the Sakyan was engaged in his work, I, sitting in the cool shade of a rose-apple tree, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, entered and abided in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. Might this be the path to enlightenment?’ Then, prince, a consciousness that followed upon that memory arose in me: ‘This indeed is the path to enlightenment.’ Then, prince, this thought occurred to me: ‘Why should I fear that happiness which is apart from sensual pleasures and apart from unwholesome states?’ Then, prince, this thought occurred to me: ‘I do not fear that happiness which is apart from sensual pleasures and apart from unwholesome states.’

“Tassa mayhaṃ, rājakumāra, etadahosi – ‘na kho taṃ sukaraṃ sukhaṃ adhigantuṃ evaṃ adhimattakasimānaṃ pattakāyena. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ oḷārikaṃ āhāraṃ āhāreyyaṃ odanakummāsa’nti. So kho ahaṃ, rājakumāra, oḷārikaṃ āhāraṃ āhāresiṃ odanakummāsaṃ. Tena kho pana maṃ, rājakumāra, samayena pañcavaggiyā bhikkhū paccupaṭṭhitā honti – ‘yaṃ kho samaṇo gotamo dhammaṃ adhigamissati taṃ no ārocessatī’ti. Yato kho ahaṃ, rājakumāra, oḷārikaṃ āhāraṃ āhāresiṃ odanakummāsaṃ, atha me te pañcavaggiyā bhikkhū nibbijja pakkamiṃsu – ‘bāhulliko bāhuliko (sī. pī.) sāratthaṭīkāya saṃghabhedasikkhāpadavaṇṇanāya sameti samaṇo gotamo padhānavibbhanto, āvatto bāhullāyā’ti.

Then, prince, this thought occurred to me: ‘It is not easy to attain that happiness with a body that has reached such a state of extreme emaciation. What if I were to take coarse food, namely rice and barley-meal?’ So I, prince, took coarse food, namely rice and barley-meal. At that time, prince, the five bhikkhus were attending on me, thinking: ‘Whatever Dhamma the ascetic Gotama attains, he will announce it to us.’ But when I, prince, took coarse food, namely rice and barley-meal, those five bhikkhus left me in disgust, thinking: ‘The ascetic Gotama has become one who lives in abundance; he has deviated from striving and reverted to a life of abundance.’

336. “So kho ahaṃ, rājakumāra, oḷārikaṃ āhāraṃ āhāretvā [T 2.0460] balaṃ gahetvā vivicceva kāmehi…pe… paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja vihāsiṃ. Vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā… dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ… tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ… catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja vihāsiṃ. So evaṃ samāhite citte parisuddhe pariyodāte anaṅgaṇe vigatūpakkilese mudubhūte kammaniye ṭhite āneñjappatte pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇāya [V 2.0298] cittaṃ abhininnāmesiṃ. So anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarāmi, seyyathidaṃ – ekampi jātiṃ dvepi jātiyo…pe… iti sākāraṃ sauddesaṃ anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarāmi. Ayaṃ kho me, rājakumāra, rattiyā paṭhame yāme paṭhamā vijjā adhigatā, avijjā vihatā, vijjā uppannā; tamo vihato, āloko uppanno – yathā taṃ appamattassa ātāpino pahitattassa viharato.

336. So I, prince, having taken coarse food and regained strength, quite secluded from sensual pleasures… entered and abided in the first jhāna. With the stilling of thought and examination… the second jhāna… the third jhāna… I entered and abided in the fourth jhāna. When my mind was thus concentrated, purified, luminous, without blemish, free from defilements, malleable, workable, steady, and had attained imperturbability, I inclined my mind towards the knowledge of recollecting past abodes. I recollected my manifold past abodes, that is, one birth, two births… thus with their aspects and details I recollected my manifold past abodes. This, prince, was the first true knowledge attained by me in the first watch of the night. Ignorance was dispelled, true knowledge arose; darkness was dispelled, light arose—as happens to one who abides diligent, ardent, and resolute.

“So evaṃ samāhite citte parisuddhe pariyodāte anaṅgaṇe vigatūpakkilese mudubhūte kammaniye ṭhite āneñjappatte sattānaṃ cutūpapātañāṇāya cittaṃ abhininnāmesiṃ. So dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena satte passāmi cavamāne upapajjamāne hīne paṇīte suvaṇṇe dubbaṇṇe sugate duggate yathākammūpage satte pajānāmi [M 2.0291] …pe… ayaṃ kho me, rājakumāra, rattiyā majjhime yāme dutiyā vijjā adhigatā, avijjā vihatā, vijjā uppannā; tamo vihato, āloko uppanno – yathā taṃ appamattassa ātāpino pahitattassa viharato.

When my mind was thus concentrated, purified, luminous, without blemish, free from defilements, malleable, workable, steady, and had attained imperturbability, I inclined my mind towards the knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings. With the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, I saw beings passing away and reappearing—inferior and superior, of good appearance and bad appearance, in good destinations and bad destinations. I understood beings as passing on according to their kamma. This, prince, was the second true knowledge attained by me in the middle watch of the night. Ignorance was dispelled, true knowledge arose; darkness was dispelled, light arose—as happens to one who abides diligent, ardent, and resolute.

“So [T 2.0461] evaṃ samāhite citte parisuddhe pariyodāte anaṅgaṇe vigatūpakkilese mudubhūte kammaniye ṭhite āneñjappatte āsavānaṃ khayañāṇāya cittaṃ abhininnāmesiṃ. So ‘idaṃ dukkha’nti yathābhūtaṃ abbhaññāsiṃ…pe… ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yathābhūtaṃ abbhaññāsiṃ; ‘ime āsavā’ti yathābhūtaṃ abbhaññāsiṃ…pe… ‘ayaṃ āsavanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yathābhūtaṃ abbhaññāsiṃ. Tassa me evaṃ jānato evaṃ passato kāmāsavāpi cittaṃ vimuccittha, bhavāsavāpi cittaṃ vimuccittha, avijjāsavāpi cittaṃ vimuccittha. Vimuttasmiṃ vimuttamiti ñāṇaṃ ahosi. ‘Khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti abbhaññāsiṃ. Ayaṃ kho me, rājakumāra, rattiyā pacchime yāme tatiyā vijjā adhigatā, avijjā vihatā, vijjā uppannā; tamo vihato, āloko uppanno – yathā taṃ appamattassa ātāpino pahitattassa viharato.

When my mind was thus concentrated, purified, luminous, without blemish, free from defilements, malleable, workable, steady, and had attained imperturbability, I inclined my mind towards the knowledge of the destruction of the taints. I directly knew, as it really is: ‘This is suffering.’ I directly knew, as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering.’ I directly knew, as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering.’ I directly knew, as it really is: ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.’ I directly knew, as it really is: ‘These are the taints.’ I directly knew, as it really is: ‘This is the origin of the taints.’ I directly knew, as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of the taints.’ I directly knew, as it really is: ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of the taints.’ Knowing thus and seeing thus, my mind was liberated from the taint of sensual pleasure, from the taint of existence, and from the taint of ignorance. When it was liberated, the knowledge arose: ‘It is liberated.’ I directly knew: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this state of being.’ This, prince, was the third true knowledge attained by me in the last watch of the night. Ignorance was dispelled, true knowledge arose; darkness was dispelled, light arose—as happens to one who abides diligent, ardent, and resolute.

337. “Tassa mayhaṃ, rājakumāra, etadahosi – ‘adhigato kho myāyaṃ dhammo gambhīro duddaso duranubodho santo paṇīto atakkāvacaro nipuṇo paṇḍitavedanīyo. Ālayarāmā kho panāyaṃ pajā ālayaratā ālayasammuditā. Ālayarāmāya kho pana pajāya ālayaratāya ālayasammuditāya [V 2.0299] duddasaṃ idaṃ ṭhānaṃ yadidaṃ – idappaccayatāpaṭiccasamuppādo. Idampi kho ṭhānaṃ duddasaṃ – yadidaṃ sabbasaṅkhārasamatho sabbūpadhipaṭinissaggo taṇhākkhayo virāgo nirodho nibbānaṃ[T 2.0462]. Ahañceva kho pana dhammaṃ deseyyaṃ, pare ca me na ājāneyyuṃ, so mamassa kilamatho, sā mamassa vihesā’ti. Apissu maṃ, rājakumāra, imā anacchariyā gāthāyo paṭibhaṃsu pubbe assutapubbā –

337. O prince, this thought occurred to me: ‘This Dhamma has been attained by me, which is profound, hard to see, hard to understand, peaceful, sublime, beyond the sphere of reasoning, subtle, knowable only by the wise. Indeed, this generation delights in attachment, is fond of attachment, and rejoices in attachment. For a generation that delights in, is fond of, and rejoices in attachment, this principle is hard to see, that is, this conditionality, Dependent Origination. This principle, too, is hard to see, that is, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all substrates of existence, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna. If I were to teach the Dhamma, and others were not to understand it, that would be a weariness for me; that would be a vexation for me.’ Moreover, O prince, these unprecedented verses, never heard before, occurred to me:

‘Kicchena me adhigataṃ, halaṃ dāni pakāsituṃ;

Rāgadosaparetehi, nāyaṃ dhammo susambudho.

‘What I have attained with difficulty, it is not fit to declare it now; by those afflicted with lust and hate, this Dhamma cannot be well understood.

‘Paṭisotagāmiṃ nipuṇaṃ, gambhīraṃ duddasaṃ aṇuṃ;

Rāgarattā na dakkhanti, tamokhandhena āvuṭā’ āvaṭā (sī.), āvutā (syā. kaṃ.) ti.

‘Going against the stream, subtle, profound, hard to see, and minute—those impassioned with lust, being covered by the mass of ignorance, will not see it.’

“Itiha [M 2.0292] me, rājakumāra, paṭisañcikkhato appossukkatāya cittaṃ namati no dhammadesanāya.

Thus, O prince, as I was reflecting, my mind inclined towards non-exertion, and not towards teaching the Dhamma.

338. “Atha kho, rājakumāra, brahmuno sahampatissa mama cetasā cetoparivitakkamaññāya etadahosi – ‘nassati vata, bho, loko; vinassati vata, bho, loko. Yatra hi nāma tathāgatassa arahato sammāsambuddhassa appossukkatāya cittaṃ namati namissati (?) no dhammadesanāyā’ti. Atha kho, rājakumāra, brahmā sahampati – seyyathāpi nāma balavā puriso samiñjitaṃ vā bāhaṃ pasāreyya pasāritaṃ vā bāhaṃ samiñjeyya, evameva – brahmaloke antarahito mama purato pāturahosi. Atha kho, rājakumāra, brahmā sahampati ekaṃsaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ karitvā yenāhaṃ tenañjaliṃ paṇāmetvā maṃ etadavoca – ‘desetu, bhante, bhagavā dhammaṃ, desetu sugato dhammaṃ. Santi sattā apparajakkhajātikā assavanatāya dhammassa parihāyanti; bhavissanti dhammassa aññātāro’ti[T 2.0463]. Idamavoca, rājakumāra, brahmā sahampati; idaṃ vatvā athāparaṃ etadavoca –

338. Then, O prince, Brahmā Sahampati, having known with his mind the thought in my mind, had this thought: ‘Alas, the world is lost! Alas, the world is perishing! For the mind of the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, inclines towards non-exertion, and not towards teaching the Dhamma.’ Then, O prince, just as a strong man might stretch out his bent arm or bend his outstretched arm, even so did Brahmā Sahampati disappear from the Brahmā world and appear before me. Then, O prince, Brahmā Sahampati, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder and having extended his joined hands towards me, said this to me: ‘Venerable sir, let the Blessed One teach the Dhamma! Let the Well-Farer teach the Dhamma! There are beings whose nature is to have little dust in their eyes. Because of not hearing the Dhamma, they are declining. There will be those who will understand the Dhamma.’ This is what Brahmā Sahampati said, O prince. Having said this, he spoke further:

‘Pāturahosi magadhesu pubbe,

Dhammo asuddho samalehi cintito;

Apāpuretaṃ avāpuretaṃ (sī.) amatassa dvāraṃ,

Suṇantu dhammaṃ vimalenānubuddhaṃ.

‘Formerly in Magadha there appeared an impure Dhamma, thought out by those with defilements. Open this door of the Deathless! Let them hear the Dhamma rightly understood by the Stainless One.

‘Sele [V 2.0300] yathā pabbatamuddhaniṭṭhito,

Yathāpi passe janataṃ samantato;

Tathūpamaṃ dhammamayaṃ sumedha,

Pāsādamāruyha samantacakkhu.

‘Just as one standing on a mountain peak of solid rock might see the people all around, so too, O One of good wisdom, O All-Seeing One, having ascended the palace made of Dhamma,

‘Sokāvatiṇṇaṃ sokāvakiṇṇaṃ (syā.) janatamapetasoko,

Avekkhassu jātijarābhibhūtaṃ;

Uṭṭhehi vīra, vijitasaṅgāma,

Satthavāha aṇaṇa anaṇa (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī. ka.), vicara loke;

Desassu desetu (syā. kaṃ. ka.) bhagavā dhammaṃ,

Aññātāro bhavissantī’ti.

‘being yourself free from sorrow, look upon this generation immersed in sorrow, overcome by birth and old age. Arise, O hero, victor in battle! O Caravan Leader, free from debt, wander in the world. Teach the Dhamma, O Blessed One; there will be those who will understand it.’

339. “Atha [M 2.0293] khvāhaṃ, rājakumāra, brahmuno ca ajjhesanaṃ viditvā sattesu ca kāruññataṃ paṭicca buddhacakkhunā lokaṃ volokesiṃ. Addasaṃ kho ahaṃ, rājakumāra, buddhacakkhunā lokaṃ volokento satte apparajakkhe mahārajakkhe tikkhindriye mudindriye svākāre dvākāre suviññāpaye [T 2.0464] duviññāpaye appekacce paralokavajjabhayadassāvine dassāvino (syā. kaṃ. ka.) viharante, appekacce na paralokavajjabhayadassāvine viharante. Seyyathāpi nāma uppaliniyaṃ vā paduminiyaṃ vā puṇḍarīkiniyaṃ vā appekaccāni uppalāni vā padumāni vā puṇḍarīkāni vā udake jātāni udake saṃvaḍḍhāni udakānuggatāni antonimuggaposīni, appekaccāni uppalāni vā padumāni vā puṇḍarīkāni vā udake jātāni udake saṃvaḍḍhāni udakānuggatāni samodakaṃ ṭhitāni, appekaccāni uppalāni vā padumāni vā puṇḍarīkāni vā udake jātāni udake saṃvaḍḍhāni udakā accuggamma ṭhitāni tiṭṭhanti (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) anupalittāni udakena, evameva kho ahaṃ, rājakumāra, buddhacakkhunā lokaṃ volokento addasaṃ satte apparajakkhe mahārajakkhe tikkhindriye mudindriye svākāre dvākāre suviññāpaye duviññāpaye, appekacce paralokavajjabhayadassāvine viharante, appekacce na paralokavajjabhayadassāvine viharante. Atha khvāhaṃ, rājakumāra, brahmānaṃ sahampatiṃ gāthāya paccabhāsiṃ –

339. Then, O prince, having understood Brahmā's request and on account of my compassion for beings, I surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye. As I surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye, O prince, I saw beings with little dust in their eyes and with much dust, with sharp faculties and with dull faculties, with good dispositions and with bad dispositions, easy to teach and difficult to teach. I saw some dwelling who perceive danger in the faults of the next world, and some dwelling who do not perceive danger in the faults of the next world. Just as in a pond of blue, red, or white lotuses, some lotuses are born in the water, grow up in the water, and are nourished while remaining immersed within the water; some lotuses are born in the water, grow up in the water, and stand at the water's surface; and some lotuses are born in the water, grow up in the water, and stand having risen above the water, unstained by the water. Even so, O prince, as I surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye, I saw beings with little dust and with much dust, with sharp faculties and with dull faculties, with good dispositions and with bad dispositions, easy to teach and difficult to teach; some dwelling who perceive danger in the faults of the next world, and some dwelling who do not. Then, O prince, I replied to Brahmā Sahampati in verse:

‘Apārutā tesaṃ amatassa dvārā,

Ye sotavanto pamuñcantu saddhaṃ;

Vihiṃsasaññī paguṇaṃ na bhāsiṃ,

Dhammaṃ paṇītaṃ manujesu brahme’ti.

‘Opened for them are the doors to the Deathless; let those who have ears release their faith. Perceiving it as a vexation, O Brahmā, I did not speak the sublime and proficient Dhamma among humans.’

340. “Atha [V 2.0301] kho, rājakumāra, brahmā sahampati ‘katāvakāso khomhi bhagavatā dhammadesanāyā’ti maṃ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā tatthevantaradhāyi.

340. Then, O prince, Brahmā Sahampati, thinking, ‘An opportunity has been granted to me by the Blessed One for the teaching of the Dhamma,’ paid homage to me, circumambulated me to the right, and disappeared right there.

“Tassa mayhaṃ, rājakumāra, etadahosi – ‘kassa nu kho ahaṃ paṭhamaṃ [T 2.0465] dhammaṃ deseyyaṃ? Ko imaṃ dhammaṃ khippameva ājānissatī’ti? Tassa mayhaṃ, rājakumāra, etadahosi – ‘ayaṃ kho āḷāro kālāmo paṇḍito viyatto medhāvī dīgharattaṃ apparajakkhajātiko. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ āḷārassa kālāmassa [M 2.0294] paṭhamaṃ dhammaṃ deseyyaṃ; so imaṃ dhammaṃ khippameva ājānissatī’ti. Atha kho maṃ, rājakumāra, devatā upasaṅkamitvā etadavoca – ‘sattāhakālaṅkato, bhante, āḷāro kālāmo’ti. Ñāṇañca pana me dassanaṃ udapādi – ‘sattāhakālaṅkato āḷāro kālāmo’ti. Tassa mayhaṃ, rājakumāra, etadahosi – ‘mahājāniyo kho āḷāro kālāmo. Sace hi so imaṃ dhammaṃ suṇeyya, khippameva ājāneyyā’ti. Tassa mayhaṃ, rājakumāra, etadahosi – ‘kassa nu kho ahaṃ paṭhamaṃ dhammaṃ deseyyaṃ? Ko imaṃ dhammaṃ khippameva ājānissatī’ti? Tassa mayhaṃ, rājakumāra, etadahosi – ‘ayaṃ kho udako rāmaputto paṇḍito viyatto medhāvī dīgharattaṃ apparajakkhajātiko. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ udakassa rāmaputtassa paṭhamaṃ dhammaṃ deseyyaṃ; so imaṃ dhammaṃ khippameva ājānissatī’ti. Atha kho maṃ, rājakumāra, devatā upasaṅkamitvā etadavoca – ‘abhidosakālaṅkato, bhante, udako rāmaputto’ti. Ñāṇañca pana me dassanaṃ udapādi – ‘abhidosakālaṅkato udako rāmaputto’ti. Tassa mayhaṃ, rājakumāra, etadahosi – ‘mahājāniyo kho udako rāmaputto. Sace hi so imaṃ dhammaṃ suṇeyya, khippameva ājāneyyā’ti.

Then, Prince, this thought occurred to me: ‘To whom should I first teach the Dhamma? Who will quickly understand this Dhamma?’ Then, Prince, this thought occurred to me: ‘This Āḷāra Kālāma is wise, astute, and intelligent; for a long time he has had little dust in his eyes. What if I were to teach the Dhamma first to Āḷāra Kālāma? He will quickly understand this Dhamma.’ Then, Prince, a deity approached me and said this: ‘Venerable sir, Āḷāra Kālāma passed away seven days ago.’ And knowledge and vision arose in me: ‘Āḷāra Kālāma passed away seven days ago.’ Then, Prince, this thought occurred to me: ‘Āḷāra Kālāma has suffered a great loss. For if he had heard this Dhamma, he would have quickly understood it.’ Then, Prince, this thought occurred to me: ‘To whom should I first teach the Dhamma? Who will quickly understand this Dhamma?’ Then, Prince, this thought occurred to me: ‘This Udaka Rāmaputta is wise, astute, and intelligent; for a long time he has had little dust in his eyes. What if I were to teach the Dhamma first to Udaka Rāmaputta? He will quickly understand this Dhamma.’ Then, Prince, a deity approached me and said this: ‘Venerable sir, Udaka Rāmaputta passed away last night.’ And knowledge and vision arose in me: ‘Udaka Rāmaputta passed away last night.’ Then, Prince, this thought occurred to me: ‘Udaka Rāmaputta has suffered a great loss. For if he had heard this Dhamma, he would have quickly understood it.’

341. “Tassa [T 2.0466] mayhaṃ, rājakumāra, etadahosi – ‘kassa nu kho ahaṃ paṭhamaṃ dhammaṃ deseyyaṃ? Ko imaṃ dhammaṃ khippameva ājānissatī’ti? Tassa mayhaṃ, rājakumāra, etadahosi – ‘bahukārā kho me pañcavaggiyā bhikkhū ye maṃ padhānapahitattaṃ upaṭṭhahiṃsu. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ pañcavaggiyānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ paṭhamaṃ dhammaṃ deseyya’nti. Tassa mayhaṃ, rājakumāra, etadahosi – ‘kahaṃ nu kho etarahi pañcavaggiyā bhikkhū viharantī’ti. Addasaṃ khvāhaṃ, rājakumāra, dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena pañcavaggiye bhikkhū bārāṇasiyaṃ viharante isipatane migadāye. Atha khvāhaṃ, rājakumāra, uruvelāyaṃ yathābhirantaṃ viharitvā yena bārāṇasī tena cārikaṃ pakkamiṃ.

341. Then, Prince, this thought occurred to me: ‘To whom should I first teach the Dhamma? Who will quickly understand this Dhamma?’ Then, Prince, this thought occurred to me: ‘The bhikkhus of the group of five were of great service to me, as they attended upon me when I was committed to striving. What if I were to teach the Dhamma first to the bhikkhus of the group of five?’ Then, Prince, this thought occurred to me: ‘Where, I wonder, are the bhikkhus of the group of five now dwelling?’ Then, Prince, with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, I saw the bhikkhus of the group of five dwelling at Bārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Isipatana. Then, Prince, having dwelt at Uruvelā for as long as I wished, I set out on a journey toward Bārāṇasī.

“Addasā kho maṃ, rājakumāra, upako ājīvako antarā ca gayaṃ antarā ca bodhiṃ addhānamaggappaṭipannaṃ[V 2.0302]. Disvāna maṃ etadavoca – ‘vippasannāni kho te, āvuso, indriyāni, parisuddho chavivaṇṇo pariyodāto. Kaṃsi tvaṃ, āvuso, uddissa pabbajito? Ko vā te satthā? Kassa vā tvaṃ dhammaṃ rocesī’ti? Evaṃ vutte, ahaṃ, rājakumāra, upakaṃ ājīvakaṃ gāthāhi ajjhabhāsiṃ –

Prince, the Ājīvaka Upaka saw me journeying on the high road between Gayā and the Bodhi tree. Having seen me, he said this: ‘Friend, your faculties are exceedingly clear, the color of your skin is pure and bright. On whose account, friend, have you gone forth? Who is your teacher? Whose Dhamma do you profess?’ When this was said, Prince, I addressed the Ājīvaka Upaka in verses:

‘Sabbābhibhū [M 2.0295] sabbavidūhamasmi,

Sabbesu dhammesu anūpalitto;

Sabbañjaho taṇhākkhaye vimutto,

Sayaṃ abhiññāya kamuddiseyyaṃ.

‘I am the all-conqueror, the all-knower, unsullied in all things. I am one who has abandoned all, liberated in the destruction of craving. Having realized this for myself through direct knowledge, whom should I point to as my teacher?

‘Na [T 2.0467] me ācariyo atthi, sadiso me na vijjati;

Sadevakasmiṃ lokasmiṃ, natthi me paṭipuggalo.

‘I have no teacher; one like me is not to be found. In the world with its devas, there is no one comparable to me.

‘Ahañhi arahā loke, ahaṃ satthā anuttaro;

Ekomhi sammāsambuddho, sītibhūtosmi nibbuto.

‘For I am the Arahant in the world, I am the unsurpassed Teacher. I alone am the Perfectly Enlightened One; I have become cool, I am extinguished.

‘Dhammacakkaṃ pavattetuṃ, gacchāmi kāsinaṃ puraṃ;

Andhībhūtasmiṃ andhabhūtasmiṃ (sī. syā. pī.) lokasmiṃ, āhañchaṃ āhaññiṃ (syā. kaṃ. ka.) amatadundubhi’nti.

‘To set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion, I go to the city of the Kāsīs. In a world that has become blind, I shall beat the drum of the Deathless.’

‘Yathā kho tvaṃ, āvuso, paṭijānāsi arahasi anantajino’ti.

‘Friend, as you profess, you are worthy of being an infinite conqueror.’

‘Mādisā ve jinā honti, ye pattā āsavakkhayaṃ;

Jitā me pāpakā dhammā, tasmāhamupaka tasmāhaṃ upakā (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) jino’ti.

‘Conquerors are indeed like me, those who have reached the destruction of the taints. Evil states have been conquered by me; therefore, Upaka, I am a Conqueror.’

“Evaṃ vutte, rājakumāra, upako ājīvako ‘hupeyyapāvuso’ti huveyyapāvuso (sī. pī.), huveyyāvuso (syā. kaṃ.) vatvā sīsaṃ okampetvā ummaggaṃ gahetvā pakkāmi.

When this was said, Prince, the Ājīvaka Upaka said, ‘It may be so, friend,’ and shaking his head, he took a different road and departed.

342. “Atha khvāhaṃ, rājakumāra, anupubbena cārikaṃ caramāno yena bārāṇasī isipatanaṃ migadāyo yena pañcavaggiyā bhikkhū tenupasaṅkamiṃ. Addasaṃsu kho maṃ, rājakumāra, pañcavaggiyā bhikkhū dūratova āgacchantaṃ. Disvāna aññamaññaṃ saṇṭhapesuṃ – ‘ayaṃ kho, āvuso, samaṇo gotamo āgacchati bāhulliko padhānavibbhanto āvatto bāhullāya. So neva [V 2.0303] abhivādetabbo, na paccuṭṭhātabbo, nāssa pattacīvaraṃ paṭiggahetabbaṃ; api ca kho āsanaṃ ṭhapetabbaṃ – sace so ākaṅkhissati nisīdissatī’ti. Yathā yathā kho ahaṃ, rājakumāra, pañcavaggiye bhikkhū [T 2.0468] upasaṅkamiṃ upasaṅkamāmi (sī. pī.), tathā tathā pañcavaggiyā bhikkhū nāsakkhiṃsu sakāya katikāya saṇṭhātuṃ. Appekacce maṃ paccuggantvā pattacīvaraṃ paṭiggahesuṃ. Appekacce āsanaṃ paññapesuṃ. Appekacce pādodakaṃ upaṭṭhapesuṃ. Api ca kho maṃ nāmena ca āvusovādena [M 2.0296] ca samudācaranti. Evaṃ vutte, ahaṃ, rājakumāra, pañcavaggiye bhikkhū etadavocaṃ – ‘mā, bhikkhave, tathāgataṃ nāmena ca āvusovādena ca samudācaratha samudācarittha (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.); arahaṃ, bhikkhave, tathāgato sammāsambuddho. Odahatha, bhikkhave, sotaṃ. Amatamadhigataṃ. Ahamanusāsāmi, ahaṃ dhammaṃ desemi. Yathānusiṭṭhaṃ tathā paṭipajjamānā nacirasseva – yassatthāya kulaputtā sammadeva agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajanti tadanuttaraṃ – brahmacariyapariyosānaṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharissathā’ti. Evaṃ vutte, rājakumāra, pañcavaggiyā bhikkhū maṃ etadavocuṃ – ‘tāyapi kho tvaṃ, āvuso gotama, iriyāya cariyāya (syā. kaṃ.) tāya paṭipadāya tāya dukkarakārikāya nājjhagamā uttarimanussadhammā alamariyañāṇadassanavisesaṃ; kiṃ pana tvaṃ etarahi bāhulliko padhānavibbhanto āvatto bāhullāya adhigamissasi uttarimanussadhammā alamariyañāṇadassanavisesa’nti? Evaṃ vutte, ahaṃ, rājakumāra, pañcavaggiye bhikkhū etadavocaṃ – ‘na, bhikkhave, tathāgato bāhulliko na padhānavibbhanto na āvatto bāhullāya. Arahaṃ, bhikkhave, tathāgato sammāsambuddho. Odahatha, bhikkhave, sotaṃ. Amatamadhigataṃ. Ahamanusāsāmi, ahaṃ dhammaṃ desemi. Yathānusiṭṭhaṃ tathā paṭipajjamānā [T 2.0469] nacirasseva – yassatthāya kulaputtā sammadeva agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajanti tadanuttaraṃ – brahmacariyapariyosānaṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharissathā’ti. Dutiyampi kho, rājakumāra, pañcavaggiyā bhikkhū maṃ etadavocuṃ – ‘tāyapi kho tvaṃ, āvuso gotama, iriyāya tāya paṭipadāya tāya dukkarakārikāya nājjhagamā uttarimanussadhammā alamariyañāṇadassanavisesaṃ; kiṃ pana tvaṃ etarahi bāhulliko padhānavibbhanto āvatto bāhullāya adhigamissasi uttarimanussadhammā alamariyañāṇadassanavisesa’nti? Dutiyampi kho ahaṃ, rājakumāra, pañcavaggiye bhikkhū etadavocaṃ – ‘na, bhikkhave, tathāgato bāhulliko na padhānavibbhanto na āvatto bāhullāya. Arahaṃ, bhikkhave, tathāgato sammāsambuddho. Odahatha, bhikkhave, sotaṃ. Amatamadhigataṃ. Ahamanusāsāmi, ahaṃ dhammaṃ desemi. Yathānusiṭṭhaṃ tathā paṭipajjamānā nacirasseva – yassatthāya kulaputtā sammadeva agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajanti tadanuttaraṃ – brahmacariyapariyosānaṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharissathā’ti[M 2.0297]. Tatiyampi kho, rājakumāra, pañcavaggiyā bhikkhū maṃ etadavocuṃ – ‘tāyapi kho tvaṃ, āvuso [V 2.0304] gotama, iriyāya tāya paṭipadāya tāya dukkarakārikāya nājjhagamā uttarimanussadhammā alamariyañāṇadassanavisesaṃ; kiṃ pana tvaṃ etarahi bāhulliko padhānavibbhanto āvatto bāhullāya adhigamissasi uttarimanussadhammā alamariyañāṇadassanavisesa’nti? Evaṃ vutte[T 2.0470], ahaṃ, rājakumāra, pañcavaggiye bhikkhū etadavocaṃ – ‘abhijānātha me no tumhe, bhikkhave, ito pubbe evarūpaṃ pabhāvitameta’nti bhāsitametanti (sī. syā. vinayepi)? ‘No hetaṃ, bhante’. ‘Arahaṃ, bhikkhave, tathāgato sammāsambuddho. Odahatha, bhikkhave, sotaṃ. Amatamadhigataṃ. Ahamanusāsāmi, ahaṃ dhammaṃ desemi. Yathānusiṭṭhaṃ tathā paṭipajjamānā nacirasseva – yassatthāya kulaputtā sammadeva agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajanti tadanuttaraṃ – brahmacariyapariyosānaṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharissathā’ti.

342. Then, O prince, wandering on tour by stages, I approached Benares, the Deer Park at Isipatana, where the bhikkhus of the group of five were. The bhikkhus of the group of five, O prince, saw me coming from afar. Having seen me, they made an agreement among themselves: ‘Friends, this ascetic Gotama is coming, who lives in abundance, has given up the struggle, and has reverted to a life of abundance. He is not to be paid homage, nor are we to rise for him, nor are his bowl and robe to be taken. However, a seat may be prepared; if he wishes, he will sit down.’

But as I approached, O prince, the bhikkhus of the group of five were unable to keep to their own agreement. Some came forward and took my bowl and robe. Some prepared a seat. Some set out water for my feet. Yet they addressed me by name and with the term ‘friend.’

When this was said, O prince, I said this to the bhikkhus of the group of five: ‘Bhikkhus, do not address the Tathāgata by name and with the term “friend.” The Tathāgata, bhikkhus, is an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One. Lend ear, bhikkhus, the Deathless has been attained. I instruct, I teach the Dhamma. Practicing in accordance with this instruction, you will, before long, in this very life, for yourselves, realize with direct knowledge and, having attained it, dwell in that unsurpassed culmination of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness.’
