When this was said, O prince, the bhikkhus of the group of five said this to me: ‘Friend Gotama, even with that deportment, that practice, and that difficult austerity, you did not attain any state beyond human states, any distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones. How then, now that you live in abundance, have given up the struggle, and have reverted to a life of abundance, will you attain any state beyond human states, any distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones?’

When this was said, O prince, I said this to the bhikkhus of the group of five: ‘Bhikkhus, the Tathāgata does not live in abundance, has not given up the struggle, and has not reverted to a life of abundance. The Tathāgata, bhikkhus, is an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One. Lend ear, bhikkhus, the Deathless has been attained. I instruct, I teach the Dhamma. Practicing in accordance with this instruction, you will, before long, in this very life, for yourselves, realize with direct knowledge and, having attained it, dwell in that unsurpassed culmination of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness.’

A second time, O prince, the bhikkhus of the group of five said this to me: ‘Friend Gotama, even with that deportment, that practice, and that difficult austerity, you did not attain any state beyond human states, any distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones. How then, now that you live in abundance, have given up the struggle, and have reverted to a life of abundance, will you attain any state beyond human states, any distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones?’

A second time, O prince, I said this to the bhikkhus of the group of five: ‘Bhikkhus, the Tathāgata does not live in abundance, has not given up the struggle, and has not reverted to a life of abundance. The Tathāgata, bhikkhus, is an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One. Lend ear, bhikkhus, the Deathless has been attained. I instruct, I teach the Dhamma. Practicing in accordance with this instruction, you will, before long, in this very life, for yourselves, realize with direct knowledge and, having attained it, dwell in that unsurpassed culmination of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness.’

A third time, O prince, the bhikkhus of the group of five said this to me: ‘Friend Gotama, even with that deportment, that practice, and that difficult austerity, you did not attain any state beyond human states, any distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones. How then, now that you live in abundance, have given up the struggle, and have reverted to a life of abundance, will you attain any state beyond human states, any distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones?’

When this was said, O prince, I said this to the bhikkhus of the group of five: ‘Bhikkhus, do you recall me ever having spoken in this way before?’

‘No, venerable sir.’

‘The Tathāgata, bhikkhus, is an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One. Lend ear, bhikkhus, the Deathless has been attained. I instruct, I teach the Dhamma. Practicing in accordance with this instruction, you will, before long, in this very life, for yourselves, realize with direct knowledge and, having attained it, dwell in that unsurpassed culmination of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness.’

“Asakkhiṃ kho ahaṃ, rājakumāra, pañcavaggiye bhikkhū saññāpetuṃ. Dvepi sudaṃ, rājakumāra, bhikkhū ovadāmi. Tayo bhikkhū piṇḍāya caranti. Yaṃ tayo bhikkhū piṇḍāya caritvā āharanti, tena chabbaggiyā chabbaggā (sī. syā. kaṃ.), chabbaggo (pī.) yāpema. Tayopi sudaṃ, rājakumāra, bhikkhū ovadāmi, dve bhikkhū piṇḍāya caranti. Yaṃ dve bhikkhū piṇḍāya caritvā āharanti [P 2.0094] tena chabbaggiyā yāpema.

I was able, Prince, to convince the group of five bhikkhus. Indeed, Prince, I would instruct two bhikkhus, while three bhikkhus went for alms. Whatever the three bhikkhus brought back from their alms-gathering, the six of us lived on that. Indeed, Prince, I would instruct three bhikkhus, while two bhikkhus went for alms. Whatever the two bhikkhus brought back from their alms-gathering, the six of us lived on that.

343. “Atha kho, rājakumāra, pañcavaggiyā bhikkhū mayā evaṃ ovadiyamānā evaṃ anusāsiyamānā nacirasseva – yassatthāya kulaputtā sammadeva agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajanti tadanuttaraṃ – brahmacariyapariyosānaṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja vihariṃsū”ti. Evaṃ vutte, bodhi rājakumāro bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “kīva cirena nu kho, bhante, bhikkhu tathāgataṃ vināyakaṃ nāyakaṃ (?) labhamāno – yassatthāya kulaputtā sammadeva agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajanti tadanuttaraṃ – brahmacariyapariyosānaṃ [T 2.0471] diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja vihareyyā”ti? “Tena hi, rājakumāra, taṃyevettha paṭipucchissāmi. Yathā te khameyya, tathā naṃ byākareyyāsi. Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, rājakumāra, kusalo tvaṃ hatthārūḷhe hatthārūyhe (sī. pī.) aṅkusagayhe aṅkusagaṇhe (syā. kaṃ.) sippe”ti? “Evaṃ, bhante, kusalo ahaṃ hatthārūḷhe aṅkusagayhe sippe”ti[M 2.0298]. “Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, rājakumāra, idha puriso āgaccheyya – ‘bodhi rājakumāro hatthārūḷhaṃ aṅkusagayhaṃ sippaṃ jānāti; tassāhaṃ santike hatthārūḷhaṃ aṅkusagayhaṃ sippaṃ sikkhissāmī’ti. So [V 2.0305] cassa assaddho; yāvatakaṃ saddhena pattabbaṃ taṃ na sampāpuṇeyya. So cassa bahvābādho; yāvatakaṃ appābādhena pattabbaṃ taṃ na sampāpuṇeyya. So cassa saṭho māyāvī; yāvatakaṃ asaṭhena amāyāvinā pattabbaṃ taṃ na sampāpuṇeyya. So cassa kusīto; yāvatakaṃ āraddhavīriyena pattabbaṃ taṃ na sampāpuṇeyya. So cassa duppañño; yāvatakaṃ paññavatā pattabbaṃ taṃ na sampāpuṇeyya. Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, rājakumāra, api nu so puriso tava santike hatthārūḷhaṃ aṅkusagayhaṃ sippaṃ sikkheyyā”ti? “Ekamekenāpi, bhante, aṅgena samannāgato so puriso na mama santike hatthārūḷhaṃ aṅkusagayhaṃ sippaṃ sikkheyya, ko pana vādo pañcahaṅgehī”ti!

343. Then, Prince, the group of five bhikkhus, being thus instructed and admonished by me, not long afterwards—for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness, that unsurpassed culmination of the holy life—realized it for themselves with direct knowledge in this very life, and having attained it, they dwelled therein. When this was said, Prince Bodhi said this to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, for a bhikkhu who has the Tathāgata as his guide, how long would it take to realize for himself with direct knowledge in this very life that unsurpassed culmination of the holy life—for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness—and having attained it, to dwell therein?” “In that case, Prince, I will question you in return on this very point. Answer as you see fit. What do you think, Prince, are you skilled in the art of elephant-riding and handling the goad?” “Yes, venerable sir, I am skilled in the art of elephant-riding and handling the goad.” “What do you think, Prince? Suppose a man were to come here, thinking: ‘Prince Bodhi knows the art of elephant-riding and handling the goad; I will learn that art from him.’ But he is without faith; he would not achieve what is to be achieved by one with faith. He is sickly; he would not achieve what is to be achieved by one with good health. He is deceitful and fraudulent; he would not achieve what is to be achieved by one who is honest and sincere. He is lazy; he would not achieve what is to be achieved by one with aroused energy. He is unwise; he would not achieve what is to be achieved by one with wisdom. What do you think, Prince, could that man learn the art of elephant-riding and handling the goad from you?” “Venerable sir, if he were endowed with even one of these factors, that man could not learn the art of elephant-riding and handling the goad from me, let alone all five!”

344. “Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, rājakumāra, idha puriso āgaccheyya – ‘bodhi [T 2.0472][P 2.0095] rājakumāro hatthārūḷhaṃ aṅkusagayhaṃ sippaṃ jānāti; tassāhaṃ santike hatthārūḷhaṃ aṅkusagayhaṃ sippaṃ sikkhissāmī’ti. So cassa saddho; yāvatakaṃ saddhena pattabbaṃ taṃ sampāpuṇeyya. So cassa appābādho; yāvatakaṃ appābādhena pattabbaṃ taṃ sampāpuṇeyya. So cassa asaṭho amāyāvī; yāvatakaṃ asaṭhena amāyāvinā pattabbaṃ taṃ sampāpuṇeyya. So cassa āraddhavīriyo; yāvatakaṃ āraddhavīriyena pattabbaṃ taṃ sampāpuṇeyya. So cassa paññavā; yāvatakaṃ paññavatā pattabbaṃ taṃ sampāpuṇeyya. Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, rājakumāra, api nu so puriso tava santike hatthārūḷhaṃ aṅkusagayhaṃ sippaṃ sikkheyyā”ti? “Ekamekenāpi, bhante, aṅgena samannāgato so puriso mama santike hatthārūḷhaṃ aṅkusagayhaṃ sippaṃ sikkheyya, ko pana vādo pañcahaṅgehī”ti! “Evameva kho, rājakumāra, pañcimāni padhāniyaṅgāni. Katamāni pañca? Idha, rājakumāra, bhikkhu saddho hoti; saddahati tathāgatassa bodhiṃ – ‘itipi so bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho vijjācaraṇasampanno sugato lokavidū anuttaro purisadammasārathi satthā devamanussānaṃ buddho bhagavā’ti; appābādho hoti appātaṅko samavepākiniyā gahaṇiyā samannāgato nātisītāya nāccuṇhāya majjhimāya padhānakkhamāya; asaṭho hoti amāyāvī yathābhūtaṃ attānaṃ āvikattā satthari [M 2.0299] vā viññūsu vā sabrahmacārīsu[T 2.0473]; āraddhavīriyo viharati akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānāya kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ upasampadāya, thāmavā daḷhaparakkamo anikkhittadhuro kusalesu dhammesu; paññavā hoti udayatthagāminiyā paññāya samannāgato ariyāya nibbedhikāya sammādukkhakkhayagāminiyā. Imāni kho, rājakumāra, pañca padhāniyaṅgāni.

344. “What do you think, Prince? Suppose a man were to come here, thinking: ‘Prince Bodhi knows the art of elephant-riding and handling the goad; I will learn that art from him.’ And he has faith; he would achieve what is to be achieved by one with faith. He has good health; he would achieve what is to be achieved by one with good health. He is honest and sincere; he would achieve what is to be achieved by one who is honest and sincere. He has aroused energy; he would achieve what is to be achieved by one with aroused energy. He has wisdom; he would achieve what is to be achieved by one with wisdom. What do you think, Prince, could that man learn the art of elephant-riding and handling the goad from you?” “Venerable sir, if he were endowed with even one of these factors, that man could learn the art of elephant-riding and handling the goad from me, let alone all five!” “In the same way, Prince, there are these five factors of striving. What five? Here, Prince, a bhikkhu has faith; he has faith in the Tathāgata’s enlightenment: ‘Thus is the Blessed One: an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, the Well-Farer, the Knower of the world, the unsurpassed trainer of persons to be tamed, the Teacher of gods and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One.’ He is free from illness and affliction, possessing a digestive system that functions evenly, being neither too cold nor too hot, but moderate and suitable for striving. He is honest and sincere, revealing himself as he truly is to the Teacher or to his wise companions in the holy life. He dwells with aroused energy for the abandoning of unwholesome states and for the attainment of wholesome states; he is steadfast, firm in his exertion, not shirking the responsibility in regard to wholesome states. He is wise, possessing the noble, penetrative wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which leads to the complete destruction of suffering. These, Prince, are the five factors of striving.”

345. “Imehi[V 2.0306], rājakumāra, pañcahi padhāniyaṅgehi samannāgato bhikkhu tathāgataṃ vināyakaṃ labhamāno – yassatthāya kulaputtā sammadeva agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajanti tadanuttaraṃ – brahmacariyapariyosānaṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja vihareyya [P 2.0096] satta vassāni. Tiṭṭhantu, rājakumāra, satta vassāni. Imehi pañcahi padhāniyaṅgehi samannāgato bhikkhu tathāgataṃ vināyakaṃ labhamāno – yassatthāya kulaputtā sammadeva agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajanti tadanuttaraṃ – brahmacariyapariyosānaṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja vihareyya chabbassāni… pañca vassāni… cattāri vassāni… tīṇi vassāni… dve vassāni… ekaṃ vassaṃ. Tiṭṭhatu, rājakumāra, ekaṃ vassaṃ. Imehi pañcahi padhāniyaṅgehi samannāgato bhikkhu tathāgataṃ vināyakaṃ labhamāno – yassatthāya kulaputtā sammadeva agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajanti tadanuttaraṃ – brahmacariyapariyosānaṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja vihareyya satta māsāni. Tiṭṭhantu, rājakumāra, satta māsāni. Imehi pañcahi padhāniyaṅgehi samannāgato [T 2.0474] bhikkhu tathāgataṃ vināyakaṃ labhamāno – yassatthāya kulaputtā sammadeva agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajanti tadanuttaraṃ – brahmacariyapariyosānaṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja vihareyya cha māsāni… pañca māsāni… cattāri māsāni… tīṇi māsāni… dve māsāni… ekaṃ māsaṃ… aḍḍhamāsaṃ. Tiṭṭhatu, rājakumāra, aḍḍhamāso. Imehi pañcahi padhāniyaṅgehi samannāgato bhikkhu tathāgataṃ vināyakaṃ labhamāno – yassatthāya kulaputtā sammadeva agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajanti tadanuttaraṃ – brahmacariyapariyosānaṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja vihareyya satta rattindivāni. Tiṭṭhantu, rājakumāra, satta rattindivāni. Imehi pañcahi padhāniyaṅgehi samannāgato bhikkhu tathāgataṃ vināyakaṃ labhamāno – yassatthāya kulaputtā sammadeva agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajanti tadanuttaraṃ – brahmacariyapariyosānaṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā [M 2.0300] upasampajja vihareyya cha rattindivāni… pañca rattindivāni… cattāri rattindivāni… tīṇi rattindivāni… dve rattindivāni… ekaṃ rattindivaṃ. Tiṭṭhatu, rājakumāra, eko rattindivo. Imehi pañcahi padhāniyaṅgehi samannāgato bhikkhu tathāgataṃ vināyakaṃ labhamāno sāyamanusiṭṭho pāto visesaṃ adhigamissati, pātamanusiṭṭho sāyaṃ visesaṃ adhigamissatī”ti. Evaṃ vutte, bodhi rājakumāro bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “aho buddho, aho dhammo, aho [T 2.0475] dhammassa svākkhātatā! Yatra hi nāma sāyamanusiṭṭho pāto visesaṃ adhigamissati, pātamanusiṭṭho sāyaṃ visesaṃ adhigamissatī”ti!

345. “Prince, a bhikkhu endowed with these five factors of striving, having obtained the Tathāgata as a guide, would, for the sake of that unsurpassed culmination of the holy life for which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness, in this very life, having realized it for himself with higher knowledge and attained it, dwell therein within seven years. Let alone seven years, Prince. A bhikkhu endowed with these five factors of striving, having obtained the Tathāgata as a guide… would dwell therein within six years… five years… four years… three years… two years… one year. Let alone one year, Prince. A bhikkhu endowed with these five factors of striving, having obtained the Tathāgata as a guide… would dwell therein within seven months. Let alone seven months, Prince. A bhikkhu endowed with these five factors of striving, having obtained the Tathāgata as a guide… would dwell therein within six months… five months… four months… three months… two months… one month… half a month. Let alone half a month, Prince. A bhikkhu endowed with these five factors of striving, having obtained the Tathāgata as a guide… would dwell therein within seven days and nights. Let alone seven days and nights, Prince. A bhikkhu endowed with these five factors of striving, having obtained the Tathāgata as a guide… would dwell therein within six days and nights… five days and nights… four days and nights… three days and nights… two days and nights… one day and night. Let alone one day and night, Prince. A bhikkhu endowed with these five factors of striving, having obtained the Tathāgata as a guide, if instructed in the evening, will attain distinction by morning; if instructed in the morning, he will attain distinction by evening.” When this was said, Prince Bodhi said to the Blessed One: “Oh, wonderful is the Buddha! Oh, wonderful is the Dhamma! Oh, how well-proclaimed is the Dhamma! For indeed, one instructed in the evening will attain distinction by morning, and one instructed in the morning will attain distinction by evening!”

346. Evaṃ [V 2.0307] vutte, sañjikāputto māṇavo bodhiṃ rājakumāraṃ etadavoca – “evameva panāyaṃ bhavaṃ bodhi – ‘aho buddho, aho dhammo, aho dhammassa svākkhātatā’ti ca vadeti vadesi (sī.), pavedeti (syā. kaṃ.); atha ca pana na taṃ bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchati dhammañca bhikkhusaṅghañcā”ti. “Mā hevaṃ, samma sañjikāputta, avaca; mā hevaṃ, samma sañjikāputta, avaca. Sammukhā metaṃ, samma sañjikāputta, ayyāya sutaṃ, sammukhā [P 2.0097] paṭiggahitaṃ”. “Ekamidaṃ, samma sañjikāputta, samayaṃ bhagavā kosambiyaṃ viharati ghositārāme. Atha kho me ayyā kucchimatī yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinnā kho me ayyā bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – ‘yo me ayaṃ, bhante, kucchigato kumārako vā kumārikā vā so bhagavantaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchati dhammañca bhikkhusaṅghañca. Upāsakaṃ taṃ bhagavā dhāretu ajjatagge pāṇupetaṃ saraṇaṃ gata’nti. Ekamidaṃ, samma sañjikāputta, samayaṃ bhagavā idheva bhaggesu viharati susumāragire bhesakaḷāvane migadāye. Atha kho maṃ dhāti aṅkena haritvā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Ekamantaṃ ṭhitā kho maṃ dhāti bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – ‘ayaṃ[T 2.0476], bhante, bodhi rājakumāro bhagavantaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchati dhammañca bhikkhusaṅghañca. Upāsakaṃ taṃ bhagavā dhāretu ajjatagge pāṇupetaṃ saraṇaṃ gata’nti. Esāhaṃ, samma sañjikāputta, tatiyakampi bhagavantaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi dhammañca bhikkhusaṅghañca. Upāsakaṃ maṃ bhagavā dhāretu ajjatagge pāṇupetaṃ saraṇaṃ gata”nti.

346. When this was said, the young man Sañjikāputta said to Prince Bodhi: “Indeed, the venerable Bodhi only says, ‘Oh, wonderful is the Buddha! Oh, wonderful is the Dhamma! Oh, how well-proclaimed is the Dhamma!’ and yet he does not go for refuge to that venerable Gotama, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.” “Do not say so, friend Sañjikāputta; do not say so, friend Sañjikāputta. I have heard this from my mother face to face, friend Sañjikāputta, I have received it face to face. On one occasion, friend Sañjikāputta, the Blessed One was dwelling at Kosambī in Ghosita’s monastery. Then my mother, who was pregnant, approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, she sat down to one side. Seated to one side, my mother said to the Blessed One: ‘Venerable Sir, this boy or girl in my womb goes for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May the Blessed One remember him or her as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forward for as long as life lasts.’ On another occasion, friend Sañjikāputta, the Blessed One was dwelling right here in the land of the Bhaggas, at Susumāragira in the Bhesakaḷā Forest, the deer sanctuary. Then my nurse, carrying me on her hip, approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, she stood to one side. Standing to one side, my nurse said to the Blessed One: ‘Venerable Sir, this Prince Bodhi goes for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May the Blessed One remember him as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forward for as long as life lasts.’ And I, friend Sañjikāputta, for the third time, go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May the Blessed One remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forward for as long as life lasts.”

Bodhirājakumārasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ pañcamaṃ.

The Discourse to Prince Bodhi, the fifth, is concluded.

6. Aṅgulimālasuttaṃ

6. The Aṅgulimāla Sutta

347. Evaṃ [M 2.0301][V 2.0308] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme. Tena kho pana samayena rañño pasenadissa kosalassa vijite coro aṅgulimālo nāma hoti luddo lohitapāṇi hatapahate niviṭṭho adayāpanno pāṇabhūtesu. Tena gāmāpi agāmā katā, nigamāpi anigamā [P 2.0098] katā, janapadāpi ajanapadā katā. So manusse vadhitvā vadhitvā aṅgulīnaṃ mālaṃ dhāreti. Atha kho bhagavā pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya sāvatthiṃ piṇḍāya pāvisi. Sāvatthiyaṃ piṇḍāya caritvā pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto senāsanaṃ saṃsāmetvā pattacīvaramādāya yena coro aṅgulimālo tenaddhānamaggaṃ paṭipajji. Addasāsuṃ kho gopālakā pasupālakā kassakā pathāvino bhagavantaṃ yena coro aṅgulimālo tenaddhānamaggapaṭipannaṃ. Disvāna bhagavantaṃ etadavocuṃ – “mā, samaṇa, etaṃ maggaṃ paṭipajji. Etasmiṃ, samaṇa, magge coro aṅgulimālo nāma luddo lohitapāṇi hatapahate niviṭṭho adayāpanno pāṇabhūtesu. Tena gāmāpi agāmā katā, nigamāpi anigamā katā, janapadāpi ajanapadā katā. So manusse vadhitvā vadhitvā aṅgulīnaṃ mālaṃ dhāreti. Etañhi, samaṇa, maggaṃ dasapi purisā vīsampi purisā tiṃsampi purisā cattārīsampi purisā paññāsampi purisā [T 2.0478] saṅkaritvā saṅkaritvā saṃharitvā saṃharitvā (sī. pī.), saṅgaritvā (syā. kaṃ.) paṭipajjanti. Tepi corassa aṅgulimālassa hatthatthaṃ gacchantī”ti. Evaṃ vutte, bhagavā tuṇhībhūto agamāsi. Dutiyampi kho gopālakā…pe… tatiyampi kho gopālakā pasupālakā kassakā pathāvino bhagavantaṃ etadavocuṃ – “mā, samaṇa, etaṃ maggaṃ paṭipajji, etasmiṃ samaṇa magge coro aṅgulimālo nāma luddo lohitapāṇi hatapahate niviṭṭho adayāpanno pāṇabhūtesu, tena gāmāpi agāmā katā, nigamāpi anigamā katā, janapadāpi ajanapadā katā. So manusse vadhitvā vadhitvā aṅgulīnaṃ mālaṃ dhāreti. Etañhi samaṇa maggaṃ dasapi purisā vīsampi purisā tiṃsampi purisā cattārīsampi purisā paññāsampi purisā saṅkaritvā [T 2.0479] saṅkaritvā paṭipajjanti. Tepi corassa aṅgulimālassa hatthatthaṃ gacchantī”ti.

347. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park. Now at that time in the realm of King Pasenadi of Kosala there was a bandit named Aṅgulimāla, who was violent, bloody-handed, intent on killing and slaying, merciless to living beings. He made villages into non-villages, towns into non-towns, and districts into non-districts. Having killed people again and again, he wore a garland of fingers. Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning, took his bowl and robe and entered Sāvatthī for alms. Having walked for alms in Sāvatthī, after the meal, on returning from the alms round, he arranged his dwelling, took his bowl and robe, and set out on the road toward the bandit Aṅgulimāla. Cowherds, shepherds, farmers, and travelers saw the Blessed One walking along the road toward Aṅgulimāla. Seeing him, they said this: “Do not, ascetic, take this road. On this road, ascetic, is the bandit Aṅgulimāla, who is violent, bloody-handed, intent on killing and slaying, and merciless to living beings. He has made villages into non-villages, towns into non-towns, and districts into non-districts. Having killed people again and again, he wears a garland of fingers. Indeed, ascetic, even groups of ten, twenty, thirty, forty, or fifty men, having banded together, travel this road. Even they fall into the hands of the bandit Aṅgulimāla.” When this was said, the Blessed One remained silent and went on. A second time... A third time the cowherds, shepherds, farmers, and travelers said this to the Blessed One: “Do not, ascetic, take this road. On this road, ascetic, is the bandit Aṅgulimāla, who is violent, bloody-handed, intent on killing and slaying, and merciless to living beings. He has made villages into non-villages, towns into non-towns, and districts into non-districts. Having killed people again and again, he wears a garland of fingers. Indeed, ascetic, even groups of ten, twenty, thirty, forty, or fifty men, having banded together, travel this road. Even they fall into the hands of the bandit Aṅgulimāla.”

348. Atha [M 2.0302][V 2.0309] kho bhagavā tuṇhībhūto agamāsi. Addasā kho coro aṅgulimālo bhagavantaṃ dūratova āgacchantaṃ. Disvānassa etadahosi – “acchariyaṃ vata, bho, abbhutaṃ vata, bho! Imañhi maggaṃ dasapi purisā vīsampi [P 2.0099] purisā tiṃsampi purisā cattārīsampi purisā paññāsampi purisā saṅkaritvā saṅkaritvā paṭipajjanti. Tepi mama hatthatthaṃ gacchanti. Atha ca panāyaṃ samaṇo eko adutiyo pasayha maññe āgacchati. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ imaṃ samaṇaṃ jīvitā voropeyya”nti. Atha kho coro aṅgulimālo asicammaṃ gahetvā dhanukalāpaṃ sannayhitvā bhagavantaṃ piṭṭhito piṭṭhito anubandhi. Atha kho bhagavā tathārūpaṃ iddhābhisaṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkhāsi abhisaṅkhāresi (syā. kaṃ. ka.) yathā coro aṅgulimālo bhagavantaṃ pakatiyā gacchantaṃ sabbathāmena gacchanto na sakkoti sampāpuṇituṃ. Atha kho corassa aṅgulimālassa etadahosi – “acchariyaṃ vata, bho, abbhutaṃ vata, bho! Ahañhi pubbe hatthimpi dhāvantaṃ anupatitvā gaṇhāmi, assampi dhāvantaṃ anupatitvā gaṇhāmi, rathampi dhāvantaṃ anupatitvā gaṇhāmi, migampi dhāvantaṃ anupatitvā gaṇhāmi; atha ca panāhaṃ imaṃ samaṇaṃ pakatiyā gacchantaṃ sabbathāmena gacchanto na sakkomi sampāpuṇitu”nti! Ṭhitova bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “tiṭṭha, tiṭṭha, samaṇā”ti. “Ṭhito ahaṃ, aṅgulimāla, tvañca tiṭṭhā”ti. Atha [T 2.0480] kho corassa aṅgulimālassa etadahosi – “ime kho samaṇā sakyaputtiyā saccavādino saccapaṭiññā. Atha panāyaṃ samaṇo gacchaṃ yevāha – ‘ṭhito ahaṃ, aṅgulimāla, tvañca tiṭṭhā’ti. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ imaṃ samaṇaṃ puccheyya”nti.

348. Then the Blessed One silently went on. The bandit Aṅgulimāla saw the Blessed One coming from afar. Seeing him, this thought occurred to him: “It is amazing, truly, it is astonishing! Indeed, even groups of ten, twenty, thirty, forty, or fifty men, having banded together, travel this road. Even they fall into my hands. And yet this ascetic comes alone, without a companion, as if to overpower me. Why should I not deprive this ascetic of life?” Then the bandit Aṅgulimāla took up his sword and shield, strung his bow and quiver, and followed closely behind the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One performed a feat of psychic power of such a kind that the bandit Aṅgulimāla, though running with all his might, could not catch up with the Blessed One who was walking at a normal pace. Then this thought occurred to the bandit Aṅgulimāla: “It is amazing, truly, it is astonishing! Previously, I could chase and catch a running elephant, a running horse, a running chariot, or a running deer; and yet now, though I am running with all my might, I cannot catch up with this ascetic who is walking at a normal pace!” Standing still, he said this to the Blessed One: “Stop, stop, ascetic!” “I am standing still, Aṅgulimāla. You, too, should stand still.” Then this thought occurred to the bandit Aṅgulimāla: “These ascetics, sons of the Sakyans, are speakers of truth, committed to the truth. And yet this ascetic, while walking, says: ‘I am standing still, Aṅgulimāla. You, too, should stand still.’ Why don't I question this ascetic?”

349. Atha kho coro aṅgulimālo bhagavantaṃ gāthāya ajjhabhāsi –

349. Then the bandit Aṅgulimāla addressed the Blessed One in verse:

“Gacchaṃ vadesi samaṇa ṭhitomhi,

Mamañca brūsi ṭhitamaṭṭhitoti;

Pucchāmi taṃ samaṇa etamatthaṃ,

Kathaṃ ṭhito tvaṃ ahamaṭṭhitomhī”ti.

“While walking, ascetic, you say, ‘I am standing still,’

And me, who am standing still, you call ‘not standing still.’

I ask you, ascetic, about this matter:

How are you standing still? How am I not standing still?”

“Ṭhito [M 2.0303] ahaṃ aṅgulimāla sabbadā,

Sabbesu bhūtesu nidhāya daṇḍaṃ;

Tuvañca [V 2.0310] pāṇesu asaññatosi,

Tasmā ṭhitohaṃ tuvamaṭṭhitosī”ti.

“I, Aṅgulimāla, am standing still always,

having laid down the rod toward all beings;

But you are unrestrained toward living beings,

Therefore, I am standing still; you are not standing still.”

“Cirassaṃ [P 2.0100] vata me mahito mahesī,

Mahāvanaṃ pāpuṇi saccavādī mahāvanaṃ samaṇoyaṃ paccupādi (sī.), mahāvanaṃ samaṇa paccupādi (syā. kaṃ.);

Sohaṃ carissāmi pahāya pāpaṃ sohaṃ cirassāpi pahāssaṃ pāpaṃ (sī.), sohaṃ carissāmi pajahissaṃ pāpaṃ (syā. kaṃ.),

Sutvāna gāthaṃ tava dhammayuttaṃ”.

“Indeed, after a long time, the revered Great Seer,

the speaker of truth, has come to this great forest for my sake.

Having heard your verse connected with the Dhamma,

I shall abandon evil and conduct myself accordingly.”

Itveva coro asimāvudhañca,

Sobbhe papāte narake akiri;

Avandi [T 2.0481] coro sugatassa pāde,

Tattheva naṃ pabbajjaṃ ayāci.

So saying, the bandit cast his sword and weapons

into a pit, a chasm, a fissure.

The bandit venerated the feet of the Sugata,

and right there, he requested the going forth from him.

Buddho ca kho kāruṇiko mahesi,

Yo satthā lokassa sadevakassa;

‘Tamehi bhikkhū’ti tadā avoca,

Eseva tassa ahu bhikkhubhāvoti.

And the Buddha, the compassionate Great Seer,

the Teacher of the world with its devas,

then said to him, “Come, bhikkhu!”

And that itself was his becoming a bhikkhu.

350. Atha kho bhagavā āyasmatā aṅgulimālena pacchāsamaṇena yena sāvatthi tena cārikaṃ pakkāmi. Anupubbena cārikaṃ caramāno yena sāvatthi tadavasari. Tatra sudaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme. Tena kho pana samayena rañño pasenadissa kosalassa antepuradvāre mahājanakāyo sannipatitvā uccāsaddo mahāsaddo hoti – “coro te, deva, vijite aṅgulimālo nāma luddo lohitapāṇi hatapahate niviṭṭho adayāpanno pāṇabhūtesu. Tena gāmāpi agāmā katā, nigamāpi anigamā katā, janapadāpi ajanapadā katā. So manusse vadhitvā vadhitvā aṅgulīnaṃ mālaṃ dhāreti. Taṃ devo paṭisedhetū”ti.

350. Then the Blessed One, having made the Venerable Aṅgulimāla his attendant monk, set out on a journey towards Sāvatthī. Traveling stage by stage, he arrived at Sāvatthī. There, indeed, the Blessed One was dwelling in Sāvatthī, in the Jeta Grove, the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍika. Now at that time, at the palace gate of King Pasenadi of Kosala, a great crowd of people had gathered and was making a loud and great noise, saying: “Your Majesty, in your realm there is a bandit named Aṅgulimāla, who is cruel, bloody-handed, devoted to killing and striking, and without compassion for living beings. By him, villages have been made into non-villages, towns into non-towns, and districts into non-districts. He, having killed people again and again, wears a garland of their fingers. May Your Majesty suppress him!”

Atha [M 2.0304][V 2.0311] kho rājā pasenadi kosalo pañcamattehi assasatehi sāvatthiyā nikkhami divā divassa. Yena ārāmo tena pāvisi. Yāvatikā yānassa bhūmi yānena gantvā yānā paccorohitvā pattikova yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā [T 2.0482] bhagavantaṃ [P 2.0101] abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinnaṃ kho rājānaṃ pasenadiṃ kosalaṃ bhagavā etadavoca – “kiṃ nu te, mahārāja, rājā vā māgadho seniyo bimbisāro kupito vesālikā vā licchavī aññe vā paṭirājāno”ti? “Na kho me, bhante, rājā māgadho seniyo bimbisāro kupito, nāpi vesālikā licchavī, nāpi aññe paṭirājāno. Coro me, bhante, vijite aṅgulimālo nāma luddo lohitapāṇi hatapahate niviṭṭho adayāpanno pāṇabhūtesu. Tena gāmāpi agāmā katā, nigamāpi anigamā katā, janapadāpi ajanapadā katā. So manusse vadhitvā vadhitvā aṅgulīnaṃ mālaṃ dhāreti. Tāhaṃ, bhante, paṭisedhissāmī”ti. “Sace pana tvaṃ, mahārāja, aṅgulimālaṃ passeyyāsi kesamassuṃ ohāretvā kāsāyāni vatthāni acchādetvā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajitaṃ, virataṃ pāṇātipātā, virataṃ adinnādānā, virataṃ musāvādā, ekabhattikaṃ, brahmacāriṃ, sīlavantaṃ, kalyāṇadhammaṃ, kinti naṃ kareyyāsī”ti? “Abhivādeyyāma vā, bhante, paccuṭṭheyyāma vā āsanena vā nimanteyyāma, abhinimanteyyāma vā naṃ cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānappaccayabhesajjaparikkhārehi, dhammikaṃ vā assa rakkhāvaraṇaguttiṃ saṃvidaheyyāma. Kuto panassa, bhante, dussīlassa pāpadhammassa evarūpo sīlasaṃyamo bhavissatī”ti?

Then King Pasenadi of Kosala set out from Sāvatthī in the middle of the day with five hundred horses. He went to the monastery, and as far as the ground was passable by vehicle, he rode in the vehicle. Then he dismounted and approached the Blessed One on foot. Having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Blessed One said to him: “What is it, Great King? Has King Bimbisāra Seniya of Magadha become angry with you, or the Licchavis of Vesālī, or some other rival king?” “It is not so, Venerable Sir. King Bimbisāra Seniya of Magadha is not angry with me, nor are the Licchavis of Vesālī, nor any other rival king. But in my realm, Venerable Sir, there is a bandit named Aṅgulimāla—cruel, bloody-handed, devoted to killing and striking, and without compassion for living beings. By him, villages have been made into non-villages, towns into non-towns, and districts into non-districts. He, having killed people again and again, wears a garland of their fingers. I, Venerable Sir, will suppress him.” “But suppose, Great King, you were to see Aṅgulimāla with his hair and beard shaved off, wearing the ochre robes, having gone forth from the household life into homelessness, abstaining from the destruction of life, abstaining from taking what is not given, abstaining from false speech, eating only one meal a day, leading the holy life, virtuous, of good principles—what would you do to him?” “We would pay homage to him, Venerable Sir, or rise up for him, or invite him to a seat. We would also invite him to accept robes, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites for the sick, or we would arrange for him a righteous guard, shelter, and protection. But how, Venerable Sir, could such moral restraint come to one who is immoral and of evil character?”

Tena kho pana samayena āyasmā aṅgulimālo bhagavato avidūre [T 2.0483] nisinno hoti. Atha kho bhagavā dakkhiṇaṃ bāhuṃ paggahetvā rājānaṃ pasenadiṃ kosalaṃ etadavoca – “eso, mahārāja, aṅgulimālo”ti. Atha kho rañño pasenadissa kosalassa ahudeva bhayaṃ, ahu chambhitattaṃ, ahu lomahaṃso. Atha kho bhagavā rājānaṃ pasenadiṃ kosalaṃ bhītaṃ saṃviggaṃ lomahaṭṭhajātaṃ viditvā rājānaṃ pasenadiṃ kosalaṃ etadavoca – “mā bhāyi, mahārāja, natthi te ito bhaya”nti. Atha kho rañño pasenadissa kosalassa yaṃ ahosi bhayaṃ vā [P 2.0102] chambhitattaṃ vā lomahaṃso vā so paṭippassambhi. Atha kho rājā pasenadi kosalo yenāyasmā aṅgulimālo [M 2.0305] tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmantaṃ aṅgulimālaṃ etadavoca – “ayyo no, bhante, aṅgulimālo”ti? “Evaṃ, mahārājā”ti. “Kathaṃgotto ayyassa pitā, kathaṃgottā mātā”ti? “Gaggo kho, mahārāja, pitā, mantāṇī mātā”ti. “Abhiramatu, bhante, ayyo gaggo mantāṇiputto. Ahamayyassa [V 2.0312] gaggassa mantāṇiputtassa ussukkaṃ karissāmi cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānappaccayabhesajjaparikkhārāna”nti.

Now at that time, the Venerable Aṅgulimāla was sitting not far from the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, extending his right arm, said to King Pasenadi of Kosala, “Great King, this is Aṅgulimāla.” Then for King Pasenadi of Kosala there arose fear, terror, and horripilation. The Blessed One, seeing that King Pasenadi of Kosala was frightened, agitated, and with his hair standing on end, said to him, “Do not be afraid, Great King. There is no danger for you from this one.” Then whatever fear, terror, or horripilation King Pasenadi of Kosala had, that subsided. Then King Pasenadi of Kosala approached the Venerable Aṅgulimāla and said to him, “Venerable Sir, is the noble one Aṅgulimāla?” “Even so, Great King.” “Of what clan is the noble one’s father, and of what clan is his mother?” “My father, Great King, is a Gagga, and my mother is a Mantāṇī.” “May the noble Gagga, son of Mantāṇī, take delight! I will endeavor to provide the noble Gagga, son of Mantāṇī, with robes, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites for the sick.”

351. Tena kho pana samayena āyasmā aṅgulimālo āraññiko hoti piṇḍapātiko paṃsukūliko tecīvariko. Atha kho āyasmā aṅgulimālo rājānaṃ pasenadiṃ kosalaṃ etadavoca – “alaṃ, mahārāja, paripuṇṇaṃ me cīvara”nti. Atha kho rājā pasenadi kosalo yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno [T 2.0484] kho rājā pasenadi kosalo bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “acchariyaṃ, bhante, abbhutaṃ, bhante! Yāvañcidaṃ, bhante, bhagavā adantānaṃ dametā, asantānaṃ sametā, aparinibbutānaṃ parinibbāpetā. Yañhi mayaṃ, bhante, nāsakkhimhā daṇḍenapi satthenapi dametuṃ so bhagavatā adaṇḍena asattheneva asatthena (syā. kaṃ.) danto. Handa ca dāni handa dāni (syā. kaṃ. pī.) mayaṃ, bhante, gacchāma; bahukiccā mayaṃ bahukaraṇīyā”ti. “Yassadāni, mahārāja, kālaṃ maññasī”ti. Atha kho rājā pasenadi kosalo uṭṭhāyāsanā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā pakkāmi.

351. Now at that time, the Venerable Aṅgulimāla was a forest-dweller, an alms-food-eater, a refuse-rag-wearer, and a triple-robe-wearer. Then the Venerable Aṅgulimāla said to King Pasenadi of Kosala: “Enough, Great King. My set of robes is complete.” Then King Pasenadi of Kosala approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, King Pasenadi of Kosala said to the Blessed One: “Wonderful, Venerable Sir! Marvelous, Venerable Sir! How well, Venerable Sir, the Blessed One tames the untamed, pacifies the unpacified, and brings to final extinguishment those who are not yet extinguished. For he whom we, Venerable Sir, were unable to tame with the rod or with the sword, has been tamed by the Blessed One without rod and without sword. Well now, Venerable Sir, we are going; we are busy and have much to do.” “Great King, it is now the time for you to do as you think fit.” Then King Pasenadi of Kosala rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping him to the right, and departed.

Atha kho āyasmā aṅgulimālo pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya sāvatthiyaṃ piṇḍāya pāvisi. Addasā kho āyasmā aṅgulimālo sāvatthiyaṃ sapadānaṃ piṇḍāya caramāno aññataraṃ itthiṃ mūḷhagabbhaṃ vighātagabbhaṃ visātagabbhaṃ (syā. kaṃ. pī. ka.). Disvānassa [P 2.0103] etadahosi – “kilissanti vata, bho, sattā; kilissanti vata, bho, sattā”ti! Atha kho āyasmā aṅgulimālo sāvatthiyaṃ piṇḍāya caritvā pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho āyasmā aṅgulimālo bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “idhāhaṃ, bhante, pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya sāvatthiṃ [M 2.0306] piṇḍāya pāvisiṃ. Addasaṃ kho ahaṃ, bhante, sāvatthiyaṃ sapadānaṃ piṇḍāya caramāno aññataraṃ itthiṃ mūḷhagabbhaṃ vighātagabbhaṃ”. Disvāna mayhaṃ etadahosi – “kilissanti vata[T 2.0485], bho, sattā; kilissanti vata, bho, sattā”ti!

Then the Venerable Aṅgulimāla, having dressed in the morning, took his bowl and robe and entered Sāvatthī for alms-food. As the Venerable Aṅgulimāla was walking for alms-food from house to house in Sāvatthī, he saw a certain woman with a malpositioned fetus and an obstructed birth. Having seen her, this thought occurred to him: 'Oh, how beings are afflicted! Oh, how beings are afflicted!' Then the Venerable Aṅgulimāla, having walked for alms-food in Sāvatthī and returned from his alms-round after his meal, approached the Blessed One. Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the Venerable Aṅgulimāla said this to the Blessed One: 'Here, Bhante, having dressed in the morning, I took my bowl and robe and entered Sāvatthī for alms-food. As I was walking for alms-food from house to house in Sāvatthī, Bhante, I saw a certain woman with a malpositioned fetus and an obstructed birth. Having seen her, this thought occurred to me: "Oh, how beings are afflicted! Oh, how beings are afflicted!"'

“Tena hi tvaṃ, aṅgulimāla, yena sā itthī tenupasaṅkama; upasaṅkamitvā taṃ itthiṃ evaṃ vadehi [V 2.0313] – ‘yatohaṃ, bhagini, jāto bhagini jātiyā jāto (sī.) nābhijānāmi sañcicca pāṇaṃ jīvitā voropetā, tena saccena sotthi te hotu, sotthi gabbhassā’”ti.

“In that case, Aṅgulimāla, go to that woman. Having approached her, say this: ‘Sister, since I was born, I do not recall intentionally depriving a living being of life. By this truth, may there be well-being for you, may there be well-being for the fetus.’”

“So hi nūna me, bhante, sampajānamusāvādo bhavissati. Mayā hi, bhante, bahū sañcicca pāṇā jīvitā voropitā”ti. “Tena hi tvaṃ, aṅgulimāla, yena sā itthī tenupasaṅkama; upasaṅkamitvā taṃ itthiṃ evaṃ vadehi – ‘yatohaṃ, bhagini, ariyāya jātiyā jāto, nābhijānāmi sañcicca pāṇaṃ jīvitā voropetā, tena saccena sotthi te hotu, sotthi gabbhassā’”ti.

“But Bhante, that would surely be a deliberate lie on my part, for I, Bhante, have intentionally deprived many living beings of life.” “In that case, Aṅgulimāla, go to that woman. Having approached her, say this: ‘Sister, since I was born with the noble birth, I do not recall intentionally depriving a living being of life. By this truth, may there be well-being for you, may there be well-being for the fetus.’”

“Evaṃ, bhante”ti kho āyasmā aṅgulimālo bhagavato paṭissutvā yena sā itthī tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā taṃ itthiṃ etadavoca – “yatohaṃ, bhagini, ariyāya jātiyā jāto, nābhijānāmi sañcicca pāṇaṃ jīvitā voropetā, tena saccena sotthi te hotu, sotthi gabbhassā”ti. Atha khvāssā itthiyā sotthi ahosi, sotthi gabbhassa.

“So be it, Bhante.” Having thus assented to the Blessed One, the Venerable Aṅgulimāla went to that woman. Having approached her, he said this: “Sister, since I was born with the noble birth, I do not recall intentionally depriving a living being of life. By this truth, may there be well-being for you, may there be well-being for the fetus.” Then there was well-being for the woman and well-being for the fetus.

Atha kho āyasmā aṅgulimālo eko vūpakaṭṭho appamatto ātāpī pahitatto viharanto nacirasseva – yassatthāya kulaputtā sammadeva agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajanti tadanuttaraṃ – brahmacariyapariyosānaṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja [T 2.0486] vihāsi. ‘Khīṇā jāti vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti [P 2.0104] abbhaññāsi. Aññataro kho panāyasmā aṅgulimālo arahataṃ ahosi.

Then the Venerable Aṅgulimāla, dwelling alone, withdrawn, heedful, ardent, and resolute, before long realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, that unsurpassed culmination of the holy life for which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness, and having entered upon it, he dwelt therein. He knew directly: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.’ And the Venerable Aṅgulimāla became one of the Arahants.

352. Atha kho āyasmā aṅgulimālo pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya sāvatthiṃ piṇḍāya pāvisi. Tena kho pana samayena aññenapi leḍḍu khitto āyasmato aṅgulimālassa kāye nipatati, aññenapi [M 2.0307] daṇḍo khitto āyasmato aṅgulimālassa kāye nipatati, aññenapi sakkharā khittā āyasmato aṅgulimālassa kāye nipatati. Atha kho āyasmā aṅgulimālo bhinnena sīsena, lohitena gaḷantena, bhinnena pattena, vipphālitāya saṅghāṭiyā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami. Addasā kho bhagavā āyasmantaṃ aṅgulimālaṃ dūratova āgacchantaṃ. Disvāna āyasmantaṃ aṅgulimālaṃ etadavoca – “adhivāsehi tvaṃ, brāhmaṇa, adhivāsehi [V 2.0314] tvaṃ, brāhmaṇa. Yassa kho tvaṃ, brāhmaṇa, kammassa vipākena bahūni vassāni bahūni vassasatāni bahūni vassasahassāni niraye pacceyyāsi tassa tvaṃ, brāhmaṇa, kammassa vipākaṃ diṭṭheva dhamme paṭisaṃvedesī”ti. Atha kho āyasmā aṅgulimālo rahogato paṭisallīno vimuttisukhaṃ paṭisaṃvedi; tāyaṃ velāyaṃ imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi –

352. Then, the Venerable Aṅgulimāla, having dressed in the morning, took his bowl and robe and entered Sāvatthī for alms-food. Now at that time, a clod thrown by someone fell on the body of the Venerable Aṅgulimāla, a stick thrown by another fell on the body of the Venerable Aṅgulimāla, and a shard thrown by yet another fell on the body of the Venerable Aṅgulimāla. Then the Venerable Aṅgulimāla—with his head split open, with blood flowing, with his bowl broken, and with his outer robe torn—approached the Blessed One. The Blessed One saw the Venerable Aṅgulimāla coming from afar. Seeing him, the Blessed One said this to the Venerable Aṅgulimāla: “Endure it, Brahmin! Endure it, Brahmin! You are experiencing in this very life the result of that kamma for which you might have been tormented in hell for many years, for many hundreds of years, for many thousands of years.” Then the Venerable Aṅgulimāla, having gone to a secluded place and dwelling in solitude, experienced the bliss of liberation. At that time, he uttered this inspired utterance:

“Yo pubbeva yo ca pubbe (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) pamajjitvā, pacchā so nappamajjati;

Somaṃ so imaṃ (sī.) lokaṃ pabhāseti, abbhā muttova candimā.

“He who was formerly heedless, but afterwards is not, illumines this world like the moon freed from a cloud.

“Yassa [T 2.0487] pāpaṃ kataṃ kammaṃ, kusalena pidhīyati pithīyati (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.);

Somaṃ lokaṃ pabhāseti, abbhā muttova candimā.

“Whose evil deed that was done is covered by a wholesome one, he illumines this world like the moon freed from a cloud.

“Yo have daharo bhikkhu, yuñjati buddhasāsane;

Somaṃ lokaṃ pabhāseti, abbhā muttova candimā.

“Indeed, a young bhikkhu who applies himself to the Buddha’s teaching illumines this world, like the moon freed from a cloud.

“Disā hi me dhammakathaṃ suṇantu,

Disā hi me yuñjantu buddhasāsane;

Disā hi me te manujā bhajantu,

Ye dhammamevādapayanti santo.

“May my enemies hear a talk on the Dhamma, may my enemies devote themselves to the Buddha’s teaching; may my enemies associate with those good people who lead others to accept the Dhamma.

“Disā [P 2.0105] hi me khantivādānaṃ, avirodhappasaṃsīnaṃ;

Suṇantu dhammaṃ kālena, tañca anuvidhīyantu.

“May my enemies listen in due season to the Dhamma of those who speak on patience and praise non-opposition, and may they act in accordance with it.

“Na hi jātu so mamaṃ hiṃse, aññaṃ vā pana kiñci naṃ kañci naṃ (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.), kañcanaṃ (?);

Pappuyya paramaṃ santiṃ, rakkheyya tasathāvare.

“May he never harm me, nor any other being whatsoever. Having attained the supreme peace, may he protect beings, both moving and still.

“Udakañhi [M 2.0308] nayanti nettikā, usukārā namayanti damayanti (ka.) tejanaṃ;

Dāruṃ namayanti tacchakā, attānaṃ damayanti paṇḍitā.

“Irrigators lead the water, fletchers straighten the arrow-shaft, carpenters shape the wood; the wise tame themselves.

“Daṇḍeneke [V 2.0315] damayanti, aṅkusehi kasāhi ca;

Adaṇḍena asatthena, ahaṃ dantomhi tādinā.

“Some tame with a rod, with goads, and with whips; I was tamed by one such, who has no rod nor any weapon.

“Ahiṃsakoti me nāmaṃ, hiṃsakassa pure sato;

Ajjāhaṃ saccanāmomhi, na naṃ hiṃsāmi kiñci naṃ kañci naṃ (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.), kañcanaṃ (?).

“‘Ahiṃsaka’ (Harmless) was my name, though formerly I was a harmer. Today I am true to my name, for I harm no one at all.

“Coro [T 2.0488] ahaṃ pure āsiṃ, aṅgulimāloti vissuto;

Vuyhamāno mahoghena, buddhaṃ saraṇamāgamaṃ.

“Formerly I was a robber, renowned as Aṅgulimāla. Swept along by the great flood, I went to the Buddha for refuge.

“Lohitapāṇi pure āsiṃ, aṅgulimāloti vissuto;

Saraṇagamanaṃ passa, bhavanetti samūhatā.

Formerly, I was one with blood-smeared hands, renowned as Aṅgulimāla. Behold my going for refuge! The craving that leads to existence has been uprooted.

“Tādisaṃ kammaṃ katvāna, bahuṃ duggatigāminaṃ;

Phuṭṭho kammavipākena, aṇaṇo bhuñjāmi bhojanaṃ.

Having done many such deeds that lead to a woeful state, I have been touched by the fruit of my kamma; now, being free from debt, I eat my food.

“Pamādamanuyuñjanti, bālā dummedhino janā;

Appamādañca medhāvī, dhanaṃ seṭṭhaṃva rakkhati.

Fools, witless people, indulge in heedlessness; but the wise guard heedfulness as their greatest treasure.

“Mā pamādamanuyuñjetha, mā kāmarati santhavaṃ;

Appamatto hi jhāyanto, pappoti vipulaṃ paramaṃ (ka.) sukhaṃ.

Do not devote yourselves to heedlessness, nor to intimacy with sensual delight. For the heedful one, meditating, attains vast happiness.

“Svāgataṃ sāgataṃ (sī. pī.) nāpagataṃ nāma sagataṃ (ka.), nayidaṃ dummantitaṃ mama;

Saṃvibhattesu suvibhattesu (syā. kaṃ.), savibhattesu (sī. ka.), paṭibhattesu (pī.) dhammesu, yaṃ seṭṭhaṃ tadupāgamaṃ.

This was a good coming, not a bad coming; this was not ill-conceived by me. Among the well-expounded teachings, I have attained that which is supreme.

“Svāgataṃ nāpagataṃ, nayidaṃ dummantitaṃ mama;

Tisso vijjā anuppattā, kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

This was a good coming, not a bad coming; this was not ill-conceived by me. The three knowledges have been attained; the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.

Aṅgulimālasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ chaṭṭhaṃ.

The Aṅgulimāla Sutta, the sixth, is concluded.

7. Piyajātikasuttaṃ

7. The Discourse on What is Born from the Dear

353. Evaṃ [T 2.0489][M 2.0309][V 2.0316][P 2.0106] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme. Tena kho pana samayena aññatarassa gahapatissa ekaputtako piyo manāpo kālaṅkato hoti. Tassa kālaṃkiriyāya neva kammantā paṭibhanti na bhattaṃ paṭibhāti. So āḷāhanaṃ gantvā kandati – “kahaṃ, ekaputtaka, kahaṃ, ekaputtakā”ti! Atha kho so gahapati yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinnaṃ kho taṃ gahapatiṃ bhagavā etadavoca – “na kho te, gahapati, sake citte ṭhitassa indriyāni, atthi te indriyānaṃ aññathatta”nti. “Kiñhi me, bhante, indriyānaṃ nāññathattaṃ bhavissati; mayhañhi, bhante, ekaputto piyo manāpo kālaṅkato. Tassa kālaṃkiriyāya neva kammantā paṭibhanti, na bhattaṃ paṭibhāti. Sohaṃ āḷāhanaṃ gantvā kandāmi – ‘kahaṃ, ekaputtaka, kahaṃ, ekaputtakā’”ti! “Evametaṃ, gahapati, evametaṃ, gahapati evametaṃ gahapati (pī. sakideva), evameva (sī. sakideva)! Piyajātikā hi, gahapati, sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā piyappabhavikā”ti. “Kassa kho kissa nu kho (sī.) nāmetaṃ, bhante, evaṃ bhavissati – ‘piyajātikā sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā piyappabhavikā’ti? Piyajātikā hi kho, bhante, ānandasomanassā piyappabhavikā”ti. Atha kho so gahapati bhagavato bhāsitaṃ [T 2.0490] anabhinanditvā paṭikkositvā uṭṭhāyāsanā pakkāmi.

353. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī, in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. Now at that time, a certain householder had a dear and beloved only son who had passed away. Due to his passing, he took no interest in his work, nor did food appeal to him. He would go to the charnel ground and weep, crying, “Where are you, my only son? Where are you, my only son?” Then that householder approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. The Blessed One said to him, “Householder, your faculties are not established in your own mind; there is an alteration in your faculties.” “Venerable sir, how could there not be an alteration in my faculties? My dear and beloved only son has passed away. Due to his passing, I take no interest in my work, nor does food appeal to me. I go to the charnel ground and weep, crying, ‘Where are you, my only son? Where are you, my only son?’” “That is so, householder, that is so! For sorrow, lamentation, pain, distress, and despair are born of what is dear, they originate from what is dear.” “Venerable sir, who would ever think that sorrow, lamentation, pain, distress, and despair are born of what is dear, that they originate from what is dear? Surely, venerable sir, joy and happiness are born of what is dear, they originate from what is dear.” Then that householder, not delighting in the Blessed One’s words and rejecting them, got up from his seat and left.

354. Tena kho pana samayena sambahulā akkhadhuttā bhagavato avidūre akkhehi dibbanti. Atha kho so gahapati yena te akkhadhuttā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā akkhadhutte etadavoca – “idhāhaṃ, bhonto, yena samaṇo gotamo [P 2.0107] tenupasaṅkamiṃ; upasaṅkamitvā samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃ. Ekamantaṃ nisinnaṃ kho maṃ, bhonto, samaṇo gotamo etadavoca – ‘na kho te, gahapati, sake citte ṭhitassa indriyāni, atthi te indriyānaṃ aññathatta’nti. Evaṃ vutte, ahaṃ, bhonto, samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ etadavocaṃ – ‘kiñhi me, bhante, indriyānaṃ nāññathattaṃ bhavissati; mayhañhi, bhante, ekaputtako piyo manāpo kālaṅkato. Tassa kālaṃkiriyāya [V 2.0317] neva kammantā paṭibhanti, na bhattaṃ paṭibhāti[M 2.0310]. Sohaṃ āḷāhanaṃ gantvā kandāmi – kahaṃ, ekaputtaka, kahaṃ, ekaputtakā’ti! ‘Evametaṃ, gahapati, evametaṃ, gahapati! Piyajātikā hi, gahapati, sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā piyappabhavikā’ti. ‘Kassa kho nāmetaṃ, bhante, evaṃ bhavissati – piyajātikā sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā piyappabhavikā? Piyajātikā hi kho, bhante, ānandasomanassā piyappabhavikā’ti. Atha khvāhaṃ, bhonto, samaṇassa gotamassa bhāsitaṃ anabhinanditvā paṭikkositvā uṭṭhāyāsanā pakkami”nti. “Evametaṃ, gahapati, evametaṃ, gahapati! Piyajātikā hi, gahapati, ānandasomanassā piyappabhavikā”ti[T 2.0491]. Atha kho so gahapati “sameti me akkhadhuttehī”ti pakkāmi. Atha kho idaṃ kathāvatthu anupubbena rājantepuraṃ pāvisi.

354. Now at that time, a number of gamblers were playing with dice not far from the Blessed One. Then that householder approached those gamblers and said to them: “Sirs, I approached the ascetic Gotama; having approached, I paid homage to the ascetic Gotama and sat down to one side. To me sitting to one side, sirs, the ascetic Gotama said this: ‘Householder, your faculties are not established in your own mind; there is an alteration in your faculties.’ When this was said, sirs, I said this to the ascetic Gotama: ‘Venerable sir, how could there not be an alteration in my faculties? My dear and beloved only son has passed away. Due to his passing, I take no interest in my work, nor does food appeal to me. I go to the charnel ground and weep, crying: “Where are you, my only son? Where are you, my only son?”’ He said: ‘That is so, householder, that is so! For sorrow, lamentation, pain, distress, and despair are born from what is dear; they originate from what is dear.’ I replied: ‘Venerable sir, who would ever think that sorrow, lamentation, pain, distress, and despair are born from what is dear, that they originate from what is dear? Surely, venerable sir, joy and happiness are born from what is dear; they originate from what is dear.’ Then, sirs, not delighting in the ascetic Gotama’s words and rejecting them, I got up from my seat and left.” The gamblers said: “That is so, householder, that is so! For joy and happiness are born from what is dear; they originate from what is dear.” Then that householder, thinking, “My view agrees with the gamblers,” departed. And this topic of conversation gradually entered the royal palace.

355. Atha kho rājā pasenadi kosalo mallikaṃ deviṃ āmantesi – “idaṃ te, mallike, samaṇena gotamena bhāsitaṃ – ‘piyajātikā sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā piyappabhavikā’”ti. “Sacetaṃ, mahārāja, bhagavatā bhāsitaṃ, evameta”nti. “Evameva panāyaṃ mallikā yaññadeva samaṇo gotamo bhāsati taṃ tadevassa abbhanumodati”. “Sacetaṃ, mahārāja, bhagavatā bhāsitaṃ evametanti. Seyyathāpi nāma, yaññadeva ācariyo antevāsissa bhāsati taṃ tadevassa antevāsī abbhanumodati – ‘evametaṃ, ācariya, evametaṃ, ācariyā’”ti. “Evameva kho tvaṃ, mallike, yaññadeva samaṇo gotamo bhāsati taṃ tadevassa abbhanumodasi”. “Sacetaṃ, mahārāja[P 2.0108], bhagavatā bhāsitaṃ evameta”nti. “Carapi, re mallike, vinassā”ti. Atha kho mallikā devī nāḷijaṅghaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ āmantesi – “ehi tvaṃ, brāhmaṇa, yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkama; upasaṅkamitvā mama vacanena bhagavato pāde sirasā vandāhi, appābādhaṃ appātaṅkaṃ lahuṭṭhānaṃ balaṃ phāsuvihāraṃ puccha – ‘mallikā, bhante, devī bhagavato pāde sirasā vandati, appābādhaṃ appātaṅkaṃ lahuṭṭhānaṃ balaṃ phāsuvihāraṃ pucchatī’ti. Evañca vadehi – ‘bhāsitā nu kho, bhante, bhagavatā esā vācā – piyajātikā sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā piyappabhavikā’ti[T 2.0492]. Yathā te bhagavā byākaroti taṃ sādhukaṃ uggahetvā mama āroceyyāsi. Na hi tathāgatā vitathaṃ bhaṇantī”ti. “Evaṃ, bhotī”ti kho nāḷijaṅgho brāhmaṇo mallikāya deviyā paṭissutvā yena bhagavā [M 2.0311] tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavatā saddhiṃ sammodi. Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ [V 2.0318] nisinno kho nāḷijaṅgho brāhmaṇo bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “mallikā, bho gotama, devī bhoto gotamassa pāde sirasā vandati; appābādhaṃ appātaṅkaṃ lahuṭṭhānaṃ balaṃ phāsuvihāraṃ pucchati; evañca vadeti – ‘bhāsitā nu kho, bhante, bhagavatā esā vācā – piyajātikā sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā piyappabhavikā’”ti.

355. Then King Pasenadi of Kosala addressed Queen Mallikā: “Mallikā, this was spoken by the ascetic Gotama: ‘Sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are born of what is dear, originate from what is dear.’” “If, great king, that was spoken by the Blessed One, then so it is.” “This Mallikā just approves of whatever the ascetic Gotama says. Just as whatever a teacher says to a student, the student approves it—‘So it is, teacher, so it is’—in the very same way, Mallikā, you approve of whatever the ascetic Gotama says.” “If, great king, that was spoken by the Blessed One, then so it is.” “Begone, you wretch, Mallikā! Perish!” Then Queen Mallikā addressed the brahmin Nāḷijaṅgha: “Come, brahmin, approach the Blessed One. Having approached, in my name bow your head to the Blessed One’s feet and inquire about his freedom from illness and affliction, his nimbleness, strength, and comfortable abiding—‘Venerable sir, Queen Mallikā bows her head to the Blessed One’s feet and inquires about his freedom from illness and affliction, his nimbleness, strength, and comfortable abiding.’ And say this: ‘Venerable sir, was this statement spoken by the Blessed One—“Sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are born of what is dear, originate from what is dear”?’ However the Blessed One explains it to you, having learned it well, you must report it back to me. For the Tathāgatas do not speak what is false.” “Yes, madam,” replied the brahmin Nāḷijaṅgha to Queen Mallikā. He then approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him. After some pleasant and memorable conversation, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the brahmin Nāḷijaṅgha said to the Blessed One: “Venerable Gotama, Queen Mallikā bows her head to your feet and inquires about your freedom from illness and affliction, your nimbleness, strength, and comfortable abiding. And she says this: ‘Venerable sir, was this statement spoken by the Blessed One—“Sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are born of what is dear, originate from what is dear”?’”

356. “Evametaṃ, brāhmaṇa, evametaṃ, brāhmaṇa! Piyajātikā hi, brāhmaṇa, sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā piyappabhavikāti. Tadamināpetaṃ, brāhmaṇa, pariyāyena veditabbaṃ yathā piyajātikā sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā piyappabhavikā. Bhūtapubbaṃ, brāhmaṇa, imissāyeva sāvatthiyā aññatarissā itthiyā mātā kālamakāsi. Sā tassā kālakiriyāya ummattikā khittacittā rathikāya rathikaṃ rathiyāya rathiyaṃ (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) siṅghāṭakena siṅghāṭakaṃ upasaṅkamitvā evamāha – ‘api me mātaraṃ addassatha addasatha (sī. pī.), api me mātaraṃ addassathā’ti? Imināpi [P 2.0109] kho etaṃ, brāhmaṇa, pariyāyena veditabbaṃ yathā piyajātikā sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā piyappabhavikāti.

356. “So it is, brahmin, so it is! For sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are indeed born from what is dear, they originate from what is dear. And in this way, brahmin, it should be understood how sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are born from what is dear, originate from what is dear. Formerly, brahmin, in this very Sāvatthī, a certain woman’s mother died. At her death, she became deranged, her mind unhinged. She went from street to street, from crossroad to crossroad, approaching people and saying, ‘Have you seen my mother? Have you seen my mother?’ In this way too, brahmin, it should be understood how sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are born from what is dear, originate from what is dear.”

“Bhūtapubbaṃ[T 2.0493], brāhmaṇa, imissāyeva sāvatthiyā aññatarissā itthiyā pitā kālamakāsi… bhātā kālamakāsi… bhaginī kālamakāsi… putto kālamakāsi… dhītā kālamakāsi… sāmiko kālamakāsi. Sā tassa kālakiriyāya ummattikā khittacittā rathikāya rathikaṃ siṅghāṭakena siṅghāṭakaṃ upasaṅkamitvā evamāha – ‘api me sāmikaṃ addassatha, api me sāmikaṃ addassathā’ti? Imināpi kho etaṃ, brāhmaṇa, pariyāyena veditabbaṃ yathā piyajātikā sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā piyappabhavikāti.

“Formerly, brahmin, in this very Sāvatthī, a certain woman’s father died… her brother died… her sister died… her son died… her daughter died… her husband died. At his death, she became deranged, her mind unhinged. She went from street to street, from crossroad to crossroad, approaching people and saying: ‘Have you seen my husband? Have you seen my husband?’ In this way too, brahmin, it should be understood how sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are born from what is dear, originate from what is dear.”

“Bhūtapubbaṃ[V 2.0319], brāhmaṇa, imissāyeva sāvatthiyā aññatarassa purisassa mātā kālamakāsi. So tassā kālakiriyāya ummattako khittacitto rathikāya rathikaṃ siṅghāṭakena siṅghāṭakaṃ upasaṅkamitvā evamāha – ‘api me mātaraṃ addassatha, api me mātaraṃ addassathā’ti[M 2.0312]? Imināpi kho etaṃ, brāhmaṇa[T 2.0494], pariyāyena veditabbaṃ yathā piyajātikā sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā piyappabhavikāti.

“Formerly, brahmin, in this very Sāvatthī, a certain man’s mother died. At her death, he became deranged, his mind unhinged. He went from street to street, from crossroad to crossroad, approaching people and saying: ‘Have you seen my mother? Have you seen my mother?’ In this way too, brahmin, it should be understood how sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are born from what is dear, originate from what is dear.”

“Bhūtapubbaṃ, brāhmaṇa, imissāyeva sāvatthiyā aññatarassa purisassa pitā kālamakāsi… bhātā kālamakāsi… bhaginī kālamakāsi… putto kālamakāsi… dhītā kālamakāsi… pajāpati kālamakāsi. So tassā kālakiriyāya ummattako khittacitto rathikāya rathikaṃ siṅghāṭakena siṅghāṭakaṃ upasaṅkamitvā evamāha – ‘api me pajāpatiṃ addassatha, api me pajāpatiṃ addassathā’ti? Imināpi kho etaṃ, brāhmaṇa, pariyāyena veditabbaṃ yathā piyajātikā sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā piyappabhavikāti.

“Formerly, brahmin, in this very Sāvatthī, a certain man’s father died… his brother died… his sister died… his son died… his daughter died… his wife died. At her death, he became deranged, his mind unhinged. He went from street to street, from crossroad to crossroad, approaching people and saying: ‘Have you seen my wife? Have you seen my wife?’ In this way too, brahmin, it should be understood how sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are born from what is dear, originate from what is dear.”

“Bhūtapubbaṃ, brāhmaṇa, imissāyeva sāvatthiyā aññatarā itthī ñātikulaṃ agamāsi. Tassā te ñātakā sāmikaṃ sāmikā (sī.) acchinditvā aññassa dātukāmā. Sā ca taṃ na icchati. Atha kho sā itthī sāmikaṃ etadavoca – ‘ime, maṃ mama (syā. kaṃ. pī.), ayyaputta, ñātakā tvaṃ tayā (sī.), taṃ (syā. kaṃ. pī.) acchinditvā aññassa dātukāmā. Ahañca taṃ na icchāmī’ti. Atha kho so puriso taṃ itthiṃ dvidhā chetvā attānaṃ [P 2.0110] upphālesi uppāṭesi (sī. pī.), ophāresi (ka.) – ‘ubho pecca bhavissāmā’ti. Imināpi kho etaṃ, brāhmaṇa, pariyāyena veditabbaṃ yathā piyajātikā sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā piyappabhavikā”ti.

“Formerly, Brahmin, in this very Sāvatthī, a certain woman went to her relatives’ home. Her relatives, intending to separate her from her husband, wanted to give her to another, but she did not want him. Then that woman said to her husband: ‘My lord, these relatives of mine intend to separate me from you and give me to another, but I do not desire him.’ Then that man cut that woman in two and ripped open his own belly, thinking: ‘We shall both be together in the next life.’ By this method too, Brahmin, it should be understood how sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are born from what is dear, have what is dear as their origin.”

357. Atha kho nāḷijaṅgho brāhmaṇo bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinanditvā anumoditvā uṭṭhāyāsanā yena mallikā devī tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā yāvatako ahosi bhagavatā saddhiṃ kathāsallāpo taṃ sabbaṃ mallikāya deviyā ārocesi. Atha kho mallikā devī yena rājā pasenadi kosalo tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā rājānaṃ pasenadiṃ kosalaṃ etadavoca – “taṃ kiṃ maññasi, mahārāja, piyā te vajirī kumārī”ti? “Evaṃ, mallike, piyā me vajirī kumārī”ti. “Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, mahārāja, vajiriyā te kumāriyā vipariṇāmaññathābhāvā uppajjeyyuṃ [T 2.0495] sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā”ti? “Vajiriyā me, mallike, kumāriyā vipariṇāmaññathābhāvā jīvitassapi siyā [M 2.0313] aññathattaṃ, kiṃ pana me na uppajjissanti sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā”ti? “Idaṃ kho taṃ, mahārāja, tena bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā sammāsambuddhena sandhāya bhāsitaṃ – ‘piyajātikā sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā piyappabhavikā’ti.

357. Then the Brahmin Nāḷijaṅgha, having rejoiced and approved of the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat and approached Queen Mallikā. Having approached, he related to Queen Mallikā all the conversation he had had with the Blessed One. Then Queen Mallikā approached King Pasenadi of Kosala and said to him: “What do you think, great king? Is Princess Vajirī dear to you?” “Yes, Mallikā, Princess Vajirī is dear to me.” “What do you think, great king? If change and alteration were to befall Princess Vajirī, would sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise in you?” “Mallikā, if change and alteration were to befall Princess Vajirī, even my life might be altered; how could sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair not arise in me?” “This, great king, is what the Blessed One—who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One—was referring to when he said: ‘Sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are born from what is dear, have what is dear as their origin.’”

“Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, mahārāja, piyā te vāsabhā khattiyā”ti? “Evaṃ, mallike, piyā [V 2.0320] me vāsabhā khattiyā”ti. “Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, mahārāja, vāsabhāya te khattiyāya vipariṇāmaññathābhāvā uppajjeyyuṃ sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā”ti? “Vāsabhāya me, mallike, khattiyāya vipariṇāmaññathābhāvā jīvitassapi siyā aññathattaṃ, kiṃ pana me na uppajjissanti sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā”ti? “Idaṃ kho taṃ, mahārāja, tena bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā sammāsambuddhena sandhāya bhāsitaṃ – ‘piyajātikā sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā piyappabhavikā’ti.

“What do you think, great king? Is Queen Vāsabhakhattiyā dear to you?” “Yes, Mallikā, Queen Vāsabhakhattiyā is dear to me.” “What do you think, great king? If change and alteration were to befall Queen Vāsabhakhattiyā, would sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise in you?” “Mallikā, if change and alteration were to befall Queen Vāsabhakhattiyā, even my life might be altered; how could sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair not arise in me?” “This, great king, is what the Blessed One—who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One—was referring to when he said: ‘Sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are born from what is dear, have what is dear as their origin.’”

“Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, mahārāja, piyo te viṭaṭūbho viḍūḍabho (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) senāpatī”ti? “Evaṃ[P 2.0111], mallike, piyo me viṭaṭūbho senāpatī”ti. “Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, mahārāja, viṭaṭūbhassa te senāpatissa vipariṇāmaññathābhāvā uppajjeyyuṃ sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā”ti? “Viṭaṭūbhassa me, mallike, senāpatissa vipariṇāmaññathābhāvā jīvitassapi siyā aññathattaṃ[T 2.0496], kiṃ pana me na uppajjissanti sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā”ti? “Idaṃ kho taṃ, mahārāja, tena bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā sammāsambuddhena sandhāya bhāsitaṃ – ‘piyajātikā sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā piyappabhavikā’ti.

“What do you think, great king? Is your general Viṭaṭūbha dear to you?” “Yes, Mallikā, my general Viṭaṭūbha is dear to me.” “What do you think, great king? If change and alteration were to befall your general Viṭaṭūbha, would sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise in you?” “Mallikā, if change and alteration were to befall my general Viṭaṭūbha, even my life might be altered; how could sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair not arise in me?” “This, great king, is what the Blessed One—who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One—was referring to when he said: ‘Sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are born from what is dear, have what is dear as their origin.’”

“Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, mahārāja, piyā te aha”nti? “Evaṃ, mallike, piyā mesi tva”nti. “Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, mahārāja, mayhaṃ te vipariṇāmaññathābhāvā uppajjeyyuṃ sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā”ti? “Tuyhañhi me, mallike, vipariṇāmaññathābhāvā jīvitassapi siyā aññathattaṃ, kiṃ pana me na uppajjissanti sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā”ti? “Idaṃ kho taṃ, mahārāja, tena bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā sammāsambuddhena sandhāya bhāsitaṃ – ‘piyajātikā sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā piyappabhavikā’ti.

“What do you think, great king, am I dear to you?” “Yes, Mallikā, you are dear to me.” “What do you think, great king, if change and alteration were to befall me, would sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise in you?” “Indeed, Mallikā, if change and alteration were to befall you, even my life might be altered; how could sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair not arise in me?” “This, great king, is what the Blessed One—who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One—was referring to when he said: ‘Sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are born from what is dear, have what is dear as their origin.’”

“Taṃ [M 2.0314] kiṃ maññasi, mahārāja, piyā te kāsikosalā”ti? “Evaṃ, mallike, piyā me kāsikosalā. Kāsikosalānaṃ, mallike, ānubhāvena kāsikacandanaṃ paccanubhoma, mālāgandhavilepanaṃ dhāremā”ti. “Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, mahārāja, kāsikosalānaṃ te vipariṇāmaññathābhāvā uppajjeyyuṃ sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā”ti? “Kāsikosalānañhi, mallike[V 2.0321], vipariṇāmaññathābhāvā jīvitassapi siyā aññathattaṃ, kiṃ pana me na uppajjissanti sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā”ti? “Idaṃ kho taṃ, mahārāja, tena bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā sammāsambuddhena [T 2.0497] sandhāya bhāsitaṃ – ‘piyajātikā sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā piyappabhavikā’”ti.

“What do you think, great king, are Kāsi and Kosala dear to you?” “Yes, Mallikā, Kāsi and Kosala are dear to me. By the influence of Kāsi and Kosala, we enjoy Kāsi sandalwood and wear garlands, perfumes, and ointments.” “What do you think, great king, if change and alteration were to befall Kāsi and Kosala, would sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise in you?” “Mallikā, if change and alteration were to befall Kāsi and Kosala, even my life might be altered; how could sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair not arise in me?” “This, great king, is what the Blessed One—who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One—was referring to when he said: ‘Sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are born from what is dear, have what is dear as their origin.’”

“Acchariyaṃ, mallike, abbhutaṃ, mallike! Yāvañca so bhagavā [P 2.0112] paññāya ativijjha maññe paṭivijjha paññāya (ka.) passati. Ehi, mallike, ācamehī”ti ācāmehīti (sī. pī.). Atha kho rājā pasenadi kosalo uṭṭhāyāsanā ekaṃsaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ karitvā yena bhagavā tenañjaliṃ paṇāmetvā tikkhattuṃ udānaṃ udānesi – “namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa, namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa, namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassā”ti.

“Wonderful, Mallikā! Amazing, Mallikā! How exceedingly that Blessed One penetrates with wisdom and sees. Come, Mallikā, bring water for rinsing.” Then King Pasenadi of Kosala rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, and, extending his joined hands in reverence toward the Blessed One, uttered this inspired utterance three times: “Homage to that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One! Homage to that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One! Homage to that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One!”

Piyajātikasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ sattamaṃ.

The Piyajātika Sutta, the seventh, is concluded.

8. Bāhitikasuttaṃ

8. The Bāhitika Sutta

358. Evaṃ [T 2.0498][V 2.0322] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme. Atha kho āyasmā ānando pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya sāvatthiyaṃ piṇḍāya pāvisi. Sāvatthiyaṃ piṇḍāya caritvā pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto yena pubbārāmo migāramātupāsādo tenupasaṅkami divāvihārāya. Tena kho pana samayena rājā pasenadi kosalo ekapuṇḍarīkaṃ nāgaṃ abhiruhitvā sāvatthiyā niyyāti divā divassa. Addasā kho rājā pasenadi kosalo āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ dūratova āgacchantaṃ. Disvāna sirivaḍḍhaṃ mahāmattaṃ āmantesi – “āyasmā no eso, samma sirivaḍḍha, ānando”ti[M 2.0315]. “Evaṃ, mahārāja, āyasmā eso ānando”ti. Atha kho rājā pasenadi kosalo aññataraṃ purisaṃ āmantesi – “ehi tvaṃ, ambho purisa, yenāyasmā ānando tenupasaṅkama; upasaṅkamitvā mama vacanena āyasmato ānandassa pāde sirasā vandāhi – ‘rājā, bhante, pasenadi kosalo āyasmato ānandassa pāde sirasā vandatī’ti. Evañca vadehi – ‘sace kira, bhante, āyasmato ānandassa na kiñci accāyikaṃ karaṇīyaṃ, āgametu kira, bhante, āyasmā ānando muhuttaṃ [P 2.0113] anukampaṃ upādāyā’”ti. “Evaṃ, devā”ti kho so puriso rañño pasenadissa kosalassa paṭissutvā yenāyasmā [T 2.0499] ānando tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Ekamantaṃ ṭhito kho so puriso āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ etadavoca – “rājā, bhante, pasenadi kosalo āyasmato ānandassa pāde sirasā vandati; evañca vadeti – ‘sace kira, bhante, āyasmato ānandassa na kiñci accāyikaṃ karaṇīyaṃ, āgametu kira, bhante, āyasmā ānando muhuttaṃ anukampaṃ upādāyā’”ti. Adhivāsesi kho āyasmā ānando tuṇhībhāvena. Atha kho rājā pasenadi kosalo yāvatikā nāgassa bhūmi nāgena gantvā nāgā paccorohitvā pattikova yenāyasmā ānando tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Ekamantaṃ ṭhito kho rājā pasenadi kosalo āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ etadavoca – “sace, bhante, āyasmato ānandassa na kiñci accāyikaṃ karaṇīyaṃ[V 2.0323], sādhu, bhante, āyasmā ānando yena aciravatiyā nadiyā tīraṃ tenupasaṅkamatu anukampaṃ upādāyā”ti. Adhivāsesi kho āyasmā ānando tuṇhībhāvena.

358. Thus have I heard: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. Then, in the morning, the Venerable Ānanda, having dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Sāvatthī for alms. Having walked for alms in Sāvatthī and returned from the alms round after the meal, he approached the Eastern Monastery, Migāramātā’s Mansion, for the day’s abiding. At that time, King Pasenadi of Kosala had mounted the elephant Ekapuṇḍarīka and was leaving Sāvatthī in the middle of the day. From a distance, King Pasenadi of Kosala saw the Venerable Ānanda approaching. Having seen him, he addressed his minister Sirivaḍḍha: “Friend Sirivaḍḍha, is that not the Venerable Ānanda?” “Yes, great king, that is the Venerable Ānanda.” Then King Pasenadi of Kosala addressed a certain man: “Come, good man, approach the Venerable Ānanda. Having approached, with my words bow your head at the Venerable Ānanda’s feet and say: ‘The king, venerable sir, Pasenadi of Kosala, bows his head at the Venerable Ānanda’s feet.’ And say this: ‘If, venerable sir, the Venerable Ānanda has no urgent duties, may the Venerable Ānanda please wait for a moment, out of compassion.’” “Yes, lord,” replied that man to King Pasenadi of Kosala. He then approached the Venerable Ānanda, paid homage to him, and stood to one side. Standing to one side, that man said to the Venerable Ānanda: “The king, venerable sir, Pasenadi of Kosala, bows his head at your feet and says: ‘If, venerable sir, the Venerable Ānanda has no urgent duties, may the Venerable Ānanda please wait for a moment, out of compassion.’” The Venerable Ānanda consented by silence. Then King Pasenadi of Kosala went as far as the elephant could go, dismounted from the elephant, and approached the Venerable Ānanda on foot. Having approached, he paid homage to the Venerable Ānanda and stood to one side. Standing to one side, King Pasenadi of Kosala said to the Venerable Ānanda: “If, venerable sir, the Venerable Ānanda has no urgent duties, it would be good if the Venerable Ānanda would approach the bank of the Aciravatī River, out of compassion.” The Venerable Ānanda consented by silence.

359. Atha kho āyasmā ānando yena aciravatiyā nadiyā tīraṃ tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā aññatarasmiṃ rukkhamūle paññatte āsane nisīdi. Atha kho rājā pasenadi kosalo yāvatikā nāgassa bhūmi nāgena gantvā nāgā paccorohitvā pattikova yenāyasmā ānando tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ abhivādetvā [T 2.0500] ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Ekamantaṃ ṭhito kho rājā pasenadi kosalo āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ etadavoca – “idha, bhante, āyasmā [M 2.0316] ānando hatthatthare nisīdatū”ti. “Alaṃ, mahārāja. Nisīda tvaṃ; nisinno ahaṃ sake āsane”ti. Nisīdi kho rājā pasenadi kosalo paññatte āsane. Nisajja kho rājā pasenadi kosalo āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ etadavoca – “kiṃ nu kho, bhante ānanda, so bhagavā tathārūpaṃ kāyasamācāraṃ samācareyya, yvāssa kāyasamācāro opārambho samaṇehi brāhmaṇehī”ti brāhmaṇehi viññūhīti (sabbattha) aṭṭhakathā ṭīkā oloketabbā? “Na kho, mahārāja, so bhagavā tathārūpaṃ kāyasamācāraṃ samācareyya, yvāssa kāyasamācāro opārambho samaṇehi brāhmaṇehi viññūhī”ti.

359. Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the bank of the Aciravatī River; having approached, he sat down on a prepared seat at the foot of a certain tree. Then King Pasenadi of Kosala, having gone as far as the elephant could go, dismounted from the elephant and approached the Venerable Ānanda on foot; having approached, he paid homage to the Venerable Ānanda and stood to one side. Standing to one side, King Pasenadi of Kosala said to the Venerable Ānanda: “Here, venerable sir, may the Venerable Ānanda sit on this elephant saddle-cloth.” “Enough, great king. You sit down; I am seated on my own seat.” King Pasenadi of Kosala sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, King Pasenadi of Kosala said to the Venerable Ānanda: “Venerable Ānanda, would that Blessed One engage in such bodily conduct that would be censurable by ascetics and brahmins?” “No, great king, that Blessed One would not engage in such bodily conduct that would be censurable by wise ascetics and brahmins.”

“Kiṃ [P 2.0114] pana, bhante ānanda, so bhagavā tathārūpaṃ vacīsamācāraṃ…pe… manosamācāraṃ samācareyya, yvāssa manosamācāro opārambho samaṇehi brāhmaṇehī”ti brāhmaṇehi viññūhīti (sabbattha) aṭṭhakathā ṭīkā oloketabbā? “Na kho, mahārāja, so bhagavā tathārūpaṃ manosamācāraṃ samācareyya, yvāssa manosamācāro opārambho samaṇehi brāhmaṇehi viññūhī”ti.

“But, Venerable Ānanda, would that Blessed One engage in such verbal conduct… or such mental conduct that would be censurable by ascetics and brahmins?” “No, great king, that Blessed One would not engage in such mental conduct that would be censurable by wise ascetics and brahmins.”

“Acchariyaṃ, bhante, abbhutaṃ, bhante! Yañhi mayaṃ, bhante, nāsakkhimhā pañhena paripūretuṃ taṃ, bhante, āyasmatā ānandena pañhassa veyyākaraṇena paripūritaṃ. Ye te, bhante, bālā abyattā ananuvicca apariyogāhetvā paresaṃ vaṇṇaṃ vā avaṇṇaṃ vā bhāsanti, na mayaṃ taṃ sārato paccāgacchāma; ye pana ye ca kho (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) te, bhante[T 2.0501], paṇḍitā viyattā byattā (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) medhāvino anuvicca pariyogāhetvā paresaṃ vaṇṇaṃ vā avaṇṇaṃ vā bhāsanti, mayaṃ taṃ sārato paccāgacchāma”.

“It is wonderful, venerable sir, it is marvelous! The very matter which we were unable to bring to completion by questioning, that matter, venerable sir, has been brought to completion by the Venerable Ānanda's explanation of the question. Those people, venerable sir, who are foolish and inept, who speak in praise or dispraise of others without investigating and without thoroughly grasping—we do not accept their words as essential. But those people, venerable sir, who are wise, skilled, and intelligent, who speak in praise or dispraise of others after investigating and thoroughly grasping—we do accept their words as essential.”

360. “Katamo pana, bhante ānanda, kāyasamācāro opārambho samaṇehi brāhmaṇehi viññūhī”ti? “Yo kho, mahārāja, kāyasamācāro akusalo”.
