402. Then the young man Assalāyana, together with a great company of brahmins, approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. After concluding the courteous and memorable talk, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the young man Assalāyana said this to the Blessed One: “Master Gotama, the brahmins say this: ‘Only the brahmin caste is superior; any other caste is inferior. Only the brahmin caste is pure; any other caste is dark. Only brahmins are purified, not non-brahmins. Brahmins alone are Brahmā’s legitimate sons, born from his mouth, born of Brahmā, created by Brahmā, and heirs of Brahmā.’ In this matter, what does Master Gotama say?” “But, Assalāyana, brahmin women are seen who menstruate, become pregnant, give birth, and nurse. And they, though born from the womb of a brahmin woman, say this: ‘Only the brahmin caste is superior; any other caste is inferior. Only the brahmin caste is pure; any other caste is dark. Only brahmins are purified, not non-brahmins. Brahmins alone are Brahmā’s legitimate sons, born from his mouth, born of Brahmā, created by Brahmā, and heirs of Brahmā.’” “Although Master Gotama says this, nevertheless, in this matter, the brahmins think thus: ‘Only the brahmin caste is superior; any other caste is inferior… heirs of Brahmā.’”

403. “Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, assalāyana, sutaṃ te – ‘yonakambojesu aññesu ca paccantimesu janapadesu dveva vaṇṇā – ayyo ceva dāso ca; ayyo hutvā dāso hoti, dāso [V 2.0364] hutvā ayyo hotī’”ti[T 2.0561]? “Evaṃ, bho, sutaṃ taṃ me – ‘yonakambojesu aññesu ca paccantimesu janapadesu dveva vaṇṇā – ayyo ceva dāso ca; ayyo hutvā dāso hoti, dāso hutvā ayyo hotī’”ti. “Ettha, assalāyana, brāhmaṇānaṃ kiṃ balaṃ, ko assāso yadettha brāhmaṇā evamāhaṃsu – ‘brāhmaṇova seṭṭho vaṇṇo, hīno añño vaṇṇo…pe… brahmadāyādā’”ti? “Kiñcāpi bhavaṃ gotamo evamāha, atha khvettha brāhmaṇā evametaṃ maññanti – ‘brāhmaṇova seṭṭho vaṇṇo, hīno añño vaṇṇo…pe… brahmadāyādā’”ti.

403. “What do you think of this, Assalāyana? Have you heard that in the lands of the Yonas and Kambojas and in other border regions, there are only two classes—master and slave; and that a master can become a slave, and a slave can become a master?” “Yes, Master, I have heard this: that in the lands of the Yonas and Kambojas and in other border regions, there are only two classes—master and slave; and that a master can become a slave, and a slave can become a master.” “In that case, Assalāyana, what strength, what assurance do the brahmins have for this, when they say, ‘Only the brahmin caste is superior; any other caste is inferior… heirs of Brahmā’?” “Although Master Gotama says this, nevertheless, in this matter, the brahmins think thus: ‘Only the brahmin caste is superior; any other caste is inferior… heirs of Brahmā.’”

404. “Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, assalāyana, khattiyova nu kho pāṇātipātī adinnādāyī kāmesumicchācārī musāvādī pisuṇavāco pharusavāco samphappalāpī abhijjhālu byāpannacitto micchādiṭṭhi kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjeyya, no brāhmaṇo? Vessova nu kho…pe… suddova nu kho pāṇātipātī adinnādāyī kāmesumicchācārī musāvādī pisuṇavāco pharusavāco samphappalāpī abhijjhālu byāpannacitto micchādiṭṭhi kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjeyya, no brāhmaṇo”ti? “No hidaṃ, bho gotama. Khattiyopi hi, bho [M 2.0357] gotama, pāṇātipātī adinnādāyī kāmesumicchācārī musāvādī pisuṇavāco pharusavāco samphappalāpī abhijjhālu byāpannacitto micchādiṭṭhi [T 2.0562] kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjeyya. Brāhmaṇopi hi, bho gotama…pe… vessopi hi, bho gotama…pe… suddopi hi, bho gotama…pe… sabbepi hi, bho gotama, cattāro vaṇṇā pāṇātipātino adinnādāyino [P 2.0150] kāmesumicchācārino musāvādino pisuṇavācā pharusavācā samphappalāpino abhijjhālū byāpannacittā micchādiṭṭhī kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjeyyu”nti. “Ettha, assalāyana, brāhmaṇānaṃ kiṃ balaṃ, ko assāso yadettha brāhmaṇā evamāhaṃsu – ‘brāhmaṇova seṭṭho vaṇṇo, hīno añño vaṇṇo…pe… brahmadāyādā’”ti? “Kiñcāpi bhavaṃ gotamo evamāha, atha khvettha brāhmaṇā evametaṃ maññanti – ‘brāhmaṇova seṭṭho vaṇṇo, hīno añño vaṇṇo…pe… brahmadāyādā’”ti.

404. “What do you think of this, Assalāyana? Would only a noble who kills living beings, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsely, speaks divisively, speaks harshly, indulges in idle chatter, is covetous, has a mind of ill will, and holds wrong view, on the breakup of the body, after death, be reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, the lower world, in hell—and not a brahmin? Would only a merchant… or only a worker who does these things be reborn in hell—and not a brahmin?” “Not so, Master Gotama. A noble, too, who kills living beings… would be reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, the lower world, in hell. A brahmin, too… A merchant, too… A worker, too… Indeed, Master Gotama, all four castes who kill living beings, take what is not given, engage in sexual misconduct, speak falsely, speak divisively, speak harshly, indulge in idle chatter, are covetous, have a mind of ill will, and hold wrong view, on the breakup of the body, after death, would be reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, the lower world, in hell.” “In that case, Assalāyana, what strength, what assurance do the brahmins have for this, when they say, ‘Only the brahmin caste is superior; any other caste is inferior… heirs of Brahmā’?” “Although Master Gotama says this, nevertheless, in this matter, the brahmins think thus: ‘Only the brahmin caste is superior; any other caste is inferior… heirs of Brahmā.’”

405. “Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, assalāyana, brāhmaṇova nu kho pāṇātipātā paṭivirato adinnādānā paṭivirato kāmesumicchācārā paṭivirato musāvādā [T 2.0563] paṭivirato pisuṇāya vācāya [V 2.0365] paṭivirato pharusāya vācāya paṭivirato samphappalāpā paṭivirato anabhijjhālu abyāpannacitto sammādiṭṭhi kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjeyya, no no ca (ka.) khattiyo no vesso, no suddo”ti? “No hidaṃ, bho gotama! Khattiyopi hi, bho gotama, pāṇātipātā paṭivirato adinnādānā paṭivirato kāmesumicchācārā paṭivirato musāvādā paṭivirato pisuṇāya vācāya paṭivirato pharusāya vācāya paṭivirato samphappalāpā paṭivirato anabhijjhālu abyāpannacitto sammādiṭṭhi kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjeyya. Brāhmaṇopi hi, bho gotama…pe… vessopi hi, bho gotama…pe… suddopi hi, bho gotama…pe… sabbepi hi, bho gotama, cattāro vaṇṇā pāṇātipātā paṭiviratā adinnādānā paṭiviratā kāmesumicchācārā paṭiviratā musāvādā paṭiviratā pisuṇāya vācāya paṭiviratā pharusāya vācāya paṭiviratā samphappalāpā paṭiviratā anabhijjhālū abyāpannacittā sammādiṭṭhī kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjeyyu”nti. “Ettha, assalāyana[M 2.0358], brāhmaṇānaṃ kiṃ balaṃ, ko assāso yadettha brāhmaṇā evamāhaṃsu – ‘brāhmaṇova seṭṭho vaṇṇo, hīno añño vaṇṇo…pe… brahmadāyādā’”ti? “Kiñcāpi bhavaṃ gotamo evamāha, atha khvettha brāhmaṇā [P 2.0151] evametaṃ maññanti – ‘brāhmaṇova seṭṭho vaṇṇo, hīno añño vaṇṇo…pe… brahmadāyādā’”ti.

405. “What do you think, Assalāyana? Is it only a brahmin who, refraining from killing living beings, refraining from taking what is not given, refraining from sexual misconduct, refraining from false speech, refraining from divisive speech, refraining from harsh speech, refraining from idle chatter, is without covetousness, has a mind free from ill will, and has right view—who, with the breakup of the body, after death, would be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world—and not a noble, not a merchant, not a worker?” “Not so, Master Gotama! A noble, too, Master Gotama, who refrains from killing living beings… and has right view, with the breakup of the body, after death, would be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. A brahmin, too, Master Gotama… A merchant, too, Master Gotama… A worker, too, Master Gotama… Indeed, Master Gotama, all four castes—if they refrain from killing living beings… and have right view—with the breakup of the body, after death, would be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world.” “In that case, Assalāyana, what strength, what assurance do the brahmins have for this, when they say, ‘Only the brahmin caste is superior; any other caste is inferior… heirs of Brahmā’?” “Although Master Gotama says this, nevertheless, in this matter, the brahmins think thus: ‘Only the brahmin caste is superior; any other caste is inferior… heirs of Brahmā.’”

406. “Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, assalāyana, brāhmaṇova nu kho pahoti asmiṃ padese averaṃ abyābajjhaṃ mettacittaṃ bhāvetuṃ, no khattiyo, no vesso no suddo”ti? “No hidaṃ, bho gotama! Khattiyopi hi, bho gotama, pahoti asmiṃ padese averaṃ abyābajjhaṃ mettacittaṃ bhāvetuṃ; brāhmaṇopi hi, bho gotama… vessopi hi[T 2.0564], bho gotama… suddopi hi, bho gotama… sabbepi hi, bho gotama, cattāro vaṇṇā pahonti asmiṃ padese averaṃ abyābajjhaṃ mettacittaṃ bhāvetu”nti. “Ettha, assalāyana, brāhmaṇānaṃ kiṃ balaṃ, ko assāso yadettha brāhmaṇā evamāhaṃsu – ‘brāhmaṇova seṭṭho vaṇṇo, hīno añño vaṇṇo…pe… brahmadāyādā’”ti? “Kiñcāpi bhavaṃ gotamo evamāha, atha khvettha brāhmaṇā evametaṃ maññanti – ‘brāhmaṇova seṭṭho vaṇṇo, hīno añño vaṇṇo…pe… brahmadāyādā’”ti.

406. “What do you think, Assalāyana? Is it only a brahmin who is able to develop a mind of loving-kindness in this region, free from enmity and ill will—and not a noble, not a merchant, not a worker?” “Not so, Master Gotama! A noble, too, Master Gotama, is able to develop a mind of loving-kindness in this region, free from enmity and ill will; a brahmin, too, Master Gotama… a merchant, too, Master Gotama… a worker, too, Master Gotama… Indeed, Master Gotama, all four castes are able to develop a mind of loving-kindness in this region, free from enmity and ill will.” “In that case, Assalāyana, what strength, what assurance do the brahmins have for this, when they say, ‘Only the brahmin caste is superior; any other caste is inferior… heirs of Brahmā’?” “Although Master Gotama says this, nevertheless, in this matter, the brahmins think thus: ‘Only the brahmin caste is superior; any other caste is inferior… heirs of Brahmā.’”

407. “Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, assalāyana, brāhmaṇova nu kho pahoti sottisināniṃ ādāya [V 2.0366] nadiṃ gantvā rajojallaṃ pavāhetuṃ, no khattiyo, no vesso, no suddo”ti? “No hidaṃ, bho gotama! Khattiyopi hi, bho gotama, pahoti sottisināniṃ ādāya nadiṃ gantvā rajojallaṃ pavāhetuṃ, brāhmaṇopi hi, bho gotama… vessopi hi, bho gotama… suddopi hi, bho gotama… sabbepi hi, bho gotama, cattāro vaṇṇā pahonti sottisināniṃ ādāya nadiṃ gantvā rajojallaṃ pavāhetu”nti. “Ettha, assalāyana, brāhmaṇānaṃ kiṃ balaṃ, ko assāso yadettha brāhmaṇā evamāhaṃsu – ‘brāhmaṇova seṭṭho vaṇṇo, hīno añño vaṇṇo…pe… brahmadāyādā’”ti? “Kiñcāpi bhavaṃ gotamo evamāha, atha khvettha brāhmaṇā evametaṃ maññanti – ‘brāhmaṇova seṭṭho vaṇṇo, hīno añño vaṇṇo…pe… [T 2.0565] brahmadāyādā’”ti.

407. “What do you think, Assalāyana? Is it only a brahmin who is able to take bathing powder, go to the river, and wash off dust and dirt—and not a khattiya, not a vessa, not a sudda?” “No, indeed, Master Gotama! A khattiya, too, Master Gotama, is able to take bathing powder, go to the river, and wash off dust and dirt; a brahmin, too, Master Gotama… a vessa, too, Master Gotama… a sudda, too, Master Gotama… Indeed, Master Gotama, all four castes are able to take bathing powder, go to the river, and wash off dust and dirt.” “In this matter, Assalāyana, what strength, what assurance do the brahmins have, that they say: ‘Only brahmins are the highest caste, other castes are inferior… heirs of Brahmā’?” “Even though Master Gotama speaks thus, still the brahmins think thus: ‘Only brahmins are the highest caste, other castes are inferior… heirs of Brahmā.’”

408. “Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, assalāyana, idha rājā khattiyo muddhāvasitto [P 2.0152] nānājaccānaṃ purisānaṃ purisasataṃ sannipāteyya – ‘āyantu bhonto ye [M 2.0359] tattha khattiyakulā brāhmaṇakulā rājaññakulā uppannā, sākassa vā sālassa vā uppannā sālassa vā (sī. pī.) salaḷassa vā candanassa vā padumakassa vā uttarāraṇiṃ ādāya, aggiṃ abhinibbattentu, tejo pātukarontu. Āyantu pana bhonto ye tattha caṇḍālakulā nesādakulā venakulā veṇakulā (sī. pī.), veṇukulā (syā. kaṃ.) rathakārakulā pukkusakulā uppannā, sāpānadoṇiyā vā sūkaradoṇiyā vā rajakadoṇiyā vā eraṇḍakaṭṭhassa vā uttarāraṇiṃ ādāya, aggiṃ abhinibbattentu, tejo pātukarontū’ti.

408. “What do you think, Assalāyana? Suppose a consecrated khattiya king were to assemble a hundred men of various births and say: ‘Come, sirs, those of you born from a khattiya family, a brahmin family, or a rājañña family, take an upper fire-stick of teak wood, sāla wood, salaḷa wood, sandalwood, or padumaka wood, and produce fire, make heat appear. And come, sirs, those of you born from a caṇḍāla family, a nesāda family, a veṇa family, a rathakāra family, or a pukkusa family, take an upper fire-stick from a dog’s trough, a pig’s trough, a washerman’s trough, or of castor-oil wood, and produce fire, make heat appear.’”

“Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, assalāyana, yo evaṃ nu kho so yo ca nu kho (syā. kaṃ. ka.) khattiyakulā brāhmaṇakulā rājaññakulā uppannehi sākassa vā sālassa vā salaḷassa vā candanassa vā padumakassa vā uttarāraṇiṃ ādāya aggi abhinibbatto, tejo pātukato, so eva nu khvāssa aggi accimā ceva ca (sī. pī.) vaṇṇavā vaṇṇimā (syā. kaṃ. pī. ka.) ca pabhassaro ca, tena ca sakkā agginā aggikaraṇīyaṃ kātuṃ; yo pana so caṇḍālakulā nesādakulā venakulā rathakārakulā pukkusakulā uppannehi sāpānadoṇiyā vā sūkaradoṇiyā vā rajakadoṇiyā vā eraṇḍakaṭṭhassa vā uttarāraṇiṃ ādāya aggi abhinibbatto, tejo pātukato svāssa aggi na ceva accimā na ca vaṇṇavā na ca pabhassaro, na ca tena sakkā agginā [T 2.0566] aggikaraṇīyaṃ kātu”nti? “No hidaṃ, bho gotama! Yopi hi so yo so (sī. pī.), bho gotama, khattiyakulā brāhmaṇakulā rājaññakulā uppannehi sākassa vā sālassa vā salaḷassa vā candanassa vā padumakassa vā uttarāraṇiṃ ādāya aggi abhinibbatto, tejo pātukato svāssa so cassa (sī. pī.), sopissa (syā. kaṃ.) aggi accimā ceva vaṇṇavā ca pabhassaro ca, tena ca sakkā agginā aggikaraṇīyaṃ kātuṃ; yopi so caṇḍālakulā nesādakulā venakulā rathakārakulā pukkusakulā uppannehi sāpānadoṇiyā vā sūkaradoṇiyā vā rajakadoṇiyā vā eraṇḍakaṭṭhassa vā uttarāraṇiṃ ādāya aggi [V 2.0367] abhinibbatto, tejo pātukato, svāssa aggi accimā ceva vaṇṇavā ca pabhassaro ca, tena ca sakkā agginā aggikaraṇīyaṃ kātuṃ. Sabbopi hi, bho gotama, aggi accimā ceva [P 2.0153] vaṇṇavā ca pabhassaro ca, sabbenapi sakkā [M 2.0360] agginā aggikaraṇīyaṃ kātu”nti. “Ettha, assalāyana, brāhmaṇānaṃ kiṃ balaṃ, ko assāso yadettha brāhmaṇā evamāhaṃsu – ‘brāhmaṇova seṭṭho vaṇṇo, hīno añño vaṇṇo; brāhmaṇova sukko vaṇṇo, kaṇho añño vaṇṇo; brāhmaṇāva sujjhanti, no abrāhmaṇā; brāhmaṇāva brahmuno puttā orasā mukhato jātā brahmajā brahmanimmitā brahmadāyādā’”ti? “Kiñcāpi bhavaṃ gotamo evamāha, atha khvettha brāhmaṇā evametaṃ maññanti – ‘brāhmaṇova seṭṭho vaṇṇo, hīno añño vaṇṇo…pe… brahmadāyādā’”ti.

“What do you think, Assalāyana? Would the fire produced by those born from a khattiya family, a brahmin family, or a rājañña family, who take an upper fire-stick of teak, sāl, salaḷa, sandalwood, or padumaka wood and kindle a fire, bringing forth heat—would that fire alone have flame, color, and radiance, and would it be possible with that fire to do what is to be done with fire? And the fire produced by those born from a caṇḍāla family, a nesāda family, a veṇa family, a rathakāra family, or a pukkusa family, who take an upper fire-stick from a dog’s trough, a pig’s trough, a washerman’s trough, or of castor-oil wood and kindle a fire, bringing forth heat—would that fire not have flame, not have color, and not have radiance, and would it not be possible with that fire to do what is to be done with fire?” “No, indeed, Master Gotama! The fire produced by those born from a khattiya family, a brahmin family, or a rājañña family, who take an upper fire-stick of teak, sāl, salaḷa, sandalwood, or padumaka wood and kindle a fire, bringing forth heat—that fire would have flame, color, and radiance, and it would be possible with that fire to do what is to be done with fire. And the fire produced by those born from a caṇḍāla family, a nesāda family, a veṇa family, a rathakāra family, or a pukkusa family, who take an upper fire-stick from a dog’s trough, a pig’s trough, a washerman’s trough, or of castor-oil wood and kindle a fire, bringing forth heat—that fire too would have flame, color, and radiance, and it would be possible with that fire to do what is to be done with fire. For, Master Gotama, all fire has flame, color, and radiance, and with all fire it is possible to do what is to be done with fire.” “In this matter, Assalāyana, what strength, what assurance do the brahmins have when they say: ‘Brahmins are the highest caste, other castes are inferior; brahmins are the fair caste, other castes are dark; only brahmins are pure, not non-brahmins; brahmins alone are the sons of Brahmā, born from his mouth, born of Brahmā, created by Brahmā, heirs of Brahmā’?” “Even though Master Gotama speaks thus, still the brahmins think thus: ‘Only brahmins are the highest caste, other castes are inferior… heirs of Brahmā.’”

409. “Taṃ [T 2.0567] kiṃ maññasi, assalāyana, idha khattiyakumāro brāhmaṇakaññāya saddhiṃ saṃvāsaṃ kappeyya, tesaṃ saṃvāsamanvāya putto jāyetha; yo so khattiyakumārena brāhmaṇakaññāya putto uppanno, siyā so mātupi sadiso pitupi sadiso, ‘khattiyo’tipi vattabbo ‘brāhmaṇo’tipi vattabbo”ti? “Yo so, bho gotama, khattiyakumārena brāhmaṇakaññāya putto uppanno, siyā so mātupi sadiso pitupi sadiso, ‘khattiyo’tipi vattabbo ‘brāhmaṇo’tipi vattabbo”ti.

409. “What do you think, Assalāyana? Suppose here a khattiya youth were to cohabit with a brahmin maiden, and on account of their cohabitation, a son were to be born. That son who is born of a khattiya youth and a brahmin maiden, being like his mother and also like his father, could he be called a ‘khattiya’ and also be called a ‘brahmin’?” “Master Gotama, that son who is born of a khattiya youth and a brahmin maiden, being like his mother and also like his father, could be called a ‘khattiya’ and also be called a ‘brahmin’.”

“Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, assalāyana, idha brāhmaṇakumāro khattiyakaññāya saddhiṃ saṃvāsaṃ kappeyya, tesaṃ saṃvāsamanvāya putto jāyetha; yo so brāhmaṇakumārena khattiyakaññāya putto uppanno, siyā so mātupi sadiso pitupi sadiso, ‘khattiyo’tipi vattabbo ‘brāhmaṇo’tipi vattabbo”ti? “Yo so, bho gotama, brāhmaṇakumārena khattiyakaññāya putto uppanno, siyā so mātupi sadiso pitupi sadiso, ‘khattiyo’tipi vattabbo ‘brāhmaṇo’tipi vattabbo”ti.

“What do you think, Assalāyana? Suppose here a brahmin youth were to cohabit with a khattiya maiden, and on account of their cohabitation, a son were to be born. That son who is born of a brahmin youth and a khattiya maiden, being like his mother and also like his father, could he be called a ‘khattiya’ and also be called a ‘brahmin’?” “Master Gotama, that son who is born of a brahmin youth and a khattiya maiden, being like his mother and also like his father, could be called a ‘khattiya’ and also be called a ‘brahmin’.”

“Taṃ [V 2.0368] kiṃ maññasi, assalāyana idha vaḷavaṃ gadrabhena sampayojeyyuṃ saṃyojeyya (ka.), tesaṃ sampayogamanvāya kisoro jāyetha; yo so vaḷavāya gadrabhena kisoro uppanno, siyā so mātupi sadiso pitupi sadiso, ‘asso’tipi vattabbo ‘gadrabho’tipi vattabbo”ti? “Kuṇḍañhi [T 2.0568] so vekurañjāya hi so (sī. pī.), so kumāraṇḍupi so (syā. kaṃ.), vekulajo hi so (?), bho gotama, assataro hoti. Idaṃ hissa[P 2.0154], bho gotama, nānākaraṇaṃ [M 2.0361] passāmi; amutra ca panesānaṃ na kiñci nānākaraṇaṃ passāmī”ti.

“What do you think, Assalāyana? Suppose here they were to mate a mare with a donkey, and on account of their union, a foal were to be born. That foal born of a mare by a donkey, being like its mother and also like its father, could it be called a ‘horse’ and also be called a ‘donkey’?” “Venerable Gotama, that foal would indeed be a mule. Here, venerable Gotama, I see this difference; but in that other case, I see no difference whatsoever.”

“Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, assalāyana, idhāssu dve māṇavakā bhātaro saudariyā, eko ajjhāyako upanīto eko anajjhāyako anupanīto. Kamettha brāhmaṇā paṭhamaṃ bhojeyyuṃ saddhe vā thālipāke vā yaññe vā pāhune vā”ti? “Yo so, bho gotama, māṇavako ajjhāyako upanīto tamettha brāhmaṇā paṭhamaṃ bhojeyyuṃ saddhe vā thālipāke vā yaññe vā pāhune vā. Kiñhi, bho gotama, anajjhāyake anupanīte dinnaṃ mahapphalaṃ bhavissatī”ti?

“What do you think, Assalāyana? Suppose here there were two young men, brothers born of the same womb—one a reciter of the Vedas and initiated, the other not a reciter and uninitiated. Whom among them would the brahmins feed first at a meal for the deceased, a pot-rice offering, a sacrifice, or for a guest?” “Venerable Gotama, the young man who is a reciter of the Vedas and initiated—him the brahmins would feed first at a meal for the deceased, a pot-rice offering, a sacrifice, or for a guest. For, venerable Gotama, what great fruit will there be from a gift given to one who is not a reciter and uninitiated?”

“Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, assalāyana, idhāssu dve māṇavakā bhātaro saudariyā, eko ajjhāyako upanīto dussīlo pāpadhammo, eko anajjhāyako anupanīto sīlavā kalyāṇadhammo. Kamettha brāhmaṇā paṭhamaṃ bhojeyyuṃ saddhe vā thālipāke vā yaññe vā pāhune vā”ti? “Yo so, bho gotama, māṇavako anajjhāyako anupanīto sīlavā kalyāṇadhammo tamettha brāhmaṇā paṭhamaṃ bhojeyyuṃ saddhe vā thālipāke vā yaññe vā pāhune vā. Kiñhi, bho gotama, dussīle pāpadhamme dinnaṃ mahapphalaṃ bhavissatī”ti?

“What do you think, Assalāyana? Suppose here there were two young men, brothers born of the same womb: one a reciter of the Vedas and initiated, but immoral and of evil nature; the other not a reciter and uninitiated, but virtuous and of good nature. Whom among them would the brahmins feed first at a meal for the deceased, a pot-rice offering, a sacrifice, or for a guest?” “Venerable Gotama, the young man who is not a reciter and uninitiated, but is virtuous and of good nature—him the brahmins would feed first at a meal for the deceased, a pot-rice offering, a sacrifice, or for a guest. For, venerable Gotama, what great fruit will there be from a gift given to one who is immoral and of evil nature?”

“Pubbe kho tvaṃ, assalāyana, jātiṃ agamāsi; jātiṃ gantvā mante agamāsi; mante gantvā [T 2.0569] tape agamāsi; tape gantvā mante gantvā tametaṃ tvaṃ (sī. pī.), mante gantvā tameva ṭhapetvā (syā. kaṃ.) cātuvaṇṇiṃ suddhiṃ paccāgato, yamahaṃ paññapemī”ti. Evaṃ vutte, assalāyano māṇavo tuṇhībhūto maṅkubhūto pattakkhandho adhomukho pajjhāyanto appaṭibhāno nisīdi.

“Formerly, indeed, Assalāyana, you went to birth; having gone to birth, you went to the Vedas; having gone to the Vedas, you went to ascetic practices; having gone to ascetic practices, you have returned to the purity of the four castes, which I am making known.” When this was said, the young brahmin Assalāyana sat silent, abashed, with shoulders drooping, downcast, brooding, and at a loss for words.

410. Atha kho bhagavā assalāyanaṃ māṇavaṃ tuṇhībhūtaṃ maṅkubhūtaṃ pattakkhandhaṃ adhomukhaṃ pajjhāyantaṃ appaṭibhānaṃ viditvā assalāyanaṃ māṇavaṃ etadavoca – “bhūtapubbaṃ, assalāyana, sattannaṃ brāhmaṇisīnaṃ araññāyatane paṇṇakuṭīsu sammantānaṃ vasantānaṃ (sī.) evarūpaṃ pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ uppannaṃ hoti [V 2.0369] – ‘brāhmaṇova seṭṭho vaṇṇo, hīno añño [P 2.0155] vaṇṇo…pe… brahmadāyādā’ti. Assosi kho[M 2.0362], assalāyana, asito devalo isi – ‘sattannaṃ kira brāhmaṇisīnaṃ araññāyatane paṇṇakuṭīsu sammantānaṃ evarūpaṃ pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ uppannaṃ – brāhmaṇova seṭṭho vaṇṇo…pe… brahmadāyādā’ti. Atha kho, assalāyana, asito devalo isi kesamassuṃ kappetvā mañjiṭṭhavaṇṇāni dussāni nivāsetvā paṭaliyo aṭaliyo (sī. pī.), agaliyo (syā. kaṃ.) upāhanā āruhitvā jātarūpamayaṃ daṇḍaṃ gahetvā sattannaṃ brāhmaṇisīnaṃ patthaṇḍile pāturahosi. Atha kho, assalāyana, asito devalo isi sattannaṃ brāhmaṇisīnaṃ patthaṇḍile caṅkamamāno evamāha – ‘handa, ko nu kho ime bhavanto brāhmaṇisayo gatā gantā (syā. kaṃ. ka.); handa, ko nu kho ime bhavanto brāhmaṇisayo gatā’ti? Atha kho, assalāyana, sattannaṃ brāhmaṇisīnaṃ etadahosi – ‘ko [T 2.0570] nāyaṃ gāmaṇḍalarūpo viya sattannaṃ brāhmaṇisīnaṃ patthaṇḍile caṅkamamāno evamāha – ‘handa, ko nu kho ime bhavanto brāhmaṇisayo gatā; handa, ko nu kho ime bhavanto brāhmaṇisayo gatāti? Handa, naṃ abhisapāmā’ti. Atha kho, assalāyana, satta brāhmaṇisayo asitaṃ devalaṃ isiṃ abhisapiṃsu – ‘bhasmā, vasala vasalī (pī.), vasali (ka.), capalī (syā. kaṃ.), hohi; bhasmā, vasala, hohī’ti bhasmā vasala hohīti abhisapavacanaṃ sī. pī. potthakesu sakideva āgataṃ. Yathā yathā kho, assalāyana, satta brāhmaṇisayo asitaṃ devalaṃ isiṃ abhisapiṃsu tathā tathā asito devalo isi abhirūpataro ceva hoti dassanīyataro ca pāsādikataro ca. Atha kho, assalāyana, sattannaṃ brāhmaṇisīnaṃ etadahosi – ‘moghaṃ vata no tapo, aphalaṃ brahmacariyaṃ. Mayañhi pubbe yaṃ abhisapāma – bhasmā, vasala, hohi; bhasmā, vasala, hohīti bhasmāva bhavati ekacco. Imaṃ pana mayaṃ yathā yathā abhisapāma tathā tathā abhirūpataro ceva hoti dassanīyataro ca pāsādikataro cā’ti. ‘Na bhavantānaṃ moghaṃ tapo, nāphalaṃ brahmacariyaṃ. Iṅgha bhavanto, yo mayi manopadoso taṃ pajahathā’ti. ‘Yo [P 2.0156] bhavati manopadoso taṃ pajahāma. Ko nu bhavaṃ hotī’ti? ‘Suto nu bhavataṃ – asito devalo isī’ti? ‘Evaṃ, bho’. ‘So khvāhaṃ, bho, homī’ti. Atha kho, assalāyana, satta brāhmaṇisayo asitaṃ devalaṃ isiṃ abhivādetuṃ upakkamiṃsu.

410. Then the Blessed One, knowing that the brahmin youth Assalāyana was silent, abashed, with shoulders drooping, downcast, brooding, and at a loss for words, said this to him: “Once upon a time, Assalāyana, this evil wrong view arose among seven conferring brahmin seers in a forest region, in their leaf-huts: ‘The brahmin is the highest caste, any other caste is inferior… heirs of Brahmā.’ The seer Asita Devala heard, Assalāyana: ‘It seems that this evil wrong view has arisen among seven conferring brahmin seers in a forest region, in their leaf-huts: “The brahmin is the highest caste… heirs of Brahmā.”’ Then, Assalāyana, the seer Asita Devala, having had his hair and beard trimmed, having put on madder-colored cloths, having mounted his layered sandals, and having taken a golden staff, appeared in the precinct of the seven brahmin seers. Then, Assalāyana, the seer Asita Devala, while walking up and down in the precinct of the seven brahmin seers, said this: ‘Where, indeed, have these venerable brahmin seers gone? Where, indeed, have these venerable brahmin seers gone?’ Then, Assalāyana, this occurred to the seven brahmin seers: ‘Who is this, like a village boy, who walks up and down in the precinct of the seven brahmin seers and says: “Where, indeed, have these venerable brahmin seers gone? Where, indeed, have these venerable brahmin seers gone?” Come, let us curse him!’ Then, Assalāyana, the seven brahmin seers cursed the seer Asita Devala: ‘Become ashes, you outcaste! Become ashes, you outcaste!’ But the more, Assalāyana, the seven brahmin seers cursed the seer Asita Devala, the more handsome, fair to see, and pleasing the seer Asita Devala became. Then, Assalāyana, this occurred to the seven brahmin seers: ‘Our asceticism is in vain, our holy life is fruitless! For previously, when we cursed someone, saying, “Become ashes, you outcaste! Become ashes, you outcaste!” he would indeed become ashes. But the more we curse this one, the more handsome, fair to see, and pleasing he becomes.’ ‘Your asceticism is not in vain, venerable sirs, nor is your holy life fruitless. Come, venerable sirs, abandon the mental corruption you have towards me.’ ‘We abandon the mental corruption we have towards you. Who might you be, venerable sir?’ ‘Have you heard of the seer Asita Devala?’ ‘Yes, venerable sir.’ ‘Indeed, venerable sirs, I am he.’ Then, Assalāyana, the seven brahmin seers set about to pay homage to the seer Asita Devala.

411. “Atha [M 2.0363] kho, assalāyana, asito devalo isi satta brāhmaṇisayo etadavoca – ‘sutaṃ metaṃ, bho, sattannaṃ kira brāhmaṇisīnaṃ araññāyatane paṇṇakuṭīsu sammantānaṃ evarūpaṃ pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ uppannaṃ [T 2.0571] – brāhmaṇova seṭṭho vaṇṇo, hīno añño vaṇṇo; brāhmaṇova sukko vaṇṇo[V 2.0370], kaṇho añño vaṇṇo; brāhmaṇāva sujjhanti, no abrāhmaṇā; brāhmaṇāva brahmuno puttā orasā mukhato jātā brahmajā brahmanimmitā brahmadāyādā’ti. ‘Evaṃ, bho’.

411. Then, Assalāyana, the seer Asita Devala said this to the seven brahmin seers: ‘I have heard this, venerable sirs, that it seems this evil wrong view has arisen among seven conferring brahmin seers in a forest region, in their leaf-huts: “The brahmin is the highest caste, any other caste is inferior; the brahmin is the fair caste, any other caste is dark; only brahmins are pure, not non-brahmins; only brahmins are Brahmā’s sons, born from his chest, born from his mouth, born of Brahmā, created by Brahmā, heirs of Brahmā.”’ ‘So it is, venerable sir.’

“‘Jānanti pana bhonto – yā janikā mātā janimātā (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) brāhmaṇaṃyeva agamāsi, no abrāhmaṇa’nti? ‘No hidaṃ, bho’.

‘But do you, venerable sirs, know this: that the mother who bore you went only to a brahmin, and not to a non-brahmin?’ ‘We do not know this, venerable sir.’

“‘Jānanti pana bhonto – yā janikāmātu janimātu (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) mātā yāva sattamā mātumātāmahayugā brāhmaṇaṃyeva agamāsi, no abrāhmaṇa’nti? ‘No hidaṃ, bho’.

‘But do you, venerable sirs, know this: that the mother of the mother who bore you, back to the seventh maternal ancestral generation, went only to a brahmin, and not to a non-brahmin?’ ‘We do not know this, venerable sir.’

“‘Jānanti pana bhonto – yo janako pitā janipitā (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) brāhmaṇiṃyeva agamāsi, no abrāhmaṇi’nti? ‘No hidaṃ, bho’.

‘But do you, venerable sirs, know this: that the father who begot you went only to a brahmin woman, and not to a non-brahmin woman?’ ‘We do not know this, venerable sir.’

“‘Jānanti pana bhonto – yo janakapitu janipitu (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) pitā yāva sattamā pitupitāmahayugā brāhmaṇiṃyeva agamāsi, no abrāhmaṇi’nti? ‘No hidaṃ, bho’.

‘But do you, venerable sirs, know this: that the father of the father who begot you, back to the seventh paternal ancestral generation, went only to a brahmin woman, and not to a non-brahmin woman?’ ‘We do not know this, venerable sir.’

“‘Jānanti pana bhonto – yathā gabbhassa avakkanti hotī’ti na mayaṃ jānāma bho yathā gabbhassa avakkanti hotīti. yathā kathaṃ pana bho gabbhassa avakkanti hotīti. (ka.)? ‘Jānāma mayaṃ, bho – yathā gabbhassa avakkanti hoti na mayaṃ jānāma bho yathā gabbhassa avakkanti hotīti. yathā kathaṃ pana bho gabbhassa avakkanti hotīti. (ka.). Idha [P 2.0157] mātāpitaro ca sannipatitā honti, mātā ca utunī hoti, gandhabbo ca paccupaṭṭhito hoti; evaṃ tiṇṇaṃ sannipātā gabbhassa avakkanti hotī’ti.

‘But do you, venerable sirs, know how the descent into the womb comes about?’ ‘We know, venerable sir, how the descent into the womb comes about. In this case, the mother and father have come together, the mother is in her season, and the being to be reborn is present. Thus, from the conjunction of these three, the descent into the womb comes about.’

“‘Jānanti pana bhonto – taggha yagghe (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.), so gandhabbo khattiyo vā brāhmaṇo vā vesso vā suddo vā’ti? ‘Na mayaṃ, bho, jānāma – taggha so gandhabbo khattiyo vā brāhmaṇo vā vesso vā suddo vā’ti. ‘Evaṃ sante, bho, jānātha – ke tumhe hothā’ti? ‘Evaṃ sante, bho[T 2.0572], na mayaṃ jānāma [M 2.0364] – ke mayaṃ homā’ti. Te hi nāma, assalāyana, satta brāhmaṇisayo asitena devalena isinā sake jātivāde samanuyuñjīyamānā samanuggāhīyamānā samanubhāsīyamānā na sampāyissanti; kiṃ pana tvaṃ etarahi mayā sakasmiṃ jātivāde samanuyuñjīyamāno [V 2.0371] samanuggāhīyamāno samanubhāsīyamāno sampāyissasi, yesaṃ tvaṃ sācariyako na puṇṇo dabbigāho”ti.

‘Furthermore, venerable sirs, do you truly know whether that being who is to take rebirth is a noble, a brahmin, a merchant, or a worker?’ ‘No, venerable sir, we do not truly know whether that being who is to take rebirth is a noble, a brahmin, a merchant, or a worker.’ ‘This being so, venerable sirs, do you know who you are?’ ‘This being so, venerable sir, we do not know who we are.’ Indeed, Assalāyana, those seven brahmin seers, when thoroughly questioned, pressed, and addressed by the seer Asita Devala regarding their own assertion about birth, could not give a complete answer. How then could you now give a complete answer when you are thoroughly questioned, pressed, and addressed by me regarding my own assertion about birth—you who, along with your teacher, are not even a complete ladle-bearer for them?’

Evaṃ vutte, assalāyano māṇavo bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “abhikkantaṃ, bho gotama…pe… upāsakaṃ maṃ bhavaṃ gotamo dhāretu ajjatagge pāṇupetaṃ saraṇaṃ gata”nti.

When this was said, the brahmin youth Assalāyana said this to the Blessed One: “Excellent, Venerable Gotama! … May the Venerable Gotama regard me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.”

Assalāyanasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ tatiyaṃ.

The Assalāyana Sutta, the third, is concluded.

4. Ghoṭamukhasuttaṃ

4. The Ghoṭamukha Sutta

412. Evaṃ [T 2.0573][V 2.0372] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ āyasmā udeno bārāṇasiyaṃ viharati khemiyambavane. Tena kho pana samayena ghoṭamukho brāhmaṇo bārāṇasiṃ anuppatto hoti kenacideva karaṇīyena. Atha kho ghoṭamukho brāhmaṇo jaṅghāvihāraṃ [P 2.0158] anucaṅkamamāno anuvicaramāno yena khemiyambavanaṃ tenupasaṅkami. Tena kho pana samayena āyasmā udeno abbhokāse caṅkamati. Atha kho ghoṭamukho brāhmaṇo yenāyasmā udeno tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmatā udenena saddhiṃ sammodi. Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā āyasmantaṃ udenaṃ caṅkamantaṃ anucaṅkamamāno evamāha – “ambho samaṇa, ‘natthi dhammiko paribbajo’ paribbājo (sī. pī.) – evaṃ me ettha hoti. Tañca kho bhavantarūpānaṃ vā adassanā, yo vā panettha dhammo”ti.

412. Thus have I heard. At one time the Venerable Udena was dwelling at Varanasi in the Khemiya Mango Grove. Now at that time the brahmin Ghoṭamukha had arrived in Varanasi for some business. Then, as the brahmin Ghoṭamukha was walking about and wandering for exercise, he approached the Khemiya Mango Grove. At that time, the Venerable Udena was walking back and forth in an open space. Then the brahmin Ghoṭamukha approached the Venerable Udena; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Udena. When they had concluded their courteous and memorable talk, while following the Venerable Udena as he was walking, he said this: ‘O recluse, it occurs to me thus: “There is no righteous ascetic.” And that is either from not seeing venerable ones such as yourself, or from not seeing whatever true principle there is in this life of an ascetic.’

Evaṃ vutte, āyasmā udeno caṅkamā orohitvā vihāraṃ pavisitvā paññatte āsane nisīdi. Ghoṭamukhopi kho brāhmaṇo caṅkamā orohitvā vihāraṃ pavisitvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Ekamantaṃ ṭhitaṃ kho ghoṭamukhaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ āyasmā udeno etadavoca – “saṃvijjanti saṃvijjante (bahūsu) kho, brāhmaṇa, āsanāni. Sace ākaṅkhasi, nisīdā”ti. “Etadeva kho pana mayaṃ [M 2.0365] bhoto udenassa āgamayamānā (na) nisīdāma. Kathañhi nāma mādiso pubbe animantito āsane [T 2.0574] nisīditabbaṃ maññeyyā”ti? Atha kho ghoṭamukho brāhmaṇo aññataraṃ nīcaṃ āsanaṃ gahetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho ghoṭamukho brāhmaṇo āyasmantaṃ udenaṃ etadavoca – “ambho samaṇa, ‘natthi dhammiko paribbajo’ – evaṃ me ettha hoti. Tañca kho bhavantarūpānaṃ vā adassanā, yo vā panettha dhammo”ti. “Sace kho pana me tvaṃ, brāhmaṇa, anuññeyyaṃ anujāneyyāsi, paṭikkositabbañca paṭikkoseyyāsi; yassa ca pana me bhāsitassa atthaṃ na jāneyyāsi, mamaṃyeva tattha uttari paṭipuccheyyāsi – ‘idaṃ, bho udena, kathaṃ, imassa kvattho’ti? Evaṃ katvā siyā no ettha kathāsallāpo”ti. “Anuññeyyaṃ khvāhaṃ bhoto udenassa anujānissāmi, paṭikkositabbañca paṭikkosissāmi; yassa ca panāhaṃ bhoto [P 2.0159] udenassa [V 2.0373] bhāsitassa atthaṃ na jānissāmi, bhavantaṃyeva tattha udenaṃ uttari paṭipucchissāmi – ‘idaṃ, bho udena, kathaṃ, imassa kvattho’ti? Evaṃ katvā hotu no ettha kathāsallāpo”ti.

When this was said, the Venerable Udena descended from the walking path, entered the dwelling, and sat down on a prepared seat. The brahmin Ghoṭamukha also descended from the walking path, entered the dwelling, and stood to one side. To the brahmin Ghoṭamukha who was standing to one side, the Venerable Udena said this: ‘Brahmin, there are seats. If you wish, sit down.’ ‘Indeed, we were waiting for the Venerable Udena’s invitation before sitting. For how could one like me think it proper to sit on a seat without being invited beforehand?’ Then the brahmin Ghoṭamukha took a certain low seat and sat to one side. Seated to one side, the brahmin Ghoṭamukha said this to the Venerable Udena: ‘O recluse, it occurs to me thus: “There is no righteous ascetic.” And that is either from not seeing venerable ones such as yourself, or from not seeing whatever true principle there is in this life of an ascetic.’ ‘If, brahmin, you would approve what should be approved and reject what should be rejected, and if you do not know the meaning of any word I have spoken, you should question me further about it, asking: “Venerable Udena, how is this? What is its meaning?” Having done so, a conversation could take place between us on this matter.’ ‘Indeed, I will approve for the Venerable Udena what should be approved and reject what should be rejected. And of whatever word spoken by the Venerable Udena I do not know the meaning, I will question the Venerable Udena further about it, asking: “Venerable Udena, how is this? What is its meaning?” Having done so, let there be a conversation between us on this matter.’

413. “Cattārome, brāhmaṇa, puggalā santo saṃvijjamānā lokasmiṃ. Katame cattāro? Idha, brāhmaṇa, ekacco puggalo attantapo hoti attaparitāpanānuyogamanuyutto. Idha pana, brāhmaṇa, ekacco puggalo parantapo hoti paraparitāpanānuyogamanuyutto. Idha pana, brāhmaṇa, ekacco puggalo attantapo ca hoti attaparitāpanānuyogamanuyutto parantapo ca paraparitāpanānuyogamanuyutto. Idha pana, brāhmaṇa[T 2.0575], ekacco puggalo nevattantapo hoti nāttaparitāpanānuyogamanuyutto, na parantapo na paraparitāpanānuyogamanuyutto. So anattantapo aparantapo diṭṭheva dhamme nicchāto nibbuto sītībhūto sukhappaṭisaṃvedī brahmabhūtena attanā viharati. Imesaṃ, brāhmaṇa, catunnaṃ puggalānaṃ katamo te puggalo cittaṃ ārādhetī”ti?

413. “Brahmin, these four individuals exist and are found in the world. Which four? Here, brahmin, a certain individual is a self-tormentor, devoted to the practice of self-torment. Here, brahmin, a certain individual is a tormentor of others, devoted to the practice of tormenting others. Here, brahmin, a certain individual is a self-tormentor, devoted to the practice of self-torment, and a tormentor of others, devoted to the practice of tormenting others. Here, brahmin, a certain individual is neither a self-tormentor nor devoted to the practice of self-torment, nor a tormentor of others nor devoted to the practice of tormenting others. Not tormenting himself and not tormenting others, in this very life he is without craving, extinguished, and cooled, experiencing bliss, dwelling with a self that has become sublime. Of these four individuals, brahmin, which one pleases your mind?”

“Yvāyaṃ, bho udena, puggalo attantapo attaparitāpanānuyogamanuyutto ayaṃ me puggalo cittaṃ nārādheti; yopāyaṃ, bho udena, puggalo parantapo paraparitāpanānuyogamanuyutto ayampi me puggalo cittaṃ nārādheti; yopāyaṃ, bho udena, puggalo attantapo ca attaparitāpanānuyogamanuyutto [M 2.0366] parantapo ca paraparitāpanānuyogamanuyutto ayampi me puggalo cittaṃ nārādheti; yo ca kho ayaṃ, bho udena, puggalo nevattantapo nāttaparitāpanānuyogamanuyutto na parantapo na paraparitāpanānuyogamanuyutto so anattantapo aparantapo diṭṭheva dhamme nicchāto nibbuto sītībhūto sukhappaṭisaṃvedī brahmabhūtena attanā viharati. Ayameva me puggalo cittaṃ ārādhetī”ti.

“Venerable Udena, whatever person is a self-tormentor, devoted to the practice of self-torment, this person does not please my mind. Venerable Udena, whatever person is a tormentor of others, devoted to the practice of tormenting others, this person also does not please my mind. Venerable Udena, whatever person is both a self-tormentor, devoted to the practice of self-torment, and a tormentor of others, devoted to the practice of tormenting others, this person also does not please my mind. But indeed, Venerable Udena, whatever person is neither a self-tormentor nor devoted to the practice of self-torment, neither a tormentor of others nor devoted to the practice of tormenting others; he, not tormenting himself and not tormenting others, in this very life is without craving, extinguished, become cool, and experiences bliss, abiding with a self that has become sublime. This very person pleases my mind.”

“Kasmā pana te, brāhmaṇa, ime tayo puggalā cittaṃ nārādhentī”ti? “Yvāyaṃ, bho udena, puggalo attantapo attaparitāpanānuyogamanuyutto so attānaṃ sukhakāmaṃ dukkhapaṭikkūlaṃ ātāpeti paritāpeti; iminā me ayaṃ puggalo cittaṃ nārādheti. Yopāyaṃ[P 2.0160], bho udena, puggalo parantapo paraparitāpanānuyogamanuyutto so paraṃ sukhakāmaṃ dukkhapaṭikkūlaṃ [T 2.0576] ātāpeti paritāpeti; iminā me ayaṃ puggalo cittaṃ nārādheti. Yopāyaṃ, bho udena, puggalo attantapo ca attaparitāpanānuyogamanuyutto parantapo ca paraparitāpanānuyogamanuyutto so [V 2.0374] attānañca parañca sukhakāmaṃ dukkhapaṭikkūlaṃ ātāpeti paritāpeti; iminā me ayaṃ puggalo cittaṃ nārādheti. Yo ca kho ayaṃ, bho udena, puggalo nevattantapo nāttaparitāpanānuyogamanuyutto na parantapo na paraparitāpanānuyogamanuyutto so anattantapo aparantapo diṭṭheva dhamme nicchāto nibbuto sītībhūto sukhappaṭisaṃvedī brahmabhūtena attanā viharati, so attānañca parañca sukhakāmaṃ dukkhapaṭikkūlaṃ neva ātāpeti na paritāpeti; iminā me ayaṃ puggalo cittaṃ ārādhetī”ti.

“But why, brahmin, do these three persons not please your mind?” “Venerable Udena, whatever person is a self-tormentor, devoted to the practice of self-torment, he torments and afflicts himself, who desires happiness and is averse to suffering. For this reason, this person does not please my mind. Venerable Udena, whatever person is a tormentor of others, devoted to the practice of tormenting others, he torments and afflicts another, who desires happiness and is averse to suffering. For this reason, this person does not please my mind. Venerable Udena, whatever person is both a self-tormentor, devoted to the practice of self-torment, and a tormentor of others, devoted to the practice of tormenting others, he torments and afflicts both himself and another, who desire happiness and are averse to suffering. For this reason, this person does not please my mind. But indeed, Venerable Udena, whatever person is neither a self-tormentor nor devoted to the practice of self-torment, neither a tormentor of others nor devoted to the practice of tormenting others; he, not tormenting himself and not tormenting others, in this very life is without craving, extinguished, become cool, and experiences bliss, abiding with a self that has become sublime. He neither torments nor afflicts himself or another, who desire happiness and are averse to suffering. For this reason, this person pleases my mind.”

414. “Dvemā, brāhmaṇa, parisā. Katamā dve? Idha, brāhmaṇa, ekaccā parisā sārattarattā maṇikuṇḍalesu puttabhariyaṃ pariyesati, dāsidāsaṃ pariyesati, khettavatthuṃ pariyesati, jātarūparajataṃ pariyesati.

414. “Brahmin, there are these two assemblies. What two? Here, brahmin, a certain assembly, being intensely passionate for those who wear jeweled earrings, seeks a wife and children, seeks female and male slaves, seeks fields and land, and seeks gold and silver.

“Idha pana, brāhmaṇa, ekaccā parisā asārattarattā maṇikuṇḍalesu puttabhariyaṃ pahāya, dāsidāsaṃ pahāya, khettavatthuṃ pahāya, jātarūparajataṃ pahāya, agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajitā. Svāyaṃ, brāhmaṇa, puggalo nevattantapo nāttaparitāpanānuyogamanuyutto na parantapo na paraparitāpanānuyogamanuyutto. So anattantapo aparantapo diṭṭheva dhamme nicchāto [M 2.0367] nibbuto sītībhūto sukhappaṭisaṃvedī [T 2.0577] brahmabhūtena attanā viharati. Idha katamaṃ tvaṃ, brāhmaṇa, puggalaṃ katamāya parisāya bahulaṃ samanupassasi – yā cāyaṃ parisā sārattarattā maṇikuṇḍalesu puttabhariyaṃ pariyesati dāsidāsaṃ pariyesati khettavatthuṃ pariyesati jātarūparajataṃ pariyesati, yā cāyaṃ parisā asārattarattā maṇikuṇḍalesu puttabhariyaṃ pahāya dāsidāsaṃ pahāya khettavatthuṃ pahāya jātarūparajataṃ pahāya agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajitā”ti?

“But here, brahmin, a certain assembly, not being intensely passionate for those who wear jeweled earrings, having abandoned wife and children, having abandoned female and male slaves, having abandoned fields and land, having abandoned gold and silver, has gone forth from the household life into homelessness. This person, brahmin, is neither a self-tormentor nor devoted to the practice of self-torment, neither a tormentor of others nor devoted to the practice of tormenting others. He, not tormenting himself and not tormenting others, in this very life is without craving, extinguished, become cool, and experiences bliss, abiding with a self that has become sublime. Now, brahmin, which person do you frequently observe, and in which assembly: in that assembly which, being intensely passionate for those who wear jeweled earrings, seeks a wife and children, seeks female and male slaves, seeks fields and land, and seeks gold and silver; or in that assembly which, not being intensely passionate for those who wear jeweled earrings, having abandoned wife and children, having abandoned female and male slaves, having abandoned fields and land, having abandoned gold and silver, has gone forth from the household life into homelessness?”

“Yvāyaṃ[P 2.0161], bho udena, puggalo nevattantapo nāttaparitāpanānuyogamanuyutto na parantapo na paraparitāpanānuyogamanuyutto so anattantapo aparantapo diṭṭheva dhamme nicchāto nibbuto sītībhūto sukhappaṭisaṃvedī brahmabhūtena attanā viharati; imāhaṃ puggalaṃ yāyaṃ parisā asārattarattā maṇikuṇḍalesu puttabhariyaṃ pahāya dāsidāsaṃ pahāya khettavatthuṃ pahāya jātarūparajataṃ pahāya agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajitā imissaṃ parisāyaṃ bahulaṃ samanupassāmī”ti.

“Venerable Udena, that person who is neither a self-tormentor nor devoted to the practice of self-torment, neither a tormentor of others nor devoted to the practice of tormenting others; he, not tormenting himself and not tormenting others, in this very life is without craving, extinguished, become cool, and experiences bliss, abiding with a self that has become sublime. I frequently observe this person in that assembly which, not being intensely passionate for those who wear jeweled earrings, having abandoned wife and children, having abandoned female and male slaves, having abandoned fields and land, having abandoned gold and silver, has gone forth from the household life into homelessness.”

“Idāneva [V 2.0375] kho pana te, brāhmaṇa, bhāsitaṃ – ‘mayaṃ evaṃ ājānāma – ambho samaṇa, natthi dhammiko paribbajo, evaṃ me ettha hoti. Tañca kho bhavantarūpānaṃ vā adassanā, yo vā panettha dhammo’”ti. “Addhā mesā, bho udena, sānuggahā vācā bhāsitā. ‘Atthi dhammiko paribbajo’ – evaṃ me ettha hoti. Evañca pana maṃ bhavaṃ udeno dhāretu. Ye ca me bhotā udenena cattāro puggalā saṃkhittena vuttā vitthārena avibhattā, sādhu me bhavaṃ, udeno ime cattāro puggale vitthārena [T 2.0578] vibhajatu anukampaṃ upādāyā”ti. “Tena hi, brāhmaṇa, suṇāhi, sādhukaṃ manasi karohi, bhāsissāmī”ti. “Evaṃ, bho”ti kho ghoṭamukho brāhmaṇo āyasmato udenassa paccassosi. Āyasmā udeno etadavoca –

“But just now, brahmin, you said this: ‘We know it to be thus: “Good ascetic, there is no righteous wanderer.” This is how it is for me here. And this is either from not seeing venerable ones such as yourself, or from not seeing what the Dhamma is in this regard.’ ‘Indeed, Venerable Udena, this speech of mine was spoken with a supporting reason. “There is a righteous wanderer”—this is how it is for me here. And may the Venerable Udena remember me thus. And as for the four persons who were spoken of by the Venerable Udena in brief but not analyzed in detail, it would be good if the Venerable Udena, out of compassion, would analyze these four persons for me in detail.’ ‘Well then, brahmin, listen and attend carefully; I will speak.’ ‘Yes, venerable sir,’ Ghotamukha the brahmin replied to the Venerable Udena. The Venerable Udena said this:

415. “Katamo ca, brāhmaṇa, puggalo attantapo attaparitāpanānuyogamanuyutto? Idha, brāhmaṇa, ekacco puggalo acelako hoti muttācāro hatthāpalekhano naehibhaddantiko natiṭṭhabhaddantiko, nābhihaṭaṃ na uddissakataṃ na nimantanaṃ sādiyati. So na kumbhimukhā paṭiggaṇhāti, na kaḷopimukhā paṭiggaṇhāti, na eḷakamantaraṃ, na daṇḍamantaraṃ, na musalamantaraṃ, na dvinnaṃ bhuñjamānānaṃ, na gabbhiniyā, na pāyamānāya[M 2.0368], na [P 2.0162] purisantaragatāya, na saṅkittīsu, na yattha sā upaṭṭhito hoti, na yattha makkhikā saṇḍasaṇḍacārinī, na macchaṃ na maṃsaṃ, na suraṃ na merayaṃ na thusodakaṃ pivati. So ekāgāriko vā hoti ekālopiko, dvāgāriko vā hoti dvālopiko…pe… sattāgāriko vā hoti sattālopiko; ekissāpi dattiyā yāpeti, dvīhipi dattīhi yāpeti…pe… sattahipi dattīhi yāpeti; ekāhikampi āhāraṃ āhāreti, dvīhikampi āhāraṃ āhāreti…pe… sattāhikampi āhāraṃ āhāreti – iti evarūpaṃ addhamāsikaṃ pariyāyabhattabhojanānuyogamanuyutto viharati. So sākabhakkho vā hoti, sāmākabhakkho vā hoti, nīvārabhakkho vā hoti, daddulabhakkho vā hoti[T 2.0579], haṭabhakkho vā hoti, kaṇabhakkho vā hoti, ācāmabhakkho vā hoti, piññākabhakkho vā hoti, tiṇabhakkho vā hoti, gomayabhakkho vā hoti, vanamūlaphalāhāro yāpeti pavattaphalabhojī. So sāṇānipi dhāreti, masāṇānipi dhāreti, chavadussānipi dhāreti, paṃsukūlānipi dhāreti, tirīṭānipi dhāreti, ajinampi dhāreti, ajinakkhipampi dhāreti, kusacīrampi dhāreti, vākacīrampi dhāreti, phalakacīrampi dhāreti, kesakambalampi dhāreti, vāḷakambalampi dhāreti, ulūkapakkhampi dhāreti; kesamassulocakopi hoti kesamassulocanānuyogamanuyutto[V 2.0376], ubbhaṭṭhakopi hoti āsanapaṭikkhitto, ukkuṭikopi hoti ukkuṭikappadhānamanuyutto, kaṇṭakāpassayikopi hoti kaṇṭakāpassaye seyyaṃ kappeti; sāyatatiyakampi udakorohanānuyogamanuyutto viharati – iti evarūpaṃ anekavihitaṃ kāyassa ātāpanaparitāpanānuyogamanuyutto viharati. Ayaṃ vuccati, brāhmaṇa, puggalo attantapo attaparitāpanānuyogamanuyutto.

415. “And what, brahmin, is the person who is a self-tormentor, devoted to the practice of self-mortification? Here, brahmin, a certain person goes naked, is of unrestrained conduct, licks his hands, does not come when asked, ‘Come, venerable sir,’ does not stop when asked, ‘Stop, venerable sir’; he does not accept food brought to him, food prepared for him, or an invitation to a meal. He does not receive food from the mouth of a pot, nor from the mouth of a bowl, nor across a threshold, nor across a stick, nor across a pestle, nor from two people eating together, nor from a pregnant woman, nor from a nursing woman, nor from a woman who has gone in between men, nor from where food is collected by subscription, nor where a dog is waiting, nor where flies are swarming; he accepts no fish or meat; he drinks no liquor, wine, or fermented brew. He is one who takes alms from only one house, or one who eats only one morsel; he is one who takes alms from only two houses, or one who eats only two morsels… he is one who takes alms from only seven houses, or one who eats only seven morsels. He subsists on one small bowl, on two small bowls… on seven small bowls. He takes food once a day, once every two days… up to once every seven days—thus he lives devoted to the practice of eating food at intervals, up to once every half-month. He is an eater of greens, or millet, or wild rice, or hide-scraps, or moss, or broken rice, or rice-scum, or sesame flour, or grass, or cow-dung. He subsists on forest roots and fruits, eating fallen fruits. He wears hemp robes, robes of mixed-hemp cloth, robes made from shrouds, rags from a dust heap, bark garments, antelope hides, strips of antelope hide, robes of kusa grass, bark-fiber garments, wood-slab garments, hair blankets, horse-tail blankets, or owl’s-wing garments. He is one who pulls out his hair and beard, devoted to the practice of pulling out hair and beard. He is one who stands continuously, rejecting seats. He is one who squats continuously, devoted to the practice of squatting. He is one who lies on a bed of thorns; he makes his bed on thorns. He is devoted to the practice of bathing in water three times a day, including in the evening. Thus he lives devoted to the various practices of mortifying and tormenting the body. This, brahmin, is called the person who is a self-tormentor, devoted to the practice of self-mortification.”

416. “Katamo [T 2.0580] ca, brāhmaṇa, puggalo parantapo paraparitāpanānuyogamanuyutto? Idha, brāhmaṇa, ekacco puggalo orabbhiko hoti sūkariko sākuṇiko māgaviko luddo macchaghātako coro coraghātako goghātako bandhanāgāriko – ye vā panaññepi keci kurūrakammantā. Ayaṃ vuccati, brāhmaṇa, puggalo parantapo paraparitāpanānuyogamanuyutto.

416. “And what, brahmin, is the person who is a tormentor of others, devoted to the practice of tormenting others? Here, brahmin, a certain person is a butcher of sheep, a butcher of pigs, a fowler, a deer-stalker, a cruel hunter, a fisherman, a thief, an executioner of thieves, a cattle-slaughterer, a jailer, or anyone else engaged in cruel occupations. This, brahmin, is called the person who is a tormentor of others, devoted to the practice of tormenting others.”

417. “Katamo [M 2.0369] ca, brāhmaṇa, puggalo attantapo ca attaparitāpanānuyogamanuyutto, parantapo ca paraparitāpanānuyogamanuyutto? Idha, brāhmaṇa, ekacco puggalo rājā vā hoti khattiyo muddhāvasitto, brāhmaṇo vā mahāsālo. So puratthimena nagarassa navaṃ santhāgāraṃ kārāpetvā kesamassuṃ ohāretvā kharājinaṃ nivāsetvā sappitelena kāyaṃ abbhañjitvā magavisāṇena piṭṭhiṃ kaṇḍuvamāno navaṃ santhāgāraṃ pavisati saddhiṃ mahesiyā brāhmaṇena ca purohitena. So tattha anantarahitāya bhūmiyā haritupalittāya seyyaṃ kappeti. Ekissāya gāviyā sarūpavacchāya yaṃ ekasmiṃ thane khīraṃ hoti tena rājā yāpeti, yaṃ dutiyasmiṃ thane khīraṃ hoti tena mahesī yāpeti, yaṃ tatiyasmiṃ thane khīraṃ hoti tena brāhmaṇo purohito yāpeti, yaṃ catutthasmiṃ thane khīraṃ hoti tena aggiṃ juhati, avasesena vacchako yāpeti. So evamāha – ‘ettakā usabhā haññantu yaññatthāya, ettakā vacchatarā haññantu yaññatthāya, ettakā vacchatariyo haññantu yaññatthāya, ettakā ajā haññantu yaññatthāya’, ettakā urabbhā haññantu yaññatthāya, ettakā assā haññantu yaññatthāya, ettakā rukkhā chijjantu yūpatthāya, ettakā dabbhā lūyantu barihisatthāyā’ti. Yepissa te honti ‘dāsā’ti vā ‘pessā’ti vā ‘kammakarā’ti vā tepi daṇḍatajjitā bhayatajjitā assumukhā rudamānā parikammāni karonti. Ayaṃ vuccati, brāhmaṇa, puggalo attantapo ca attaparitāpanānuyogamanuyutto[T 2.0581], parantapo ca paraparitāpanānuyogamanuyutto.

417. “And what, brahmin, is the person who is a self-tormentor, devoted to the practice of self-mortification, and a tormentor of others, devoted to the practice of tormenting others? Here, brahmin, a certain person is a king, a head-anointed noble, or a wealthy brahmin. He has a new sacrificial hall built to the east of the city, shaves off his hair and beard, dresses in a rough animal hide, smears his body with ghee and oil, scratches his back with a deer’s horn, and enters the new sacrificial hall together with his chief queen and his brahmin chaplain. There he lies on the bare ground, which is smeared with fresh cow-dung. The king sustains himself on the milk from one teat of a single cow with a calf of similar appearance; the chief queen sustains herself on the milk from the second teat; the brahmin chaplain sustains himself on the milk from the third teat; with the milk from the fourth teat they offer to the fire; and the calf sustains itself on what is left over. He declares: ‘Let so many bulls be slaughtered for the sacrifice, let so many young bullocks be slaughtered for the sacrifice, let so many young heifers be slaughtered for the sacrifice, let so many goats be slaughtered for the sacrifice, let so many rams be slaughtered for the sacrifice, let so many horses be slaughtered for the sacrifice, let so many trees be cut down for the sacrificial posts, let so much kusa grass be cut for the sacred ground.’ And those who are his slaves, messengers, or workers, threatened by the rod and by fear, with tearful faces, weeping, carry out the preparations. This, brahmin, is called the person who is a self-tormentor, devoted to the practice of self-mortification, and a tormentor of others, devoted to the practice of tormenting others.”

418. “Katamo ca, brāhmaṇa, puggalo nevattantapo nāttaparitāpanānuyogamanuyutto, na parantapo na paraparitāpanānuyogamanuyutto; so anattantapo aparantapo diṭṭheva dhamme nicchāto nibbuto [V 2.0377] sītībhūto sukhappaṭisaṃvedī brahmabhūtena attanā viharati? Idha, brāhmaṇa, tathāgato loke uppajjati arahaṃ sammāsambuddho vijjācaraṇasampanno sugato lokavidū anuttaro purisadammasārathi satthā devamanussānaṃ buddho bhagavā. So imaṃ lokaṃ sadevakaṃ samārakaṃ sabrahmakaṃ sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiṃ pajaṃ sadevamanussaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā pavedeti. So dhammaṃ deseti ādikalyāṇaṃ majjhekalyāṇaṃ [M 2.0370] pariyosānakalyāṇaṃ sātthaṃ sabyañjanaṃ, kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ parisuddhaṃ brahmacariyaṃ pakāseti. Taṃ dhammaṃ suṇāti gahapati vā gahapatiputto vā aññatarasmiṃ vā kule paccājāto. So taṃ dhammaṃ sutvā tathāgate saddhaṃ paṭilabhati. So tena saddhāpaṭilābhena samannāgato iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘sambādho gharāvāso rajopatho abbhokāso pabbajjā. Nayidaṃ sukaraṃ agāraṃ ajjhāvasatā ekantaparipuṇṇaṃ ekantaparisuddhaṃ saṅkhalikhitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ carituṃ. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ kesamassuṃ ohāretvā kāsāyāni vatthāni acchādetvā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajeyya’nti. So aparena samayena appaṃ vā bhogakkhandhaṃ pahāya mahantaṃ vā bhogakkhandhaṃ pahāya, appaṃ vā ñātiparivaṭṭaṃ pahāya [T 2.0582] mahantaṃ vā ñātiparivaṭṭaṃ pahāya, kesamassuṃ ohāretvā kāsāyāni vatthāni acchādetvā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajati. So evaṃ pabbajito samāno bhikkhūnaṃ sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno pāṇātipātaṃ pahāya pāṇātipātā paṭivirato hoti, nihitadaṇḍo nihitasattho lajjī dayāpanno sabbapāṇabhūtahitānukampī viharati.

418. “And what, brahmin, is the person who is neither a self-tormentor, not devoted to the practice of self-mortification, nor a tormentor of others, not devoted to the practice of tormenting others; who, not tormenting himself and not tormenting others, is in this very life without craving, extinguished, cooled, and experiences bliss, dwelling with a self that has become divine? Here, brahmin, a Tathāgata arises in the world, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, perfect in knowledge and conduct, the Well-Farer, knower of the world, unsurpassed trainer of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One. He makes known this world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its deities and humans, having realized it himself with direct knowledge. He teaches the Dhamma which is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with its meaning and phrasing; he reveals the perfectly complete and pure spiritual life. A householder or a householder’s son, or one born in some other family, hears that Dhamma. Having heard the Dhamma, he gains faith in the Tathāgata. Possessing that faith, he reflects thus: ‘Household life is confining, a path of dust; the life of going forth is like the open air. It is not easy, while living in a house, to lead the perfectly complete, perfectly pure spiritual life, polished like a conch shell. Suppose I shave off my hair and beard, put on the ochre robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness.’ Then, after some time, having abandoned a small or large fortune, having abandoned a small or large circle of relatives, he shaves off his hair and beard, puts on the ochre robes, and goes forth from the household life into homelessness. Having thus gone forth, and possessing the training and livelihood of the bhikkhus, he abandons the taking of life and refrains from taking life. Having laid down the rod and laid down the weapon, he is conscientious, compassionate, and dwells with empathy for the welfare of all living beings.

“Adinnādānaṃ pahāya adinnādānā paṭivirato hoti dinnādāyī dinnapāṭikaṅkhī. Athenena sucibhūtena attanā viharati.

“He abandons taking what is not given and refrains from taking what is not given. He takes only what is given, expecting only what is given. He dwells with a self that is pure and free from theft.

“Abrahmacariyaṃ pahāya brahmacārī hoti ārācārī virato methunā gāmadhammā.

“He abandons unchastity and is celibate, living aloof, refraining from sexual intercourse, the practice of villagers.

“Musāvādaṃ pahāya musāvādā paṭivirato hoti saccavādī saccasandho theto paccayiko avisaṃvādako lokassa.

“He abandons false speech and refrains from false speech. He is a speaker of truth, devoted to truth, reliable, trustworthy, and not a deceiver of the world.

“Pisuṇaṃ vācaṃ pahāya pisuṇāya vācāya paṭivirato hoti; ito sutvā na amutra akkhātā imesaṃ bhedāya, amutra vā sutvā na imesaṃ akkhātā amūsaṃ bhedāya. Iti bhinnānaṃ vā sandhātā sahitānaṃ vā anuppadātā, samaggārāmo samaggarato samagganandī samaggakaraṇiṃ vācaṃ bhāsitā hoti.

“He abandons divisive speech and refrains from divisive speech. Having heard something here, he does not repeat it elsewhere to cause division among these people; or having heard something elsewhere, he does not repeat it to these people to cause division among those people. Thus, he is a reconciler of those who are divided and a promoter of those who are united. He delights in harmony, is fond of harmony, rejoices in harmony, and speaks words that create harmony.

“Pharusaṃ [V 2.0378] vācaṃ pahāya pharusāya vācāya paṭivirato hoti. Yā sā vācā nelā kaṇṇasukhā pemanīyā hadayaṅgamā porī bahujanakantā bahujanamanāpā tathārūpiṃ vācaṃ bhāsitā hoti.

“He abandons harsh speech and refrains from harsh speech. He speaks such words as are gentle, pleasing to the ear, affectionate, going to the heart, courteous, liked by many people, and agreeable to many people.

“Samphappalāpaṃ [M 2.0371] pahāya samphappalāpā paṭivirato hoti, kālavādī bhūtavādī atthavādī dhammavādī vinayavādī, nidhānavatiṃ vācaṃ bhāsitā kālena sāpadesaṃ pariyantavatiṃ atthasaṃhitaṃ.

“He abandons frivolous talk and refrains from frivolous talk. He speaks at the proper time, speaks what is factual, speaks what is beneficial, speaks on the Dhamma and the Vinaya. He speaks words that are worth treasuring, timely, reasoned, well-defined, and connected with benefit.

“So bījagāmabhūtagāmasamārambhā paṭivirato hoti[T 2.0583]. Ekabhattiko hoti rattūparato virato vikālabhojanā. Naccagītavāditavisūkadassanā paṭivirato hoti. Mālāgandhavilepanadhāraṇamaṇḍanavibhūsanaṭṭhānā paṭivirato hoti. Uccāsayanamahāsayanā paṭivirato hoti. Jātarūparajatapaṭiggahaṇā paṭivirato hoti. Āmakadhaññapaṭiggahaṇā paṭivirato hoti. Āmakamaṃsapaṭiggahaṇā paṭivirato hoti. Itthikumārikapaṭiggahaṇā paṭivirato hoti. Dāsidāsapaṭiggahaṇā paṭivirato hoti. Ajeḷakapaṭiggahaṇā paṭivirato hoti. Kukkuṭasūkarapaṭiggahaṇā paṭivirato hoti. Hatthigavassavaḷavapaṭiggahaṇā paṭivirato hoti. Khettavatthupaṭiggahaṇā paṭivirato hoti. Dūteyyapahiṇagamanānuyogā paṭivirato hoti. Kayavikkayā paṭivirato hoti. Tulākūṭakaṃsakūṭamānakūṭā paṭivirato hoti. Ukkoṭanavañcananikatisāciyogā paṭivirato hoti. Chedanavadhabandhanaviparāmosaālopasahasākārā paṭivirato hoti.

He refrains from destroying seed-life and plant-life. He eats only one meal a day, refraining from eating at night and abstaining from food at the wrong time. He refrains from watching dancing, singing, instrumental music, and shows. He refrains from wearing garlands, using perfumes, and anointing with cosmetics, and from adornments and embellishments. He refrains from high and large beds. He refrains from accepting gold and silver. He refrains from accepting uncooked grain. He refrains from accepting raw meat. He refrains from accepting women and girls. He refrains from accepting male and female slaves. He refrains from accepting goats and sheep. He refrains from accepting chickens and pigs. He refrains from accepting elephants, cattle, horses, and mares. He refrains from accepting fields and lands. He refrains from undertaking errands and messages. He refrains from buying and selling. He refrains from cheating with weights, currency, and measures. He refrains from bribery, deception, fraud, and crooked practices. He refrains from cutting, killing, binding, highway robbery, plundering, and violence.

“So santuṭṭho hoti kāyaparihārikena cīvarena, kucchiparihārikena piṇḍapātena. So yena yeneva pakkamati samādāyeva pakkamati. Seyyathāpi nāma pakkhī sakuṇo yena yeneva ḍeti sapattabhārova ḍeti, evameva bhikkhu santuṭṭho hoti kāyaparihārikena cīvarena, kucchiparihārikena piṇḍapātena. So yena yeneva pakkamati samādāyeva pakkamati. So iminā ariyena sīlakkhandhena samannāgato ajjhattaṃ anavajjasukhaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti.

He is content with robes that suffice for the maintenance of his body and with almsfood that suffices for the maintenance of his belly. Wherever he goes, he sets out taking just these with him. Just as a winged bird, wherever it flies, flies with the burden of its wings, so too is the bhikkhu content with robes that suffice for the maintenance of his body and with almsfood that suffices for the maintenance of his belly. Wherever he goes, he sets out taking just these with him. Endowed with this noble aggregate of virtue, he experiences within himself the bliss of blamelessness.

419. “So cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā na nimittaggāhī hoti nānubyañjanaggāhī. Yatvādhikaraṇamenaṃ cakkhundriyaṃ [T 2.0584] asaṃvutaṃ viharantaṃ abhijjhādomanassā pāpakā akusalā dhammā anvāssaveyyuṃ tassa saṃvarāya paṭipajjati, rakkhati cakkhundriyaṃ, cakkhundriye saṃvaraṃ āpajjati. Sotena saddaṃ sutvā…pe… ghānena gandhaṃ ghāyitvā… jivhāya rasaṃ sāyitvā… kāyena phoṭṭhabbaṃ phusitvā… manasā dhammaṃ viññāyana na nimittaggāhī hoti nānubyañjanaggāhī[V 2.0379]. Yatvādhikaraṇamenaṃ [M 2.0372] manindriyaṃ asaṃvutaṃ viharantaṃ abhijjhādomanassā pāpakā akusalā dhammā anvāssaveyyuṃ tassa saṃvarāya paṭipajjati, rakkhati manindriyaṃ, manindriye saṃvaraṃ āpajjati. So iminā ariyena indriyasaṃvarena samannāgato ajjhattaṃ abyāsekasukhaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti.

419. Having seen a form with the eye, he is not one who grasps at signs or at secondary characteristics. Inasmuch as evil, unwholesome states of covetousness and displeasure might assail him were he to dwell with the eye faculty unrestrained, he practices for its restraint, he guards the eye faculty, he undertakes restraint of the eye faculty. Having heard a sound with the ear… having smelled an odor with the nose… having tasted a flavor with the tongue… having touched a tangible with the body… having cognized a mental object with the mind, he is not one who grasps at signs or at secondary characteristics. Inasmuch as evil, unwholesome states of covetousness and displeasure might assail him were he to dwell with the mind faculty unrestrained, he practices for its restraint, he guards the mind faculty, he undertakes restraint of the mind faculty. Endowed with this noble restraint of the faculties, he experiences within himself an unblemished bliss.

“So abhikkante paṭikkante sampajānakārī hoti, ālokite vilokite sampajānakārī hoti, samiñjite pasārite sampajānakārī hoti, saṅghāṭipattacīvaradhāraṇe sampajānakārī hoti, asite pīte khāyite sāyite sampajānakārī hoti, uccārapassāvakamme sampajānakārī hoti, gate ṭhite nisinne sutte jāgarite bhāsite tuṇhībhāve sampajānakārī hoti.

He acts with clear comprehension when going forward and returning; he acts with clear comprehension when looking ahead and looking around; he acts with clear comprehension when bending and stretching; he acts with clear comprehension in wearing his double-robe, bowl, and outer robe; he acts with clear comprehension when eating, drinking, chewing, and savoring; he acts with clear comprehension when defecating and urinating; he acts with clear comprehension when walking, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, and in being silent.

“So iminā ca ariyena sīlakkhandhena samannāgato, (imāya ca ariyāya santuṭṭhiyā samannāgato,) passa ma. ni. 1.296 iminā ca ariyena indriyasaṃvarena samannāgato, iminā ca ariyena satisampajaññena samannāgato vivittaṃ senāsanaṃ bhajati araññaṃ rukkhamūlaṃ pabbataṃ kandaraṃ giriguhaṃ susānaṃ vanapatthaṃ abbhokāsaṃ palālapuñjaṃ. So pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto nisīdati pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā, ujuṃ [T 2.0585] kāyaṃ paṇidhāya, parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā. So abhijjhaṃ loke pahāya vigatābhijjhena cetasā viharati, abhijjhāya cittaṃ parisodheti; byāpādapadosaṃ pahāya abyāpannacitto viharati sabbapāṇabhūtahitānukampī, byāpādapadosā cittaṃ parisodheti; thinamiddhaṃ pahāya vigatathīnamiddho viharati ālokasaññī sato sampajāno, thīnamiddhā cittaṃ parisodheti; uddhaccakukkuccaṃ pahāya anuddhato viharati ajjhattaṃ vūpasantacitto, uddhaccakukkuccā cittaṃ parisodheti; vicikicchaṃ pahāya tiṇṇavicikiccho viharati akathaṃkathī kusalesu dhammesu, vicikicchāya cittaṃ parisodheti.

Endowed with this noble aggregate of virtue, with this noble restraint of the faculties, and with this noble mindfulness and clear comprehension, he resorts to a secluded lodging: a forest, the foot of a tree, a mountain, a ravine, a mountain cave, a charnel ground, a forest thicket, an open space, a heap of straw. After the meal, having returned from the alms-round, he sits down, having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness before him. Having abandoned covetousness for the world, he dwells with a mind devoid of covetousness; he purifies his mind from covetousness. Having abandoned ill will and malevolence, he dwells with a mind free from ill will, compassionate for the welfare of all living beings; he purifies his mind from ill will and malevolence. Having abandoned sloth and torpor, he dwells free from sloth and torpor, perceiving light, mindful, and clearly comprehending; he purifies his mind from sloth and torpor. Having abandoned restlessness and remorse, he dwells unagitated, with a mind internally calmed; he purifies his mind from restlessness and remorse. Having abandoned doubt, he dwells having crossed over doubt, without uncertainty regarding wholesome states; he purifies his mind from doubt.

“So ime pañca nīvaraṇe pahāya cetaso upakkilese paññāya dubbalīkaraṇe vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā ajjhattaṃ sampasādanaṃ cetaso ekodibhāvaṃ avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ samādhijaṃ pītisukhaṃ dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Pītiyā ca virāgā upekkhako ca viharati sato ca sampajāno, sukhañca kāyena paṭisaṃvedeti[M 2.0373], yaṃ taṃ ariyā ācikkhanti – ‘upekkhako satimā sukhavihārī’ti tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Sukhassa ca pahānā dukkhassa ca pahānā, pubbeva somanassadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamā, adukkhamasukhaṃ upekkhāsatipārisuddhiṃ catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati.

Having abandoned these five hindrances—defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom—secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by initial and sustained application, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. With the stilling of initial and sustained application, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without initial and sustained application, with rapture and happiness born of concentration. With the fading away of rapture, he dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending, and experiences happiness with the body—that of which the noble ones declare: ‘Equanimous and mindful, he dwells happily.’ He enters and dwells in the third jhāna. With the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and displeasure, he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.

420. “So [T 2.0586][V 2.0380] evaṃ samāhite citte parisuddhe pariyodāte anaṅgaṇe vigatūpakkilese mudubhūte kammaniye ṭhite āneñjappatte pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇāya cittaṃ abhininnāmeti. So anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati, seyyathidaṃ – ekampi jātiṃ dvepi jātiyo tissopi jātiyo catassopi jātiyo pañcapi jātiyo dasapi jātiyo vīsampi jātiyo tiṃsampi jātiyo cattālīsampi jātiyo paññāsampi jātiyo jātisatampi jātisahassampi jātisatasahassampi, anekepi saṃvaṭṭakappe anekepi vivaṭṭakappe anekepi saṃvaṭṭavivaṭṭakappe – ‘amutrāsiṃ evaṃnāmo evaṃgotto evaṃvaṇṇo evamāhāro evaṃsukhadukkhappaṭisaṃvedī evamāyupariyanto; so tato cuto amutra udapādiṃ; tatrāpāsiṃ evaṃnāmo evaṃgotto evaṃvaṇṇo evamāhāro evaṃsukhadukkhappaṭisaṃvedī evamāyupariyanto; so tato cuto idhūpapanno’ti. Iti sākāraṃ sauddesaṃ anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati.

420. When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, without blemish, free from defilements, become malleable, workable, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he inclines and directs his mind to the knowledge of the recollection of past abodes. He recollects his manifold past abodes, that is: one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births; many eons of contraction, many eons of expansion, many eons of contraction and expansion. ‘In that place I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, experienced such pleasure and pain, and had such a life-span. Passing away from there, I reappeared elsewhere. There too I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, experienced such pleasure and pain, and had such a life-span. Passing away from there, I have arisen here.’ Thus he recollects his manifold past abodes with their aspects and details.

“So evaṃ samāhite citte parisuddhe pariyodāte anaṅgaṇe vigatūpakkilese mudubhūte kammaniye ṭhite āneñjappatte sattānaṃ cutūpapātañāṇāya cittaṃ abhininnāmeti. So dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena satte passati cavamāne upapajjamāne hīne paṇīte suvaṇṇe dubbaṇṇe sugate duggate yathākammūpage satte pajānāti – ‘ime vata bhonto sattā kāyaduccaritena samannāgatā…pe… ariyānaṃ upavādakā micchādiṭṭhikā micchādiṭṭhikammasamādānā[T 2.0587], te kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapannā. Ime vā pana bhonto sattā kāyasucaritena samannāgatā…pe… ariyānaṃ anupavādakā sammādiṭṭhikā sammādiṭṭhikammasamādānā, te kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapannā’ti. Iti dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena satte passati cavamāne upapajjamāne hīne paṇīte suvaṇṇe dubbaṇṇe sugate duggate yathākammūpage satte pajānāti.

When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of defilements, malleable, workable, steady, and having attained imperturbability, he directs and inclines his mind to the knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings. With the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, he sees beings passing away and reappearing—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma: ‘Indeed, these beings who were endowed with bodily misconduct… revilers of the noble ones, holding wrong view, and undertaking actions based on wrong view, with the breakup of the body, after death, have reappeared in the plane of misery, in a bad destination, in the lower world, in hell. But these beings who were endowed with good bodily conduct… not revilers of the noble ones, holding right view, and undertaking actions based on right view, with the breakup of the body, after death, have reappeared in a good destination, in a heavenly world.’ Thus, with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, he sees beings passing away and reappearing—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma.

“So [M 2.0374] evaṃ samāhite citte parisuddhe pariyodāte anaṅgaṇe vigatūpakkilese mudubhūte kammaniye ṭhite āneñjappatte āsavānaṃ khayañāṇāya cittaṃ abhininnāmeti. So ‘idaṃ dukkha’nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, ‘ayaṃ dukkhasamudayo’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodho’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti; ‘ime āsavā’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, ‘ayaṃ āsavasamudayo’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, ‘ayaṃ āsavanirodho’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, ‘ayaṃ āsavanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Tassa evaṃ jānato evaṃ passato kāmāsavāpi cittaṃ vimuccati, bhavāsavāpi cittaṃ vimuccati, avijjāsavāpi [V 2.0381] cittaṃ vimuccati. Vimuttasmiṃ vimuttamiti ñāṇaṃ hoti. ‘Khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti pajānāti.

When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of defilements, malleable, workable, steady, and having attained imperturbability, he directs and inclines his mind to the knowledge of the destruction of the taints. He understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering.’ He understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering.’ He understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering.’ He understands as it really is: ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.’ He understands as it really is: ‘These are the taints.’ He understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of the taints.’ He understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of the taints.’ He understands as it really is: ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of the taints.’ As he knows and sees thus, his mind is liberated from the taint of sensual desire, his mind is liberated from the taint of existence, and his mind is liberated from the taint of ignorance. When it is liberated, the knowledge arises: ‘It is liberated.’ He understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.’

“Ayaṃ vuccati, brāhmaṇa, puggalo nevattantapo nāttaparitāpanānuyogamanuyutto, na parantapo na [T 2.0588] paraparitāpanānuyogamanuyutto. So anattantapo aparantapo diṭṭheva dhamme nicchāto nibbuto sītībhūto sukhappaṭisaṃvedī brahmabhūtena attanā viharatī”ti.

This, brahmin, is called a person who is neither a self-tormentor nor devoted to the practice of self-torment, neither a tormentor of others nor devoted to the practice of tormenting others. He, not a self-tormentor and not a tormentor of others, in this very life dwells without craving, extinguished, cooled, experiencing bliss, with a self that has become supreme.

421. Evaṃ vutte, ghoṭamukho brāhmaṇo āyasmantaṃ udenaṃ etadavoca – “abhikkantaṃ, bho udena, abhikkantaṃ, bho udena! Seyyathāpi, bho udena, nikkujjitaṃ vā ukkujjeyya, paṭicchannaṃ vā vivareyya, mūḷhassa vā maggaṃ ācikkheyya, andhakāre vā telapajjotaṃ dhāreyya – cakkhumanto rūpāni dakkhantīti – evamevaṃ bhotā udenena anekapariyāyena dhammo pakāsito. Esāhaṃ bhavantaṃ udenaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi dhammañca bhikkhusaṅghañca. Upāsakaṃ maṃ bhavaṃ udeno dhāretu ajjatagge pāṇupetaṃ saraṇaṃ gata”nti. “Mā kho maṃ tvaṃ, brāhmaṇa, saraṇaṃ agamāsi. Tameva bhagavantaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāhi yamahaṃ saraṇaṃ gato”ti. “Kahaṃ pana, bho udena, etarahi so bhavaṃ gotamo viharati arahaṃ sammāsambuddho”ti? “Parinibbuto kho, brāhmaṇa, etarahi so bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho”ti.

421. When this was said, the brahmin Ghoṭamukha said to the Venerable Udena: 'Excellent, Venerable Udena, excellent, Venerable Udena!
