Seyyathāpi, bho gotama, nikkujjitaṃ vā ukkujjeyya, paṭicchannaṃ vā vivareyya, mūḷhassa vā maggaṃ ācikkheyya, andhakāre vā telapajjotaṃ dhāreyya – cakkhumanto rūpāni dakkhantīti – evamevaṃ bhotā gotamena anekapariyāyena dhammo pakāsito. Ete mayaṃ bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāma dhammañca bhikkhusaṅghañca. Upāsake no bhavaṃ gotamo dhāretu ajjatagge pāṇupetaṃ saraṇaṃ gate”ti.

461. When this was said, the young men Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja said to the Blessed One: “Excellent, Master Gotama, excellent! Just as, Master Gotama, one might set upright what was overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or hold up an oil lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—in the very same way, the Dhamma has been made clear by Master Gotama in many ways. We go for refuge to Master Gotama, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May Master Gotama remember us as lay followers who have gone for refuge from this day forward, for as long as life lasts.”

Vāseṭṭhasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ.

The Vāseṭṭha Sutta, the eighth, is concluded.

9. Subhasuttaṃ

9. The Subha Sutta

462. Evaṃ [V 2.0421] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme. Tena kho pana samayena subho māṇavo todeyyaputto sāvatthiyaṃ paṭivasati aññatarassa gahapatissa nivesane kenacideva karaṇīyena. Atha kho subho māṇavo todeyyaputto yassa gahapatissa nivesane paṭivasati taṃ gahapatiṃ etadavoca – “sutaṃ metaṃ, gahapati – ‘avivittā sāvatthī arahantehī’ti. Kaṃ nu khvajja samaṇaṃ vā brāhmaṇaṃ vā payirupāseyyāmā”ti? “Ayaṃ, bhante, bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme. Taṃ, bhante, bhagavantaṃ payirupāsassū”ti. Atha [P 2.0197] kho subho māṇavo todeyyaputto tassa gahapatissa paṭissutvā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavatā saddhiṃ sammodi. Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho subho māṇavo todeyyaputto bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “brāhmaṇā, bho gotama, evamāhaṃsu – ‘gahaṭṭho ārādhako hoti ñāyaṃ dhammaṃ kusalaṃ, na pabbajito ārādhako hoti ñāyaṃ dhammaṃ kusala’nti. Idha bhavaṃ gotamo kimāhā”ti?

462. Thus have I heard. At one time, the Blessed One was dwelling in Sāvatthī, at Jeta’s Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. Now at that time, the young man Subha, son of Todeyya, was residing in Sāvatthī in the house of a certain householder on some business. Then the young man Subha, son of Todeyya, said to the householder in whose residence he was staying: ‘Householder, I have heard this: “Sāvatthī is not devoid of Arahants.” Which recluse or brahmin should we attend upon today?’ ‘Venerable sir, the Blessed One is dwelling in Sāvatthī, at Jeta’s Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. Venerable sir, you should attend upon that Blessed One.’ Then the young man Subha, son of Todeyya, having respectfully listened to the householder’s words, approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he exchanged joyful greetings with the Blessed One. Having concluded the joyful and memorable conversation, he sat down at a suitable place. Seated at a suitable place, the young man Subha, son of Todeyya, said this to the Blessed One: ‘Venerable Gotama, the brahmins say this: “A householder is one who accomplishes the righteous and wholesome Dhamma; a renunciate is not one who accomplishes the righteous and wholesome Dhamma.” Regarding this, what does the Venerable Gotama say?’

463. “Vibhajjavādo kho ahamettha, māṇava; nāhamettha ekaṃsavādo. Gihissa vāhaṃ, māṇava, pabbajitassa vā micchāpaṭipattiṃ na vaṇṇemi. Gihī vā [M 2.0414] hi[T 2.0651], māṇava, pabbajito vā micchāpaṭipanno micchāpaṭipattādhikaraṇahetu na ārādhako hoti ñāyaṃ dhammaṃ kusalaṃ. Gihissa vāhaṃ, māṇava, pabbajitassa vā sammāpaṭipattiṃ vaṇṇemi. Gihī vā hi, māṇava, pabbajito vā sammāpaṭipanno sammāpaṭipattādhikaraṇahetu ārādhako hoti ñāyaṃ dhammaṃ kusala”nti.

463. “Young man, in this matter I speak analytically; I do not speak categorically. Young man, I do not praise the wrong practice of either a householder or a renunciate. Indeed, young man, whether a householder or a renunciate, one who has undertaken wrong practice, by reason of that wrong practice, does not accomplish the righteous and wholesome Dhamma. Young man, I praise the right practice of either a householder or a renunciate. Indeed, young man, whether a householder or a renunciate, one who has undertaken right practice, by reason of that right practice, accomplishes the righteous and wholesome Dhamma.”

“Brāhmaṇā, bho gotama, evamāhaṃsu – ‘mahaṭṭhamidaṃ mahākiccaṃ mahādhikaraṇaṃ mahāsamārambhaṃ gharāvāsakammaṭṭhānaṃ mahapphalaṃ hoti; appaṭṭhamidaṃ appakiccaṃ appādhikaraṇaṃ appasamārambhaṃ pabbajjā kammaṭṭhānaṃ appaphalaṃ hotī’ti. Idha bhavaṃ gotamo kimāhā”ti.

“Venerable Gotama, the brahmins say this: ‘The occupation of the householder has great purpose, great duties, great undertakings, and great exertion; it is of great fruit. The occupation of the renunciate has little purpose, few duties, few undertakings, and little exertion; it is of little fruit.’ Regarding this, what does the Venerable Gotama say?”

“Etthāpi [V 2.0422] kho ahaṃ, māṇava, vibhajjavādo; nāhamettha ekaṃsavādo. Atthi, māṇava, kammaṭṭhānaṃ mahaṭṭhaṃ mahākiccaṃ mahādhikaraṇaṃ mahāsamārambhaṃ vipajjamānaṃ appaphalaṃ hoti; atthi, māṇava, kammaṭṭhānaṃ mahaṭṭhaṃ mahākiccaṃ mahādhikaraṇaṃ mahāsamārambhaṃ sampajjamānaṃ mahapphalaṃ hoti; atthi, māṇava, kammaṭṭhānaṃ appaṭṭhaṃ appakiccaṃ appādhikaraṇaṃ appasamārambhaṃ vipajjamānaṃ appaphalaṃ hoti; atthi, māṇava, kammaṭṭhānaṃ appaṭṭhaṃ appakiccaṃ appādhikaraṇaṃ appasamārambhaṃ sampajjamānaṃ mahapphalaṃ hoti. Katamañca, māṇava[P 2.0198], kammaṭṭhānaṃ mahaṭṭhaṃ mahākiccaṃ mahādhikaraṇaṃ mahāsamārambhaṃ vipajjamānaṃ appaphalaṃ [T 2.0652] hoti? Kasi kho, māṇava, kammaṭṭhānaṃ mahaṭṭhaṃ mahākiccaṃ mahādhikaraṇaṃ mahāsamārambhaṃ vipajjamānaṃ appaphalaṃ hoti. Katamañca, māṇava, kammaṭṭhānaṃ mahaṭṭhaṃ mahākiccaṃ mahādhikaraṇaṃ mahāsamārambhaṃ sampajjamānaṃ mahapphalaṃ hoti? Kasiyeva kho, māṇava, kammaṭṭhānaṃ mahaṭṭhaṃ mahākiccaṃ mahādhikaraṇaṃ mahāsamārambhaṃ sampajjamānaṃ mahapphalaṃ hoti. Katamañca, māṇava, kammaṭṭhānaṃ appaṭṭhaṃ appakiccaṃ appādhikaraṇaṃ appasamārambhaṃ vipajjamānaṃ appaphalaṃ hoti? Vaṇijjā kho, māṇava, kammaṭṭhānaṃ appaṭṭhaṃ appakiccaṃ appādhikaraṇaṃ appasamārambhaṃ vipajjamānaṃ appaphalaṃ hoti. Katamañca māṇava, kammaṭṭhānaṃ appaṭṭhaṃ appakiccaṃ appādhikaraṇaṃ appasamārambhaṃ sampajjamānaṃ mahapphalaṃ hoti? Vaṇijjāyeva kho, māṇava, kammaṭṭhānaṃ appaṭṭhaṃ appakiccaṃ appādhikaraṇaṃ appasamārambhaṃ sampajjamānaṃ mahapphalaṃ hoti.

“Here too, young man, I speak analytically; I do not speak categorically. There is, young man, an occupation that has great purpose, great duties, great undertakings, and great exertion, which, when it fails, is of little fruit. There is, young man, an occupation that has great purpose, great duties, great undertakings, and great exertion, which, when it succeeds, is of great fruit. There is, young man, an occupation that has little purpose, few duties, few undertakings, and little exertion, which, when it fails, is of little fruit. There is, young man, an occupation that has little purpose, few duties, few undertakings, and little exertion, which, when it succeeds, is of great fruit. And what, young man, is the occupation that has great purpose, great duties, great undertakings, and great exertion, which, when it fails, is of little fruit? Farming, young man, is an occupation that has great purpose, great duties, great undertakings, and great exertion, which, when it fails, is of little fruit. And what, young man, is the occupation that has great purpose, great duties, great undertakings, and great exertion, which, when it succeeds, is of great fruit? Farming itself, young man, is an occupation that has great purpose, great duties, great undertakings, and great exertion, which, when it succeeds, is of great fruit. And what, young man, is the occupation that has little purpose, few duties, few undertakings, and little exertion, which, when it fails, is of little fruit? Trade, young man, is an occupation that has little purpose, few duties, few undertakings, and little exertion, which, when it fails, is of little fruit. And what, young man, is the occupation that has little purpose, few duties, few undertakings, and little exertion, which, when it succeeds, is of great fruit? Trade itself, young man, is an occupation that has little purpose, few duties, few undertakings, and little exertion, which, when it succeeds, is of great fruit.”

464. “Seyyathāpi, māṇava, kasi kammaṭṭhānaṃ mahaṭṭhaṃ mahākiccaṃ mahādhikaraṇaṃ mahāsamārambhaṃ vipajjamānaṃ appaphalaṃ hoti; evameva kho, māṇava, gharāvāsakammaṭṭhānaṃ mahaṭṭhaṃ mahākiccaṃ mahādhikaraṇaṃ mahāsamārambhaṃ vipajjamānaṃ [M 2.0415] appaphalaṃ hoti. Seyyathāpi, māṇava, kasiyeva kammaṭṭhānaṃ mahaṭṭhaṃ mahākiccaṃ mahādhikaraṇaṃ mahāsamārambhaṃ sampajjamānaṃ mahapphalaṃ hoti; evameva kho, māṇava, gharāvāsakammaṭṭhānaṃ mahaṭṭhaṃ mahākiccaṃ mahādhikaraṇaṃ mahāsamārambhaṃ sampajjamānaṃ mahapphalaṃ hoti. Seyyathāpi, māṇava, vaṇijjā kammaṭṭhānaṃ appaṭṭhaṃ appakiccaṃ appādhikaraṇaṃ appasamārambhaṃ vipajjamānaṃ appaphalaṃ hoti; evameva [T 2.0653] kho, māṇava, pabbajjā kammaṭṭhānaṃ appaṭṭhaṃ appakiccaṃ appādhikaraṇaṃ appasamārambhaṃ vipajjamānaṃ appaphalaṃ hoti. Seyyathāpi, māṇava, vaṇijjāyeva kammaṭṭhānaṃ appaṭṭhaṃ appakiccaṃ appādhikaraṇaṃ appasamārambhaṃ sampajjamānaṃ mahapphalaṃ hoti; evameva kho[P 2.0199], māṇava, pabbajjā kammaṭṭhānaṃ appaṭṭhaṃ appakiccaṃ appādhikaraṇaṃ appasamārambhaṃ sampajjamānaṃ mahapphalaṃ hotī”ti.

464. Young man, just as the work of farming—of great purpose, great task, great affair, and great exertion—when it fails, yields little fruit; even so, young man, the work of the household life—of great purpose, great task, great affair, and great exertion—when it fails, yields little fruit. Young man, just as the very work of farming—of great purpose, great task, great affair, and great exertion—when it succeeds, yields great fruit; even so, young man, the work of the household life—of great purpose, great task, great affair, and great exertion—when it succeeds, yields great fruit. Young man, just as the work of trade—of little purpose, little task, little affair, and little exertion—when it fails, yields little fruit; even so, young man, the work of going forth—of little purpose, little task, little affair, and little exertion—when it fails, yields little fruit. Young man, just as the very work of trade—of little purpose, little task, little affair, and little exertion—when it succeeds, yields great fruit; even so, young man, the work of going forth—of little purpose, little task, little affair, and little exertion—when it succeeds, yields great fruit.

“Brāhmaṇā[V 2.0423], bho gotama, pañca dhamme paññapenti puññassa kiriyāya, kusalassa ārādhanāyā”ti. “Ye te, māṇava, brāhmaṇā pañca dhamme paññapenti puññassa kiriyāya, kusalassa ārādhanāya – sace te agaru – sādhu te pañca dhamme imasmiṃ parisati bhāsassū”ti. “Na kho me, bho gotama, garu yatthassu bhavanto vā nisinno bhavantarūpo vā”ti nisinnā bhavantarūpā vāti (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.). “Tena hi, māṇava, bhāsassū”ti. “Saccaṃ kho, bho gotama, brāhmaṇā paṭhamaṃ dhammaṃ paññapenti puññassa kiriyāya, kusalassa ārādhanāya. Tapaṃ kho, bho gotama, brāhmaṇā dutiyaṃ dhammaṃ paññapenti puññassa kiriyāya, kusalassa ārādhanāya. Brahmacariyaṃ kho, bho gotama, brāhmaṇā tatiyaṃ dhammaṃ paññapenti puññassa kiriyāya, kusalassa ārādhanāya. Ajjhenaṃ kho, bho gotama, brāhmaṇā catutthaṃ dhammaṃ paññapenti puññassa kiriyāya, kusalassa ārādhanāya. Cāgaṃ kho, bho gotama, brāhmaṇā [T 2.0654] pañcamaṃ dhammaṃ paññapenti puññassa kiriyāya, kusalassa ārādhanāya. Brāhmaṇā, bho gotama, ime pañca dhamme paññapenti puññassa kiriyāya, kusalassa ārādhanāyāti. Idha bhavaṃ gotamo kimāhā”ti?

“Venerable Gotama, brahmins prescribe five principles for the making of merit, for the accomplishment of the wholesome.” “Young man, regarding those five principles that the brahmins prescribe for the making of merit, for the accomplishment of the wholesome—if it is not a burden for you, it would be good to speak of those five principles in this assembly.” “It is no burden for me, Venerable Gotama, where the venerable one is seated, or one like the venerable one.” “Then, young man, speak.” “Venerable Gotama, the brahmins prescribe truthfulness as the first principle for the making of merit, for the accomplishment of the wholesome. Venerable Gotama, the brahmins prescribe austerity as the second principle for the making of merit, for the accomplishment of the wholesome. Venerable Gotama, the brahmins prescribe the holy life as the third principle for the making of merit, for the accomplishment of the wholesome. Venerable Gotama, the brahmins prescribe study as the fourth principle for the making of merit, for the accomplishment of the wholesome. Venerable Gotama, the brahmins prescribe generosity as the fifth principle for the making of merit, for the accomplishment of the wholesome. Venerable Gotama, these are the five principles that the brahmins prescribe for the making of merit, for the accomplishment of the wholesome. Regarding this, what does the Venerable Gotama say?”

465. “Kiṃ pana, māṇava, atthi koci brāhmaṇānaṃ ekabrāhmaṇopi yo evamāha – ‘ahaṃ imesaṃ pañcannaṃ dhammānaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā vipākaṃ pavedemī’”ti? “No hidaṃ, bho gotama”. “Kiṃ pana, māṇava, atthi koci brāhmaṇānaṃ ekācariyopi ekācariyapācariyopi yāva sattamā ācariyamahayugāpi yo evamāha – ‘ahaṃ imesaṃ pañcannaṃ dhammānaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā [M 2.0416] vipākaṃ pavedemī’”ti? “No hidaṃ, bho gotama”. “Kiṃ [P 2.0200] pana, māṇava, yepi te brāhmaṇānaṃ pubbakā isayo mantānaṃ kattāro mantānaṃ pavattāro yesamidaṃ etarahi brāhmaṇā porāṇaṃ mantapadaṃ gītaṃ pavuttaṃ samihitaṃ tadanugāyanti tadanubhāsanti bhāsitamanubhāsanti vācitamanuvācenti, seyyathidaṃ – aṭṭhako vāmako vāmadevo vessāmitto yamataggi aṅgīraso bhāradvājo vāseṭṭho kassapo bhagu, tepi evamāhaṃsu – ‘mayaṃ imesaṃ pañcannaṃ dhammānaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā vipākaṃ pavedemā’”ti? “No hidaṃ, bho gotama”.

465. “But, young man, is there any single brahmin who says thus: ‘Having realized it for myself through direct knowledge, I declare the result of these five principles’?” “That is not so, Venerable Gotama.” “But, young man, is there any single teacher of the brahmins, or a teacher of a teacher, even up to the seventh generation of teachers, who says thus: ‘Having realized it for myself through direct knowledge, I declare the result of these five principles’?” “That is not so, Venerable Gotama.” “But, young man, what of those ancient seers of the brahmins, the creators of the hymns, the promulgators of the hymns—whose ancient hymn-verse, chanted, proclaimed, and compiled, the brahmins of today now chant along with and recite along with, repeating what was spoken and reciting what was taught—namely, Aṭṭhaka, Vāmaka, Vāmadeva, Vessāmitta, Yamataggi, Aṅgīrasa, Bhāradvāja, Vāseṭṭha, Kassapa, and Bhagu? Did even they say thus: ‘Having realized it for ourselves through direct knowledge, we declare the result of these five principles’?” “That is not so, Venerable Gotama.”

“Iti kira, māṇava, natthi koci brāhmaṇānaṃ ekabrāhmaṇopi yo evamāha – ‘ahaṃ imesaṃ pañcannaṃ dhammānaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā [T 2.0655] sacchikatvā vipākaṃ pavedemī’ti; natthi koci brāhmaṇānaṃ ekācariyopi ekācariyapācariyopi yāva sattamā ācariyamahayugāpi yo evamāha [V 2.0424] – ‘ahaṃ imesaṃ pañcannaṃ dhammānaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā vipākaṃ pavedemī’ti; yepi te brāhmaṇānaṃ pubbakā isayo mantānaṃ kattāro mantānaṃ pavattāro, yesamidaṃ etarahi brāhmaṇā porāṇaṃ mantapadaṃ gītaṃ pavuttaṃ samihitaṃ, tadanugāyanti tadanubhāsanti bhāsitamanubhāsanti vācitamanuvācenti, seyyathidaṃ – aṭṭhako vāmako vāmadevo vessāmitto yamataggi aṅgīraso bhāradvājo vāseṭṭho kassapo bhagu. Tepi na evamāhaṃsu – ‘mayaṃ imesaṃ pañcannaṃ dhammānaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā vipākaṃ pavedemā’ti.

“So it seems, young man, there is not any single brahmin who says thus: ‘Having realized it for myself through direct knowledge, I declare the result of these five principles.’ There is not any single teacher of the brahmins, or a teacher of a teacher, even up to the seventh generation of teachers, who says thus: ‘Having realized it for myself through direct knowledge, I declare the result of these five principles.’ And even those ancient seers of the brahmins, the creators of the hymns, the promulgators of the hymns—whose ancient hymn-verse, chanted, proclaimed, and compiled, the brahmins of today now chant along with and recite along with, repeating what was spoken and reciting what was taught—namely, Aṭṭhaka, Vāmaka, Vāmadeva, Vessāmitta, Yamataggi, Aṅgīrasa, Bhāradvāja, Vāseṭṭha, Kassapa, and Bhagu—did not say thus: ‘Having realized it for ourselves through direct knowledge, we declare the result of these five principles.’”

“Seyyathāpi, māṇava, andhaveṇi paramparāsaṃsattā purimopi na passati majjhimopi na passati pacchimopi na passati; evameva kho, māṇava, andhaveṇūpamaṃ maññe brāhmaṇānaṃ bhāsitaṃ sampajjati – purimopi na passati majjhimopi na passati pacchimopi na passatī”ti.

“Young man, just as with a line of blind men linked together, the first one does not see, the middle one does not see, and the last one does not see; even so, young man, the statement of the brahmins, I think, proves to be like a line of blind men: the first one does not see, the middle one does not see, and the last one does not see.”

466. Evaṃ vutte, subho māṇavo todeyyaputto bhagavatā andhaveṇūpamena vuccamāno kupito anattamano bhagavantaṃyeva khuṃsento bhagavantaṃyeva vambhento bhagavantaṃyeva vadamāno – ‘samaṇo gotamo pāpito bhavissatī’ti bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “brāhmaṇo, bho gotama, pokkharasāti opamañño subhagavaniko evamāha – ‘evameva [M 2.0417] panidhekacce panimeke (sabbattha) samaṇabrāhmaṇā uttarimanussadhammā alamariyañāṇadassanavisesaṃ [T 2.0656] paṭijānanti. Tesamidaṃ bhāsitaṃ [P 2.0201] hassakaṃyeva sampajjati, nāmakaṃyeva sampajjati, rittakaṃyeva sampajjati, tucchakaṃyeva sampajjati. Kathañhi nāma manussabhūto uttarimanussadhammā alamariyañāṇadassanavisesaṃ ñassati vā dakkhati vā sacchi vā karissatīti – netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatī’”ti?

466. When this was said, the young man Subha, son of the brahmin Todeyya, being addressed by the Blessed One with the simile of the string of blind men, became angry and displeased. Wanting to revile the Blessed One, wanting to disparage the Blessed One, and wanting to accuse the Blessed One, he thought, 'The ascetic Gotama will be brought low,' and said this to the Blessed One: 'Venerable Gotama, the brahmin Pokkharasāti of the Opamañña clan, lord of Subhagavana, says thus: “Indeed, some ascetics and brahmins here claim a state superior to the human state, a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones. Their statement becomes merely laughable, becomes merely a name, becomes merely empty, becomes merely void. For how could a human being know or see or realize a state superior to the human state, a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones? This is not possible.”'

“Kiṃ pana, māṇava, brāhmaṇo pokkharasāti opamañño subhagavaniko sabbesaṃyeva samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ cetasā ceto paricca pajānātī”ti? “Sakāyapi hi, bho gotama, puṇṇikāya dāsiyā brāhmaṇo pokkharasāti opamañño subhagavaniko cetasā ceto paricca na pajānāti, kuto pana sabbesaṃyeva samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ cetasā ceto paricca pajānissatī”ti?

“But what do you think, young man? Does the brahmin Pokkharasāti of the Opamañña clan, lord of Subhagavana, know the minds of all ascetics and brahmins by encompassing them with his own mind?” “Venerable Gotama, the brahmin Pokkharasāti of the Opamañña clan, lord of Subhagavana, does not even know the mind of his own slave-woman Puṇṇikā by encompassing it with his own mind. How then could he know the minds of all ascetics and brahmins by encompassing them with his own mind?”

“Seyyathāpi, māṇava, jaccandho puriso na passeyya kaṇhasukkāni rūpāni, na passeyya nīlakāni [V 2.0425] rūpāni, na passeyya pītakāni rūpāni, na passeyya lohitakāni rūpāni, na passeyya mañjiṭṭhakāni rūpāni, na passeyya samavisamaṃ, na passeyya tārakarūpāni, na passeyya candimasūriye. So evaṃ vadeyya – ‘natthi kaṇhasukkāni rūpāni, natthi kaṇhasukkānaṃ rūpānaṃ dassāvī; natthi nīlakāni rūpāni, natthi nīlakānaṃ rūpānaṃ dassāvī; natthi pītakāni rūpāni, natthi pītakānaṃ rūpānaṃ dassāvī; natthi lohitakāni rūpāni, natthi lohitakānaṃ rūpānaṃ dassāvī; natthi mañjiṭṭhakāni rūpāni, natthi mañjiṭṭhakānaṃ rūpānaṃ dassāvī; natthi samavisamaṃ, natthi samavisamassa [T 2.0657] dassāvī; natthi tārakarūpāni, natthi tārakarūpānaṃ dassāvī; natthi candimasūriyā, natthi candimasūriyānaṃ dassāvī. Ahametaṃ na jānāmi, ahametaṃ na passāmi; tasmā taṃ natthī’ti. Sammā nu kho so, māṇava, vadamāno vadeyyā”ti?

“Suppose, young man, a man blind from birth would not see black and white forms, would not see blue forms, would not see yellow forms, would not see red forms, would not see crimson forms, would not see the even and the uneven, would not see the forms of the stars, and would not see the moon and sun. He might say: ‘There are no black and white forms, and no one who sees black and white forms; there are no blue forms, and no one who sees blue forms; there are no yellow forms, and no one who sees yellow forms; there are no red forms, and no one who sees red forms; there are no crimson forms, and no one who sees crimson forms; there is no even and uneven, and no one who sees the even and uneven; there are no forms of the stars, and no one who sees the forms of the stars; there are no moon and sun, and no one who sees the moon and sun. I do not know this, I do not see this; therefore, it does not exist.’ Speaking thus, young man, would he be speaking rightly?”

“No hidaṃ, bho gotama. Atthi kaṇhasukkāni rūpāni, atthi kaṇhasukkānaṃ rūpānaṃ dassāvī; atthi nīlakāni rūpāni, atthi nīlakānaṃ rūpānaṃ dassāvī; atthi pītakāni rūpāni, atthi pītakānaṃ rūpānaṃ dassāvī; atthi lohitakāni rūpāni, atthi lohitakānaṃ rūpānaṃ dassāvī; atthi mañjiṭṭhakāni rūpāni, atthi mañjiṭṭhakānaṃ rūpānaṃ dassāvī; atthi samavisamaṃ, atthi samavisamassa dassāvī; atthi tārakarūpāni, atthi tārakarūpānaṃ dassāvī[M 2.0418]; atthi candimasūriyā, atthi candimasūriyānaṃ dassāvī. ‘Ahametaṃ na [P 2.0202] jānāmi, ahametaṃ na passāmi; tasmā taṃ natthī’ti; na hi so, bho gotama, sammā vadamāno vadeyyā”ti.

“Certainly not, Venerable Gotama. There are black and white forms, and there is one who sees black and white forms; there are blue forms, and there is one who sees blue forms; there are yellow forms, and there is one who sees yellow forms; there are red forms, and there is one who sees red forms; there are crimson forms, and there is one who sees crimson forms; there is the even and the uneven, and there is one who sees the even and the uneven; there are the forms of the stars, and there is one who sees the forms of the stars; there are the moon and sun, and there is one who sees the moon and sun. For him to say, ‘I do not know this, I do not see this; therefore, it does not exist’—speaking thus, Venerable Gotama, he would not be speaking rightly.”

“Evameva kho, māṇava, brāhmaṇo pokkharasāti opamañño subhagavaniko andho acakkhuko. So vata uttarimanussadhammā alamariyañāṇadassanavisesaṃ ñassati vā dakkhati vā sacchi vā karissatīti – netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati”.

“In this very way, young man, the brahmin Pokkharasāti of the Opamañña clan, lord of Subhagavana, is blind and without eyes. That he should know or see or realize a state superior to the human state, a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones—this is not possible.”

467. “Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, māṇava, ye te kosalakā brāhmaṇamahāsālā, seyyathidaṃ – caṅkī brāhmaṇo tārukkho brāhmaṇo pokkharasāti brāhmaṇo jāṇussoṇi brāhmaṇo pitā ca vā (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) te todeyyo, katamā nesaṃ seyyo seyyā (syā. kaṃ.), yaṃ vā te sammuccā [T 2.0658] sammusā (sī. pī.) vācaṃ bhāseyyuṃ yaṃ vā asammuccā”ti? “Sammuccā, bho gotama”.

467. “What do you think, young man? Regarding those Kosalan brahmins of great wealth—such as the brahmin Caṅkī, the brahmin Tārukkha, the brahmin Pokkharasāti, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi, and your father Todeyya—which of these is better: that they speak words that are conventional, or words that are unconventional?” “Conventional words, Venerable Gotama.”

“Katamā [V 2.0426] nesaṃ seyyo, yaṃ vā te mantā vācaṃ bhāseyyuṃ yaṃ vā amantā”ti? “Mantā, bho gotama”.

“Which of these is better: that they speak words with understanding, or words without understanding?” “With understanding, Venerable Gotama.”

“Katamā nesaṃ seyyo, yaṃ vā te paṭisaṅkhāya vācaṃ bhāseyyuṃ yaṃ vā appaṭisaṅkhāyā”ti? “Paṭisaṅkhāya, bho gotama”.

“Which of these is better: that they speak words after consideration, or words without consideration?” “After consideration, Venerable Gotama.”

“Katamā nesaṃ seyyo, yaṃ vā te atthasaṃhitaṃ vācaṃ bhāseyyuṃ yaṃ vā anatthasaṃhita”nti? “Atthasaṃhitaṃ, bho gotama”.

“Which of these is better: that they speak words connected with benefit, or words not connected with benefit?” “Words connected with benefit, Venerable Gotama.”

“Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, māṇava, yadi evaṃ sante, brāhmaṇena pokkharasātinā opamaññena subhagavanikena sammuccā vācā bhāsitā asammuccā”ti asammusā vāti (pī.) evamitarapañhattayepi vāsaddena saha dissati? “Asammuccā, bho gotama”.

“What do you think, young man? This being the case, was the speech spoken by the brahmin Pokkharasāti of the Opamañña clan, lord of Subhagavana, conventional or unconventional?” “Unconventional, Venerable Gotama.”

“Mantā vācā bhāsitā amantā vā”ti? “Amantā, bho gotama”.

“Was the speech spoken with understanding or without understanding?” “Without understanding, Venerable Gotama.”

“Paṭisaṅkhāya vācā bhāsitā appaṭisaṅkhāyā”ti? “Appaṭisaṅkhāya, bho gotama”.

“Was the speech spoken after consideration or without consideration?” “Without consideration, Venerable Gotama.”

“Atthasaṃhitā vācā bhāsitā anatthasaṃhitā”ti? “Anatthasaṃhitā, bho gotama”.

“Was the speech spoken connected with benefit or not connected with benefit?” “Not connected with benefit, Venerable Gotama.”

“Pañca [M 2.0419][P 2.0203] kho ime, māṇava, nīvaraṇā. Katame pañca? Kāmacchandanīvaraṇaṃ, byāpādanīvaraṇaṃ, thīnamiddhanīvaraṇaṃ uddhaccakukkuccanīvaraṇaṃ, vicikicchānīvaraṇaṃ – ime kho, māṇava, pañca nīvaraṇā. Imehi kho māṇava, pañcahi nīvaraṇehi brāhmaṇo pokkharasāti opamañño subhagavaniko āvuto nivuto ophuṭo ovuto (sī.), ophuto (syā. kaṃ. pī.) pariyonaddho. So vata uttarimanussadhammā alamariyañāṇadassanavisesaṃ ñassati vā dakkhati vā sacchi vā karissatīti – netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati.

“There are these five hindrances, young man. Which five? The hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill will, the hindrance of sloth and drowsiness, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, and the hindrance of doubt. These, young man, are the five hindrances. The brahmin Pokkharasāti of the Upamañña clan, from Subhagavana, is shrouded, obstructed, covered, and enveloped by these five hindrances. That he should know or see or realize a superior human state, a distinction of noble knowledge and vision—this is impossible.”

468. “Pañca [T 2.0659] kho ime, māṇava, kāmaguṇā. Katame pañca? Cakkhuviññeyyā rūpā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā rajanīyā, sotaviññeyyā saddā…pe… ghānaviññeyyā [V 2.0427] gandhā… jivhā viññeyyā rasā… kāyaviññeyyā phoṭṭhabbā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā rajanīyā – ime kho, māṇava, pañca kāmaguṇā. Imehi kho, māṇava, pañcahi kāmaguṇehi brāhmaṇo pokkharasāti opamañño subhagavaniko gathito mucchito ajjhopanno anādīnavadassāvī anissaraṇapañño paribhuñjati. So vata uttarimanussadhammā alamariyañāṇadassanavisesaṃ ñassati vā dakkhati vā sacchi vā karissatīti – netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati.

468. “There are these five strands of sensual pleasure, young man. Which five? Forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, pleasing, of a nature to be cherished, connected with sensual pleasure, and alluring; sounds cognizable by the ear… smells cognizable by the nose… tastes cognizable by the tongue… tangibles cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, pleasing, of a nature to be cherished, connected with sensual pleasure, and alluring. These, young man, are the five strands of sensual pleasure. The brahmin Pokkharasāti of the Upamañña clan, from Subhagavana, enjoys these five strands of sensual pleasure, being greedy, infatuated, and immersed in them, not seeing their danger and lacking the wisdom for escape. That he should know or see or realize a superior human state, a distinction of noble knowledge and vision—this is impossible.”

“Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, māṇava, yaṃ vā tiṇakaṭṭhupādānaṃ paṭicca aggiṃ jāleyya yaṃ vā nissaṭṭhatiṇakaṭṭhupādānaṃ aggiṃ jāleyya, katamo nu khvāssa aggi accimā ceva vaṇṇavā ca pabhassaro cā”ti? “Sace taṃ, bho gotama, ṭhānaṃ nissaṭṭhatiṇakaṭṭhupādānaṃ aggiṃ jāletuṃ, svāssa aggi accimā ceva vaṇṇavā ca pabhassaro cā”ti. “Aṭṭhānaṃ kho etaṃ, māṇava, anavakāso yaṃ nissaṭṭhatiṇakaṭṭhupādānaṃ aggiṃ jāleyya aññatra iddhimatā. Seyyathāpi, māṇava, tiṇakaṭṭhupādānaṃ paṭicca aggi jalati tathūpamāhaṃ, māṇava, imaṃ pītiṃ vadāmi yāyaṃ pīti pañca [P 2.0204] kāmaguṇe paṭicca. Seyyathāpi, māṇava, nissaṭṭhatiṇakaṭṭhupādāno nissaṭṭhatiṇakaṭṭhupādānaṃ paṭicca (sī. pī. ka.) aggi jalati tathūpamāhaṃ, māṇava[T 2.0660], imaṃ pītiṃ vadāmi yāyaṃ pīti aññatreva kāmehi aññatra akusalehi dhammehi.

“What do you think, young man? If one were to light a fire in dependence on fuel of grass and wood, and another were to light a fire without fuel of grass and wood, which of those fires would have a greater flame, be more splendid, and be more luminous?” “If it were possible, Master Gotama, to light a fire without fuel of grass and wood, that fire would have a greater flame, be more splendid, and be more luminous.” “It is impossible, young man, it is not feasible to light a fire without fuel of grass and wood, except for one with psychic power. Just as, young man, a fire burns in dependence on fuel of grass and wood, so too, I say, is the rapture that arises in dependence on the five strands of sensual pleasure. Just as, young man, a fire burns without fuel of grass and wood, so too, I say, is the rapture that is apart from sensual pleasures and apart from unwholesome states.”

“Katamā ca, māṇava, pīti aññatreva kāmehi aññatra akusalehi dhammehi? Idha, māṇava, bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehi…pe… paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Ayampi kho, māṇava, pīti aññatreva kāmehi aññatra akusalehi [M 2.0420] dhammehi. Puna caparaṃ, māṇava, bhikkhu vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā…pe… dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Ayampi kho, māṇava, pīti aññatreva kāmehi aññatra akusalehi dhammehi.

“And what, young man, is the rapture that is apart from sensual pleasures and apart from unwholesome states? Here, young man, a monk, quite secluded from sensual pleasures… enters and abides in the first jhāna. This, young man, is a rapture that is apart from sensual pleasures and apart from unwholesome states. Furthermore, young man, a monk, with the stilling of applied and sustained thought… enters and abides in the second jhāna. This too, young man, is a rapture that is apart from sensual pleasures and apart from unwholesome states.”

469. “Ye te, māṇava, brāhmaṇā pañca dhamme paññapenti puññassa kiriyāya kusalassa ārādhanāya, katamettha kamettha (ka. sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) brāhmaṇā dhammaṃ mahapphalataraṃ paññapenti puññassa kiriyāya kusalassa ārādhanāyā”ti? “Yeme, bho gotama, brāhmaṇā pañca dhamme paññapenti puññassa kiriyāya [V 2.0428] kusalassa ārādhanāya, cāgamettha brāhmaṇā dhammaṃ mahapphalataraṃ paññapenti puññassa kiriyāya kusalassa ārādhanāyā”ti.

469. “Young man, of those five principles that the brahmins declare for the performance of merit and for the accomplishment of the wholesome, which principle do the brahmins declare to be more fruitful for the performance of merit and for the accomplishment of the wholesome?” “Master Gotama, of those five principles that the brahmins declare for the performance of merit and for the accomplishment of the wholesome, they declare generosity to be the principle that is more fruitful for the performance of merit and for the accomplishment of the wholesome.”

“Taṃ ki maññasi, māṇava, idha aññatarassa brāhmaṇassa mahāyañño paccupaṭṭhito assa. Atha dve brāhmaṇā āgaccheyyuṃ – ‘itthannāmassa brāhmaṇassa mahāyaññaṃ anubhavissāmā’ti. Tatrekassa tatthekassa (pī.) brāhmaṇassa evamassa – ‘aho vata! Ahameva labheyyaṃ bhattagge aggāsanaṃ aggodakaṃ aggapiṇḍaṃ, na añño brāhmaṇo labheyya bhattagge aggāsanaṃ aggodakaṃ aggapiṇḍa’nti. Ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ, māṇava[T 2.0661], vijjati yaṃ añño brāhmaṇo labheyya bhattagge aggāsanaṃ aggodakaṃ aggapiṇḍaṃ, na so brāhmaṇo labheyya bhattagge aggāsanaṃ aggodakaṃ aggapiṇḍaṃ. ‘Añño brāhmaṇo labhati bhattagge aggāsanaṃ aggodakaṃ aggapiṇḍaṃ, nāhaṃ labhāmi bhattagge aggāsanaṃ aggodakaṃ aggapiṇḍa’nti – iti so [P 2.0205] kupito hoti anattamano. Imassa pana, māṇava, brāhmaṇā kiṃ vipākaṃ paññapentī”ti? “Na khvettha, bho gotama, brāhmaṇā evaṃ dānaṃ denti – ‘iminā paro kupito hotu anattamano’ti. Atha khvettha brāhmaṇā anukampājātikaṃyeva anukampajātikaṃyeva (syā. kaṃ. ka.) dānaṃ dentī”ti. “Evaṃ sante, kho, māṇava, brāhmaṇānaṃ idaṃ chaṭṭhaṃ puññakiriyavatthu hoti – yadidaṃ anukampājātika”nti. “Evaṃ sante, bho gotama, brāhmaṇānaṃ idaṃ chaṭṭhaṃ puññakiriyavatthu hoti – yadidaṃ anukampājātika”nti.

“What do you think, young man? Suppose a great sacrifice has been prepared for a certain brahmin. Then two brahmins might arrive, thinking, ‘We shall partake of the great sacrifice of the brahmin so-and-so.’ It might occur to one of those brahmins: ‘Oh, may I alone receive the best seat, the best water, and the best portion of food in the dining hall! May no other brahmin receive the best seat, the best water, and the best portion of food!’ Now, it is possible, young man, that another brahmin might receive the best seat, the best water, and the best portion of food in the dining hall, and that first brahmin might not. Thinking, ‘Another brahmin receives the best seat, the best water, and the best portion of food in the dining hall, but I do not!’ he becomes angry and displeased. Now, young man, what result do the brahmins declare for this?” “Indeed, Master Gotama, brahmins do not give gifts in such a way, thinking, ‘By this, may another become angry and displeased!’ Rather, brahmins give gifts that are solely of a compassionate nature.” “In that case, young man, this becomes a sixth basis for meritorious action for the brahmins, that is, the compassionate nature of the act.” “In that case, Master Gotama, this becomes a sixth basis for meritorious action for the brahmins, that is, the compassionate nature of the act.”

“Ye te, māṇava, brāhmaṇā pañca dhamme paññapenti puññassa kiriyāya kusalassa ārādhanāya, ime tvaṃ pañca dhamme kattha bahulaṃ samanupassasi – gahaṭṭhesu vā pabbajitesu vā”ti? “Yeme, bho gotama, brāhmaṇā pañca dhamme paññapenti puññassa kiriyāya kusalassa ārādhanāya, imāhaṃ pañca dhamme pabbajitesu [M 2.0421] bahulaṃ samanupassāmi appaṃ gahaṭṭhesu. Gahaṭṭho hi, bho gotama, mahaṭṭho mahākicco mahādhikaraṇo mahāsamārambho, na satataṃ samitaṃ saccavādī [T 2.0662] hoti; pabbajito kho pana, bho gotama, appaṭṭho appakicco appādhikaraṇo appasamārambho, satataṃ samitaṃ saccavādī hoti. Gahaṭṭho hi, bho gotama, mahaṭṭho mahākicco mahādhikaraṇo mahāsamārambho na satataṃ samitaṃ tapassī hoti… brahmacārī hoti… sajjhāyabahulo hoti… cāgabahulo hoti; pabbajito kho pana, bho gotama, appaṭṭho appakicco appādhikaraṇo appasamārambho satataṃ samitaṃ tapassī hoti… brahmacārī hoti… sajjhāyabahulo hoti… cāgabahulo [V 2.0429] hoti. Yeme, bho gotama, brāhmaṇā pañca dhamme paññapenti puññassa kiriyāya kusalassa ārādhanāya, imāhaṃ pañca dhamme pabbajitesu bahulaṃ samanupassāmi appaṃ gahaṭṭhesū”ti.

“Young man, those five things that the brahmins prescribe for the doing of merit and the accomplishment of the wholesome—where do you mostly see these five things: among householders or among renunciants?” “Master Gotama, those five things that the brahmins prescribe for the doing of merit and the accomplishment of the wholesome—I mostly see these five things among renunciants, and seldom among householders. For a householder, Master Gotama, has much business, many duties, many responsibilities, and much involvement; he is not one who constantly and continually speaks the truth. But a renunciant, Master Gotama, has little business, few duties, few responsibilities, and little involvement; he is one who constantly and continually speaks the truth. A householder, Master Gotama, has much business, many duties, many responsibilities, and much involvement; he is not one who constantly and continually practices austerity… observes celibacy… engages much in recitation… engages much in generosity. But a renunciant, Master Gotama, has little business, few duties, few responsibilities, and little involvement; he is one who constantly and continually practices austerity… observes celibacy… engages much in recitation… engages much in generosity. Master Gotama, those five things that the brahmins prescribe for the doing of merit and the accomplishment of the wholesome—I mostly see these five things among renunciants, and seldom among householders.”

“Ye te, māṇava, brāhmaṇā pañca dhamme paññapenti puññassa kiriyāya kusalassa ārādhanāya cittassāhaṃ ete parikkhāre [P 2.0206] vadāmi – yadidaṃ cittaṃ averaṃ abyābajjhaṃ tassa bhāvanāya. Idha, māṇava, bhikkhu saccavādī hoti. So ‘saccavādīmhī’ti labhati atthavedaṃ, labhati dhammavedaṃ, labhati dhammūpasaṃhitaṃ pāmojjaṃ. Yaṃ taṃ kusalūpasaṃhitaṃ pāmojjaṃ, cittassāhaṃ etaṃ parikkhāraṃ vadāmi – yadidaṃ cittaṃ averaṃ abyābajjhaṃ tassa bhāvanāya. Idha, māṇava, bhikkhu tapassī hoti…pe… brahmacārī hoti…pe… sajjhāyabahulo hoti…pe… cāgabahulo hoti. So ‘cāgabahulomhī’ti labhati atthavedaṃ, labhati dhammavedaṃ, labhati dhammūpasaṃhitaṃ pāmojjaṃ. Yaṃ taṃ kusalūpasaṃhitaṃ pāmojjaṃ, cittassāhaṃ etaṃ parikkhāraṃ vadāmi – yadidaṃ cittaṃ averaṃ abyābajjhaṃ tassa bhāvanāya. Ye [T 2.0663] te māṇava, brāhmaṇā, pañca dhamme paññapenti puññassa kiriyāya kusalassa ārādhanāya, cittassāhaṃ ete parikkhāre vadāmi – yadidaṃ cittaṃ averaṃ abyābajjhaṃ tassa bhāvanāyā”ti.

“Young man, those five things that the brahmins prescribe for the doing of merit and the accomplishment of the wholesome, I declare these to be requisites of the mind—that is, for the development of a mind that is without enmity and without affliction. Here, young man, a bhikkhu is a speaker of truth. Thinking, ‘I am a speaker of truth,’ he obtains the experience of the goal, he obtains the experience of the Dhamma, and he obtains joy connected with the Dhamma. Whatever joy is connected with the wholesome, I declare this to be a requisite of the mind—that is, for the development of a mind that is without enmity and without affliction. Here, young man, a bhikkhu is one who practices austerity… is one who observes celibacy… is one who engages much in recitation… is one who engages much in generosity. Thinking, ‘I am one who engages much in generosity,’ he obtains the experience of the goal, he obtains the experience of the Dhamma, and he obtains joy connected with the Dhamma. Whatever joy is connected with the wholesome, I declare this to be a requisite of the mind—that is, for the development of a mind that is without enmity and without affliction. Young man, those five things that the brahmins prescribe for the doing of merit and the accomplishment of the wholesome, I declare these to be requisites of the mind—that is, for the development of a mind that is without enmity and without affliction.”

470. Evaṃ vutte, subho māṇavo todeyyaputto bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “sutaṃ metaṃ, bho gotama – ‘samaṇo gotamo brahmānaṃ sahabyatāya maggaṃ jānātī’”ti.

470. When this was said, the young man Subha, son of Todeyya, said this to the Blessed One: “I have heard this, Master Gotama: ‘The ascetic Gotama knows the path to companionship with Brahmā.’”

“Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, māṇava, āsanne ito naḷakāragāmo, na yito dūre naḷakāragāmo”ti?

“What do you think, young man? Is the reed-workers’ village near here? Is the reed-workers’ village not far from here?”

“Evaṃ, bho, āsanne ito naḷakāragāmo[M 2.0422], na yito dūre naḷakāragāmo”ti.

“So it is, Master. The reed-workers’ village is near here; it is not far from here.”

“Taṃ, kiṃ maññasi māṇava, idhassa puriso naḷakāragāme jātavaddho jātavaḍḍho (syā. kaṃ. ka.); tamenaṃ naḷakāragāmato tāvadeva avasaṭaṃ apasakkaṃ (syā. kaṃ. ka.) naḷakāragāmassa maggaṃ puccheyyuṃ; siyā nu kho, māṇava, tassa [V 2.0430] purisassa naḷakāragāme jātavaddhassa naḷakāragāmassa maggaṃ puṭṭhassa dandhāyitattaṃ vā vitthāyitattaṃ vā”ti?

“What do you think, young man? Suppose there were a man born and raised in the reed-workers’ village. And suppose someone were to ask him, just as he had left the village, for the path to the reed-workers’ village. Would there be, young man, any slowness or hesitation on the part of that man, born and raised in the reed-workers’ village, when asked for the path to the reed-workers’ village?”

“No hidaṃ, bho gotama”.

“Certainly not, Master Gotama.”

“Taṃ kissa hetu”?

“For what reason?”

“Amu hi, bho gotama, puriso naḷakāragāme jātavaddho. Tassa sabbāneva naḷakāragāmassa maggāni suviditānī”ti. “Siyā nu kho, māṇava, tassa purisassa naḷakāragāme jātavaddhassa naḷakāragāmassa maggaṃ puṭṭhassa dandhāyitattaṃ [P 2.0207] vā vitthāyitattaṃ vāti, na tveva tathāgatassa brahmalokaṃ vā brahmalokagāminiṃ vā paṭipadaṃ puṭṭhassa dandhāyitattaṃ vā vitthāyitattaṃ vā. Brahmānañcāhaṃ, māṇava, pajānāmi brahmalokañca brahmalokagāminiñca paṭipadaṃ; yathāpaṭipanno ca brahmalokaṃ upapanno tañca pajānāmī”ti[T 2.0664].

“Because, Master Gotama, that man was born and raised in the reed-workers’ village. All the paths to the reed-workers’ village are well-known to him.” “Young man, there might be some slowness or hesitation for that man born and raised in the reed-workers’ village when asked for the path to the reed-workers’ village. But for the Tathāgata, when asked about the Brahmā world or the practice leading to the Brahmā world, there would certainly be no slowness or hesitation. For I, young man, directly know Brahmā, and the Brahmā world, and the practice leading to the Brahmā world. And I directly know how one who has practiced accordingly is reborn in the Brahmā world.”

“Sutaṃ metaṃ, bho gotama – ‘samaṇo gotamo brahmānaṃ sahabyatāya maggaṃ desetī’ti. Sādhu me bhavaṃ gotamo brahmānaṃ sahabyatāya maggaṃ desetū”ti.

“I have heard this, Master Gotama: ‘The ascetic Gotama teaches the path to companionship with Brahmā.’ It would be good if Master Gotama would teach me the path to companionship with Brahmā.”

“Tena hi, māṇava, suṇāhi, sādhukaṃ manasi karohi, bhāsissāmī”ti. “Evaṃ bho”ti kho subho māṇavo todeyyaputto bhagavato paccassosi. Bhagavā etadavoca –

“Well then, young man, listen and apply your mind well. I will speak.” “Yes, Master,” the young man Subha, son of Todeyya, replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:

471. “Katamo ca, māṇava, brahmānaṃ sahabyatāya maggo? Idha, māṇava, bhikkhu mettāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharati, tathā dutiyaṃ, tathā tatiyaṃ, tathā catutthaṃ; iti uddhamadho tiriyaṃ sabbadhi sabbattatāya sabbāvantaṃ lokaṃ mettāsahagatena cetasā vipulena mahaggatena appamāṇena averena abyābajjhena pharitvā viharati. Evaṃ bhāvitāya kho, māṇava, mettāya cetovimuttiyā yaṃ pamāṇakataṃ kammaṃ na taṃ tatrāvasissati, na taṃ tatrāvatiṭṭhati. Seyyathāpi, māṇava, balavā saṅkhadhamo appakasireneva cātuddisā viññāpeyya evameva kho māṇava evaṃ bhāvitāya mettāya (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī. dī. ni. 1.556) tathāpi idha pāṭhoyeva upamāya saṃsandiyamāno paripuṇṇo viya dissati; evameva kho, māṇava…pe… evaṃ bhāvitāya kho, māṇava, mettāya evameva kho māṇava evaṃ bhāvitāya mettāya (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī. dī. ni. 1.556) tathāpi idha pāṭhoyeva upamāya saṃsandiyamāno paripuṇṇo viya dissati cetovimuttiyā yaṃ pamāṇakataṃ [V 2.0431] kammaṃ na taṃ tatrāvasissati, na taṃ tatrāvatiṭṭhati. Ayampi kho, māṇava, brahmānaṃ sahabyatāya maggo. “Puna [M 2.0423] caparaṃ, māṇava, bhikkhu karuṇāsahagatena cetasā…pe… muditāsahagatena cetasā…pe… upekkhāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharati, tathā dutiyaṃ, tathā tatiyaṃ, tathā catutthaṃ; iti uddhamadho tiriyaṃ sabbadhi sabbattatāya sabbāvantaṃ lokaṃ upekkhāsahagatena cetasā vipulena [T 2.0665] mahaggatena appamāṇena [P 2.0208] averena abyābajjhena pharitvā viharati. Evaṃ bhāvitāya kho, māṇava, upekkhāya cetovimuttiyā yaṃ pamāṇakataṃ kammaṃ na taṃ tatrāvasissati, na taṃ tatrāvatiṭṭhati. Seyyathāpi, māṇava, balavā saṅkhadhamo appakasireneva cātuddisā viññāpeyya; evameva kho, māṇava…pe… evaṃ bhāvitāya kho, māṇava, upekkhāya cetovimuttiyā yaṃ pamāṇakataṃ kammaṃ na taṃ tatrāvasissati, na taṃ tatrāvatiṭṭhati. Ayampi kho, māṇava, brahmānaṃ sahabyatāya maggo”ti.

471. “And what, young man, is the path to companionship with Brahmā? Here, young man, a bhikkhu dwells pervading one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth; so above, below, around, everywhere, and in all circumstances, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness—vast, exalted, immeasurable, without hostility, without ill will. When, young man, the liberation of mind by loving-kindness is thus developed, any limited sense-sphere action does not remain there, does not persist there. Just as, young man, a strong conch-blower can easily make himself heard in the four directions; so too, young man… when the liberation of mind by loving-kindness is thus developed, any limited sense-sphere action does not remain there, does not persist there. This too, young man, is the path to companionship with Brahmā. Furthermore, young man, a bhikkhu dwells pervading one direction with a mind imbued with compassion… with a mind imbued with appreciative joy… with a mind imbued with equanimity, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth; so above, below, around, everywhere, and in all circumstances, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with equanimity—vast, exalted, immeasurable, without hostility, without ill will. When, young man, the liberation of mind by equanimity is thus developed, any limited sense-sphere action does not remain there, does not persist there. Just as, young man, a strong conch-blower can easily make himself heard in the four directions; so too, young man… when the liberation of mind by equanimity is thus developed, any limited sense-sphere action does not remain there, does not persist there. This too, young man, is the path to companionship with Brahmā.”

472. Evaṃ vutte, subho māṇavo todeyyaputto bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “abhikkantaṃ, bho gotama, abhikkantaṃ, bho gotama! Seyyathāpi, bho gotama, nikkujjitaṃ vā ukkujjeyya, paṭicchannaṃ vā vivareyya, mūḷhassa vā maggaṃ ācikkheyya, andhakāre vā telapajjotaṃ dhāreyya – cakkhumanto rūpāni dakkhantīti – evamevaṃ bhotā gotamena anekapariyāyena dhammo pakāsito. Esāhaṃ bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi dhammañca bhikkhusaṅghañca. Upāsakaṃ maṃ bhavaṃ gotamo dhāretu ajjatagge pāṇupetaṃ saraṇaṃ gataṃ. Handa, ca dāni mayaṃ, bho gotama, gacchāma; bahukiccā mayaṃ bahukaraṇīyā”ti. “Yassadāni tvaṃ, māṇava, kālaṃ maññasī”ti. Atha kho subho māṇavo todeyyaputto bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinanditvā anumoditvā uṭṭhāyāsanā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā pakkāmi.

472. When this was said, the young man Subha, Todeyya’s son, said to the Blessed One: “Excellent, Master Gotama! Excellent, Master Gotama! Just as one might set upright what was overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or hold up an oil lamp in the dark so that those with eyes could see forms—in the same way the Dhamma has been made clear in many ways by Master Gotama. I go to Master Gotama for refuge, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May Master Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forward, for as long as life lasts. And now, Master Gotama, we must go. We have much to do, many duties to attend to.” “You may go, young man, when you think it is time.” Then the young man Subha, Todeyya’s son, having delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping his right side toward him, and departed.

Tena kho pana samayena jāṇussoṇi brāhmaṇo sabbasetena vaḷavābhirathena vaḷabhīrathena (sī.) sāvatthiyā niyyāti divā divassa. Addasā kho jāṇussoṇi [T 2.0666] brāhmaṇo subhaṃ māṇavaṃ todeyyaputtaṃ dūratova āgacchantaṃ. Disvāna subhaṃ māṇavaṃ todeyyaputtaṃ etadavoca – “handa, kuto nu bhavaṃ bhāradvājo āgacchati divā divassā”ti? “Ito hi kho ahaṃ, bho[M 2.0424], āgacchāmi samaṇassa gotamassa santikā”ti. “Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, bhavaṃ bhāradvājo, samaṇassa gotamassa paññāveyyattiyaṃ paṇḍito maññeti”? “Ko [P 2.0209] cāhaṃ, bho, ko ca samaṇassa gotamassa paññāveyyattiyaṃ [V 2.0432] jānissāmi? Sopi nūnassa tādisova yo samaṇassa gotamassa paññāveyyattiyaṃ jāneyyā”ti. “Uḷārāya khalu, bhavaṃ bhāradvājo, samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ pasaṃsāya pasaṃsatī”ti. “Ko cāhaṃ, bho, ko ca samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ pasaṃsissāmi? Pasatthapasatthova so bhavaṃ gotamo seṭṭho devamanussānaṃ. Ye cime, bho, brāhmaṇā pañca dhamme paññapenti puññassa kiriyāya kusalassa ārādhanāya; cittassete samaṇo gotamo parikkhāre vadeti – yadidaṃ cittaṃ averaṃ abyābajjhaṃ tassa bhāvanāyā”ti.

At that time, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi was leaving Sāvatthī in the middle of the day in an all-white chariot drawn by mares. The brahmin Jāṇussoṇi saw the young man Subha, son of Todeyya, coming from a distance. Having seen him, he said to the young man Subha, son of Todeyya: “Well now, where is Master Bhāradvāja coming from in the middle of the day?” “Sir, I am coming from the presence of the ascetic Gotama.” “What do you think of this, Master Bhāradvāja? Do you consider the ascetic Gotama a wise man, on account of his penetrating wisdom?” “Who am I, sir, to know the penetrating wisdom of the ascetic Gotama? Surely, only one like him could know the penetrating wisdom of the ascetic Gotama.” “Indeed, Master Bhāradvāja, you praise the ascetic Gotama with exceedingly high praise.” “Who am I, sir, to praise the ascetic Gotama? That Master Gotama is praised by the praiseworthy, the best of gods and humans. Sir, those brahmins who prescribe five things for the performance of merit and the attainment of the wholesome—the ascetic Gotama declares these to be the equipment of the mind, that is, for the development of a mind free from enmity and ill will.”

Evaṃ vutte, jāṇussoṇi brāhmaṇo sabbasetā vaḷavābhirathā orohitvā ekaṃsaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ karitvā yena bhagavā tenañjaliṃ paṇāmetvā udānaṃ udānesi – “lābhā rañño pasenadissa kosalassa, suladdhalābhā rañño pasenadissa kosalassa yassa vijite tathāgato viharati arahaṃ sammāsambuddho”ti.

When this was said, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi descended from his all-white chariot drawn by mares, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, raised his joined palms towards the Blessed One, and uttered this inspired utterance: “It is a gain for King Pasenadi of Kosala, a great gain for King Pasenadi of Kosala, that in his realm the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, dwells.”

Subhasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ navamaṃ.

The Subha Sutta, the ninth, is concluded.

10. Saṅgāravasuttaṃ

10. The Saṅgārava Sutta

473. Evaṃ [T 2.0667][V 2.0433] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā kosalesu cārikaṃ carati mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ. Tena kho pana samayena dhanañjānī dhānañjānī (sī. pī.) nāma brāhmaṇī cañcalikappe maṇḍalakappe (sī.), paccalakappe (syā. kaṃ.), caṇḍalakappe (pī.) paṭivasati abhippasannā buddhe ca dhamme ca saṅghe ca. Atha kho dhanañjānī brāhmaṇī upakkhalitvā tikkhattuṃ udānaṃ udānesi – “namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa. Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa. Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassā”ti[P 2.0210].

473. Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was wandering in the Kosala country with a large Saṅgha of bhikkhus. At that time, a brahmin woman named Dhanañjānī was living in Cañcalikappa, deeply devoted to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha. Then, having stumbled, the brahmin woman Dhanañjānī uttered this inspired utterance three times: “Homage to that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One! Homage to that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One! Homage to that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One!”

Tena kho pana samayena saṅgāravo nāma māṇavo cañcalikappe paṭivasati tiṇṇaṃ vedānaṃ pāragū sanighaṇḍukeṭubhānaṃ sākkharappabhedānaṃ itihāsapañcamānaṃ[M 2.0425], padako, veyyākaraṇo, lokāyatamahāpurisalakkhaṇesu anavayo. Assosi kho saṅgāravo māṇavo dhanañjāniyā brāhmaṇiyā evaṃ vācaṃ bhāsamānāya. Sutvā dhanañjāniṃ brāhmaṇiṃ etadavoca – “avabhūtāva ayaṃ avabhūtā cayaṃ (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) dhanañjānī brāhmaṇī, parabhūtāva ayaṃ parābhūtā cayaṃ (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) dhanañjānī brāhmaṇī, vijjamānānaṃ (tevijjānaṃ) ( ) sī. syā. kaṃ. pī. potthakesu natthi brāhmaṇānaṃ, atha ca pana tassa muṇḍakassa samaṇakassa vaṇṇaṃ bhāsissatī”ti bhāsatīti (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī). “Na hi pana tvaṃ, tāta bhadramukha, tassa bhagavato sīlapaññāṇaṃ jānāsi. Sace tvaṃ, tāta bhadramukha, tassa bhagavato sīlapaññāṇaṃ jāneyyāsi, na tvaṃ, tāta bhadramukha, taṃ bhagavantaṃ akkositabbaṃ paribhāsitabbaṃ maññeyyāsī”ti. “Tena hi, bhoti, yadā samaṇo gotamo cañcalikappaṃ anuppatto hoti atha [T 2.0668] me āroceyyāsī”ti. “Evaṃ, bhadramukhā”ti kho dhanañjānī brāhmaṇī saṅgāravassa māṇavassa paccassosi.

At that time, a young brahmin named Saṅgārava was residing in Cañcalikappa. He was a master of the three Vedas, complete with the glossaries, poetics, and phonetics, with the legends as the fifth; he was a master of the verses, a grammarian, and he was fully skilled in worldly philosophy and the marks of a great man. The young brahmin Saṅgārava heard the brahmin woman Dhanañjānī speaking these words. Having heard her, he said this to the brahmin woman Dhanañjānī: “This Dhanañjānī is indeed inauspicious, this Dhanañjānī is indeed ruined! While there are brahmins who possess the threefold knowledge, yet she praises that shaven-headed, contemptible ascetic!” “But, dear one of pleasant face, you do not know the virtue and wisdom of the Blessed One. If you, dear one of pleasant face, knew the virtue and wisdom of the Blessed One, you would not think that Blessed One should be reviled or disparaged.” “Then, madam, when the ascetic Gotama comes to Cañcalikappa, you must inform me.” “Yes, pleasant-faced one,” the brahmin woman Dhanañjānī replied to the young brahmin Saṅgārava.

Atha kho bhagavā kosalesu anupubbena cārikaṃ caramāno yena cañcalikappaṃ tadavasari. Tatra sudaṃ bhagavā cañcalikappe viharati todeyyānaṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ ambavane. Assosi kho dhanañjānī brāhmaṇī – “bhagavā kira cañcalikappaṃ anuppatto, cañcalikappe viharati todeyyānaṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ ambavane”ti. Atha kho dhanañjānī brāhmaṇī yena saṅgāravo māṇavo tenupasaṅkami[V 2.0434]; upasaṅkamitvā saṅgāravaṃ māṇavaṃ etadavoca – “ayaṃ, tāta bhadramukha, so bhagavā cañcalikappaṃ anuppatto, cañcalikappe viharati todeyyānaṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ ambavane. Yassadāni, tāta bhadramukha, kālaṃ maññasī”ti.

Then the Blessed One, while wandering by stages in the Kosala country, arrived at Cañcalikappa. There the Blessed One stayed in Cañcalikappa, in the mango grove of the Todeyya brahmins. Dhanañjānī the brahmin woman heard: “The Blessed One, it seems, has arrived at Cañcalikappa and is staying in the mango grove of the Todeyya brahmins.” Then Dhanañjānī the brahmin woman approached the young man Saṅgārava; having approached, she said this to the young man Saṅgārava: “This Blessed One, dear one of pleasant face, has arrived at Cañcalikappa and is staying in the mango grove of the Todeyya brahmins. Now, dear one of pleasant face, is the time for whatever you think fit.”

474. “Evaṃ, bho”ti kho saṅgāravo māṇavo dhanañjāniyā brāhmaṇiyā paṭissutvā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavatā saddhiṃ sammodi. Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ [P 2.0211] sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho saṅgāravo māṇavo bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “santi kho, bho gotama, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā diṭṭhadhammābhiññāvosānapāramippattā, ādibrahmacariyaṃ paṭijānanti. Tatra, bho gotama, ye [M 2.0426] te samaṇabrāhmaṇā diṭṭhadhammābhiññāvosānapāramippattā, ādibrahmacariyaṃ paṭijānanti, tesaṃ bhavaṃ gotamo katamo”ti? “Diṭṭhadhammābhiññāvosānapāramippattānaṃ, ādibrahmacariyaṃ paṭijānantānampi [T 2.0669] kho ahaṃ, bhāradvāja, vemattaṃ vadāmi. Santi, bhāradvāja, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā anussavikā. Te anussavena diṭṭhadhammābhiññāvosānapāramippattā, ādibrahmacariyaṃ paṭijānanti; seyyathāpi brāhmaṇā tevijjā. Santi pana, bhāradvāja, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā kevalaṃ saddhāmattakena diṭṭhadhammābhiññāvosānapāramippattā, ādibrahmacariyaṃ paṭijānanti; seyyathāpi takkī vīmaṃsī. Santi, bhāradvāja, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā pubbe ananussutesu dhammesu sāmaṃyeva dhammaṃ abhiññāya diṭṭhadhammābhiññāvosānapāramippattā, ādibrahmacariyaṃ paṭijānanti. Tatra, bhāradvāja, ye te samaṇabrāhmaṇā pubbe ananussutesu dhammesu sāmaṃyeva dhammaṃ abhiññāya diṭṭhadhammābhiññāvosānapāramippattā, ādibrahmacariyaṃ paṭijānanti, tesāhamasmi. Tadamināpetaṃ, bhāradvāja, pariyāyena veditabbaṃ, yathā ye te samaṇabrāhmaṇā pubbe ananussutesu dhammesu sāmaṃyeva dhammaṃ abhiññāya diṭṭhadhammābhiññāvosānapāramippattā, ādibrahmacariyaṃ paṭijānanti, tesāhamasmi.

474. “Yes, madam,” replied the young brahmin Saṅgārava to the brahmin woman Dhanañjānī, and then he approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. When the courteous and memorable conversation was concluded, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the young brahmin Saṅgārava said this to the Blessed One: “Master Gotama, there are some ascetics and brahmins who, having realized with higher knowledge in this very life, claim to have reached the final consummation and to profess the fundamental holy life. Among those ascetics and brahmins who, having realized with higher knowledge in this very life, claim to have reached the final consummation and to profess the fundamental holy life, of which kind are you, Master Gotama?” “Bhāradvāja, among those who, having realized with higher knowledge in this very life, claim to have reached the final consummation and to profess the fundamental holy life, I declare there is a difference. There are, Bhāradvāja, some ascetics and brahmins who are traditionalists. They claim to have reached the final consummation and to profess the fundamental holy life based on tradition—such as the brahmins versed in the three Vedas. Then there are, Bhāradvāja, some ascetics and brahmins who do so based on mere faith—such as the reasoners and investigators. And there are, Bhāradvāja, some ascetics and brahmins who, regarding teachings not heard before, have directly known the Dhamma by themselves and, having realized with higher knowledge in this very life, claim to have reached the final consummation and to profess the fundamental holy life. Among those ascetics and brahmins who, regarding teachings not heard before, have directly known the Dhamma by themselves and, having realized with higher knowledge in this very life, claim to have reached the final consummation and to profess the fundamental holy life, I am one. By this line of reasoning, Bhāradvāja, it should be understood how, among those ascetics and brahmins who, regarding teachings not heard before, have directly known the Dhamma by themselves and, having realized with higher knowledge in this very life, claim to have reached the final consummation and to profess the fundamental holy life, I am one.”

475. “Idha me, bhāradvāja, pubbeva sambodhā anabhisambuddhassa bodhisattasseva sato etadahosi – ‘sambādho gharāvāso rajāpatho, abbhokāso pabbajjā. Nayidaṃ sukaraṃ agāraṃ ajjhāvasatā ekantaparipuṇṇaṃ ekantaparisuddhaṃ saṅkhalikhitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ carituṃ. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ kesamassuṃ ohāretvā kāsāyāni vatthāni acchādetvā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ [T 2.0670] pabbajeyya’nti. So kho ahaṃ, bhāradvāja, aparena [P 2.0212] samayena daharova samāno susukāḷakeso bhadrena yobbanena samannāgato [V 2.0435] paṭhamena vayasā akāmakānaṃ mātāpitūnaṃ assumukhānaṃ rudantānaṃ kesamassuṃ ohāretvā kāsāyāni vatthāni acchādetvā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajiṃ. So evaṃ pabbajito samāno kiṃkusalagavesī anuttaraṃ santivarapadaṃ pariyesamāno yena āḷāro kālāmo tenupasaṅkamiṃ; upasaṅkamitvā āḷāraṃ kālāmaṃ etadavocaṃ – ‘icchāmahaṃ, āvuso kālāma, imasmiṃ dhammavinaye brahmacariyaṃ caritu’nti. Evaṃ vutte, bhāradvāja, āḷāro kālāmo maṃ etadavoca – ‘viharatāyasmā. Tādiso ayaṃ dhammo yattha viññū puriso nacirasseva sakaṃ ācariyakaṃ sayaṃ [M 2.0427] abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja vihareyyā’ti. So kho ahaṃ, bhāradvāja, nacirasseva khippameva taṃ dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇiṃ. So kho ahaṃ, bhāradvāja, tāvatakeneva oṭṭhapahatamattena lapitalāpanamattena ‘ñāṇavādañca vadāmi, theravādañca jānāmi, passāmī’ti ca paṭijānāmi, ahañceva aññe ca. Tassa mayhaṃ, bhāradvāja, etadahosi – ‘na kho āḷāro kālāmo imaṃ dhammaṃ kevalaṃ saddhāmattakena sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharāmīti pavedeti; addhā āḷāro kālāmo imaṃ dhammaṃ jānaṃ passaṃ viharatī’ti.

475. Bhāradvāja, before my enlightenment, while I was still an unenlightened Bodhisatta, this thought occurred to me: ‘The household life is confining, a path of dust; the going forth is the open air. It is not easy for one living in a house to lead the holy life that is utterly complete, utterly pure, and polished like a conch shell. What if I were to shave off my hair and beard, put on the ochre robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness?’ So, Bhāradvāja, on a later occasion, while still a youth, a black-haired young man endowed with the blessing of youth, in the prime of life—though my parents were unwilling and wept with tear-stained faces—I shaved off my hair and beard, put on the ochre robes, and went forth from the household life into homelessness. Having thus gone forth, seeking what is wholesome, searching for the supreme, unsurpassed state of peace, I approached Āḷāra Kālāma. Having approached him, I said to Āḷāra Kālāma: ‘Friend Kālāma, I wish to lead the holy life in this Dhamma and Vinaya.’ When this was said, Bhāradvāja, Āḷāra Kālāma said this to me: ‘May the venerable one dwell. This Dhamma is such that an intelligent person could, in no long time, realize for himself with higher knowledge his own teacher’s doctrine, and having attained it, dwell therein.’ So, Bhāradvāja, in no long time, very quickly, I learned that Dhamma. And so, Bhāradvāja, with just that much, by mere lip-recital and verbal repetition, I could speak the ‘word of knowledge’ and the ‘word of the elders,’ and I could profess, ‘I know, I see’—both I and others. Then, Bhāradvāja, this thought occurred to me: ‘Āḷāra Kālāma does not declare this Dhamma merely from faith, saying, “Having realized it for myself with higher knowledge and having attained it, I dwell therein.” Surely, Āḷāra Kālāma dwells knowing and seeing this Dhamma.’

“Atha khvāhaṃ, bhāradvāja, yena āḷāro kālāmo tenupasaṅkamiṃ; upasaṅkamitvā āḷāraṃ kālāmaṃ etadavocaṃ – ‘kittāvatā no, āvuso kālāma, imaṃ dhammaṃ [T 2.0671] sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharāmīti pavedesī’ti? Evaṃ vutte, bhāradvāja, āḷāro kālāmo ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ pavedesi. Tassa mayhaṃ, bhāradvāja, etadahosi – ‘na kho āḷārasseva kālāmassa atthi saddhā, mayhaṃpatthi saddhā; na kho āḷārasseva kālāmassa atthi vīriyaṃ…pe… sati… samādhi… paññā, mayhaṃpatthi paññā. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ yaṃ dhammaṃ āḷāro kālāmo sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharāmīti pavedeti tassa dhammassa sacchikiriyāya padaheyya’nti. So kho ahaṃ, bhāradvāja, nacirasseva khippameva taṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja vihāsiṃ. Atha khvāhaṃ, bhāradvāja, yena āḷāro kālāmo tenupasaṅkamiṃ; upasaṅkamitvā āḷāraṃ kālāmaṃ etadavocaṃ – ‘ettāvatā no, āvuso kālāma, imaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja pavedesī’ti? ‘Ettāvatā kho ahaṃ, āvuso, imaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja pavedemī’ti. ‘Ahampi kho, āvuso, ettāvatā imaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharāmī’ti. ‘Lābhā no, āvuso, suladdhaṃ no, āvuso, ye mayaṃ āyasmantaṃ tādisaṃ sabrahmacāriṃ passāma. Iti yāhaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja pavedemi taṃ tvaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharasi; yaṃ tvaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharasi tamahaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja [T 2.0672] pavedemi. Iti yāhaṃ dhammaṃ jānāmi [V 2.0436] taṃ tvaṃ dhammaṃ jānāsi, yaṃ tvaṃ dhammaṃ jānāsi tamahaṃ dhammaṃ jānāmi[M 2.0428]. Iti yādiso ahaṃ tādiso tuvaṃ, yādiso tuvaṃ tādiso ahaṃ. Ehi dāni, āvuso, ubhova santā imaṃ gaṇaṃ pariharāmā’ti. Iti kho, bhāradvāja, āḷāro kālāmo ācariyo me samāno attano antevāsiṃ maṃ samānaṃ attanā samasamaṃ ṭhapesi, uḷārāya ca maṃ pūjāya pūjesi. Tassa mayhaṃ, bhāradvāja, etadahosi – ‘nāyaṃ dhammo nibbidāya na virāgāya na nirodhāya na upasamāya na abhiññāya na sambodhāya na nibbānāya saṃvattati, yāvadeva ākiñcaññāyatanūpapattiyā’ti. So kho ahaṃ, bhāradvāja, taṃ dhammaṃ analaṅkaritvā tasmā dhammā nibbijja apakkamiṃ.

Then, Bhāradvāja, I approached Āḷāra Kālāma. Having approached him, I said to Āḷāra Kālāma: ‘Friend Kālāma, to what extent do you declare this Dhamma, having realized it for yourself with higher knowledge and having attained it?’ When this was said, Bhāradvāja, Āḷāra Kālāma declared the sphere of nothingness. Then, Bhāradvāja, this thought occurred to me: ‘It is not only Āḷāra Kālāma who has faith; I too have faith. It is not only Āḷāra Kālāma who has energy… mindfulness… concentration… wisdom; I too have wisdom. What if I were to strive for the realization of that Dhamma which Āḷāra Kālāma declares he has realized for himself with higher knowledge and has attained?’ So, Bhāradvāja, in no long time, very quickly, I realized that Dhamma for myself with higher knowledge, and having attained it, I dwelt therein. Then, Bhāradvāja, I approached Āḷāra Kālāma. Having approached him, I said to Āḷāra Kālāma: ‘Friend Kālāma, is it to this extent that you declare this Dhamma, having realized it for yourself with higher knowledge and having attained it?’ ‘Friend, it is to this extent that I declare this Dhamma, having realized it for myself with higher knowledge and having attained it.’ ‘Friend, I too, to this extent, have realized this Dhamma for myself with higher knowledge, and having attained it, I dwell therein.’ ‘It is a gain for us, friend, it is well-gained by us, that we see such a venerable one as a fellow practitioner of the holy life. Thus, the Dhamma that I declare, having realized it for myself with higher knowledge and having attained it, that Dhamma you dwell in, having realized it for yourself with higher knowledge and having attained it. The Dhamma that you dwell in, having realized it for yourself with higher knowledge and having attained it, that Dhamma I declare, having realized it for myself with higher knowledge and having attained it. Thus, the Dhamma that I know, that Dhamma you know; the Dhamma that you know, that Dhamma I know. Thus, as I am, so are you; as you are, so am I. Come now, friend, let us both together lead this group.’ Thus, Bhāradvāja, Āḷāra Kālāma, being my teacher, placed me, his pupil, on the very same level as himself and honored me with great honor. Then, Bhāradvāja, this thought occurred to me: ‘This Dhamma does not conduce to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to higher knowledge, to enlightenment, nor to Nibbāna, but only to rebirth in the sphere of nothingness.’ So, Bhāradvāja, finding that Dhamma insufficient, I became disenchanted with that Dhamma and departed.

476. “So kho ahaṃ, bhāradvāja, kiṃkusalagavesī anuttaraṃ santivarapadaṃ pariyesamāno yena udako rāmaputto tenupasaṅkamiṃ; upasaṅkamitvā udakaṃ rāmaputtaṃ etadavocaṃ – ‘icchāmahaṃ, āvuso passa ma. ni. 1.278 pāsarāsisutte, imasmiṃ dhammavinaye brahmacariyaṃ caritu’nti. Evaṃ vutte, bhāradvāja, udako rāmaputto maṃ etadavoca – ‘viharatāyasmā. Tādiso ayaṃ dhammo yattha viññū puriso nacirasseva sakaṃ ācariyakaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja vihareyyā’ti. So kho ahaṃ, bhāradvāja, nacirasseva khippameva taṃ dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇiṃ. So kho ahaṃ, bhāradvāja, tāvatakeneva oṭṭhapahatamattena lapitalāpanamattena ‘ñāṇavādañca vadāmi, theravādañca jānāmi, passāmī’ti ca paṭijānāmi, ahañceva aññe ca[T 2.0673]. Tassa mayhaṃ, bhāradvāja, etadahosi – ‘na kho rāmo imaṃ dhammaṃ kevalaṃ saddhāmattakena sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharāmīti pavedesi; addhā rāmo imaṃ dhammaṃ jānaṃ passaṃ vihāsī’ti. Atha khvāhaṃ, bhāradvāja, yena udako rāmaputto tenupasaṅkamiṃ; upasaṅkamitvā udakaṃ rāmaputtaṃ etadavocaṃ – ‘kittāvatā no, āvuso, rāmo imaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharāmīti pavedesī’ti? Evaṃ vutte, bhāradvāja, udako rāmaputto nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ pavedesi. Tassa mayhaṃ, bhāradvāja, etadahosi – ‘na kho rāmasseva ahosi saddhā, mayhaṃpatthi saddhā; na kho rāmasseva ahosi vīriyaṃ…pe… sati… samādhi… paññā, mayhaṃpatthi paññā. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ yaṃ dhammaṃ rāmo sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja [M 2.0429] viharāmīti pavedesi tassa dhammassa sacchikiriyāya padaheyya’nti. So kho ahaṃ, bhāradvāja, nacirasseva khippameva taṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja vihāsiṃ.

476. Indeed, Bhāradvāja, seeking what is wholesome, searching for the unsurpassed, supreme state of peace, I approached Udaka Rāmaputta. Having approached, I said this to Udaka Rāmaputta: ‘Friend, I wish to lead the holy life in this Dhamma and Vinaya.’ When this was said, Bhāradvāja, Udaka Rāmaputta said this to me: ‘May the venerable one dwell. This Dhamma is such that a wise person, before long, having realized for himself with higher knowledge his own teacher's doctrine, might attain it and dwell therein.’ Indeed, Bhāradvāja, not long after, very quickly, I mastered that Dhamma. Indeed, Bhāradvāja, with just that much, by mere lip-service, by mere recitation, I spoke the claim of knowledge and the doctrine of the elders, and I professed, 'I know, I see'—both I and others. Then, Bhāradvāja, this thought occurred to me: ‘Surely Rāma did not declare this Dhamma, saying, "I dwell having realized it for myself with higher knowledge and attained it," based on mere faith alone; certainly, Rāma dwelt knowing and seeing this Dhamma.’ Then, Bhāradvāja, I approached Udaka Rāmaputta. Having approached, I said this to Udaka Rāmaputta: ‘Friend, to what extent did Rāma declare this Dhamma, having realized it for himself with higher knowledge and attained it?’ When this was said, Bhāradvāja, Udaka Rāmaputta declared the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Then, Bhāradvāja, this thought occurred to me: ‘It was not only Rāma who had faith; I too have faith. It was not only Rāma who had energy… mindfulness… concentration… wisdom; I too have wisdom. What if I were to strive for the realization of that Dhamma which Rāma declared he had realized for himself with higher knowledge and attained it?’ Indeed, Bhāradvāja, not long after, very quickly, having realized that Dhamma for myself with higher knowledge, I attained it and dwelt therein.

“Atha khvāhaṃ, bhāradvāja, yena udako rāmaputto tenupasaṅkamiṃ; upasaṅkamitvā udakaṃ rāmaputtaṃ etadavocaṃ – ‘ettāvatā no, āvuso, rāmo imaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja [V 2.0437] pavedesī’ti? ‘Ettāvatā kho, āvuso, rāmo imaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja pavedesī’ti. ‘Ahampi kho, āvuso, ettāvatā imaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharāmī’ti. ‘Lābhā no, āvuso, suladdhaṃ [T 2.0674] no, āvuso, ye mayaṃ āyasmantaṃ tādisaṃ sabrahmacāriṃ passāma. Iti yaṃ dhammaṃ rāmo sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja pavedesi taṃ tvaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharasi; yaṃ tvaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharasi taṃ dhammaṃ rāmo sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja pavedesi. Iti yaṃ dhammaṃ rāmo abhiññāsi taṃ tvaṃ dhammaṃ jānāsi, yaṃ tvaṃ dhammaṃ jānāsi taṃ dhammaṃ rāmo abhiññāsi. Iti yādiso rāmo ahosi tādiso tuvaṃ, yādiso tuvaṃ tādiso rāmo ahosi. Ehi dāni, āvuso, tuvaṃ imaṃ gaṇaṃ pariharā’ti. Iti kho, bhāradvāja, udako rāmaputto sabrahmacārī me samāno ācariyaṭṭhāne maṃ ṭhapesi, uḷārāya ca maṃ pūjāya pūjesi. Tassa mayhaṃ, bhāradvāja, etadahosi – ‘nāyaṃ dhammo nibbidāya na virāgāya na nirodhāya na upasamāya na abhiññāya na sambodhāya na nibbānāya saṃvattati, yāvadeva nevasaññānāsaññāyatanūpapattiyā’ti. So kho ahaṃ, bhāradvāja, taṃ dhammaṃ analaṅkaritvā tasmā dhammā nibbijja apakkamiṃ.

Then, Bhāradvāja, I approached Udaka Rāmaputta. Having approached, I said this to Udaka Rāmaputta: ‘Friend, was it to this extent that Rāma declared this Dhamma, having realized it for himself with higher knowledge and attained it?’ ‘Indeed, friend, it was to this extent that Rāma declared this Dhamma, having realized it for himself with higher knowledge and attained it.’ ‘Friend, I too dwell having realized this Dhamma for myself with higher knowledge and attained it to this extent.’ ‘It is a gain for us, friend, a great gain for us, that we see such a venerable companion in the holy life. Thus, the Dhamma that Rāma declared, having realized it for himself with higher knowledge and attained it, that Dhamma you dwell in, having realized it for yourself with higher knowledge and attained it. The Dhamma that you dwell in, having realized it for yourself with higher knowledge and attained it, that Dhamma Rāma declared, having realized it for himself with higher knowledge and attained it. Thus, the Dhamma that Rāma knew with higher knowledge, that Dhamma you know; the Dhamma that you know, that Dhamma Rāma knew with higher knowledge. Thus, as Rāma was, so are you; as you are, so was Rāma. Come now, friend, you lead this group.’ Thus, Bhāradvāja, Udaka Rāmaputta, being my companion in the holy life, placed me in the position of a teacher and honored me with great honor. Then, Bhāradvāja, this thought occurred to me: ‘This Dhamma does not lead to disenchantment, not to dispassion, not to cessation, not to peace, not to higher knowledge, not to enlightenment, not to Nibbāna; it leads only as far as rebirth in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.’ Indeed, Bhāradvāja, finding that Dhamma insufficient, I became disenchanted with that Dhamma and departed.

477. “So kho ahaṃ, bhāradvāja, kiṃkusalagavesī anuttaraṃ santivarapadaṃ pariyesamāno magadhesu anupubbena cārikaṃ caramāno yena uruveḷā senānigamo tadavasariṃ. Tatthaddasaṃ ramaṇīyaṃ bhūmibhāgaṃ, pāsādikañca vanasaṇḍaṃ, nadiñca sandantiṃ setakaṃ supatitthaṃ ramaṇīyaṃ, samantā [T 2.0675] ca gocaragāmaṃ. Tassa mayhaṃ, bhāradvāja, etadahosi – ‘ramaṇīyo vata, bho, bhūmibhāgo, pāsādiko ca vanasaṇḍo, nadī ca sandati setakā supatitthā ramaṇīyā, samantā ca gocaragāmo. Alaṃ vatidaṃ kulaputtassa padhānatthikassa padhānāyā’ti[M 2.0430]. So kho ahaṃ, bhāradvāja, tattheva nisīdiṃ – ‘alamidaṃ padhānāyā’ti. Apissu maṃ, bhāradvāja, tisso upamā paṭibhaṃsu anacchariyā pubbe assutapubbā.

477. Indeed, Bhāradvāja, seeking what is wholesome, searching for the unsurpassed, supreme state of peace, while wandering on tour in due course through the Magadhan country, I eventually arrived at Uruvelā, at the market town of Senā. There I saw a delightful stretch of land, a pleasant grove, a flowing river with clear water and good, delightful bathing places, and a village for alms-round all around. Then, Bhāradvāja, this thought occurred to me: ‘Sirs, this stretch of land is truly delightful, the grove is pleasant, and the river flows with clear water and good, delightful bathing places, and there is a village for alms-round all around. This is indeed suitable for a clansman intent on striving to make an effort.’ Indeed, Bhāradvāja, I sat down right there, thinking: ‘This is suitable for striving.’ And then, Bhāradvāja, three similes occurred to me, unprecedented, never heard before.

“Seyyathāpi, bhāradvāja, allaṃ kaṭṭhaṃ sasnehaṃ udake nikkhittaṃ. Atha puriso āgaccheyya uttarāraṇiṃ ādāya – ‘aggiṃ abhinibbattessāmi, tejo pātukarissāmī’ti. Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, bhāradvāja, api nu so puriso amuṃ allaṃ kaṭṭhaṃ sasnehaṃ udake nikkhittaṃ uttarāraṇiṃ ādāya abhimanthento aggiṃ abhinibbatteyya, tejo pātukareyyā”ti? “No hidaṃ, bho gotama. Taṃ kissa hetu? Aduñhi, bho gotama, allaṃ kaṭṭhaṃ sasnehaṃ, tañca [V 2.0438] pana udake nikkhittaṃ; yāvadeva ca pana so puriso kilamathassa vighātassa bhāgī assā”ti. “Evameva kho, bhāradvāja, ye hi keci samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā kāyena ceva cittena ca kāmehi avūpakaṭṭhā viharanti, yo ca nesaṃ kāmesu kāmacchando kāmasneho kāmamucchā kāmapipāsā kāmapariḷāho so ca ajjhattaṃ na suppahīno hoti na suppaṭippassaddho, opakkamikā cepi te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā dukkhā tibbā kharā kaṭukā vedanā vedayanti, abhabbāva te ñāṇāya dassanāya anuttarāya sambodhāya. No capi te [T 2.0676] bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā opakkamikā dukkhā tibbā kharā kaṭukā vedanā vedayanti abhabbāva te ñāṇāya dassanāya anuttarāya sambodhāya. Ayaṃ kho maṃ, bhāradvāja, paṭhamā upamā paṭibhāsi anacchariyā pubbe assutapubbā.

“Just as, Bhāradvāja, a wet, sappy piece of wood is placed in water. Then a man might come along with an upper fire-stick, thinking: ‘I will produce fire, I will make heat manifest.’ What do you think, Bhāradvāja, could that man, taking that wet, sappy piece of wood placed in water and rubbing it with an upper fire-stick, produce fire and make heat manifest?” “No, indeed, venerable Gotama. For what reason? Because, venerable Gotama, that wood is wet and sappy, and it is also placed in water; that man would only partake of weariness and distress.” “Even so, Bhāradvāja, whatever ascetics or brahmins dwell with body and mind unwithdrawn from sensual pleasures—and whose sensual desire, sensual affection, sensual infatuation, sensual thirst, and sensual fever for sensual pleasures are not internally well abandoned and well calmed—even if those venerable ascetics and brahmins experience painful, sharp, harsh, and bitter feelings due to their striving, they are incapable of knowledge, vision, and unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. And even if those venerable ascetics and brahmins do not experience painful, sharp, harsh, and bitter feelings due to their striving, they are still incapable of knowledge, vision, and unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. This, Bhāradvāja, was the first simile that occurred to me—amazing and never heard before.”

478. “Aparāpi kho maṃ, bhāradvāja, dutiyā upamā paṭibhāsi anacchariyā pubbe assutapubbā. Seyyathāpi, bhāradvāja, allaṃ kaṭṭhaṃ sasnehaṃ ārakā udakā thale nikkhittaṃ. Atha puriso āgaccheyya uttarāraṇiṃ ādāya – ‘aggiṃ abhinibbattessāmi, tejo pātukarissāmī’ti. Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, bhāradvāja, api nu so puriso amuṃ allaṃ kaṭṭhaṃ sasnehaṃ ārakā udakā thale nikkhittaṃ uttarāraṇiṃ ādāya abhimanthento aggiṃ abhinibbatteyya tejo pātukareyyā”ti? “No hidaṃ, bho gotama. Taṃ kissa hetu? Aduñhi, bho gotama, allaṃ kaṭṭhaṃ sasnehaṃ, kiñcāpi ārakā udakā thale nikkhittaṃ; yāvadeva ca pana so puriso kilamathassa vighātassa [M 2.0431] bhāgī assā”ti. “Evameva kho, bhāradvāja, ye hi keci samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā kāyena ceva cittena ca kāmehi vūpakaṭṭhā viharanti, yo ca nesaṃ kāmesu kāmacchando kāmasneho kāmamucchā kāmapipāsā kāmapariḷāho so ca ajjhattaṃ na suppahīno hoti na suppaṭippassaddho, opakkamikā cepi te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā dukkhā tibbā kharā kaṭukā vedanā vedayanti, abhabbāva te ñāṇāya dassanāya anuttarāya sambodhāya. No cepi te [T 2.0677] bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā opakkamikā dukkhā tibbā kharā kaṭukā vedanā vedayanti, abhabbāva te ñāṇāya dassanāya anuttarāya sambodhāya. Ayaṃ kho maṃ, bhāradvāja, dutiyā upamā paṭibhāsi anacchariyā pubbe assutapubbā.

478. “Furthermore, Bhāradvāja, a second simile occurred to me—amazing and never heard before. Just as, Bhāradvāja, a wet, sappy piece of wood is placed on dry land, far from water.
