Then a man might come along with an upper fire-stick, thinking: ‘I will produce fire, I will make heat manifest.’ What do you think, Bhāradvāja, could that man, taking that wet, sappy piece of wood placed on dry land, far from water, and rubbing it with an upper fire-stick, produce fire and make heat manifest?” “No, indeed, venerable Gotama. For what reason? Because, venerable Gotama, that wood is wet and sappy, even though it is placed on dry land, far from water; that man would only partake of weariness and distress.” “Even so, Bhāradvāja, whatever ascetics or brahmins dwell with body and mind withdrawn from sensual pleasures, but whose sensual desire, sensual affection, sensual infatuation, sensual thirst, and sensual fever for sensual pleasures are not internally well abandoned and well calmed—even if those venerable ascetics and brahmins experience painful, sharp, harsh, and bitter feelings due to their striving, they are incapable of knowledge, vision, and unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. And even if those venerable ascetics and brahmins do not experience painful, sharp, harsh, and bitter feelings due to their striving, they are still incapable of knowledge, vision, and unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. This, Bhāradvāja, was the second simile that occurred to me—amazing and never heard before.”

479. “Aparāpi [V 2.0439] kho maṃ, bhāradvāja, tatiyā upamā paṭibhāsi anacchariyā pubbe assutapubbā. Seyyathāpi, bhāradvāja, sukkhaṃ kaṭṭhaṃ koḷāpaṃ ārakā udakā thale nikkhittaṃ. Atha puriso āgaccheyya uttarāraṇiṃ ādāya – ‘aggiṃ abhinibbattessāmi, tejo pātukarissāmī’ti. Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, bhāradvāja, api nu so puriso amuṃ sukkhaṃ kaṭṭhaṃ koḷāpaṃ ārakā udakā thale nikkhittaṃ uttarāraṇiṃ ādāya abhimanthento aggiṃ abhinibbatteyya, tejo pātukareyyā”ti? “Evaṃ bho gotama. Taṃ kissa hetu? Aduñhi, bho gotama, sukkhaṃ kaṭṭhaṃ koḷāpaṃ, tañca pana ārakā udakā thale nikkhitta”nti. “Evameva kho, bhāradvāja, ye hi keci samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā kāyena ceva cittena ca kāmehi vūpakaṭṭhā viharanti, yo ca nesaṃ kāmesu kāmacchando kāmasneho kāmamucchā kāmapipāsā kāmapariḷāho so ca ajjhattaṃ suppahīno hoti suppaṭippassaddho, opakkamikā cepi te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā dukkhā tibbā kharā kaṭukā vedanā vedayanti, bhabbāva te ñāṇāya dassanāya anuttarāya sambodhāya. No cepi te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā opakkamikā [T 2.0678] dukkhā tibbā kharā kaṭukā vedanā vedayanti, bhabbāva te ñāṇāya dassanāya anuttarāya sambodhāya. Ayaṃ kho maṃ, bhāradvāja, tatiyā upamā paṭibhāsi anacchariyā pubbe assutapubbā. Imā kho maṃ, bhāradvāja, tisso upamā paṭibhaṃsu anacchariyā pubbe assutapubbā.

479. “Furthermore, Bhāradvāja, a third simile occurred to me—amazing and never heard before. Just as, Bhāradvāja, a dry, sapless piece of wood is placed on dry land, far from water. Then a man might come along with an upper fire-stick, thinking: ‘I will produce fire, I will make heat manifest.’ What do you think, Bhāradvāja, could that man, taking that dry, sapless piece of wood placed on dry land, far from water, and rubbing it with an upper fire-stick, produce fire and make heat manifest?” “Yes, venerable Gotama. For what reason? Because, venerable Gotama, that wood is dry and sapless, and it is also placed on dry land, far from water.” “Even so, Bhāradvāja, whatever ascetics or brahmins dwell with body and mind withdrawn from sensual pleasures, and whose sensual desire, sensual affection, sensual infatuation, sensual thirst, and sensual fever for sensual pleasures are internally well abandoned and well calmed—even if those venerable ascetics and brahmins experience painful, sharp, harsh, and bitter feelings due to their striving, they are capable of knowledge, vision, and unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. And even if those venerable ascetics and brahmins do not experience painful, sharp, harsh, and bitter feelings due to their striving, they are still capable of knowledge, vision, and unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. This, Bhāradvāja, was the third simile that occurred to me—amazing and never heard before. These, Bhāradvāja, are the three similes that occurred to me—amazing and never heard before.”

480. “Tassa [M 2.0432] mayhaṃ, bhāradvāja, etadahosi – ‘yaṃnūnāhaṃ dantebhidantamādhāya, jivhāya tāluṃ āhacca, cetasā cittaṃ abhiniggaṇheyyaṃ abhinippīḷeyyaṃ abhisantāpeyya’nti. So kho ahaṃ, bhāradvāja, dantebhidantamādhāya, jivhāya tāluṃ āhacca, cetasā cittaṃ abhiniggaṇhāmi abhinippīḷemi abhisantāpemi. Tassa mayhaṃ, bhāradvāja, dantebhidantamādhāya, jivhāya tāluṃ āhacca, cetasā cittaṃ abhiniggaṇhato abhinippīḷayato abhisantāpayato kacchehi sedā muccanti. Seyyathāpi, bhāradvāja, balavā puriso dubbalataraṃ purisaṃ sīse vā gahetvā khandhe vā gahetvā abhiniggaṇheyya abhinippīḷeyya abhisantāpeyya, evameva kho me, bhāradvāja, dantebhidantamādhāya, jivhāya tāluṃ āhacca, cetasā cittaṃ abhiniggaṇhato abhinippīḷayato abhisantāpayato kacchehi sedā muccanti. Āraddhaṃ kho pana me, bhāradvāja, vīriyaṃ hoti asallīnaṃ, upaṭṭhitā sati asammuṭṭhā; sāraddho ca pana me kāyo hoti appaṭippassaddho, teneva dukkhappadhānena padhānābhitunnassa sato.

480. Bhāradvāja, this thought occurred to me: ‘What if, pressing my teeth together and pressing my tongue against the palate, I should restrain, crush, and torment the mind with the mind?’ So, Bhāradvāja, pressing my teeth together and pressing my tongue against the palate, I restrain, crush, and torment the mind with the mind. As I, Bhāradvāja, was pressing my teeth together, pressing my tongue against the palate, and restraining, crushing, and tormenting the mind with the mind, sweat flowed from my armpits. Just as, Bhāradvāja, a strong man, having seized a weaker man by the head or by the shoulders, might restrain, crush, and torment him, in the very same way, Bhāradvāja, as I was pressing my teeth together, pressing my tongue against the palate, and restraining, crushing, and tormenting the mind with the mind, sweat flowed from my armpits. Indeed, Bhāradvāja, my energy was aroused and unshrinking, my mindfulness was established and unconfused; but my body was agitated and uncalmed, being pierced by that painful striving.

481. “Tassa [T 2.0679][V 2.0440] mayhaṃ, bhāradvāja, etadahosi – ‘yaṃnūnāhaṃ appāṇakaṃyeva jhānaṃ jhāyeyya’nti. So kho ahaṃ, bhāradvāja, mukhato ca nāsato ca assāsapassāse uparundhiṃ. Tassa mayhaṃ, bhāradvāja, mukhato ca nāsato ca assāsapassāsesu uparuddhesu kaṇṇasotehi vātānaṃ nikkhamantānaṃ adhimatto saddo hoti. Seyyathāpi nāma kammāragaggariyā dhamamānāya adhimatto saddo hoti, evameva kho me, bhāradvāja, mukhato ca nāsato ca assāsapassāsesu uparuddhesu kaṇṇasotehi vātānaṃ nikkhamantānaṃ adhimatto saddo hoti. Āraddhaṃ kho pana me, bhāradvāja, vīriyaṃ hoti asallīnaṃ, upaṭṭhitā sati asammuṭṭhā; sāraddho ca pana me kāyo hoti appaṭippassaddho, teneva dukkhappadhānena padhānābhitunnassa sato.

481. Bhāradvāja, this thought occurred to me: ‘What if I were to enter upon the breathless jhāna?’ So, Bhāradvāja, I stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths through my mouth and nose. As I, Bhāradvāja, had stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths through my mouth and nose, there was an exceedingly loud sound of winds issuing from my ear-holes. Just as there is an exceedingly loud sound from a blacksmith's bellows when it is being blown, in the very same way, Bhāradvāja, when the in-breaths and out-breaths were stopped through my mouth and nose, there was an exceedingly loud sound of winds issuing from my ear-holes. Indeed, Bhāradvāja, my energy was aroused and unshrinking, my mindfulness was established and unconfused; but my body was agitated and uncalmed, being pierced by that painful striving.

“Tassa mayhaṃ, bhāradvāja, etadahosi – ‘yaṃnūnāhaṃ appāṇakaṃyeva jhānaṃ jhāyeyya’nti. So kho ahaṃ, bhāradvāja, mukhato ca nāsato ca kaṇṇato ca assāsapassāse uparundhiṃ. Tassa mayhaṃ, bhāradvāja, mukhato ca nāsato ca kaṇṇato ca assāsapassāsesu uparuddhesu adhimattā vātā muddhani ūhananti. Seyyathāpi, bhāradvāja, balavā puriso, tiṇhena sikharena muddhani abhimattheyya, evameva kho me, bhāradvāja, mukhato ca nāsato [M 2.0433] ca kaṇṇato ca assāsapassāsesu uparuddhesu adhimattā vātā muddhani ūhananti. Āraddhaṃ kho pana me, bhāradvāja, vīriyaṃ hoti asallīnaṃ[T 2.0680], upaṭṭhitā sati asammuṭṭhā; sāraddho ca pana me kāyo hoti appaṭippassaddho, teneva dukkhappadhānena padhānābhitunnassa sato.

Bhāradvāja, this thought occurred to me: ‘What if I were to enter upon the breathless jhāna?’ So, Bhāradvāja, I stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths through my mouth, nose, and ears. As I, Bhāradvāja, had stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths through my mouth, nose, and ears, exceedingly strong winds struck my head. Just as, Bhāradvāja, a strong man might bore into his head with a sharp point, in the very same way, Bhāradvāja, when the in-breaths and out-breaths were stopped through my mouth, nose, and ears, exceedingly strong winds struck my head. Indeed, Bhāradvāja, my energy was aroused and unshrinking, my mindfulness was established and unconfused; but my body was agitated and uncalmed, being pierced by that painful striving.

“Tassa mayhaṃ, bhāradvāja, etadahosi – ‘yaṃnūnāhaṃ appāṇakaṃyeva jhānaṃ jhāyeyya’nti. So kho ahaṃ, bhāradvāja, mukhato ca nāsato ca kaṇṇato ca assāsapassāse uparundhiṃ. Tassa mayhaṃ, bhāradvāja, mukhato ca nāsato ca kaṇṇato ca assāsapassāsesu uparuddhesu adhimattā sīse sīsavedanā honti. Seyyathāpi, bhāradvāja, balavā puriso daḷhena varattakkhaṇḍena sīse sīsaveṭhaṃ dadeyya, evameva kho, bhāradvāja, mukhato ca nāsato ca kaṇṇato ca assāsapassāsesu uparuddhesu adhimattā sīse sīsavedanā honti. Āraddhaṃ kho pana me, bhāradvāja, vīriyaṃ hoti asallīnaṃ, upaṭṭhitā sati asammuṭṭhā; sāraddho ca pana me kāyo hoti appaṭippassaddho, teneva dukkhappadhānena padhānābhitunnassa sato.

Bhāradvāja, this thought occurred to me: ‘What if I were to enter upon the breathless jhāna?’ So, Bhāradvāja, I stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths through my mouth, nose, and ears. As I, Bhāradvāja, had stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths through my mouth, nose, and ears, exceedingly severe pains arose in my head. Just as, Bhāradvāja, a strong man might tighten a strong leather thong around his head as a headband, in the very same way, Bhāradvāja, when the in-breaths and out-breaths were stopped through my mouth, nose, and ears, exceedingly severe pains arose in my head. Indeed, Bhāradvāja, my energy was aroused and unshrinking, my mindfulness was established and unconfused; but my body was agitated and uncalmed, being pierced by that painful striving.

“Tassa mayhaṃ, bhāradvāja, etadahosi – ‘yaṃnūnāhaṃ appāṇakaṃyeva jhānaṃ jhāyeyya’nti. So kho ahaṃ, bhāradvāja, mukhato ca nāsato ca kaṇṇato ca assāsapassāse uparundhiṃ. Tassa mayhaṃ, bhāradvāja, mukhato ca nāsato ca kaṇṇato ca assāsapassāsesu uparuddhesu adhimattā [V 2.0441] vātā kucchiṃ parikantanti. Seyyathāpi[T 2.0681], bhāradvāja, dakkho goghātako vā goghātakantevāsī vā tiṇhena govikantanena kucchiṃ parikanteyya, evameva kho me, bhāradvāja, mukhato ca nāsato ca kaṇṇato ca assāsapassāsesu uparuddhesu adhimattā vātā kucchiṃ parikantanti. Āraddhaṃ kho pana me, bhāradvāja, vīriyaṃ hoti asallīnaṃ upaṭṭhitā sati asammuṭṭhā; sāraddho ca pana me kāyo hoti appaṭippassaddho, teneva dukkhappadhānena padhānābhitunnassa sato.

Bhāradvāja, this thought occurred to me: ‘What if I were to enter upon the breathless jhāna?’ So, Bhāradvāja, I stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths through my mouth, nose, and ears. As I, Bhāradvāja, had stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths through my mouth, nose, and ears, exceedingly strong winds cut through my belly. Just as a skilled cow-butcher or his apprentice might carve up a belly with a sharp butcher's knife, in the very same way, Bhāradvāja, when the in-breaths and out-breaths were stopped through my mouth, nose, and ears, exceedingly strong winds cut through my belly. Indeed, Bhāradvāja, my energy was aroused and unshrinking, my mindfulness was established and unconfused; but my body was agitated and uncalmed, being pierced by that painful striving.

“Tassa mayhaṃ, bhāradvāja, etadahosi – ‘yaṃnūnāhaṃ appāṇakaṃyeva jhānaṃ jhāyeyya’nti. So kho ahaṃ, bhāradvāja, mukhato ca nāsato ca kaṇṇato ca assāsapassāse uparundhiṃ. Tassa mayhaṃ, bhāradvāja, mukhato ca [M 2.0434] nāsato ca kaṇṇato ca assāsapassāsesu uparuddhesu adhimatto kāyasmiṃ ḍāho hoti. Seyyathāpi, bhāradvāja, dve balavanto purisā dubbalataraṃ purisaṃ nānābāhāsu gahetvā aṅgārakāsuyā santāpeyyuṃ samparitāpeyyuṃ, evameva kho me, bhāradvāja, mukhato ca nāsato ca kaṇṇato ca assāsapassāsesu uparuddhesu adhimatto kāyasmiṃ ḍāho hoti. Āraddhaṃ kho pana me, bhāradvāja, vīriyaṃ hoti asallīnaṃ, upaṭṭhitā sati asammuṭṭhā, sāraddho ca pana me kāyo hoti appaṭippassaddho, teneva dukkhappadhānena padhānābhitunnassa sato. Apissu maṃ, bhāradvāja, devatā disvā evamāhaṃsu – ‘kālaṅkato samaṇo gotamo’ti. Ekaccā [T 2.0682] devatā evamāhaṃsu – ‘na kālaṅkato samaṇo gotamo, api ca kālaṅkarotī’ti. Ekaccā devatā evamāhaṃsu – ‘na kālaṅkato samaṇo gotamo, nāpi kālaṅkaroti; arahaṃ samaṇo gotamo, vihārotveva so arahato evarūpo hotī’ti.

Then, Bhāradvāja, this thought occurred to me: ‘What if I were to enter the fourth jhāna, which is without in-and-out breathing?’ So, Bhāradvāja, I stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths from my mouth, from my nose, and from my ears. When my in-breaths and out-breaths were stopped from my mouth, from my nose, and from my ears, Bhāradvāja, an excessive burning arose in my body. Just as, Bhāradvāja, two strong men might seize a weaker man by his various arms and heat him, and roast him all over on a pit of embers, even so, Bhāradvāja, when my in-breaths and out-breaths were stopped from my mouth, from my nose, and from my ears, an excessive burning arose in my body. Indeed, Bhāradvāja, my energy was aroused and unflagging, my mindfulness was established and unconfused; yet my body was agitated and uncalmed, being assailed by that painful striving. And, Bhāradvāja, some deities, seeing me, said this: ‘The ascetic Gotama is dead.’ Other deities said: ‘The ascetic Gotama is not dead, but he is dying.’ Still other deities said: ‘The ascetic Gotama is neither dead nor dying; the ascetic Gotama is an Arahant, and for an Arahant, such is this manner of abiding.’

“Tassa mayhaṃ, bhāradvāja, etadahosi – ‘yaṃnūnāhaṃ sabbaso āhārupacchedāya paṭipajjeyya’nti. Atha kho maṃ, bhāradvāja, devatā upasaṅkamitvā etadavocuṃ – ‘mā kho tvaṃ, mārisa, sabbaso āhārupacchedāya paṭipajji. Sace kho tvaṃ, mārisa, sabbaso āhārupacchedāya paṭipajjissasi, tassa te mayaṃ dibbaṃ ojaṃ lomakūpehi ajjhohāressāma. Tāya tvaṃ yāpessasī’ti. Tassa mayhaṃ, bhāradvāja, etadahosi – ‘ahañceva kho pana sabbaso ajajjitaṃ paṭijāneyyaṃ, imā ca me devatā dibbaṃ ojaṃ lomakūpehi ajjhohāreyyuṃ, tāya cāhaṃ yāpeyyaṃ. Taṃ mamassa musā’ti. So kho ahaṃ, bhāradvāja, tā devatā paccācikkhāmi, ‘hala’nti vadāmi.

Then, Bhāradvāja, this thought occurred to me: ‘What if I were to practice the complete cutting off of food?’ Then, Bhāradvāja, deities approached me and said this: ‘Good sir, do not practice the complete cutting off of food. If you, good sir, were to practice the complete cutting off of food, we would infuse divine nutritive essence through the pores of your hair, and you would be sustained by that.’ Then, Bhāradvāja, this thought occurred to me: ‘If I were to profess complete abstinence from food, and these deities were to infuse divine nutritive essence through the pores of my hair, and I were to be sustained by that, it would be a falsehood on my part.’ So, Bhāradvāja, I rejected those deities, saying, ‘That is not proper!’

“Tassa mayhaṃ, bhāradvāja, etadahosi – ‘yaṃnūnāhaṃ thokaṃ thokaṃ āhāraṃ āhāreyyaṃ pasataṃ pasataṃ[V 2.0442], yadi vā muggayūsaṃ, yadi vā kulatthayūsaṃ, yadi vā kaḷāyayūsaṃ, yadi vā hareṇukayūsa’nti. So kho ahaṃ, bhāradvāja, thokaṃ thokaṃ āhāraṃ āhāresiṃ pasataṃ pasataṃ, yadi vā muggayūsaṃ[T 2.0683], yadi vā kulatthayūsaṃ, yadi vā kaḷāyayūsaṃ, yadi vā hareṇukayūsaṃ. Tassa mayhaṃ, bhāradvāja, thokaṃ thokaṃ āhāraṃ [M 2.0435] āhārayato pasataṃ pasataṃ, yadi vā muggayūsaṃ, yadi vā kulatthayūsaṃ, yadi vā kaḷāyayūsaṃ, yadi vā hareṇukayūsaṃ, adhimattakasimānaṃ patto kāyo hoti. Seyyathāpi nāma āsītikapabbāni vā kāḷapabbāni vā, evamevassu me aṅgapaccaṅgāni bhavanti tāyevappāhāratāya; seyyathāpi nāma oṭṭhapadaṃ, evamevassu me ānisadaṃ hoti tāyevappāhāratāya; seyyathāpi nāma vaṭṭanāvaḷī, evamevassu me piṭṭhikaṇṭako uṇṇatāvanato hoti tāyevappāhāratāya; seyyathāpi nāma jarasālāya gopānasiyo oluggaviluggā bhavanti, evamevassu me phāsuḷiyo oluggaviluggā bhavanti tāyevappāhāratāya; seyyathāpi nāma gambhīre udapāne udakatārakā gambhīragatā okkhāyikā dissanti, evamevassu me akkhikūpesu akkhitārakā gambhīragatā okkhāyikā dissanti tāyevappāhāratāya; seyyathāpi nāma tittakālābu āmakacchinno vātātapena saṃphuṭito hoti sammilāto, evamevassu me sīsacchavi saṃphuṭitā hoti sammilātā tāyevappāhāratāya. So kho ahaṃ, bhāradvāja, ‘udaracchaviṃ parimasissāmī’ti piṭṭhikaṇṭakaṃyeva pariggaṇhāmi, ‘piṭṭhikaṇṭakaṃ parimasissāmī’ti udaracchaviṃyeva pariggaṇhāmi; yāvassu me, bhāradvāja, udaracchavi piṭṭhikaṇṭakaṃ allīnā hoti tāyevappāhāratāya. So kho ahaṃ, bhāradvāja[T 2.0684], ‘vaccaṃ vā muttaṃ vā karissāmī’ti tattheva avakujjo papatāmi tāyevappāhāratāya. So kho ahaṃ, bhāradvāja, imameva kāyaṃ assāsento pāṇinā gattāni anumajjāmi. Tassa mayhaṃ, bhāradvāja, pāṇinā gattāni anumajjato pūtimūlāni lomāni kāyasmā papatanti tāyevappāhāratāya. Apissu maṃ, bhāradvāja, manussā disvā evamāhaṃsu – ‘kāḷo samaṇo gotamo’ti. Ekacce manussā evamāhaṃsu – ‘na kāḷo samaṇo gotamo, sāmo samaṇo gotamo’ti. Ekacce manussā evamāhaṃsu – ‘na kāḷo samaṇo gotamo napi sāmo, maṅguracchavi samaṇo gotamo’ti; yāvassu me, bhāradvāja, tāva parisuddho chavivaṇṇo pariyodāto upahato hoti tāyevappāhāratāya.

Then, Bhāradvāja, this thought occurred to me: ‘What if I were to take food little by little, a hollowed handful at a time—whether it be mung bean soup, horse gram soup, chickpea soup, or pea soup?’ So, Bhāradvāja, I took food little by little, a hollowed handful at a time—whether it be mung bean soup, horse gram soup, chickpea soup, or pea soup. As I took food little by little, a hollowed handful at a time, Bhāradvāja, my body reached a state of extreme emaciation. Because of eating so little, my limbs became like the joints of withered reeds. Because of eating so little, my backside became like a camel’s hoof. Because of eating so little, my spine became uneven with highs and lows like a string of beads. Because of eating so little, my ribs jutted out, drooping and dangling like the rafters of a dilapidated old hall. Because of eating so little, the pupils in my eye sockets appeared deep down and sunken, like the reflection of stars in a deep well. Because of eating so little, the skin of my head became shrunken and withered, like a bitter gourd cut while raw and withered by wind and sun. Bhāradvāja, when I thought, ‘I will touch the skin of my belly,’ I grasped the backbone itself. When I thought, ‘I will touch my backbone,’ I grasped the skin of my belly itself. So much, Bhāradvāja, had the skin of my belly clung to my backbone because of eating so little. Bhāradvāja, when I thought, ‘I will relieve myself of feces or urine,’ I would fall face down right there because of eating so little. Bhāradvāja, as I, seeking to comfort this very body, rubbed my limbs with my hand, the hairs, their roots rotted, fell from my body because of eating so little. And, Bhāradvāja, people who saw me said this: ‘The ascetic Gotama is black.’ Some people said: ‘The ascetic Gotama is not black; the ascetic Gotama is golden-skinned.’ Some people said: ‘The ascetic Gotama is neither black nor golden-skinned; the ascetic Gotama has the complexion of a mangura fish.’ To such an extent, Bhāradvāja, was my pure and bright skin-complexion ruined because of eating so little.

482. “Tassa mayhaṃ, bhāradvāja, etadahosi – ‘ye kho keci atītamaddhānaṃ samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā opakkamikā dukkhā tibbā kharā kaṭukā vedanā vedayiṃsu[M 2.0436], etāvaparamaṃ, nayito bhiyyo; yepi hi keci anāgatamaddhānaṃ samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā opakkamikā dukkhā tibbā kharā kaṭukā vedanā vedayissanti, etāvaparamaṃ, nayito bhiyyo; yepi hi keci [V 2.0443] etarahi samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā opakkamikā dukkhā tibbā kharā kaṭukā vedanā vedayanti, etāvaparamaṃ, nayito bhiyyo. Na kho panāhaṃ imāya kaṭukāya dukkarakārikāya adhigacchāmi uttari manussadhammā alamariyañāṇadassanavisesaṃ. Siyā nu kho añño maggo bodhāyā’ti[T 2.0685]? Tassa mayhaṃ bhāradvāja, etadahosi – ‘abhijānāmi kho panāhaṃ pitu sakkassa kammante sītāya jambucchāyāya nisinno vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharitā. Siyā nu kho eso maggo bodhāyā’ti? Tassa mayhaṃ, bhāradvāja, satānusāri viññāṇaṃ ahosi – ‘eseva maggo bodhāyā’ti. Tassa mayhaṃ, bhāradvāja, etadahosi – ‘kiṃ nu kho ahaṃ tassa sukhassa bhāyāmi yaṃ taṃ sukhaṃ aññatreva kāmehi aññatra akusalehi dhammehī’ti? Tassa mayhaṃ, bhāradvāja, etadahosi – ‘na kho ahaṃ tassa sukhassa bhāyāmi yaṃ taṃ sukhaṃ aññatreva kāmehi aññatra akusalehi dhammehī’ti.

482. Then, Bhāradvāja, this thought occurred to me: ‘Whatever striving ascetics or brahmins in the past have experienced painful, sharp, harsh, and severe feelings, this was the utmost—nothing more than this. And whatever striving ascetics or brahmins in the future will experience painful, sharp, harsh, and severe feelings, this will be the utmost—nothing more than this. And whatever striving ascetics or brahmins now experience painful, sharp, harsh, and severe feelings, this is the utmost—nothing more than this. But by this severe, difficult-to-perform practice, I do not attain any state superior to the human state, any distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones. Could there be another path to awakening?’ Then, Bhāradvāja, this thought occurred to me: ‘I recall that during the plowing ceremony of my father, the Sakyan, while sitting in the cool shade of a rose-apple tree, being quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, I entered and dwelled in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. Could this be the path to awakening?’ Following that memory, Bhāradvāja, the consciousness arose: ‘This is indeed the path to awakening.’ Then, Bhāradvāja, this thought occurred to me: ‘Why should I fear that happiness which is apart from sensual pleasures and apart from unwholesome states?’ Then, Bhāradvāja, this thought occurred to me: ‘I do not fear that happiness which is apart from sensual pleasures and apart from unwholesome states.’

483. “Tassa mayhaṃ, bhāradvāja, etadahosi – ‘na kho taṃ sukaraṃ sukhaṃ adhigantuṃ evaṃ adhimattakasimānaṃ pattakāyena. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ oḷārikaṃ āhāraṃ āhāreyyaṃ odanakummāsa’nti. So kho ahaṃ, bhāradvāja, oḷārikaṃ āhāraṃ āhāresiṃ odanakummāsaṃ. Tena kho pana maṃ, bhāradvāja, samayena pañcavaggiyā bhikkhū paccupaṭṭhitā honti – ‘yaṃ kho samaṇo gotamo dhammaṃ adhigamissati taṃ no ārocessatī’ti. Yato kho ahaṃ, bhāradvāja, oḷārikaṃ āhāraṃ āhāresiṃ odanakummāsaṃ, atha me te pañcavaggiyā bhikkhū nibbijja pakkamiṃsu – ‘bāhulliko samaṇo gotamo padhānavibbhanto āvatto bāhullāyā’ti.

483. Then, Bhāradvāja, this thought occurred to me: ‘It is not easy to attain that happiness with a body so excessively emaciated. What if I were to take substantial food, rice and barley-gruel?’ So, Bhāradvāja, I took substantial food, rice and barley-gruel. At that time, Bhāradvāja, the group of five bhikkhus were attending on me, thinking, ‘Whatever Dhamma the ascetic Gotama attains, he will announce it to us.’ But when I took substantial food, rice and barley-gruel, those five bhikkhus left me in disgust, saying, ‘The ascetic Gotama has become indulgent, has given up the striving, and has reverted to indulgence.’

“So kho ahaṃ, bhāradvāja, oḷārikaṃ āhāraṃ āhāretvā balaṃ [T 2.0686] gahetvā vivicceva kāmehi…pe… paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja vihāsiṃ. Vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā ajjhattaṃ sampasādanaṃ cetaso ekodibhāvaṃ avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ [M 2.0437] samādhijaṃ pītisukhaṃ dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ… tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ… catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja vihāsiṃ.

Then, Bhāradvāja, having taken substantial food and regained strength, being quite secluded from sensual pleasures... and so on... I entered and dwelled in the first jhāna. With the stilling of thought and examination, bringing about internal confidence and unification of mind, being without thought and without examination, born of concentration, with rapture and happiness, I entered and dwelled in the second jhāna... in the third jhāna... and I entered and dwelled in the fourth jhāna.

“So evaṃ samāhite citte parisuddhe pariyodāte anaṅgaṇe vigatūpakkilese mudubhūte kammaniye [V 2.0444] ṭhite āneñjappatte pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇāya cittaṃ abhininnāmesiṃ. So anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarāmi, seyyathidaṃ – ekampi jātiṃ dvepi jātiyo…pe… iti sākāraṃ sauddesaṃ anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarāmi. Ayaṃ kho me, bhāradvāja, rattiyā paṭhame yāme paṭhamā vijjā adhigatā, avijjā vihatā, vijjā uppannā; tamo vihato, āloko uppanno; yathā taṃ appamattassa ātāpino pahitattassa viharato.

When my mind was thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of defilements, pliable, workable, steady, and had attained imperturbability, I directed it to the knowledge of the recollection of past lives. I recollected many kinds of past lives, that is, one birth, two births... and so on... Thus with their aspects and details I recollected many kinds of past lives. This, Bhāradvāja, was the first true knowledge attained by me in the first watch of the night. Ignorance was dispelled, true knowledge arose; darkness was dispelled, light arose, as happens for one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute.

484. “So evaṃ samāhite citte parisuddhe pariyodāte anaṅgaṇe vigatūpakkilese mudubhūte kammaniye ṭhite āneñjappatte sattānaṃ [T 2.0687] cutūpapātañāṇāya cittaṃ abhininnāmesiṃ. So dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena satte passāmi cavamāne upapajjamāne hīne paṇīte suvaṇṇe dubbaṇṇe sugate duggate yathākammūpage satte pajānāmi…pe… ayaṃ kho me, bhāradvāja, rattiyā majjhime yāme dutiyā vijjā adhigatā, avijjā vihatā, vijjā uppannā; tamo vihato, āloko uppanno; yathā taṃ appamattassa ātāpino pahitattassa viharato.

484. When my mind was thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of defilements, pliable, workable, steady, and had attained imperturbability, I directed my mind to the knowledge of the passing away and arising of beings. With the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, I saw beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and I understood beings passing on according to their deeds... and so on... This, Bhāradvāja, was the second true knowledge attained by me in the middle watch of the night. Ignorance was dispelled, true knowledge arose; darkness was dispelled, light arose—as happens for one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute.

“So evaṃ samāhite citte parisuddhe pariyodāte anaṅgaṇe vigatūpakkilese mudubhūte kammaniye ṭhite āneñjappatte āsavānaṃ khayañāṇāya cittaṃ abhininnāmesiṃ. So ‘idaṃ dukkha’nti yathābhūtaṃ abbhaññāsiṃ, ‘ayaṃ dukkhasamudayo’ti yathābhūtaṃ abbhaññāsiṃ, ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodho’ti yathābhūtaṃ abbhaññāsiṃ, ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yathābhūtaṃ abbhaññāsiṃ; ‘ime āsavā’ti yathābhūtaṃ abbhaññāsiṃ, ‘ayaṃ āsavasamudayo’ti yathābhūtaṃ abbhaññāsiṃ, ‘ayaṃ āsavanirodho’ti yathābhūtaṃ abbhaññāsiṃ, ‘ayaṃ āsavanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yathābhūtaṃ abbhaññāsiṃ. Tassa me evaṃ jānato evaṃ passato kāmāsavāpi cittaṃ vimuccittha, bhavāsavāpi cittaṃ vimuccittha, avijjāsavāpi [M 2.0438] cittaṃ vimuccittha. Vimuttasmiṃ vimuttamiti ñāṇaṃ ahosi. ‘Khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti abbhaññāsiṃ. Ayaṃ kho me, bhāradvāja, rattiyā pacchime yāme tatiyā [T 2.0688] vijjā adhigatā, avijjā vihatā, vijjā uppannā; tamo vihato, āloko uppanno; yathā taṃ appamattassa ātāpino pahitattassa viharato”ti.

With my mind thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of defilements, malleable, wieldy, steady, and having attained imperturbability, I directed it to the knowledge of the destruction of the taints. I understood, as it actually is: ‘This is suffering.’ I understood, as it actually is: ‘This is the origin of suffering.’ I understood, as it actually is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering.’ I understood, as it actually is: ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.’ I understood, as it actually is: ‘These are the taints.’ I understood, as it actually is: ‘This is the origin of the taints.’ I understood, as it actually is: ‘This is the cessation of the taints.’ I understood, as it actually is: ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of the taints.’ Knowing thus and seeing thus, my mind was liberated from the taint of sensual desire, my mind was liberated from the taint of becoming, and my mind was liberated from the taint of ignorance. When it was liberated, the knowledge arose: ‘It is liberated.’ I understood: ‘Birth is destroyed, the spiritual life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.’ This, Bhāradvāja, was the third knowledge I attained in the last watch of the night. Ignorance was dispelled, knowledge arose; darkness was dispelled, light arose, as happens for one who dwells diligently, ardently, and resolutely.

485. Evaṃ vutte, saṅgāravo māṇavo bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “aṭṭhitavataṃ aṭṭhita vata (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) bhoto gotamassa padhānaṃ ahosi, sappurisavataṃ sappurisa vata (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) bhoto gotamassa padhānaṃ ahosi; yathā taṃ arahato sammāsambuddhassa. Kiṃ nu kho, bho gotama, atthi devā”ti adhidevāti (ka.) evaṃ sabbesu ‘atthi devā’tipadesu? “Ṭhānaso metaṃ kho panetaṃ (syā. kaṃ. ka.), bhāradvāja, viditaṃ yadidaṃ – adhidevā”ti atthi devāti (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.), atidevāti (?) evaṃ sabbesu ‘adhidevā’tipadesu. “Kiṃ nu kho, bho gotama, ‘atthi devā’ti puṭṭho samāno ‘ṭhānaso metaṃ, bhāradvāja[V 2.0445], viditaṃ yadidaṃ adhidevā’ti vadesi. Nanu, bho gotama, evaṃ sante tucchā musā hotī”ti? “‘Atthi devā’ti, bhāradvāja, puṭṭho samāno ‘atthi devā’ti [P 2.0213] yo vadeyya, ‘ṭhānaso me viditā’ti ṭhānaso viditā me viditāti (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.), ṭhānaso me viditā atidevāti (?) yo vadeyya; atha khvettha viññunā purisena ekaṃsena niṭṭhaṃ gantabbaṃ gantuṃ (ka.), gantuṃ vā (syā. kaṃ.) yadidaṃ – ‘atthi devā’”ti. “Kissa pana me bhavaṃ gotamo ādikeneva na byākāsī”ti gotamo ādikeneva byākāsīti (ka.), gotamo atthi devāti na byākāsīti (?)? “Uccena sammataṃ kho etaṃ, bhāradvāja, lokasmiṃ yadidaṃ – ‘atthi devā’”ti.

485. When this was said, the young man Saṅgārava said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Gotama, your striving has been that of one who is steadfast, your striving has been that of a good man—as it is for an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One. But, Venerable Gotama, are there gods?" "It is known to me on principle, Bhāradvāja, that there are higher gods." "But, Venerable Gotama, when asked, 'Are there gods?' you say, 'It is known to me on principle, Bhāradvāja, that there are higher gods.' In that case, Venerable Gotama, is not your statement empty and false?" "Bhāradvāja, if someone, when asked, 'Are there gods?' were to say, 'There are gods,' and were to say, 'This is known to me on principle'; then a wise person should certainly arrive at the conclusion: 'There are gods.'" "Then why did the Venerable Gotama not declare this to me at the very beginning?" "This is widely acknowledged in the world, Bhāradvāja, that 'there are gods.'"

486. Evaṃ vutte, saṅgāravo māṇavo bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “abhikkantaṃ, bho gotama, abhikkantaṃ, bho gotama! Seyyathāpi, bho gotama, nikkujjitaṃ vā ukkujjeyya, paṭicchannaṃ vā vivareyya, mūḷhassa vā maggaṃ ācikkheyya, andhakāre vā telapajjotaṃ dhāreyya – cakkhumanto rūpāni dakkhantīti – evamevaṃ bhotā gotamena anekapariyāyena [T 2.0689] dhammo pakāsito. Esāhaṃ [M 2.0439] bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi dhammañca bhikkhusaṅghañca. Upāsakaṃ maṃ bhavaṃ gotamo dhāretu ajjatagge pāṇupetaṃ saraṇaṃ gata”nti.

486. When this was said, the young man Saṅgārava said to the Blessed One: "Excellent, Venerable Gotama! Excellent, Venerable Gotama! Just as one might set upright what was overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or hold up an oil lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—in the very same way, the Dhamma has been made clear by the Venerable Gotama in many ways. I go for refuge to the Venerable Gotama, to the Dhamma, and to the Bhikkhu Saṅgha. May the Venerable Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forward for as long as life lasts."

Saṅgāravasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ dasamaṃ.

The Saṅgārava Sutta, the tenth, is concluded.

Brāhmaṇavaggo niṭṭhito pañcamo.

The Chapter on Brahmins, the fifth, is concluded.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary thereof:

Brahmāyu selassalāyano, ghoṭamukho ca brāhmaṇo;

Caṅkī esu dhanañjāni, vāseṭṭho subhagāravoti.

Brahmāyu, Sela, Assalāyana, and the brahmin Ghoṭamukha; Caṅkī, Esukārī, Dhanañjāni, Vāseṭṭha, Subha, and Saṅgārava.

Idaṃ vaggānamuddānaṃ –

This is the summary of the chapters:

Vaggo gahapati bhikkhu, paribbājakanāmako;

Rājavaggo brāhmaṇoti, pañca majjhimaāgame.

The Chapter of Householders, of Bhikkhus, the one named Wanderers; the Chapter of Kings, and of Brahmins—these five are in the Middle Collection.

Majjhimapaṇṇāsakaṃ samattaṃ.

The Middle Fifty is completed.
